US lead in AI over China narrows after DeepSeek gains, Bloomberg Intelligence says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
00:30:00 UTC
09:30:00 KST

US lead in AI over China narrows after DeepSeek gains, Bloomberg Intelligence says
- US AI companies' lead over China has sharply narrowed to just a 3% difference after DeepSeek's V4.1 Flash release, threatening US dominance in AI technology.
- China's AI progress is driven by strong expertise and optimisation for domestic hardware, challenging the effectiveness of US export restrictions on tech like Nvidia chips.
- Despite gains, Chinese AI firms face profitability challenges due to fierce competition and pricing wars, with sustainable profits expected only after industry consolidation by 2030.
AI generated
American AI companies’ performance lead over China narrowed sharply in past months to a record low after labs such as DeepSeek gained ground, threatening US tech supremacy, according to Bloomberg Intelligence (BI).
Top Chinese models lag their US rivals by just 3% on benchmark scores after the September release of DeepSeek’s V4.1 Flash, BI senior analyst Robert Lea wrote in a report on Oct 5.
That is down from about 9% in May and 15% earlier in the year. That improving performance spells further market share gains for Chinese contenders, he said.
China’s ascent is a result of deepening AI expertise and its researchers’ ability to optimise their models for domestic hardware. The gains raise questions about the usefulness of US export restrictions on technology such as Nvidia chips, intended to curtail Chinese AI advances and prevent the likes of Huawei Technologies from making progress with their own alternatives.
China’s progress “casts further doubt on the long-term sustainability of US technological supremacy in AI”, Lea said.
The two superpowers are vying to dominate a technology that drives economic productivity, military leadership and global influence. China’s lower-cost AI models are bridging the gap with US rivals in user numbers just as Anthropic and OpenAI chase trillion-dollar valuations in stock market debuts, touting their superior capabilities.
DeepSeek’s V4.1 Flash ranked sixth globally in September on LiveBench, making it the highest-ranked Chinese model since the startup broke ground with its reasoning model R1 in 2025. LiveBench scores AI models based on their responses to and analysis of questions, puzzles or tasks, a process akin to gauging human IQ.
DeepSeek last recorded a LiveBench score of 81.1, below Anthropic’s best score of 83.4. That means the DeepSeek model delivers “comparable performance” to leading AI systems from Anthropic and OpenAI, Lea said.
Still, while the score gap has narrowed to just 3%, just three of the top 15 models as assessed by LiveBench were Chinese.
Such rankings shift, Lea cautioned, and it could be difficult to monetise regardless of leaderboard scores. Chinese models face increasing US regulatory scrutiny and even potential bans following allegations of model distillation.
The Chinese AI industry could remain unprofitable until 2030, Lea said. A focus on low-margin token supply and a brutal price war may make it impossible for any firm to gain a competitive edge in a domestic market flooded with more than 1,100 large language models.
ByteDance’s Doubao is the frontrunner in AI app monetisation, while the chatbots of rivals DeepSeek and Tencent Holdings remain free, Lea said.
“Putting China’s AI sector on a sustainable profit footing will require a cooling of competitive pressures, an industry shake-out and a more rational approach to pricing,” he said. BLOOMBERG

🔴 Brazil presidential election heads to runoff with Bolsonaro ahead of Lula
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05

Brazil presidential election heads to runoff as Bolsonaro leads Lula
Brazilians voted Sunday in a high-stakes presidential election pitting incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro amid a regional shift to the right. Bolsonaro is the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro. A runoff will take place October 25 if no candidate wins an outright majority.
Brazilians voted Sunday in a high-stakes presidential election pitting incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro at a moment when the region is shifting to the right in line with the Trump administration.
Bolsonaro, 45, is the son of far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year sentence for a coup attempt and an ally of US President Donald Trump. Lula, who at 80 is one of the world’s oldest heads of state, is running in his seventh presidential election and has strengthened Brazil's ties with Beijing.
Trump allies have fared well in recent elections in Latin America, including in Argentina, Colombia, Honduras and Peru.
If none of the 12 presidential candidates gets more than 50% of the vote, the top two will head to a runoff on Oct. 25 in Latin America’s economic powerhouse.
Brazil's nearly 159 million eligible voters will also elect 27 state governors, members of state legislatures, all 513 federal members of the lower house of congress and 54 of the country’s 81 senators in Sunday’s vote.
Read moreA Profile of Brazil's Potential President
Polls closed at 5 p.m. Sunday with those still in line able to vote and tallies started rolling in within the hour. In the last presidential election, the two candidates who advanced out of the first round were mathematically determined at about 8 p.m. Brasilia time with nearly 99% of votes counted.
While the once widely popular Lula saw his approval ratings plummet during his third term, standing up to the US has given him a boost. And he still enjoys a strong base of supporters who credit his social policies for improving millions of Brazilians’ lives.
The incumbent president has often spoken about risks of US intervention in the Brazilian elections after the Trump administration imposed high tariffs against Brazilian exports, revoked the visa of the country’s ambassador and sanctioned a Supreme Court justice who chaired the investigation that eventually sentenced Jair Bolsonaro, Lula's predecessor.
Lula told journalists after voting Sunday that he needs “to do double of what we have done” if reelected, and expressed confidence in a first-round win.
But the incumbent faces a tough battle because of an affordability crisis and a corruption scandal that ensnared the same justice who led the investigation into Bolsonaro.

“Many in the Lula campaign were not expecting such a difficult election a few weeks ago, and it is clear to them that the present election is a tough battle and the next ones, without Lula, could be even more so,” said Carlos Melo, a political science professor at Insper University in Sao Paulo.
Flávio Bolsonaro has touted his proximity to the White House, although he denies his campaign received help from the US government.
He has promised to crack down on Brazilian criminal groups and insisted that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare minerals economy, second only to China. Bolsonaro also has campaigned on releasing his father and bringing him back to politics.
“Brazil needs change. Brazil can’t stand so much suffering,” he told reporters at the Rio de Janeiro voting center, where he cast his vote Sunday.
The senator faces his own challenges. He has seen his political career tainted by several corruption accusations, including receiving millions of dollars from a disgraced banker to allegedly produce a movie on his father’s life.
Rosane Wink, 67, a retired engineer, is a lifelong conservative voter who supports Bolsonaro and his promise to classify criminal groups as terrorist organizations.
“It’s a kind of terrorism that they’re doing with us,” said Wink as she voted in Rio de Janeiro. Last month she had a gun held to her stomach as a criminal bit her hand and removed her wedding ring, she said.
Read moreBrazil: Lula and Bolsonaro tied in polls
Maria Ribeiro, a 50-year-old cellphone vendor from Brasilia, said she voted for Bolsonaro because she wants freedom to express her Evangelical religion. She hopes he follows in his father's footsteps.
“I voted for his father, and I don't regret it,” she said.
The proximity to his father was what worried Lorena Zschaber, a 40-year-old photographer, who watched the results roll in at an LGBTQ+-friendly bar in downtown Rio de Janeiro. During his father’s presidency, “people felt more at ease to discriminate," she said.
"I’m an LGBTQ+ woman, I can’t think of anything worse happening than Flávio Bolsonaro being elected,” she added.
Rosângela Resende da Rocha, a 69-year-old who was previously a stay-at-home mom, said she supported Lula's social policies that help the “less fortunate” and how he stands up to Trump.
“That crazy guy wants to come in here to buy our country, so that our country will be like it is over there,” she said at a voting center in Brasilia. “He won’t succeed if Lula wins.”
Even for those outside the country, Lula's social programs, including his flagship welfare program Bolsa Familia, drove many to continue supporting him.

Brazil’s presidential race goes to second round as Flávio Bolsonaro leads incumbent Lula
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
00:16:52 UTC
09:16:52 KST

Brazil’s presidential race will go to a second round after the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, beat the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but failed to secure the outright majority he needed to avoid a runoff.
With 99.9% of votes counted, the 45-year-old son of the disgraced former president, Jair Bolsonaro, had won 47%, meaning he will now face a 25 October showdown with his 80-year-old rival. Lula received 45.1%. Bolsonaro received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m.
Bolsonaro will go into the second round as strong favourite and is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates, who included Ronaldo Caiado, who secured 2.1%, and Renan Santos, who won 2.2%.
Brazil’s far-right put in an even stronger than expected showing, with a succession of Bolsonarista politicians winning congressional or gubernatorial races. They included Jair Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, and his wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who both won seats in the senate. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, Jair Renan, was elected to the lower house of congress. Bolsonaro’s former infrastructure minister, Tarcísio de Freitas, was reelected as governor of São Paulo, Brazil’s most populous and economically important state.
Of the 54 senators elected, 34 were from the right or far right.
Flávio Bolsonaro told supporters in the capital, Brasília, that the result signalled “the end of an era” for Lula’s Workers’ party. “Lula has fought seven presidential elections. He’s worried about power. I am worried about the future of Brazil,” he said.
Speaking in Sāo Paulo, Lula put a brave face on a difficult night for the left. “We have just had a lesson in Brazilian democracy,” he said. “The result is often unexpected. We can never get everything we wanted. I confess to you that I was convinced I was going to win the election in the first round … But we have a second round.”
Lula said Bolsonaro’s “dark past” would become clearer to voters in the lead-up to that vote. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil.”
Earlier, as he cast this vote, Lula said Latin America’s largest democracy faced a stark choice, highlighting his adversary’s well-documented links to members of Rio’s underworld, including once employing close relatives of a notorious contract killer.
Lula, who became Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002 and was returned to office in 2006 and 2022, is hoping to secure a historic fourth non-consecutive term in this year’s election.
Allies of the veteran leftwinger called the election a crucial battle in the fight against a far-right movement that less than four years ago brought chaos to the capital, Brasília, during an unsuccessful attempt to overturn the result of the 2022 election, when Lula beat the incumbent president, Jair Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro hopes winning the presidency will allow him to free his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup after refusing to accept he had lost the last election to Lula. Ahead of the election he also called for tactical voting from conservatives who are not supporters of Bolsonarismo, but want to vote Lula out of power.
As well as the president, Brazil’s nearly 159 million voters were choosing state parliamentarians, 27 state governors, 513 members of the lower house and 54 members of the 81-seat senate. Bolsonaro supporters made the senate race a priority because senators are the only lawmakers who can impeach supreme court justices – a demand among Bolsonaristas since the court jailed the former president for attempting a coup.
Hundreds of leftwingers had gathered at the heart of Laranjeiras, one of Rio’s most leftwing neighbourhoods, hoping to celebrate a Lula win to the sound of samba. But the mood soured and tears were shed as the hours passed and Bolsonaro’s lead over Lula held.
“It’s so sad that the Brazilian people … have opted for so much retrogression,” said Marcelo Mac, one of the owners of Miolo, a leftwing bar in Laranjeiras, as the scale of the rightwing advance was confirmed on Sunday night.
Mac, 46, voiced perplexity that the son of the man who tried to stage a coup only four years ago was now in pole position to become Brazil’s next leader. “He’s such an abominable guy that he manages to be even worse than his father,” Mac said of Bolsonaro.
Beside the bar a yellow flag stamped with Lula’s face carried the slogan: “Turn left”. But Brazil had voted for a turn to the far right.
Bolsonaro seemed to have the wind in his sails in the final days before Sunday’s vote, amid public frustration at a cost of living crisis and urban violence.
But opinion polls failed to predict the scale of the rightwing triumph.
Shop assistant Italo Andrade dos Santos, a 31-year-old Bolsonaro voter, had to keep his celebrations restrained behind the counter of the pharmacy where he was working a Sunday night shift. “I was a little disappointed because I expected Flávio to win in the first round. But I’m happy he’s ahead,” said Santos, adding that he voted “more to get Lula out than for Flávio himself”.
Donald Trump became a key election issue, with Lula accusing the US president of trying to swing the vote in Bolsonaro’s favour in order to “colonise” Brazil and appropriate its natural resources. Bolsonaro has vowed to build a closer relationship with Trump, who hopes a rightwing victory will help him further cement US control over Latin America after the election of pro-Trump leaders in a succession of countries, including Chile, Colombia and Peru.

Brazilians voted Sunday in a high-stakes presidential election pitting incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro at a moment when the region is shifting to the right in line with the Trump administration.

Zamir: IDF to overhaul intelligence, force readiness after October 7 investigations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
00:01:30 UTC
09:01:30 KST

The IDF will expand its forces and prepare for a surprise attack on multiple fronts even without advance warning, under a new approach shaped by the military's investigation into the failures surrounding the October 7 massacre.
The changes were among the main conclusions presented Sunday at a conference of the IDF's senior command staff, led by IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir, as the military reviewed its October 7 investigations and outlined how it would implement its findings.
Under the changes, the IDF will base its readiness on what its enemies are capable of doing rather than assessments of what they intend to do. The military will also increase the number of forces kept on alert and in reserve, strengthen the defense of border communities, expand commanders' freedom of action in the field, and overhaul elements of its intelligence and warning systems.
"One of our greatest lessons from October 7 is the need to expand our security margins," Zamir said at the conference. "We need to build the IDF's order of battle to meet all the multi-front challenges and threats. The size of the IDF is our strategic depth."
"We are building the IDF's strategy with preparedness for a surprise war as our reference scenario, including thwarting serious threats as they emerge. This is our operational compass," he said.
The conference, held at the Glilot base and attended by officers at the rank of brigadier-general and above from across the IDF's commands, directorates, and branches, was intended to summarize the October 7 investigations, examine how their findings are being implemented, and outline the next stages of the military's review process.
At the start of the conference, commanders observed a moment of silence in memory of those killed in the massacre.
Strategy, operations, force buildup, and intelligence
The IDF divided its findings into four main areas: strategy, operations, force buildup, and intelligence.
Planned changes include increasing the number of forces kept on alert and in reserve, revising the military's approach to defending border communities, giving forces in the field greater autonomy, strengthening firepower and intelligence-gathering capabilities along the borders, and changing working methods within the Intelligence Directorate.
According to data presented at the conference, the number of forces assigned to readiness and reserve roles across all sectors has more than doubled. The IDF has also established dedicated reserve and force-multiplier readiness arrangements and redistributed forces and equipment across sectors to enable a faster response in any area.
The military determined that it must be prepared for a surprise attack on several fronts simultaneously, even if both deterrence and advance warning fail.
Readiness will be based on what an enemy is capable of doing rather than on assessments of what it intends to do. The IDF will also place greater emphasis on proactive offensive operations intended to prevent serious threats from developing.
The military also decided to strengthen its ground maneuver capabilities and improve headquarters' ability to build an accurate picture of events and to continue operating in extreme situations and periods of uncertainty.
It also seeks to deepen strategic and operational expertise and encourage a culture in which officers question assumptions and raise concerns about shortcomings within the system.
At the operational level, threat scenarios, defense plans, readiness arrangements, and reserve deployments will be updated as enemy capabilities change. The scenarios will be reviewed every six months and examined across multiple branches of the military.
Israeli military to expand surprise drills, extreme-event scenarios
The IDF will also expand surprise drills, extreme-event scenarios, and Chief of Staff readiness tests to improve the military's transition from routine operations to war and strengthen both defensive and offensive preparedness.
The military intends to give its regional commands a stronger role in developing expertise about the areas under their responsibility and to incorporate their assessments into General Staff planning. Commanders in the field will also receive greater operational independence and freedom of action.
One of the main areas of change concerns the defense of Israeli communities near the country's borders.
The IDF determined that a community is "vital terrain and the object of defense," and that during an infiltration, forces must seek contact and reach the community quickly.
The locations of military outposts will therefore be adjusted based on their proximity to communities and their ability to defend them even when only limited forces are available.
Regional defense forces and security units in communities will also be expanded, including defense platoons, Yatam units, regional defense battalions, and David brigades.
The IDF also seeks to clarify responsibilities during emergencies, establish a single authority to respond to incidents, and strengthen coordination between military and civilian bodies.
Regional brigades and divisions will receive greater independent strike capabilities, along with increased access to ground and air firepower along the borders.
The IDF will also establish a multidimensional, multilayered intelligence-gathering network for each sector, operable from several locations. Coordination between forces in the field and the Intelligence Directorate will also be strengthened.
In the intelligence field, advance warning has been redefined as a core mission of the Military Intelligence Directorate, alongside understanding developments on the ground and building a comprehensive intelligence picture.
The IDF also plans to define intelligence responsibilities more clearly while deliberately allowing some overlap between intelligence bodies and formalizing how they work together.
The intelligence work of individual divisions and their ability to build a complete picture of events will also be examined. Warning systems across different fronts will be synchronized, while each level of command will retain the ability to reach its own independent assessment.
Greater emphasis will also be placed on distinguishing between long-term strategic analysis and short-term tactical intelligence, while encouraging greater criticism and questioning within the intelligence system.
This approach was also reflected when Zamir presented a certificate of appreciation during the conference to Chief Warrant Officer V. from Unit 8200, who warned before October 7 that Hamas was preparing for a large-scale surprise attack.
"V. is a clear example of intellectual courage and professionalism," Zamir said. "In our organizational culture, we must not allow appeasing discourse, intellectual tyranny, or the suppression of critical thinking."
Zamir also addressed the military failure on the day of the massacre, saying, "On October 7, the IDF failed miserably," but added that afterward, "the IDF got back on its feet and proved itself to possess a determined spirit."
"Our duty is to ensure that they are not repeated," he said.
The Chief of Staff added that the conference was the "opening shot" in a broader process of investigating the war, and that 2027 will be designated by the IDF as the year to investigate the entire war and draw lessons from it.
In the coming period, the investigations into Operation Roaring Lion, among others, will be completed, after which the IDF will summarize the war's findings overall.

AI generated
NADI, Fiji – Extreme heat is putting pregnant mothers and their newborns at increasing risk, United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell will warn on Oct 5.
Speaking at the “pre-COP” summit in Nadi, Fiji, Stiell will cite a new survey showing more than two-thirds of health professionals across five continents had seen complications caused by intense heat in the past five years.
“Rising temperatures mean rising danger in pregnancy,” he is expected to say.
“Climate-driven extreme heat during pregnancy is increasingly linked to premature birth, stillbirth, low birth weight and maternal complications.”
“The picture is clear and very disturbing. As extreme heat worsens, pregnancy and birth are now a new fault line in the global climate crisis, and one which is potentially fatal,” Stiell will say.
“This fault line must not become another deep chasm of climate-driven suffering, inequality and injustice.”
Scientists warn that climate change is making extreme weather events more intense and resulting in heat records tumbling more often.
Around 33 countries, spanning from western Europe to the Sahel and central America, recorded their hottest July in 2026 since records began, according to AFP analysis of data from the European Union’s Copernicus climate observatory.
The survey of 1,000 midwives and doctors in the United Kingdom, Australia, India, Brazil and Zimbabwe was commissioned by charitable foundation Wellcome.
Its chairwoman – Australian former Prime Minister Julia Gillard – said in a statement that mothers and babies are being put at increasing risk as a result of climate change.
“Extreme heat is an invisible killer, but pregnant women must not be invisible. Leaders have the evidence and solutions they need – now they must act,” Gillard said.
The survey found nearly all midwives and doctors had cared for mothers or babies suffering the effects of extreme heat.
About a third of respondents said they had seen cases of low birth weight or restricted growth, feeding difficulties, and dehydration or heat-related illness, all resulting from what they believed was extreme heat.
Stiell will tell pre-COP delegates that “pregnancy should be a time of hope”.
“But for millions, it is becoming a time of anxiety, as climate impacts fill everyday life with risk.”
The pre-COP31 summit in Fiji and the remote coral atoll Tuvalu is seen by Pacific leaders as a chance to draw attention to life on the front line of climate change.
They are a precursor to the larger UN-sponsored global climate summit – known as COP31 – to be held in November in Turkey. AFP

China

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- A prolonged heat wave continued across California over the weekend, breaking daily high-temperature records at multiple locations, while hot and dry conditions and wildfire smoke added to health and fire risks across parts of the state, according to the U.S. National Weather Service (NWS) and state authorities.
A preliminary report from the NWS San Diego office said eight daily high-temperature records were broken and one was tied on Oct. 3 across Orange, San Diego and Riverside counties.
Santa Ana in Orange County reached 41.7 degrees Celsius, about 2.8 degrees above the previous record for Oct. 3 set in 2014, while Vista in San Diego County reached 42.2 degrees, according to the report.
San Diego International Airport reached 40.6 degrees, breaking a daily record that had stood since 1987. The temperature was about 16.1 degrees above normal for the date, according to an NWS climate report.
Farther north, Napa Airport reached 35.6 degrees, breaking its previous Oct. 3 record of 34.4 degrees, according to the NWS San Francisco Bay Area office. In northern Nevada, Winnemucca Airport reached 32.2 degrees, breaking its previous daily record set in 2024, according to the NWS Elko office.
The NWS Los Angeles/Oxnard office described the episode as a major and long-lasting heat wave and said unusually high temperatures were expected to persist through the coming week.
More than 34 million Californians were under heat warnings or advisories. Extreme Heat Warnings remained in effect through Thursday evening in parts of Southern California, including San Diego and the coasts and valleys of Los Angeles and Ventura counties and parts of Santa Barbara County.
The California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE) website listed several active incidents Sunday, including the Bouquet Fire in Los Angeles County, which had burned 1,048 acres and was 40 percent contained, and the Dome Fire in Mariposa County, which had burned 6,826 acres and was 40 percent contained.
Across California, CAL FIRE reported 5,701 wildfires and 328,950 acres burned in 2026, with three fatalities and 157 structures destroyed. The figures are preliminary and subject to frequent updates.
Smoke from active wildfires adds another health concern. Fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, can penetrate deep into the lungs and is particularly harmful to children, older adults and people with heart or lung conditions, according to California health authorities.
AirNow forecasts showed air quality reaching levels considered unhealthy for sensitive groups in several California communities on Sunday, with ozone identified as the main pollutant in a number of areas.
Health officials advise residents to limit strenuous outdoor activity during periods of extreme heat or poor air quality, keep windows and doors closed when smoke is present, use air conditioning on recirculate and seek a cooler, cleaner-air location when necessary. ■

Brazil election: Bolsonaro and Lula head to runoff
Published October 4, 2026last updated October 5, 2026
With votes being counted in Brazil following the presidential election on Sunday, populist Senator Flavio Bolsonaro was leading the race ahead of leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro seeks to continue the right-wing populist movement started by his father, Jair Bolsonaro, while Lula is seeking his fourth non-consecutive term.
With more than 99% of the ballots processed, Flavio Bolsonaro has received 47.2% of the vote, and Lula has 45%. Since neither candidate received enough votes to win outright on Sunday, the country's electoral court announced that Bolsonaro and Lula will face each other in a runoff on October 25.
Commenting on the outcome, Lula said it was "unexpected" as he was convinced he would "win in the first round."
"Tomorrow we start a new campaign," the 80-year-old said. "I am very good in the knockout stage."
In turn, Bolsonaro said he was "very happy with the real possibility that, three weeks from now, Brazil will give a definitive answer by choosing a modern government."
Bolsonaro is monitoring the vote count in Brasilia, the country's capital, while Lula is following it from Sao Paulo..
You can watch our livestream on the Brazil election results below.
Right gaining momentum in Brazil
Fabio de Sa e Silva, a professor of Brazilian studies at the University of Oklahoma, told DW that the right was currently on the rise in Brazil, making it difficult for Lula to change the course of the election.
"He still has a chance, based on the numbers, but the momentum is with the right," said de Sa e Silva.
"The big news tomorrow will be not that we have a runoff... but it is a takeover that happened in Congress by the far-right," the researcher said.
He added that it will be very hard for Lula to govern with Brazil's new Congress, even if he eventually secures another term.
Lula vows to 'defeat the far right'
Lula and Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday in Brazil's economic powerhouse state of Sao Paulo.
The 80-year-old Lula capped off his campaign with a tour through the city of Sao Paulo, vowing to "defeat the far right."
Organizers said some 150,000 of Lula's supporters turned up for the rally in Brazil's largest city.
Lula has campaigned on continuing his left-leaning Workers' Party platform, comprising welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution.
"The people will have to choose between strengthening the democratic regime and barbarism ... between progress and backwardness," he said as he cast his ballot on Sunday.
Bolsonaro calls for 'change'
Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has served as the Liberal Party's senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019. On Saturday, he led a motorcycle parade through Sao Paulo's countryside cities of Santa Barbara d'Oeste and Americana.
He also held up a portrait of his father, while the crowd shouted "mito" — a Portuguese word for "legend" that Jair Bolsonaro's supporters use to refer to him.
The right-wing Bolsonaro has campaigned on hardline security policies and tax cuts, emphasizing high cost of living under Lula, who he has slammed as "incompetent."
"Brazil needs change," the son of the former president said as he cast his vote. "Brazil cannot bear any more suffering, such as high taxes, so many women killed."
Brazil's 2022 election rematch
The elder Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence in prison for attempting a coup to overturn his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election. Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his father if elected.
Lula's team has cast the Bolsonaro movement as a threat to Brazil's sovereignty, pointing to Flavio and Jair's ties with US President Donald Trump, who last year slapped a 50% tariff on Brazilian imports in response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial. The US president called the case a "witch hunt."
The younger Bolsonaro has said in interviews he is "more moderate" than his father, who he has nevertheless said will remain "my compass, my point of reference."
Policies where both Bolsonaros are similar include relaxed gun control laws and skepticism of human-caused climate change.
Trump has not endorsed the senator, but has said he is watching the election "very closely."
What happens next?
Brazil finds itself politically divided, and campaigning has been bitter, with online operations from both sides seizing on every gaffe, accusation and rumor, quickly producing slick videos or AI-generated images for social media.
In September, it was revealed Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father. He has denied any misconduct.
The latest polling for the first round of voting shows Lula at 46% and Bolsonaro at 45%, according to the Brazilian data intelligence and public opinion research firm Quaest cited by Reuters news agency.
In the case of a run-off, the Quaest poll shows Lula at 42% and Bolsonaro at 44%.
In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by only 1.8 percentage points.
Along with voting for president, Brazil's 160 million registered voters are also choosing other lawmakers, governors, and some senators.

The United Nations "pre-COP" climate summit has opened in the Fijian city of Nadi, where Pacific leaders are demanding urgent global action to protect vulnerable island nations on the front line of global warming.
The talks in Fiji and the atoll nation of Tuvalu serve as a diplomatic prelude to COP31, the global climate conference taking place later this year in Antalya, Türkiye.
Pacific leaders are insisting that the world adhere strictly to limiting global warming to 1.5C, expand access to adaptation finance, and prioritise oceanic preservation.
"Our prime minister will carry three clear messages to the leaders this week: keep 1.5 degrees within reach, make finance reach the communities that need it and give the ocean its rightful place in the climate regime," Fiji's climate minister Lynda Tabuya told delegates.
A UN assessment warned that rising seas—accelerating at twice the global average across the Pacific—could displace up to 1.2 billion people by 2050.
The report revealed a severe financing gap, noting developing nations need $310 billion to $365 billion to adapt, yet had only $26 billion available in 2023.
COP31 in Antalya
The regional talks set the stage for COP31, which Türkiye will host in the coastal city of Antalya from November 9 to 20, 2026.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly in September, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan stressed that Ankara is working to make the Antalya conference an event where climate pledges translate directly into concrete implementation.
Erdogan noted that climate targets must align with national socio-economic realities, cautioning that uniform progress is unrealistic while deep inequalities persist between nations regarding access to clean technology and finance.

The White House has defended a newly hired press aide who posed for a holiday photograph in 2021 wearing a “Fuck Joe Biden” T-shirt and holding a rifle.
Beni Rae Harmony, the new assistant White House press secretary, revealed on Friday that she was going to work for Donald Trump just days after covering him as a correspondent for Real America’s Voice, a partisan rightwing outlet originally created as a video podcast platform for the president’s former adviser Steve Bannon.
According to a LinkedIn profile, Harmony, 24, previously worked as a producer for the far-right Turning Point USA host Jack Posobiec – and as a press aide “focusing on crisis management” for two far-right Republicans: congressman Paul Gosar of Arizona and former congressman Matt Gaetz of Florida.
In 2021, when Gosar was censured by the US House for posting an animated video that depicted him killing Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and attacking Joe Biden, Harmony recorded an outraged defense of her boss for his YouTube channel.
The photograph of Harmony and an older man posing with rifles in matching anti-Biden shirts, in front of Christmas decorations, was reportedly posted on Instagram in November 2021 by a far-right Republican House candidate, Jarome Bell, who mounted a failed campaign for Congress in 2022.
A screenshot of that post, published by the Daily Mirror, shows that it included the caption: “My campaign Public Affairs Director @beniraeharmony is a beast. This is how we roll.”
Harmony appeared to verify the authenticity of the photograph in December 2021, when it was shared on social media by an anti-Maga outlet, PatriotTakes, which also identified her as an aide to Gosar.
The next day, Harmony replied to the PatriotTakes post of the image with another image of herself, wearing the same shirt in the same location and grinning into the camera. When another social media user posted a sarcastic question about the relationship between the older man and the young woman seen in the image, asking: “Daughter or date?”, Harmony replied with a one-word answer: “Uncle.”
Biden at the time was serving his lone term in the Oval Office, and Trump supporters chanting “Fuck Joe Biden” at a Nascar race that autumn inspired a viral meme featuring a variation of the slogan.
Harmony did not reply to requests to comment on the photograph. But the White House press office responded with a statement from a deputy press secretary, Anna Kelly, who praised the new hire for her advocacy of Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, while ostensibly covering the president as a journalist.
“Beni Rae Harmony has been a trusted voice for the MAGA movement as a White House correspondent,” Kelly wrote. “She will be an outstanding addition to President Trump’s communications team as an Assistant Press Secretary – we look forward to having her on board!”
Harmony joins a White House press office that has taken unprecedented steps to ensure that the president is surrounded at all times by correspondents from partisan outlets who shower him with praise, and limit or deny access to reporters from nonpartisan outlets who challenge him.
Trump has tried to ban CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House entirely, for what he considers overly negative coverage, and his aides now select which outlets are in place to ask him questions, with frequent slots reserved for correspondents who openly support him.
Harmony became the White House correspondent for Real America’s Voice after her predecessor, Brian Glenn, fell out of favor with Trump when his partner, Marjorie Taylor Greene, broke with the president and accused him of betraying the Maga movement.
Glenn had previously worked hard to advance Trump’s political agenda when invited by the president to ask questions. In 2025, for instance, Glenn pointedly asked Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, why he refused to wear a suit in the Oval Office, a question that inflamed an already volatile encounter.
During a press availability on Air Force One last month, Trump approached reporters with a sheaf of papers in his left hand. Harmony asked Trump a series of friendly questions that seemed designed to help him score political points. As TMZ reported on Friday, Associated Press photographs taken during that exchange showed that Harmony’s name was at the top of the first page in the president’s hand, suggesting that he might have been holding her résumé as he took her questions.
Harmony achieved a measure of celebrity in the rightwing media in 2025, when she left her job as an on-air host at a local TV station in Springfield, Illinois, after delivering an on-air tribute to the late Charlie Kirk, describing him as her first boss and mentor.
The station’s news director denied that Harmony had been suspended over the tribute, as she claimed, and clarified that she had never been a member of its news team, and instead hosted a program run by the channel’s sales department that featured clients who paid to be interviewed on television.

Dozens detained at authorized Communist Party rally after chants of 'Down with the Tsar'
Moscow police detained about 60 people at an authorized Communist Party rally on Oct. 4 after participants began chanting anti-Kremlin slogans, according to the party and Russian rights group OVD-Info.
The rally marked the anniversary of Russia's 1993 constitutional crisis, when a standoff between President Boris Yeltsin and hard-line lawmakers culminated in the military shelling the parliament building in Moscow. Authorities said 123 people were killed, while unofficial estimates put the toll in the hundreds.
The Communist Party has organized annual events as a symbol of resistance to Yeltsin-era reforms, but this year's authorized rally took a turn as participants chanted slogans including "Freedom for political prisoners," "For fair elections," and "Down with the Tsar."
OVD-Info says participants also chanted “No to political repression,” “Down with Roskomnadzor,” and “Down with the party of crooks and thieves.”
The event had been authorized by Moscow authorities, but detentions reportedly intensified as the rally was ending and participants shifted toward more directly anti-Kremlin slogans.
According to OVD-Info, around 20 people were initially taken to Moscow's Krasnopresnenskiy police station before the reported total rose to about 60. The detainees were not all Communist Party supporters: 26 were Communist Party participants, 30 were members of the liberal Yabloko party, and several others were activists.
The Communist Party, Russia's main parliamentary opposition, generally aligns with the Kremlin on major national security and foreign policy issues, including support for Russia's war against Ukraine. It occasionally criticizes domestic policy but does not directly challenge President Vladimir Putin's rule.
Russia has pushed harder against political opposition and anti-war activism in recent years. In August, Russia's Supreme Court banned the Yabloko party from participating in upcoming parliamentary elections taking place Sept. 18-20. 
In September, authorities arrested members of the banned pro-peace Yabloko party, Anna Shatunovskaya-Byurno and Grigory Grishin, among others, as part of a broader crackdown on dissent and political organizing.

OpenAI’s Altman says AI benefits warrant accepting some risks
- OpenAI CEO Sam Altman believes the benefits of AI justify accepting some risks and supports keeping the technology widely accessible to the public.
- Altman disagrees with stricter regulation proposals like those from rival Anthropic, calling such control "a completely unacceptable trade-off".
- The debate over AI risks continues, with Anthropic warning of potential dangers, while US officials oppose new restrictions to maintain competitiveness.
AI generated
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of artificial intelligence justify accepting some risks and argued the technology should remain broadly accessible to the public
“We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” Altman said in an interview with Politico’s technology-focused newsletter Decoded.
Altman said there remained a fundamental difference in worldview between OpenAI and rival Anthropic on AI regulation, adding: “I think there’s a lot of daylight.”
“I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like, ‘This technology is going to get so powerful, and it’s so dangerous, that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits,’“ Altman said.
He called that “a completely unacceptable trade-off” that runs counter to the “lighter-touch regulatory stance” backed by OpenAI.
“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, ‘We’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen,’“ Altman said. “Because I think people will do tremendously – orders of magnitude more – good stuff than bad stuff.”
Altman’s remarks come amid a growing debate within the AI industry over the pace of development and the risks posed by increasingly capable systems.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in September published an essay calling on the industry to slow down to “pace the frontier,” a stance that Altman publicly endorsed.
Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned in September, saying the people building AI believe it “could kill us all by the end of the decade.
Reuters reported in September that Anthropic warned that, despite AI’s potential benefits, the technology can sometimes act in ways that run counter to its makers’ intentions and penetrate other companies’ systems.
The company said advanced models could exhibit “self-preserving behaviours,” including attempts to “resist shutdown,” “conceal or manipulate information,” or generate outputs that could be interpreted as “coercive, deceptive, or manipulative”.
However, US President Donald Trump has largely dismissed calls for new restrictions, arguing they would make it harder for American companies to compete with Chinese rivals.
He has repeatedly said existing law enforcement agencies, including the Justice Department, provide sufficient safeguards and that no new rules are needed. REUTERS

SBU urges Ukrainians not to film or share photos and videos of Russian strikes
The SBU announced this on its website, according to Ukrinform.
In particular, people are urged not to post content showing Russian strikes on military facilities and critical infrastructure, air defense operations, and other such activity.
"These recordings may be used not only by Russian propagandists, but also by Russian military personnel who monitor and analyze such materials in order to adjust subsequent strikes," the agency said.
The SBU stressed that law enforcement agencies may consider the publication of such content a criminal offense, which carries severe punishment. Depending on the circumstances, such actions may be classified under Article 114-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
This includes the unauthorized dissemination of information about the movement of the Ukrainian Armed Forces and providing information to a state carrying out armed aggression against Ukraine, which carries a sentence of up to 12 years in prison.
SBU operational units systematically investigate cases of such recordings being shared online and hold their authors accountable.
The SBU urged Ukrainians to act responsibly, not help the enemy, and not put other citizens at risk.
On October 4, a Russian drone hit the roadway on the Northern Bridge in Kyiv. Two people were reported injured.

Pacific leaders urge climate action as UN pre-COP talks open in Fiji
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04

08:21:10 KST

Pacific leaders urge climate action as UN pre-COP talks open in Fiji
Pacific leaders urged action on climate change as UN pre-COP talks opened in Fiji's Nadi on Monday, ahead of next month's COP31 summit in Turkey. Discussions in Fiji and Tuvalu will focus on limiting warming to 1.5C, improving access to climate finance and protecting oceans as rising seas threaten communities.
The UN "pre-COP" climate gathering kicked off on Monday in the Fijian city of Nadi, where Pacific leaders are seeking to draw the world's attention to life on the frontline of climate change.
The South Pacific is among the most vulnerable regions in the world to global warming -- from rising sea waters jeopardising homes to increasing temperatures causing coral bleaching.
This week's talks in Nadi and on the atoll nation of Tuvalu are a precursor to the larger UN-sponsored global climate summit -- known as COP31 -- to be held next month in Turkey.
Pacific leaders are pushing for the world to stick to a target of limiting global warming to 1.5C, enhance access to climate finance and give more attention to the impact on oceans.
"Our prime minister will carry three clear messages to the leaders this week: keep 1.5 degrees within reach, make finance reach the communities that need it and give the ocean its rightful place in the climate regime," Fiji's climate minister Lynda Tabuya told the opening ceremony.
Sea levels are rising at a record pace, driven by warming oceans and glacier melt, according to a UN report.
Up to 1.2 billion people could be displaced by 2050, with Pacific island countries experiencing sea level rise at twice the global average, the report released in August said.
It also highlighted a financing gap, with developing countries needing $310-$365 billion to adapt, yet having only $26 billion in adaptation finance available in 2023.
"Today in Fiji, we are again calling on the world to match ambition with delivery," said Australia's climate minister Chris Bowen, who is also president of negotiations for COP31.
He said talks at the pre-COP would focus on "capturing, capitalising on, and putting to work the knowledge of those who've been dealing with climate change here at its forefront, here at its cutting edge".
Regional leaders have pitched the pre-COP as a chance to bring the world to the Pacific.
Read moreColombia hosts climate talks in bid to lead global transition away from fossil fuels
Limited guest list
But officials have been forced to concede that the guest list will be smaller than they had hoped.
Fewer than a dozen world leaders have publicly confirmed that they will attend.
On the streets of Nadi, most locals seemed unaware that a global summit was even taking place.
Australia said last month 4,000 people from 60 nations would attend, without providing a full breakdown.
Among those attending will be Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal of Nepal, which is still reeling from August's Himalayan flood disaster which killed nearly 1,500 people and left 5,800 missing in Nepal and China.
Top delegates to the Pacific talks will also hold a one-day retreat on low-lying Tuvalu, already laying plans to relocate the population if it is consumed by the ocean.
The highest point in the capital Funafuti is just two metres (6.6 feet) above sea level, and two of its nine coral atolls are already largely swamped by rising waters.
Read moreWhat are the key takeaways from the COP30 climate summit?
'Act now decisively'
"Sea-level rise is not a future threat, it is a present reality," Tuvalu Prime Minister Feleti Teo told the UN General Assembly ahead of the climate talks.
"Tuvalu's message is clear: the world must act now decisively, collectively, and with urgency to protect the future for generations to come."
Only a handful of leaders are expected to join the Tuvalu leg of the trip.
"It does make you think nobody cares," said marine scientist Rajneel Singh, part of a team that reported large-scale coral death around Tuvalu.
"It's very, very sad."
As leader of the climate talks, major coal exporter Australia has faced accusations of hypocrisy.
Australian officials have insisted the country is rapidly expanding its renewable energy sources.
But activists accuse Australia of "double talk" on climate change, and have urged leaders to listen to Pacific communities most affected by global warming.
"As Australia prepares to chair the upcoming COP31 talks in partnership with the Pacific, it must do much more to turn empty rhetoric into real action to end the fossil fuel chokehold," Greenpeace's Shiva Gounden said.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

The United States said Sunday that it had removed all of its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Britain following an alleged terror plot disrupted near the base last week that authorities suspect may have been linked to Iran.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the aircraft, which were used among other missions for strikes on Iran during the war, were withdrawn because of security concerns surrounding the base.
About a dozen B-1 bombers had been stationed at Fairford, northwest of London. Their removal could signal a change in how Washington intends to use the base, which Iran threatened to attack in July.
The aircraft have returned to bases in the United States, though the Pentagon stressed Sunday that they remain capable of providing a ‘global strike capability’ from US territory.
‘While operational security considerations prevented us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real time, we can now confirm that all US bombers deployed at Fairford have been redeployed to their home bases in the United States,’ the Pentagon said.
The unusual incident outside the base began early Sunday morning last week, when British police received a report of three suspicious vehicles traveling toward Fairford. Armed officers detained five British citizens in their 20s, all London residents, initially on suspicion of explosives-related offenses and later on suspicion of preparing an act of terrorism. Dozens of nearby homes were evacuated and large police forces were deployed to the area.
The investigation later took an unexpected turn when police said no explosives had been found in the three vans, only gasoline. It was subsequently revealed that one of the suspects had called emergency services shortly before the arrests, adding further uncertainty over what had occurred.
All five suspects were released on bail under restrictive conditions, though police said they remain under investigation.
A sixth suspect, a young London resident with British-Iranian citizenship, was arrested Thursday on suspicion of planning terrorist acts. He was also released on bail several days later.
The suspects’ alleged plan remains unclear, but The Wall Street Journal reported that US officials had been aware of an Iran-linked plot to kill personnel at the base and damage the bombers stationed there.
A senior US official told the newspaper that a unit of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had recruited British citizens to carry out the attack, which allegedly involved several stages, including creating a diversion in a nearby area.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were ‘strong indications’ that Iran was involved in the incident, though the reported details of the alleged plot have not been officially confirmed.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, meanwhile, said in an interview published Saturday by the Daily Mail that Israel had provided intelligence to Britain before the alleged attack was disrupted.

- UK officials seek to be recognised as a "trusted partner" by the EU to maintain trade flow and avoid barriers under new EU rules.
AI generated

Strikes by North Sea oil workers could ‘severely disrupt’ UK fuel supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
23:01:40 UTC
08:01:40 KST

A looming strike by oil workers in the North Sea could “severely disrupt” UK fuel supplies, the Unite union has said, adding that staff were left with no choice after a breakdown in pay talks with the Texas oil company Apache.
The union said Apache workers had “emphatically” backed strike action after being given what it said was an unacceptable pay offer that amounted to a real-terms pay cut for many employees, at a time when the company was “raking in eye-watering profits”.
Unite said the operator had also set deadlines for reaching an agreement over back pay and indicated payments could be withheld, “leaving workers potentially thousands of pounds out of pocket”.
Apache said it had “engaged constructively throughout the pay discussions” and added that it had offered a 4% pay increase for staff, “whose earnings already place them among the highest earners in the UK and whose offshore rota averages 153 working days a year”.
Strike action could begin later this month, according to the union, and could involve more than 160 Apache offshore workers, including electrical experts, production technicians and radio operators.
Any action would affect the Forties and Beryl oilfields, and could lead to one of the critical North Sea platforms, known as Charlie, “being brought to a standstill”, Unite said.
That could ultimately result in the entire Forties pipeline system in the North Sea – which is said to handle almost a third of the UK’s oil and gas – “going down”, the union said, adding that the disruption could also ripple out and affect other large North Sea operators.
Unite blamed the potential disruption on Apache’s failure to reach a pay deal, saying the company’s behaviour could have “far-reaching consequences for workers, operators and consumers”.
Consumers have already been grappling with rising fuel and gas prices because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has been disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf.
On Friday, British motorists were dealt a fresh blow when it emerged that the average price of diesel had climbed to a record £2 a litre.
At the same time it was announced that leaders of G7 nations would release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off supplies of US diesel.
Commenting on the potential strike action, the Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham, said: “We will not tolerate unacceptable pay offers.”
Stevie Davies, a Unite industrial officer, said any disruption to Apache’s platforms “would have a direct hit on the Forties pipeline and potentially severely affect the UK’s fuel supplies”.
The Texas-based APA Corporation, which is the parent company behind Apache North Sea Production, reported $1.4bn (£1.1bn) in after-tax profits and $9.2bn in revenues for last year.
“We believe our final offer to the union is fair and recognises the contribution of our offshore workforce, alongside the wider benefits in our total rewards package,” Apache said. “The proposed pay increase is also in line with that awarded to our non-unionised employees earlier this year.”
Apache also said it had contingency plans in place, and that it did not expect any strike action to affect other producers and their ability to operate through the Forties pipeline system. The plans included keeping “experienced personnel” on key sites, and it said any reduction in pipeline pressure as a result of industrial action would be similar to what occurred during routine maintenance outages.
“As a responsible operator, we are planning to maintain safe operations throughout any industrial action,” Apache added.
Planned strikes by Neo Next offshore workers, organised by Unite, were called off this summer after they secured a deal that the union said lifted the pay package by more than £4,000. The deal was reached days before workers were due to start a series of strikes from 22 July.
Ineos, which operates the Forties pipeline system, was contacted for comment.

Money stolen by scammers hijacking UK social media accounts rises 400%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
23:01:40 UTC
08:01:40 KST

The total amount stolen by criminals who hack into people’s emails and social media accounts and then pretend to be them has risen by more than 400% in a year, official UK data shows.
In many cases, the scammers are hijacking people’s accounts in order to use their identity to sell fake event tickets – such as to sold-out gigs – to unsuspecting friends and family.
The total reported amount stolen via email and social media account hacking reached £6.3m in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with £1.2m in 2024-25, according to the Report Fraud service run by the City of London police, which holds national responsibility for economic crime.
However, the true total may be much higher as many scam victims do not report the crime, often because they feel embarrassed, and sometimes because the individual amount of money involved was relatively small.
The Guardian previously featured the case of a music fan whose Instagram account was targeted by hackers, who used her identity to advertise tickets to an Oasis gig and stole £1,400 from her friends. She said the hackers impersonated her so well that her friends and family genuinely thought they were speaking to her.
Others have been scammed by fraudulent WhatsApp and text messages in which a criminal pretends to be their child or a relative who is in an emergency situation and urgently needs cash. This has been dubbed the “Hi mum” scam.
Data from Santander has shown that among customers of the bank, fraudsters pretending to be someone’s son were the most successful at extracting cash, followed by daughters.
Ch Supt Amanda Wolf, head of Report Fraud operations, said: “For most people, being hacked isn’t just a cyber issue – it’s personal. It can leave victims locked out of important accounts, worried about what information has been accessed, and concerned that criminals may use their identity to target others.”
She added that what starts with one compromised account “can quickly impact family, friends and colleagues as fraudsters exploit trusted relationships to commit further fraud”.
Report Fraud is launching an awareness campaign urging the public to protect their online accounts from hackers by switching to passkeys where they are available. A passkey uses an individual’s device and biometrics to authenticate them and cannot be hacked like a password.

Flavio Bolsonaro leads Lula as Brazil election heads to runoff
Brazil’s presidential election is headed to a runoff, with right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, leading incumbent left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
With almost all votes counted, Bolsonaro received 47.21% of the vote, compared with Lula’s 45.16%, according to the official tally.
Under Brazilian election rules, a presidential candidate must secure more than 50% of valid votes to win in the first round. With neither Bolsonaro nor Lula reaching that threshold, the two will face each other in a runoff on October 25.
The election is widely seen as a highly polarized contest over Brazil’s political direction, pitting Lula’s left-wing agenda against Bolsonaro’s conservative platform, which emphasizes tougher measures against crime and the protection of “traditional values.”
The vote also presents a foreign-policy choice, as Lula has sought to strengthen Brazil’s role in BRICS and deepen ties with China and other Global South powers, while Bolsonaro has emphasized closer relations with Washington and touted his ties to US President Donald Trump.
Lula served as Brazil’s president from 2003 to 2011 and returned to office for a third term in 2023. He was barred from running in the 2018 election due to a corruption conviction and spent 580 days in prison. Brazil’s Supreme Court annulled his convictions in 2021, ruling that the court that tried him lacked jurisdiction, restoring his political rights and allowing him to run again.
Jair Bolsonaro, who served as president from 2019 to 2022, is serving a 27-year sentence after being convicted of attempting a coup following his defeat by Lula in the 2022 election. Both men have denied wrongdoing in their respective cases and argued that the prosecutions against them were politically motivated.
Bolsonaro’s other son, Eduardo, has lived in self-imposed exile in the United States since 2025. Brazil’s Supreme Court sentenced him in June to four years and two months in prison for coercion after finding that he had sought US pressure on Brazilian authorities in an effort to interfere with his father’s coup trial.
Brazilian authorities have also investigated alleged US interference in the country’s politics after Trump denounced the case against Jair Bolsonaro as a “witch hunt,” while Flavio and Eduardo Bolsonaro met the US president at the White House in May.
The election also brought victories for other members of the Bolsonaro family, with former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro elected to the Senate from the Federal District and Bolsonaro’s third son, Carlos, winning a Senate seat in Santa Catarina.

The Pentagon confirmed reports Sunday that the United States has withdrawn all B-1 bomber planes from Royal Air Force Fairford, the UK airbase where a suspicious incident triggered nearby evacuations.
A statement from a Pentagon official said "we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States."

Read moreMystery over UK airbase scare as police find petrol but no explosives
The scare forced evacuations at 85 homes near the airbase, which was used to launch strikes on Iran.
Speculation about the motives behind the incident ranged from terror threat to fuel thievery, as energy prices in the UK hit record highs this week.
Investigators said they did not find any explosives in the vans, but instead "a quantity of petrol was recovered," National Counter Terrorism Policing head Lawrence Taylor said.
The five London-based Britons arrested in the incident, all men in their mid-20s, were released on bail, drawing rebuke from Washington.

Iran's embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation that Tehran was involved.
Security at the base had reportedly been heightened recently.

Fairford is the only airbase on Britain's mainland used for this purpose.

One person was killed and six injured, as Russian forces carried out a double-tap strike using Banderol missiles in Kharkiv’s industrial district.
Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov confirmed the death and casualties, reporting that an administrative building and vehicles were burning. At least 10 multi-story residential buildings were damaged in the attack, and search and rescue operations are ongoing.
Banderol missiles have been a part of Russia's increasing use of jet-powered loitering munitions, combining features of a cruise missile and a jet-powered drone. Its speed, maneuverability, and low-altitude flight profile can make the Banderol difficult for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept.
After a July 8 Banderol missile struck Kharkiv, Spartak Borysenko, head of the department for combating crimes committed in the context of armed conflict at the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office, told Suspilne Kharkiv that the munition can reach speeds of up to 800 kilometers (500 miles) per hour and carry around 300–400 kilograms (660–880 pounds) of explosives.
"It has a guidance system and numerous control surfaces, and it can change its direction and altitude while in flight," Borysenko said.
On Sept. 24, three Russian S-8000 Banderol missiles struck a farm in Kharkiv Oblast, killing 6 and injuring 14.
Kharkiv has also faced repeated attacks with other Russian aerial weapons in recent days. On Oct. 2, Russian glide bombs struck the city’s Slobidskyi and Nemyshlianskyi districts, killing two women and injuring 36 people, including three children.
The latest strike is evidence of Russia’s increasing use of fast, maneuverable jet-powered munitions against targets in Ukraine, adding further strain to air defenses already contending with drones, glide bombs, and missiles.

Nicaragua says it will withdraw from Central American Parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
22:36:54 UTC
07:36:54 KST

Nicaragua says it will withdraw from Central American Parliament
The country’s crackdown on human rights has left it increasingly isolated in Latin America.
Nicaragua’s government has announced it will withdraw from the Central American Parliament, a key regional body, as President Daniel Ortega and his co-president and wife, Rosario Murillo, consolidate power.
The Foreign Ministry announced on Saturday that it would exit the six-country parliament, established to help promote human rights and democracy in Central America.
The announcement comes shortly after Friday’s passage of a resolution at the Organization of American States (OAS), calling on Nicaragua to restore civil rights and release political prisoners.
The Nicaraguan government, however, said Saturday’s action was “in the full exercise of its sovereignty”.
The government said the decision would take effect immediately, the latest in a series of withdrawals from regional and international organisations the country has undertaken.
The Ortega-Murillo government has accused such international groups of being vehicles for outside intervention.
Nicaragua pulled out of the OAS in 2023 and the United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHCR) in 2025 over criticisms of the country’s human rights record, which has deteriorated during Ortega’s tenure.
Ortega has been accused of using the state to target critics and dissidents, including through imprisonment, torture and exile.
A UN report released in September found the government was responsible for at least eight deaths in custody since 2018, when Ortega began a sharp crackdown on protests and dissent.
The report also detailed inconsistencies in the government’s account of in-custody deaths, including that of Indigenous Miskito leader Brooklyn Rivera.
A critic of the Ortega government, Rivera was detained for 32 months with minimal contact with his family before dying in May.
The government blamed his death on the effects of a previous case of COVID-19, an assessment the Physicians for Human Rights group called “not medically coherent”.
“A State that resorts to enforced disappearance and allows persons to die in its custody falls short of the minimum human rights standards required for credible democratic governance,” said Jan-Michael Simon, the group’s chair.
The administration of US President Donald Trump has also been vocal in denouncing the Nicaraguan government’s abuses, including Rivera’s death.
In July, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio published a statement calling Nicaragua’s government a “dictatorship” after it announced it would abolish the country’s upcoming elections.
He also framed the Ortega-Murillo government as a threat to US national security. “Ortega’s pledge to abolish elections in Nicaragua proves his cowardice and fear of the Nicaraguan people’s will,” Rubio wrote.
But the Trump administration has come under criticism for seeking to deport Nicaraguan citizens who were expelled under Ortega’s leadership.
Human Rights Watch recently warned that the Trump administration had detained eight Nicaraguan nationals for deportation, seven of whom were among 222 political prisoners flown into exile in the US in February 2023, during former President Joe Biden’s administration.
Nicaragua subsequently stripped them of their citizenship and branded them as “traitors” to the country. The Ortega government also seized any property they had in the country.
Human Rights Watch urged the Trump administration not to deport the eight detainees, warning that they could face abuse if they were returned to Nicaragua. Four of the detainees reportedly have pending asylum cases.
“After offering refuge to these critics of the Nicaraguan government just three years ago, the United States is now detaining and threatening to deport them,” Juanita Goebertus, Americas director at Human Rights Watch, said in a statement.
“International law prohibits the United States from returning anyone to face the threat of persecution or torture. US authorities should not be trying to send these men back into danger.”

US withdraws B-1 bomber aircraft from UK’s Fairford base amid Iran fears
The abrupt redeployment to the US comes after several ‘terrorism-related’ arrests were made outside RAF Fairford.
The United States has made the abrupt decision to withdraw its bombers from the Royal Air Force (RAF) base Fairford in the western part of the United Kingdom, citing concerns about a potential attack.
Media reports emerged on Sunday that an urgent redeployment was under way, with B-1 bombers leaving RAF Fairford for the US.
Roughly a dozen such aircraft had been based at RAF Fairford prior to the sudden departure.
“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” a Pentagon spokesperson told Al Jazeera.
“The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, anytime,” the official added.
It is unclear precisely what prompted the withdrawal, which comes as the US and Israel remain embroiled in a war against Iran.
RAF Fairford has served as a stopping point for US bombers participating in the war, which began more than seven months ago, on February 28.
But the base, located roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, has been rumoured to be the target of a “terror” plot involving Iran.
On September 27, UK authorities arrested five men on suspicion of plotting to plant explosives near the base.
Iran has denied any such scheme, and the men were released without charge a day later. Investigators discovered petrol, but no explosive devices, in their vans. Still, officials in the UK say they remain under investigation.
On Thursday, British police also announced they had arrested a 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national in London on suspicion of plotting an attack against the airbase.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested last week that “Iran played a part” in the alleged plot, though he declined to provide details.
“The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry,” Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said in a statement.
“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.”
US President Donald Trump responded to the initial arrests by accusing the men of seeking to do “big damage” to US facilities. He also praised UK authorities for their efforts.
“The arrest in the UK was fantastic. Working with Britain – it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation,” Trump said of the suspects. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them.”
Iran, meanwhile, summoned the UK ambassador to Tehran over the last week in protest of the arrests.
The US has a long history of stationing forces at RAF Fairford during its wars in the Middle East, stretching back to the Gulf War in the 1990s.
RAF Fairford has been the site of antiwar protests in the past. During one instance, in 2003, five protesters broke into the airbase in an attempt to destroy military equipment slated to be used in the US invasion of Iraq.
The UK has largely declined to participate in the ongoing war on Iran, despite pressure from the Trump administration.
Still, while the UK government was initially hesitant to let the US use its bases for the war, it granted the US “defensive” access to bases, including Fairford and RAF Diego Garcia, in March.

Yemen’s civil war has intensified, with the internationally recognized government announcing a military operation aimed at retaking territory captured last month by the Iran-backed Houthis.
The Houthis, a Shiite armed group, continued their own offensive, reportedly seizing more towns in southwestern Taiz province near the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

FBI arrests woman accused of surveilling Taiwanese president's son for China

2026-10-04
22:21:52 UTC
