FBI arrests alleged Chinese agent at LAX after she allegedly surveilled son of Taiwanese president
The FBI arrested a suspected Chinese agent at Los Angeles International Airport after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's U.S.-based son, law enforcement sources told CBS News.
Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was cuffed by federal law enforcement on Sunday before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China, from LAX, on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.
Zhang's husband Edric Ding, a realtor at the same firm, told CBS News when reached by phone Sunday: "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.
It was not immediately clear if Zhang has an attorney.
A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of traveling to Seattle, Washington, in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.
Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.
Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.
"If the PRC [People's Republic of China] wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to the PRC," wrote FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt in the Oct. 3, 2026, criminal complaint.
Taiwan has been the focus of high geopolitical tensions for decades. It asserts its independence, while the Chinese government claims it is part of China. The island is in a key position astride major shipping lanes, and is where many of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips are manufactured.
CBS News reached out to the Taiwanese consulate for comment.
The complaint said Zhang, 34, and a man named only as "Individual 1" flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan Rogue and drove to their target's home.
Images from a neighbor's security camera included in the complaint allegedly show the two "appearing to film" Ting-Yu, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening.
CBS News matched the images to an address near Seattle owned by Ting-Yu.
Zhang allegedly texted her Chinese government handler: "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," followed by two license plate numbers, according to the complaint.
The FBI agent wrote that the texts from the Chinese messaging app WeChat were obtained from a search warrant on Zhang's iCloud account.
"Zhang was in contact with at least two people whom she appeared to acknowledge worked for the PRC government," the agent wrote.
The complaint claims Zhang was introduced in June 2025 to one of the Chinese government officials by a classmate from her alma mater, Beijing's University of International Relations, which Holt said has close ties to the Ministry of State Security.
Holt's affidavit claims Zhang booked a private room in Changsha, China, during a June 2025 trip, where she allegedly met the government official and received her surveillance mission.
She later texted the official, "I can take care of this thing," according to the complaint.
On Aug. 26, 2025, Zhang wrote: "I will be busy with work in L.A. this week. I will probably go to Seattle next week," and the official replied: "Ok. Thank you for your hard work," the complaint said.
Zhang is a licensed California realtor with JC Pacific Capital Inc. Her Zillow profile says she has 130 sales and listings around Los Angeles and neighboring counties.
Ting-Yu received his bachelor's in electrical engineering from Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio, in 2012; a master's in Bioengineering Innovation and Design from Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, the following year; then a PhD from the Department of Bioengineering at the University of Washington, according to a profile from one of his academic publications.
Taiwan TV news station SETN reported that he met his Taiwanese wife while studying for his doctorate. They married in 2018 and had a child in the U.S. in 2020, according to CNA, Taiwan's national news agency.
Chinese government agents have previously been caught spying on and harassing Chinese dissidents and pro-democracy activists in the U.S.
Federal prosecutors said Shujun Wang, 75, infiltrated and informed on a Chinese pro-democracy group in Queens, New York, for the Chinese Ministry of State Security for 17 years. He was convicted in 2024 of acting as a foreign agent.
Two people were arrested in April 2023 for their involvement in an unofficial Chinese police station in Manhattan set up to monitor Chinese dissidents.
The Justice Department has warned of a plan by the Chinese security services called Operation Fox Hunt aimed at repatriating wanted Chinese nationals around the world, which targets enemies of the regime.
New York-based Quanzhong An, who prosecutors say is a leader of the U.S. wing of Operation Fox Hunt, was sentenced in March 2025 after harassing a Chinese dissident in an attempt to bring them back to China.
In California, former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang was charged with acting as a Chinese agent in May. She admitted to being paid to spread pro-Chinese government propaganda in the U.S., including an essay on her blog denying "forced labor" in China.

Nationalist Parties, Dodik Dominate Bosnian Election Amid Low Turnout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
22:20:58 UTC
07:20:58 KST

SARAJEVO -- Milorad Dodik, the Russia-friendly former leader of Bosnia-Herzegovina's Serbian-led entity, declared victory for his party in the region, with nationalist parties also scoring wins in Bosnia's complex electoral system -- results likely to keep tensions high in the country and the region.
"I am declaring that we have won," Dodik told supporters in Banja Luka late on October 4, saying preliminary figures assure that his SNSD -- the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats -- will remain in power in Republika Srpska (RS).
Voters cast ballots for the country's central tripartite presidency and national parliament, alongside regional legislative races, such as in the RS, in a complex political system set up under the Dayton accords that ended the country's devastating 1992-95 war.
As part of the Dayton agreements, Bosnia was divided into two semi-autonomous entities -- the Serb-run RS and a Muslim Bosniak-Croat federation -- linked by a sometimes weak central government.
In his victory speech, Dodik said the SNSD’s Zeljka Cvijanovic will become a member of Bosnia's tripartite presidency, based on results with 92 percent of ballots counted.
Pro-West incumbent Denis Becirovic was on course to win the Bosniak seat in the presidency and is expected to be joined by Darijana Filipovic of the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), who is projected to win the Croat seat.
At 39, Filipovic is set to become the youngest member of the Bosnian presidency since the end of the 1992-95 conflict.
Thanks For Trump, Putin
Dodik, who has pushed for greater autonomy from the state government for the Serbian entity -- often along with secessionist rhetoric -- was quick to thank the US and Russian presidents for the victory.
"If it had not been for Donald Trump's magnificent victory...we would probably be political corpses today," he told supporters.
"But now, thanks to the new environment, we are political winners," he said, also offering thanks to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Our political positions remain firm and we will not abandon them. We will continue working for the benefit of our people," Dodik said.
Dodik, 67, was not on any ballot, having been banned from public office, but his face was visible on billboards across Republika Srpska, where he remains a highly influential voice.
Dodik and other RS officials previously faced US sanctions over allegations related to violations of the Dayton peace accords that ended Bosnia's 1992-95 war and for refusing to implement actions of an international peace envoy.
However, the US Treasury Department announced on October 29, 2025, that Dodik and dozens of his allies had been removed from the US sanctions list.
The Treasury did not elaborate on the move, but it followed Washington’s statement welcoming the appointment of an interim president to replace Dodik, who had been stripped of his presidency after a court ruling.
Throughout his tenure as RS president, Dodik faced criticism for authoritarian tendencies, undermining democratic institutions, and fostering a culture of political patronage.
In one preelection rally, Dodik called for the border between RS and Serbia to be erased. Other nationalist politicians have called for a merger with Serbia.
SDA Leads Parliament Vote
Meanwhile, ethnic-nationalist forces appear to have scored success in the BiH’s national parliament in Sarajevo on October 4.
According to preliminary results, the nationalist Party of Democratic Action (SDA) has the largest number of votes in the federation parliament, trailed by the Social Democratic Party of BiH (SDP-BH), and the Croatian Democratic Union of BiH (HDZ BiH).
The SNSD and Dodik are openly pro-Russian and anti-NATO, while the SDA, HDZ, and SDP are pro-EU and favor NATO.
Outgoing Croat presidency member Zeljko Komsic said the strong results by nationalist parties reflected growing ethnic consolidation among voters.
"It is evident that ethnic homogenization of the electorate has taken place across all parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina," Komsic said, adding that the election suggested that "the idea of a civic state currently lacks broad electoral support."
While the political divide still reflects the 1990s conflict, a new element in this election was biometric voter checks and ballot scanners. This led to some polling stations opening later than scheduled amid technical hiccups.
Bosnia is the first country in the Western Balkans to implement the system nationwide, a measure imposed by the international High Representative's Office as part of election-integrity reforms under the framework established by the Dayton accords.

American bomber fleet departs Britain
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
23:17:02 BST
07:17:02 KST

All US bombers deployed to RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire have returned to their home stations in the United States, ending the latest sustained deployment of American heavy bombers at the British airbase, according to US European Command.
European Command confirmed on 4 October that the aircraft “are redeploying to their home stations”, while a US Department of Defense official separately confirmed that every American bomber deployed to Fairford had now left the base.
“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States,” a US Air Force statement said.
The aircraft remaining at Fairford before the departure were B-1B Lancer bombers. The New York Times, citing two US officials, reported that 12 B-1s were involved in the redeployment and that at least three had reached South Dakota by Sunday. No reason for the withdrawal has been given publicly by the Pentagon or US European Command.
European Command said American bombers routinely deploy internationally as part of global readiness and operational requirements, without providing further detail on the decision to bring the Fairford aircraft home. “US Air Force bombers routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements,” the US statement said.
The service added that its bomber force remained capable of carrying out long-range operations directly from the continental United States. “The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, anytime.”
RAF Fairford is a Royal Air Force station used extensively by the United States Air Force and serves as a forward operating location for US strategic bomber deployments to Europe. Its long runway and supporting infrastructure allow aircraft including the B-1B Lancer, B-2 Spirit and B-52 Stratofortress to operate from the Gloucestershire base.
The airfield has hosted a substantial US bomber presence during 2026. B-1 and B-52 aircraft operated from Fairford during American military operations connected with the war with Iran, making the base one of the principal European locations supporting the deployment of US long-range strike aircraft.
Six B-52 Stratofortress bombers had already departed Fairford earlier in the year, leaving B-1 Lancers as the remaining deployed bomber force at the base by the beginning of October.
The B-1B is a supersonic long-range conventional bomber operated by the US Air Force. Although originally developed during the Cold War with a nuclear role, the aircraft was subsequently converted to a conventional-only mission and has been used extensively for long-range strike operations.

UK warships to enter South China Sea despite China protest
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
23:08:16 BST
07:08:16 KST

Royal Navy patrol ships HMS Spey and HMS Tamar are to enter the South China Sea for a ten-day multinational exercise with Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand and Singapore, continuing a British naval presence in waters where Beijing has repeatedly objected to UK military activity and policy, according to the Royal Navy.
The two Batch 2 River-class offshore patrol vessels will take part in Exercise Bersama Lima 26, the annual tri-service exercise conducted under the Five Power Defence Arrangements, or FPDA, which links the United Kingdom with Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand and Singapore.
Bersama Lima, meaning “Together Five” in Malay, will involve ships, aircraft and troops operating across maritime, land and air scenarios. Forces committed to the exercise include frigates, patrol vessels, a corvette, tanker and submarine, as well as divers and specialist boarding teams.
Australian F-35A Lightning II fighters will lead the air element of the exercise, while planned scenarios include troops directing naval gunfire, boarding and searching vessels at sea, anti-submarine warfare and naval air defence supported by participating air forces.
The deployment takes place against a long-running dispute between Beijing and several regional governments over territorial and maritime claims in the South China Sea, as well as wider disagreements over the activities of military forces from countries outside the region. China has repeatedly criticised British involvement. In 2018, Beijing said it had lodged stern representations with the UK after HMS Albion sailed close to the Paracel Islands, which China calls the Xisha Islands. China said the ship had entered waters it regarded as its territorial sea without permission, while Britain has consistently maintained the importance of navigational rights under international law.
Beijing again objected in 2021 as the UK increased its naval presence in the Indo-Pacific, accusing Britain of deploying its Carrier Strike Group to the South China Sea to “flex its naval muscles”. More recently, in July 2026, the Chinese Embassy in London strongly condemned the UK for joining an international statement supporting the 2016 South China Sea arbitration award and urged Britain to stop what it described as “stirring up trouble” in the region.
HMS Tamar has also recently conducted a freedom-of-navigation activity in the South China Sea. In a parliamentary answer published on 8 September, the Ministry of Defence confirmed that the patrol ship operated alongside the Royal Australian Navy on 1 September as part of the UK’s stated commitment to freedom of navigation and overflight under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
The Royal Navy says HMS Spey and HMS Tamar have themselves conducted freedom-of-navigation missions in disputed waters during their five-year deployment to the Indo-Pacific, sometimes operating independently and sometimes alongside regional partners.
Before Bersama Lima moves into its main operational phase, personnel from the five participating nations will spend time familiarising themselves with different vessels, equipment, procedures and terminology, while senior officers carry out planning for the live exercise.
According to a Royal Navy news update, Lieutenant Commander Cheryl Goodwin, HMS Tamar’s Executive Officer, said: “We’re looking forward to being a part of Bersama Lima 26 – an exercise which unites some of our closest allies, tests the crew in a traditional war-fighting role, and demonstrates the UK’s resolve to maintain stability in the Indo-Pacific region through supporting our partners.”
HMS Tamar is also carrying a Royal New Zealand Navy boarding team during the exercise, adding another element of direct integration between the participating forces.
Lieutenant Williams, a Royal New Zealand Navy officer embarked aboard Tamar, said: “It’s a first for me and my team, but it’s a well-trodden path which has been established through a deep history of our navies working together.”
He added: “We’ve got a lot of experience to share, are always looking to improve and we’re ready to go.”
The Five Power Defence Arrangements were established in 1971 and provide a framework for defence cooperation between the five member states. Regular exercises bring together naval, land and air forces, particularly around Malaysia and Singapore, to practise combined operations and develop common procedures. Both British patrol ships have been forward deployed to the Indo-Pacific since 2021. Their mission, known as Operation Highwall, has included multinational exercises, maritime security operations, sanctions enforcement, humanitarian assistance, defence engagement and freedom-of-navigation activity.
Bersama Lima marks a return to operations for HMS Spey after the vessel spent the summer undergoing maintenance in Singapore. HMS Tamar has remained active across the region, including participation in the US-led Pacific Partnership humanitarian exercise and a visit to Cambodia before its September activity with the Royal Australian Navy in the South China Sea.
The ships passed five years continuously deployed to the Indo-Pacific in September, making them the first Royal Navy vessels to maintain a persistent presence in the region since the handover of Hong Kong in 1997.
During Bersama Lima, Spey and Tamar will operate as part of a larger multinational force, with the live phase testing the five FPDA nations across areas including maritime interdiction, anti-submarine warfare and air defence in and around the South China Sea.

Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea, Somalia issue declaration on Red Sea governance, state sovereignty, water rights
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:04:15 CST
07:04:15 KST

CAIRO, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- The leaders of Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea and Somalia on Sunday issued a joint declaration on state sovereignty, Red Sea governance, and water rights, stressing the necessity of adhering to international law as the foundation for regional stability and cooperation.
In the El Alamein Joint Declaration issued following the quadrilateral consultative summit in Egypt's New Alamein, the leaders rejected interference in the internal affairs of the region's states "under any pretext."
The summit was attended by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, and Abdel Fattah Al-Burhan, chairman of Sudan's Transitional Sovereign Council.
The leaders discussed regional and international developments, and ways to strengthen political, economic, trade and cultural cooperation among the four countries, and addressed a number of regional issues.
On Sudan, the leaders support the unity, sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national institutions of the Republic of Sudan, rejecting the establishment of any parallel entities.
They reject any recognition of or support for the so-called "Somaliland" and affirm that the governance of the Red Sea is the exclusive responsibility of the littoral states.
The declaration also stressed the importance of respecting international law regarding transboundary rivers, including the Nile River, particularly the principle of "no harm" and the obligation to cooperate through prior notification, consultation, and consensus.
They categorically reject "any unilateral measures that harm the existing water uses of the two downstream Nile states."
The summit came amid growing Egyptian efforts to strengthen coordination with countries in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea region over regional security and stability. ■

News Analysis: British PM reopens Brexit debate, but return to EU remains uncertain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:04:08 CST
07:04:08 KST

by Xinhua writers Zhang Feng, Chen Shulin
LONDON, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has reopened the debate over Britain's relationship with the European Union (EU), putting eventual membership among the options.
His remarks challenge Labour's previous red lines and raise a central question: how far is Britain prepared to go in rebuilding ties with the bloc?
In his first Labour Party conference speech as prime minister on Tuesday, Burnham said "Brexit has done more harm than good," and laid out options for "Britain's long-term relationship with our European partners."
In an interview broadcast by the BBC the next day, he said rejoining the EU was one option. "I would like to see Britain rejoin in my lifetime," he said, but added that he would "look at the different options."
Those options range from maintaining the current relationship to joining a customs union, participating in the single market or returning to full EU membership. They involve different degrees of economic integration and political commitment.
The openness to reconsidering those options contrasts with Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out returning to the single market or customs union and restoring freedom of movement. Burnham had also previously pledged not to reopen "divisive arguments about rejoining the EU," according to the Financial Times.
The debate comes a decade after 52 percent of voters backed leaving the EU in the June 2016 referendum. Britain formally left in 2020.
ECONOMIC CASE, POLITICAL RISKS
Burnham has made economic growth a critical argument for reconsidering Britain's relationship with the EU.
"I think we have seen growth harmed by Brexit and it's hard to see how we can get back to the higher levels of growth we once had by staying too distant from our largest market," he said in an interview broadcast by ITV News on Wednesday.
Polling also points to public support for closer ties, although that does not necessarily amount to a mandate for full membership.
A Public First poll found that 70 percent of British voters wanted the government to build a closer relationship with the EU, the Independent reported Wednesday. YouGov data published on the same day showed 59 percent support for rejoining the EU.
Reopening the debate also carries political risks. Labour MP Graham Stringer said it would be a "betrayal" for Britain to go back on the vote, and warned that the debate could be "more acrimonious" than in 2016.
WELCOME SIGNALS, BUT NO EASY RETURN
French President Emmanuel Macron and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez welcomed the prospect of Britain's return. Macron said in English, "welcome back," describing a possible British return to the EU as great news for Britain and Europe.
Sanchez said Brexit had been a "huge loss" for both the British people and the EU.
Those responses signal political goodwill, but they do not establish agreement across the bloc on the conditions for British membership.
Rejoining would require negotiations over membership terms, the European Parliament's consent, unanimous approval by the Council of the EU and ratification of an accession treaty by Britain and all EU member states. Support from individual European leaders would be only part of that process.
A forthcoming UK-EU summit could provide an early indication of how Burnham intends to translate his remarks into policy. The summit originally scheduled for July was postponed and could be held in November. British media have suggested that Burnham wants it also to address the broader framework of UK-EU relations.
The immediate test is whether the government sets out a concrete negotiating position. That would help clarify whether Burnham is pursuing closer practical cooperation or preparing for a more fundamental change in Britain's relationship with the EU. ■

U.S. military removes bombers from U.K. air base following security incident
The U.S. Air Force has removed all of its bombers from a U.K. air base following a security incident that led to the arrest of five British men and one U.K.-Iranian national last month, a Pentagon spokesperson confirmed to CBS News on Sunday.
All U.S. bombers deployed to RAF Fairford have been returned to their home stations in the United States, the spokesperson said. The Wall Street Journal was first to report on the bombers' return.
"U.S. Air Force bombers routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements," the Pentagon spokesperson's statement said. "The Airmen that operate America's bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, anytime."
On Sept. 27, five men, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran. Police say they found a quantity of an accelerant — gasoline — in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.
The suspects have since been released on bail.
A dual U.K.-Iranian national was also later arrested on suspicion of plotting a terror attack. The 25-year-old man was taken into custody in London on Thursday, and on Saturday, Counter Terrorism Policing announced he had been released on bail.
The British government believes Iran "played a part" in the incident at the air base, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week.
"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America," the prime minister told the BBC.
Iranian officials have said several times since the beginning of the war that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets. But the Iranian Embassy in London said in a statement last week that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.

Israeli troops shot and killed a man suspected of trying to infiltrate an IDF post in southern Syria overnight, the military said Monday.
The incident occurred in an Israeli-controlled security zone near the Syrian village of al-Hamidiyah, close to the border with Israel. The man approached one of the military posts in the area, prompting Carmeli Brigade troops to begin a standard procedure for confronting a suspected intruder.
According to the military, the man continued climbing an embankment toward the post despite orders to stop and was eventually shot and killed outside the position.
The IDF said it was investigating the incident, including whether the man was armed and attempting to carry out an attack. No Israeli troops were injured.
“A short while ago, IDF soldiers identified a suspect attempting to infiltrate an IDF post in the Security Zone in southern Syria,” the military said shortly after the incident. “Following a quick identification, the soldiers fired toward the suspect and eliminated him. No IDF injuries were reported.”
“The IDF will continue to operate in the Security Zone in southern Syria in order to remove any threat to Israeli civilians and IDF soldiers,” it added.
The incident began when soldiers at one of the observation posts spotted a person climbing an embankment outside the military position. The troops called on him to stop and said he appeared to be holding something in his hand.
The man did not comply and continued advancing, according to the soldiers, prompting them to open fire. He was killed in the shooting.
Troops were searching the surrounding area afterward to rule out the presence of additional suspects.
A reserve officer serving in the buffer zone in Syria told ynet that it was not the first incident in recent weeks involving people approaching IDF positions.
“They are testing the area,” the officer said. “They send people, they send cells, they do all kinds of things to see where we operate and how we respond.”
“It reminds me of the period before Oct. 7,” he added, referring to the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. “Disturbances, one person here, another person there. They see how long it takes you to respond, how you respond and from where you detect them.”
Several weeks ago, another Syrian man, allegedly armed with a knife, was suspected of attempting to infiltrate one of the IDF posts in the buffer zone and was detained. An investigation later determined that he was suffering from mental illness.

Iran says no military solution to war as peace talks with US stall

Iran says no military solution to war as peace talks with US stall
Iran's diplomat said on Sunday there was no military solution to the US war against Iran as peace talks appeared stalled. Washington has scaled back attacks in favour of economic pressure, while Iran's attempted Hormuz blockade remains contentious. A UK maritime agency reported another tanker hit by an unidentified projectile.
Iran's top diplomat insisted on Sunday that there would be no military solution to the United States' war against the Islamic republic, with talks on ending the conflict apparently at an impasse.
A campaign of heavy bombardment failed to bring a decisive close to the war launched by the US and Israel in late February, and Washington in recent weeks has dialled back military operations in favour of economic pressure.
The main point of contention remains Iran's attempt to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, a vital conduit for Gulf oil and gas where a UK maritime agency reported on Sunday another tanker was struck by an unknown projectile.
"If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said at a gathering of foreign ambassadors.
"There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions," he continued, adding "only negotiations based on justice and fairness" could end the conflict.
Read moreG7 members will release 100 million barrels of diesel after US threatens export ban
The two sides agreed a memorandum of understanding in June that spelled out a framework for a permanent resolution, but Iranian attacks on vessels in the Hormuz prompted a return to US military operations.
Iran has sought to impose its control over the vital shipping lane since the start of the war, striking vessels that attempt to transit without its authorisation.
The US has imposed its own counterblockade of Iranian ports, and has also struck vessels it accuses of violating it.
On Sunday, the British maritime security agency UKMTO said a tanker in the Hormuz "reported being struck by an unknown projectile, causing damage to the engine room", though the crew were reported safe and no environmental impact was recorded.
The agency did not specify the date of the incident, the vessel's origin or destination, or whether it was an oil tanker or LNG carrier.
In Iran, oil minister Mohsen Paknejad has resigned, the president's office said on Sunday, as the US maintains a blockade on the country's oil exports.
In a news bulletin on the minister's resignation, state television ran an interview with an official from the Iranian presidential office who said Paknejad initially offered to quit a while ago "due to personal issues" but this was rejected.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had asked Paknejad to continue in his post but was now accepting his departure as the minister had insisted on leaving, the official added.
Paknejad has been replaced by Hamid Bovard, the chief executive of the National Iranian Oil Company, the presidency said.
Focused on Hormuz
Iranian and US officials last week held indirect talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, with Tehran saying it presented seven conditions for reopening the strait.
Iran has demanded, among other things, a ceasefire across the Middle East, the unfreezing of its assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade.
Trump, however, rejected the proposal, while leaving the door open both to further talks or renewed military operations.
Read moreIran says it expects US response Tuesday on plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Sunday that the US had expressed its views on the proposal and said they were being reviewed.
"The Americans, through intermediaries, have also conveyed their views on this proposal, and these views are currently being examined inside the country through the relevant channels and procedures," he told reporters, according to state news agency IRNA.
"Whenever the final position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is ready, appropriate steps will be taken accordingly. At the same time, the Islamic Republic of Iran is also preparing itself for any other possible scenario."
Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei on Sunday characterised the latest US counterproposal as being "in line with their previous proposals concerning nuclear issues".
"We have clearly indicated that we are focusing on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz," he said, adding that reopening the waterway required "an end to the disruptions to Iranian commercial maritime traffic and the lifting of sanctions".
The United States and Israel have said the war is necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons -- a goal it has long denied pursuing -- though the focus soon shifted to reopening the Hormuz after its closure sent shockwaves through world energy markets.
The United States has not struck Iran since September 1, but it has recently pursued a fresh military buildup in the region.

Cornell case puts New York’s progressive image at odds with its rape laws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
21:39:55 UTC
06:39:55 KST

Cornell case puts New York’s progressive image at odds with its rape laws
New York lawmakers will review sexual-assault laws, including the ‘voluntary intoxication’ rule at the heart of the Cornell case.
Last month, a woman identified as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit against Cornell University, the fraternity Chi Phi and the seven fraternity members she accused of gang-raping her on the night of October 19, 2024.
Her allegations have triggered a nationwide reckoning in the United States over the prevalence of sexual assault on college campuses.
But the case has also reignited efforts to reform laws in the state of New York.
While the left-leaning state has long presented itself as a leader in women’s rights, advocates say sexual assault survivors still face pervasive legal barriers when they seek justice.
Erica Vladimer, a lawyer and founding director of Harassment-Free New York, a survivor-led nonprofit, told Al Jazeera that much of the legislation currently in the spotlight is the culmination of years, if not decades, of work.
“These are bills that we have been fighting for for years when sexual violence is not in the news,” Vladimer said.
She drew a line between the #MeToo movement, which began in 2017 as an online campaign to denounce sexual misconduct, and the current wave of outrage following Doe’s allegations.
“It speaks to the fact that the #MeToo movement is not dead. It is a movement, not a moment,” Vladimer said.
Already, leaders in Albany, the state capital, have signalled they would take action following the Cornell case.
On Wednesday, the New York Assembly announced it had formed a working group to examine the state’s sexual-assault laws and develop recommendations for the 2027 legislative session.
Still, advocates say more concrete measures are needed to address the crisis.
“I appreciate that this work is happening,” said Lindsey Boylan, a New York City Council candidate. “It doesn’t undo the fact that rape culture is pervasive in the United States and very much so alive and well in New York.”
Boylan was the first woman to publicly accuse former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo of sexual harassment in another high-profile misconduct case, back in 2020. She is among those calling for greater reform.
Here are some of the measures advocates are pushing state lawmakers to adopt or amend:
‘Voluntary intoxication’ statute
The Cornell University case has brought renewed attention to New York’s “voluntary intoxication” statute, a legal loophole that can make it harder to prosecute sexual assault when a person has willingly consumed alcohol or drugs.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul pledged on Friday to work with lawmakers to close the gap.
“It should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol. Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape. Period,” Hochul said.
Under the current state law, a person who voluntarily drinks or takes drugs is not considered “mentally incapacitated” during an assault, even if they become too intoxicated to consent.
That can make it harder for prosecutors to bring a sex-crime charge. The law primarily recognises incapacitation in the context of sexual assault when a person was involuntarily intoxicated, unconscious or otherwise “physically helpless”.
That distinction has become central to the Cornell case. Doe has acknowledged that she consumed substances before the alleged rape, saying that she was pressured into drinking alcohol and taking the dissociative drug ketamine.
The Tompkins County district attorney initially declined to bring charges, pointing to the law’s stance on “voluntary intoxication”. But the investigation has since been reopened, amid public pressure.
New York is one of 19 states in the US that distinguish between “voluntary” and “involuntary” intoxication when it comes to determining consent in sexual violence cases.
But the Cornell case has spurred a push to remove the distinction from the law books. Critics have argued that sexual assault is no less grievous if a victim is drunk or has chosen to take drugs.
“I mean, to have New York, a supposedly progressive state, penalise people who are sexually abused for drinking is disgusting,” Boylan told Al Jazeera.
Vladimer, for her part, explained that distinguishing between “voluntary” and “involuntary” intoxication as a means for pursuing sexual assault cases shifts the focus onto the actions of victims, rather than perpetrators.
“We essentially have codified victim-blaming by saying if you become voluntarily intoxicated and then are sexually assaulted, you essentially cannot seek justice in our court system,” Vladimer told Al Jazeera.
In June, the New York state Senate unanimously passed a bill to allow sexual assault charges regardless of whether a victim is intoxicated voluntarily or involuntarily.
But the legislation has yet to be taken up in the state Assembly.
The rape-shield gap
New York’s rape-shield protections limit the use of evidence about a complainant’s sexual history and conduct in criminal proceedings. But those protections do not currently extend to civil cases.
This distinction could matter in the Cornell case because Doe filed a civil lawsuit.
Vladimer said questions about a survivor’s behaviour could come up in the discovery process of a civil case, as well as in court.
“There is the potential of her having to face questions about things like her sexual history,” Vladimer said.
Bridie Farrell, the director of victim rights advocacy and legislation at the law firm Weitz and Luxenberg, told Al Jazeera that she has seen major differences in how male and female survivors are questioned in civil cases where this practice is still permitted.
In one case involving a brother and sister who were both sexually assaulted, Farrell said the man was not questioned about his sexual history while the woman was “grilled on it”.
A bill sponsored by State Senator Liz Krueger would extend rape-shield protections to civil proceedings. The measure passed the Senate in June and is currently before the Assembly Judiciary Committee.
Retaliatory defamation lawsuits
Advocates are also pushing for legislation to prevent retaliatory defamation lawsuits.
Boylan said she has spent more than $2m defending herself in legal proceedings connected to her accusations against Cuomo, who stepped down as New York governor in 2021.
He has repeatedly denied any allegations of wrongdoing, despite a state attorney general’s report that concluded he “engaged in conduct constituting sexual harassment”.
“Every step of the way, we have a system that penalises people for speaking up about their own harm,” Boylan said.
Boylan and Charlotte Bennett, a former aide who also accused Cuomo of sexual harassment, are proponents of the Speak Your Truth Act, which would provide legal protections for people who publicly report sexual assault, harassment or discrimination.
The bill, sponsored by Assembly member Jessica Gonzalez-Rojas, would make certain communications about sexual assault, harassment or discrimination privileged when they are made without malice.
It would also allow survivors of sexual misconduct who successfully defend themselves against a defamation lawsuit to recover legal fees and costs. The bill remains in an Assembly committee.
A recent win, a long way to go
For Bridie Farrell, the victims’ rights advocate, the fight for legal change is personal.
Farrell was a 15-year-old competitive speed skater in 1997 when she said she was sexually abused by her 33-year-old teammate and mentor. She came forward with her story of abuse in 2013.
By then, the statute of limitations in her case had expired. Farrell later became an advocate for changes to New York’s laws, helping to pass the Child Victims Act in 2019 that extended the time available for survivors of childhood sexual abuse to pursue criminal and civil claims.
The law allowed Farrell to file her own case, which she did in 2020. She tells Al Jazeera that a trial has finally been scheduled for June 2027.
“Before we passed the Child Victims Act in 2019, New York was one of the worst in the country,” Farrell said of the situation for sexual assault survivors seeking justice.
Farrell considers the legal impediments to Doe’s case — like the “voluntary intoxication” statute — all too predictable. “I’m not surprised if we haven’t updated a law that is archaic,” she said.
Still, lawmakers have signalled willingness to reform such laws. In announcing the state Assembly’s working group on sexual-assault laws, Speaker Carl Heastie pledged to “thoughtfully” consider how the state can strengthen its laws.
“The allegations being reported out of Cornell University are truly horrifying,” Heastie said on Wednesday. “We want to do everything we can to ensure victims of sexual assault see justice served.”
But survivors and sexual violence advocates say the Cornell case points to problems that go beyond any single law. They hope to see widespread systemic and societal change.
“Changing legislation is incredibly important. But legislation in a lot of cases can only go [as far as] the paper that it’s written on,” Boylan said. “It would be amiss to orient this horrible, tragic, unacceptable, infuriating case in isolation without looking at the broader rape culture of our state and our country.”

====================================================================================================

Nearly three years after Oct. 7, Israeli donations keep climbing as philanthropy shifts to recovery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
21:36:05 UTC
06:36:05 KST

Nearly three years after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 massacre, Israel’s philanthropic sector is showing signs that the surge in charitable giving triggered by the attack has become more than a temporary emergency response. According to Ori Ben-Shlomo, CEO of Israeli donation platform JGive, donations have continued to rise even as the country has moved from immediate wartime relief toward long-term rehabilitation.
In the days after October 7, normal life across Israel was upended. Soldiers were called into reserve duty, hundreds of thousands of Israelis were evacuated, families sought assistance, nonprofits scrambled to identify urgent needs, and private citizens stepped in as state systems struggled to respond.
At the same time, an unprecedented wave of donations began flowing into Israel. Israelis and Jews abroad sought ways to quickly support evacuees, soldiers, affected families, and organizations providing food, equipment, housing, and other emergency assistance, turning digital fundraising platforms into a central part of the civilian response.
Nearly three years later, the questions facing the sector have changed. Diaspora Jewish communities are balancing support for Israel with mounting needs at home, emergency fundraising has increasingly given way to rehabilitation, and Israelis themselves appear to have developed a different relationship with philanthropy.
Ben-Shlomo said JGive’s figures indicate that the shift has endured.
“I think it tells the story of Israeli society through our eyes,” Ben-Shlomo said. “In the year before October 7, 2023, around NIS 160 million passed through our platform. When October 7 came, that rose to something like NIS 330 million in donations. We are talking about hundreds of thousands of donors a year.”
The initial increase was dramatic, but JGive executives did not know whether it would last. During the first months of the war, most donations went toward immediate needs, including food, supplies, assistance for evacuees, and support for soldiers.
“At a certain point, when the immediate emergency began to subside, we thought perhaps the burst of generosity, from Israel and abroad, would also fade,” Ben-Shlomo said. “But the numbers continued to rise.”
He said the platform finished last year with close to NIS 400 million in donations, while the amount passing through JGive this year has already increased further.
“We saw a significant change in Israeli society’s attitude toward donations, solidarity, and the understanding that this is genuinely important for our resilience,” he said.
Israelis increasingly choose direct donations
Although Israel received substantial financial support from Jewish communities abroad following October 7, Ben-Shlomo said most of the money processed through JGive still comes from Israeli donors.
“It is true that during the war the balance changed and more money came from abroad, mainly from the United States,” he said. “But the bigger picture is that most still comes from Israel.”
The trend suggests that the post-October 7 solidarity story was not solely one of Diaspora Jews supporting Israel. Israelis themselves also increased their charitable giving.
At the same time, Ben-Shlomo said the war strengthened financial and emotional links between Israel and Jewish communities overseas, although those relationships have also become more complex.
One major change has been the rise of direct giving.
“In the past, central institutions and organizations had much more power,” he said. “Today, people like to give directly. If you want to donate to a specific nonprofit, you do not necessarily need an intermediary.”
Ben-Shlomo compared the shift to broader consumer behavior, in which people increasingly seek direct access instead of working through middlemen.
The change is particularly visible in the United States, he said, where donors can use digital tools to select a specific Israeli organization or project rather than automatically routing their contribution through established communal institutions.
“That does not mean the federations do not have a role,” he said. “They still have a very significant role, especially in philanthropy and large donations. But alongside that, there is now much more direct giving.”
Emergency fundraising gives way to rehabilitation
Immediately after October 7, JGive concentrated on helping nonprofits raise money as quickly as possible.
“When everything happened on that day, we understood that we needed to do two things,” Ben-Shlomo said. “One was to give nonprofits the time and tools and help them raise as much money as possible, as quickly as possible.”
The organization established an emergency operation to assist nonprofits using its platform. At the same time, JGive began receiving inquiries from donors around the world asking where their money was most urgently needed.
“We received calls from literally all over the globe asking, ‘How can we help?’” he said. “Then we understood there was a serious problem. Many donors simply did not know where to give. They wanted to donate, including companies, but they did not know where the money should go.”
That led to the creation of a national emergency fund intended to rapidly distribute money to organizations responding to needs on the ground.
“We were distributing money every evening,” Ben-Shlomo said. “Our approach was that the funds needed to reach many organizations because there were many needs.”
Nearly three years later, however, the definition of “need” has changed.
“At the beginning of the war, everyone stopped donating to routine causes, culture, education, health, everything that happens in ordinary life,” he said. “Almost everything stopped, and donations moved toward the emergency.”
Those initial needs were often basic, including food and assistance for evacuees. Over time, traditional areas of charitable giving began to recover, while an entirely new rehabilitation sector emerged around the consequences of October 7 and the war.
“There are many organizations that were established for needs created by October 7, and there is now an entire world moving toward rehabilitation,” Ben-Shlomo said.
Mental health, wounded soldiers drive new philanthropic needs
Ben-Shlomo said rehabilitation now includes wounded soldiers, mental-health care, civilian recovery, and long-term assistance for communities and families affected by the war.
“There are a great many needs,” he said. “There is the rehabilitation of soldiers, which is a very complicated event. There is mental health, and there is the civilian rehabilitation of many people following everything that happened.”
“The world of rehabilitation is a new chapter,” he added. “It is also bringing many good people into this field who were not part of it before.”
One notable development, he said, has been the arrival of professionals who previously had little involvement with nonprofits.
“You see organizations being established by doctors, psychologists, or other professionals who were not previously part of the nonprofit world,” he said. “It is very refreshing because people recognize a need and come with their professional expertise.”
The transition comes as Israel continues to face significant psychological consequences from the war, with health organizations reporting sustained demand for mental-health services.
Diaspora communities balance Israel support with needs at home
Ben-Shlomo described the relationship between Israel and Diaspora Jewry since October 7 as increasingly important but also increasingly complicated.
“I think it is a very complex situation,” he said. “The connection to Israel is more important than ever.”
He said rising antisemitism and security concerns around the world have strengthened some Diaspora Jews’ sense of connection to Israel.
“Because of everything happening around Jews in the world today, antisemitism and all of these terrible phenomena, it strengthens many people’s connection to Israel,” he said. “Israel is also a kind of more stable and secure anchor that they want to strengthen their connection with.”
At the same time, Jewish communities abroad are facing growing local expenses.
“Their local challenges are becoming more and more significant,” Ben-Shlomo said. “They need to invest more in protecting people, strengthening their own communities, and building resilience.”
“That makes philanthropy a more complicated issue,” he added. “But the willingness of Diaspora Jewry to create a strong connection with Israel and support important causes is still there.”
Younger donors want to know where their money goes
Donor behavior is also changing, Ben-Shlomo said, reflecting broader developments in philanthropy rather than October 7 alone.
“The new generation goes much further into the details and is interested in where its money goes,” he said. “It is not very different from the way people behave in the investment world.”
Donors increasingly expect transparency and want to understand how their money is being used.
October 7 accelerated that process by exposing many Israelis, particularly younger people, to nonprofits and volunteer activity for the first time.
“If, before October 7, we saw the world of donations as something that was nice to do, something reserved for a particular group, one of the changes we have undergone is that today everyone understands that it is essential and critical,” Ben-Shlomo said.
He recalled a conversation with a friend serving on the board of a business who described how social involvement had become part of professional identity.
Before board members even began discussing business, she told him, participants began describing the nonprofits where they volunteered or served in leadership positions.
“It naturally became a form of self-identity,” Ben-Shlomo said. “Many people feel they need to say that they are involved, whether through donations or volunteering.”
Nearly 90,000 donations in one holiday month
One figure that particularly surprised Ben-Shlomo was not a single major philanthropic contribution, but the sheer number of individual donors.
“In the last holiday month, there were almost 90,000 donations in one month, totaling NIS 60 million,” he said.
“That is one of the figures that always amazes me. It is not one major philanthropist giving a significant amount. It is a huge number of people donating, including small amounts.”
Many of JGive’s donors are young Israelis, he added.
“That really proves something about the Israeli DNA,” Ben-Shlomo said.
The larger question now is whether the solidarity that emerged after October 7 can be sustained during ordinary times.
“In an emergency, there is no question,” he said. “We saw that it happens.”
“The thing that concerns me more, and that we are working on a great deal, is how we take all the enthusiasm that existed during the emergency and turn it into something that happens in ordinary life,” he said. “That requires a great deal of work.”
Ben-Shlomo said the long-term goal should be to make social responsibility a permanent feature of Israeli life.
“I think our mission over the coming decades is to make Israel a social superpower as well,” he said. “There should truly be solidarity and a culture of mutual responsibility in which every person takes action, even if only in their own small area around their home, to look after the people there and those who need help.”

Time Magazine showcases prominent Jewish leaders in 'world's most influential rising stars' list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
21:36:00 UTC
06:36:00 KST

From artists and actors to technologists to politicians advancing visions for the future, Time Magazine has recognized Jewish figures on its list of “the world’s most influential rising stars.”
The magazine launched the Time100 Next list in 2019 to highlight people whose influence is still taking shape. This year’s list reflected shifts in popular culture, the AI revolution and responses to global crises from the United States to Israel.
Jewish members of Time100 Next have talked about their Jewishness as a source of inspiration, angst and activism. Here’s what nine have said about their Jewish identity.
Marisa Abela
Abela, an actress who rose to fame for her role in the TV financial drama series “Industry” and portrayed Amy Winehouse in the 2024 biopic “Back to Black,” grew up in England. She has described drawing from her mixed heritage to inhabit her characters.
“I am someone whose mum and dad come from completely different cultures, my dad is Maltese Arab, and my mum is from a family of Polish Jewish refugees,” Abela told The National in 2022.
While Abela’s background differs from that of her “Industry” character Yasmin Kara-Hanani, whose parents are Lebanese, she said that she understood the character’s family tensions. “The thing I relate to most is that those two cultures can be quite divisive, and you can feel like you’re being pulled in different directions,” she said.
To play Winehouse, Abela said she tapped into shared features of their early lives in Jewish households.
“The more I got to know her, the more I felt a major connection to this spiky Jewish girl from London who had a lot to say, and was really quite unafraid,” she told Harper’s Bazaar in a 2024 interview.
“I remembered how I felt when I was young, seeing that woman who was proud and cool, wearing a big Star of David in between a cleavage and a nice bra. I understood what a Friday-night dinner would look like in her home, the humor in her family.”
Jake Auchincloss
Massachusetts Democratic Rep. Auchincloss is one of his party’s staunchest advocates for centrism amid a rising wave of Democratic Socialists. He represents the state’s 4th Congressional District, spanning the heavily Jewish Boston suburbs of Brookline and Newton, where he grew up with a Jewish mother and Episcopalian father.
After a record of bolstering the Democrats’ pro-Israel wing in Congress, Auchincloss was among the majority of House Democrats who voted in July to cut $3.3 billion in military aid to Israel.
Auchincloss argued the vote did not contradict his support for Israel. Instead, he said it was a vote against President Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who he said had sacrificed the trust of Congress “with their disastrous war against Iran, their empowerment of settler violence in the West Bank, and their strategic incoherence against Islamist terrorism.”
He has also fended off progressive Democrats who denounce the United States-Israel alliance. In September, Auchincloss defeated a primary challenge from AI and policy researcher Jason Poulos, who said that he was animated by watching the United States send military aid to Israel and “participate actively in the genocide of the Palestinian people.”
Auchincloss told the Jerusalem News Syndicate in 2022 that “Judaism is important” to him even though he is “not a religious person.” He added that his parents’ interfaith marriage in the 1970s, which took place at the Harvard Memorial Church with a rabbi officiating, was “still a bit unusual” and made him more appreciative of his Jewish heritage as he was growing up.
Auchincloss has cited his family history as a factor in his decision to join the Marine Corps. In a 2021 interview with Roll Call, Auchincloss said his maternal grandfather enlisted in the Marines in 1942. Instead of deploying the 17-year-old in combat, the Marines sent him to study biomedical engineering at Purdue University, and he became a pioneer in artificial limbs.
“I just think about that, in one of the lowest moments of World War II, one of the lowest moments for Jews in our history, the U.S. government sent a Jewish kid in the Marine Corps to school,” said Auchincloss.
Molly Gordon
Actress and filmmaker Gordon has said that her Jewishness resonates throughout her career, not through observance, but through comedy.
Her Jewish roles span the 2020 comedy “Shiva Baby,” the 2023 mockumentary “Theater Camp,” which she also co-created, and the Hulu series “Ramy,” where she plays a Jewish woman who dates the title character, a Muslim. Gordon’s star has also risen through roles that are not identifiably Jewish, as in FX’s hit series “The Bear.”
“Being Jewish in West LA, my religion was watching comedy. That felt like God to me,” Gordon told Vulture in 2021.
The painter Sasha Gordon, who has no relation to Molly Gordon, won acclaim for her self-portraits set in surreal and nightmarish scenes. She has had multiple solo exhibitions in major cities, including “Haze” at the David Zwirner Gallery in New York City last year.
Gordon grew up in Somers, New York, with a Korean mother and a Polish American Jewish father. She told Vogue in 2023 that she and her brother were bullied in the predominantly white small town for being different.
“I don’t think I’m religious in any way, but I’d say that I’m culturally very Jewish,” said Gordon.
South African-born fashion designer Kallmeyer is the founder of Kallmeyer, a New York-based brand that specializes in suiting. She also became known for hosting pop-up Shabbat dinners that celebrated the Jewish queer community of New York.
In an interview with Gossamer, Kallmeyer described herself as a “gay Jewish business owner” with all the accompanying “anxiety.”
Joey King
King has been an actress since childhood, from the 2010 film “Ramona and Beezus” to the “Kissing Booth” series, which ran from 2018 to 2021, and the 2019 crime drama “The Act,” which won her an Emmy nomination. Her latest film, “Practical Magic 2,” premiered last month.
King opened up about her Jewish identity after starring in “We Were the Lucky Ones,” a 2024 Hulu miniseries based on a true story about Polish siblings who survived the Holocaust while scattered across the globe.
King told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency in 2024 that she jumped at her first opportunity to play a Jewish woman.
“I couldn’t be prouder of who I am and my Jewish heritage,” said King. “When you get presented with a story like this, it’s just a once-in-a-lifetime feeling. It’s an immediate yes — to feel that you get to play a Jewish woman, and you are a Jewish woman.”
Naama Lazimi
Lazimi has been dubbed by Haaretz a “superstar” of the Israeli left. The lawmaker in Israel’s Knesset built her political profile with a focus on poverty and public housing, while protesting against Netanyahu’s government and calling for a state commission of inquiry into government failures surrounding the Hamas attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
Lazimi said on social media that Time’s recognition came just before “the most important elections the State of Israel has ever known.” Lazimi’s Democrats Party hopes to join a centrist governing coalition after the Oct. 27 elections.
“This is not just a personal achievement, but a badge of honor for an entire camp in Israel, a glorious and determined camp that fights for the democratic character of our country, and for solidarity and social justice,” she said.
Lazimi is a longtime ally of Smol Emuni, or “Faithful Left,” a movement of religious left-wing Jews who advocate for peace and oppose the Gaza war. At a conference of Smol Emuni’s U.S. branch in New York, Lazimi said, “Peace is not just true security; it is also the most moral, and the most Jewish, choice.”
Yotam Segev
Israeli-born Segev is the leader of Cyera, a company that creates systems to defend sensitive data against attackers in the AI age. Founded in 2021, Cyera is now valued at $12 billion, according to Time.
Segev, who moved to New York four years ago, told CTech that he became more aware of being “a Jew in the U.S.” since the Gaza war. He cited rising incidents of antisemitism and the fear of being “perceived as someone’s enemy just because of where I come from.”
“When I walk around with my child, I don’t speak loudly in Hebrew without being aware of my surroundings,” said Segev.
Troye Sivan
Australian singer and actor Sivan went from performing the “shul circuit” as a child to Grammy-nominated pop stardom. He was raised in an Orthodox Jewish household. At 15, he came out after his father shared the belief that “it really doesn’t make sense” for religion to ban being gay, according to a 2019 interview with the New Yorker.
Sivan launched a lifestyle brand in 2023 called Tsu Lange Yor, the Yiddish phrase for “to long years.” He told W Magazine his great-grandmother spoke Yiddish at home when he was a child. While not himself “particularly religious,” Sivan said his Jewish identity formed a “huge part” of his cultural identity, and he continued to hold Shabbat dinners.
“Considering I’m not very religious and I’m queer, my Jewish identity was something I grappled with and was unsure about,” said Sivan. “I liked the idea of reclaiming it and proudly saying, even to other Jewish people, ‘I’m queer, and I’m also a Jew — and these are things that are both equally important in the makeup of who I am.’”

October 7 testimonies reach US audiences with new video archive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
21:35:39 UTC
06:35:39 KST

Friends of the Israel Defense Forces (FIDF) is launching a digital library of English-language video testimonies from soldiers, former hostages, bereaved families and others who experienced the Oct. 7 attacks and their aftermath, the organization said.
The archive, being launched ahead of the third anniversary of the Hamas-led attacks, is intended to make firsthand accounts accessible to FIDF donors and other supporters of Israel in the United States, including members of Jewish and Christian communities.
The library will initially include more than 50 filmed testimonies totaling over 12 hours of footage collected by FIDF. The organization said the archive will continue to expand as additional testimonies are recorded and added.
The project brings together accounts from IDF soldiers, lone soldiers, reservists, bereaved relatives, former hostages, community leaders and experts. The videos are divided into categories, allowing viewers to explore the events of Oct. 7 and the period that followed from different perspectives.
Among those featured are Moshe and Shira Shapira, the parents of Staff Sgt. Aner Shapira, who was killed during the attack; Rabbi Doron Perez, father of Capt. Daniel Perez, who was killed and whose body was taken to Gaza; and Col. Elad Edri, who recounts the attack on the IDF's Zikim base.
The archive also features Izzy Ezagui, an IDF veteran who lost an arm after being wounded during his military service and later returned to serve in the reserves.
Testimonies from former hostages include Noa Argamani, Amit Soussana, Maya Regev, Almog Meir Jan, Edan Alexander and Maxim Harkin.
FIDF said the initiative is intended both to preserve firsthand accounts for future generations and to give supporters abroad direct access to the people behind the events. The organization said the archive seeks to document stories of courage and resilience while helping communities outside Israel understand the personal experiences of those affected by the attacks and the war that followed.
"Since October 7, we have been moved by the surge of supporters across Jewish and Christian communities in the United States who want to understand more closely what happened in Israel on that devastating day and the days that followed and hear directly from the people who experienced it," said Maj. Gen. (res.) Nadav Padan, CEO of FIDF.
"Three years later, it is important not only to preserve these testimonies, but also to make them accessible in English to the communities that support Israel and IDF soldiers," Padan said. "This library allows them to hear firsthand from soldiers, hostage survivors and families, and to learn the personal stories behind October 7."

US removes bombers from UK base after security incident
Redeployment from RAF Fairford comes as British authorities link thwarted plot to Tehran
The US Air Force has removed its bombers stationed at a US-run military airbase in England used to strike Iran following an investigation into a planned terror attack at the RAF Fairford base.
The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the United States, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorised to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on Sunday on condition of anonymity.

Brazil’s Flavio Bolsonaro beats polls in presidential vote, faces incumbent Lula in runoff
- Senator Flavio Bolsonaro leads Brazil's presidential election first round with 49.58%, but is projected to face a runoff against President Lula, who has 42.25%, as no candidate passed 50%.
- The campaign focused on corruption scandals, economic worries, and accusations of US interference, with voters showing frustration and many undecided ahead of the runoff.
- Economic challenges, rising public debt, and a major fraud investigation involving Bolsonaro and judiciary figures overshadow the election, while legislative races increase political stakes.
AI generated
BRASILIA/SAO PAULO/RIO DE JANEIRO – Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro will face President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the runoff of a presidential election, the country’s electoral authority said on Oct 4.
With just over 97% of the ballots counted, the right-wing challenger took 47.45% of valid votes in the first round, beating the forecasts in most private surveys. 
Leftist Lula received 44.66% of the votes.
The two leading candidates will advance to the second round of voting on Oct 25, beating out a field of 12 candidates in a campaign focused on concerns about the growing cost of living, corruption and insecurity in Brazilians’ daily lives.
Flavio, the 45-year-old son of former president Jair Bolsonaro who hopes to return his father’s right-wing movement to power, led Lula, 80, who is seeking a fourth term, following a campaign dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling.
A candidate must pass 50% in order to win outright in the first round.
The two leading candidates were expected to head into a second round vote, Brazilian pollster Datafolha said. Surveys have shown Lula and Flavio polling roughly even in an Oct 25 run-off.
Early results showed southern states that lean to Bolsonaro reporting faster, while votes from Lula’s north-east stronghold are tallied more slowly.
Analysts told Reuters they believed Flavio was receiving “protest votes” of people voting against Lula rather than for the right-wing senator – votes they had been expected to save until a second round.
A victory for the senator would extend a wave of wins across Latin America by right-wing candidates aligned with US President Donald Trump, while Lula’s reelection could create a headache for Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.
Despite growing worries over Brazil’s public finances and sluggish economic growth, the campaign offered meagre policy debate, as both leading candidates skipped the major TV debates.
Undecided voters
While polls right up until Oct 3 showed Lula would likely lead the first round but not avoid a runoff, Flavio told journalists in Rio de Janeiro he was confident he could win the presidency in the first round, citing voters’ frustration with his chief opponent.
Flavio was counting on “a protest vote from people who would otherwise vote for another candidate but are opposed to Lula”, he said. “I hope it’s enough to secure a victory in the first round.”
Thaise Lima, a 41-year-old lawyer on her way to vote in Sao Paulo, said her main goal was to get Lula’s Workers’ Party out of office.
“I don’t think Flavio is the best candidate, but I might decide to vote for him in the next few minutes,” she said, adding that she wished psychiatrist and author Augusto Cury were a more viable candidate.
Fernando Tempel, 49, a management consultant, told Reuters he was voting for Flavio despite initially planning to vote for Romeu Zema, the former governor of Minas Gerais state.
Outside interference
On the other hand, Lula’s allies have warned that the Trump administration might refuse to recognise election results if he wins, pointing to an aborted effort to send US officials to Brazil.
“What is at stake is the future of Brazil,” Lula said after voting in Sao Bernardo do Campo, in Sao Paulo state.
Trump has not formally endorsed a candidate, though he hosted Senator Flavio Bolsonaro at the White House and praised him publicly.
“I’m a little worried about everything that’s been happening recently, including internationally. I feel this election has had a lot of outside influence, more than in previous elections,” said Cristiano, 34, a doctor in Brasilia who voted for Lula and preferred to withhold his surname.
“We are confident in our President Lula, who will fight for national sovereignty,” said Pedro Palacio, 45, who was voting in Brasilia alongside his wife, Andreia, and their two sons and two dogs, all of whom wore outfits supporting the president.
As at the afternoon of Oct 4, the election was proceeding normally, Brazil’s electoral court chief Kassio Nunes Marques said in a press conference.
“Teams monitoring international risks have not identified any risks whatsoever,” he said.
Reuters reported on Sept 30 that Brazilian intelligence officials briefed a French and German delegation on alleged US and Russian interference before the election. The US has rejected claims of interference in Brazil’s affairs.
Economic headwinds
Despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over voters grappling with high living costs, heavy household debt and the threat of street crime and more pervasive gang activity.
Flavio Bolsonaro has sought to capitalise on cost-of-living concerns, while Lula has moved to ban online gambling and, as the race tightened, expanded welfare and proposed fresh debt relief for families.
Rising spending and public debt above 82% of gross domestic product have stoked fiscal concerns that Brazil’s next president will need to address. The government lowered its economic growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 to just 2.0% and 2.3% respectively.
“I voted for Brazil to start growing again,” said Marciano de Souza e Silva, a 52-year-old public servant in Brasilia and former Lula voter who moved right, voting for Jair Bolsonaro in 2018 and 2022 and Flavio on Oct 4.
“The best social programme is one that encourages people to start businesses, to actually produce real wealth,” he said.
Scandal-plagued campaigns
Overshadowing the policy debate, a scandal surrounding the now-defunct Banco Master has engulfed much of Brazil’s political class and renewed public anger over corruption.
Daniel Vorcaro, who ran the bank, was arrested earlier in 2026 and accused of a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme.
The investigation has probed the banker’s ties to figures from Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes to Flavio Bolsonaro, who is being investigated for money laundering tied to the case by the federal police.
The candidate has denied any wrongdoing, although he confirmed raising millions of dollars from Vorcaro to make a movie about his father.
The banker’s connections to Moraes, widely perceived as a Lula ally, plunged the court into crisis a month before the vote, creating fresh problems for the President.
Moraes has said the case against him is politically motivated for his role in the conviction of the elder Bolsonaro.
On Oct 4, voters will also elect all 513 lower house members and two-thirds of the Senate, where some lawmakers have pushed to impeach Moraes.
Congress has gained greater influence in Brazilian politics since the impeachment of former president Dilma Rousseff, a Lula ally, in 2016, raising the stakes of those legislative races. REUTERS
