Israel lashes out as UK’s Green Party formally defines Zionism as ‘racism’
Israel’s president declared that the ‘antisemitic lie’ deliberately endangers Jews and Israelis.
Israel has reacted with anger after the United Kingdom’s Green Party voted to define Zionism as a form of racism.
Israel, as well as British Jewish groups, lashed out on Sunday following the vote by the small political party. The Israeli government declared that it now views the left-leaning Greens as giving “legitimacy to terrorism”.
The Green Party, which received 6 percent of the vote in the UK’s national elections in 2024, said it regarded Zionism as “an ethnonationalist political project” and repeated its call for Britain’s Labour government to end all arms trade with Israel.
In a swift response, Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the policy went “far beyond the boundaries of legitimate political debate” and called on other British political parties to condemn the resolution.
“The Greens have adopted not only the green of Hamas, but also its ideology: the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle,” the ministry wrote on social media.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog labelled the move “a disgrace and a shame”. Writing on social media, he said: “Those who claim the antisemitic lie that ‘Zionism is racism’ deliberately endanger Jews and Israelis everywhere.”
Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid said it is “not Zionism that’s racism, it is the Green Party”.
The Movement for Progressive Judaism, a British group, said: “The Green Party has made antisemitism party policy and become a racist party”.
It added that the support of some Jews for the motion did not mean it would not be used to discriminate against others.
During the vote, the Green Party also reaffirmed its “commitment to Palestinian liberation, the right of return, Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS), and a full arms embargo against Israel”.
It also reiterated support for “the establishment of a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine”, the party said in a statement.
The motion was backed by a majority of 1,022 to 813. Party leader Zack Polanski, who is running for Parliament in former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s London constituency, did not vote.
In an interview with UK media outlet Sky News, the Greens’ co-deputy leader Mothin Ali said that the heavy casualty toll during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and its ongoing attacks were the context for the vote.
The Green Party has five sitting members in the UK’s 650-seat parliament.
Following the passage of the resolution, Polanski and other Green Party members said in a joint statement they would “continue to stand in opposition to genocide, ethnic cleansing, apartheid and the illegal occupation” and “call out the heinous crimes of the Netanyahu government”.

====================================================================================================

Trump Is Promising Health Care Checks Before the Midterms. How Far Will They Go?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
20:38:29 UTC
05:38:29 KST

President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 2 that 20.8 million eligible Medicare enrollees will receive a one-time $90 premium rebate from the government.
It represents the latest payout that the President has made or promised Americans ahead of midterm elections, at a time when 66% of rural voters are worried about affording health care for themselves or their families, according to a KFF/AP poll released Sept. 23. The same survey found that 54% disapproved of Trump’s handling of health care.
The $90 payout is intended to help older Americans pay for their Medicare Part B premiums, which jumped by a record amount from 2025 to 2026.
“I am pleased to announce that my Administration will, immediately, begin sending ‘Checks’ of nearly $100 to over 20 MILLION wonderful Seniors to help pay for their Medicare Part B premiums, which we have already reduced by significant amounts,” the President wrote in a Truth Social post.
Trump said the payments would come from the roughly $2 billion Medicare Improvement Fund, which Congress established in 2008 to improve Original Medicare, the traditional program covering hospital and medical services. The fund’s authorized uses include adjusting payments to health care providers, but its mandate is broader than those payments alone.
The Administration is presenting the rebates as another way to improve the program by making coverage more affordable. The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) said in an FAQ that the payments would put money “in the hands of our Medicare beneficiaries.” It does not spell out the legal basis for using the fund to send checks directly to enrollees.
The CMS said most eligible beneficiaries will receive the $90 payment by direct deposit in early October, while others will receive a mailed check.
The Medicare rebates follow Trump’s Sept. 10 announcement of $500 refunds for some Affordable Care Act enrollees, who the Administration claims paid excessive fees under Biden.
Trump touted these refunds during a rally in Vandalia, Ohio, during which he claimed that his Administration had already sent out nearly a million $500 refund checks—with about 70,000 going to families in Ohio.
“You'll be getting them in the next couple of days,” he told the Ohio crowd. He also said, without evidence, that Democrats “kept millions and millions of dollars” from Americans.
The White House said that the refunds come from a surplus of ACA marketplace user fees collected under the Biden Administration, which it claimed exceeded the amount needed to operate the federal exchange.
For eligible ACA enrollees, the $500 refund could help cover health expenses, but it is a one-time payment—not a reduction in their ongoing insurance premiums.
The distinction between a one-time payment and recurring costs is crucial, says Lindsay Allen, a health economist and policy researcher at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine.
“Getting $90 once doesn't change anyone's Medicare costs,” Allen says.
According to the CMS, the standard monthly Medicare Part B premium rose from $185 in 2025 to $202.90 in 2026. That amounts to an additional $214.80 over a full year, meaning a $90 rebate would cover about 42% of the annual increase for eligible enrollees paying the standard premium—or less than half of a single month’s payment.
Why are older Americans feeling financial pressure?
According to the American Association of Retired Persons’ Financial Security Trends Survey, this year saw a growing number of Americans ages 50 and older feeling financially squeezed.
New census data this year also found that the poverty rate has increased the most for Americans 65 and older, growing from 9.1% in 2020 to 13.1% in 2025.
Those pressures also underpin expectations for next year’s cost-of-living adjustment from the Social Security Administration.
The Senior Citizens League projects a 3.5% increase for 2027, though the official adjustment will be announced Oct. 14. An increase of that size would raise average monthly benefits from $1,941.76 to $2,009.72. These annual adjustments are designed to help ensure that beneficiaries’ monthly payments help them keep pace with inflation, and an increase—potentially the largest cost-of-living adjustment since 2023—underscores the continuing pressure of rising prices on older Americans.
Some analysts note the timing of the payouts, with the midterms approaching and Republicans facing a potential backlash over Trump’s second term. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report says the party is on track to lose its House majority.
Public dissatisfaction extends across the economy and the war in Iran. An AP-NORC poll released Oct. 1 found that 65% of Americans attributed higher-than-usual prices to Trump’s policies, while 64% said he had gone too far in imposing tariffs. The same survey found that 69% believed the Iran war had not been worth fighting. About half (49%) of respondents said they were “extremely” or “very” concerned about being able to fill their tanks, up from 39% in July.
The payments also come as changes to federal health policy threaten to add to some beneficiaries’ costs, raising questions about how much lasting relief the rebates can provide.
How much will Trump’s Medicare rebate help?
Several Trump Administration policy decisions will soon begin affecting Medicare and other health care programs for senior adults.
The Administration announced in July that it would end the Medicare Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration program on Jan. 1, 2027—a year earlier than originally planned, which is something that advocate groups like Medicare Rights Center worry “will unnecessarily erode beneficiary choice, health, and financial security.”
“It is likely to make it harder for older adults and people with disabilities to access and afford needed care,” the group said in its response to the decision in July, urging the Administration to reconsider.
Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill was also signed into law in summer 2025 and had massive implications for older adults’ health care benefits—including delaying the implementation of a 2023 rule that would have streamlined enrolling in the Medicare Savings Programs, which help low-income beneficiaries pay for Medicare premiums and cost-sharing, until 2034.
Allen doubts that the refunds can offset the big issue at hand: “Medicare costs are increasing every year, but incomes for older adults aren’t.”
William Dow, a professor of health policy at University of California, Berkeley, reiterates Allen’s point, saying that the check “will have minimal effects in mitigating the overall increased cost of living among older adults.”
“This is particularly true because lower-income Medicare enrollees, for whom every dollar is most important, are not eligible for the checks,” Dow says. Beneficiaries whose premiums are already paid by Medicaid do not qualify, according to the White House.
“This makes sense given that the payment is a premium rebate and these beneficiaries don’t pay their own premiums. It does, however, mean that the payment leaves out the most financially vulnerable people in the program,” Allen says.
She points out that premiums are likely to go up again in 2027.
“People will get a small one-time check before the election, and then likely hear about next year's premium increase after it,” she says, calling it “notable” that people are likely to receive these checks within the next few weeks, just shortly before the midterm elections.
She believes that short-term relief might sway some voters—even though those people will continue to feel the premium increases “every month” after. According to health policy nonprofit KFF, the standard Part B premium has doubled in costs over the last decade and it is projected to increase even further in 2027.
“The payment is also limited relative to everyday expenses,” Allen says. “At current prices, $90 will get you about one tank of gas.”
Dow says that the move might eventually backfire, arguing that distributing roughly $1.9 billion in rebates will leave less money available for future improvements to Medicare.
“While perhaps good politics on the eve of an election, these checks are being paid from a fund intended by Congress to improve Medicare operations,” he says. “By diverting these funds, the long-term net effect will instead be to undermine Medicare operations.”

A second suspected member of the group, identified as a 24-year-old from Amsterdam, was arrested on Sept. 15 on suspicion of being a member of ShinyHunters, Dutch National Police and the FBI previously reported. planted roof extends garden over tato architects’ timber house in mibu, japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
20:35:47 UTC
05:35:47 KST

planted roof extends garden over tato architects’ timber house in mibu, japan
the house is clad in charred cedar, or yakisugi, beneath a corrugated galvanized steel roof.
house’s rotated timber volume responds to the existing backyard
House in Mibu is a two-story timber house for a couple and their three children, designed by Tato Architects in the backyard of the family’s parental home in Mibu, Tochigi Prefecture, Japan. The living floor is sunk about 500 millimeters into the ground, while its planted roof extends the garden over the house.
A large, weathered barn in the backyard is used for parking and as a workspace and is being repaired and retained. To keep the garden open, Tato Architects rotated the house at an angle following the path of cars that continue to pass through the site. This creates sheltered areas where the roof reaches toward the barn and gaps where it pulls away.
Tato connects the living room and garden through Split levels
The half-sunken living room is enclosed by earth and a low wooden roof while opening broadly toward the garden. From the lowered floor, the garden appears almost at eye level beyond the glass. The second floor forms a more enclosed counterpart, with small, nest-like rooms connected by two staircases and a raised loft that functions as both a desk and sleeping area.
The change in levels also creates visual connections between family members in the garden and those inside the living room. This extends Kobe-based studio Tato Architects’ use of split-level relationships from the interior to the relationship between the house and its surroundings.
- Charred cedar and a grass roof connect house and landscape
The roof acts as an ‘in-between’ element, drawing on Aldo van Eyck’s idea of a space where enclosure and openness coexist. From inside, it reads as a ceiling; from the garden, it becomes an extension of the ground, covered with grass and watered automatically from the site’s existing well.
The house is clad in charred cedar, or yakisugi, beneath a corrugated galvanized steel roof. Inside, lauan plywood is combined with troweled mortar floors. By sinking the living space and extending the garden across the roof, the design integrates the new house with the existing backyard and barn.
project info:
name: House in Mibu
architects: Tato Architects – Yo Shimada | @yo_shimada
design team: Yo Shimada, Nobuhiko Sato, Yohei Uchino
structural engineer: tmsd Takashi Manda
structural design team: Takashi Manda, Moeka Magari, Hideki Oda
location: Mibu, Japan
photographer: DAICI ANO

What's next?
Australia plays the first of three Tests against South Africa in Durban starting on Friday.
Marnus Labuschagne has responded to the debate over whether he merits a place in Australia's Test future by just doing what he likes doing best — scoring runs.
After a difficult year, the under-pressure 32-year-old chose the most timely moment to score his first century in any form of cricket for 11 months in Potchefstroom, just five days before Australia play their first Test in South Africa since the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.
Former skipper Ricky Ponting had joined the chorus that Labuschagne's place in Australia had become "untenable" after three years and 43 Tests without a Test ton, capped by three failures in the recent Bangladesh series.
Yet the South African-born batter looks sure to fill the number three spot once more in the first Test that starts in Durban on Friday after his swift century against a modest Cricket South Africa Invitation XI attack.
Labuschagne was largely untroubled as he raced to a 76-ball ton, going on to 111 from 89, decorated with 19 fours, before retiring to let his colleagues also get in some batting practice on the final day of the two-day warm-up match.
They enjoyed the opportunity too, with Steve Smith also retiring after making 61 while Alex Carey, fresh from his fine form in the third ODI, hit another half-century (57) as Pat Cummins' Australian side rattled up 6-368 in the drawn game.

Those four could all play on Friday.
Renshaw looked completely recovered from a knock to his right wrist, but may feel he missed out by being dismissed for 32 off his 50 balls, as may his fellow opener Travis Head (21 off 22 balls).
Beau Webster brushed off a few cobwebs with his 42 off 88 balls before he retired.
All eyes, though, were on Labuschagne, who even had a bit of local support as he took the crease at Senwes Park, a venue less than 50km from where he was born in Klerksdorp and the emotional scene of his first ODI hundred for Australia back in 2020.
Australia will see it as a useful workout after they gave 11 bowlers a run-out on Saturday when the Invitation XI declared on 7-318 after a century from former Proteas captain Neil Brand.
Meanwhile, South Africa paceman Anrich Nortje is in line for a remarkable return to first-class cricket after an absence of three-and-a-half years to help the injury-hit Proteas' attack.
With fitness doubts over key strike bowler Kagiso Rabada and three others, Nortje could return to Tests for the first time since March 2023 after a series of back and hip problems that left him concentrating on white-ball formats to reduce the strain on his body.
"I'll be very excited if I can put my Test cap on again. Growing up, it's the format you want to play," he said on Sunday, the day before he's expected to be named in South Africa's Test squad of 15.

Brazilians head to polls in pivotal election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
20:12:22 UTC
05:12:22 KST

Polls close in Brazil’s pivotal election
Polls have closed in Brazil’s hotly contested presidential election, which could reshape the country’s domestic and foreign policy.
The race is dominated by incumbent left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his right-wing challenger, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Lula is seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term in office. More than a dozen other candidates are also on the ballot.
Polls released on the eve of the election showed Lula and Bolsonaro neck and neck. Quaest put them at 46% and 45%, respectively, while Datafolha had Lula at 45% and Bolsonaro at 42%, with both surveys showing a statistical tie. If neither candidate wins more than half of votes, a runoff will be held on October 25. All other candidates are polling in the low single digits, but their endorsements could prove important in a second round.
Brazilians will also elect all 513 federal congress members, 54 of the country’s 81 senators, 27 governors and some regional legislatures.
Lula campaigned on his left-leaning Workers’ Party platform, promising continued welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution. He has framed the vote as a choice between “strengthening democracy and barbarism.”
Bolsonaro called for “change,” blaming Lula’s policies for high living costs and promising tougher security policies and tax cuts. The 45-year-old senator for Rio de Janeiro has also leaned heavily on the image of his father, known to supporters as “mito” – “the legend.”
Jair Bolsonaro, 71, was sentenced to 27 years behind bars over attempting to overturn the results of the 2022 presidential election, which he lost to Lula. He has denied wrongdoing. He spent several months in prison after breaking house arrest monitoring rules before being hospitalized in March 2026 over health issues and eventually transferred back to “temporary” house arrest that has since been extended.
Why does this vote matter?
Brazil is a founding member of BRICS and has played a prominent role in the group. Under Lula, Brasilia has pursued a policy focused on strengthening multipolarity and resisting Western pressure, particularly from Washington.
The Trump administration has placed renewed emphasis on US dominance in the Western Hemisphere under what it calls the “Donroe Doctrine,” a modern reinterpretation of the 19th-century hegemonic political strategy known as the Monroe Doctrine.
Washington has said it intends to strengthen US influence across the Americas while preventing rival powers, particularly China, from gaining strategic footholds there.
Opposing ‘colonization’
During his current term, Lula has repeatedly criticized the US over what he described as attempts to undermine multipolarity and impose its will on other nations.
Last year, India and Brazil stepped up talks on trade and investment after both countries were hit with 50% tariffs by the US. Lula also called for a coordinated BRICS response to Washington’s tariff policies, accusing Trump of attempts to “dismantle multilateralism” and promote “unilateralism, where he negotiates one-on-one with other countries.”
The Brazilian president also sharply condemned the US kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in early 2026. In March, he proposed boosting defense cooperation with South Africa to reduce reliance on foreign weapons, arguing that both nations could be vulnerable to “invasion.”
In late September, he openly accused Trump of seeking to “colonize” Brazil and gain control of its natural resources. “What Trump wants is to colonize Brazil, to take our wealth, steal our future and leave us behind,” he stated at the time.
‘Trump’s candidate’?
Flavio Bolsonaro, whom Lula has described as “Trump’s candidate,” has emphasized his affinity with the US president and repeatedly praised him, while denying receiving assistance from Washington for his campaign. He has insisted that Brazil should seek better deals with the US, including on rare earth minerals – a topic that has been repeatedly invoked by US President Donald Trump in his talks with various nations, including Ukraine and Russia.
The senator also promised a “flood of investments” from the US if he wins. “Brazil and the United States will once again have a high-level and long-term relationship, including the largest trade and investment agreement in our history!” Bolsonaro wrote in a post on X in June.
He has also vowed to “truly combat Brazilian terrorist organizations and restore sovereignty to more than 50 million Brazilians who live in areas dominated by them,” without specifying which groups he meant.
Bolsonaro has also reportedly pledged to join the US campaign against drug cartels. The American military has at times targeted boats supposedly belonging to traffickers, killing dozens of people.
Shadow of interference
Brazilian authorities have opened a probe into allegations that the US government funded activities aimed at interfering in the election and undermining the legitimacy of the country’s Supreme Federal Court, Agencia Brasil reported on Friday.
That followed a report by the Guardian earlier in the week, claiming that the White House had planned to allocate $1 million for a project titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil.”
US social media giant Meta also blocked the advertising account on Facebook used by Lula’s campaign, preventing it from running new ads just days before the first round. The account was restored later the same day, with Meta providing no immediate explanation.
In September, Lula cited a confidential assessment by the Brazilian Intelligence Agency, which warned that a risk of US interference in the vote was allegedly at a “critical level.”
Trump avoided openly endorsing any candidates ahead of the elections but stated he was following the vote “very closely.”
“Brazil is a very important country. The people of Brazil are fantastic. These are very important elections,” he said on Thursday.
Moscow has expressed its hope that the Sunday vote would be held “without any adverse external interference.” “We are open to… continuing our cooperation with our Brazilian partners across the entire agenda,” the head of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Latin American Department, Aleksandr Shetinin, told TASS.

Australian services sector activity slows
The Australian services sector has continued to expand, but at slower pace, according to the latest S&P Global Purchasing Managers' Index survey.
The Australian services PMI remained in expansionary territory (above 50 points) for the fourth consecutive month in September, but new orders slowed and costs rose.
"Softer growth of new orders, meanwhile, led to a resumption of job shedding as companies looked to limit costs. Business confidence also declined," S&P Global noted.
Prices in both inputs and outputs rose, a theme in line with recent ABS inflation surveys.
S&P Global economist Jingyi Pan said the services sector's expansion was in contrast to the deepening contraction in the manufacturing sector.
"Elevated price pressures in the service sector do not bode well for demand recovery as growth in services new business softened for the second month in a row," she said.
"Overall, the acceleration of output price inflation in the Australian private sector suggests that CPI could remain elevated in the coming months, which could keep the Australian central bank on a hawkish bias."

Key Event
Federal Court finds ANZ global markets team was "reckless and dangerous" (and often drunk)
The wrongful dismissal case between ANZ's former head of global balance sheet management Etienne Alexiou and the bank has been smouldering away in the Federal Court since late last year — finally, late on Friday there was a finding and it was damning for the ANZ.
It wasn't much better in reputational terms for Mr Alexiou but at least he won a degree of compensation, but well short of the $100 million he was seeking from the bank. It looks be closer to around $3.3 million in shares that ANZ tried to claw back on his way out the door.
The ANZ initially sacked Mr Alexiou in 2011 over what it claimed were breaches of its Code of Conduct and other policies, relating to an abundance of crude, vulgar, sexist and offensive messages he sent in Bloomberg chats and other messaging systems.
Veteran banking writer and editor of the Banking Day newsletter Ian Rogers says he has studied many complex and illuminating court judgements relating to the banking industry in Australia over the years and "this is the best one ever."
"(Mr) Alexiou … failed on the most material claims made against ANZ following a lengthy trial in the Federal Court late last year, but (he) has more than succeeded in humiliating ANZ and exposing the toxic, masculine and sexist culture that pervades financial markets, and not just ANZ," Mr Rogers said.
The judgement from Justice Nye Perran runs to 260 pages and 130,000 words had been delayed for two weeks to allow the parties to agree on any necessary redactions.
"While Justice Perran concluded that the credit of the plaintiff, Etienne Alexiou, was worse than dubious on many points, including numerous findings that Alexiou was a liar, it is to Alexiou's credit that he had the guts to agitate these matters in the public domain," Mr Rogers said.
As part of his unfair dismissal case Mr Alexiou said observed irregular trading at ANZ in the BBSW market on September 30, 2011, a day's trading that had been targeted by ASIC which then took ANZ to court in a separate case.
Justice Perran found that while Mr Alexiou had raised concerns about the day's trading here was no whistleblower disclosure made at that time that could have been the basis for an unfair dismissal claim.
However, Justice Perran's observations about the culture of ANZ's global markets division between 2011 and late 2013 were caustic.
"I find that senior management openly engaged in excessive consumption of alcohol, at times reckless and dangerous conduct [and] sexist behaviour which did not by any means stop short of sexual harassment. The attitude to women that is revealed is particularly problematic.
"Since the fish rots from the head, I find that this culture permeated down to the traders for whom senior management was responsible and that the workplace was affected by it to a non-trivial degree.
"The boorish attitude to women is reflected in many of the chat messages which emerged from the Code of Conduct Review.
"The culture of Global Markets was, indeed, one of toxic masculinity."
Justice Perran found Mr Alexiou was not involved in any manipulation of the BBSW rate.
"It is apparent that because of the harm done to his reputation Mr Alexiou had become persona non grata in the banking industry and was not going to obtain employment in it."
Justice Perran did find in favour of Mr Alexiou and against ANZ in relation to the withholding of deferred bonuses following his dismissal.
Mr Rogers said the judge ordered ANZ to calculate the compensation owed to Mr Alexiou on this element of his claim in line with analysis outlined in the judgement.

CSL signs deal to develop kidney and liver treatment
Australia's biotech heavyweight CSL has signed a major deal with a Swiss-based drug firm Alentis to co-develop and promote a treatment for a rare autoimmune kidney and liver disease.
The collaboration centres on the drug Lixudebartm, which is currently being evaluated in an ongoing phase two trial on patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN).
AAV is a rare autoimmune disease that causes inflammation and damage in small and medium blood vessels, potentially affecting multiple organs such as kidneys and liver.
The associated RPGN is characterised by a rapid loss of kidney function in a matter of days.
"We believe Lixudebart has the potential to become an important new therapeutic option to help improve kidney function and prevent progression to end-stage kidney disease," CSL head of R&D Bill Mezzanotte said.
CSL will make an initial payment to Alentis of $US355 million, with Alentis eligible to receive up to an additional $US1.2 billion in commercial milestone payments.
If commercialised, global profits will be shared 55% to CSL and 45% to Alentis.
"Our collaboration with Alentis reflects CSL's commitment to building a leading global nephrology franchise and our strategic intent to create high-value external partnerships," Dr Mezzanotte said.

Is the bond market rout overdone?
Capital Economics markets strategy team posted an interesting note asking the question "was the bond market rout" — that is, falling bond prices and rising interest rates — "overdone?"
"Perhaps" seems to be the answer, but that doesn't mean equity markets are about to be given a leg up if interest rates stop rising and edge lower.
Quite the opposite, according to Capital Economics (CE), which sees see the AI-driven equity rally as bubble waiting to burst.
CE noted that markets in the past quarter have been dominated by three stories that have been important all year: the waxing and waning of investors' enthusiasm for AI-exposed equities, big swings in commodity prices, and a sharp rise in bond yields.
"We think all three trends are approaching turning points," CE's Chief Markets Economist Jonas Goltermann wrote in a note.
"We suspect the AI-driven equity rally has become stretched and will turn into a rout at some point.
"We also expect commodity prices to fall back, with the caveat that energy prices will continue to depend heavily on developments in the Strait of Hormuz.
"And we think that government bonds will recover as tightening cycles underwhelm expectations."
On the bond rout, Mr Goltermann expects a reversal before too long.
"We expect the sell-off in DM (Developed Market) government bonds to unwind over the coming year or so as energy prices drop back and most central banks tighten policy by less than is now discounted, generating good returns from bonds.
"We think corporate bond spreads will widen markedly given our view that the AI stock market boom will turn to bust, especially given that huge AI-related bond issuance has increased the direct exposure of that asset class to AI."
CE's view is that the AI boom's day of reckoning may be sooner rather than later.
"While timing such crashes is hard, our forecasts envisage one happening next year. That allows for the possibility of a final 'blow-off' phase in which tech stocks, in particular, make further gains before heading sharply lower."
Key Event
OPEC+ agrees to keep November oil output targets steady
OPEC+ agreed to keep oil production targets steady for November at a meeting on Sunday, the producer group said, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments are unlikely until next year.
Seven core members of the group comprising the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia made the decision for November in a brief online meeting on Sunday.
The core members are Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman.
Gulf OPEC+ producers have been pumping well below output targets in the face of continuing export disruptions from the US-Israeli war on Iran, with exports fluctuating at 60% to 80% of normal levels in recent months.
"The OPEC+ group of seven kept their production ceilings unchanged, in line with market expectations. That said, despite rising flows through the Strait of Hormuz, their output levels remain well below quota," UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo said.
"Consequently, the oil market remains tight."
Oil prices had dropped on Friday after European leaders agreed to US President Donald Trump's request to release diesel reserves. Even so, Brent crude remains above $US100 a barrel, up from about $US73 before the Iran war started in late February.
The Iran war has also delayed the group's output capacity review — crucial to determine members' 2027 output quotas — because it has thrown estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, industry sources told Reuters last week.
OPEC+ has been raising output targets for much of 2026 after years of production cuts, but most of the increases stayed on paper because of the Middle East conflict.
The seven core OPEC+ members pumped 25 million barrels per day in August, up 630,000 bpd from July, yet still roughly 5 million bpd below prewar levels in February, OPEC data shows.

Calling AI 'other intelligence' better describes the advent of a new lifeform
Finance guru Alan Kohler says humanity has essentially created a new lifeform in the form of artificial intelligence (AI).
In his latest column, Alan wrote:
The hack of Medicare by an OpenAI agent, which followed other hacks by AI agents, illuminated the fact that these companies are not building a screwdriver that exists only as a tool for humans; they're building agents that turn passive AI into active autonomy.
And cyber security experts I've spoken to tell me we are rapidly approaching a situation where only autonomous AI agents will be able to defend against other autonomous AI agents.
The use of AI by agents — that is the buying of tokens from large language models (LLMs) — went past human usage by volume in February and has since increased 14-fold while human token buying has merely tripled, according to Open Router, an LLM marketplace.
Agents now use five times as much AI as humans and that gap is continuing to widen rapidly.

US tech rally

Protests by school students in France are continuing; on Monday, up to 500 schools will not hold classes
Kyiv • UNN
Up to 500 schools in France will be closed on Monday due to student protests. Students and education unions are preparing a new action for Tuesday.
Massive protests by high school students are continuing in France. They began back in September and have spread to many cities across the country. On Monday, classes will be suspended at between 400 and 500 schools, while on Tuesday students and education unions are preparing a new nationwide action, Le Monde reports, writes UNN.
Details
Minister of National Education Édouard Geffray said that approximately the same number of institutions had also not been operating on Friday. According to him, schools are being closed where it is impossible to guarantee safety, logistical problems have arisen, or staff have become direct targets of attacks.
The most difficult situation is expected in the Île-de-France region, where more than 160 schools will not operate on Monday—more than a third of the region's total.
The protests will continue
The movement began on September 17 in Île-de-France and later spread to other cities across the country. Students are demanding increased education funding, the filling of vacant teaching positions, repairs to dilapidated school buildings, changes to excessively packed schedules, and improvements to the university admissions system, Parcoursup.
According to the minister, 78 education-sector employees have been affected since the protests began, while 24 schools have been set on fire or damaged by vandals. In Île-de-France, the damage is already estimated at €7 million.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu instructed authorities to resume classes wherever the security situation permits, and to speed up the replacement of absent teachers and the filling of vacancies.
However, after talks with the government, protesters said they had not received sufficiently concrete solutions. For Tuesday, October 6, student organizations announced the "third act" of the protests, which education unions also plan to join with a strike.

In Latvia, they plan to form a pro-Ukrainian coalition after the elections and continue supporting Kyiv

Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs plans to remain in power and form a pro-Ukrainian coalition after his party, the "United List," won a convincing victory in the parliamentary elections. Kulbergs has already promised to continue supporting Ukraine and maintain a tough stance toward russia, Reuters reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
After 97% of the ballots were counted, the "United List" received 35.3% of the vote, giving the party 42 of the 100 seats in parliament. Reuters calls this the biggest victory in Latvia's parliamentary elections since the restoration of independence in 1991.
Kulbergs will still need partners to secure a parliamentary majority. According to political scientist Roberts Kīts, the "United List" could form a majority either with the "National Alliance," which takes a hard line toward the kremlin, or with the liberal "Progressives."
Kulbergs promises not to change course on Ukraine
After the election, the prime minister confirmed that Latvia would continue to support Ukraine and maintain a tough policy toward moscow.
Any economic ties with russia make us weaker. Yes, they may bring in additional money, but this is a weakness that russia can exploit
The populist "Latvia First" came second in the election with 13.1%, while the pro-russian "Sovereign Power" received 11.7%. The "National Alliance" garnered 8.9%. Although pro-russian forces increased their representation, according to Kīts's assessment, they remain politically isolated and are unlikely to have a significant influence on the policy of the new government.
During the election campaign, Kulbergs also promised to strengthen Latvia's counter-drone capabilities and maintain defense spending at 5% of GDP – one of the highest levels among NATO countries.

SIR strikes at heart of Constitution: Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
20:04:02 UTC
05:04:02 KST

File photo: Supreme Court of India Judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan (PTI Photo)
NEW DELHI: Launching a scathing attack on special intensive revision (SIR) that has resulted in large-scale deletion of names from voter lists across states, Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan on Sunday said any process disenfranchising millions of Indian citizens was intrinsically arbitrary as it struck at the heart of the Constitution.Discounting the reasons given by govt and EC to justify SIR, which was upheld in the case of the revision of rolls in West Bengal by SC with modifications, Justice Bhuyan said, "No amount of whataboutery can justify it. It strikes at the very heart of Constitution. I would go to the extent of saying that it is a negation of the constitutional order which we have adopted under the Constitution."
-
He was speaking at the moot court valedictory function at Nalsar, Hyderabad.Nalsar students, who had opposed CJI Surya Kant's participation in the convocation ceremony recently, came in for praise from Justice Bhuyan.Also read| Democracy in peril as voters illegally ousted: Former SC judge Justice Rohinton Fali Nariman"One last word about the brilliant students of Nalsar. You have shown to the country and to the world what a university student, that too a student of law, should be. You are brilliant, you are bold, and you are brave," he said.
Detaching right to vote from citizen is like taking soul out of body: Bhuyan
Justice Bhuyan said a citizen’s right to vote was central to the holding of free and fair elections.
“Except in the case of a dead voter, the name of a voter once enlisted in the electoral roll cannot be deleted without notice and hearing,” he added.The SC judge said the right to vote or be included in the voters’ list could not be detached from the persona of an Indian citizen.Also read: EC orders special drive to add genuine electors 'left out' during SIR“If it is done, it will be like taking out the soul from the body,” he added. Justice Bhuyan said the Indian Constitution does not provide for two classes of citizens: citizens with voting rights and citizens without voting rights. “Any process which leads to wholesale disenfranchisement of Indian citizens, making them citizens without voting rights, would be violative of Articles 326 and 14 of Constitution of India,” he said.“If any process results in disenfranchising millions and millions of Indian citizens, making them second class citizens in their own country in the sense of being citizens without voting rights, such a process is intrinsically arbitrary,” he added, his remarks coinciding with attacks on EC and govt over SIR by the opposition and others.
Justice Bhuyan said the right to vote was intertwined with India’s years of struggle against foreign rule. “It is a manifestation of our freedom achieved after so much struggle and sacrifice. Article 326 (universal adult franchise) cannot be tinkered with at all. No authority can do it, no court can condone it. No one is above Constitution,” he said.

Early neglect may disrupt how the brain fine-tunes itself during adolescence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
20:00:27 UTC
05:00:27 KST

Children exposed to severe psychosocial deprivation early in life showed lasting differences in how their brain activity developed during adolescence, according to a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. These altered brain dynamics were associated with poorer performance on a task requiring attention and self-control.
Adolescence is a major period of brain development. During these years, young people generally become faster and more accurate at controlling their attention, managing distractions, and responding to changing demands. Brain networks also become more stable and efficient, partly through a process called synaptic pruning, in which weaker connections between brain cells are eliminated and stronger ones are reinforced.
Computer models suggest that pruning helps brain activity settle back to its typical pattern more quickly after being knocked off course, which may support more efficient thinking. The researchers wanted to know whether severe deprivation early in life could interrupt this process.
Psychosocial deprivation can occur when children grow up without consistent caregiving, stimulation, and social interaction. Institutional settings may provide food and shelter but still fail to offer the stable, responsive relationships that are important for healthy development.
Led by Marta Andujar of the National Institute of Mental Health, the team used data from the Bucharest Early Intervention Project, a long-running randomized controlled trial in Romania. When the project began, young children living in state-run institutions, all younger than about two and a half, were randomly assigned either to move into high-quality foster care or to continue receiving the usual institutional care.
The analysis included 163 participants. Fifty-two had been randomly placed in foster care, and 51 had been randomly assigned to continue in institutional care, although Romanian child protection authorities later moved many children in that group to other placements. A comparison group of 60 children who had never lived in an institution was recruited from the community. Participants were assessed in follow-ups that began at ages 12, 16, and 21, with average ages at those visits of about 12.7, 16.9, and 23.3 years.
Participants completed a Flanker task, which involves responding to a central arrow while ignoring surrounding arrows that point either in the same direction or in the opposite direction. The task measures the ability to focus attention and override an automatic response.
While participants completed the task, the researchers recorded the brain’s electrical activity using electroencephalography (EEG). They then used a mathematical model to measure how quickly moment-to-moment deviations in each person’s brain activity, the ways a single trial differed from that person’s typical response, faded back toward the typical pattern. A higher value indicated that these deviations lingered longer before settling back.
Across all groups, these values decreased with age, suggesting that brain activity normally becomes quicker to stabilize during adolescence. However, participants who had experienced institutional care showed consistently higher values than those who had never been institutionalized. The foster care group did not differ from the group assigned to continued institutional care, meaning this brain measure showed no clear benefit of foster care. That contrasts with earlier findings in the same children, which showed some recovery after foster care in other brain signals, though the new study used a different and more fine-grained measure.
Behavioral results told a similar story. Never-institutionalized participants were more accurate overall than both groups with institutional histories, which did not differ from each other. On a measure combining speed and accuracy, foster care appeared to help somewhat, but the authors describe this recovery as modest and limited.
Participants whose brain activity took longer to settle also tended to perform less efficiently on the task, based on the combined measure of speed and accuracy. This link was negligible at age 12 but grew stronger at 16 and 21. Statistical analyses suggested that the neural differences accounted for part of the performance gap between participants with and without institutional histories.
“These findings demonstrate that early deprivation leaves a lasting imprint on the developmental trajectory of neural dynamics, affecting the maturation of brain systems underlying cognitive control,” the authors concluded.
The study has some limitations. Although children were randomly assigned to foster care or institutional care, the never-institutionalized comparison group was not randomized, so differences between that group and the others could partly reflect factors other than deprivation. The sample was also relatively small, and children’s placements and later life experiences varied after the trial began.
In addition, the link to synaptic pruning is an interpretation rather than a direct measurement, since EEG cannot measure connections between brain cells. The authors note that this explanation still needs to be tested directly, for example in animal studies that combine brain recordings with anatomical data.
The study, “Early psychosocial deprivation alters the refinement of neural dynamics across adolescence,” was authored by Marta Andujar, Lucrezia Liuzzi, Daniel S. Pine, Charles A. Nelson III, Charles H. Zeanah, Nathan A. Fox, and Bruno B. Averbeck.

Brazil: Polls close in tight race between Lula and Bolsonaro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
20:00:00 UTC
05:00:00 KST

Brazil election: Bolsonaro and Lula head to runoff
Published October 4, 2026last updated October 5, 2026
With votes being counted in Brazil following the presidential election on Sunday, populist Senator Flavio Bolsonaro was leading the race ahead of leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro seeks to continue the right-wing populist movement started by his father, Jair Bolsonaro, while Lula is seeking his fourth non-consecutive term.
With more than 99% of the ballots processed, Flavio Bolsonaro has received 47.2% of the vote, and Lula has 45%. Since neither candidate received enough votes to win outright on Sunday, the country's electoral court announced that Bolsonaro and Lula will face each other in a runoff on October 25.
Commenting on the outcome, Lula said it was "unexpected" as he was convinced he would "win in the first round."
"Tomorrow we start a new campaign," the 80-year-old said. "I am very good in the knockout stage."
In turn, Bolsonaro said he was "very happy with the real possibility that, three weeks from now, Brazil will give a definitive answer by choosing a modern government."
Bolsonaro is monitoring the vote count in Brasilia, the country's capital, while Lula is following it from Sao Paulo..
You can watch our livestream on the Brazil election results below.
Right gaining momentum in Brazil
Fabio de Sa e Silva, a professor of Brazilian studies at the University of Oklahoma, told DW that the right was currently on the rise in Brazil, making it difficult for Lula to change the course of the election.
"He still has a chance, based on the numbers, but the momentum is with the right," said de Sa e Silva.
"The big news tomorrow will be not that we have a runoff... but it is a takeover that happened in Congress by the far-right," the researcher said.
He added that it will be very hard for Lula to govern with Brazil's new Congress, even if he eventually secures another term.
Lula vows to 'defeat the far right'
Lula and Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday in Brazil's economic powerhouse state of Sao Paulo.
The 80-year-old Lula capped off his campaign with a tour through the city of Sao Paulo, vowing to "defeat the far right."
Organizers said some 150,000 of Lula's supporters turned up for the rally in Brazil's largest city.
Lula has campaigned on continuing his left-leaning Workers' Party platform, comprising welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution.
"The people will have to choose between strengthening the democratic regime and barbarism ... between progress and backwardness," he said as he cast his ballot on Sunday.
Bolsonaro calls for 'change'
Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has served as the Liberal Party's senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019. On Saturday, he led a motorcycle parade through Sao Paulo's countryside cities of Santa Barbara d'Oeste and Americana.
He also held up a portrait of his father, while the crowd shouted "mito" — a Portuguese word for "legend" that Jair Bolsonaro's supporters use to refer to him.
The right-wing Bolsonaro has campaigned on hardline security policies and tax cuts, emphasizing high cost of living under Lula, who he has slammed as "incompetent."
"Brazil needs change," the son of the former president said as he cast his vote. "Brazil cannot bear any more suffering, such as high taxes, so many women killed."
Brazil's 2022 election rematch
The elder Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence in prison for attempting a coup to overturn his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election. Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his father if elected.
Lula's team has cast the Bolsonaro movement as a threat to Brazil's sovereignty, pointing to Flavio and Jair's ties with US President Donald Trump, who last year slapped a 50% tariff on Brazilian imports in response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial. The US president called the case a "witch hunt."
The younger Bolsonaro has said in interviews he is "more moderate" than his father, who he has nevertheless said will remain "my compass, my point of reference."
Policies where both Bolsonaros are similar include relaxed gun control laws and skepticism of human-caused climate change.
Trump has not endorsed the senator, but has said he is watching the election "very closely."
What happens next?
Brazil finds itself politically divided, and campaigning has been bitter, with online operations from both sides seizing on every gaffe, accusation and rumor, quickly producing slick videos or AI-generated images for social media.
In September, it was revealed Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father. He has denied any misconduct.
The latest polling for the first round of voting shows Lula at 46% and Bolsonaro at 45%, according to the Brazilian data intelligence and public opinion research firm Quaest cited by Reuters news agency.
In the case of a run-off, the Quaest poll shows Lula at 42% and Bolsonaro at 44%.
In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by only 1.8 percentage points.
Along with voting for president, Brazil's 160 million registered voters are also choosing other lawmakers, governors, and some senators.

WikiLeaks at 20: The leaks that shook the world (VIDEOS)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
19:57:47 UTC
04:57:47 KST

WikiLeaks at 20: The leaks that shook the world (VIDEOS)
Sunday marks 20 years since Australian journalist and activist Julian Assange founded WikiLeaks, the whistleblowing platform that would publish some of the most consequential leaks of the internet age, exposing classified US war records, CIA hacking tools, mass surveillance and other closely guarded government secrets.
Registered in 2006, the website provided a secure and anonymous channel for whistleblowers to submit material for publication. Its early releases included operating procedures for the US detention camp at Guantanamo Bay, banking and corporate secrets, and internal documents from the Church of Scientology.
However, it was the scoops published in 2010 that made WikiLeaks a global phenomenon. That year, the website released “Collateral Murder,” raw classified US footage of a 2007 Apache helicopter attack in Baghdad which killed over a dozen people, including two Reuters news staff. WikiLeaks later published more than 91,000 documents from the Washington-led war in Afghanistan and some 391,000 reports from the US invasion of Iraq.
In 2012, Assange hosted ‘The World Tomorrow’ on RT. The 12-episode program covered a number of hotly debated topics and featured guests including Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah, former Guantanamo Bay inmate Moazzam Begg, and Imran Khan – who would later become Pakistan’s Prime Minister.
Later that year, Assange sought refuge in the Ecuadorian Embassy in London after losing a legal battle against extradition to Sweden over a sexual assault investigation that was later discontinued. He jumped bail, was granted asylum by Ecuador, and remained in the embassy for nearly seven years.
Major disclosures continued, including leaks exposing surveillance of US allies by the National Security Agency (NSA). Documents released in 2015 indicated that the NSA had spied on French presidents Jacques Chirac, Nicolas Sarkozy, and Francois Hollande, leading to a diplomatic row. In 2017, WikiLeaks’ Vault 7 releases exposed an arsenal of CIA hacking capabilities, including techniques aimed at smartphones and internet-connected TVs.
The following year, US plans to seek Assange’s extradition and prosecution became public. In 2019, Ecuador revoked Assange’s asylum and he was arrested by the British authorities and sent to the high-security Belmarsh prison. That year, Washington charged the journalist under the Espionage Act over WikiLeaks’ acquisition and publication of classified material. In 2024, after more than five years in prison, Assange agreed to take a plea deal with the US under which he was sentenced to time already served and returned to Australia.
Assange has since argued that his prosecution set a dangerous precedent for press freedom, telling the Council of Europe that he was freed after having “pleaded guilty to journalism.”

BELGRADE, October 4. /TASS/. Milorad Dodik, leader of the ruling Alliance of Independent Social Democrats in Republika Srpska (one of the two constituent entities of Bosnia and Herzegovina), has announced the victory of his political force at Sunday’s elections and thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for his support ahead of the voting.
"I announce our victory at all levels. Thank you all. We thank everyone who supported us," he told a news conference, adding that his party and its coalition partners will get two thirds of seats in the new parliament of the Republika Srpska.
"I want to thank our friends who contributed to this victory. I also thank [Russian] President Vladimir Putin who received us before the elections," he stressed.
Earlier, the Central Election Commission of Bosnia and Herzegovina said that the party’s candidates, Savo Minic and Zeljka Cvijanovic, are winning the elections of the Republika Srpska’s president and the entity’s member of the Presidency (Presidium) of Bosnia and Herzegovina, respectively.
Under the constitution envisaged by the General Framework Agreement for Peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina (Dayton Agreement) of 1995, Bosnia and Herzegovina is comprised of two entities, namely the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (around 51% of the territory) and the Republic of Srpska (around 49%), as well as the Brcko District. The three key ethno-religious groups, i.e. Bosniaks (Slavs professing Islam), Serbs (Orthodox Christians), and Croats (Catholics), are proportionally represented in the state governance system.

The flydubai attack was a failure before it was a plot - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
19:50:50 UTC
04:50:50 KST

Officials in Oman have said the flydubai co-pilot was taken off flying duties there over concerns about extremism.
Australian intelligence kept a file on him from his student years, when he allegedly visited radical mosques and extremist websites, The Financial Times reported.
Royal Air Maroc, the national airline of Morocco, trained him for three months in 2025 and then declined to hire him. They won’t say why. None of it kept him out of the cockpit. Whatever investigators eventually find about any connections with Tehran, that is the part they have to explain.
Political motive to link the attack as backed by a state
It is easy to see why some governments would rather talk about Iran. A state sponsor makes the threat bigger and the diplomacy more serious, and it puts off indefinitely any discussion of who failed to read what.
It wouldn’t come free. A proven Iranian role would force the Emiratis into a confrontation with a neighbor they have worked hard to manage, and it would put pressure on Jerusalem to respond. But it would also move the conversation away from the hiring files.
The incentive is strongest in Jerusalem. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been warning about Tehran’s reach for most of his career, and a trail leading there would vindicate him.
He would have allies to rally and a response to discuss. Explaining which Israeli agency was supposed to have checked the crew, a question Israeli officials are now arguing about among themselves, offers none of that.
What is on the record is thin. A possible Iranian connection is being examined, among other hypotheses, a senior Emirati source familiar with the matter told The Jerusalem Post.
There is no publicly established evidence tying Tehran to the attack, and Iran denies any role. US President Donald Trump has raised the possibility. Netanyahu said it is too early to say.
The working assessment was still that the attacker acted on his own, an Israeli official told the Post on October 1.
Three governments, one unfinished investigation, and they don’t agree.
The suspect’s reported exposure to al-Qaeda ideology cuts both ways. Sunni jihadists and Iran’s Shi’ite regime have been at odds for decades and have cooperated when it suited them.
The US State Department said senior al-Qaeda figure Saif al-Adl is based in Iran. The 9/11 Commission documented Iranian help with al-Qaeda transit, although it found no evidence that Iran or Hezbollah knew about the plot.
The oddest chapter came in August 2020, when al-Qaeda’s deputy leader, Abu Muhammad al-Masri, was shot dead in his car in Tehran, along with his daughter Miriam, the widow of Hamza bin Laden, Osama bin Laden’s son.
According to The New York Times, he had been living freely in an upscale part of the city for years, and Israeli operatives killed him at Washington’s request. Iranian state media first reported the dead man as a Lebanese history teacher. Tehran said the Times story was invented.
So, the history makes the question legitimate, and that is about all it does. Whether this pilot had anything to do with Iran depends on evidence about this pilot.
Establishing a connection is useful to politicians
Whoever eventually announces a “connection” should be made to say what they mean. Contact with somebody linked to Iran is one thing. Assistance is another, and operational direction is something else again, with very different consequences for policy. Until somebody defines the term, it is mostly useful to politicians.
Netanyahu’s statement that Israel had no specific warning may well be accurate. It also answers a question nobody was asking.
Intelligence that names a plot is one kind of information. Doubt about whether a particular man should be flying passengers is a different kind, and that is what a vetting system exists to catch.
You don’t need a date or a target to ground a pilot. What Israelis are entitled to know is whether anyone in the chain, here or abroad, knew enough about him to stop him, and what they did with it.
The chronology that is emerging suggests the information never traveled. Emirati sources said what Oman and Australia knew reached them only after the attack.
Someone in Oman wrote down the concerns about this man. Australia compiled a file. Royal Air Maroc had its reasons for turning him down sitting in a drawer somewhere. Investigators should establish what each contained, who was entitled to see it, and whether anyone ever asked.
Israel’s own warning about the system predates all of this. A 2024 State Comptroller’s Report called for a review of aviation security responsibilities, including for incoming foreign flights, and urged the political leadership to formulate a comprehensive policy.
Netanyahu and Transportation Minister Miri Regev should be asked, specifically, what was done with that recommendation. If an Iranian handler turns up, the question only gets more pointed.
The UAE has handled this better than most of the governments now pointing fingers. Its prosecutor general called it an attempted terrorist attack in public, and Emirati authorities are running the inquiry.
In this region, that is unusual. Flydubai’s own hiring checks are still under scrutiny, as they should be, alongside the complaints about what other countries allegedly held back.
Saudi Arabia took in the aircraft and looked after the passengers, and it reportedly refused to let Israeli military planes come to collect them. Cooperation was negotiated one decision at a time, in public, during an emergency.
It would be worth knowing how those same channels worked in the months before, when nobody was watching, and a shared file might have changed the outcome.
If Iran was involved, the uncomfortable conclusion is that a hostile service walked through gaps several institutions had plenty of time to close. State sponsorship makes an operation more capable. It doesn’t tell you which safeguards were beaten and which were never there to begin with.
I would want an inquiry that follows the attacker’s communications and his paperwork with the same seriousness. Whatever evidence of outside direction exists belongs in the same file as the employment records, the requests for information, the replies, and the security clearances. Read together, they will show who had enough to act, even if nobody had the whole picture.
If the evidence leads to Tehran, the response should be serious. The governments whose job it was to protect those passengers will still owe them an explanation of how this became possible.
An Iranian connection would widen the investigation – and the list of people who owe answers along with it.

Hapoel Tel Aviv sweeps EuroLeague basketball doubleheader, Maccabi Tel Aviv still winless
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
19:50:41 UTC
04:50:41 KST

Hapoel Tel Aviv swept its EuroLeague double week, while Maccabi Tel Aviv’s record dropped to a disappointing 0-3 on the season as it will face Valencia and Milano, respectively, later this week.
Hapoel Tel Aviv downed Real Madrid 102-98 as Elijah Bryant picked up both MVPs of the week and scored with ease in the final frame to break a 75-75 deadlock and notch the win to sweep the EuroLeague double and improve to 2-1.
Dimitrios Itoudis’s team jumped out to a 63-43 lead at the half with Bruno Caboclo, Zach LeDay and Vasilije Micic leading the way, but Theo Maledon, Timothe Luwawu-Cabarrot and Walter Tavares all scored to knot the game up by the end of the third quarter. However, Bryant put the Reds on his back in the fourth quarter to lead his side to the victory.
Bryant scored 22 points, 13 rebounds, and seven assists; Micic added 22 points, while LeDay and Caboclo both scored 15 points in the win. Maledon scored 26 points, Cabarrot put in 21 points, and Tavares scored 14 points in the loss.
Itoudis talked about the win.
“It looks like we beat Real Madrid in the same game twice. We started the game well both offensively and defensively, and we wanted to not get outscored in transition as they have the tools to run. In the second half, and specifically in the third quarter, we lost the entire lead. We talked about this being a character game and not cracking at the timeout. We analyzed what was going wrong and changed the approach of the attack. This win was important and the way it happened.”
Real Madrid coach reflects on loss to Hapoel Tel Aviv
Real Madrid coach Pedro Martinez discussed the defeat from his side’s perspective.
“Two different halves in this game. The first half we saw bad defense and a slow offense with no rhythm. It was a very bad half. But in the second half, with aggressiveness, we were able to come back and even take the lead, but we had to rotate, and that didn’t work. Hapoel deserved to win the game.”
Meanwhile, Maccabi Tel Aviv fell to Panathinaikos 90-67 to drop to 0-3 on the season and now finds itself at the bottom of the standings.
Oded Katash’s team was without injured big man Daniel Theis, as well as captain John DiBartolomeo, who was attending his brother’s wedding. The yellow-and-blue got off to a brutal start and trailed 25-10 by the end of the first quarter as the Greeks cruised from that point to take the win at the OAKA Arena in Athens.
Roman Sorkin scored 13 points, Keaton Wallace added nine points, and Oshae Brissett scored eight points in the loss, while Gershon Yabusele led the way for Pana with 17 points. Nigel Hayes-Davis scored 13 points, while Sylvain Francisco and Lefteris Mantzoukas scored 11 points each.
Katash lamented yet another defeat.
“It is the third game that we’re losing our structure way too early and the way we want to play. It’s not about the result. We can miss shots, we can lose games. We’re playing against a really good quality team in a tough gym. What worries me is that too early we started having bad body language and a lot of turnovers. We have to learn from this.”
Panathinaikos coach Zeljko Obradovic spoke about the win.
“We played good and we played all 40 minutes. There were some moments when the players relaxed, which is normal, but they like to play. They played like a team, and this is very positive. I hope we continue the same way.”
Iffe Lundberg reflects on Maccabi Tel Aviv’s defeat
Maccabi’s Iffe Lundberg also talked about the defeat.
“I think we play with a lack of energy and lack of intensity along with a lack of execution. I think in all three games, we’ve had a pretty good game plan, but it’s up to us to go out there and execute it. Lucky for us, it’s still early in the season, so there’s no reason to panic. But, obviously, understanding the magnitude of the EuroLeague and the importance of each game. We have to fix it, of course. We still believe, obviously, like I said, because it’s early. So, we just have to lock in, look within and then go out there and do our job.”

Texas wins case forcing Galveston school district to display Ten Commandments posters in classrooms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
19:50:33 UTC
04:50:33 KST

A Texas judge has ordered a Gulf Coast school district to display posters of the Ten Commandments in all classrooms, marking a victory for the state in a long series of legal battles over religious freedom in public education.
District Judge Jeth Jones ruled on Thursday that the Galveston Independent School District must comply within 10 days, while also scheduling a non-jury trial to resolve the case next June.
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican, had sued the school district last November after the school board voted against exhibiting the Protestant version of the Ten Commandments. Paxton’s petition argued that the board violated a June 2025 state law, SB10, which required the “conspicuous” display of Ten Commandments posters in all public school classrooms.
Two rabbis challenging the Texas law at the US Supreme Court
That law is at the center of multiple lawsuits across the state, including one effort led by two rabbis seeking to bring a case to the US Supreme Court. Along with non-Jewish clergy and parents, they are arguing that the mandatory inclusion of these texts in classrooms is unconstitutional and infringes upon religious freedom. Their case is separate from the Galveston case.
“These are religious documents,” Mara Nathan, the lead petitioner and senior rabbi at Temple Beth-El in San Antonio, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.
“They do not belong in a secular public school space,” she continued. “If people want to be in a school space where religious instruction is part of that, then they can choose to send their kids to parochial school.”
In their case, Nathan and more than two dozen parties are asking the US Supreme Court to weigh in on the controversial Ten Commandments law. Their petition, filed in August, asks the court to protect the religious freedom of students by ensuring that families, rather than politicians, are able to determine what role religion plays in their children’s lives.
Joining Nathan in the case is Joshua Fixler, associate rabbi at Congregation Emanu El in Houston, as well as Jewish, Christian, Hindu, Baha’i, Unitarian Universalist and nonreligious families statewide. The defendants include a long list of school districts, such as the Alamo Heights Independent School District and the Houston Independent School District, where Nathan and Fixler send their children, respectively.
Their decision to petition the Supreme Court is the culmination of a lengthy legal process that began after Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, signed the SB10 bill into law in June 2025.
'Uncomfortable and outraged'
“When I heard about this law, I was really uncomfortable and outraged,” Nathan said. “When I found out there was an opportunity to speak up and be part of litigation to oppose it, I was like, ‘Please sign me up.’”
Fixler echoed these sentiments, with hopes of protecting children from “seeing this Protestant Christian text every day in every classroom, and having it shape their understanding of what religious freedom should look like in America.”
The Jewish and Protestant versions of the commandments differ in wording, order, and emphasis, with the Jewish commandments beginning with God’s declaration that he brought the Israelites out of Egypt.
Nathan, Fixler and the other plaintiffs filed a federal lawsuit in July 2025 seeking to block the display at their children’s schools. The next month, they secured a brief victory in district court when they won a preliminary injunction to block the displays.
Last October, Paxton issued a formal legal advisory to all Texas school districts, reiterating their obligation to exhibit the display. He warned that Texas would vigorously enforce the law, while acknowledging temporary exceptions for 11 school districts that were party to the litigation at the time.
The attorney general described the commandments as “a cornerstone of America’s moral and legal heritage,” stressing a need for “these timeless principles” in schools “now more than ever.”
Appellate court ruled the law didn't violate the First Amendment
The pendulum swung in Paxton’s favor in April 2026, when the US Court of Appeals for the 5th District reversed the district court’s ruling. The judges, who sit on one of the most conservative federal appellate courts nationwide, determined that the law does not violate the First Amendment’s free exercise clause, which prohibits government from regulating religious beliefs.
They maintained that the SB 10 law “looks nothing like a historical religious establishment,” a bar that the judges said was set in a 2022 lawsuit. The Texas legislation, they wrote in the ruling, doesn’t “tell churches or synagogues or mosques what to believe or how to worship or whom to employ as priests, rabbis, or imams.”
“It punishes no one who rejects the Ten Commandments, no matter the reason,” they added.
Unwilling to concede defeat, Nathan and her colleagues in August asked the high court to review the case. Whether the Supreme Court will decide to take on the case is still uncertain, as four of its nine justices must agree to do so.
Fixler noted that the law requires posters of the commandments to be big enough to be read anywhere in the classroom and contain no other texts or context.
“I’m hearing from parents all over the state that their kids know that the state is elevating literally one religious tradition over all others,” he said, relating that although he prepared his kids for the displays, they “expressed a lot of anxiety” about needing “to see these words posted on the wall of their classroom.”
Fixler also expressed concern that the prominence of these posters could lead kids to ask “questions that some teachers aren’t going to want to answer,” such as, “What is adultery, and what does it mean to covet your neighbor’s wife?”
The families are represented by the American Civil Liberties Union of Texas, the national ACLU, Americans United for Separation of Church and State, and the Freedom From Religion Foundation, with pro bono counsel from the Simpson Thacher & Bartlett law firm.
In their Supreme Court petition, the families accused the appeals court of defying a 1980 Supreme Court decision, Stone v. Graham, which they said “struck down a nearly identical Kentucky statute almost 50 years ago.” While the Texas appellate court had claimed that precedents set in a later case had superseded the Stone ruling, the families argued that the core principles of the Stone judgment were untouched by that later suit.
The forced display of the Protestant Ten Commandments in public school classrooms is not unique to Texas, although the Lone Star State case has emerged as one of the most prominent battlefields for the issue in recent months.
Other states that have required public schools to exhibit the Ten Commandments include Arkansas, Louisiana and Alabama, while Tennessee and North Dakota allow optional displays.
'America is a Christian nation'
A group of complainants in Arkansas, including one Jewish family, is urging the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit to block school districts from implementing a state law on the subject. Meanwhile, in Tennessee, the ACLU and other groups have sent letters seeking records relating to school district plans to begin displaying the Ten Commandments.
In Galveston, the school board president told local media on Thursday that the school district would comply with the order, as demanded in the November lawsuit. Alongside the filing, Paxton had declared that “there is no valid legal basis” to prevent schools from complying with the law, claiming that their refusal was rooted in “the misconception that a ‘separation of church and state’ phrase appears in the Constitution.”
“It does not,” Paxton stated.
While Galveston is not a party to Fixler and Nathan’s Supreme Court petition, the plaintiffs cited the year-long saga as evidence. The situation in Galveston, the petition argues, demonstrates that “injuries” to families who oppose the Ten Commandments displays “are actual or imminent,” a requirement to hear a case in federal courts.
The attorney general accused Galveston’s school board of voting “to flout SB 10” in its refusal “to display the Ten Commandments in accordance with State law.” At the time, he alleged that Galveston decided to “blatantly ignore the legislature,” while emphasizing that “America is a Christian nation.”
Notably, Fixler and Nathan’s Supreme Court petition flags the Galveston case in its appendix, even though the district is not a party to the case. The petition argues that the situation in Galveston shows “injuries” to families “are actual or imminent.”
“I hope that the Supreme Court will take our case and rule in our favor,” Nathan said, affirming that any decision made here could set a precedent for similar cases nationwide.
“It would be really exciting to be written into history in a positive way, as part of a movement to really protect our religious freedom and separation between public school spaces and the private religious lives of people,” she added.

Ukraine's deep strikes have wrecked over half of Russia's oil refining capacity, Defense Ministry says

Unknown Publisher
