Ukraine's deep strikes have wrecked over half of Russia's oil refining capacity, Defense Ministry says
Over 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity has been disabled by Ukrainian attacks, the Defense Ministry reported on Oct. 4.
Ukraine has systematically targeted Russia's oil and gas infrastructure in long-range strikes, dramatically increasing its campaign against oil refineries in the past two years. Kyiv considers refineries valid military targets, as they supply both fuel and funds to the Russian armed forces.
Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara reported on the consequences of Ukraine's strategy in an update on Oct. 4. Citing analysts from Ukraine's intelligence services, Defense Ministry, and General Staff, Khmara said that over 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity has been disabled.
"This is the result of carefully planned, systematic, and comprehensive actions aimed at crippling the Russian war machine and destroying its military-economic potential," Khmara said.
"Fifty-one percent of the damaged oil refining capacity is a significant blow to the enemy's economy, to its ability to wage aggression, and to supply its military formations."
The Defense Ministry listed recent attacks at Russia's Moscow, Yaroslavl, Kirishi, Perm, Ilsky, Saratov, and Syzran refineries in its report.
The ministry's assessment marks an increase from the 45% drop in Russian refining capacity reported by Ukraine's General Staff on Sept. 21.
It also follows a decree from Russian President Vladimir Putin, signed Sept. 28, restricting access to data on the country's oil refineries and energy exports amid Ukraine's escalating deep strikes.
Ukraine's long-range strike drones and missiles have proved capable of regularly reaching targets more than 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukrainian-controlled territory. The military reported a new record on Sept. 9, after a Fire Point FP-1 drone struck a Russian gas facility 3,200 kilometers (1,988 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The Defense Ministry reported on Oct. 4 that Ukraine tripled its production and procurement of long-range strike drones in 2026 — and that it hopes to keep growing.
"This is not the limit," the ministry said. "We will continue to scale up our long-range strike capabilities."

Five quakes rattle south Turkey, no injuries reported
ISTANBUL - Five shallow quakes rattled southern Turkey on Oct 4 with the tremors also felt in northern Syria, but caused no injuries or damage, the authorities on both sides said.
Three of them occurred during the early afternoon, with two more during the evening, Turkey’s AFAD disaster relief agency said on X, saying they caused “no adverse situation”.
The area is about 150km from the epicentre of two massive earthquakes in February 2023 that killed at least 53,000 people in Turkey and around 6,000 in Syria.
Four of them shook the Saimbeyli district in Adana province: a 4.8 magnitude quake at 2.19pm, one measuring 4.9 at 2.36pm, a third of 4.4 at 7pm and a fourth of 4.3 magnitude at 8.28pm, AFAD said.
There was also a 5.2 quake in the Sumbas district, about 80km further south, at 2.43pm.
In a statement on Telegram, Syria’s national earthquake centre said all five quakes had been felt in parts of northern Syria, without mentioning any injuries or damage.
Turkey is crisscrossed by several geological fault lines that have previously caused catastrophes in the country. AFP

France to shutter up to 500 schools as more student protests called

France to shutter up to 500 schools as more student protests called
French education minister cites safety concerns for closures as resumption of protests are called for by organisers.
France plans to fully or partially close up to 500 schools on Monday amid a series of student protests that have become increasingly violent.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced the precautionary measures on Sunday as part of a bid for a “partial, progressive return to lessons”. However, after a weekend lull, student protestors announced they plan to resume demonstrations – launched last month over complaints regarding class sizes, lack of teachers, and other complaints – early in the week.
Lessons will be “totally or partly suspended” in some “400-500” high schools as the security conditions “have not been fulfilled”, the minister said. He added that 24 schools had been “burned or ransacked” since the start of the protests.
Geffray said the closures were a security precaution. Protest organisers have called for a return to large-scale demonstrations on Tuesday, citing a lack of “concrete measures” from President Emmanuel Macron’s government.
At least 170 students and 78 educational personnel have been injured since the student demos first erupted in the Paris region in mid-September, according to Geffray.
The Ministry of National Education reported that at least 400 of the 3,700 high schools in France were closed on Friday, while 560 faced protests or disruptions.
The number of schools affected on Monday would be comparable to the figure from Friday, Geffray said.
Teachers and students first mobilised at a high school in a Paris suburb on 17 September over a lack of teaching staff, excessive school-day hours and other grievances. The protests have since spread nationwide, resulting in class strikes, blockades and demonstrations.
According to the interior minister, more than 5,000 people have been arrested in the last week; 85 percent of them minors.
Critics have criticised “disproportionate” police violence in response to the demonstrations. Rights group Amnesty International said the student protestors “must be listened to, not repressed”.
In an interview on French public radio, Geffray claimed far-left activists “infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves and engaged in extreme violence.”

Three Russian Strategic Aviation Officers Responsible for Missile Strikes on Ukraine Killed in Tu-95MS Crash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
19:37:22 UTC
04:37:22 KST

Three officers involved in missile strikes on Ukraine were among those killed in the crash of a Russian Tu-95MS strategic bomber in the Amur Region.
A photo of the crew members killed in the crash was published by Mikhail Piven, head of the Mazanovsky Municipal District in the Amur Region.
They were Lt. Col. Fedor Pavlyukov and Majors Andrei Gerasimov and Andrei Lobanov.
The crash occurred on September 29, 2026, during a training flight in the Amur Region, near the village of Krasnoyarovo.
According to an official statement by the Russian Defense Ministry, six crew members were killed and another was injured and evacuated to a medical facility.
According to OSINT researcher Duke BG, photographs of eight people killed in the crash are arranged according to their positions within the crew, while the last two were passengers.
One of those killed was Lt. Col. Fedor Pavlyukov. According to the Ukrainian Book of Executioners project, Pavlyukov served as deputy commander for flight training of the 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment. Previously, from August 2021 to April 2024, he commanded a Tu-95MS aviation squadron of the same regiment.
Pavlyukov was responsible for preparing flight crews to carry out combat missions and commanded a unit. Ukrainian researchers link him to the organization and execution of missile strikes against Ukraine.
The 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment is part of the 326th Heavy Bomber Aviation Division and operates Tu-95MS strategic bombers. The 182nd Regiment had about 16 Tu-95MS aircraft.
The second identified officer was Maj. Andrei Gerasimov. According to the Book of Executioners, he was commander of a Tu-95MS aviation squadron of the 121st Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment of the 22nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Division. Before that, from June 2022 to October 2024, he served as deputy squadron commander.
Gerasimov personally took part in combat sorties and may have been involved in organizing and carrying out cruise missile launches during mass strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The 121st Regiment is associated with Engels-2 air base in the Saratov Region, one of Russia’s key strategic aviation airfields. On August 28, long-range drones operated by the SSU’s Special Operations Center “A” hit a Russian Tu-95MS there.
Another person killed was Maj. Andrei Lobanov, deputy commander of a Tu-95MS aviation squadron of military unit 75715. According to 24 Kanal, on May 29, 2023, Lobanov carried out a combat sortie as the commander of a Tu-95MS, during which the crew launched six air-launched missiles in succession at critical infrastructure facilities in Ukraine.
The crash occurred amid a significant workload on Russia’s strategic bomber fleet. Following Ukrainian strikes on strategic aviation airfields, Russia began actively moving Tu-95MS aircraft between Engels-2 air base and Ukrainka in the Amur Region.
At Engels-2, the aircraft can undergo preparation and be armed with Kh-101 cruise missiles before combat sorties, while the remote Ukrainka air base is used, among other purposes, to disperse strategic aviation and reduce its vulnerability to Ukrainian attacks.
As a result, the bombers have to make lengthy flights between the Russian Far East and the European part of Russia. The total range of an individual combat sortie can exceed 12,000 kilometers, while its duration can approach 24 hours.
Such a workload accelerates wear on the aircraft, many of which were manufactured during the Soviet era, while also increasing the burden on flight crews and maintenance personnel.

Pro-Imran Khan mass rally launched after Pakistan government talks fail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
19:20:08 UTC
04:20:08 KST

Pro-Imran Khan mass rally launched after Pakistan government talks fail
Government warns of crackdown as supporters of jailed former prime set off from northwest Pakistan towards Islamabad.
Supporters of jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan have set off on a protest march from the country’s northwest after talks with the government to call off the demonstration failed.
More than 5,000 were reported to have begun the rally on Sunday. The march, planned by Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party, was originally scheduled for September 27 but was postponed until October 4 to allow talks between the government and the PTI leadership to take place.
However, two rounds of talks over the weekend failed to break the deadlock, and the PTI decided to carry out its plan, which is the latest attempt to pressure the government into releasing Khan, the country’s most popular political figure according to polls, who has been behind bars since August 2023 following a series of convictions that his party calls politically motivated.
All but one of the convictions against the former PM have since been suspended or overturned on appeal.
Videos posted on the PTI’s official social media showed supporters joining the march in different areas of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province, which is ruled by the party, and setting off in convoys.
Sohail Afridi, the region’s chief minister, had earlier posted on social media that the demonstration in support of Khan would go ahead.
He said the march will make its way to Khairabad, 80 kilometres (50 miles) west of Islamabad, by Thursday, where the plan for the “next phase” will be announced.
Government warns protesters
The government has been preparing for weeks for the arrival of PTI demonstrators in Islamabad. It has erected barriers using shipping containers to block main access routes to the capital.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi confirmed earlier on Sunday that the talks between the two sides had failed. He accused Afridi of “sabotaging” the negotiations, and added that the government would not allow the PTI to “create a disturbance”.
He also cited an Islamabad High Court order from September 14, ruling that no political party or its leadership has the “lawful right to occupy public roads, highways, interchanges, toll plazas and buildings in Islamabad”.
“If they violate the orders, whether they are workers or politicians, whether they are protesting within KP or outside KP, we will pursue them one by one. This time, we want to ensure that these repeated episodes of creating disturbance in Islamabad come to an end,” Naqvi said.
Concerns about the 73-year-old Khan’s health, in particular the condition of his right eye that has required months of specialist treatment, have prompted the PTI’s campaign for his release.
The party has also called for the release of Khan’s three sisters, whose arrests last month further heightened tensions.
James Dorsey, a fellow at the National University of Singapore, said Khan was “essentially a populist leader” with “a genuine popular movement that had broad popular support”.
That is behind the “determination by the government to prevent [the protesters] from entering Islamabad,” he told the AFP news agency.
Given Pakistan’s security concerns, particularly following its unresolved February 2026 conflict with Afghanistan, Islamabad wants to avoid escalation in the face of the protests, he added.
“It’s a problem for the government, but I don’t think it’s an existential threat,” he said.

Polls close in Bosnia-Herzegovina's divisive election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
19:15:00 UTC
04:15:00 KST

Nationalists top Bosnia-Herzegovina's divisive election
Published October 4, 2026last updated October 5, 2026
Bosnian officials reported a record-low turnout following the Sunday vote, with only 41.5% out of the country's 3.4 million voters taking part in the general election in Bosnia-Herzegovina.
Nationalist parties dominated races as citizens chose officials across multiple tiers of government; including members of the country's multiethnic, tripartite presidency.
With counting nearly concluded, Serb nationalist Zeljka Cvijanovic, Bosniak moderate leftist Denis Becirovic and Croat nationalist Darijana Filipovic have been announced as the winners of the presidential seats of their respective ethnicities.
Cvijanovic had been backed by the Republika Srpska's former secessionist leader Milorad Dodik, who was barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.
"I am declaring that we have won," Dodik told supporters in Banja Luka on Sunday night. He said his SNSD party had retained the Serb seat in the presidency and remained power in Republika Srpska.
With counting nearly over, Cvijanovic looked to have won with 55.6% of the vote.
Social Democrat Becirovic won the race for the Bosniak seat with 38.1% of the vote, while Croat Filipovic took 48.2% of the vote.
Nationalist and ethnic political division
Voters also chose lawmakers for the federal parliament and the heads of institutions for the country's two largely autonomous entities — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) and the Serb-run Republika Srpska (RS).
Currently, about 50% of Bosnia and Herzegovina's citizens are Muslim Bosniaks, 31% are Orthodox Serb and another 15% are Catholic Croat.
Between 1992 and 1995, more than two million people were displaced and nearly 100,000 killed in a civil war. Despite the country being peaceful for decades, ethnonationalist parties have kept divisions alive as a way to hold on to power. Many voters, however, say they want to move on from the war-era rhetoric.
The election comes at a time when the country is struggling with a number of challenges.
There's been an economic downturn, sluggish progress toward EU membership, and sustained political gridlock — with dominant ethnic parties from these entities repeatedly stalling decisions by the weak central government that binds them.
The election saw contests that pitted the Bosniak SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH against multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party.
Polls closed at 7 p.m. local time (1700 GMT), with preliminary results to be released later in the evening — though complex constitutional order and drawn out coalition talks mean that the true result of Sunday's election could remain unclear for months.
What is the system that governs Bosnia-Herzegovina?
The economic, administrative and political responsibilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina are divided between the multiethnic central government, the two semi-autonomous entities FBiH and RS, and the self-governing neutral Brcko district.
These entities are further split into several cantons and communities.
The complicated framework — divided along ethnic lines — was set up during the US-brokered 1995 Dayton Peace Accords, following the 1992-95 Bosnian war, itself a consequence of the breakup of Yugoslavia.
Milorad Dodik still powerful figure in Republika Srpska
In Republika Srpska, secessionist leader Milorad Dodik of the SNSD party remained the key figure of the election despite not being on the ballot.
Dodik, the former president of the Serb-majority entity, is barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.
Dodik-backed Savo Minic decisively won the Republika Srpska's presidency and RS increased its heft by taking 39% of the parliamentary tally, up from 34.6% in 2022.
After the vote, Dodik, who just returned from meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, thanked Putin and also credited "Donald Trump's magnificent victory" for keeping his political camp alive.
He added that "now, thanks to the new environment, we are political winners."
Dodik, wants close ties to Serbia and Russia and secession from Bosnia and Herzegovina.
"Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead, it is an impossible country," Dodik told supporters at the final rally of his in Banja Luka on Friday.
What is happening in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?
In the Muslim-Croat federation, Bosniak parties are advocating for a stronger central state.
The main Bosniak SDA party is focused on efforts to keep the country united against Serb separatism.
Bosnian Croats are also largely backing their ethnic parties, including the Bosnian branch of Croatia's ruling conservative Croatian Democratic Union.
Meanwhile, Denis Becirovic, the incumbent Bosniak presidency member, has vowed a renewed path to the EU and NATO.
Bosnia and Herzegovina has been a candidate for EU membership since 2022.
But the actual start of membership talks depends on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, including strengthening judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption laws.

North Korea Claims Test of Ballistic Missile With Four Flight Profiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
19:14:41 UTC
04:14:41 KST

North Korea launched a missile toward the Sea of Japan that Pyongyang described as a “strategic intermediate-range missile.”
Details of the launch were reported by the Japanese Ministry of Defense.
According to Japan’s Defense Ministry, at around 6:36 a.m. local time, North Korea launched at least one ballistic missile from the country’s east coast in a northeastern direction.
The missile reached a maximum altitude of about 90 kilometers, traveled approximately 680 kilometers and fell into the Sea of Japan outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone. There were no reports of damage to aircraft or vessels in the area where the missile fell.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) reported that the launch was detected at around 6:30 a.m. from the area of Wonsan and that the missile traveled more than 700 kilometers. South Korean and U.S. intelligence agencies tracked the launch from an early stage and exchanged the data they collected.
Japan’s Ministry of Defense said Tokyo continues to analyze the missile’s characteristics jointly with the United States and South Korea.
After the missile launch was detected, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi instructed government agencies to promptly collect and analyze information, check the safety of aircraft and vessels, and prepare for possible contingencies.
The state-run KCNA published a statement by Kim Yo Jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, in which she confirmed that missile-firing exercises had been conducted.
According to her, a “strategic intermediate-range missile” was used during the exercises, while Kim Jong Un personally observed the launch by a special fire unit.
According to the North Korean side, the missile can alter its trajectory at low altitude and has at least four flight profiles that can be selected depending on the target and mission.
Kim Yo Jong also claimed that AI elements were used in the system, although there is currently no independent confirmation of these characteristics.
The North Korean side also cited the difference between the flight-range estimates released by South Korea and Japan as evidence supporting its claim that the missile is difficult to track.
This may have involved a quasi-ballistic missile capable of performing maneuvers during different stages of flight and deviating from a conventional ballistic trajectory.
Such missiles can combine a ballistic flight phase with gliding and active maneuvering in the atmosphere. This makes their trajectory less predictable and complicates the operation of missile defense systems, which must continuously track the target and predict the point at which it will meet the interceptor missile.
In addition, flying at a relatively low altitude can reduce radar detection range and the time available for air defense systems to respond. Combined with maneuvering, this makes it more difficult to maintain stable tracking of the missile and establish a predictable trajectory for interception.
The Russian 9M723 ballistic missile of the Iskander-M system is one example of this class of weapons.
At the same time, the development of similar capabilities in North Korea could be linked both to its own development of the Hwasong-11 family and to military-technical cooperation with Russia.
Ukrainian military engineers, after examining North Korean KN-23 missiles, determined that the missiles are not direct copies of the Iskander missile, but could be a modified version of one of the earlier designs associated with the Russian system.
In addition, amid deepening military cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang, there have been reports that Russia has transferred missile technologies to North Korea. In particular, Kyrylo Budanov, who was then Chief of Defense Intelligence of Ukraine, said that Russia had helped North Korea improve the KN-23 and significantly increase its accuracy.
At the same time, there is currently no confirmed data that would directly link the missile’s claimed four flight profiles to the transfer of specific Russian technologies.
On September 20, North Korea launched a ballistic missile from the country’s east coast toward the Sea of Japan.
According to the Japanese side, during that launch the missile reached an altitude of about 60 kilometers and traveled approximately 440 kilometers. South Korean military officials also identified the Wonsan area as the launch site.
North Korea later released photographs of a test of a new missile that was identified as the Hwasong-11Ma-1. During the September 20 tests, South Korean military officials detected two launches from the Wonsan area at an interval of approximately three hours.
The latest launch took place amid renewed tensions between the countries following a mine explosion in the demilitarized zone on September 21 that injured three South Korean servicemen.

Roosters were always more than just the villain in Newcastle's fairytale
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
19:12:47 UTC
04:12:47 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Roosters spoil Knights' NRL party as grand final won by Daly Cherry-Evans's class
The week leading up to the NRL grand final was all about the Knights.
The Steel City. The rugby league heartland. The undermanned and outgunned team had somehow made it back to the big show for the first time in 25 years.
Newcastle is everything Bondi isn't, of course.
Miners sinking tins, rather than the work-from-homers sipping oat flat whites. In the 25 years since Newcastle's previous journey to the men's decider, the Roosters have made it eight times for five premierships.
The Roosters are undeniably one of the NRL's "haves".
Roosters chairman Nick Politis is the closest thing Australian football has to an American-style club owner; the sort of bloke who would get on stage to accept the championship trophy before any of his players touch it.
He didn't quite go that far after the Roosters' thrilling one-point win over the Knights, but broadcaster Channel Nine did make sure to find him in the midst of the celebrations, talking to a few kids over the fence.
"They're my best customers; future customers. And I love them all," Politis told former stablemate Brad Fittler.
As he celebrated his team winning the men's and women's premierships, he pledged the all-conquering, undefeated NRLW champions would get better next year.
"We've got that rugby sevens girl coming. I can't remember her name, but she's very good," he said.
It doesn't scream close-knit family unit, but it's the sort of cold, hard business operation that is so often the formula for success at this level.
The famed salary sombrero has allowed them to be in the hunt or end up as the final destination for just about every big-name off-contract player in recent years.
Years ago they ripped James Tedesco from the Tigers (and arguably the Raiders). The Rabbitohs were powerless to hang on to Angus Crichton when Uncle Nick came calling. They pinched Mark Nawaqanitawase from the Wallabies. And, perhaps most pivotally, they gave Daly Cherry-Evans one last NRL payday and a shot at premiership glory.
Sam Walker was their future, Hugo Savala was a ready-made option, and Sandon Smith had proved an able utility or deputy half.
But the Roosters wanted more. They wanted an assurance of class and quality,
So, like Cooper Cronk before him, Cherry-Evans made the journey to Moore Park and did what he was paid handsomely to do.
When the moment came, he took it upon himself to step up and ice the moment with what turned out to be the decisive field goal.
He did it.
But no, not according to him.
"We did it," he stressed to Channel Nine.
"I didn't do anything."
That team-first mentality is as much a part of the Roosters as it is any team in the NRL, because of course all the hyperbole isn't true.
For all the battler energy of the Knights and Newcastle, in Kalyn Ponga and Dylan Brown they boast the two most expensive players of either grand final team (and reportedly two of the league's top seven).
And for all the glitz and glamour that comes with being a Rooster, centres Rob Toia and Billy Smith have been through five torn ACLs and two broken jaws between them to play in this grand final.
Crichton has battled through mental demons you wouldn't wish on your worst enemy and literally cut off his left middle finger to keep playing footy.
All the while the Roosters, this big business, stood by them. On Sunday night, those well-paid battlers returned the faith (and the sizeable investment).
And if we're talking about communities showing resilience to bounce back from tough times, they don't come much tougher than what Bondi experienced last summer.
Even DCE, the blond-haired boy from Manly. One of the NRL's great villains, mostly for being a little too media trained and polished, has never really been a safe bet when it comes to this sort of thing.
The oldest NRL grand finalist and now the oldest premiership winner at 37, burst onto the scene with a premiership in his 2011 rookie year with Manly, but the ensuing decade-and-a-half were slim pickings for the State of Origin hero, with just four top-eight finishes in his last 11 Sea Eagles seasons.
But it only took one in Bondi for him to rediscover that winning form and deliver on the promise he made, either explicitly or implicitly, when he signed that contract.
"I don't know what it means, but it feels amazing," he told Nine.
"This is not just about me, it's about my teammates and my family. The journey is all about the ups and downs and it's so amazing to finish here."
The Roosters were no neutrals' favourites in this grand final. In many ways, Cherry-Evans winning with the Roosters may be even less popular than if he'd won another with Manly.
It's not much fun seeing the rich get richer, and rugby league's Richie Rich Roosters don't really need the love as long as they have the titles to keep them warm at night.
But they do deserve our respect.

The Palestinian Red Crescent told WAFA that they rushed to the scene after receiving a report of a critically ill Palestinian, who died at the scene.

Kashmiri teacher fights period stigma, one village at a time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
19:03:15 UTC
04:03:15 KST

BARAMULLA: While most schools are quiet on Sundays, Aasima Jan heads into north Kashmir’s remote tribal villages to talk to girls and families about a subject many still avoid: menstruation. For years, the 42-year-old govt school teacher has conducted awareness sessions on menstrual health, hygiene and stigma, while also persuading families to re-enrol children who have dropped out of school. Her efforts earned her J&K’s “Best Teacher Award” in 2023.Recruited in 2003, Aasima spent seven years teaching at a govt school in Bandipora. In 2009, she noticed many girls missing classes for up to a week during their periods. Some said their parents barred them from attending school while menstruating.The turning point came when she found a student crying over the shame surrounding periods. “It broke my heart. I felt a deep sense of responsibility and resolved to do something about it,” Aasima said. The next day, she began taking extra classes on menstruation and started counselling parents. “I tell girls this is natural. It is not a disease, but a sign that they are growing up,” she said.
Attendance among girls improved.Aasima then moved beyond the classroom, conducting monthly awareness sessions at schools and visiting villages on Sundays and holidays. She continued the sessions even after her transfer to neighbouring Baramulla district. Her outreach expanded to remote areas such as Gurez and Uri, and to nomadic Gujjar and Bakerwal communities.
Every Sunday, she picks a village, contacts local panches and sarpanches, and conducts sessions centred on “awareness, acceptance and action”. In remote areas, she often finds girls using cloth during periods while families, including mothers, are reluctant to discuss menstruation. Aasima spends her own money buying sanitary pads to distribute during visits, while explaining their use and disposal.Her social media page, with around 40,000 followers, also promotes menstrual health and other social causes. For Aasima, the biggest reward is seeing students continue the work by spreading awareness and positivity about menstrual health.

How Andy Burnham ate the Greens’ policy lunch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

BRIGHTON, England — Zack Polanski won a landslide victory to lead the Green Party last September with a vow to “replace” Labour on the left of British politics.
Today, Andy Burnham’s new-look Labour is gobbling up Polanski’s policies — and, rather than supplanting the governing Labour Party, the Greens are sliding down the polls.
Burnham used a conference speech last week to frame the next general election as a fight on left-of-center, progressive issues familiar to Polanski’s brand of eco-populism — such as electoral reform, a new adult social care system, and forging closer ties with the EU.
Advertisement
“Vote Green, and watch Labour move,” Polanski told his own party’s conference this past weekend, arguing that Labour’s leftward lurch on policy was down to pressure exerted via Green breakthroughs in local and parliamentary by-elections.
But experts warn that it’s precisely such moves from Burnham, which the Greens chalk up as wins, that ultimately undermine the party’s electoral prospects.
The Green Party is “slightly a victim of their own success,” said Luke Tryl, boss of the More in Common think tank and polling agency.
Party insiders insist they still have the policies to take the fight to Labour.
But Tryl compared the Greens to the UK Independence Party after 2010. The Euro-skeptic outfit under Nigel Farage had an “outsized impact on the whole of politics” — but never made substantial breakthroughs into parliament.
Sinking
Six months ago, Polanski had dragged the Greens to 18% with voters, a single percentage point ahead of Labour, according to POLITICO’s poll of polls, as Keir Starmer’s ruling party struggled in the doldrums.
Advertisement
Now the Green Party has sunk back to 11%, and Burnham’s Labour has reopened a lead over the Greens of 14 points. The initial surge in Green support is mostly over, More in Common argued in a presentation on the fringes of the party’s annual conference, as Burnham claws back voters on the left.
Zack Polanski participates in a protest in London on Nov. 25, 2025. | Guy Smallman/Getty Images
John Curtice, Britain’s leading political scientist, compared the party’s fortunes to another force in British politics. “This reminds me of the kind of arguments that the Liberal Democrats used to use,” he said: “‘We are the party that comes up with all the clever ideas first, and other people gobble them up.’”
He added: “I think the challenge they [the Greens] now face is how do they hang on to — or in a sense recapture — the support that they did have six months ago, that seems to have eroded back to Labour.”
To the left, to the left
Burnham’s speech to Labour conference last Tuesday — which the party faithful met with tears and applause — indicates the size of that challenge.
Burnham proposed a state-funded social care system in the mold of the NHS, as well as promising electoral reform and a new long-term relationship between Britain and the EU. (He later left the door open to another referendum.)
“They are all policies that we already have,” Sian Berry, Green MP for Brighton Pavilion, answered when POLITICO reeled through Burnham’s priorities. “It is hard to imagine that speech ... without the influence of the Green Party,” Tryl said.
Advertisement
The principle of a care system free at the point of need, for example, “has been in Green Party policy for some years now,” said Adrian Ramsay, MP for Waveney Valley. The party also backs “closer ties” with the EU post-Brexit and, eventually, rejoining the bloc.
On electoral reform, the Greens are left agreeing with Labour but urging Burnham to move faster. A commission, tasked with suggesting how to shake up the electoral system before the next election, could “just be the way to kick this into the long grass,” said Natalie Bennett, a Green Party peer. “What we are saying is PR [proportional representation] now.”
Being distinctive
Green Party politicians are keen to talk up areas where they still offer voters something distinct from Labour.
Polanski’s main policy announcement in his speech was a temporary “emergency brake” on private rent, which would stop rents rising above 2%, inflation, or levels of wage growth, whichever was lowest. Burnham, when mayor of Manchester, voiced support for rent controls — only for his government to rule it out this summer.
John Curtice said those plans could help shore up the Green vote. “Polanski’s policy on rent is very, very clearly designed to appeal to precisely the kind of people that Greens have been most successful among,” he said.
“We’re not afraid to say that there should be more regulation on landlords,” said Zoë Garbett, the Green mayor of Hackney, who won her seat from Labour in May’s local elections.
Advertisement
Green members also passed a policy motion ditching the Office for Budget Responsibility and scrapping fiscal rules seen to constrain public spending.
The party has drawn dividing lines with the government, too, on climate, its founding cause. Alongside Gaza, it was Polanski’s call to ban new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea that received the loudest applause in the hall.
A pro-Palestine demonstration takes place during the Green Party conference in Brighton, England on Oct. 3, 2026. | Alishia Abodunde/Getty Images
“The Andy Burnham speech was impressive in its oratory, and it was clearly a shift from what we saw from Keir Starmer, but there wasn’t a single mention of climate and nature in the whole speech,” Ramsay said.
The same More in Common data referenced above showed that Green voters, and those considering voting for the Greens, think the party is at its best when talking about nature and clean power.
Rethinking climate goals
And yet, the Green’s Brighton conference also saw the party waver on its ambitious, flagship climate pledge.
The Greens went into the 2024 general election with a promise to reduce U.K. greenhouse gas emissions to net zero by 2040, a full decade ahead of Labour’s target.
Advertisement
But that bold commitment has gone.
“We would need to review [the pledge],” said Ramsay, when asked if the net-zero target still stood. “We did a really thorough exercise ahead of the 2024 manifesto to look at what’s the quickest it can be achieved from that point in time. We will do the same ahead of the next general election.” He blamed slow progress on net zero by “repeated governments.”
Meantime, said Curtice, the political scientist, the Greens should focus on offering answers to short-term challenges on issues like cost of living and turning around the health service. Hannah Spencer — the MP for Gorton and Denton, who beat Labour in a by-election earlier this year — last week accused the government of “dithering” over intervening with support for energy bills, which are expected to surge in January.
There is always a chance for the Greens in “profiting from disillusion with Labour,” argued Curtice. The party’s task, he added, is to come up at the same time with policies that “encourage people.”

Netanyahu orders security review of flights to Israel after flydubai attack
JERUSALEM - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered a security review of international flights to Israel on Oct 4, after an attempt by an Omani co-pilot to crash an Israel-bound plane from Dubai.
Netanyahu “has instructed the head of the National Security Council, Shmuel Ben Ezra, to appoint an examiner to conduct a thorough review of all security aspects of foreign civil aviation to Israel”, a statement from the premier’s office said.
Calls have mounted in Israel for an investigation into the security lapse that allowed the Omani co-pilot of a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Sept 30 to attempt to bring down the aircraft after stabbing the Indian captain.
Israeli media has reported that the co-pilot intended to crash the aircraft on Israeli territory.
Critics have focused on how a pilot from a country with no diplomatic relations with Israel was cleared to operate a flight bound for Tel Aviv.
Transport Minister Miri Regev rejected responsibility for the failure, saying security oversight for flights operated by foreign airlines falls under the remit of the Mossad and Shin Bet, Israel’s foreign and domestic intelligence agencies.
A 2024 report by the state comptroller found there was no clear division of responsibility for the security of foreign airlines operating in Israel, and recommended that the government address the issue.
Israeli media have reported that pilots from countries hostile to Israel have repeatedly flown into the country in recent years.
Keren Terner, who previously served as director-general of the transport ministry and is now running for Parliament for the opposition, blamed Regev for the security failure, noting that the Civil Aviation Authority was under the “direct subordination” of her ministry.
“You are responsible for the security of foreign companies. Not the Shin Bet, not Mossad. You. That’s what the government decided, and that’s what the law stipulates,” Terner wrote on X.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid dismissed Netanyahu’s announcement of a security review as a “sham investigation”.
“The chain of failures that preceded the incident could have led to a disaster of historic proportions, and this is how an Israeli prime minister responds?” Lapid wrote on X.
“Just as Netanyahu escaped an investigation into the October 7 massacre, he is now running away again,” he added.
Gadi Eisenkot, a leading challenger to Netanyahu ahead of the Oct 27 election, wrote on X that “in a proper and functioning government, the minister of transportation would have submitted a letter of resignation last night”. AFP

Antalya hosts IAC 2026: What to know about the global space gathering
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:52:05 UTC
03:52:05 KST

Once a year, the world’s space community gathers to debate where humanity goes next beyond Earth.
This year, the list is long: weapons in orbit, artificial intelligence data centres in space, overcrowded skies and a new race to the moon.
Those issues top the agenda of the 77th International Astronautical Congress, or IAC, widely described as the largest international gathering of the space sector. It will be held October 5-9 at the NEST Convention Center in Belek, near the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya. It marks the first time Türkiye has hosted the congress since its launch in 1950.
Organisers expect more than 10,000 registered participants, from space agency chiefs and company executives to engineers, scientists and students. This year’s theme is “The World Needs More Space.”
Here is a look at what will be discussed, who is coming and why the meeting matters.
What is IAC?
The congress is organised every year by the International Astronautical Federation, a nonprofit organisation founded in 1951 to connect space organisations across national borders. The first such congress was held in Paris a year earlier, when spaceflight was still largely a dream.
Today, the IAC works as a mix of scientific conference, trade fair and diplomatic summit. Researchers present thousands of technical papers, companies show off rockets and satellites in a large exhibition hall, and leaders of several space powers share the same stage.
The event has also served as a launch pad for big announcements. At the 2016 congress in Guadalajara, Mexico, SpaceX founder Elon Musk first laid out his plan to build a giant rocket to carry people to Mars, the design that later became the company’s Starship. A year later, in Adelaide, Australia used the congress to announce it would create its own national space agency.
The host country changes every year, usually rotating among different continents. Last year’s congress was held in Sydney, Australia.
What’s on agenda?
The official programme covers a wide range, from moon exploration to space medicine.
One headline session is titled “Geopolitics vs. Innovation,” another looks at how regional organisations govern space, and a third tackles what organisers call “orbital oversaturation.”
The European Space Agency said it expects space security, exploration and the ethics of activities beyond Earth to be among the week’s themes.
NASA plans to present results from its Artemis II mission and hold a news conference on the Artemis Accords, a set of US-led principles for peaceful exploration. Its Jet Propulsion Laboratory will also present its work on “trusted AI on Mars,” with a session examining how an autonomous planning system has been used to operate the Perseverance rover and how such technology could support future missions searching for life beyond Earth.
The harder questions sit just outside the programme’s titles.
On September 14, US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said the US Space Force already has weapons in orbit designed for “space control,” without saying what they are. It was a rare public admission that a country has operational weapons in space.
Washington is also building Golden Dome, a missile shield backed by President Donald Trump that would include interceptors stationed in orbit. Officials say it could be operational by the summer of 2028, and the White House first estimated its cost at $175 billion.
Critics say orbiting interceptors could double as satellite killers and push rivals to build more anti-satellite weapons of their own. Russia and China have both tested anti-satellite weapons.
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the founding law of space, bans nuclear weapons in orbit but says little about conventional arms.
Artificial intelligence is the other new pressure.
In January, SpaceX asked US regulators for permission to launch up to 1 million satellites that would work as data centres in orbit. Google is sending its own AI chips into space for testing this week under a project called Suncatcher.
Supporters say orbit offers steady solar power for energy-hungry AI. Skeptics point to high costs, radiation damage and the risk of adding still more hardware to increasingly crowded orbits, where debris from a single collision can threaten other satellites.
A separate lecture at the congress will look at the safety of giant satellite networks from the viewpoint of Starlink, SpaceX’s internet constellation. Michael Nicolls, SpaceX’s senior vice president of Starlink engineering and president of SpaceXAI, will discuss the safety and sustainability challenges involved in operating a constellation on that scale.
Who is coming?
The Global Space Leaders Summit on October 6 will bring together heads and senior officials from space agencies and offices from more than 40 countries.
NASA’s delegation will be led by Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson. European Space Agency Director General Josef Aschbacher will also attend, along with India’s ISRO Chairman V. Narayanan, China’s CNSA Chief Engineer Li Guoping, JAXA President Hiroshi Yamakawa and Canadian Space Agency Acting President Jean-Claude Piedboeuf.
The summit will also bring together space officials from countries including the United Arab Emirates, Brazil, Spain, the UK, France, Germany, South Korea, Pakistan, South Africa and Poland.
Aarti Holla-Maini, director of the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs, is also set to attend the congress.
The congress will also feature more than 25 astronauts, along with ministers and aerospace executives.
Jonathan Cirtain, CEO and president of Axiom Space, and Mike Gold, president of Redwire, are among the industry executives attending. Other prominent industry figures include Awais Ahmed, founder and CEO of Indian space company Pixxel, and Murat Ikinci, CEO of Turkish defence and aerospace company Roketsan.
The event is coordinated by Türkiye’s Ministry of Industry and Technology, hosted by the Turkish Space Agency (TUA) and co-hosted by SAHA Istanbul, a defence and aerospace industry cluster, with Anadolu as its global communications partner.

Daniel invited a religious group to stay on his farm. He says they soon told him to 'submit'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:41:38 UTC
03:41:38 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
Everyone has a breaking point, but once we decide to take action, how can we be sure it's the right move? From toxic relationships to high-stress jobs and religious beliefs, Insight hears from people who've reached their final straw.
Nine years ago, Daniel invited a group of people he'd never met before to stay on his farm. This decision led to him later testifying in a parliamentary inquiry into cults.
He and his wife had recently returned to their Christian faith when they were feeling significant pressure due to the breakdown of their business and the birth of their twins.
"We were physically, financially, and emotionally wrecked," Daniel told Insight.
"I basically leaned on that because everything else was crumbling around me."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Daniel started watching online videos about Jesus made by a little-known religious group. He soon contacted the leader, and they began exchanging emails.
"Because they told me they were a travelling group … I [said] 'We've got a farm; you can camp here while you're passing through,'" Daniel said.
"But then within the two weeks, we had the whole Australian group there."
'Your children are not your children'
Daniel says that at first, the group was "super friendly" and helped around the farm and with taking care of Daniel and his wife's 11 children.
But things took a turn after a few weeks, and "the 'straws' started raining down".
"They became very demanding, very [critical] of everything we did — especially our parenting," Daniel said.
"It just got worse and worse to the point where they were even physically punishing our kids without us even being there — locking them in rooms, hitting them to the ground, pulling them out of vehicles."
When the group said they were thinking of leaving for Sydney after a few months, Daniel and his wife felt relieved.
"But then the next day, two of the members came up to us … and said, 'We will stay if you want, but you have to understand: your children are not your children, and you have to submit to us fully'."
That was the breaking point for Daniel, and he said it'd be best if they followed through with going to Sydney.
"After they left, I turned to my wife and said, 'What the f--- was that?'
"I'd never sworn up until that point."
Daniel said that when the group tried to return a month later, he called the police, and they left before the officers arrived.
Two of the members came up to us … and said, 'We will stay if you want, but you have to understand: your children are not your children, and you have to submit to us fully'.
Daniel
Daniel believes the whole experience was also the final straw for his Christian faith.
He says he was forced to ask himself, "Can I be a good person without believing in God?"
"It takes a long time to break it all down," he said.
"I went through many years of literally questioning every thought that came up in my head, every action I was about to do — and reprogram it."
'Not really about that one small event'
Monique Crane, a professor at the School of Psychological Sciences at Macquarie University, says a final straw is "often not really about that one small event".
"Usually, the person has been feeling uncomfortable, stressed, disappointed, angry or unhappy for a long time ... they may have been trying to understand what is wrong — even if they have not been thinking about it consciously ..." Crane told Insight.
"However, one moment can bring a sense of clarity ..."
The Sydney-based psychologist and researcher says that psychologists sometimes describe this type of sudden understanding as an "insight".
"An insight happens when ideas or experiences that have been building over time suddenly come together and make sense," Crane said.
She said this might come in the form of realising a job is unsustainable or a relationship conflicts with someone's values or beliefs about how they should be treated.
Crane said that a final straw moment can help the person recognise there is a gap between their current situation and something important to them.
"That is why a small event can sometimes lead to a large decision," she said.
"The reaction is usually not just about what happened that day; it is about what that event helped the person finally understand about everything that came before it."
Leaving Montana
For Wendy, a decision arising from a final straw caused her regret.
She had hired a builder her friends recommended to build her dream home in the mountains of Montana, US, where she used to live. But she grew concerned.
"He would present me with bills that, in my opinion, did not seem accurate … he really never worked an eight-hour day … he was a fellow who liked a very long lunch."
Wendy eventually let the builder go when she thought the construction was not progressing quickly enough.
She was "heartbroken" when he handed her the final bill of $200,000 as it was much larger than she expected, but she paid it after he threatened legal action.
"I really couldn't afford to finish the home at this point," she said.
"I felt [people I trusted] had betrayed me by saying he was a great guy… I went with him, and it was disastrous for me ... That was the final straw with him and with Montana."
Wendy felt she needed to change her whole situation.
After selling everything and rehoming her 27 dogs, she moved to Sydney, Australia, where her son lives.
She says it took time to adjust to the change and that she "sobbed" for the first two-and-a-half years of being in Australia.
"I didn't realise how much I would miss my life in Montana, my ice fishing, my hunting, my friends — it was very hard."
"I felt that I had made the wrong decision, but it was an economic impossibility to move back."
Wendy has since taken up ocean fishing and now loves living here and feels like she has found herself again.
'A frog in boiling water'
Jenny didn't have any regrets about leaving her situation when she reached a breaking point in her career.
She loved being a teacher but likens her time as a school principal to being "a frog in boiling water".
"The water just kept getting hotter and hotter and hotter until it got to the point where I was completely overwhelmed and burnt out," she said.
She says it only got more difficult when she became the principal of a special education school, where she encountered "challenging behaviours [such as] biting, kicking, pinching, running away".
"It wasn't malicious; they were just really challenging students."
It was a text that spelled the end of Jenny's career.
"My phone went off in my pocket and I just snuck a look at it and it said, 'Please come back to school. A student has really injured a teacher'," she said.
After returning to school and calling a crisis meeting, Jenny turned to her deputy principal and said: "You're going to have to ring the district director and tell them that the principal's left."
"I picked up my handbag and drove away. It was gut-wrenching to leave them behind."
While she initially felt she had let her students and staff down, Jenny is now involved in education in a different way — as a leadership coach for school principals struggling in their careers.
"I think life brings you to where you're supposed to be," she said.
"I'm in and around schools all the time, but the difference that I can make is to keep people well, happy and successful in their jobs."
Resilience in leaving a situation
Psychologist Crane, who specialises in resilience, workplace mental health and human performance, says, "There is no single point at which everyone decides that 'enough is enough'".
"People have different values, goals, expectations and circumstances; so the same situation can feel manageable to one person and unacceptable to another."
"People will often have tried to cope, hoped things would improve, changed the way they approached the situation or tried to fix the problem. Then, after all that, they reach the realisation that ... a more substantial re-orientation is necessary."
The professor said that when changing or fixing the situation isn't possible, leaving the situation may be the most resilient response.
"Resilience ... is about adapting, solving problems and making choices that help us continue to live and work in ways that are consistent with what matters to us."
Learning about cults
Daniel later gave evidence about what happened when a religious group moved onto his farm as part of a parliamentary inquiry into cults.
He and his family left their farm after the experience and travelled for two years.
"Everything was just about having fun, joking about what had happened, then trying to understand why this had happened."
Daniel now lives happily without religion but says, "It took many years to rebuild … to some sort of normalcy."
He says podcasts have helped him "understand cults and how they worked".
"It was a lot of working on yourself to get yourself out of that sort of thinking, that extreme thinking ... "

Medicinal cannabis prescriber scrubs false claims but won't notify customers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:41:22 UTC
03:41:22 KST

in brief
- MOCA admits its products were wrongly described as TGA-approved.
- More than 99 per cent of medicinal cannabis products are not TGA-approved.
An online medicinal cannabis prescriber has admitted it wrongly described its products as approved by Australia's medicines regulator.
But it says it will only "consider" notifying clients about the change.
Medicinal Organic Cannabis Australia (MOCA) had claimed its entire product range was approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA), whereas in fact the products it sells, while legal, are unapproved therapeutic goods and have not been assessed by TGA for safety, quality or effectiveness.
Experts have told SBS News the claim is one example of concerns about how medicinal cannabis products are described and marketed to patients.
Earlier this year, the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) wrote to the TGA calling for reforms to the way medicinal cannabis is prescribed and regulated.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
SBS investigation uncovers misleading claims
As part of its research into the online medicinal cannabis industry, SBS News found examples of clinics and online retailers using language that could give prospective patients the impression their cannabis products had been "approved" by the TGA.
One example was MOCA, which lists a Sydney address on its website.
Managing director Alessandro Sorbello stated on the website that the company's "complete product range is approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) and is ready for practitioners to prescribe to patients in Australia".
The website also said its "approved medical cannabis product range includes capsules, sublingual oils, isolates, vape pens and whole cannabis flowers".
However, the TGA's Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG) lists only two cannabis medicines as approved products: Epidyolex, an oral solution used for specific forms of epilepsy and Sativex, a mouth spray used for multiple sclerosis-related spasticity. Combined, these two products make up less than 1 per cent of medicinal products available in Australia.
In a statement to SBS News, MOCA acknowledged that the wording "did not accurately reflect the regulatory status" of its products and said it had removed it.
The company said it was also reviewing its broader website to ensure information about its products and their regulatory status was "accurate and consistent with current requirements".
Asked whether it would communicate the changes to patients, MOCA said it "will consider whether any further communication is appropriate as part of that process".
In a statement to SBS News, a spokesperson for the TGA said it was unable to say whether the information identified by the investigation constituted unlawful advertising, saying advertising of therapeutic goods "must undergo robust assessment on a case-by-case basis and in the context in which it is viewed".
However, the regulator said the Therapeutic Goods Act 1989 prohibits advertisements that imply a therapeutic good has been approved or recommended by the government or a government authority.
"Businesses are responsible for understanding and complying with their regulatory obligations when advertising and supplying therapeutic goods, including advertising through online platforms," the spokesperson said.
Calls to better regulate prescribing
More than 99 per cent of medicinal cannabis products in Australia are not included in the ARTG and have not been assessed by the TGA for safety, quality or effectiveness.
However, this does not mean they can't be prescribed. Doctors can lawfully prescribe some of these unapproved but legal products through regulatory pathways, including the Special Access Scheme (SAS) and Authorised Prescriber Scheme (APS), subject to relevant requirements. The SAS allows doctors to access unapproved products on a case-by-case basis, while the APS doesn't require individual approvals.
Medicinal cannabis contains the same primary compounds found in cannabis more broadly, including THC, the main psychoactive compound and CBD, which does not produce the same intoxicating effects. Their strength, cannabinoid content and composition can vary between products.
The regulatory framework has also attracted scrutiny from the RACGP, which raised concerns about the prescribing of unapproved medicinal cannabis products in a submission to a TGA consultation.
The college said the system isn't working as it should and has called for changes.
"It is the view of the RACGP that the absence of ARTG processes leave Australians vulnerable to unsafe products and devices," the submission states.

'Cheap, quick, and easy': What Alex's prescription reveals about Australia after a major change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:39:49 UTC
03:39:49 KST

10 min read
Feature
'Cheap, quick, and easy': What Alex's prescription reveals about Australia after a major change
For Alex, getting a prescription for medicinal cannabis was remarkably simple.
The Sydney-based part-time worker had used cannabis recreationally for years, taking it to switch off and wind down after a hard day's work. She struggles with sleep, anxiety and depression, and says cannabis has significantly improved her quality of life.
"I'm aware it doesn't work for everybody ... but it's an amazing substance for me," she tells SBS News.
Friends who used medicinal cannabis later recommended the prescription route, and after researching providers online, she found a clinic offering what she describes as a "cheap, quick and easy" service.
But the evidence for using medicinal cannabis for conditions such as anxiety, insomnia and depression remains limited, with the Australian Medical Association saying there is little or no evidence base for some of these uses.
Alex's experience is increasingly part of the way Australians access cannabis. SBS News has withheld her surname for privacy reasons.
Ten years after medicinal cannabis was legalised, prescribing has expanded and a large commercial market has emerged around it. Australians aged 18 and over can access medicinal cannabis through online prescribing services, which patients can then take to a pharmacy.
But as access has grown, so too have concerns about how medicinal cannabis is prescribed and marketed, the evidence behind some of its uses and whether patients fully understand the products they are being prescribed.
What 'medicinal cannabis' really means
For patients, getting a prescription can make a cannabis product feel much like any other medicine. But the word "medicinal" does not necessarily mean a product has been assessed and registered by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA).
Most medicinal cannabis products in Australia are not included in the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG) and have not been assessed by the TGA for safety, quality or effectiveness.
However, doctors can lawfully prescribe some of these unapproved products through regulatory pathways, including the Special Access Scheme and Authorised Prescriber Scheme. Sponsors are also legally responsible for ensuring these products comply with applicable Australian standards, including requirements relating to quality and labelling.
Medicinal cannabis contains the same primary compounds found in cannabis more broadly, including THC, the main psychoactive compound and CBD, which does not produce the same intoxicating effects. Their strength, cannabinoid content and composition can vary between products.
That regulatory distinction is central to the debate over medicinal cannabis, with some doctors and researchers questioning whether the language around the treatment can sometimes give greater weight to its medical benefits than the evidence supports.
Matthew Large, a conjoint professor from the School of Psychiatry at the University of New South Wales, says the term "medicinal cannabis" can overstate its benefits and downplay its risks.
[I believe] the medicalisation of cannabis is the biggest public health bungle in Australia's history.
"As a medicine, cannabis has not come with the appropriate health warnings. And because it's become a medicine, it's become more and more difficult to talk with patients about its harms around addiction and psychosis," he tells SBS News.
As part of its research, SBS News found examples of clinics and online retailers using language that could give prospective patients the impression their cannabis products had been "approved" by the TGA.
One example was online prescriber Medicinal Organic Cannabis Australia (MOCA), which lists a Sydney address on its website.
Managing director Alessandro Sorbello stated on the website that the company's "complete product range is approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) and is ready for practitioners to prescribe to patients in Australia".
The website also said its "approved medical cannabis product range includes capsules, sublingual oils, isolates, vape pens and whole cannabis flowers".
In a statement to SBS News, MOCA acknowledged the wording "did not accurately reflect the regulatory status" of its products and said it had been removed.
The company said it was also reviewing its broader website to ensure information about its products and their regulatory status was "accurate and consistent with current requirements".
Asked whether it would communicate the changes to patients, MOCA said it "will consider whether any further communication is appropriate as part of that process".
In response to questions from SBS News about the MOCA material identified by the investigation, a TGA spokesperson said the regulator was unable to say whether it constituted unlawful advertising.
The spokesperson said advertising of therapeutic goods "must undergo robust assessment on a case-by-case basis and in the context in which it is viewed".
However, the regulator said the Therapeutic Goods Act 1989 prohibits advertisements that imply a therapeutic good has been approved or recommended by the government or a government authority.
Businesses are responsible for understanding and complying with their regulatory obligations when advertising and supplying therapeutic goods, including advertising through online platforms.
The ARTG lists only two cannabis medicines as registered products, including Epidyolex, an oral solution used for specific forms of epilepsy, and Sativex, a mouth spray used for multiple sclerosis-related spasticity.
Combined, these two products make up less than 1 per cent of medicinal products available in Australia. Other medicinal cannabis products are not listed on the ARTG.
A spokesperson for the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (Ahpra) told SBS News it has concerns "some registered health practitioners are prioritising profits over patient safety".
"Ahpra has put the medicinal cannabis industry on notice about its expectations and will continue to use data, including from other regulators, to identify and investigate practitioners who are not prescribing safely," they said in a statement.
Ahpra confirmed regulatory action had been taken against 80 practitioners since 2019 in relation to the prescribing or dispensing of medicinal cannabis.
Large says since the COVID-19 pandemic there has been an "explosion" in cannabis prescribing, particularly for anxiety and depression.
He argues that cannabis can make people feel calmer in the short term without necessarily treating the underlying condition.
His concern is particularly focused on products containing high levels of THC — the psychoactive component of cannabis.
He says THC's effects can be delayed, creating a gap between taking the drug and experiencing its negative effects.
This is a slow-moving problem with a delay between ingestion and toxicity.
Large points to research examining cannabis use and psychosis, saying the findings are concerning, and says the risk of psychosis may increase with greater cannabis exposure and potency.
Research has found an association between frequent use of high-potency cannabis and psychosis, although this does not establish that prescribed medicinal cannabis causes psychosis.
He also warns of the potential for dependence.
"I think it's quite possible that we are going to have a much greater proportion of our population addicted to yet another compound."
He stresses that not all medicinal cannabis products carry the same risks.
Low-THC products and topically applied products such as ointments are likely to be much less toxic, he says.
Concerns over prescribing
Melbourne-based Vicki Kotsirilos was among the first Australian GPs authorised to prescribe medicinal cannabis.
She initially obtained approval to treat patients suffering from chronic, severe cancer pain and neuropathic pain.
But a decade on, she is concerned about how easily some patients can obtain cannabis.
Prescribing medicinal cannabis should always be a last-resort treatment, after other non-cannabis options have been explored.
"We now have clinics and telehealth companies that solely prescribe cannabis to patients. That shows a lack of ethical guidance and professionalism," she tells SBS News.
Kotsirilos says the greatest concern is not necessarily CBD-dominant products, but products containing high levels of THC.
Australian medicinal cannabis products are grouped into five categories according to their cannabinoid content. Categories 1 and 2 are CBD-dominant; category 3 is balanced; and categories 4 and 5 are generally THC-dominant.
Kotsirilos says doctors need to be particularly cautious when prescribing high-THC products to people with conditions such as anxiety.
"THC can aggravate anxiety, can cause illusions and psychosis, and aggravate mental health conditions," she says.
She also warns that high doses can cause sedation and drowsiness and can lead to cannabis use disorder.
Kotsirilos says doctors should first consider behavioural and non-drug treatments, particularly when patients present with anxiety or sleep problems.
"For anxiety, it's really important to first deal with the patient's stresses in their lives, look at their behaviour, exercise, talk to them about sleep and how to correct sleep," she says.
If medicinal cannabis is ultimately prescribed, she advocates starting with lower doses and gradually increasing them where appropriate, while favouring CBD-dominant products over high-THC products.
The potency problem
Large says the potency of cannabis available today is substantially higher than that of cannabis that was commonly available decades ago.
"In the 1970s, illegal cannabis typically had THC concentrations of approximately 2 to 5 per cent at the very most," he says.
"It's possible now to ring up a doctor with a relatively minor complaint and get sent, within 24 hours, multiple scripts, some of which contain 35 per cent THC."
The availability of high-THC products is one reason he believes the risks of cannabis need to be communicated more clearly to patients.
There are so many misconceptions about the toxicity of cannabis.
That makes the language clinics use particularly important.
For patients, the word "medicinal" can suggest that a product has been rigorously tested, is proven to work and is safer than recreational cannabis.
But those assumptions do not necessarily follow from the fact that a product has been prescribed.
The Royal Australian College of General Practitioners has called for changes to the regulatory framework, including greater safeguards around prescribing, and has expressed concerns about how some products are accessed through telehealth services.
The appeal of access
For patients like Alex, however, the distinction between the benefits and risks can feel less complicated.
She says medicinal cannabis has helped with her health concerns, and that the cost of accessing it fits within her budget.
She had a free video call with a nurse, followed by a consultation with a doctor and subsequent appointments every few weeks or months.
Each doctor's appointment was substantially less than she would have paid at her private GP, which she says made the service attractive to her.
The accessibility did not mean the cannabis itself was necessarily cheaper.
Alex says the cost of the products themselves was comparable to cannabis she had previously bought illegally.
She was prescribed flower containing 25 per cent THC, as well as gummies and CBD oil.
Alex says her doctor was prepared to prescribe a higher-THC product because of her experience using cannabis recreationally.
She says she has not experienced the paranoia, dizziness or discomfort that can accompany cannabis use.
For Alex, the ease of accessing medicinal cannabis was part of its appeal. But experts say the question is whether patients are getting enough information to understand the potential benefits and risks.
