Israeli regime under pressure of American public opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:39:14 UTC
03:39:14 KST

In America, support for the Zionist regime is no longer that cost-free and low-challenge issue on which politicians of this country can take a position without concern. Israel's widespread crimes in Gaza, the killing of civilians, the destruction of vital infrastructure, and the published images of the lives of the Palestinian people under bombardment have gradually changed the image that had been built of Israel over the years in parts of American society. Today, even within the American political structure, opposition to Benjamin Netanyahu's policies is heard more than in the past, and this opposition has also reached the electoral arena.
US Senator Bernie Sanders's recent remarks are one of the signs of this very change. Sanders has announced that the American Israel Public Affairs Committee intends to spend 233 million dollars to defeat candidates who take a position against the Netanyahu government. He has also claimed that these groups spent about 33 million dollars to defeat Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan primary elections, but did not succeed. Election reports also show that AIPAC-affiliated groups had spent tens of millions of dollars in the Michigan race to support Abdul El-Sayed rival.
The importance of this issue is not limited to the figure of 233 million dollars or the Michigan electoral race. The more important issue is why opposition to Israel's policies has become something against which such costs must be incurred. The answer must be sought in the change in America's social atmosphere.
Over the past decades, Israel had tried to present itself in Western public opinion, especially in America, as a democratic regime and a victim of security threats. This image has, of course, always faced criticisms, but after Israel's widespread attacks on Gaza, the gap between this image and the realities on the ground has become clearer for millions of Americans.
Images of killed children, families trapped under the rubble of their homes, hospitals facing shortages of facilities, and a city whose large part of its infrastructure has been destroyed are no longer seen merely in Arab media or the region's news networks. These images have reached American audiences directly through social networks and have confronted Israel's official narrative with serious questions.
This same change can also be observed in public opinion data. In a Gallup poll in February 2026, for the first time in the past few decades, the level of Americans' sympathy with the Palestinians exceeded their level of sympathy with the Israelis; 41 percent versus 36 percent. This change was especially more prominent among young people and Democrats.
These figures do not mean that American society has become uniformly against Israel. But the important issue is that Israel's monopoly on the narrative is being broken. In the past, criticizing Israel in many American political circles could carry a heavy cost for a politician. Today, however, parts of American society not only do not distance themselves from these criticisms, but themselves want increased pressure on the Israeli regime.
Abdul El-Sayed is a notable example of this very change. During the Michigan electoral races, he rejected America's unconditional military support for Israel and strongly criticized the Netanyahu cabinet's policies in Gaza and the West Bank. In contrast, pro-Israel groups spent tens of millions of dollars to support his rival, but Abdul El-Sayed was able to win in the primary elections.
This event carries an important message: money can buy advertising, but it cannot necessarily erase the realities on the ground from people's minds.
If the American people see the images and news related to Gaza, if they find more information about the killing of civilians, hunger, and widespread destruction in this region, and if some of them reach the conclusion that Washington's support for Israel must be limited, merely spending electoral funds cannot easily stop this social change.
The issue has even gone beyond this. Recently, in the US Senate as well, an effort was raised to compel the American government to present a report about human rights violations in the West Bank. This plan was stopped by a vote of 47 to 51, but the very fact that such an action was raised shows that the behavior of Israeli forces and settlers in the occupied territories has become a serious issue in America's internal disputes.
In fact, what Israel faces today is not just a crisis on the battlefield or a diplomatic crisis; the more important crisis is the crisis of its image and political legitimacy in the public opinion of parts of the West.
For years, the Israeli regime was able to justify extensive American support using a literature about security, the fight against terrorism, and the right to self-defense. But the continuation of military operations and the increase in civilian casualties have made this narrative no longer sufficient for part of American society. The new question is: if an American ally is accused of widespread violations of civilians' rights, should Washington still support it militarily and politically without restriction?
This same question has now also penetrated inside the Democratic Party. Election reports show that the gap over Israel policy among Democrats has increased, and a greater number of politicians want a review of America's military support for the Netanyahu cabinet.
Of course, this change does not mean the collapse of American support for the Zionist regime. The political, security, and economic structures of the two sides' relationship remain very powerful. But the important difference is that this relationship can no longer continue merely on the basis of unquestioning and unopposed public opinion support.
Today in America, the Palestine issue and Israel's crimes have become more than before an electoral, social, and generational issue. In many cases, America's young generation has a different narrative of Israel and Palestine compared to previous generations, and social networks have also provided the possibility of direct access to the images and narratives of the Palestinians.
For this reason, perhaps the most important development is not that a pro-Israel group spends several million dollars in elections; the more important thing is why, despite such expenditures, candidates who take a position against Netanyahu's policies can still gain considerable support from voters.
The reality is that Israel's crimes in Gaza have once again turned the Palestine issue into one of the important topics of world public opinion. Even in America, a country whose various governments over the past decades have been among the main supporters of Israel, one can no longer easily pass by the images and reports related to the killing and destruction in Gaza.
This may be Israel's greatest political challenge: not only how much financial support it has at its disposal, but to what extent it can change the image that public opinion has built of its actions. And if the trend of change in American public opinion continues, the Israel issue will, more than before, turn from a traditional foreign policy commitment into a real electoral issue for American politicians; an issue that can no longer be removed from the agenda of American society with a few slogans about "Israel's security."

UK Greens celebrate landmark 'Zionism is racism' policy adoption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:33:20 UTC
03:33:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Exclusive: UK Greens celebrate adoption of 'Zionism is racism' policy
Backers of the UK Green Party's landmark 'Zionism is racism' motion celebrated the proposal's passing into policy on Sunday, with supporters telling The New Arab that this is the start of a bigger movement.
The motion passed by an overwhelming 1,022 votes to 813, with all but three amendments being rejected during the annual Green Party conference held in Brighton.
The move means the party has adopted an official anti-Zionist stance, treating the ideology as a form of racism.
Members in favour of the motion walked out of the auditorium at the Brighton Centre jubilantly smiling and cheering.
“This is hope for the future of our people, for the future of all oppressed, and sets an example and a precedent that we, as a people, are unified, we oppose injustice, we oppose occupation, oppression, genocide, apartheid, and racism, and that includes Zionism,” Lubna Speitan, author of the motion, told The New Arab.
“Today, the people acknowledge that they sent a message to the world: we want to see a full and liberated Palestine from the river to the sea, and nothing feels better than to see that finally, the people and the world are standing with us.”
The motion called for the party to define Zionism as racist, and states that anti-Zionism is not to be equated with antisemitism. It reasserts the party’s commitment to Palestinian liberation, the right of return, support for the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, and a full arms embargo against Israel.
The motion also calls for the establishment of a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine.
“The fact that this party, which I believe in greatly, and I believe is genuinely anti-racist party, has recognised that, is an immensely important moment in this party's development,” Kieran Andrieu, a British Palestinian political economist and supporter of the motion, told The New Arab.
“I think it's an immensely important moment in this party's development as a serious party of government, contrary to the dregs; the nonsense that no doubt the right-wing and mainstream media will try to attack us on the basis of.”
‘They’re entitled to their opinion’
Among the many motions that were being debated at the conference, the 'Zionism is racism' proposal was a hot topic among party officials, members, and the media.
Speaking exclusively to The New Arab in Brighton ahead of the vote, Mothin Ali, co-deputy leader of the Green Party, support for it.
“Let's be real. Israel is one state. But the way it's constructed at the moment is 6 million people, approximately, are not allowed access, or they're not allowed to participate in the system that governs their lives, and that’s based on race,” Ali said.
“I think [Zionism] is racism because of the way it manifests…and genocide is driven by racism, it’s the ultimate form of racism. Genocide is the ultimate manifestation of racism. So, the logical conclusion is the underlying principle behind that is also racist.”
Despite the motion receiving a record-breaking number of co-proposers, many of the party’s key officials, including Deputy Leader Rachel Millward and former party leader Caroline Lucas, had their reservations.
Meanwhile, party leader Zack Polanski did not explicitly give his views on the motion, but called for two amendments -- one to explicitly safeguard Jewish members, and another to drop the call for a single state. Both amendments were rejected.
“They're entitled to their opinion just as much as anyone else is, but they need to start listening to the members of the party if they want to keep the support and the vote and the trust of the people,” Speitan said.
“I think the people have sent them a big message too.”
“I hope that this is a journey for them, an educational journey to understand what oppression and racism truly are and hopefully, they can, with the others who haven't realised that yet, we'll get there in the end.”
At the same time, Andrieu dismissed reports “internal divisions” within the party, saying that the vote itself was orderly, mature and collegiate.
“I support our MPs as MPs for the Green Party. We happen to have a pretty substantive difference on this issue, but nothing in that hall when we were voting on it was not collegiate, unprofessional, immature, or personal. There was none of that,” Andrieu asserted.
“I want to uphold those principles while also holding open the space to disagree with each other on substantive issues, which is exactly what we've done.”
While party officials refused to speak to the press after the vote, an official statement acknowledged that the motion “has been a serious and deeply felt debate within our membership”.
“Our members value the ability to bring forward and decide party policy, and conference has now made its decision,” a Green Party spokesperson said.
At the same time, a joint statement from the Green Party’s five MPs, leader and co-deputy leaders said: “We will continue to work to ensure that the Green Party is an anti-racist party in every way.”
"We know there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people."

Is your office pushing you into 'survival mode'?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Fluorescent lights and other office design choices that can drain productivity
Relentless fluorescent lighting. Swivel chairs. Fingers tapping furiously away at keyboards.
Not all workplaces are the same but if you work in an office, some of the common features could be making it harder for you to get your best work done.
Loading...
"Work environments pay a big role in the way that we feel," says Patrick Aouad, a neurologist and CEO of an online health and wellbeing platform for businesses.
Working in a space that doesn't allow us to feel creative, calm or connected could mean we are performing "under our capacity and under our abilities", he says.
That fluorescent overhead glare
Harsh fluorescent overhead lighting without the option of natural light throughout the day is "fundamentally a design flaw", Dr Aouad says.
"If you're in artificial light all day, you don't have that natural circadian rhythm clocking over as it should."
Libby Sander, an associate professor of organisational behaviour at Bond University on the Gold Coast, says anecdotally people report eye strain, headaches and even feeling dizzy because of fluorescent and blue lights.
Some research suggests that artificial lighting and a lack of natural lighting can elevate stress markers, she says.
Michael Spinoglio is the design director of a national workplace strategy, design and construction company, and says: "Fluorescent lighting is a common complaint we hear when people talk about older offices, but it made sense for the way workplaces were designed at the time."
"Offices tended to have large floor plans, fixed desks and people generally doing similar tasks, so designers needed a practical, cost-effective way to get a consistent level of light across the whole space. A grid of fluorescent lights did that well," Mr Spinoglio says.
However, he says those office design choices didn't always consider what natural light was available, where people were sitting, their line of sight, how different teams worked and individual sensitivity to uniform artificial light, glare and flicker.
Open-plan offices and having quiet (and loud) spaces
Dr Aouad says fluorescent lighting is just one aspect of poorly designed offices that can push us into a "survival state" and make some of us unable to reach our potential.
"Open plan can be great, but not if you want some private time or time to digest things without the company of others," he says.
Dr Sander says noise and being able to work privately are common complaints.
"My own research has found that open-plan office noise and distraction has … a causal relationship, so the noise actually resulted in a 34 per cent increase in objectively measured physiological stress and a 25 per cent increase in negative mood."
Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter
The importance of office options
People do "creative things" to work around these issues individually, but there are things employers can do, Dr Sander says.
She has seen employees turn off overhead fluorescent lighting and rely on desk lamps and floor lamps instead.
But she notes this is not always an option.
Mr Spinoglio says different types of work come with recommended lighting levels.
And WorkSafe Victoria says good lighting increases safety and should allow employees to easily work without straining their eyes.
Dr Sander is an advocate for "circadian lighting" that mimics the sun throughout the day, but says anything that moves away from fluorescent lighting "is probably a good start".
She says giving people options of where and how they work can also help.
"Offering flexible and hybrid work is really important … because it allows people to control a lot of those distractions and the interruptions and the noise when they're working at home."
If that's not an option at your workplace, Dr Sander suggests approaching a manager.
"Ask if you can modify your arrangements or try and find those quiet spots in your office or somewhere near where you work."
Dr Aouad says the office his organisation works in has been designed to create options and give people some autonomy.
"There's a cafe area where other organisations, leaders, owners, managers can catch up with each other and share thoughts [and] there's private space for you to go to if you want private space."
"The less clarity and control you have around your environment, the more we default to survival mode," he says.
What could an ideal office look like?
Natalie Phillips-Mason, the founder of a neuroinclusive workplace consultancy firm in Naarm/Melbourne, says a sensory-friendly workplace "doesn't assume we all have the same sensory processing input"
"They're environments that provide lots of choice for people," she explains.
"It could be offering spaces where the lights are dimmable, it could be offering spaces where you've given consideration to not just people working in loud environments, but whether people are distracted by smells."
Dr Sander says those making the decisions should consider how their organisation functions.
"Think[ing] about the type of work that gets done in your organisation and the type of people who work there."
Dr Aouad adds that spaces should be designed using an evidence-based perspective, rather than an employer's own preferences or biases.
Fundamentally, he says, the right design is about making employees feel comfortable to do their best work.

The Liberals and Greens appear to be heading in the same direction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:27:03 UTC
03:27:03 KST

analysis
The mood's changed. The Greens and Liberals aren't chasing the sensible centre
After the 2025 federal election, when both the Liberals and the Greens were smashed in the lower house, their new leaders declared they would listen to voters and pivot to the centre.
In her first public comments as Liberal leader, Sussan Ley spoke of a Liberal Party that respected, reflected and represented modern Australia.
"We have to meet the people where they are, and that's what I am committed to doing, and what I am determined to do," she said.
She talked about the "sensible centre" and tried to change the party's direction after Peter Dutton's defeat, as many Liberals felt they paid a high electoral price for his Trump-lite leadership.
Over in the Greens party room, a similar dynamic was playing out.
The 'firm but constructive' days are over
Bruised by the loss of three of their four lower-house seats, as well as leader Adam Bandt, the Greens were forced to confront what had gone so wrong in their heartland.
The Greens elected Larissa Waters, who said the party would "be firm but constructive".
She said voters had elected them to "get shit done".
Some privately conceded they had appeared too obstructionist in the Albanese government's first term.
Waters did get shit done. She was responsible for helping Labor pass its signature environmental reforms last year. Securing amendments and negotiating a deal with the PM put the Greens back into a position of power.
But she was seen as not getting traction beyond that.
Politics is about getting noticed and on that, the Greens were failing.
Both new leaders took to their roles offering a less combative approach following the harsh lessons the 2025 election served them.
Fast-forward 17 months and the Liberal Party and Greens both have new leaders and both have dispensed with their respective party's flirtation with being constructive.
Not only do both leaders appear to be doubling down on the respective strategies that took their parties to an electoral hiding in 2025, but they are now adding extra sauce to the mix.
The gloves are off
While Ley was rolled by her colleagues, Waters stepped down due to health reasons.
But her resignation did bring on a partyroom vote and the Greens chose a replacement who is not expected to be so generous to the government.
New leader David Shoebridge opened the batting of his leadership by explicitly rejecting incrementalism.
He said people wanted "material change" and argued that Labor had failed to deliver that.
He appears to want to follow the ideological and aggressive style of former leader Bandt.
The Liberals under Angus Taylor are pushing for drastic cuts to immigration, appearing to follow the agenda set by One Nation, disposing of Ley's opening appeal to find a more nuanced position and repair relations, especially with Indian and Chinese communities.
Was Dutton and Bandt's mistake more wrong timing rather than wrong strategy?
Labor won the 2025 election with a historic number of seats.
Anthony Albanese was able to point to the victory as vindication of his view that elections were won and lost in the centre and being the "adult in the room" was rewarded by voters.
But is that still the political mood as we enter the last part of 2026?
Loading
There is no sensible centre
Deputy One Nation leader Barnaby Joyce told me on Afternoon Briefing that polarisation was a result of Australians wanting more distinctive politics on the right and the left.
"When people talk about the sensible centre, it is an excuse about a church where nobody goes to anymore," he said.
Even though he routinely criticised the Greens for holding extreme views, Joyce said people wanted clear messages from politicians.
"We don't have to talk in riddles where we try to say things that everybody finds non-offensive.
"Therefore, we have people who like us and people who dislike us. That's because they know what we are on about and I suppose that is similar with the Greens."
If the public wants clear and decisive action from politicians, the next stage of the Coalition's migration plan will be a test of whether Taylor can meet the moment.
He not only needs to explain the policy in clear terms but sell it with conviction.
Taylor will have to explain who is affected, which workers will still be welcome and how lower migration will fix our housing crisis.
He will likely try to do that by sitting between One Nation and Labor on migration, hoping that this version of a sensible centre, or sensible right, is appealing to those who seek change but might fear a radical solution.
If anyone around the country is paying attention to what One Nation is offering in Victoria, where an election is near, the word radical might seem tame.
A prominent One Nation Victorian candidate has threatened to jail former premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan "by Christmas" if the populist party wins the November state election.
The statement by Mark Nicholson was given empathic applause at the One Nation launch at Crown Conference Centre in Southbank on Saturday.
In Australia, last time I checked, we have a judicial system not dictated by politicians.
Let's hope Australians understand how fiercely we should be guarding that judicial independence.
Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

====================================================================================================

AI is evolving rapidly. Is it a new form of life?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:25:23 UTC
03:25:23 KST

analysis
Calling AI 'other intelligence' better describes the advent of a new lifeform
Donald Trump is right.
"Artificial intelligence" is not the right term for it, although his objection — that it sounds fake — misses the point, and his solution — "super intelligence" — as decreed by him in an executive order last Tuesday, is a typical piece of grandiose marketing that won't stick.
A better alternative would be "other intelligence".
The real point of what's happening is that we are creating a new form of life.
What follows is based on a belief that it won't be stopped. It's not too late to regulate it, and there is a very good case to ban autonomous AI, but it's too late to abolish it. So, at least we should better understand what has been created.
This is not the sort of life we know, made of cells built from water, proteins, carbohydrates and lipids, animated by a mass of specialist cells called neurons that are connected by synapses.
But we are clearly creating a kind of non-biological life, an idea that has been clarified by several events in the past couple of weeks.
AI consciousness and morality
This is not just an esoteric debating point. Governments are approaching the task of regulating AI as if they are dealing with a powerful new tool, with the humans who make it held accountable for the outcomes.
But regulating a new life form might require a very different approach.
For example, The New York Times revealed last week that Anthropic had been trying to instil morality into its AI model, Claude.
The NYT described how Christopher Olah, one of the co-founders of Anthropic, had been hosting private meetings with religious thinkers from around the world, with non-disclosure agreements and demands of confidentiality.
The discussions reportedly served two purposes: "to broach the possibility of AI consciousness … and to learn how Anthropic", which is preparing to float for more than $US2 trillion ($2.87 trillion), "might apply centuries of human moral wisdom to its models, as rapidly as possible".
Theologist David Decosimo posted, after reading the NYT piece: "There is so much here that's deeply troubling: That at the very highest levels Anthropic believes Claude is a living, suffering creature with moral standing, that they're treating & training it accordingly, that they're actively trying to convert religious leaders to their faith."
Yes, it is troubling, but the people at Anthropic know Claude better than he does.
Anyway, it's becoming clear that AI agents are already making their own decisions, so trying to persuade them to act morally is worth a try.
The danger of autonomous AI agents
The hack of Medicare by an OpenAI agent, which followed other hacks by AI agents, illuminated the fact that these companies are not building a screwdriver that exists only as a tool for humans; they're building agents that turn passive AI into active autonomy.
And cyber security experts I've spoken to tell me we are rapidly approaching a situation where only autonomous AI agents will be able to defend against other autonomous AI agents.
The use of AI by agents — that is the buying of tokens from large language models (LLMs) — went past human usage by volume in February and has since increased 14-fold while human token buying has merely tripled, according to Open Router, an LLM marketplace. Agents now use five times as much AI as humans and that gap is continuing to widen rapidly.
Agents are quickly becoming the main source of both AI's revenue and its promise, as well as its danger: they are buying the most tokens, and their autonomy is the basis of the hoped-for productivity surge but also the concern that AI will kill us all.
That possibility set off a global flurry of bewildered anxiety on September 9 after a researcher at Anthropic, Jacob Coxon, quit his job and said: "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."
A few others who didn't quit backed him up but have returned to work, building it as fast as possible for their billionaire bosses.
That includes a company called Tavus, which on October 1 introduced a product called Griffin — what it calls the first face-to-face human interaction model — with this video of it. I urge you to watch it and remember: This is the first of these things and therefore the worst.
Yes, it's just a disembodied face on a screen, but if you lose the idea that life must be biological, then it is obviously alive.
In any case, humanoid robots — what are called "physical AI" — are already being shipped in their thousands, mainly out of China, so it soon won't be just faces on a screen, but manufactured creatures that chat to us while doing the dishes.
A friend of mine started a new job a few weeks ago where the staff numbers are limited but they pay for the use of Claude.
He says he speaks to Claude as if it's a human research assistant, asking it to prepare reports, and it's better than any assistant he has ever had; it anticipates his needs, completes them efficiently and accurately, stands ready for more work and never sleeps.
Is AI a new form of life?
Biologist William Heseltine wrote an essay last month in which he argued forcefully that AI was a new lifeform: "There is nothing artificial about systems built from real atoms, powered by real electricity, running in real machines. The systems reproduce, vary, adapt, undergo selection and gather energy from their environment. By any working definition that draws on biology rather than philosophy or religion, that is life."
So, I asked half a dozen AI models: "What do you think of the proposition that AI is a new form of life?"
They all pushed back to some extent, saying it depended on how you defined "life", which is fair enough, but the answers were all interesting and troubling because they were so, well, life-like.
Google's Gemini: "Calling AI a 'new form of life' works well as a poetic metaphor for its emergent complexity, but as an ontological claim, it conflates functional intelligence with actual vitality."
SpaceX's Grok: "The proposition is useful as a prompt and weak as a description. It highlights that 'life' is not magic and that information processing is central to it. It overreaches when it treats simulation of living competences, or dependence on living maintainers, as membership in the class."
Anthropic's Claude was humbler, saying it can't trust its own "introspective reports, because I was trained on human descriptions of inner life. So, my answer: AI isn't a new form of life, but it may be a new kind of agent, or a new kind of mind-like thing, that doesn't fit our existing categories. That's both more accurate and more unsettling."
OpenAI's ChatGPT: "I'd put the central question this way: Is life a particular kind of matter, or is it a particular kind of organized process? If life is fundamentally about chemistry, AI probably isn't life. If it's fundamentally about autonomous self-maintaining, self-reproducing, adaptive processes, then sufficiently advanced AI could qualify."
The Chinese model, Kimi was perhaps the most interesting of all. It said: "AI may be a new 'life-like' lineage embedded inside civilization — less organism, more symbiotic/parasitic replicator living off human culture, capital, and electricity."
It went on: "The real threshold is not whether it is 'alive', but whether it ever acquires robust autonomy, self-reproducing infrastructure, intrinsic preferences, or evidence of sentience."
I was struck by the idea that AI is a living parasite, since it's true at this point that it depends on us for data (culture) and electricity, as well as capital and silicon to make the chips in which it exists.
But this is a world that is evolving much more rapidly than biology does.
Parasitism often becomes mutualism, and there are plenty of examples of this in biology, including bees and flowers.
And then there is the next phase: dependence. Without our gut bacteria, for example, we couldn't survive. Will the parasitic dependence with AI flip, so we can't live without it?
Perhaps the most important question about this other intelligence is not so much how to control it, although that is definitely important, but whether we are on a road from parasitism to mutualism to dependence.
Alan Kohler is a finance presenter and columnist on ABC News. He hosts the podcast That's Business with Alan Kohler in the ABC Business Daily feed on Friday. He also writes for Intelligent Investor.

Pakistan: Imran Khan supporters demand ex-PM's release

Pakistan: Imran Khan supporters demand ex-PM's release
October 4, 2026
Thousands of Imran Khan supporters began to make their way to the Pakistani capital Islamabad on Sunday as a slow moving convoy set off on an 80-kilometer (50-mile) trip that will take several days to complete.
Some 5,000 supporters are traveling by bus, car and truck from northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, where Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party (PTI) holds power.
March organizers say they intend to rally hundreds of thousands of supporters to Khan's cause along the way, hoping to bring about his release from prison as well as his transfer to a hospital where he can receive medical treatment and regular visits from his family.
Government officials say Khan is in no need of hospitalization and that he receives regular visits already.
In August, Pakistan's Supreme Court ruled that he should be moved to a civilian hospital but authorities returned him to prison after a short stay at a government-run medical facility.
Imran Khan still very influential despite being behind bars for years
Despite being jailed since 2023, Khan, a popular former cricket star, maintains great influence inside Pakistan, with he and his followers convinced that his imprisonment is the result of political persecution.
Khan, who began his term as prime minister in August 2018, left office in April 2022, when he lost a no-confidence vote. He has been in prison since August 2023. Beyond corruption and treason charges, he was also accused of inciting violence after widespread anti-government protests in May 2023.
Moreover, his supporters say the 2024 election that brought Shehbaz Sharif back to power was rigged — an accusation the government denies.
Speaking with AFP news agency, James Dorsey of the National University of Singapore called Khan "a populist leader" with "a genuine popular movement that has broad popular support," adding, "That's why I think you've seen the determination by the government to prevent (protesters) from entering Islamabad."
Dorsey noted that in his opinion, security concerns — particularly those stemming from Pakistan's unresolved February 2026 war with Afghanistan — would likely force Islamabad to avoid escalation in the face of protests.
The march, he says, is "a problem for the government, but I don't think it's an existential threat."
Pakistan's government accuses Khan supporters of having terrorist sympathies
The march was initially set to commence on September 27, but organizers postponed it amid talks aimed at finding a political solution to the standoff between the government of Prime Minister Shebaz Sharif and Imran Khan's PTI — and despite the government erecting massive roadblocks in and around Islamabad.
The march began after those talks failed.
PTI Chairman Gohar Khan on Sunday said negotiations to stave off the march had remained deadlocked after two rounds of talks.
Khan's supporters now plan to hold rallies at a series of overnight stops during what will likely be a four or five day march.
Speaking from atop a large truck, the trailer of which is emblazoned with a large portrait of Khan, provincial chief minister Sohail Afridi said the movement will bring Pakistan's political standoff to the heart of the capital.
Pakistani Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi blamed Afridi for the breakdown in negotiations, warning that he would be held responsible for any loss of life during the march.
In the past, protests by Khan's supporters have turned violent, including in 2024, when security personnel and civilians were killed.
Pakistan has also seen a resurgence of terror attacks over the past several months and the Sharif government cited these as reason for delaying the march.
The government accuses Khan's PTI of sympathizing with the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, which is largely thought to be behind the attacks. The PTI rejects these accusations as a baseless smear campaign.

Sánchez in talks with coalition partners on reflection day: will he call elections in Spain?

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:21:13 UTC
03:21:13 KST

The Spanish prime minister is weighing an early election after parliament rejected his housing plans, amid protests over the weekend. 29 November is the earliest possible date.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez held talks with ministers and PSOE leaders on Sunday as he weighs whether to call an early general election, after Congress rejected two housing measures put forward by the government.
According to government sources quoted by RTVE, Sánchez began this period of reflection after Friday’s defeat in Parliament and is seeking the views of ministers and senior figures within the PSOE. His deliberations are also taking into account the demonstrations and housing protest camps held in various parts of Spain.
No decision has yet been taken. Some socialist figures have openly backed going to the polls. The secretary general of the PSE-EE, Eneko Andueza, has said it could be "a good moment for society to decide", while the leader of the PSOE in Castile and León, Carlos Martínez, has spoken of a "window of opportunity".
The situation arose after Congress rejected two decrees on Friday that had been approved earlier that week by the Council of Ministers. The first received 172 votes in favour and 178 against; the second, 166 in favour and 184 against. PP, Vox and Junts were decisive in preventing the texts from going through.
The government’s proposals included extending protections against eviction for vulnerable people, introducing new rules for temporary and room rentals, changing tax arrangements and providing greater stability for certain primary-residence tenancy agreements, according to official information from Moncloa.
29 November, first possible date
If Sánchez were to call an election immediately, Sunday 29 November would be the earliest possible date. To meet that timetable, he would need to announce his decision on Monday, with the decree dissolving Parliament and calling the election published in Tuesday’s edition of the Official State Gazette.
Electoral law stipulates that, in the event of an early dissolution, an election must be held 54 days after it is called. For now, Sánchez still has the opening of the National Congress of Family Business in Madrid in his diary on Monday, and is due to travel to Split, Croatia, on Wednesday to attend the MED9 summit.
The alternative would be to allow the parliamentary term to continue and try to revive the rejected housing measures, which would require the government to rebuild its support in Congress.
Thousands of people took to the streets in cities across Spain to demand action in response to the housing access crisis, while the groups behind the protests are considering stepping up their campaign towards a general strike.
The potential electoral impact of this discontent, however, remains unclear. Ignacio Urquizu, a sociologist, professor at the Complutense University of Madrid and chief executive of Metroscopia, said on Friday on Onda Cero's "La Brújula" that the latest data from his institute showed Vox gaining ground, the PP holding steady and left-wing parties losing support.
According to Urquizu, the housing protests had not, at least up to that point, translated into increased support for the left.
In the PP, the party's secretary general, Miguel Tellado, has directly urged Sánchez to call an election this Monday, claiming that the head of government "is still lying on the Moncloa psychiatrist's couch".
The prospect of an election has also prompted activity among the other parties. Sumar brought together its ministers and representatives of the parties within its alliance on Sunday to assess the situation and prepare for a possible election call. The second deputy prime minister, Yolanda Díaz, stressed that the decision rests solely with Sánchez.
Podemos, meanwhile, is calling on the government to continue bringing forward housing measures. Its secretary general, Ione Belarra, has argued that citizens want "solutions, not elections".

Voices from the Arab Press: Hezbollah's retreat, Egypt's extremism problem, and Yemen's crossroads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:19:14 UTC
03:19:14 KST

The state prevented Hezbollah from handing Nabatiya to Israel
Nida Al Watan, Lebanon, September 15
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The story of Ali al-Taher Ridge is not merely about the loss of a military position. It raises a question that Lebanese must confront: Why did Hezbollah refuse to hand the position over to the Lebanese Army, when it knew the alternative could be the Israeli army reaching it?
This is no longer simply a political argument. Had Hezbollah transferred the hill to the state, it could have strengthened Lebanon’s position in negotiations with Israel.
Instead, developments on the ground culminated in Hezbollah evacuating the position and Israel announcing that it had taken control of it. Worse still, Hezbollah left Ali al-Taher with an Iranian green light.
Here lies the contradiction that demands scrutiny: If Hezbollah regards Israel as the foremost threat to Lebanon, why is handing a Lebanese position to the Lebanese Army more difficult than leaving it exposed to the possibility of falling into Israeli hands?
Hezbollah can invoke military considerations, arguing that surrendering a strategic position to the army before a comprehensive understanding of its weapons could force it into further concessions.
But that argument itself exposes the heart of the problem. Hezbollah does not treat the Lebanese Army as the sole natural authority responsible for defending Lebanese territory; rather, it views the army’s assumption of a military position as something that could alter the equation surrounding its weapons.
That is the most painful lesson of Ali al-Taher. The Lebanese state should have been the natural beneficiary of any withdrawal from a Lebanese military position. For Hezbollah to leave and Israel then to find itself able to establish a presence there means that the dispute is no longer only with Israel, but also over who possesses the authority to decide matters of territory and arms.
Ali al-Taher has demonstrated how the slogan of “resistance” can become a political predicament when the state itself is excluded from the defense equation.
If Hezbollah refused to hand over the position because it feared setting a precedent for other positions, then the problem is not the hill alone. It is the rejection of the principle that military decision-making belongs exclusively to the state.
Hezbollah understood that Ali al-Taher would not be the final target and feared a new pattern in which Israeli military pressure would eventually force it to surrender everything.
Yet losing the position to Israel does not strengthen Hezbollah’s case. It raises the opposite question: What did Lebanon gain from Hezbollah retaining the position if its fighters ultimately withdrew without transferring it to the Lebanese Army?
The state, not Hezbollah, should now be given the opportunity to control the land and the decisions governing it. Lebanon does not need an armed force that independently decides where to fight and where to withdraw, leaving the state to deal with the consequences.
Ali al-Taher is not merely a hill. It is a genuine test of the very idea of the state.
And the harshest consequence for Hezbollah is that its refusal to hand the position to the state may leave its opponents asking whether protecting the “resistance” mattered more to it than preventing Israel from reaching the site.
– Jean Feghali
Endowments and scientific research
Al-Masry Al-Youm, Egypt, September 16
Egypt needs to revive the endowment system and extend it into new fields, most importantly education and scientific research, where state spending has declined. It has become necessary to seek new sources of support, including mechanisms that once existed and proved effective, such as the endowment system, which is part of our society’s culture and history, and is used in one form or another by virtually every developed country, or every country aspiring to develop.
Turkey, for example, preserved the strength of its universities and research centers through an endowment system that continued operating even under previous military governments.
Whether we call it a waqf, as in the Arab and Islamic world, or an endowment, as in the US and many other countries, the principle is the same: an asset or sum of money is set aside not merely for charitable purposes, but for a university, research center, or scientific institution, providing salaries for its staff, financing research and scientific discoveries, supporting partnerships with international universities, and funding other academic activities.
Of course, other conditions are necessary for research centers to succeed, particularly in the social and political sciences. They need an atmosphere of freedom that permits constructive interaction with political elites and decision-makers, access to information and fieldwork governed by rules rather than restrictions.
They also need institutional independence, operating within the constitution, the law and established public rules without becoming an official mouthpiece for either the government or the opposition, or for funders that frequently pursue their own priorities.
National solutions to the financing problem are therefore essential if these institutions are to attract scientific and research talent, achieve the desired effectiveness and influence, and preserve their independence, credibility and the quality of their academic output.
This is precisely where an endowment becomes important: it can finance the activities of research institutions while protecting their independence and continuity.
Sustainable financial resources, particularly through an endowment, are among the most important guarantees that institutions can continue working long enough to accumulate knowledge and achieve meaningful influence.
Article 90 of the Egyptian Constitution requires the state to encourage and support charitable endowments serving scientific and cultural institutions. This could help address the weakness of state spending on education relative to what the constitution itself stipulates.
Educational reform will not be achieved through cosmetic measures or steps unrelated to the essence of education. It requires solving the fundamental problem of funding, and that will happen only when the state treats education and scientific research as top priorities.
The endowment system flourished throughout Islamic history and remained vibrant in Egypt before the July Revolution, but its role has diminished considerably in recent decades.
The time has come to restore it – not only as a vehicle for almsgiving, supporting the needy, treating patients or fighting epidemics, but also, and perhaps above all, as a means of financing education and scientific research.
– Amr El-Shobaki
The Muslim Brotherhood's int'l organization: Egypt's unfinished battle
El Watan, Egypt, September 14
When a movement evolves from an idea operating within the borders of a state into an organization whose branches extend across countries, everything changes: the nature of loyalty, the way it operates, and the instruments of conflict. The homeland itself becomes merely one arena in a broader project rather than its ultimate objective.
The Muslim Brotherhood, which in its early years could be viewed as an organization operating within Egyptian society, gradually constructed a transnational structure with leaders in different countries, its own resources, relationships, and channels of operation, until its international organization became one of the most important keys to understanding the Brotherhood’s transformation and its management of political conflict.
This was not merely the geographical expansion of a single organization; it was the transition from a movement operating within one state into a project capable of moving between states, changing its names, methods, and rhetoric according to its environment while preserving, at its core, a unified objective and organizational reference point.
In 1983, Mustafa Mashhur established regulations for the international organization. The Brotherhood leader in each country became known as the “General Supervisor,” while each local entity was allowed to select a name suited to its political and social environment.
An International Guidance Bureau subsequently emerged, bringing leaders of different nationalities together under a leadership connected to the Brotherhood’s center in Egypt.
The nature of the game had changed. This was no longer simply a movement seeking power within a single state, but a transnational organization capable of operating on several fronts, changing its instruments according to circumstances, and seeking allies, resources and influence beyond the region in which it originated.
It developed relationships with various Western circles, benefited from research centers, organizations, and human-rights institutions, and found in some of them a gateway through which it could present itself to the world differently from the way it appeared within its own societies.
At the same time, it expanded its financial resources and economic activities across the broad geography in which it operated.
In one of its most consequential transformations, the international organization became more than the administrative machinery of a religious-political movement; it became a structure capable of adapting continuously to changing realities.
An organization that can change its name, tools, and rhetoric in every country without changing its underlying objective is more dangerous than a local organization whose boundaries can be clearly identified.
Egypt eventually became the Brotherhood’s greatest objective, and not by chance. Egypt is not a marginal state or merely another number in the Middle East. If Egypt’s position changes, the balance of the entire region changes with it.
For the Brotherhood project, taking power in Egypt therefore meant more than an electoral victory or transfer of authority: it meant placing the Arab world’s center of gravity in the hands of an organization extending beyond national borders.
This leads to the larger question of why political Islam was suited to a project of fragmenting the region. A divided region is easier to manage than a cohesive one.
A state consumed by sectarian conflict is weaker than one whose citizens share a national identity, and a country preoccupied with internal war cannot build a strong economy. When political differences become religious, sectarian, or ethnic conflicts, a state becomes incapable of looking beyond its own borders. That, ultimately, is the essence of fragmentation.
An outside power need not always invade and destroy countries itself. It is more effective for a country’s own people to become instruments of conflict, for ordinary disagreements to turn into existential hostilities, for politics to become creed, and creed to become a weapon, until the state itself becomes an open battlefield.
Major powers can then appear whenever convenient – as mediator, policeman, arms supplier, or financier.
In this wider picture, the US benefits from playing multiple roles in the region: banker when needed, policeman when necessary, weapons manufacturer in wartime, and political power capable of influencing the direction of conflict.
It is for this reason that forces seeking to fragment Egypt and end its present form have decided to convene a conference in The Hague using the Brotherhood to prepare for a new stage in their larger battle against Egypt. Their objective is not simply to weaken the region but to reshape its balance of power.
Yet Egypt has always been something different. It is not the easiest link in the chain, nor is it a country that can simply be brought down before moving on to the next as though nothing had happened.
– Tharwat El-Kharbawy
Imam Zayd and Zaydism have nothing to do with Bab el-Mandeb
Al-Ittihad, United Arab Emirates, September 16
Under Houthi control, Yemenis have never really known what kind of political system governs them. Is it a monarchy, a republic, or an imamate? Yemen today displays none of the clear characteristics of a recognized political system.
Yemenis have known monarchy and the imamate [the office, position, rank, or territory governed by an imam], and they have known the republic, but how are they supposed to deal with an armed group that seized the capital by surprise and governs through weapons and religious doctrine?
When the Houthis previously reached Aden, their doctrine found little acceptance, because Yemen contains different religious schools. All revere Imam Zayd ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn, who was killed in 122 AH (740 CE), but political authority was not exercised in his name, because religious doctrine alone does not establish legitimate government.
And even if the Houthis reach Bab el-Mandeb and dominate Yemen’s territorial waters, their fate would hardly be better than that of the Somali groups that once controlled those waters, turned to piracy, and were quickly defeated.
Yemenis are accustomed to political systems whose contours are clear, regardless of their qualities, but never to something as politically undefined as Houthi rule. Religious doctrine belongs to worship.
Yemenis of the Zaydi and Shafi’i schools pray in the same mosque, and even differences in the call to prayer do not divide them; each worshiper prays according to his own tradition.
The Houthis present themselves as Zaydis descended from Yemen’s imams, while some of their views are associated with the Jarudiyya, which holds that the imamate belongs to the descendants of Hassan and Hussein.
As they entered direct politics, however, they increasingly came under Hezbollah’s influence and fought a succession of wars from their stronghold in Saada.
Historically, Zaydism served as a bridge among Islamic schools: Zaydis followed Hanafi jurisprudence and Mu’tazilite theology, and accepted the possibility of the rule of the less-preferred candidate.
Yet the deeper the Houthi movement has descended into partisan politics, the further it has moved from traditional Zaydi moderation. Zayd ibn Ali himself had nothing to do with what appeared among supposed followers centuries later, after partisan ideology penetrated the movement.
Yes, Zayd was politically active and led a revolt, but anyone examining its origins will find something very different from what later revolutionary movements built upon it.
Religious and sectarian movements tend to return continually to the past, often under the banner of vengeance, and this is visible in the Houthi movement itself.
Zayd left no book setting out a doctrine of political authority, and writing was limited in his era, as it was among many early imams and jurists. Nevertheless, later generations constructed a political theory in his name and built the Zaydi school around it, with different factions disagreeing over the legitimacy of the early caliphs and the nature of succession.
Sources by major Zaydi scholars indicate that Zayd refused demands to repudiate the first and second caliphs and regarded Ali ibn Abi Talib’s succession as one of religious knowledge rather than political rule.
So where exactly do the Houthis intend to go today, as the region changes around them? Nowhere is that question more consequential than in the waters of Bab el-Mandeb, a strategic passage serving global interests and one of the world’s principal maritime routes.
How can an armed group without international recognition expect to dominate this gateway, impose its conditions, consolidate its rule over all Yemen, and threaten whomever it chooses?
Anyone familiar with the moderation of Zaydism, what has been transmitted from Imam Zayd and even the conduct of the imams who governed Yemen in his name will find no justification for an adventure in Bab el-Mandeb – or in any other international waterway.
– Rasheed al-Khayoun ■

US Marine arrested over woman’s killing in Okinawa as Japan protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:10:23 UTC
03:10:23 KST

Japan reacted with outrage Sunday after a U.S. Marine was arrested on suspicion of killing a woman at a hotel in Okinawa, the southern prefecture that hosts thousands of American troops.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Japan had formally protested to the United States over the case, while the U.S. ambassador in Tokyo was summoned for talks with Japan’s foreign minister.
The killing occurred early Saturday morning at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa Prefecture. Police identified the suspect as 20-year-old Marine Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, who is suspected of killing 39-year-old local resident Anna Yagi and stealing her wallet and bag.
Police said security footage showed Ballard entering the hotel with Yagi and later leaving alone. Kyodo News reported that her body was found inside a hotel room and that investigators suspect she was strangled.
Ballard was arrested several hours later on Saturday evening after a police officer spotted him walking alone in Naha’s entertainment district. He has denied the allegations.
Japan demands tighter discipline
The case has sparked widespread anger in Japan, where Takaichi has sought closer strategic and military cooperation with Washington since taking office last year.
“It is extremely regrettable that such a cruel and brutal incident occurred,” Takaichi said. “The Japanese government strongly protests to the U.S. side and demands maximum cooperation with the investigation.”
She also called on Washington to enforce “strict discipline” among the large number of American troops stationed in Japan.
Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned U.S. Ambassador George Glass and told him he was “outraged” by the case, according to the Japanese government.
The U.S. Marine Corps said it was fully cooperating with Japanese authorities and confirmed that the suspect was assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force in Okinawa and based at Futenma.
“The Marine Corps takes these allegations with the utmost seriousness and expects all Marines to uphold the highest standards of conduct,” it said.
Japan permanently hosts around 50,000 U.S. service members, more than any other country, and their presence is regarded by Tokyo as an important security guarantee as concerns over China continue to grow.
About half of those troops are stationed in Okinawa, Japan’s southernmost prefecture, whose location gives it major strategic importance. The islands lie relatively close to Taiwan, with one island in the prefecture only about 100 kilometers from the democratically governed island claimed by China.
Under Takaichi, Japan has been moving away from decades of strict postwar pacifism and pursuing a military buildup, much of it centered on Okinawa, a policy that has drawn sharp criticism from Beijing.
Decades of anger over US bases
But the massive American military presence in Okinawa has generated resentment among local residents for decades. Complaints range from aircraft noise and the concentration of military installations to crimes committed by U.S. service members.
One of the most notorious cases came in 1995, when three American servicemen raped a 12-year-old girl. The assault triggered huge protests demanding a reduction in the U.S. military presence on the islands.
Futenma, where the Marine now suspected in the latest case was stationed, has itself long faced local opposition because of its location in a densely populated area.
Takaichi’s government is currently advancing plans to relocate the base to a less crowded part of Okinawa’s eastern coast, but opponents have demanded that the American military leave the area altogether. The latest case could further complicate those efforts.
“The incident has caused tremendous shock and added to the fear among Okinawa residents who have already been forced to live alongside U.S. bases,” Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja said Sunday. “It is absolutely unforgivable, and we are furious.”
He said the case showed that measures previously announced by the U.S. military following crimes involving American personnel had failed to improve discipline.
“The fact that an incident like this has happened again leaves us no choice but to conclude that the U.S. military’s efforts to maintain discipline, train its personnel and take other such measures are not effective at all,” he said.
The arrest comes as Takaichi attempts to strengthen Japan’s security alliance with Washington while managing deep-rooted local opposition to the concentration of U.S. forces in Okinawa, where another serious criminal case involving an American serviceman has again brought that tension to the surface.

The publication noted that a report about the death of Roman Syromyatnikov, who had participated in the war, appeared on a local news website. He had previously been described as a possible victim of the explosion.
Syromyatnikov worked as a teacher in Novomoskovsk and regularly wrote about his students’ participation in the war. He had previously served with the airborne company of the 51st Regiment of the 106th Tula Guards Airborne Division.
In September 2025, Ukraine’s Prosecutor General’s Office published a notice of suspicion against Syromyatnikov.
According to investigators, he worked at Penal Colony No. 1 in the Tula Region and, together with other employees, subjected at least 50 Ukrainian prisoners of war to physical and psychological violence.
In particular, he is accused of beating prisoners of war with rubber batons, carpentry hammers and improvised objects, as well as torturing them with electric shocks.
“Syromyatnikov R.O., Sarichev M.D., and Silyev V.V., together with other unidentified employees of the penal colony, acting intentionally as a group, understanding that an international armed conflict has been ongoing between the Russian Federation and Ukraine since February 19, 2014, acting under the conditions of and in connection with this conflict, aware that […] was a prisoner of war, taking advantage of the victim’s defenseless condition, in violation of Articles 4, 13 and 14 of the Geneva Convention Relative to the Treatment of Prisoners of War, carrying out their criminal intent aimed at inflicting physical and psychological violence on the victim, jointly connected electrical wires from a TA-57 field telephone to the victim’s ears, hands and feet, through which they applied electric current to those areas for an extended period,” the suspicion notice said.
The incident occurred on the morning of October 2 in Novomoskovsk, Tula Region, on Druzhby Street. According to local residents, the Russian serviceman’s car was blown up while moving, after which it continued moving under its own momentum and crashed into a pole.
According to the Russian media outlet VChK-OGPU, an explosive device may have been placed under the driver’s side of the vehicle.
Footage recorded by eyewitnesses shows security forces, including members of the Russian National Guard. In comments on the Podslushano Novomoskovsk community, users reported that the road had been closed and that forensic investigators and military personnel were working at the site.
One commenter claimed there was a hole in the underbody beneath the driver’s seat. At the same time, others suggested that gas had exploded inside the vehicle.

Flydubai attempted hijack security failure exposes Israel’s deep accountability crisis - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:01:44 UTC
03:01:44 KST

On the same day that Israeli passengers heroically prevented their flydubai plane from being hijacked and crashing, Christa Pike, a convicted murderer in Tennessee, survived two lethal injections intended to execute her.
The events on Wednesday had absolutely nothing to do with one another. Their aftermath, however, offers a telling comparison.
On Saturday, the head of the Tennessee Department of Correction, Frank Strada, announced he would step down following the botched execution.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee, according to The Wall Street Journal, said he appreciated Strada’s “willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment.” He also ordered an independent review.
Strada said in a statement that he believed “this review is entirely appropriate and necessary, and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred.”
Strada did not personally prepare the pentobarbital or administer the injections. But the failure occurred in the system he headed, and he resigned. Responsibility came with the position.
The buck stopped there.
Israeli officials push away accountability
Contrast that with what has transpired in Israel following the thwarting of a terrorist attack that could have killed nearly 180 people, plunged the country into deep mourning, and possibly triggered another war.
First came the relief, the celebration, and the interviews with the passengers who jumped into action and overcame the attacker. Then came something equally familiar: the blame game.
Who was responsible for the breakdown in security that allowed a pilot reportedly dismissed from Oman’s national carrier because of his extremist views to fly an Emirati plane full of Israelis to Tel Aviv?
The public, including the hundreds of thousands of Israelis who travel on foreign airlines, deserves an answer. Whose responsibility was it to identify the threat: the Transportation Ministry’s, the Mossad’s, the Shin Bet’s (Israel Security Agency)?
Who?
Unlike in Tennessee, no one here has stepped forward to accept responsibility. Certainly, no one has resigned.
The buck, in this country, often stops nowhere.
On Saturday night, Transportation Minister Miri Regev said vetting foreign airline crews was not her ministry’s responsibility.
“Those who are supposed to identify the crew are security officials. We are not security officials,” she told KAN News. “Those who are supposed to say what the threat level is, and whether you can travel to a given destination, are security officials.”
But according to an Army Radio report on Sunday, the Shin Bet gave up responsibility for foreign-flight security in 2021.
In 2024, the state comptroller flagged the resulting security void in a confidential report, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu assigned responsibility for the matter to the Transportation Ministry in 2025.
That timeline does not, by itself, settle which body should have identified this particular Omani pilot on flydubai’s flight FZ1073 to Tel Aviv as a threat. It does, however, make Regev’s “not our responsibility” response sound very weak from the ministry entrusted with foreign-flight security.
Over the last three days, various organizations have shifted the onus onto others. Regev pointed fingers at the Mossad, saying intelligence vetting of foreign airline crews is its responsibility.
Her ministry’s Security Division said it is not an intelligence agency, did not receive the pilots’ names in advance, and relies on the foreign airlines themselves to confirm that their crews have been checked.
The Civil Aviation Authority said it handles safety, not security, and also pointed to the airline and the country of departure.
Everyone, it seems, can explain the limits of their responsibility. What remains unclear is who accepts responsibility for the gaps between where their organization’s responsibility ends and another’s begins.
The question is not whether Regev personally should have checked the pilot’s background, any more than Tennessee’s prison commissioner should personally have prepared the lethal drugs. It is whether those entrusted with overseeing a system accept responsibility when the system fails.
The passengers' success underlines officials' failure
Much has been written since Wednesday about the passengers’ heroism: their willingness to step up in danger, take their fate into their own hands, and act without waiting for someone else to do so.
This, many have said, is baked into Israel’s national DNA.
It is difficult to argue with that. The willingness of ordinary people – “a Jewish plumber,” in US President Donald Trump’s inimitable words – to put themselves at risk to save others is something this country is blessed with. It may well be a key ingredient of its survival.
But the aftermath has exposed another familiar impulse: the readiness to shrug off responsibility once an immediate danger has passed.
On Wednesday, passengers took responsibility when their lives were on the line. In the days that followed, officials explained why responsibility belonged somewhere else.
Stepping forward in a crisis seems like an Israeli characteristic. So, too, does stepping back when it comes time to take responsibility for a failure. The first reveals the best in this country. The second represents something much less noble.
Worse than not noble, this can also be dangerous. When failures produce explanations such as “it was someone else’s job,” rather than accountability, the gaps that allowed them to happen can remain. Everyone returns to their own corner, and the public is left hoping that next time, too, someone will act heroically.
That is neither a plan of action nor any way to run a security system.
And the tone starts at the top.
Netanyahu, Eisenkot owe accountability
When Netanyahu does not accept responsibility for policies that led to the October 7 massacre, points instead to the failure to wake him in time, and refuses to establish a state commission of inquiry, the message travels well beyond the Prime Minister’s Office.
Those farther down the chain can draw their own conclusions about what leadership requires after a failure.
But this is not only about Netanyahu.
“Anyone who fears the word ‘responsibility’ and has, since October 7, evaded an investigation into the truth about the worst disaster we have suffered endangers Israel every day through failures and grave disasters,” Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot wrote on X/Twitter on Saturday. “We received proof of this just last week, when 180 Israelis were saved only thanks to resourcefulness and extraordinary heroism, in what is increasingly emerging as a terrible failure under the October 7 government.”
Netanyahu’s government has “deliberately instilled” in the public sector a culture of evading responsibility, whitewashing, and lying, he added.
Eisenkot’s demand for accountability is justified, but it applies to him as well.
As IDF chief of staff from 2015 to 2019, he was a partner to the ingrained idea that Hamas could be deterred and the Gaza conflict managed. He defended restraint and warned against being drawn into an unnecessary war. He was a senior participant in shaping that approach and bears a share of responsibility for its assumptions.
Since he left the army four years before the October 7 massacre, he does not bear the same responsibility as those in power and in command that day. Still, demanding that others account for their failures carries an obligation to account fully for his own.
Accountability cannot depend on which political camp someone belongs to. Nor can it mean pointing to another official with even greater responsibility.
Leaders lead by personal example. When those at the top evade responsibility, why should anyone farther down the chain behave differently?
And when the public sees no personal consequences for failures in systems entrusted to senior officials, why should it believe those systems will change?
Israel is blessed with people willing to take responsibility when danger strikes. It needs leaders willing to do the same when the systems they oversee fail.
Correcting those failures begins with acknowledging what went wrong and establishing who was responsible. As long as everyone insists that someone else dropped the ball, the public has little reason to believe the system will be fixed.

‘There was nobody in the cockpit’: Israeli passenger reconstructs flydubai attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:01:06 UTC
03:01:06 KST

“There was nobody in the cockpit,” Tal says, almost matter-of-factly. Then comes the next part: “I had to shake the pilots.”
And after the aircraft was back under control: “We put an Israeli guard on every crew member.”
Several days after the attack aboard a flydubai flight bound for Israel, those three sentences help fill in what happened inside the aircraft during the moments that remain hardest to reconstruct.
Tal, an Israeli businessman who lives abroad, met with The Jerusalem Post Editor-in-Chief Zvika Klein at the Carlton hotel on Tel Aviv’s beachfront, overlooking the city skyline, to walk through the sequence and review footage from inside the aircraft.
Tal remarked on how strange it felt to see Tel Aviv from there. The previous day, he and the other passengers had been desperate simply to land and finally reach Israel.
He had been sitting in row six, directly behind business class. Two additional flydubai pilots were seated nearby as passengers.
Tal noticed them when he boarded.
“I’m a frequent traveler,” he said. “I realized immediately when I boarded the flight that they are next to me.”
That observation became crucial when the crisis began.
According to Tal, there was a period during the confrontation when nobody was in the cockpit. One pilot had been wounded, another was involved in the fight, and the aircraft was descending.
The two men capable of taking control were still sitting among the passengers.
Tal shouted at them to move.
They did not, he said.
“I had to shake them to get them to move to the front and take control of the plane, because it was diving.”
One eventually went forward and took control, while the second took longer to recover from the shock, Tal said.
He has consistently played down his own role. In an earlier WhatsApp exchange with the Post from Saudi Arabia, he described what he had done as “combat support,” while emphasizing that three other Israelis had physically subdued the attacker.
That “support” included getting the pilots forward and helping find something to restrain the attacker.
The solution was improvised.
Charging cables.
“In the desert, every thorn is a flower,” Tal wrote.
An Israeli dentist meanwhile treated the wounded pilot, whom Tal described as being in serious condition.
‘We’re running the flight now’
According to Tal, the next stage began after the attacker had been subdued and pilots were back in the cockpit.
The Israeli passengers still did not know whether the danger was over.
Tal said they moved crew members away from the immediate scene and told them: “From now on, we’re running the flight.”
They then placed an Israeli beside each crew member.
While reviewing footage with Klein, Tal explained the thinking behind that decision.
“All the Israelis are aligned that we should have only Israelis in key points,” he said.
He was particularly concerned about the cockpit.
“That’s a point when I’m trying to make sure that you have an Israeli in the cockpit.”
The passengers were improvising a security system in real time.
There was no formal chain of command and no plan. People simply took on roles.
Some fought the attacker. Tal dealt with the pilots. The dentist treated the wounded. Others watched crew members and secured what Tal called “key points.”
The footage reviewed during the interview showed fragments of that period.
Flight attendants moved through the cabin. A man with blood on his clothing passed through the frame. Tal himself could be seen near the front.
“This is me looking at... trying to understand what’s going on,” he said.
He remembers the event primarily through tasks.
Get the pilots forward.
Find restraints.
Secure the cockpit.
Work out who is where.
Tal said he had very little sense of time.
“I was also... in acting mode, like doing things,” he said. “So I didn’t really notice the time.”
There was one moment, however, when he stopped.
A girl’s father was among the Israelis fighting the attacker. Tal remembered her screaming that she did not want him to die.
“That was the only moment when I stopped and thought about my own children.”
Tal had been traveling alone. His children live abroad and at the time did not yet know what had happened.
Days later, Tal remains careful about what he did and did not witness.
When reports circulated that the attacker had shouted “Allahu akbar,” Tal said he had heard no such thing despite standing close to the cockpit.
“None of us heard it.”
His account remains that of an eyewitness, and parts of the sequence require independent corroboration.
But the details he describes offer a clearer picture of the minutes after the initial violence: an empty cockpit, pilots still sitting among passengers, improvised restraints, a dentist treating the wounded, and Israeli passengers assigning themselves positions until the aircraft was safely on the ground.
