Republican-aligned actors issued nearly three-quarters of fact-checked 2024 election hoaxes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:00:38 UTC
03:00:38 KST

During the 2024 United States presidential election, political actors and anonymous online users regularly spread false information as an open campaign strategy. A recent study identifies who promoted these hoaxes and who was targeted, revealing that political figures and regular citizens approach the creation of fake content in distinct ways. The research was published in American Behavioral Scientist.
False narratives in politics can distort public perception and erode trust in democratic systems. The spread of fabricated claims often spikes during election seasons, when voters are paying close attention to public discourse.
In the past decade, digital platforms have made it easier for people to circulate misleading material. Disinformation is characterized by the intentional spread of false content to gain a strategic advantage or cause harm.
Much of the academic research on this topic has focused on the content of fake news stories or how fast they travel across the internet. Fewer studies have examined the specific people generating and fielding these falsehoods.
Understanding the individuals who launch unverified claims and the people they target helps build a better picture of modern political communication. Alba Córdoba-Cabús and Andreu Casero-Ripollés, communication researchers at the Universitat Jaume I in Spain, led the recent project. They wanted to categorize the spreaders of political hoaxes, known as issuers, and the subjects of those hoaxes, known as recipients.
The researchers analyzed a sample of 374 false messages related to the 2024 U.S. presidential election. They collected these items from PolitiFact, a prominent journalistic organization that verifies political claims. The analyzed period spanned from January 2024 through the presidential inauguration in January 2025.
For each verified hoax, the research team systematically categorized multiple details. They recorded the channel where the message appeared, the specific topic, and the exact type of falsehood. They also identified the political affiliations and public roles of both the people spreading the claims and the people the claims were about.
In more than 90 percent of the cases, the team could readily identify the person or group issuing the false statement. Spreading falsehoods appears to be a normalized, public tactic rather than a secretive operation. People generating this content did not typically try to hide their identities.
The researchers suggest this reflects a political environment where actors do not fear being penalized by voters for sharing unverified claims. Anonymous online users were the most common source, responsible for nearly 40 percent of the false messages. Political candidates and celebrities or internet influencers tied for the second most common sources.
Each of these latter groups accounted for roughly 16 percent of the items. The data revealed an association between the type of person sharing the claim and the medium they used to share it. Anonymous users and influencers relied almost exclusively on social media platforms to circulate their messages.
Political candidates and public officials took a different approach. They distributed unverified claims across a wider variety of channels, including campaign rallies, television interviews, and press releases. This strategy suggests an effort to reach voters across many different formats, rather than relying solely on internet algorithms.
The subject matter of the hoaxes also varied depending on who was talking. Politicians tended to center their false statements around public policies, such as the economy, immigration, and crime.
Conversely, anonymous users and influencers focused heavily on the mechanics of the campaign itself. Their posts frequently targeted the voting process, polling numbers, or the private lives of political figures.
The study found differences in the mechanics of the deception. Political actors often used misleading content, which involves twisting real statistics or misinterpreting data to fit a specific narrative.
Anonymous users and influencers more frequently relied on false context. This occurs when real images, videos, or quotes are shared alongside fabricated background details to change their original meaning.
When looking at political affiliations, actors aligned with the Republican party issued about 73 percent of the hoaxes. Democratic actors were responsible for roughly 22 percent of the unverified claims in the sample.
Most of this fake content was designed to attack political rivals. Candidates were the primary targets, appearing as the subject in 38 percent of the analyzed items. Democratic figures were on the receiving end of about 57 percent of the falsehoods, while Republicans were targeted by about 22 percent.
The researchers also identified a growing trend of constructive disinformation. While false claims are traditionally used as attacks, Republican actors directed nearly 20 percent of their false claims at their own party or candidate in a positive manner. These messages were intended to inflate accomplishments or bolster public support, rather than tear down an opponent.
Democratic actors used this same supportive tactic, though at a lower rate of roughly 7 percent. This highlights an evolution in political deception. It shows that fake news is not strictly used as an offensive weapon against adversaries, but can also act as an artificial booster to make a candidate appear more attractive to the electorate.
The findings rely on data collected by a single fact-checking organization. Because fact-checkers cannot review every questionable statement made during an election, the sample likely does not capture all the unverified content that circulated online. The study is based on a specific subset of verified falsehoods rather than the entirety of the internet’s political discourse.
The study focuses entirely on the 2024 U.S. presidential election. The communication tactics observed in this specific political environment might not translate to other countries or local political races. Future studies will need to examine elections in different global regions to see if these patterns hold steady across different political systems.
The study, “Actors of Disinformation: Issuers and Recipients of Hoaxes in the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election,” was authored by Alba Córdoba-Cabús and Andreu Casero-Ripollés.

Nearly all women who try to reach the UK in small boats from northern France have been raped on their journey, Shabana Mahmood has claimed.
In an interview with The Rest Is Politics podcast, the home secretary said far-right, balaclava-wearing activists would “kill” or “kick me out of my own country” if they took power.
Speaking to the former Tory minister Rory Stewart and Tony Blair’s former close adviser Alastair Campbell, she said sexual abusers would exploit most asylum seekers as long as traffickers continued to decide who came to the UK.
She said: “We’re not in control of this border. The sifting of the people that end up in the north of France and are about to get on a dinghy is done by criminal gangs who are also, by the way, people traffickers.
“You can almost guarantee that every woman that’s in the north of France has probably been raped along the journey. Some of the men too, they’ve certainly been abused and threatened. That is not the model that should decide whether somebody gets to come to the UK, make this their place of sanctuary and ultimately become one of us.”
Asked by Campbell about balaclava-wearing protesters shutting down ports and praising her policies, she said they should “sod off”.
She added: “They’re just troublemakers. You know, they’d kill me in a minute if they could, and they’d definitely kick me out of my own country. So let’s just be really clear about who and what they are. They don’t think I’m a true Brit and they hate the fact that I’m a Muslim.”
Mahmood also said she considered herself “part of the pro-Palestinian cause” and felt “very uncomfortable” over the arrests of activists opposing the ban imposed on Palestine Action.
Merseyside police arrested 82 people on Monday at the Labour party conference on suspicion of wearing or carrying articles supporting a proscribed organisation.
In a protest organised by Defend Our Juries, scores of people sat outside the conference centre in Liverpool, many holding handmade banners saying they supported Palestine Action.
Mahmood said: “For those of us who have been in the pro-Palestinian cause all of our lives, these are people – sometimes you’ll know who they are, you know, you’ve been on the marches with them – it feels very uncomfortable to see them falling foul of section 13 of the Terrorism Act.”
However, she defended enforcing the ban, regardless of her views: “You’ve got to be able to apply your principles, even when it’s uncomfortable for you, because you’re going to really want to apply them when it’s something you, you know, with your whole heart, are feeling very passionately about.”
Authorities were preparing on Sunday for the arrival of a migrant dinghy heading for the south coast. The boat was being shadowed by French coastguard and rescue vessels and moving toward the Channel boundary line, according to ship tracking data.
It appeared to have set off from near the Utah Beach area of Normandy on Sunday morning.
Caroline Dinenage, the Conservative MP for Gosport in Hampshire, said there was “nothing to suggest” the boat would land on the county’s coast but police were “making preparations should that situation change”.
A government spokesperson said: “The Border Security Command works around the clock to monitor the Channel and protect our border. It is vital we continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival.”
Imran Hussain, a director at the Refugee Council, welcomed the home secretary’s acknowledgment of widespread sexual violence, but questioned why the government had closed safe and legal routes which could help asylum seekers avoid falling into the hands of predators.
“We know from our services that women and girls fleeing war and persecution face sexual violence both in the conflicts they have escaped and on the journeys they are forced to make in search of safety,” he said.
“That is why in welcoming the government’s announcement last week of new safe routes we called for them not to be limited to a few hundred people. Last year the government closed family reunion, the safe route for refugees which overwhelmingly benefits women and children.
“It is entirely right to talk about the dangers women face on these journeys but we should not be closing the safe routes that could keep them out of harm’s way. Protecting women means more safe routes, not fewer.”

Study links anti-trans content to worse mental health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Study links exposure to anti-trans content with mental health harms
In short:
In a new study, trans and gender-diverse people described the stigma they encountered online and in traditional media as "relentless" and "inescapable".
The study linked frequent exposure to anti-trans stigma with negative mental health outcomes.
What's next?
A government spokesperson says it is strengthening its cyberbullying and cyber-abuse schemes, but the study's lead researcher wants more action.
An Australian study has linked more frequent exposure to anti-trans stigma with statistically higher rates of anxiety, depression, self-harm thoughts and suicidal thoughts.
In Australia, trans and gender-diverse people experience poor mental health outcomes than the general population, and this gap has widened over the past 22 years.
As social media has continued to integrate itself into modern life, the study's lead author River Zwickl said they wanted to understand more about the impact anti-trans content had on a person's mental health.
For the study, published in Frontiers of Public Health, the team surveyed 807 trans and gender-diverse people aged 16 and over, some of whom described the stigma they encountered online or in traditional media as "relentless", "omnipresent" and "inescapable".
"We found that anti-trans content in the news and social media is close to unavoidable," said Dr Zwickl, a University of Melbourne researcher.
"Over 70 per cent of people we surveyed had seen or heard anti-trans remarks online multiple times weekly in the previous month."
Dr Zwickl said, as someone who was trans, the results were not surprising.
"It's something that I experience personally as well."
Three in four trans participants had cut back on news media to avoid harmful content.
This, Dr Zwickl said, meant they also missed out on valuable online connections and keeping informed.
Negative exposure and mental health
Researchers asked participants about whether they saw any anti-trans remarks online or in the news media, and if so, how often.
They then compared the mental health outcomes for people who were exposed to anti-trans stigma multiple times a week and people exposed less frequently.
People who had seen or heard about anti-trans remarks in the news media, multiple times weekly, compared to those who had experienced this less often, were:
- 37 per cent more likely to report anxiety
- 25 per cent more likely to report depression
- 23 per cent more likely to report self-harm ideation
- 38 per cent more likely to report self-harm behaviour
- 33 per cent more likely to report suicidal Ideation
- 43 per cent more likely to report suicide planning.
Dr Zwickl said the correlation was "extraordinary".
"It's certainly one of the highest, most clear findings in that respect between looking at an exposure [to anti-trans context] and [mental health] outcomes," they said.
Estimates from the Australian Bureau of Statistics suggest nearly 1 per cent of Australians, about 178,900 Australians, are trans and gender-diverse.
Dr Zwickl said given the relatively small percentage of trans and gender-diverse people living in Australia, their cohort of 807 was a representative sample and they would expect similar results in a larger cohort.
Damien Riggs, professor in social work at Flinders University, who did not contribute to the study, agreed.
Although the research did not prove causation, Professor Riggs said the strong association supported clinical observations.
"What it does is name something we already knew clinically, we already knew in the community," he said.
"When trans people are exposed to higher rates of discrimination in any form, it has negative impacts to their mental health."
Study points to potential solutions
Avery (not their real name) was one of the 807 people who took part in the study.
He said while there had "always" been a lot of anti-trans content online, the amount of negative content on social media appeared to have either increased or become more prominent in the past 12 months.
"It's deeply unpleasant and often quite upsetting," he said.
Avery said he was concerned about the impact this content had on others, especially young trans and gender-diverse people and their families.
Dr Zwickl said there were a few things on a policy level that could improve outcomes for trans and gender-diverse people.
Specifically, they wanted media outlets to be held accountable for publishing anti-trans information and for social media platforms to introduce greater protections for minority groups.
Australia's broadcast radio industry codes, which have recently been updated, state material cannot incite hatred, serious contempt or sever ridicule towards a person or group because of attributes including transgender status.
But Dr Zwickl wants the codes strengthened, with serious penalties for non-compliance.
In a statement, a spokesperson for the Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts said the government was strengthening its cyberbullying and cyber-abuse schemes.
Part of this, they said, would give the eSafety commissioner power to respond more quickly to such content.
They also said Australia's proposed digital duty of care laws would force online service providers to be "proactive" in preventing harm rather than putting the onus on users to report harm after it had occurred.

Zelensky: European politicians should support Ukraine even from pragmatic perspective

Zelensky: European politicians should support Ukraine even from pragmatic perspective
The head of state expressed this view during a conversation with the media, according to Ukrinform.
Zelensky noted that Ukraine has good relations with its partners, but some political parties in those countries oppose supporting Kyiv. According to him, it is up to the societies of other countries to determine their own policies, but Ukraine sees risks to itself and is engaging with political forces and governments in those countries, particularly Germany.
“It’s important that today the majority of the German people are on our side. That helps. But what will happen tomorrow? I don’t know. However, it’s also in Germany’s own interest to prevent more ‘Leipzigs’ [referring to the sabotage at Leipzig Airport] and not to support Putin,” the President said.
He explained: when the Kremlin leader supports someone, it may seem like a path to establishing dialogue, but it will only work for a short time.
“Because if you’re not strong, the Russians won’t respect you. If you’re not strong enough, they’ll try to break you. If you’re weak, they will inevitably break you and occupy you. That is the situation we find ourselves in,” the politician emphasized.
Zelensky also believes that European politicians should support Ukraine even from a pragmatic standpoint, since otherwise they will have to deal with the Russians on their own.
“There is no war right now in Germany, Poland, the Czech Republic, or the Baltic states. Is that a bad thing? It’s wonderful that there’s no war there. It really is wonderful. So let’s preserve this situation. Let’s support Ukraine,” the head of state stressed.
As reported by Ukrinform, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered near a Ukrainian An-124 transport aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport; police specialists subsequently defused it.

Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito has "thought about" retiring after the high court's last term but decided against it, believing he could still make "a valuable contribution," he said in an interview with CBS News.
Alito, 76, is the second-oldest justice on the bench, and speculation had swirled that he would retire while Republicans control the Senate and the White House — when the chances of swiftly confirming a GOP-backed candidate to the bench would be high.
The possibility that the Senate could flip to Democrats after November's midterm election may make confirmation of any potential nominee of President Donald Trump more difficult or impossible if Democrats control the Senate.
"I've been bemused by the retirement speculation; it's not too pleasant to look up and see the vultures circling," Alito said in a separate interview with "Fox News Sunday." "I don't have a calculation for it ... I think it would be foolhardy to make a calculation [that] I'm going to serve for a certain number of additional years."
Alito's status as one of the court's most conservative justices has sparked the speculation that he would retire ahead of the midterms — a decision the justice ultimately has not made. Should Democrats take control of the Senate, they would effectively have veto power over a Supreme Court nomination.
Justice Clarence Thomas, 78 — the court's oldest justice and a member of its conservative bloc — has also been on retirement watch.
The politics and timing of Supreme Court vacancies have been closely watched since Justice Antonin Scalia died in 2016. Then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell refused to take up President Barack Obama's nomination of Merrick Garland to the Supreme Court until after the 2016 presidential election, allowing Trump the time to nominate and confirm Justice Neil Gorsuch.
Then, after Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg died in 2020, McConnell moved quickly to confirm Trump's nominee, Amy Coney Barrett, just over a week before the 2020 presidential election.
The Court is now controlled by a 6-3 conservative majority.
Democrats currently hold an edge in national House polling and in the CBS News Battleground Tracker model, which estimates a narrow Democratic majority after the midterm election, which looms just 30 days away. The Senate is also now in play, with Republicans locked in unexpectedly tight races across the country amid voter ire over prices and the economy.
Democrats need to net at least four seats while defending all the seats they currently have to win a Senate majority.

What happens to Israel if Arab citizens lose their political representation? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
17:44:42 UTC
02:44:42 KST

A non-Jewish, non-Christian friend who has no ax to grind against either Jews or Muslims has friends in both circles.
One Jewish friend whom he describes as “a friendly radical” is vehemently anti-Arab, and whenever the two meet for lunch, he embarks on a rant about how all Arabs are killers who want to murder all the Jews.
My friend listens, then gently changes the subject, whereupon there is a change in the demeanor of the friendly radical, whose anger dissipates.
On one occasion, the rant became too much for my friend to tolerate, and he asked the friendly radical what his reaction would be if he repeated exactly what had been said but substituted the word Jew for Arab.
The friendly radical was taken aback, but didn’t argue. He merely stopped his rant.
But he is far from being the only Israeli Jew who is anti-Arab.
There is a move afoot by right-wing parties to disqualify the Arab parties from running in the Knesset elections. Such a measure is unlikely to succeed, though individual Arab politicians have been disqualified in the past.
To disqualify citizens who have done nothing to endanger the state, and whose only “sins” are to support the notion of a Palestinian state and to refuse to publicly say that Hamas is a terrorist organization, is totally undemocratic.
We should remember that 80 years ago, secular Jews who did not believe in the Bible and were Jews in name only were among the most active campaigners for a Jewish state, even though there had not been one for two millennia.
So why should Palestinians who were born in Israel, and whose parents, grandparents, and great-grandparents were born in what was British Mandate Palestine, not campaign for a Palestinian state?
It may be argued that Mandate Palestine was not a Palestinian state. It was under Ottoman rule for 400 years, and before that, the region was ruled by a series of foreign conquerors, and at one stage by the Hasmoneans, who were equivalent to the Jewish people.
There never was a Palestinian state as such, but Palestinians did hold high positions in the land, and some can trace their Israel-Palestine ancestry back to the 14th century.
As for calling Hamas a terrorist organization, the reluctance is born out of fear. We do not know how many Hamas operatives live in Israel. The high rate of violence and killings in the Arab sector is usually attributed to criminal gangs and feuds between families.
But it’s possible that some may also be related to criticism of Hamas.
Some Israeli broadcast journalists, when interviewing Arab politicians, persist in asking, “Why can’t you say that Hamas is a terrorist organization?”
The question may be asked repeatedly in the course of an interview, even though the politician may have publicly condemned the October 7 attack and called for the release of hostages in Gaza.
The interviewer doesn’t take into account that the politician may have relatives in Gaza, and that any criticism of Hamas on his part will put the lives of his relatives at risk.
Getting back to the attempt to disqualify Arab parties from running in the Knesset elections, what would happen if a domino effect were to follow if such a proposal is accepted?
Arab contributions to Israeli society
First and foremost, it would affect the Arab vote. Then let’s suppose that all Arabs working in Israeli enterprises would go on strike. Arabs serve as doctors, nurses, judges, lawyers, technologists, construction workers, street sweepers, and more.
In other words, they occupy positions at all levels of society and community.
How would it affect the country if they all stopped working? Some of Israel’s leading medical experts are Arabs.
That’s not surprising, as medicine and law are among the two most sought-after professions by minorities seeking a foothold in mainstream society.
Children and grandchildren of semi-literates who migrated to New York’s Lower East Side became prominent in medicine, law, economics, and academia, and in Israel the ratio of Arabs in medical professions is higher than in the overall population. Visit any hospital to check.
What would we do without them? As things stand, Israel suffers from a severe shortage of medical professionals.
An inferno can start by striking a single match. A single dislodged rock can start an avalanche. A collapsed building can cause damage to an entire neighborhood. By depriving the Arab sector of representation in the Knesset, we may be creating a demographic tsunami.
Instead of progressing, we will be regressing, and may be responsible for what future historians will call “the destruction of the Third Temple.”
We are already on that path by allowing Israeli anarchists to continue engaging in violent persecution of Palestinian villagers. This is outright racism. It goes against the principles of both Judaism and Zionism. Allowing it to continue is outrageous.
These anarchists are Jewish terrorists and should be punished in the same way that Arab terrorists are punished. Terrorism is terrorism is terrorism.
Terrorism is not mitigated by religious, national, or ethnic pride. Terrorism is a vicious, inhuman act that must be dealt with accordingly.

Jewish-Arab families show how Israeli identities are changing - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
17:44:32 UTC
02:44:32 KST

A while back, I met an Israeli woman from a mixed family: one parent Jewish, the other Arab.
Her background struck me less than her way of thinking and how she saw Israeli society and the region. She does not fit neatly into the boxes we tend to use from far away.
How should we describe her: by her father’s side, her mother’s, or just as Israeli?
The question probably tells us more about our own habits than about who she is. We are trying to squeeze someone shaped by a different social reality into molds built by a decades-long conflict.
That meeting prompted me to look at Israeli society in a new way. It is deeply diverse, and its communities hold on to their religious, national, and cultural identities.
But decades of living in the same state have loosened the boundaries between them in daily life, much more than politics and the conflict would have you believe.
We, in the Arab world, usually see Israel through the lens of war, the Palestinian-Israeli conflict, the army, and the government. Those are real and fundamental. But they are only part of the picture.
Behind them is everyday life, built over generations among Jews, Arabs, Druze, Christians, and Muslims, and even within each of those categories, among groups that differ in origin and how they define themselves.
Israel holds a strange tension. Religion runs deep in the structure of society and the state, while liberal norms shape social, cultural, and economic life.
Plenty of problems, gaps, and disputes remain, and there is no reason to deny them or romanticize what exists.
Even so, spaces of citizenship and shared life have opened up. They have allowed Arab citizens to become doctors, judges, university professors, and members of the Knesset, and, in some communities, officers and soldiers.
Diversity of Arabs in Israel
The phrase “Arabs in Israel” also conceals more diversity than it suggests. There are Israeli Palestinians for whom Palestinian identity sits at the core of who they are. There are Bedouins, Druze, Christians, and Muslims.
Some families have roots in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, and beyond. Some see themselves as Arab and Israeli, some as Palestinian and Israeli, and some put their Israeli identity first.
This does not match the story that parts of the traditional Arab media have settled on: the Arab in Israel as a citizen with no real belonging to the state.
The reality is more complicated. Recent polls show that a large majority of Arabs in Israel would rather stay in the State of Israel even if they had the chance to live in a Western country.
Interviews and public statements also reveal Arab Israelis who see staying in Israel as preferable to moving to an Arab country. These positions fall short of satisfaction, but they point to something real: Arab origin and Israeli identity can coexist.
What interests me most is not this overlap in its political or civic form, but the moment it enters the family itself. Marriage between Jews and Arabs in Israel is still limited, and the religious and social barriers around it are strong on both sides.
It would be wrong to present it as a broad demographic trend, or to talk about a large generation about to transform society. Its value lies less in the numbers than in what it says: that shared life can produce identities the old divisions fit poorly.
A person born to a Jewish father and an Arab mother, or the other way around, carries inside one home what the conflict has always presented as two separate worlds.
Such a person may hear Arabic and Hebrew, know Jewish and Arab relatives, and grow up moving between two cultures and two memories, maybe more than one religion or social tradition.
The Arab side might be Palestinian Israeli, Druze, Bedouin, or from a family with other Arab roots. For this person, the line between “us” and “them” can run inside the home rather than outside it. Sometimes it runs right through the family tree.
MY VIEW shifted after I met that woman. Her significance lies not in representing a large demographic segment, for she represents no such thing, but in her being a model of a human being produced by Israeli society itself.
The old definitions no longer describe such a person easily. I see no point in deciding whether she is an Arab Jew or a Jewish Arab.
What matters is that she is an Israeli with a composite identity, and the way she was formed says something about the society that raised her.
The October 7 massacre put this idea to a much harsher test. The attack did not spare Arab citizens who were in the areas that were hit. Arabs were killed, among them Israeli Palestinians and Bedouins, and others were taken hostage.
At the same time, Arab citizens joined rescue and defense efforts, and soldiers and officers from the Druze and Bedouin communities helped protect towns and fight.
When danger comes, identity stops being abstract. A person can keep their Arab origin or Palestinian identity and still see Israel as the state where they live. Defending its citizens means defending their family, their home, their future.
For people from mixed marriages, this becomes even more layered, because, for them, a Jew and an Arab were never two completely separate worlds. Both were always there – in the family and in their own formation.
So, I would say it is inaccurate to describe these people as a generation of peace. One of them might be right-wing or left-wing, nationalist or liberal, for the government or against it. Mixed marriage does not produce uniform politics nor immunity from the conflicts the society is going through.
This generation complicates the traditional map of the conflict. Political discourse usually needs fixed boundaries: this one is Jewish, that one is Arab. This one is Israeli, that one is Palestinian. These are here, those are there.
Inside mixed families, those boundaries can pass through the same house, sometimes through a single person’s identity.
That is why, I think, Jewish-Arab marriage matters less for its current size than for what it means. It shows that decades of living in one society can, even amid conflict and tension, produce people that a single word cannot adequately describe.
The paradox is that politics and the media can go on describing Jews and Arabs as two separate worlds, while life itself, even in small numbers, keeps producing people who belong, in varying degrees, to both.
The conflict and disagreements are not going anywhere. But that reality makes complete separation between identities harder to sustain as conditions slowly shift within society.
Perhaps what will matter in the future is not the number of these marriages, but what they produce: people who see no need to make a forced choice among the parts of their identity.
And what happens to a conflict when the boundaries it rests on no longer run cleanly between people, but start running through their identities, their families, their everyday lives?
The writer is a UAE political analyst and former Federal National Council candidate.

Cornell University has recently been under fire in various headlines and on social media for its light punishments for the seven men who allegedly gang-raped Jane Doe in 2024.
However, recent reporting from the New York Times, citing detailed discipline summaries, 1,000 pages of interview transcripts, police reports, and other records gathered by Cornell investigators, shows the initial punishments the university gave each of the seven accused Chi Phi fraternity members in a closed proceeding.
The lawsuit filed by Jane Doe added fuel to the fire online when it stated that the accused were “afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell.”
The university has said that the characterization of the punishments is inaccurate.
How did Cornell punish seven fraternity members accused of sexual assault?
Notably, none of the seven accused men were ever criminally charged. All seven have also denied any wrongdoing.
Their fraternity, Chi Phi, was barred from campus.
The Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office declined to prosecute the case in 2024.
But Jane Doe said that the incident left her “destroyed” and “utterly ashamed,” in recently released text messages to a member of Chi Phi.
Cornell opened a closed disciplinary investigation into the matter. A three-member panel, which enforces federal civil rights at the university under Title IX provisions, was appointed to dole out punishments. The NYT noted that the panel did not conclude that Jane Doe was sexually assaulted by all seven of the men she has accused.
The lightest of the punishments doled out were “reflection papers” and sexual misconduct trainings. The most severe was expulsion from Cornell.
What happened between Jane Doe and the Cornell 7?
In October 2024, Jane Doe went to the Chi Phi fraternity house to visit Matthew Ingalls. Once she was there, he asked her if she wanted to have a threesome with Jonathan Newell.
Once she was there, both men gave her alcohol and ketamine. Jane Doe has consistently stated that, because she was severely intoxicated, she was unable to give consent to any sexual act.
After that encounter, other men engaged in sexual acts with her without her consent after Newell sent a Snapchat message saying that there was “free p*ssy upstairs.”
Jane Doe told police in November 2024 that Newell left bruises on her buttocks and manipulated her into taking ketamine.
At one point, when she was near hallucinating, other men entered to have sex with her.
Both Ingalls and Newell were expelled from Cornell and were found responsible for sexual assault.
Ingalls, in particular, was found to be willing to “manipulate, exploit and endanger Jane Doe for his own self-interest and the entertainment of others,” the NYT reported, citing Cornell discipline summaries.
Winston Lee and Gillio Lopes were given suspensions and disciplinary probation for their alleged part in the rape.
Jane Doe accused Lee of snorting ketamine off of her and forcing oral sex on her without her consent. She accused Lopes of having sex with her without her consent.
Lee was given a two-year suspension from campus with multiple semesters of disciplinary probation.
Lopes was given a three-semester suspension and two years of probation.
Both men were given an order not to contact Jane Doe, were required to take a course on sexual harassment, and write “reflection papers.”
Diego Sarabia was issued a persona non-grata order by the university; he had graduated by the time of the discipline panel’s ruling.
Jane Doe accused Sarabia of kissing her without her consent.
He was banned from campus for three years.
Jane Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said in a statement on Friday that the punishments “did not reflect the severity of the charges.”
The final two men, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar, were accused of entering the room where Jane Doe was undressed on the bed after Newell’s Snapchat message.
They were ordered not to contact Jane Doe, to study sexual harassment, social media use, and bystander intervention, and also had to write “reflection papers.”
Kretzschmar was specifically not found responsible for sexual assault, the NYT added, but Cornell said he did commit attempted sexual exploitation.
Jeremy Saland, Kretzschmar’s lawyer, said that his client was “never accused of, nor found responsible for, rape,” in response to a request for comment from the NYT.
“He was not even present during any sexual activity,” Saland added.
Lawyers, family members, and direct requests for commentary to any other former member of Chi Phi from the NYT either went unanswered or were denied.
Jane Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said in a Friday statement that the punishments Cornell gave the seven men “did not reflect the severity of the charges.”
“With the exception of two of these men, all of them will be able to graduate with a Cornell diploma and live their lives reaping the benefits of this coveted degree,” Giuffra said. “In contrast, as of today, it is doubtful whether Ms. Doe will even graduate from college or ever live a normal life due to what these men did to her.”

Syria condemns Israel's 'violations' of its sovereignty

02:44:05 KST

Syria on Sunday condemned Israel’s continued “violations” of Syrian territory, Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), Syria’s official news agency, reported.
It accused Israel of creating a new line of control inside Syria called the “Sufa 53 Line,” the report said.
Israel took over an area of Syrian territory on December 8, 2024, when the Assad regime fell.
The IDF has continued to operate in this area, which runs along part of the 1974 ceasefire line, essentially extending control into a buffer zone that had existed before. Previously, it was administered by the Syrian regime and patrolled by the UN.
“The Syrian Arab Republic on Sunday condemned in the strongest terms the ongoing violations committed by the Israeli occupation against Syrian territory, the latest of which was the completion of work on the so-called ‘Sufa 53 Line,’ in flagrant violation of the 1974 Disengagement Agreement and international law,” SANA reported.
This is one of several recent indications that Syria is increasingly concerned about Israel’s role in the area, which the IDF conquered in 2024. Israel also seized the peak of Mount Hermon. Israeli officials have said the area will not be returned to Syria.
Almost 300 Israeli 'incursions' into Syrian territory in single month
Syrian media outlets frequently accuse Israel of carrying out raids inside Syrian villages and shelling them near the buffer zone. There have been more than 1,300 Israeli “incursions,” including 280 in September, Syrian news site Levant24 recently reported.
Israeli officials over the past year have accused the Syrian government of being “jihadists” and predicted that Israel and Turkey will clash over Syria.
The Syrian Foreign Ministry “said the continued aggressive approach of the Israeli occupation, along with its attacks and field incursions, constitutes a direct threat to regional security and stability and undermines international law,” SANA reported. “The ministry called on the international community to assume its responsibilities and take effective deterrent measures to put an end to these violations and prevent their recurrence.”
Syria wants to see the international community pressure Israel more on this issue. It would like to see the border area demarcated and stabilized.
Israel has demanded that Syria demilitarize the areas in southern Syria near the border. Without Syrian Interior Ministry forces along the border line, there has been low-level chaos since 2024. This has also led to a power vacuum.
Syria said it detained a Hezbollah cell in the Yarmouk Basin near the Golan last week. This area is also near the Jordanian border.
Syria appears to believe that rather than reaching an agreement with Damascus, Israel is entrenching itself in Syria.
“Israeli forces resumed excavation west of al-Asha village in southern Quneitra as part of a project launched in mid-2022 inside the 1974 buffer zone,” Levant24 reported on October 4. “The works include an eight-meter military road, five-meter berms, trenches, and observation posts toward the Golan Heights.”
Israeli, Syrian officials met in Paris this year
The US had worked on an agreement between Israel and Syria toward the end of 2025 and early 2026.
On January 6, the US State Department said: “Under the auspices of the United States, senior Israeli and Syrian officials met in Paris. President Donald J. Trump’s leadership in the Middle East enabled productive discussions, centered on respect for Syria’s sovereignty and stability, Israel’s security, and prosperity for both countries. The State of Israel and the Syrian Arab Republic (the “Sides”) have reached the following understandings.”
“The Sides reaffirm their commitment to strive toward achieving lasting security and stability arrangements for both countries,” it said. “Both Sides have decided to establish a joint fusion mechanism – a dedicated communication cell – to facilitate immediate and ongoing coordination on their intelligence sharing, military de-escalation, diplomatic engagement, and commercial opportunities under the supervision of the United States.”
Jordan has also been increasingly concerned and outspoken about Israel’s role in Syria.
“Jordan’s King Abdullah II renewed his warning over Israeli escalation in southern Syria in a call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, affirming Jordan’s support for Syria’s security and sovereignty, and urged a comprehensive de-escalation agreement that guarantees the security and sovereignty of Arab states,” Levant24 reported on October 3. “Jordan hosted the US-mediated Syrian-Israeli talks in Amman in August and co-signed the 2025 [Sweida] road map with Damascus and Washington.”

Ireland’s football snub of Israel was more than a political protest - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
17:43:57 UTC
02:43:57 KST

I watched the Republic of Ireland football team’s treatment of Israel in Debrecen with mounting disbelief, and then with fury.
The bowed heads during “Hatikvah.” The refusal to shake Israeli hands. The captains’ failure to exchange pennants, one of football’s simplest gestures of mutual respect. The black armbands.
This was not a spontaneous act by a lone protester. It was a calculated, collective humiliation of Israel’s national team, performed before an international audience. What breathtaking chutzpah.
Criticism of Israel is legitimate. Israelis themselves engage in it loudly and relentlessly. But the Irish players were not debating government policy. They were publicly shunning individual Israeli footballers, as if merely representing Israel rendered them contaminated.
They shook hands with the match officials, yet withheld that elementary courtesy from their Israeli opponents.
That distinction tells us everything: This was not an appeal for peace. It was an exercise in national ostracism.
Had I been responsible for the Israeli team, I would have seriously considered walking off the pitch the moment the Irish players turned our anthem into a prop for their political theater.
Israel should not have to beg for the courtesies routinely extended to every other nation. If our flag, anthem, and players are considered beneath basic respect, why lend legitimacy to the spectacle by participating in it? Play someone whose hand you are prepared to shake.
The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) and the players will undoubtedly insist that their actions concerned Gaza, not Jews or Israelis as people. But intentions do not erase consequences.
When Israelis alone are treated as untouchables, when their anthem is singled out, their hands refused, and their national symbols ostentatiously rejected, the performance crosses from political criticism into collective condemnation.
Arab Israelis in Israel's national team
And here is another inconvenient detail for Ireland’s moral dramatists: Our so-called “genocidal” Israeli football team contains Arab citizens of Israel.
Anan Khalaili, an Arab Israeli from Sakhnin, was in the starting lineup against Ireland. Other Arab footballers have represented Israel at every level.
So how does that work, exactly? Were the Irish players nobly refusing to shake the hands of “oppressors,” even when one of the men in the Israeli shirt was himself an Arab?
Was Khalaili transformed into a suitable object of Irish contempt because he chose to represent the country of his birth? Does inclusion suddenly become apartheid when it appears in an Israeli uniform?
The reality of Israel is considerably more complicated than the cartoon version promoted by those who regard every Israeli as guilty before kickoff.
Jews, Muslims, Christians, Druze, and Circassians play in Israeli football. Yet the Irish protest reduced every player to a single supposedly shameful identity: Israeli. That is not solidarity. It is prejudice disguised as virtue.
That cannot simply be waved away as harmless activism. It carries the unmistakable stench of antisemitic exclusion, whether every participant understands that or not.
What makes this sanctimony particularly galling is Ireland’s own history.
I remember precisely where I was when the Provisional IRA detonated its enormous bomb in central Manchester on June 15, 1996. It was a Saturday morning, and I was in a synagogue less than three miles away. I heard and felt the blast.
Over 200 people were injured, and the commercial heart of the city was devastated. To some extent, it has never recovered.
That bombing did not emerge from some remote medieval conflict. It happened within living memory.
There was also the 1984 Brighton hotel bombing, an attempt to murder British prime minister Margaret Thatcher and members of her government while they slept. Five people were killed.
In 1974, IRA bombs in two Guildford pubs killed five and injured dozens. The Troubles brought kneecappings, punishment shootings, abductions, bombings, and grotesque acts of intimidation, including tar and feather attacks, against those accused of fraternizing with the “wrong” people.
None of this means that “the Irish” collectively were responsible. The Irish state did not speak for the IRA, and countless Irish people rejected republican terrorism.
Britain and loyalist paramilitaries also have blood on their hands. Historical honesty requires those distinctions.
But that is precisely the point.
A country with Ireland’s history should understand better than most the moral necessity of distinguishing a population from an armed organization, a footballer from a government, and a national community from those committing violence in its name.
Irish people rightly objected when IRA atrocities were used to smear every Irish citizen. Yet the Irish team has now participated in precisely that kind of collective stigmatization against Israelis.
Where was this ostentatious moral clarity after Hamas murdered, raped, and kidnapped Israelis on October 7? Where was the insistence that Israeli victims be seen as human beings rather than inconvenient obstacles to a fashionable political narrative?
Why is Irish outrage so often thunderous when Israel fights back, but strangely qualified when Jews are slaughtered?
Black armbands for “all lives lost” sound admirably universal. Yet universalism that cannot name the aggressor who began the war, cannot acknowledge the hostages, and cannot extend a handshake to an Israeli footballer is not universalism at all. It is selective morality dressed in ceremonial black.
The argument is not that Ireland’s troubled past permanently disqualifies Irish people from criticizing anyone. That would be absurd. Nations are entitled to learn, change, and speak.
But moral authority demands humility, consistency, and some awareness of history. It does not permit a football association to transform a sporting fixture into a public ritual of Israeli degradation while presenting itself as the conscience of Europe.
The FAI had choices. Its officials and players could have issued a statement supporting civilians on both sides.
They could have called for peace, condemned terrorism, mourned Palestinian suffering, and remembered the Israeli victims of October 7. They could have competed fiercely while treating their opponents as human beings.
Instead, they selected the politics of the snub.
And let us be clear: Refusing a handshake does nothing for a Palestinian child. Bowing one’s head through “Hatikvah” does not end a war. Denying a pennant to Manor Solomon saves no life.
These gestures cost the Irish players nothing, achieve nothing, and enlighten no one. Their only tangible purpose is to make Israelis feel despised.
Ireland has nothing to teach Israel about surviving terrorism. Israelis have endured suicide bombings, rocket attacks, massacres, and hostage-taking while much of Europe lectures them about the etiquette of self-defense.
We do not require moral instruction from people who treat our existence as something shameful.
Perhaps we should not be entirely surprised: In May 1945, Taoiseach Éamon de Valera personally visited Nazi Germany’s representative in Dublin to offer condolences following Hitler’s death, an act defended as diplomatic protocol but remembered as a stain on Ireland’s wartime record.
Ireland won the match 3 to 0. Congratulations to its players on their football.
But before a ball was kicked, they lost something more important. They surrendered the sportsmanship that makes international competition possible and the moral seriousness their protest purported to display.
So yes, I am angry. Israelis should be angry. Decent football supporters should be angry.
If Irish football wants respect, it should begin by showing some. Until then, the FAI can keep its sanctimony, its theatrical gestures, and its chutzpah.
Israel should accept criticism. It should never accept humiliation.
The writer is a rabbi and physician. He writes and teaches on Jewish ethics, leadership, and resilience. His work appears on rabbidrjonathanlieberman.substack.com and youtube.com. @rabbidrjonathanlieberman

Iran’s oil minister resigns, replaced by oil executive
DUBAI - Iran’s oil minister Mohsen Paknejad has resigned and been replaced by the country’s top oil executive, the president’s office said in a statement on Oct 4, amid a blockade on Tehran’s oil exports by the United States.
“Following the acceptance of Mohsen Paknejad’s resignation, Hamid Bovard”, the CEO of the National Iranian Oil Company, “has been appointed as acting Minister of Oil by a decree from the president”, said the statement carried by state broadcaster IRIB.

The crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway has been the focal point of the Middle East war, as a fifth of the world’s oil and LNG passed through it before the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in late February.
Tehran has been blocking the passage of commercial ships, firing on vessels it accuses of unauthorised crossings.
Washington responded with a counterblockade of Iranian ports in an effort to prevent Tehran from exporting its oil.
Earlier in the war, capital Tehran and other Iranian cities at times saw queues build up at petrol stations as Washington choked the country’s economy. AFP

Flydubai suspect planned to crash plane into Ben Gurion Airport, Israeli officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
17:38:08 UTC
02:38:08 KST

Israeli officials say the investigation of Omani co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami, who tried to hijack a flydubai flight to Israel, indicates that he intended to crash the aircraft at Ben Gurion Airport and cause mass casualties.
According to the officials, al-Hammami began his attempt to seize control of the aircraft only after it reached Jordanian airspace because he intended to continue toward Israel as though the flight were making a normal landing at Ben Gurion Airport, then crash the plane into the airport.
If he was unable to reach Ben Gurion, investigators believe al-Hammami planned to crash the aircraft into a U.S. military base in Jordan.
The investigation also found that the Omani pilot had planned to carry out the attack as early as July but postponed it because of a personal connection with one of the crew members aboard his flight at the time, deciding to “spare him” and wait for another opportunity.
According to the findings so far, al-Hammami had previously landed in Israel in June and was preparing himself to become a “martyr.”
Al-Hammami’s plan to crash flydubai Flight FZ1023 was thwarted by the actions of Israeli passengers aboard the aircraft and the pilots who ultimately landed it safely, as well as the struggle put up by Indian captain Smit Machchhar.
Machchhar fought for his life and those of his passengers after being attacked in the cockpit. Investigators say al-Hammami had planned to strike the captain repeatedly with an emergency ax until he lost consciousness, then take control of the aircraft and crash it.
Channel 13 reported that al-Hammami told investigators he had deliberately sought employment with an airline that flew to Tel Aviv.
“I searched and checked which company flies to Tel Aviv, and that’s why I chose flydubai,” he was quoted as saying. “I tried to get accepted by all the airlines. I planned the operation even before I was hired by the company.”
Earlier Sunday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office announced a review of the security arrangements governing foreign civil aviation to Israel, following scrutiny of security gaps exposed by the incident.
According to the Prime Minister’s Office, Netanyahu instructed National Security Council chief Shmuel Ben Ezra to “appoint an examiner to conduct a thorough review of all aspects of security for foreign civil aviation to Israel.”
It was not immediately clear how quickly the review would proceed or whether security gaps identified during the process would be addressed promptly.
The move effectively revisits recommendations made by State Comptroller Matanyahu Englman in May 2024, when his office warned of shortcomings in oversight of foreign aircrews arriving in Israel.
The decision to order a comprehensive review follows years of warnings over gaps in the security of foreign aviation.
In May 2024, Englman published a report on the security of international civil aviation to and from Israel that identified serious shortcomings and gaps, including in security arrangements involving aircraft operated by foreign airlines.
One of the report’s central recommendations was for the National Security Council to lead a comprehensive review involving the Transportation Ministry, Finance Ministry, Israel Airports Authority, Shin Bet domestic security agency and police and formulate an updated overall aviation security policy.
An official close to Netanyahu rejected criticism of the decision to launch another review.
“It is healthy and legitimate that when an incident like this occurs and points to a gap in a particular area, the prime minister acts to have the deficiencies examined and corrected, with the aim of preventing such an incident from happening again,” the official said.
“You can’t have it both ways — point an accusing finger when something goes wrong and then point an accusing finger when action is taken to fix it.”
The review ordered by Netanyahu, however, will be an internal examination only, and the person appointed to lead it will not have investigative or enforcement powers.
Ben Ezra, who has been tasked with overseeing the new review, has until now been responsible for handling the issue through the National Security Council, without resolving the security gaps highlighted in previous assessments.

Saab expands its engagement in the space domain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
17:37:57 UTC
02:37:57 KST

Saab intends to take a broader role in the space domain as a system integrator, leveraging its expertise in sensors, communications and system integration to strengthen sovereign Swedish and Nordic capability across the space value chain. As a step in that direction, Saab has signed MoUs with SSC Space, OHB Sweden and Ericsson.
The aim of the three Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) is to explore cooperation in key areas for future multi-domain and space-enabled capabilities.
Space is becoming increasingly important as a strategic, operational, and tactical domain within defence and security. Military capabilities are also becoming ever more reliant on space-based solutions within areas including communications, navigation, surveillance and early warning.
While a number of actors in Sweden have strong capabilities in many parts of the space value chain, Saab sees opportunities to connect these strengths more closely and combine technologies and capabilities into operational systems through partnerships.
“With space becoming increasingly important for defence and security, Saab wants to contribute to a stronger and more coherent Swedish capability in this domain by building on our experience in integrating advanced defence and security solutions. Our recently signed MoUs with SSC Space, OHB Sweden and Ericsson are important steps in that direction and reflect our ambition to take a broader role as a system integrator in the space domain,” says Marcus Wandt, head of Group Strategy & Technology at Saab.
Saab’s MoU with SSC Space sets out joint exploration of how Saab’s system integration capabilities could be combined with SSC Space’s services, such as ground station network, mission engineering, high-altitude platform services and orbital launch infrastructure including the Esrange Space Center. The ambition is to enable relevant space capabilities with the aim of supporting multi-domain operations.
The MoU with OHB Sweden focuses on how existing and future satellite systems and platforms can be integrated into Saab’s multi-domain solutions. The cooperation is intended to support stronger operational awareness, connectivity and resilience by integrating space-based capabilities into solutions across air, land, sea and cyber domains.
With Ericsson, Saab will explore opportunities for collaboration and will examine how terrestrial and space-based communication solutions can be integrated to support future defence, security and societal resilience.
Source: saab.com

Jet-Powered Interceptor Likely Developed Based on Bars Missile-Drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
17:22:55 UTC
02:22:55 KST

A jet-powered interceptor was likely developed based on the Bars missile-drone. It is currently demonstrating the highest effectiveness against Russian drones.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said this during a joint news conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv.
“Second, interceptor drones. The Bars have shown positive results. They currently have the highest percentage. Others are also catching up. God willing, there will be competition in the good sense of the word,” he said.
Although it is probably impossible to determine whether Zelensky was referring specifically to an adaptation of Bars missile-drones or to a jet-powered interceptor with the same name, a number of factors support the adaptation theory. Ukraine and Germany already have an agreement on the joint production of these missile-drones.
In addition, RBC-Ukraine previously reported, citing its own sources in military circles, that Ukrainian jet-powered drone platforms currently used for long-range strikes were being adapted. According to the publication’s sources, “some solutions based on them have already demonstrated good results in the role of interceptors.”
According to the president, the Bars jet-powered interceptor currently has an interception rate of about 30% against aerial targets.
The president also spoke separately about agreements with Germany on the production of interceptor drones. According to him, Ukraine is to receive 2,000 Bars drones, which will be manufactured as part of joint production. Funding for the program has already been provided by the German side.
Overall, according to the president, the Defense Forces intercept about 50-55% of Russian jet-powered drones, and “sometimes 60%,” while the rate for conventional Shahed drones is 85-92%, depending on the composition of the Russian attack.
It was previously reported that the main obstacles to the production of jet-powered interceptor drones are a shortage of engines and limited budget funding.
“Engines are a key element; we really import them in large quantities. There are also domestically produced engines, but there are not enough of them,” Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times.
The Bars has been under development since 2023, but its first photos appeared only recently. During that time, its design underwent more than 40 engineering upgrades.
The platform currently has several variants: some modifications have a range of up to 1,000 kilometers, a payload of up to 60 kilograms, and a speed exceeding 700 km/h.
According to the stated specifications, the Bars is a modular platform that allows the aircraft to be rapidly adapted to specific missions. Its modularity enables three main categories of use: DeepStrike, MiddleStrike and FrontStrike.
Changing the configuration allows the balance between fuel tank volume and warhead weight to be adjusted to create different modifications.
“We use the capabilities provided by AI technologies today and are not afraid to apply them at all levels — from development and solving engineering tasks to implementing machine vision in our target-guidance systems,” the developer said.

United List wins Latvia’s parliamentary election as six parties secure seats

Latvia’s United List, led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, has won the October 3 parliamentary election, securing approximately 35% of the vote and a projected 42 seats in the 100-member Saeima. The preliminary results put Kulbergs in a strong position to lead negotiations on the next government.
With virtually all votes counted, six political forces have crossed the 5% threshold required to enter parliament. United List holds a substantial lead over its nearest competitors, although it will still need coalition partners to secure a parliamentary majority.
The Union of Greens and Farmers fell below the electoral threshold and is set to lose its parliamentary representation.
A coalition bringing together United List, the National Alliance and New Unity would control 59 seats, providing a working majority. United List and the National Alliance could also reach a narrower majority of 52 seats. These remain possible arrangements rather than an agreed government.
Latvia First and Sovereign Power/New Latvians together are projected to hold 32 seats, giving them a substantial parliamentary presence. Their ability to shape government policy will depend on the outcome of coalition negotiations.
Voter turnout reached approximately 51.8%, compared with around 59.4% in the previous parliamentary election in 2022. Despite the decisive result for the leading party, nearly half of eligible voters did not participate.
Security and economic concerns featured prominently in the campaign. Kulbergs has pledged to continue supporting Ukraine, strengthen Latvia’s defence capabilities and improve governance while reducing bureaucracy.
Attention now turns to the formation of the next government. President Edgars Rinkēvičs will nominate a candidate for prime minister, who must assemble a cabinet capable of winning parliamentary approval.
The election results remain preliminary pending formal confirmation. The new Saeima will serve a four-year term.

Britain's Green Party votes to class Zionism as a form of racism
LONDON, Oct 4 - Britain's Green Party voted on Sunday to class Zionism as a form of racism, drawing criticism from British Jews and from the Israeli government which said it now viewed the party as "a body that gives legitimacy to terrorism".
The party – which received 6% of the vote in national elections in 2024 – said it regarded Zionism as "an ethnonationalist political project" and repeated its call for Britain's Labour government to end all arms trade with Israel.
"The motion also restates the Green Party's backing for the right to self-determination and calls for the establishment of a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine," the party said in a statement.
The definition of Zionism – which inspired the foundation of the modern state of Israel in the 20th century – and what it implies for the rights of non-Jews in Israel and neighbouring territory, is contentious. Jewish groups sometimes define it as a right to Jewish self-determination.
The Green Party motion passed by a majority of 1,022 to 813 despite opposition from many senior figures. Party leader Zack Polanski, who is seeking election to Parliament on Thursday in former Prime Minister Keir Starmer's now-vacant London constituency, did not vote.
The result was condemned by British Jewish groups.
"The Green Party has made antisemitism party policy and become a racist party," the Movement for Progressive Judaism said, adding that the support of some Jews for the motion did not mean it would not be used to discriminate against others.
Israeli foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar has decided to declare Polanski barred from entering Israel, the foreign ministry said in a post on X Sunday.
It said the Green Party motion "constitutes a clear antisemitic text according to the IHRA (International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance) definition, as it denies the Jewish people’s right to self-determination," the ministry said.
Mothin Ali, deputy leader of the Green Party and a supporter of the motion, told Sky News on Saturday that the heavy Palestinian death toll in Israel's conflict with Hamas – which followed the Palestinian militant group's deadly 2023 attack on an Israeli music festival – was the key context for the vote.
"The motion defines Zionism quite clearly. It defines it as an ethnonationalist movement. It defines it as ethnic cleansing. It defines it as genocide," Ali said.
Britain's government views Israeli settlers' actions in the West Bank as amounting to ethnic cleansing but has said courts must decide if other Israeli actions qualify as genocide.
Israel – which rejects claims of ethnic cleansing and genocide – called on Sunday for other British political parties to condemn the Green Party vote. "The Greens have adopted not only the green of Hamas, but also its ideology: the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle," it said.
Polanski and other senior Green Party figures said they would "continue to call out the heinous crimes of the Netanyahu government," and that "there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people." REUTERS

Anthropic report: Is Russia using AI for disinformation in the Central African Republic and elsewhere?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
17:15:00 UTC
02:15:00 KST

Anthropic: Is Russia using AI for disinformation in CAR?
October 4, 2026
In Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic, Russian agents are said to have deliberately used the AI assistant Claude to promote pro-Russian influence. A report titled "Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI," published by US-based company Anthropic in September, detailed how opposition politicians were monitored, propaganda content was created and disinformation campaigns were supported.
The report claimed that Claude was used primarily to produce content broadcast by Radio Lengo Songo, a radio station that, according to the international investigative collective All Eyes on Wagner, is funded by Russia. The collective, made up of journalists, academics and experts, investigates the activities of the Russian mercenary group Wagner Group and its successor structures, such as the Africa Corps, around the world.
Pro-Russian propaganda, surveillance of the opposition
The Anthropic report said the content was pro-Russian and portrayed the Central African government and the Africa Corps mercenaries in a positive light, while taking a critical stance on France and the opposition.
Lou Osborn, a member of All Eyes on Wagner, was involved in the research for the latest report. He believes these methods are part of a practice that has already been observed in connection with the Wagner Group in the Central African Republic. "There have been several arrests of people who were not necessarily closely affiliated with the Touadera regime," he told DW. "They’ve been doing this for several years now."Faustin-Archange Touadera has been president of the Central African Republic since 2016.
"The arrests were the subject of online campaigns in newspapers and on the radio which portrayed those individuals either as proxies for France or Western intelligence services, or as people preparing a coup against Touadera," Osborn added.
Anthropic also reported that Claude was prompted to portray opposition figures as armed militants in an effort to provoke security forces into taking action against them. Anthropic says Claude refused the request. However, the report did not name the opposition figures who were monitored, specify the exact nature of the data collected, or say who received it.
'The government wants to get rid of us,' opposition says
For the opposition, the Anthropic report underscored the determination of the government in Bangui and its Russian allies to get rid of them. Martin Ziguele, chairman of the Movement for the Liberation of the Central African People, referred to an earlier case. "We have been observing this since 2020, when the CPC, a coalition of rebel groups, attacked Bangui. Strangely enough, several media outlets did everything in their power to establish alleged links between certain opposition leaders and the CPC," Ziguele told DW.
"There were also attacks against the opposition claiming that we were being paid by foreign countries. There was an attempt to pass a law stating that foreign agents were present in the country. All of this relates to the activities of the Wagner Group, as does this latest revelation."
DW also sought a statement from Russia. "Yes, I heard about [the report] in the news," said Dmitri Sytyi, a representative of the Russian mission in the Central African Republic. "But there are no concrete facts in it. [...] These are vague allegations, without precision and without evidence."
AI influence operations across the DRC, Kenya, Sudan and Mali?
Russia firmly denies the allegations, but the report indicates that the Central African Republic was not an isolated case. According to the report, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Kenya, Sudan and Mali were also affected.
In the DRC, Anthropic identified 318 articles that, according to the report, were published by a network of about 70 fake news sites and subsequently distributed by more than 250 fictitious accounts on X. The content supported the positions of the Congolese government against the backdrop of the conflict with Rwanda.
In Kenya, Claude was allegedly used to generate batches of 50 messages at a time that supported the government and were hostile toward the opposition.
In Sudan, Anthropic says AI was used as part of an operation attributed to individuals in the United Arab Emirates — particularly to create fabricated witness statements for the United Nations.
In Mali, meanwhile, an adviser with ties to intelligence services allegedly used Claude to develop a platform for monitoring telecommunications. According to the report, it was designed to target 25 million SIM cards and circumvent the requirement to obtain judicial authorization.
Anthropic says it uncovered and shut down all of these different operations between December 2025 and August 2026, primarily by deleting the accounts involved and strengthening its detection systems.
This article was originally published in German.
