For Kemi, being the Nasty party is not toxic but a badge of honour | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
17:13:49 UTC
02:13:49 KST

It’s a thought. A bold one. Possibly a career-ending one. But a thought nonetheless. When Theresa May told the Tory conference in 2002 that under Iain Duncan Smith the Conservatives had become “the Nasty party”, many members took that to mean they had become undesirable. Within a few years, David Cameron had moved the Tories closer to the “hug a husky” centre and by 2010 he was prime minister.
Kemi Badenoch takes a rather different view. For her, being the Nasty party is a badge of honour. An aspiration. People had had it far too good with austerity, Brexit, Covid and the Liz Truss mini-budget. The country needed a reality check; a return to old-fashioned unpleasantness. A taste of genuine hardship. People had got far too used to getting something for nothing. Especially the physically and mentally ill. What they needed was a short sharp shock of intense labour from 8am to 8pm. That would make them feel better. And anyone found skiving would be banged up for a short time in prison. Say 10 years.
And take a bow, her cheerleader-in-chief. The man whose sycophancy consistently goes above and beyond the call of duty. We’re talking, of course, of the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp. He had chosen to mark the beginning of Tory conference with an interview to the Sun in which he had identified himself as a one-man vigilante force. For the next four days, he had personally guaranteed that Birmingham would be a crime-free zone. The Philpster would be on guard night and day to arrest all shoplifters and to check up on people who hadn’t paid their TV licence. From now on he would be a superhero. BatTwat.
For Kemi, the beginning of conference was marked with the traditional BBC interview with Laura Kuenssberg. One where she would try to be the cosiest version of herself. The nasty leader with the heart of gold. A woman who could say in all honesty that “this was hurting her more than it was hurting you” as she removed someone’s benefits. This was Kemi returning in triumph. A year ago, her position as leader had looked ropey. Now the Tories have had a long, hard look around and concluded there actually isn’t anyone better.
“Is this a return to the nasty party?” asked Kuenssberg. Kemi was trying not to phrase it in precisely those terms. Nasty was only a word to be implied. Rather, she would prefer it if we could use the words “commonsense” party. Common sense, as in it was plain to everyone that something had to be done. And that something was to pick on the poorest and most vulnerable people in society. For years now, these parasites had been lounging around and getting fat on benefits. Asking themselves not what they could do for the Tory party but what the Tory party could do for them.
To illustrate her point, Kemi proudly drew Laura’s attention to her rather desperate pamphlet The Right Way, which the Tories have published as their new credo. Six principles of Conservatism to get them through the bad times. To remind them they are right even when the country thinks they are unelectable. Kemi’s Kemistry, as she hopes we will call it. The first rule is that Kemi never makes mistakes. Asked to name anything she has changed her mind about, she comes up with nothing. The laws of physics will change long before Kemi. She wants us to think of The Right Way as her foundational document that will be spoken of in hushed tones for decades to come. It will be lucky to survive until tomorrow.
We then moved on to Kemi’s latest big idea: to give everyone who makes more than £100,000 a year unlimited free childcare. The case was unarguable, said Kemi. Free childcare was totally wasted on people on the minimum wage because they couldn’t be trusted to spend the money wisely. It would probably all be wasted on Happy Meals at McDonald’s or a Sky subscription. Let’s face it, it was just chucking good money after bad. Most working-class kids were bound to end up on benefits anyway, so why encourage them from the moment they were born? It’s time they learned to be self-sufficient. What a contrast with the top 5% of the country. They could at least spend their benefits on something worthwhile. Like baby yoga.
Kemi was also keen to keep pensioners happy. We will retain the triple lock, she said. Even though half the shadow cabinet know it’s completely unaffordable. Old people definitely had to be kept sweet, as they were about the last section of the country who actually voted Tory. Not that this was any factor in shaping current policy. Because Kemi had just published The Right Way, in which she had declared that her principles were whatever she wanted them to be on the day. And, by the way, this would all be paid for by cutting benefits for the 10 million scroungers who were cheating the system. Could you verify that figure? Laura asked. Kemi shook her head. It was just a well-known fact that she had made up. So no need.
After going on to say she would be building 50,000 more prison spaces for all the criminals BatTwat arrested in the next four days, the interview meandered to a close. In the studio, Penny Mordaunt declared it to be the best interview a Tory leader had ever given. Penny is beside herself with joy at having passed the test to be admitted to the MPs’ candidate list. Answering yes to questions such as: “Are you mad?” and “Are you happy to trash the Good Friday agreement?” It was Penny’s performance in the Sky reality show The War Game that swung it. As defence secretary she couldn’t wait to start a nuclear apocalypse. Come friendly bombs.
Over in the conference centre, the complex was strangely quiet. Maybe the news that everything is going swimmingly for the Tories hasn’t yet filtered down to MPs and members. Even the main hall wasn’t full, and there was nothing going on elsewhere. But those who were there seemed happy enough. Perhaps they are genuinely delighted that things aren’t going even worse. That they are still only four points in the polls off their disastrous 2024 election result. That it doesn’t matter that the so-called Keminaissance exists largely in their imaginations.
But on we go. A party the country still regards as toxic is determined to double down on its toxicity. Desperate to track ever further to the right and abandon its centre right to Labour and the Lib Dems. It feels like madness. But this conference is all about Kult Kemi. There is even an AI slop, sub-Beano reproduction of the Bayeux tapestry. A series of tableaux leading to the moment Kemi saves the world. She looks on beatifically as several easily identified journalists take dictation. Curiously, I’m not one of them.

Good palliative care and assisted dying can go hand in hand | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
17:06:32 UTC
02:06:32 KST

Jane Turner is right that end-of‑life care needs fixing (MPs, you told us clearly that end-of-life care in the UK is broken. So now we need you to fix it, 28 September), and I argue that it needs fixing on two fronts at once. My husband, John, died in March aged 43 after nearly six years of bowel cancer treatment. He endured more than 70 rounds of chemotherapy, determined to watch our children grow up. He spent his last three months in a hospice, receiving the best palliative care on offer. Even so, he suffered terribly.
Some pain cannot be controlled quickly, and some suffering cannot be treated at all. One evening he screamed in agony while stranded in a bath, unable to move, for nearly an hour before relief took effect. As the cancer swelled his torso, he slowly suffocated – and no drug could prevent it. He was fully aware throughout, and told me repeatedly that he could not go on. In his last hours, I wore earplugs to bear the sound of his gasping.
Most hospices are charities that receive very little state funding – that must change. Better palliative care will spare many people needless suffering. But it cannot spare everyone, and no amount of funding would have given John what he wanted: the chance to face the inevitable on his own terms.
Improving palliative care and legalising assisted dying are not rivals. Doing both would also free hospice beds for those who want them; John occupied one for three months.
John was always going to die from his cancer, but the trauma of his final months, for him and for our children, was preventable. MPs should not choose between fixing care and offering choice. They must do both.
Liz Wilson
Coventry
Jane Turner is absolutely right that we need to invest in palliative and end-of life care. She is also correct that the greatest unmet needs are seen in NHS hospitals, and that it is here where investment is most urgent. That all sounds very expensive, but if we look at the headline financial figures, we see that actually it might cost very little in terms of new money. The Nuffield Trust tells us that the UK spends £6.6bn on emergency hospital care in the last year of life. This contrasts with only £1.1bn to run all 204 UK hospices, including the 24 NHS hospices.
I was a consultant physician at one of these units for 20 years, and I am told that it now costs around £5m annually to provide a comprehensive specialist palliative care service to a population of 250,000, delivered across all settings, including hospital wards. This implies a total cost of around £1.4bn to provide this NHS service across the UK population of 70 million people. The NHS has complete access to the patient activity and financial figures of these 24 units, so these figures can easily be confirmed.
One of the strengths of specialist palliative care services is that they always try to help patients and their families to plan for the future: when you get more poorly, where would you want to be cared for? If this planning enabled us to avert only 10% of emergency admissions in the last year of life, the money saved would more than fill the funding gap. If emergency admissions fell by more than 10%, it would, overall, save the nation money.
Stephen Kirkham
Lytchett Minster, Dorset
Jane Turner is absolutely right that palliative and end-of-life care must be properly funded and available to everyone who needs it. Those of us who campaigned for assisted dying have never argued otherwise. Better palliative care and greater choice at the end of life should not be competing ambitions.
But there is an important question that cannot be lost now the parliamentary vote is over: what happens to the people whose suffering even excellent palliative care cannot adequately relieve?
I am living with incurable secondary breast cancer. I love my life and want to be here for my daughter for as long as possible. But I also know from painful personal experience that I am allergic to opioid painkillers. After the birth of my daughter, when I needed multiple operations, my pain could not be properly controlled. It was frightening. So when I am told that better palliative care will remove the need for assisted dying, I have a very simple question: what if it cannot?
Jane is right that even with the best quality care, some deaths can still be difficult. Those people matter too. Since the fall of the terminally ill adults (end of life) bill, terminally ill people have not suddenly become less frightened about what lies ahead. Our diagnoses have not changed, and neither have the limits of medicine.
So yes: fix palliative care. End the postcode lottery. Make sure nobody reaches the end of their life without the support, expertise and compassion they deserve. But we should be able to hold two thoughts at once. Excellent palliative care can transform many deaths. It cannot guarantee that every dying person’s suffering can be relieved.
The question for those who opposed assisted dying therefore remains: what is the answer for those people?
Sophie Blake
Hove, East Sussex

Let’s build a better future for female scaffolders | Letter

Adrian Chiles is right: scaffolding is hard work (Britain’s scaffolding should be a source of national pride – instead we’re struggling to recruit workers, 1 October). It demands physical resilience, skill, judgment and proper training. That will naturally mean it is not a job for everyone – men or women.
Which is why the conversation about the skills shortage should be less about who traditionally became a scaffolder, and more about who is willing and able to learn the trade and meet the same standards.
As the industry is already facing the significant shortfall that Chiles describes, we need to widen the pool of people who can see scaffolding as a genuine career.
That includes women, but the bigger issue is attracting capable people into the trade, training them properly and keeping standards high. That is part of what the Women in Scaffolding Association (WiSA) is trying to do.
We support women already working on the tools, make them visible and connected, and show women and girls that scaffolding is a genuine skilled career. We also work to bring more people into construction generally.
Nobody is suggesting lowering the bar. Scaffolding requires strength, but also technique, teamwork, training and considerable skill. The standards should remain the standards.
Chiles also makes an important point about AI. Scaffolding is practical, skilled work that cannot simply be automated away. Britain still needs people who can build, solve problems and work safely with their hands. If scaffolders are becoming a dying breed, perhaps the answer is to look more widely for the next generation. Some of them will be women.
Emma Claassen
Founder, WiSA

Singeetham Srinivasa Rao: Seven decades, many worlds of cinema
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
17:06:15 UTC
02:06:15 KST

BENGALURU: Singeetham Srinivasa Rao, who died in Chennai on Saturday aged 95, had a career that spanned more than seven decades of Indian cinema. He entered films in 1954 as an apprentice to legendary Telugu filmmaker KV Reddy, assisting him on Donga Ramudu and Mayabazar.From those early days on the sets of a Telugu classic, Rao went on to become one of Indian cinema’s most inventive filmmakers, leaving a particularly rich mark on Kannada cinema while also making acclaimed films in Tamil, Telugu and other languages.His Kannada journey began before he became a director. Rao was the executive director of Samskara (1970), Pattabhirama Reddy’s landmark adaptation of UR Ananthamurthy’s novel. The film, which won the National Film Award for Best Feature Film, became a defining work of Kannada parallel cinema. It was an early indication of the range of a filmmaker who would later move comfortably between art-house cinema and popular entertainment.His directorial debut in Kannada came with Rajkumar in Haalu Jenu in 1982. What followed was one of the notable actor-director collaborations in Kannada cinema, with Chalisuva Modagalu, Eradu Nakshatragalu, Shravana Banthu, Jwaalamukhi, Bhagyada Lakshmi Baramma and Devatha Manushya — all after Gogak Chaluvali.
The films moved across family drama, romance, crime and comedy, with Rao adapting his craft to each. Devatha Manushya was also Rajkumar’s 200th film.His association with the Rajkumar family extended beyond the thespian himself. In Anand (1986), Rao introduced Shivarajkumar as a leading man. He later directed Raghavendra Rajkumar in Chiranjeevi Sudhakar. His association with the Rajkumar banner also included work on other films produced by the family.There was another side to Rao’s Kannada work that is less often remembered: music. A disciple of composer S Rajeswara Rao, he also composed music, giving Kannada cinema some memorable albums. He composed the songs and score for Bhagyada Lakshmi Baramma and the songs for Samyuktha, moving between direction and music with the same ease with which he moved between genres.Then came Pushpaka Vimana (1987), the dialogue-free film starring Kamal Haasan. The movie, which became one of the most distinctive films of its time, was another example of Rao refusing to be confined by conventional cinematic language. Though often remembered primarily through its Tamil connection, it was produced as a Kannada entry and won the National Award for Best Popular Film Providing Wholesome Entertainment.
His apprenticeship under KV Reddy had taken him through some of Telugu cinema’s landmark films. Decades later, he returned to Telugu cinema as a director with films such as Aditya 369 and Bhairava Dweepam. In Tamil, his collaborations with Kamal Haasan produced films including Raja Paarvai, Apoorva Sagodharargal and Michael Madana Kama Rajan. His work also extended to Hindi, Malayalam and English.Across more than seven decades, Rao’s filmography was less a straight line than a series of departures. He began as a young apprentice learning from KV Reddy on films such as Mayabazar, became part of the Kannada New Wave through Samskara, worked extensively with Rajkumar, introduced two of his sons, experimented with a dialogue-free film and continued moving between languages and genres almost until the end.
Chethan Kumar is a Senior Assistant Editor with the Times of India. Aside from specialising in Space & Science, he has reported extensively on varied topics, with special focus on defence, policy and data stories. He has covered multiple elections, too. As a young democracy grows out of adolescence, Chethan feels, there are reels of tales emerging which need to be captured. To do this, he alternates between the mundane goings-on of the Common Man and the wonder-filled worlds of scientists and scamsters, politicians and soldiers. In a career spanning nearly 18 years, he has reported from multiple datelines — Houston, Florida, Kochi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Sriharikota (AP), NH-1 (J&K Highway), New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Raichur, Bhatkal, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, to name a few — but is based out of Bengaluru, India’s science capital that also hosts the ISRO HQ.

Parental alienation and the pain of custody battles in the the family courts | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
17:06:15 UTC
02:06:15 KST

Hannah Summers’ article raises disturbing concerns about the misuse of parental alienation allegations in family courts (‘Just like that, I lost my girls’: the mother who feels betrayed by the family courts, 29 September). However, I believe that it would benefit from a clearer distinction between the discredited theory of “parental alienation syndrome” (PAS) and genuine, demonstrable alienating behaviour.
PAS proposed that a child’s unjustified rejection of a parent could be identified as a distinct syndrome. It is no longer an accepted clinical diagnosis, since a child’s rejection of a parent cannot itself establish manipulation, therefore treating it as diagnostic risks overlooking abuse or other legitimate reasons for the child’s feelings.
However, rejecting PAS as a clinical diagnosis should not obscure the reality that one parent can manipulate a child into rejecting the other. Persistent denigration, emotional pressure and demands for loyalty can leave a child feeling that loving one parent means betraying the other. No child should have to carry that burden.
The Children and Family Court Advisory and Support Service (Cafcass) deliberately uses the term “alienating behaviours”, recognising that these can damage children’s identity, self-worth and wider family relationships, and that manipulation or coercion may amount to emotional abuse. The Family Justice Council similarly distinguishes the unsupported syndrome from behaviour whose existence and consequences courts must determine as matters of fact.
For a child, being made to feel that loving one parent betrays the other is an intolerable burden. For the rejected parent, losing a relationship with a living child can bring devastating grief. These experiences deserve recognition alongside the suffering caused to both the child and rejected parent.
Children must be heard, domestic abuse taken seriously and allegations carefully examined. Rejecting an unsupported diagnosis should strengthen that scrutiny, without obscuring the reality of harmful parental manipulation.
Balanced reporting should acknowledge both the danger of unfounded allegations and the anguish caused by proven manipulation. These are not competing concerns. Both demand our attention if children and families are to be protected.
Name and address supplied
Reading this article was painfully familiar. I lost custody of my daughters in 2013 after initially applying for shared, 50/50 care.
My experience was complicated by the fact that my barrister argued that it was my ex-husband who was alienating the children from me. My daughters, now adults, have since told me that their father and his family coached them on how to answer Children and Family Court Advisory and Support Service (Cafcass) questions and encouraged them to believe that I was mentally ill and did not want to care for them.
At the time, Fathers4Justice and fathers’ rights were receiving considerable media attention. The judge in my case was approaching retirement, and my barrister told me she believed his decision to award my ex-husband full custody was intended to make a wider statement. I cannot know whether she was right.
Central to the judgment was the claim that I was mentally unstable. After my ex-husband abruptly removed the children from school and obtained an ex parte order preventing me from seeing them, I was distraught and called the Samaritans. My ex subsequently obtained my phone records and used that call as evidence. The judge treated calling the Samaritans as evidence that I might be suicidal and therefore unsafe to care for my children.
At my barrister’s suggestion, I obtained an independent psychiatric/psychological assessment. It found no reason why I could not care for my daughters. As I remember it, that report was simply ignored.
So I struggle with the suggestion that parental alienation is not “real”. The label may be problematic, but parents can manipulate and coach children against another parent. My daughters have since confirmed to me that this happened to them.
Name and address supplied
Your report on Sarah’s case raises concerns about reliance on flawed psychological assessment. My experience in Zurich highlights the consequences of failing to obtain any such assessment.
I am a father living in England, whose son lives with his mother in Switzerland. Despite joint legal custody, court orders providing for contact and repeated enforcement proceedings, I have not seen him since July 2023.
Zurich court decisions recognised his mother’s interference with contact. Two sets of social workers, involved at different times, recommended psychological assessments of the parents to assess parenting capacity. Yet the authorities never acted on those recommendations. Without those assessments, my son has remained with the parent whose behaviour I regard as emotionally manipulative, while his relationship with me has been allowed to disappear.
Reliable psychological assessment can help authorities understand family relationships; its absence can leave damaging behaviour unexamined. The answer to poor expert evidence should be rigorous assessment where warranted, alongside careful examination of the facts.
A child’s expressed wishes matter, but so does understanding how they developed. Refusal of contact may reflect harmful experiences, pressure, divided loyalties or several factors together.
We should therefore resist drawing general conclusions from individual cases. Misusing allegations of alienation to dismiss genuine abuse is an injustice. Ignoring deliberate obstruction and denigration can also deprive a child of a loving parent. Rejecting a disputed diagnostic label does not establish that the underlying behaviours never occur.
Neither mothers nor fathers have a monopoly on suffering or causing harm. My case cannot establish what happened in Sarah’s family, any more than hers settles mine. Both call for competent investigation, timely intervention and scrutiny of outcomes. Years lost to a parent and child cannot be restored by a later acknowledgment that the system failed them.
Name and address supplied

Ansarallah extends gains in Yemen's Taiz
Yemen's Ansarallah made fresh territorial gains in the southwestern province of Taiz on Sunday, pressing its advance as the Saudi-backed government in Yemen announced the start of a large-scale military campaign to retake what it called the remaining Ansarallah-held areas.
A local security official, speaking to Xinhua on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Ansarallah fighters had entered At Turbah, a strategic center in southern Taiz province, without fighting after Saudi-led forces withdrew earlier in the day.
He added that troops and allied fighters had pulled back to mountainous positions outside At Turbah, while some retreated farther south into neighboring Lahj province following "battlefield setbacks and losses." Ansarallah fighters subsequently moved into the city, deploying at key locations and its main entrances and exits.
Residents said Ansarallah spread along major streets and around public facilities in At Turbah, while many merchants closed their shops before the arrival. They said Ansarallah also used mosque loudspeakers to urge residents not to resist.
The capture of At Turbah marks the first time Ansarallah has taken control of the city since Yemen's conflict erupted in late 2014, extending the group's recent territorial gains across southwestern Yemen.
Earlier Sunday, a military official told Xinhua that Ansarallah forces had advanced through parts of Ash Shamayatayn and neighboring Al-Ma'afer districts, seizing several key positions and forcing government troops to retreat.
Ansarallah�s advances came as Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council (PLC) and commander-in-chief of the armed forces, announced from the Saudi capital Riyadh the start of a large-scale military campaign to retake what he described as the remaining areas under Ansarallah control.
In a televised address, al-Alimi said the government was moving "from the preparation phase to the action phase" after weeks of military mobilization.
The developments marked a rapidly shifting battlefield after years of largely frozen front lines. Since launching a major offensive in early September, Ansarallah has expanded across parts of Taiz and neighboring Lahj, seizing the Red Sea port city of Mocha on Sept. 10 and Mayyun Island, also known as Perim, a day later, while tensions have intensified in the highlands overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.

Bennett: 'Direct line' connects flydubai attempted hijacking, Oct. 7 after gov. trades blame

17:05:06 UTC
02:05:06 KST

Former prime minister and B’Yachad co-chairman Naftali Bennett drew a connection between the October 7 massacre and the flydubai attempted hijacking in a Sunday statement.
This comes after Transportation Minister Miri Regev denied responsibility for the incident, despite the fact that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu assigned her ministry the responsibility of conducting intelligence background checks on foreign airline pilots.
“There is a direct line connecting the plane failure to the October 7 massacre,” Bennett said.
“The arrogance of Netanyahu and his ministers: they fall asleep on guard duty and abandon us and Israel’s security. Any prime minister who cared about Israel’s security would have demanded answers from his transportation minister and thrown her out,” he added.
“But instead of investigating and drawing lessons in order to prevent the next disaster, Netanyahu and Miri Regev are celebrating the failure that happened on their watch.”
Bennett said Israelis were questioning what the Netanyahu administration was doing to prevent the next disaster, and urged Israelis to vote Netanyahu out in the upcoming October elections.
“We will replace them, put an end to the chaos, and return to governing Israel,” Bennett said.
Former transportation minister: 'Failure's name is Miri Regev'
Former transportation minister and the third person on B'Yachad's list, Keren Turner-Eyal, joined Bennett in the address and directly blamed Regev for the incident.
“This failure has a name: Miri Regev. She is the one who chose to make a decision contrary to the positions of the Shin Bet and the National Security Council, and who decided to ignore a severe State Comptroller’s report that states clearly: The Transportation Ministry’s security division does not have the ability to meet the required security objectives,” Turner-Eyal said.
“But for a few more powers and a few more jobs, Miri Regev chose to endanger all of our lives. This government is no longer going to investigate anything or draw any lessons," Turner-Eyal added.
“Fortunately for all of us, in 23 days we will replace them and prove to the public that it is possible to run a country without backroom deals and without endless failures.”
Regev denies responsibility for flydubai flight hijacking
The Transportation Ministry and Regev have come under scrutiny following the attempted terror hijacking by an Omani flydubai pilot who had previously landed at Ben-Gurion Airport, raising questions over what checks were carried out on foreign airline crews and which Israeli body was responsible for them.
On Saturday, Regev denied that her agency was responsible for vetting foreign airline crews.
"Aviation security is a very complex issue. The entire intelligence issue is divided between the Mossad and the Shin Bet," Regev said in an interview with KAN News.
She alleged the agencies had a clear division of responsibility.
"The Shin Bet is responsible for Israeli flights, and the Mossad is responsible for foreign companies. Flydubai is a foreign company. It is not connected to the Shin Bet but to the Mossad,” she added.
Notably, in 2021, the Shin Bet removed itself from responsibility for securing foreign flights while the Transportation Ministry did not act to assume that responsibility, according to a report published Sunday by Army Radio. The State Comptroller subsequently highlighted the issue in a classified report issued in May 2024, Army Radio reported.
Regev maintained that the Transportation Ministry was not sent a passenger or crew list.
"The list did not come to us because the body that is supposed to identify the crew is an intelligence body. We are not an intelligence body," she said.
However, in 2023, a law was enacted to regulate the security of Israeli aviation. It aimed to decentralize enforcement and monitoring powers so each body could access information without interfering with the others.
The law established Customs as the relevant government body responsible for collecting and analyzing flight and passenger data. The body is called the National Center for Passenger Data Analysis, known by its Hebrew acronym MALAN.
The center was established under dedicated legislation with the aim of receiving advance data from airlines on flights, passengers, and crew members entering or leaving Israel.
The body is intended to provide continuous information to each of the relevant organizations. Police receive information concerning criminals, individuals wanted for questioning, or information related to the transfer of drugs and illicit funds.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s criminal trial entered its new five-day-a-week schedule on Sunday. The Jerusalem District Court wants to accelerate the six-year-old case before the presiding judge retires.
The court ordered hearings from Sunday through Thursday, between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m., despite objections from both the prosecution and the defense. It also instructed the defense teams to prepare replacement witnesses to prevent hearings from being canceled.
Presiding Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman is expected to retire in March 2028 when she turns 70. The expanded schedule is intended to move the trial through the remaining evidence while leaving the panel time to hear closing arguments and write its verdict.
Former Labor MK Eitan Cabel took the stand Sunday to testify about Case 2000, which concerns recorded conversations between Netanyahu and Yediot Aharonot publisher Arnon “Noni” Mozes.
Prosecutors allege that Netanyahu and Mozes had discussed a possible arrangement under which Netanyahu would receive more favorable coverage in exchange for steps that could weaken Yediot’s principal rival, Israel Hayom.
Netanyahu is charged with fraud and breach of trust. Mozes is charged with offering and promising a bribe. They both deny wrongdoing.
Former Labor MK Eitan Cabel testifies in Case 2000
Cabel led legislation that would have restricted the free distribution of Israel Hayom. He was questioned under caution during the Case 2000 investigation, but the case against him was later closed without charges. His testimony had previously been postponed because he was serving in the IDF reserves.
The trial is now in the defense stage. Netanyahu, its first witness, completed his testimony in June after 98 hearings, spanning about a year and a half. The court is now hearing other witnesses called on his behalf.
Mandelblit set to testify weeks before October 27 election
Former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit, who approved the investigations and later decided to indict Netanyahu, is scheduled to testify on October 11-12 and October 18-22, during the final weeks before the October 27 election.
The court last week declined to postpone Mandelblit’s testimony until November or December. It left open the possibility of reconsidering if the defense can provide other witnesses for those dates.
Once Netanyahu’s witnesses have finished, his three co-defendants will be able to present their cases. The parties will then submit closing arguments before the judges deliver a verdict. No date has been set for a decision.

Mass protests demanding poll chief resignation shake India for third day
Protesters say the election commission’s voter-roll revision has removed millions of eligible voters to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling BJP party.
Thousands of youth and opposition protesters have rallied for a third day in India demanding the resignation of the country’s election commission chief.
Thousands marched in Mumbai on Sunday, while others gathered for a third day of demonstrations in New Delhi. The protests began on Friday demanding that Election Commission of India (ECI) chief Gyanesh Kumar step down due to reports that he has overseen voter-roll revisions removing millions from electoral lists.
Protesters say the disenfranchisement stands to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the ECI and the BJP have denied the allegations.
Led by opposition leaders Raj Thackeray and Uddhav Thackeray, thousands marched in Mumbai on Sunday, waving Indian flags and calling for Kumar to step down.
In the capital, New Delhi, protesters started gathering in the early evening. As on previous days, some were detained by police as they arrived, according to the Reuters news agency.
Police in the capital have clamped down in a bid to prevent protesters from assembling over the last two days, detaining dozens and taking them away by bus.
Some of the detainees were released later on Friday and Saturday, but police registered cases against some on charges of violating orders banning mass gatherings in the centre of the capital.
“I just want to tell the ruling party this much … We are angry about how you are wielding that power. It’s the people of this country who should decide who sits in power and who sits in opposition, not the election commission,” Raj Thackeray told the crowd in Mumbai.
The ECI says the voter-roll revision is designed to remove duplicate, deceased or ineligible entries and maintain electoral integrity. On Friday, it directed its officials to register eligible voters inadvertently omitted from electoral rolls.
Kumar has not publicly responded to the demands for his resignation or commented on the protests, which look set to continue over the coming days, with more rallies planned.
An alliance of India’s opposition parties plans to launch protests to “save democracy” with a march to the election commission office on Tuesday. The Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has announced plans for a major rally in New Delhi on October 10.

Macron laments the EU’s nosedive like he’s not one of the pilots

Macron laments the EU’s nosedive like he’s not one of the pilots
So, big bad US President Donald Trump just successfully strong-armed French President Emmanuel Macron and the EU into dumping their precious ‘rainy day’ diesel from strategic reserves.
Why? Because Trump, threatening a disastrous cutoff of diesel exports to Europe altogether, wanted to keep domestic gas prices looking perky ahead of next month’s American midterms.
“We have decided to release strategic reserves of diesel and crude oil, under the coordination of the International Energy Agency – which will meet in the coming hours or days to organize this… This process will begin by prioritizing diesel,” Macron declared.
Wait, aren’t those the exact same strategic reserves that have given Brussels a collective nervous breakdown over imminent winter shortages? Oh well, what’s a leader to do when he’s just a helpless, innocent little cog in a grand G7 multilateral machine? It’s not like Macron is directly engineering this self-inflicted disaster in any sense, right?
Oh, hang on. He’s not done digging yet.
“In any case, France will make this effort regarding its own reserves, which also reflects a desire to send a clear signal to the market,” Macron added. Yeah, the signals are about as subtle as a flare gun to the face.
Visionary European leaders like Macron have long since handed the wheel to Washington because they apparently thought that it was a better look in the eyes of their Ukrainian girlfriend, Zelensky, than dealing with Russia and its cheap gas.
And now we get yet another Macronian capitulation to a more recent bogeymen that he’s been whining about on the global stage: Trump.
All this drama peaked amid a state visit to Madrid, where Macron dropped by a local university to jam out some avant-garde thoughts on Europe alongside prominent Spanish cultural figures. A local writer teed up a softball right across the center of the plate, invoking Trump and the global rise of populism in the same breath as fascism to frame them as an existential threat to democracy. Which, of course, was the ultimate cue for Macron to explain whose fault this mess actually is. And the short answer is: absolutely, unequivocally not his.
“The great blow for France was the 2008–2012 crisis. And who paid the bill? The middle classes. Even in countries that were less affected, some categories have still not fully recovered in terms of purchasing power and living standards they had before that crisis. And this has been a betrayal,” he said.
The same guy who’s been running the joint for nearly a full decade has to time-travel back 15 to 20 years to find someone responsible for the fact that French middle class is currently on economic life support. Because obviously, he couldn’t possibly have had anything to do with it despite holding the royal scepter for the past ten years.
He chalks up current reality to the 2010 European debt crisis as though he were just an innocent tourist snapping selfies outside the Elysee Palace rather than the captain of the ship.
“A key factor in European competitiveness was very cheap gas coming from Russia. That ended in 2022,” Macron pontificated. “But our great export market was China. That is over too. Europe now has a trade deficit with China. Today, every day, we lose €1 billion in trade with China.”
You’ve got to admire the poetry – if not the gall – of the passive tense there. It ended in 2022. Like a rainstorm! It just happened to end. Totally out of his hands. What can a mere mortal do? Same with selling things to China. Poof, it’s over now! Who knows why? A total mystery. Bleeding a billion euros a day while standing there and shrugging.
Never mind his other brilliant policy hits, like trying to flatline French nuclear power before panicking and awkwardly resurrecting it as the next greatest thing in green renewables, or selling off French industrial crown jewels to Americans only to proudly buy them back later at a massive taxpayer loss. Or riffing to the press on his private jet about how Europe shouldn’t be an American vassal – right before making French citizens and industry pay through the nose for the privilege of heating or cooling their homes as a result of doing precisely that.
It’s the exact same laissez-faire energy that he’s currently bringing to France’s annual far-left protest-and-smashfest season. This fall, the usual professional malcontents have managed to rope some high schoolers into doing their dirty work, meaning that we get to endure teenagers setting fire to their own academic institutions because they believe that their school days are too grueling – in a country where they enjoy a mandatory two-week vacation every six weeks of the academic calendar.
And the government’s cutting-edge counterinsurgency strategy to clear the streets is... online classes. Because the cure for revolutionary zeal is apparently to invite the sons and daughters of Che to hang out near the family fridge and the TV remote while mom and dad are out breaking their backs at work. Perhaps they figure that it’s more inviting than hanging out in the streets and chewing the scenery.
Every single year, the same script plays out, and the authorities just hunker down and wait it out. That appears to be Macron’s playbook for everything, even as he enjoys his 18% approval rating. Just wait for the fire to burn out, and then casually chalk it up to something entirely out of your control. He can’t even bother to unroll the hose at this point.
Looks like maybe the French will just have to wait out Macron himself, and for his term to end, before having a shot at anyone actually doing something useful to reverse course on any of this.

Reaching the core: could Russia cut Ukrainians off from the internet and mobile communications?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
19:47:00 EEST
01:47:00 KST

Reaching the core: could Russia cut Ukrainians off from the internet and mobile communications?
Over the past week, the Kremlin has been expanding its campaign of terror to include new targets. In addition to hitting energy infrastructure and logistics hubs, Russia is now attacking the data centres that house equipment used by internet service providers, government services, banks and other digital systems, launching a wave of strikes on buildings where vital telecoms infrastructure is concentrated.
Telecoms industry representatives say it is not possible to cut Kyiv or Ukraine off from the internet by hitting data centres. There is no single facility whose destruction would take the country offline. But the objective of these attacks is not merely to carry out acts of terror. The goal is not the total destruction of the internet, but to degrade internet quality and overload backup routes, which could increase latency and destabilise networks.
And that may not be the worst-case scenario. The Russians have also started targeting mobile operator infrastructure, which may have more far-reaching consequences. Could these attacks disrupt communications across Ukraine? Where are the weak points in the country's telecoms infrastructure, and why is it that mobile networks could turn out to be significantly more vulnerable? Read on to find out.
From data centres to mobile network operators
On 23 September, Russian drones attacked a building in central Kyiv that housed one of the capital's data centres. A business centre was hit by several jet-powered Shahed drones in the course of an hour, and a fire then broke out.
Later that day, drones struck a similar data centre in another part of the city, and that evening, Russian forces hit yet another facility housing a data centre.
In one day, Russia had attacked at least three data centres in different parts of Kyiv. All housed equipment belonging to internet service providers. Some, notably the cloud service Fex.net, reported disruptions to their services. Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Transformation said around 100,000 users had problems accessing the internet.
Ekonomichna Pravda estimates that at least nine data centres in Kyiv may have been targeted since September, some of them more than once. The Protasiv Yar business centre, which housed the Cosmonova data centre, has been hit twice. Cosmonova suspended operations at the site as a result.
Four days later, the Russians turned their attention to mobile operators' infrastructure. Kyivstar, Ukraine's largest mobile operator, reported that a drone had struck one of its buildings, and Russia's Defence Ministry claimed that equipment belonging to Vodafone Ukraine had been damaged.
Internet service providers and mobile operators have suffered attacks to their networks before, but since 23 September the attacks have been on a different scale. Several data centres were hit within a few days, including some facilities that are critical to the telecoms industry.
For instance, a Russian attack destroyed a data centre that housed infrastructure belonging to hosting provider MiroHost. Founder Oleksandr Olshanskyi said MiroHost won't be able to bring its Ukraine-based infrastructure back online for at least the next three months.
Government digital services have also been disrupted, including state registries and electronic registration at centres run by Ukraine's Ministry of Internal Affairs that provide administrative services related to vehicles and driving licences.
The attacks on data centres have affected television broadcasts too. Disruptions have been reported by Army TV, Novyny.Live, We Are Ukraine, Pershyi, STB, 1+1, Channel 5, Suspilne Sport and Suspilne Culture.
Further evidence of the attacks is contained in a video posted by the Varyag Brigade, which is regarded as one of Russia's elite drone units alongside the better-known Rubicon unit. In the footage, Russian military personnel claim to have struck at least 11 data centres in Kyiv.
The exact dates of the strikes shown in the video cannot be established, but some appear to have taken place between 23 and 27 September. The footage clearly shows a strike on the Datagroup data centre on 25 September.
Read more: Fahrenheit 451: Russia has destroyed one-third of the books printed in Ukraine this year
The Ukrainian authorities had to respond. Following a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said specific decisions had been taken to protect data centres and other critical communications infrastructure. The government is preparing for the worst. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said the risk of widespread internet disruptions will persist for as long as Russia continues its strikes.
There is no one-size-fits-all way to protect this infrastructure. Some equipment can be moved underground; some can migrate to cloud environments or be relocated abroad. For some systems, a combination of these approaches may be used.
The government has allocated UAH 518.3 million (about US$11.5 million) to establish backup environments at separate locations, cloud infrastructure, and additional sites for state information systems. The funds will also be used to purchase server equipment, software, and data backup and recovery systems.
What happens if a data centre is attacked?
Much of the digital infrastructure Ukrainians rely on every day is built around data centres. The servers and storage systems they house keep websites, apps, state registers and banking services running.
Data centres are critical for internet service providers, as they house essential resources such as web, email and Domain Name System (DNS) servers, cloud infrastructure, and equipment belonging to providers and their clients.
Dmytro Kokhmaniuk, an expert on internet infrastructure and DNS, says some companies rent capacity in several data centres, others have their own facilities, and some combine both approaches. Spreading infrastructure across multiple sites helps make networks more resilient.
Repairing a data centre after an attack is a complex and lengthy process. "It's not just a room full of servers," Kokhmaniuk says. "It's a vast engineering system that includes a power supply, generators, cooling systems, ventilation, physical access control and network infrastructure. Damage to one or more of these elements can render the entire facility inoperable."
Consequently, a strike on a data centre can disrupt its operations even if the servers themselves escape damage. That does not necessarily mean, however, that the data stored there would be lost.
If up-to-date backups are stored at another independent site, the data can be restored. But getting everything back up and running requires computing resources, system configuration, and time. The impact of an attack therefore depends on how the particular service is set up and operated.
Since the start of Russia's full-scale war, a significant proportion of Ukraine's state registers and digital infrastructure has been moved to cloud services and backup environments in other countries.
So even if Russia destroys a Ukrainian data centre, the resulting outage may not last long. The attack may, however, cause temporary disruptions, loss of access and damage to equipment, and make it necessary to repair or relocate infrastructure.
Internet connectivity must also be restored separately. Damage to routers or an internet provider's cables can cut users off even when the service itself continues to operate. In that case, access can be restored using backup routes and equipment that survived intact, or by repairing the damaged network.
Internet speeds may drop
The events of 23 September offer some insight into what Russia may be trying to achieve by targeting Ukrainian network infrastructure.
One of the organisations affected that day was the internet service provider Pavutyna, which notified users of disruptions to its network. Co-owner and director Oleksandr Arutiunian said it was the third strike on the company's infrastructure, but the latest attack hit equipment at several locations almost simultaneously.
"The first two attacks were less disruptive because the backup systems worked better and the damage didn't all happen at the same time," Arutiunian says. "During the third attack, two locations were hit at once. The network could not recover automatically, so some users were left without a connection for between one and two hours. Repair crews then brought the network back online."
It appears that the Russians' target is not so much individual government services as the infrastructure that provides internet access. To this end, they are striking large data centres that house equipment used by several providers.
The telecoms industry representatives interviewed by Ekonomichna Pravda say these attacks cannot cut Ukrainians off from the internet entirely, because providers' network nodes are not only located in data centres.
"Networks have become much more decentralised in recent years," Arutiunian explains. "An operator can have far more than just one, two or five nodes. If necessary, backup equipment can be deployed at another site. In many cases this happens automatically, and engineers only need to step in when the damage is more serious."
If Ukrainian networks have numerous connections and backup routes, then what can Russia realistically achieve by attacking data centres?
Ekonomichna Pravda's sources say providers' network nodes and internet exchange points (IXPs) could potentially be targets. Network nodes support the operation of providers' networks, while IXPs allow different networks to exchange data. There are around 20 IXPs in Ukraine, and their equipment can be located at a single site or several.
The destruction of some of these facilities would not result in a nationwide internet blackout. As long as alternative connections are intact, internet service providers could reroute traffic through other operators, direct connections and international IXPs, just as traffic is diverted when a road is closed. Networks without an alternative route, however, could lose connectivity if their infrastructure is damaged.
The problem may lie elsewhere. Backup routes often have less capacity and are not set up to handle additional traffic. This could result in slower internet speeds and dropped connections for users.
That is what happened to internet provider Fiberlink after Russian attacks damaged the infrastructure of one of its backbone partners. The company rerouted traffic through a backup channel and warned users that internet speeds could temporarily drop. Further damage could lead to more significant disruptions.
According to Kokhmaniuk, poorer connection quality and slower data transfer speeds could be likely. In any event, operators will also have to absorb the additional cost of repairing infrastructure, deploying emergency repair crews and constructing backup lines. If the attacks continue, this could ultimately drive up the cost of broadband for subscribers.
"Operators will need to decentralise their networks further and expand the number of nodes and backup sites, which will increase the cost of providing services," Arutiunian says. "They will need more equipment, more staff and more resources to maintain and support this infrastructure."
Mobile network operator infrastructure
Mobile communications are another area of concern. If Russia continues to hit facilities belonging to mobile network operators, as it did on 27 September, this could have more serious consequences than attacks on data centres.
The Russians would not need to strike tens of thousands of base stations. The mobile core network, which manages subscriber registration, calls, text messages and mobile internet access, may be a far more vulnerable target.
If attacks were to disrupt critical functions of a core network beyond what its backup systems can handle, the consequences could be similar to those of the cyberattack on Kyivstar, which left millions of subscribers without access to calls, text messages or mobile internet.
Operators maintain backup infrastructure, but a fully-fledged mobile core network cannot simply be replicated by installing spare equipment at another node. Ekonomichna Pravda's sources estimate that building an additional core could cost each operator US$40-50 million. How many layers of redundancy would be needed if attacks on this infrastructure became sustained is an open question.
Ekonomichna Pravda's sources say the state and operators are taking steps to build more redundancy into critical network components. Some of these measures have been introduced only recently and will take time to implement. Russian attacks on mobile infrastructure could therefore pose a greater risk to communications.
What does this mean for users? In a critical situation, it's best to have more than one way of accessing the internet – for example, broadband from one provider and mobile internet from another. The more independent connections there are, the lower the risk of losing access during a large-scale attack.

Not just Dubai: Small airports expose Israel’s aviation security gaps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:43:06 UTC
01:43:06 KST

The attempted attack aboard a flydubai flight to Israel was thwarted and the security incident ended without disaster, but it also exposed a system in which no single agency bears full responsibility. The state comptroller warned about the problem in 2024; recommendations to create a coordinating authority were shelved and the Transportation Ministry, Shin Bet, National Security Council and Prime Minister’s Office are now pointing fingers at one another.
Dozens of flights operated by foreign airlines land in Israel every day carrying Israeli citizens. Most passengers are unaware that security arrangements on those flights are fundamentally different from those aboard Israel’s El Al, Arkia and Israir airlines.
The drama aboard flydubai Flight FZ1073 raised a simple question with no simple answer: Who, exactly, checks those aircraft and their crews?
ynet examined what the state comptroller wrote, what has been done since and what two former senior officials who worked inside the system have to say: Danny Shenar, who headed the Transportation Ministry’s Security, Emergency and Cyber Division for 25 years, and Eyal Hulata, who served as national security adviser and head of the National Security Council under the government of former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
What did the state comptroller say?
In May 2024, State Comptroller Matanyahu Englman issued a report on security for international civil aviation to and from Israel. The report, covering 2022 and 2023, remained classified by the Knesset’s State Control Committee, but its main findings are known: There were serious gaps and failures in aviation security, including the protection of aircraft operated by foreign airlines.
Its central recommendation was clear. The National Security Council was asked to lead a review with the Transportation Ministry, Finance Ministry, Israel Airports Authority, Shin Bet domestic security agency and police and formulate a new, comprehensive aviation security policy.
“Basically, the comptroller was right about everything he wrote, from A to Z,” Shenar said.
“He says a national authority needs to be established, that everything cannot rest with MAMLAT,” Shenar said, referring to the Hebrew acronym for the Aviation Security Operations Center, an operational body under the Transportation Ministry’s security division that is responsible for issuing security clearance for foreign flights seeking to land in Israel. “He said a comprehensive review had to be conducted. And they didn’t do it.”
Hulata was equally blunt.
“Nothing has been done since the comptroller’s report in 2024,” he said. “It’s a failure that cries out to the heavens.”
Who is responsible for what?
On paper, the answer regarding foreign flights is straightforward: the Transportation Ministry.
Under Israeli law and government decisions, the ministry’s Security, Emergency and Cyber Division, including MAMLAT, is responsible for conducting security assessments of foreign flights to Israel and issuing security instructions to airlines. According to the ministry, it has held that responsibility since 1977.
In practice, Shenar said aviation security is now divided among seven different bodies, resulting in “chaos and misunderstandings.” MAMLAT, he said, handles only about 20% of the sector: foreign and private flights.
In response to the criticism, the Transportation Ministry itself stressed the limits of its authority and capabilities.
“The Transportation Ministry is not an intelligence agency and does not have the tools to conduct intelligence background checks on crew members and passengers,” the ministry said. “Its procedures rely on security in the countries of origin, written commitments from the airlines and inspections at airports abroad.”
The “chaos” described by Shenar was also reflected in a report by Haaretz concerning Avri Cohen, head of the Transportation Ministry’s security division, who according to the newspaper simultaneously holds another job.
In addition to heading the division, Cohen reportedly works as a reserve security officer responsible for security at an overseas airport on behalf of Israeli airlines. It is paid work, separate from his official government position, for which he receives additional compensation. According to Haaretz, Cohen said the Transportation Ministry’s director-general approved the arrangement in 2018. Such an arrangement is highly unusual given the heavy workload associated with the positions.
Haaretz reported that Cohen also works with Ofek, a state aviation security apparatus operating on behalf of the Shin Bet to protect passengers on Israeli airlines overseas. Ofek security officers are deployed to airports around the world, where they oversee screening procedures for Israeli carriers. The job requires them to spend several days abroad at a time.
Cohen previously served in the system, which offers former personnel opportunities to fill in when staffing shortages arise. The Transportation Ministry said simply that “the management approved it in 2018.”
Why was a coordinating authority never established?
The idea is not new.
In 2011, the Transportation Ministry submitted a proposal to the prime minister to establish a national aviation security authority as a ministry-affiliated government agency responsible for all aspects of aviation security in Israel and abroad.
Shenar, who led the planning effort, said he coordinated the work of the various government ministries before presenting the proposal to senior officials.
“I coordinated all the government ministries and brought it to the director-general and the minister, and they brought it to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu,” he said. “There was a three-and-a-half-hour discussion, and the prime minister rejected the recommendation by Israel Katz, Dan Harel and me. There is no such body, and all the failures stem from that.”
According to the Transportation Ministry, two committees led by the National Security Council also previously recommended establishing a national authority responsible for all flights. The ministry said it supported the proposal then and continues to support it, but the recommendations were never implemented. Establishing such an authority would require a government decision.
Hulata placed responsibility on Netanyahu.
“He has an obligation to conduct a comprehensive review, identify gaps and identify who is not doing their part,” Hulata said. “The prime minister doesn’t want to touch anything.”
What has been addressed?
Very little, according to the former officials, and mostly around the edges.
The Transportation Ministry said that “after decades” it secured a dedicated budget to upgrade MAMLAT’s computer systems.
A gap involving charter flights — flights operated by Israeli airlines using foreign aircraft — was also addressed. Until 2021, all such flights were under Shin Bet security. That year, the security Cabinet decided the Shin Bet would secure only high-risk flights. The others were left without a clear security framework, a gap also identified by the state comptroller.
At the beginning of 2026, the Transportation Ministry assumed responsibility for those flights despite its reservations and subject to receiving the necessary budget and staffing.
So why are private aircraft, considered less dangerous, subjected to thorough checks?
“Because it’s easier, simpler,” Shenar said, arguing that the system had functioned better in the past.
MAMLAT was established following a 2003 government decision and began operating in 2006.
“We identified aircraft from 180 miles away, and within three or four minutes we could determine whether an aircraft was the one that had received clearance,” Shenar said.
At its peak, he said, fighter jets were scrambled about 19 times a month to intercept civilian aircraft, while officials from the United States, Britain and Canada came to study the Israeli model.
But after Shenar retired in 2017, he said, the security officer position remained vacant for a year and a half amid disputes over the appointment and petitions to the High Court of Justice.
Can Israel realistically check every crew?
With dozens of foreign flights arriving each day and hundreds of crew members involved, checking everyone may sound impossible for a single agency. Shenar rejects that argument.
“Technically, there’s no problem doing it,” he said. “Today, you enter a list of 5,000 pilots into a computer and get an answer within a minute.”
The legal basis already exists, he said. According to Shenar, the 1997 Aviation Law governing civil aviation security allows the transportation minister to demand the names of crew members flying aircraft to Israel and submit them to an intelligence agency for screening.
The problem is that, in practice, those lists are not being received.
In the flydubai case, according to the Transportation Ministry, the Emirati airline had committed to vetting its crews and said in writing that it had incorporated nationality restrictions into its crew scheduling system. Those restrictions were supposed to prevent pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel — including Oman, Syria, Iran and Pakistan — from operating flights to the country.
The Transportation Ministry said it did not receive the crew list for Flight FZ1073 and that its security division does not have access to flight crew lists.
In other words, Israel relied on a written declaration from a foreign airline.
After the incident, the blame game began.
An internal National Security Council document concluded last year that the Transportation Ministry was failing to fulfill its role in securing foreign flights. According to the document, professional officials in the ministry’s security division opposed transferring the responsibility to them, the director-general of the Civil Aviation Authority insisted on the move and Transportation Minister Miri Regev and Netanyahu ultimately approved it.
Hulata apportioned responsibility differently.
“It’s clear to us that Dubai is the first line of defense,” he said. “They should have checked who the Omani pilot was. The first line of contact collapsed.”
Had the Transportation Ministry conducted spot checks, Hulata argued, it could have determined whether flydubai was honoring its commitments.
“I’m not absolving the Shin Bet of responsibility,” he added, though he said the Mossad foreign intelligence agency had no direct responsibility unless there were gaps in understanding the threat.
Hulata also pointed to an earlier dispute with the United Arab Emirates. Israel did not allow Israeli airlines to fly there because Emirati authorities refused to permit Israeli security screening using CT scanners. The result, he said, was that Israelis instead flew aboard Emirati airlines that did not use the same screening procedures.
“The State of Israel abandoned its citizens,” Hulata said. “Who are we protecting here, El Al’s reputation? What about the Israeli citizen? They simply abandoned them.”
What happens next?
For now, the Transportation Ministry says security authorities are examining the circumstances of the flydubai incident.
“If it emerges that there was a deviation from the guidelines, it will be addressed accordingly,” the ministry said.
No agency, however, has announced any change to the underlying division of responsibilities.
Shenar pointed to what he sees as the next danger. Flights from major airports such as Athens operate with a strong security framework and advanced screening equipment, he said.
“But in most peripheral destinations and on the islands — Kos, Mykonos — the level of security is very poor,” he warned. “These are tiny airports, and aircraft fly from there to Israel without a security envelope. That’s where the danger lies.”
What should be done immediately?
Shenar said the first step is to establish the facts. In the longer term, he said, Israel should create the national aviation security authority that has repeatedly been proposed.
In the meantime, he said, Israel could require the names of all foreign pilots flying into the country, submit them for intelligence screening and prevent crew members from Iran, Syria, Iraq or Turkey from operating flights to Israel.
“At least an initial screening,” he said, acknowledging: “I understand there is no agreement on these things.”
If the current situation continues, Shenar warned, Israel could face “instability in the security of incoming foreign aviation.”
The latest incident ended safely. Next time, he said, Israel cannot afford to rely on luck.

Syria condemns Israeli excavation work near occupied Golan Heights as ‘flagrant breach’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:41:48 UTC
01:41:48 KST

Syria strongly condemned on Sunday Israeli excavation work near a separation line with the occupied Syrian Golan Heights, calling it a “flagrant breach” of the 1974 disengagement agreement.
In a statement, the Foreign Ministry denounced work on the project known as “Sofa 53,” as Israeli forces resumed excavations west of al-Asha village in the countryside of the southern Quneitra province.
The ministry described the work as part of continuing Israeli violations in the buffer zone covered by the disengagement agreement.
“The continuation of the Israeli occupation’s aggressive approach, accompanied by attacks and incursions on the ground, poses a direct threat to regional security and stability and undermines international law,” the ministry warned.
It urged the international community to take deterrent measures to halt such practices and prevent their recurrence.
Reasserting territorial sovereignty
The ministry also reaffirmed Syria’s right to exercise full sovereignty over all its territory under international law and relevant UN resolutions, calling on the international community to fulfill its legal and moral responsibilities to protect state sovereignty and respect borders.
According to Syria’s Al-Ikhbariya television channel, the project involves excavation and construction of a military road along the separation line within the buffer zone.
Israel began working on the project, also referred to as the “Great Storm” or “Sofa 53,” in mid-2022 near Hader in northern Quneitra, before extending it through Jabata al-Khashab, al-Hamidiyah, al-Qahtaniyah, Ruweihina, Bir Ajam and Bariqa.
Its route continues south through al-Asha toward the point where the Syrian, Jordanian and Israeli boundaries meet.
Israeli military expansion accelerates
As part of the project, the Israeli army built a military road approximately 8 metres wide, flanked by earth berms reaching around 5 metres in height, according to the Syrian broadcaster. It also established observation posts and military positions along the route adjacent to the ceasefire line in the occupied Golan Heights.
Syrian accounts indicate that Israeli forces have advanced between 300 and 1,000 metres beyond the ceasefire line, with military construction accelerating in late 2024, particularly after the fall of Bashar al Assad’s regime.
Residents previously told Anadolu that the project’s expansion had rendered thousands of dunams of agricultural land in rural Quneitra unsuitable for farming and grazing, while disrupting water flows and altering the area’s natural landscape.
Since Assad’s fall on December 8, 2024, Israel has expanded its military operations in Syria, moving troops into the Golan buffer zone and nearby positions.
Syria demands the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the areas they occupied and maintains its commitment to the 1974 disengagement agreement. Israel claims its movements are driven by security considerations.

U.S.-Russia negotiations on ending the war in Ukraine have expanded to include a multibillion-dollar oil deal that would benefit US and Middle Eastern businessmen linked to President Donald Trump’s circle.
The New York Times reported this.
The deal, which requires approval from the U.S. and Russian governments, concerns a large network of oil fields, refineries and gas stations in various countries owned by Russia’s Lukoil.
The New York Times learned about the talks, which have been underway for several months, from eight people familiar with them. The sources agreed to speak on condition of anonymity because of the negotiations’ sensitivity.
According to three people familiar with the meeting, Russian President Vladimir Putin raised the deal during talks with Witkoff and Kushner at the Kremlin on September 5. One source said Putin proposed the deal to show Russians they could do business with the United States.
Witkoff and Kushner, who have traveled to Russia repeatedly for meetings with Putin, argue that the prospect of restoring economic ties with the West could persuade the Russian president to compromise on Ukraine. The Trump administration has signaled that it is ready to pursue deals with Russia before the war ends to demonstrate its seriousness about resetting U.S.-Russia relations. According to people familiar with the matter, the sale of Lukoil’s assets is one such deal.
A group led by Todd Boehly, a billionaire and Trump supporter, is the leading bidder for a substantial portion of Lukoil’s international assets. Influential Middle Eastern figures and the U.S. government have joined the group.
Boehly is a co-owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers baseball team. In December 2025, he donated $1 million to MAGA Inc., a political action committee supporting Trump. He also contributed another $1 million through his investment company Eldridge Industries to Trump’s inauguration.
The U.S. government is expected to receive a stake in the deal through the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), an institution that invests in overseas projects and provides them with loans. A DFC representative said that a potential deal involving Lukoil would support the Trump administration’s commitments to strengthen U.S. economic security, advance American foreign policy, and lower energy prices for ordinary Americans.
A significant stake is expected to go to a Qatari conglomerate controlled by brothers Mutaz al-Khayyat and Ramez al-Khayyat. Both attended Trump’s 2025 inauguration and later partnered with Kushner and his wife, Ivanka Trump, one of the U.S. president’s daughters. They are helping finance a multibillion-dollar luxury hotel resort project in southern Albania.
Another major participant is expected to be an investment fund from Abu Dhabi controlled by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the United Arab Emirates’ national security adviser. He also controls another fund that acquired a significant stake in the Trump family cryptocurrency company World Liberty.
In September, Donald Trump said he had warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of the need to stop striking Russian oil refineries. Ukraine, for its part, proposed that its partners seek a mutual agreement with Russia to end strikes on critical infrastructure.

Breadcrumb
Future of far-right RN star Bardella in balance after antisemitism claims
After one of the most meteoric rises in the history of French politics, Jordan Bardella, the 31-year-old top ally of Marine Le Pen, is fighting for his political life after allegations he made antisemitic comments as a teenager in 2013.
Just a week ago, all was looking rosy for Bardella, with polls predicting Le Pen is on course to win the presidency at the fourth attempt, and the young leader of her National Rally (RN) party subsequently set to take the job of prime minister.
But then came the bombshell allegations published on Monday by the Mediapart website, which accused Bardella of writing a string of antisemitic messages in 2013. On Thursday, it posted screenshots of the messages written on Facebook Messenger.
Bardella chose a strategy of all-out attack to deny the allegations, accusing his opponents of launching a "total war" to derail the RN's rise to the presidency and vowing to take Mediapart to court for publishing what he described as fakes.
Le Pen, addressing party MPs side-by-side with Bardella on Tuesday, echoed his denial.
But she fell into an uncharacteristic silence after the screenshots were published on Thursday, broken only by a brief comment of "I have complete confidence in Jordan" to La Tribune Dimanche newspaper this weekend.
According to the report, Bardella wrote, among other comments, in a chat: "The Jew has to dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them; a Zionist is necessarily a Jew, and fundamentally so."
'Pull the plug' on Bardella?
Bardella's defiance indicated that he hopes to ride out the crisis, with his future depending on whether Mediapart has more allegations in the pipeline and above all, Le Pen herself.
He has been instrumental in implementing her strategy of "de-demonisation" to try and rid the party of the toxic legacy of its founder, her father Jean-Marie Le Pen, who was openly antisemitic.
Bardella made an unprecedented visit to Israel in 2025, the first by a French far-right leader, in a bid to demonstrate the RN's new credentials.
He was invited by Amichai Chikli, a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's hard-right government, who has cultivated ties with several European far-right parties despite their history of antisemitism.
"Marine Le Pen had to back Jordan Bardella so as not to alienate voters who would not forgive her for abandoning him," said sociologist Erwan Lecoeur, a specialist on the far-right.
But he added: "My belief is that Marine Le Pen will pull the plug on" Bardella, arguing that the more Bardella defends himself "the deeper he digs himself into a hole -- taking the RN down with him".
The allegations also surfaced after months of reports of tensions between Bardella and Le Pen -- notably over a policy to ban the Muslim headscarf in public -- even though the tandem maintained an outward united front.
"I don't think she necessarily has to get rid of him," said Marta Lorimer, lecturer in politics at Cardiff University.
"They will try to use whatever they can to defend his position," she told AFP.
"But my suspicion is if we see Bardella ousted it is not going to be because of this but because of possibly broader tensions with Le Pen. For the time being that does not seem to be the case."
'Contaminate the candidate'
There have also been suggestions that some in the RN would like to see Bardella exit and be replaced as Le Pens' de-facto running mate by another figure such as Eric Ciotti, the leader of an allied far-right party, or her niece Marion Marechal, who leads her own extreme-right movement.
Murmurs have also echoed on social media that the allegations could have come from within the RN, sparking a furious hunt for the "taupe" (mole).
Bardella has acknowledged what is at stake, saying that the aim is to "kill my political career".
His strategy of flat-out denial has also left him open to accusations of lying.
"Do we want a prime minister who is not only antisemitic but also lies to the French people in the face of damning evidence?" asked Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin.
Socialist leader Olivier Faure said: "We are dealing with two things here - his antisemitism and lying in politics. Neither is forgivable."
But with the RN lining up to back Bardella, Le Monde daily warned this had risks for Le Pen herself.
"The RN is closing ranks... in the hope that the storm will pass, at the risk of seeing the discredit attached to Jordan Bardella contaminate the presidential candidate," it said.
