Russia’s growing bear population: What you need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:40:08 UTC
01:40:08 KST

Russia’s growing bear population: What you need to know
Russia’s brown bear population has more than doubled over the past three decades, while a rise in attacks in recent years has prompted authorities and lawmakers to consider new ways to reduce the risks.
An independent online project has also begun mapping reports of bear encounters across the country.
What does the bear map show?
WhereBear brings together reports of bear sightings, attacks and tracks from official sources, media reports, open publications, and users, plotting them on an interactive map of Russia.
The independent service also accepts user submissions. It does not track animals in real time: markers show where and when bears were reported, rather than their current location.
How serious is the problem?
Russia is home to 307,900 brown bears, according to the Natural Resources Ministry.
The largest populations are concentrated in Siberia and the Far East, led by Krasnoyarsk Region with 26,600, Khabarovsk Region with 26,200 and Kamchatka with 24,200. Irkutsk Region has an estimated 22,400 and Yakutia 18,800.
Are bear attacks becoming more common?
Authorities have recorded 59 attacks so far this year, leaving 21 people dead and 38 injured across 22 regions.
The figure compares with 34 attacks in 2025 and 19 in 2024. Officials say around 20 to 30 attacks have typically been recorded annually in recent years, although there have been exceptional spikes. In 2014, 166 attacks were registered.
In the Krasnoyarsk Region, six people died in confirmed or suspected bear attacks in September alone, prompting investigators to open a criminal negligence case.
Heightened-alert regimes have been introduced in several parts of Siberia and the Far East. In Zakamensk, Buryatia, two schools and a technical college switched to remote learning after a bear appeared inside the town.
Why are bears approaching people?
Experts point to several factors, including the growing population, shortages of natural food, and easy access to human food.
Russian hunting inspectors and biologists have pointed to an unusually poor crop of nuts and berries this year. Researchers said that an early, dry spring caused berries to ripen and fall earlier than usual, leaving bears with less natural food as they prepared for hibernation.
Open rubbish containers, dumps, and food waste around homes and tourist facilities provide an easy source of calories. Once animals successfully find food near people, they may return. Wildlife authorities warn that bears accustomed to human food can gradually lose their natural caution and become more dangerous.
How are Russian authorities responding?
The Russian government is preparing additional measures following this year’s attacks.
Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Patrushev said on Wednesday that regions struggling to control bear numbers could receive additional federal funding. The government is also considering regulatory changes that would allow regional authorities to act more quickly, including potentially removing brown bears from the list of species subject to hunting limits.
”As the bear population grows, so does the number of problems,” Patrushev said at a government meeting on the issue.
Natural Resources Minister Aleksandr Kozlov has also proposed giving his ministry greater powers to verify regional estimates of bear numbers and setting baseline population levels for individual areas.
Separately, State Duma lawmaker Dmitry Novikov has proposed creating a public map showing areas where bears, wolves, and other predators regularly approach communities. His proposal includes camera traps and remote monitoring, as well as alerts for residents.
Why aren’t more bears being hunted?
Existing hunting limits are far from being reached. In 2025, hunters killed 12,700 bears nationwide, or around 27% of the nearly 47,000 they were permitted to hunt, according to the Association of Hunters and Fishermen.
Hunting groups have attributed the low uptake partly to the cost of hunting and weak demand for bear meat and skins. The association has proposed scrapping the fee to boost interest.
Why is the bear so closely associated with Russia?
Beyond the current concerns over their growing numbers, bears have featured in Russian culture for centuries, from folklore and literature to heraldry – long before they became an international stereotype associated with the country.
In Russian folk tales, bears can be powerful and fearsome, but also good-natured, naïve, or easily outwitted. They are often called Misha, a familiar form of the name Mikhail.
Trained bears were once common at fairs and public festivities, where handlers had them perform tricks, dance, and imitate people. Bears also made their way into Russian literature, appearing in works by writers including Leo Tolstoy and Mikhail Saltykov-Shchedrin. One appears prominently in Tatyana’s famous dream in Alexander Pushkin’s Eugene Onegin, drawing on a folk belief that dreaming of the animal could foretell marriage.
Bears have also appeared in Russian heraldry for centuries, including on the coats of arms of Yaroslavl, Perm, and Veliky Novgorod. Some of these images can be traced to the 16th and 17th centuries. Yaroslavl’s bear is linked to a legend about the city’s founding, while Perm’s carries a Gospel on its back.
Outside Russia, the animal gradually became a visual shorthand for the country, particularly in European political cartoons. British caricaturists were depicting Russia as a bear by the late 18th century, often using the image to convey size, strength, aggression, and menace. The stereotype persisted through the Russian Empire and the Soviet era and remains common today, with the ‘Russian bear’ often portrayed as a powerful and threatening beast.
From Olympic Misha to ‘Masha and the Bear’
One of the most famous modern versions of the image came with the 1980 Moscow Olympics, when a smiling bear cub named Misha was chosen as the Games’ mascot. Designed by Soviet children’s-book illustrator Viktor Chizhikov, Misha appeared on everything from stamps and posters to toys and souvenirs.
At the closing ceremony, thousands of participants in the stands formed a giant mosaic of Misha, with a tear appearing to roll down the bear’s cheek. The emotional farewell moved many spectators as an enormous inflatable version of the mascot was lifted into the air by balloons and floated out of the stadium to the song ‘Farewell, Moscow.’
Decades later, another Russian bear reached an even larger global audience. The traditional folk tale Masha and the Bear inspired the Russian animated series of the same name, which has become an international children’s hit. One episode, Recipe for Disaster, became the most-viewed animated video on YouTube, according to Guinness World Records.
Are other countries facing similar problems?
Russia is not the only country reporting an increase in encounters between bears and people.
Japan has faced similar problems, recording a record 238 bear-related casualties in fiscal 2025 and prompting the government to step up measures aimed at reducing encounters.
Human-bear conflicts are also reported in parts of North America and Europe. Wildlife authorities have similarly warned that bears attracted to rubbish and other human food can become accustomed to people and repeatedly return.
While circumstances vary by country and bear species, expanding or recovering populations, natural food availability, and access to human food can all affect how often bears and people cross paths.

Trump-Xi summit hard to swallow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:39:11 UTC
01:39:11 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) received two different welcomes within the space of 10 days — one in New Delhi and the other in Washington. In diplomatic protocol, the two could hardly have been more different. Yet, in their own ways, neither appeared particularly easy for Xi to digest. The discomfort seemed to show not merely in diplomacy, but almost physically.
Xi appeared distinctly uneasy in India. At one point during the BRICS summit, it was noticeable enough for host Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi to interrupt himself and ask Xi: “Are you OK?”
Xi did not attend the dinner that evening and left New Delhi early the next day.
Ten days later, when he landed in the world’s most powerful country, the reception was dramatically different. US President Donald Trump broke with decades of tradition to personally receive Xi at the airport.
During that visit, Xi’s face did not betray the same discomfort visible in India, but neither did he appear entirely at ease. At the White House dinner, Taiwanese music played in the background, and a choir performed songs from Les Miserables. To assume that the symbolism embedded in such music escaped the attention of the Chinese leadership would itself be diplomatic naivety.
These contrasting styles of welcome reveal something about the changing world order.
Who accords importance to whom — and how much? Why does one country embrace another while a third keeps its distance? Behind ceremonial protocol lie friendship and hostility, competition and rivalry, strategic proximity and strategic distance. These signals might also tell us something about the direction in which the world is heading.
In India, it was neither practical nor appropriate for Modi to personally receive every head of state at the airport. Protocol demands broadly comparable treatment at summits such as BRICS. That is why even Russian President Vladimir Putin, despite his close relationship with Modi, was received by the same level of ministerial representation that greeted Xi.
India was, in many ways, a reluctant host for Xi. He was visiting the country for the first time in seven years. The dark shadow of Galwan might have faded somewhat, but the wounds have not entirely healed. Troops might have disengaged from face-to-face positions along parts of the disputed Himalayan border, but mutual trust has hardly been restored — and Washington was watching.
Throughout the summit, India appeared deliberately restrained. That control manifested itself in several ways. Even the official briefing on the summit was conducted at the Sherpa-secretary level. Forget the Indian minister of external affairs — even the foreign secretary did not address the press briefing.
The BRICS declaration was a substantial achievement precisely because it accommodated widely differing interests. Yet neither Modi nor Indian Minister of External Affairs Subrahmanyam Jaishankar appeared eager to publicly claim political credit for it.
There was a reason for that restraint: Washington was watching with considerable suspicion. It was concerned about de-dollarization. It was also watching a gathering representing nearly half of humanity.
In that entire constellation, India — and perhaps Oman — could hardly be described as instinctively anti-Western. That left New Delhi with little incentive to display excessive enthusiasm about BRICS becoming an explicitly anti-Western platform.
What kind of diplomacy leads Washington to offer such an extraordinary welcome to the leader of the country it regards as its principal strategic competitor?
What does Trump want from China that he believes can be obtained by keeping Xi happy?
What does the US need from a country on which it imposes tariffs, and the rise of which it seeks to contain — or at least performs the diplomatic theater of containing? What does Washington seek from a China that stands behind Iran and provides Russia crucial support in its war on Ukraine?
The truth is that the US’ behavior is difficult for much of the world to digest.
That is why there is unease — from Taipei to Washington, Tel Aviv, Tehran, Ankara and New Delhi. Where exactly is this difficult-to-digest diplomacy of rebuking friends and embracing adversaries taking the US?
The G7, G20 and NATO increasingly risk looking less like partnerships and more like competing geopolitical gangs. Through the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, another grouping appears to be taking shape, one that is already being described in some quarters as an “Islamic NATO.” BRICS, and to some extent the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, represent counterweights to these formations.
However, the US’ diplomatically unpredictable behavior is scrambling established equations.
Xi is no less unpredictable. What exactly does he want? He is almost as difficult to decipher as Trump. By contrast, the strategic objectives of Putin, Modi and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whether one agrees with them or not, are easier to read.
When the leaders of the world’s two competing powers become simultaneously so unpredictable — and their diplomacy so difficult for everyone else to digest — it might not necessarily mean that catastrophe is imminent, but it certainly does not make for a reassuring world order.
Mukesh Kaushik is an Indian journalist and commentator on strategic affairs, defense and geopolitics. He is a researcher at National Chengchi University on the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Taiwan Fellowship.

He has a presence that commands attention, and a combination of qualities that appear to be the result of powerful political currents. What is it that makes Shen different? Throughout the past decades of local elections, I have not seen anyone seriously discuss a long-term vision for urban planning, let alone with the kind of clarity and insight that Shen possesses that compels people to keep listening. He is an exceptional storyteller, with an ability to present a vision

Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising

Four more people have been reported missing in China, bringing the total number of Taiwanese who have been reported missing, detained for questioning or suspected of having their freedom of movement restricted from Jan. 1, 2024, to Friday to 453, the Mainland Affairs Council said in its weekly report issued on Saturday.
The council’s latest report showed that 172 Taiwanese have been reported missing, up from 168 the previous week, while 39 have been detained for questioning, unchanged from last week, and 242 have been held by Chinese authorities, also unchanged.
It added that it had received reports of four civil servants being questioned by Chinese authorities, including a Criminal Investigation Bureau officer, a tax official and a nurse at a Ministry of Health and Welfare hospital.
Photo: Chung Li-hua, Taipei Times
The nurse was questioned by Chinese state security personnel about the military hospital she had previously worked at, making it the first known case of a Taiwanese nurse being subjected to such questioning.
Asked whether any of the Taiwanese reported missing in China might have had their organs removed, a government official familiar with cross-strait affairs said that authorities “do not know.”
The missing people have not been located and no relatives have reported circumstances suggesting organ harvesting had taken place, the official added.
The Taoyuan District Prosecutors’ Office last month indicted seven people following an investigation into a suspected human trafficking ring that allegedly attempted to capture people to take to China for organ harvesting. The group allegedly recruited people with promises of high-paying jobs. Three people were deceived, but were never transported out of Taiwan.
The official said human trafficking operations could involve another layer: groups that perform organ-removal surgeries.

Paprika makers fight to save national spice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:39:09 UTC
01:39:09 KST

Working from before dawn until midnight, farmers Nikoletta Pajsan Nagy and Laszlo Pajsan fought Europe’s driest summer ever to save their red pepper harvest in Hungary.
Unable to irrigate much of their two-and-a-half-hectare land because power lines run across it, they repeatedly loosened the soil around the plants, which are used to make the central European country’s signature spice, paprika.
“I was absolutely convinced that we’d have to take on part-time jobs because they’d burn out,” Pajsan Nagy, 44, said, while selling her family’s products at the annual town fair in Kalocsa, in southern Hungary.
Photo: AFP
“But somehow the crop turned out bigger and more beautiful than in previous years. It was a miracle,” she said, recalling some 20-hour days in the field.
The couple see themselves as a dwindling profession, as cultivation of paprika — an indispensable ingredient in traditional cuisine — has declined over the past several decades in Hungary, with many small producers going out of business.
The area devoted to paprika peaked at 13,029 hectares in 1979 and had fallen to 1,410 hectares by 2024, official statistics showed.
While cheap imports from China and parts of South America are squeezing producers, climate change is making paprika production more difficult and costly, said Robert Braj, an adviser at Dutch-owned BWA Kft, one of Hungary’s top food-seasoning manufacturers.
“There are longer droughts, more extreme heatwaves, while new pests and diseases are spreading,” Braj said.
Along with some other EU nations, Hungary experienced its driest summer since records began in 1901 and its second-hottest on record, the national weather service HungaroMet said. Labor shortages are also a problem.
At the fair, paprika seller Agnes Toth recalled picking up peppers as a child, taking part in the family business.
“Back then, we grew paprika on six hectares. Now it’s around three hectares because there aren’t enough seasonal workers to harvest it by hand,” the 44-year-old said.
“A family couldn’t make a living from this anymore... Everyone has a full-time job. I’m a teacher, my brother is a firefighter,” she said.
Hungary’s Agriculture and Food Economy Ministry said it seeks to bolster producers’ competitiveness, but it is yet to announce any new measures.
At last month’s annual fair in Kalocsa, one of Hungary’s main paprika-growing regions, the aroma of meat stews and fish soups laced with the vibrant scarlet spice filled the air as teams poured generous amounts into their cauldrons at a cooking contest.
“For us Hungarians, paprika is a wonder,” one of the competitors, local fast-food restaurant owner Imre Zseni said, while stirring a beef stew.
Booths were adorned with strings of dried red peppers — the raw ingredient used to make paprika — recalling a sight once common on houses in the surrounding countryside every autumn.
Originating from the Americas, peppers found their way to Hungary’s sun-drenched, fertile river plains around Kalocsa and Szeged in the 16th century.
The two historic paprika-production centers are recognized with the EU’s protected designation of origin status.
Ethnographer Imre Romsics said paprika became an important symbol of Hungarian identity during the 19th century, “alongside costume, folk art and other traditions.”
However, younger generations cook fewer traditional Hungarian recipes, and they prefer food “that is faster and easier to prepare,” specialist Braj said.

US still top debtor of Taiwan’s banks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:39:07 UTC
01:39:07 KST

The US remained the largest debtor of Taiwanese banks for the 44th consecutive quarter at the end of June, with its share of Taiwanese banks’ total exposure surpassing 30 percent for the first time, the central bank said on Friday.
Taiwanese banks’ exposure to the US on an immediate counterparty basis reached a new high of US$222.53 billion at the end of the second quarter, up 6.47 percent from a quarter earlier, central bank data showed.
According to the Bank for International Settlements, the immediate counterparty basis is a methodology under which positions are allocated to the primary party to a contract.
Photo: Reuters
Department of Financial Inspection Deputy Director-General Hsieh Jen-chun (謝人俊) said the increase in exposure to the US resulted from growth in interbank loans and investments.
The increase in investments largely came from investments and fund deposits in US marketable securities amid a booming stock market, Hsieh said.
At the end of June, total international claims of Taiwan’s banks on an immediate counterparty basis, consisting of investments, deposits, loans and other holdings, rose 4.61 percent from a quarter earlier to US$735 billion, driven by increased lending to the global non-bank private sector.
Exposure to the US accounted for 30.28 percent of the local banking sector’s total at the end of June, a new high, up from 29.75 percent at the end of March, data showed.
The Taiwanese banking sector’s second-largest area of exposure was Luxembourg, at US$54.84 billion, up 6.07 percent from a quarter earlier, the central bank said.
Hsieh described Luxembourg as an important hub for mutual fund registration, meaning many local investors invest through banks in the country.
China came in third, with exposure totaling US$51.76 billion, up 4.94 percent from a quarter earlier, the central bank said.
Hsieh said the gap in exposure between the US and China widened gradually to a new high of US$170.7 billion at the end of June. Since the second quarter of 2023, the quarterly gap has exceeded US$100 billion for 13 consecutive quarters.
Australia was the fourth-largest debtor of Taiwan’s banks, with exposure totaling US$47.82 billion, up 2.06 percent from a quarter earlier, central bank data showed.
The next-largest areas of exposure for Taiwanese banks were Japan (US$41.46 billion, up 8.26 percent), Hong Kong (US$38.01 billion, up 11.67 percent), the UK (US$24.83 billion, down 1.35 percent), Singapore (US$23.87 billion, up 6.38 percent), France (US $20.83 billion, up 1.00 percent), and Vietnam (US$20.66 billion, up 7.74 percent), data showed.
The central bank said exposure to the top 10 debtor nations totaled US$546.62 billion at the end of June, rising 5.80 percent from a quarter earlier and representing 74.37 percent of total international claims by Taiwanese banks.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi yesterday urged “dialogue, not confrontation” ahead of talks among African leaders as concerns grow that Ethiopia’s escalating violence could spill across borders.
Al-Sisi was due to meet the leaders of Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan in El-Alamein later in the day, with the Ethiopian conflict expected to feature prominently on the agenda.
Those three countries have strained relations with Addis Ababa, which has accused Eritrea of backing Tigray rebels with support from Sudan and Egypt, allegations all three nations deny.
Photo obtained by Reuters
Addressing the African Union’s mid-year coordination summit, Al-Sisi said Egypt opposed foreign interference in African states and called for relations to be based on “mutual respect, good neighborliness, dialogue and consultation, far from unilateral policies or narrow interests.”
Cross-border challenges “require cooperation, not competition, and dialogue, not confrontation,” including in managing natural resources and transboundary rivers in accordance with international law, he said.
The remarks come against the backdrop of Egypt’s long-running dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile.
Cairo and Khartoum have for years sought a legally binding agreement governing the dam’s operation, citing concerns over water security, while Ethiopia says the project is crucial to its economic development and energy needs.
Renewed fighting in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region has revived fears of a return to the country’s devastating 2020-2022 civil war.
The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) launched attacks on federal forces last month and Ethiopian troops were reported yesterday to have taken full control of Mekelle, the regional capital.
The TPLF on Saturday said it had pulled out. It had done so in the previous two-year war, which ended with a peace agreement in 2022, apparently to spare the city from destruction.
Fighters loyal to the TPLF seized the airport on Sept. 23, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to Mekelle and the Tigrayan cities of Axum and Shire.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has tried and failed to subdue Tigray’s rebellious leaders over the past few months, with TPLF chairman Debretsion Gebremichael openly challenging him.
Debretsion on Thursday said the fighting was a “continuation of the previous war” and that his fighters would keep attacking and defending Tigray from its enemies.
After federal troops take control of Mekelle, Abiy is likely to leave regional security in the hands of the Tigray Peace Force, ACLED analyst for Ethiopia Jalale Getachew Birru said.

New Tainan train station opens up later this month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:39:04 UTC
01:39:04 KST

Taiwan Railway Corp’s new station in Tainan is scheduled to open on Oct. 17 as part of a project to shift the mainline rail infrastructure in the city underground, the Railway Bureau under the Ministry of Transportation and Communications said yesterday.
Built next to the historic Tainan Station, completion of the new station allows the surrounding area to be redeveloped with a plaza, parking facilities, a transport hub and green space to improve connectivity and passenger access, the bureau said.
The new station is the first Taiwan Railway station to use a color-coded wayfinding system similar to that of the Taiwan High Speed Rail, with blue for northbound trains and green for southbound trains, according to the railroad.
Photo: CNA
The new station is part of the Tainan Urban District Railway Underground Project, which aims to reconnect areas of the city divided by street-level railway tracks. The historic Tainan Station is to be preserved as a heritage site, the bureau said.
The project covers an 8.23km section from the southern end of Daciao Station (大橋車站) to about 600m south of Dalin Road, according to the bureau.
It includes two new underground commuter stations, Linsen (林森) and South Tainan (南台南), which are scheduled to open in 2029 and 2030, respectively.
After the new station opens, the street-level railway would be gradually dismantled, allowing work on the second phase, including landscaping and other above-ground facilities, to proceed.
Once completed, the project is expected to eliminate 23 railway crossings and other grade-separated intersections, including nine level crossings, eight underpasses and four overpasses, the bureau said.
Approved in 2009 as part of a broader effort to modernize Taiwan’s railway system in metropolitan areas, the project is expected to be completed in stages through 2031, it said.

The army plans to commission the National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST) to build dedicated testing facilities for its indigenously developed Lu Chien II (陸射劍二, “Land Sword II”) missile systems, with a budget of more than NT$295 million (US$9.27 million), marking move toward fully self-reliant air defense logistics, sources said yesterday.
The move came as the navy’s missile inspection and testing capacity has become increasingly strained by growing demand associated with its next-generation light frigates and the Kang Ding-class frigate, as well as demand for the production and testing of Hai Chien II missiles (海劍二, “Sea Sword II”), a senior military official said on condition of anonymity.
From 2028, the navy would no longer support testing for the army’s surface-launched Land Sword II missiles, they said.
Photo: Tsai Tsung-hsien, Taipei Times
As the NCSIST had prioritized developing the Hai Chien II missiles, during the early development of the Land Sword II system, it relied heavily on naval equipment and vessels to verify launch ignition, radar integration and terminal seeker performance, they said.
The navy’s test ship, the Kaohsiung, served as a missile-testing platform, they added.
To prevent gaps in air defense readiness, the army has decided to abandon the cross-service testing arrangement and invest nearly NT$260 million in building an independent support capability, they said.
While the budget does not cover new missile acquisitions, it is a crucial step toward self-reliant logistics, the official said.
The funding would be used to comprehensively refurbish facilities, install temperature and humidity-controlled systems, upgrade ammunition safety infrastructure and procure dedicated testing equipment, they said.
The new systems would be capable of simulating radar signals and midcourse guidance commands, as well as conducting full-circuit diagnostics on missiles, they added.
The facility would allow the army to carry out inspections, functional tests and seeker calibration for Land Sword II missiles without relying on the navy, significantly improving maintenance flexibility and operational readiness, they said.
The move aligns with the army’s upcoming five-year, NT$3.65 billion procurement program to acquire additional Land Sword II missiles, which begins in the next fiscal year, the official said.
The NCSIST is upgrading its Land Sword II system to cut reload times from nearly 30 minutes after firing to less than 10 minutes, they said, adding that a standardized launcher canister would also be adopted.
The new testing facility is expected to open alongside the army’s procurement of upgraded missiles from next year to 2031, allowing newly manufactured missiles to undergo immediate intake testing, the official said.
With the delivery of the initial batch of 246 land-based Land Sword II missiles, the synchronized logistics model gives field air defense units complete operational autonomy, the official said.
In-house intake of new missiles, life extension for older units and routine overhauls will form a streamlined, end-to-end process within the army, they added.
The initiative would improve the readiness of the army’s mobile air defense units during precision firing exercises, which would be another significant step in bolstering Taiwan’s asymmetric warfare capabilities, integrated air defense network and logistics resilience, they said.

Taitung could use more urban green space: MOENV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:39:01 UTC
01:39:01 KST

Taitung County has the highest forest coverage nationwide, but has insufficient urban green cover, Minister of Environment Peng Chi-ming (彭?明) said yesterday, adding that urban forests could mitigate heat from foehn winds.
Peng made the remarks during a briefing hosted by the Ministry of Environment (MOENV) in Taitung on the government’s national green cover initiative.
Peng said the plan was launched by President William Lai (賴清德) last year, promoting urban green cover as resilience infrastructure alongside things such as water and power supply.
Photo: Screen grab from Taitung County Government’s Web site
The ministry on April 30 launched the urban forest expansion plan, he said, adding it would put forward an urban forest special act by the end of this year.
Taitung County’s green cover is limited to mountainous areas, Peng said.
Green cover remains insufficient in the county’s low-lying urban areas, where heat issues are usually compounded by foehn winds, he said.
Local foehns often reached 40°C, while urban streets without green cover could be heated to higher than 40°C under direct sunlight, Peng said.
The ministry is planning to create a national evaluation mechanism based on the EU’s experience with the European Green Capital Award, Peng said, adding that the county could become Taiwan’s “green capital.”
The ministry would coordinate resources from public and private sectors to assist local governments in implementing urban forest planning, he said.
Climate Change Administration Deputy Director-General Chang Ken-mu (張根穆) said trees not only help cool down urban temperatures, but can mitigate flooding by absorbing rainfall.
The ministry has found that the county’s Jinfeng Township (金峰) had the highest average noon temperature this summer, followed by Taitung City, Taimali Township (太麻里) and Dawu Township (大武), he said.
Trees should first be planted in sites where heat-vulnerable groups such as children, older people or those with disabilities gather, Chang said.
The goal is to plant the right tree species and encourage long lives with cultivation, he said.
Trimmed branches or fallen trees would be recycled as wood resources to reduce the burden on incinerators, Chang said.
National Taitung University vice president for administration Hu Cho-chun (胡焯淳) supported Peng’s idea of introducing a “green capital” evaluation mechanism to encourage local government’s urban forest development.
The Society of Wilderness’ Taitung branch spokeswoman Su Ya-ting (蘇雅婷) called for incorporating the national green cover climate adaptation scheme into the nation’s spatial planning.

Amazon makes vow to data center towns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:39:01 UTC
01:39:01 KST

Amazon.com Inc on Friday pledged more than US$1 billion over five years for US communities that host its data centers, the latest tech giant seeking to win over residents increasingly hostile to the artificial intelligence (AI)-fueled construction boom.
The Built Together program, unveiled by Amazon Web Services (AWS) chief Matt Garman in a 3,000-word blog post, would fund free community college degrees and trades training as well as energy-efficiency upgrades for schools and homes.
The company also announced a Data Center Commitment, promising that its facilities would not drive up local electricity bills and that it would publish annual figures on energy and water use.
Photo: AFP
Garman said AWS would stop using nondisclosure agreements with government agencies on its projects, a practice that has become a major flashpoint for the movement opposing data centers.
Microsoft Corp made a similar move in March, the first major tech firm to do so.
Garman cast the buildout as a national security imperative on par with the 1950s interstate highway system.
He warned that with more than 100 local moratoriums under consideration nationwide, the US “could be writing its own losing ticket” in the AI race and that “the consequences would last generations.”
He also took aim at what he called myths about data centers, disputing as false arguments that they drive up power costs, deplete water supply and cause pollution from diesel fumes. Citing “widespread reports,” Garman said some countries were deliberately seeding misinformation in the US to slow construction — an argument also made by US President Donald Trump’s administration.
Disinformation researchers and fact-checkers say such claims overstate the role of foreign influence campaigns in a grassroots movement that spans the political spectrum and nearly every US state.
Trump, a vocal champion of the buildout, has warned that communities rejecting the facilities would “end up being backwards and poor.”
Amazon’s rivals have made similar overtures. In January, Microsoft pledged to fully cover its data centers’ power costs and stop requesting local tax breaks, and OpenAI promised that its Stargate data centers would not raise local electricity prices.
In March, Amazon, Google, Meta Platforms Inc, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle Corp and SpaceXAI signed a White House pledge to provide their own power for new data centers and pay for any grid upgrades they require.

Health study shows the efficacy of drug treatments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:59 UTC
01:38:59 KST

A local public health study found that methadone maintenance treatment and needle and syringe programs are highly cost-effective in reducing HIV transmission, Centers for Disease Control (CDC) Director-General Philip Lo (羅一鈞) said yesterday.
Lo made the remarks amid a heated debate online over methadone maintenance treatment and needle and syringe programs between supporters of Taipei mayoral candidates over the weekend.
Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) said on Saturday that drug prevention measures include needle exchange and methadone treatment programs, while Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安), currently seeking re-election, on Saturday said in a Facebook post that the danger lies in blurring the line between illegal drugs and medication, and urged against using methadone treatment as a smokescreen.
Photo: Lin Hui-chin, Taipei Times
The post sparked a fierce response from their respective supporters, drawing more 100,000 comments within two hours.
Lo yesterday posted on Facebook a link to a local public health study, saying that needle and syringe programs and methadone maintenance treatment proved to be highly cost-effective in reducing HIV transmission among people who take drugs intravenously, a public health policy where every NT$1 invested saves NT$19 in medical expenditure.
The two harm reduction policies have prevented 13,664 intravenous drug users from being diagnosed with HIV between 2005 and 2020, and they are expected to prevent 10,821 HIV transmissions between 2021 and 2040, he said.
The two policies cost NT$21 billion between 2005 and 2020, but saved in HIV-related medical expenditure by NT$404.1 billion during the same period. The policies cost NT$28 billion between 2021 and 2024, but are expected to save NT$321.3 billion in HIV-related medical expenditure, he said, adding that the benefit-cost ratios are 18.94 and 11.47, respectively.
Disease prevention transcends political parties, and the central and local governments would continue to implement cost-effective public health policies, Lo said, adding that he hoped everyone continued to support harm reduction policies as well as encourage the frontline workers and the participants in the programs.

Unknown Publisher

16:38:59 UTC
01:38:59 KST

CPC Corp, Taiwan (台灣中油) said on Saturday that it would keep its domestic gasoline and diesel prices unchanged this week, even though international crude oil prices still hovered at high levels.
Formosa Petrochemical Corp’s (台塑石化) Web site also indicates that it would maintain its fuel prices at the same levels.
The decisions marked the third consecutive week that CPC and Formosa have kept their domestic fuel prices steady as part of the government’s efforts to ease inflationary pressure.
Last week, international crude oil prices stayed volatile with Brent, the global benchmark, moving lower, but the West Texas Intermediate in the US moving higher amid conflict in the Middle East.
State-run CPC said its floating price mechanism, based on a weighted average of 70 percent Dubai and 30 percent Brent crude, showed that the average international crude oil price fell from US$115.33 per barrel last week to US$112.54 this week.
However, a weaker New Taiwan dollar, which averaged NT$31.850 against the US dollar last week, compared with NT$31.741 in the previous week, slightly raised purchasing costs for CPC.
Retail gasoline prices this week are to remain at NT$31.2, NT$32.7 and NT$34.7 per liter for 92, 95 and 98-octane unleaded gasoline respectively at CPC and Formosa stations, while prices of premium diesel would stay at NT$29.9 per liter at CPC stations and NT$29.7 per liter at Formosa pumps, the companies said.

Mayoral candidates bicker over drug policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:55 UTC
01:38:55 KST

Democratic Progressive Party Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) and Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) continued to clash over drug policy yesterday.
The dispute began after Shen introduced a campaign platform with four strategies to combat drug use in schools last Friday, including interdicting the supply of drugs, improving life-skills education and implementing drug screening, complemented by judicial measures.
KMT lawmakers Lo Chih-chiang (羅智強) and Hsu Chiao-hsin (徐巧芯) and KMT Taipei City Councilor Yang Chih-tou (楊植斗) the next day cited a 2014 op-ed in which Shen discussed decriminalization and wrote that illegal drugs and medicines should be treated on the same conceptual footing, and that Taiwan should establish community centers like in some countries to provide drug users with clean needles and controlled substances.
Photo: George Tsorng, Taipei Times
Asked for comment, Shen on Saturday said Taipei’s needle and syringe programs — providing sterile injecting equipment and safe disposal options to people who use drugs intravenously — started when Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九) of the KMT was mayor of Taipei, and is a policy that is still being implemented across the nation.
Illegal drugs and medicine are both called “drugs” in English, Shen said, adding that the main issue is risk management, and the KMT lawmakers might have misunderstood, as he also said that Taiwan’s institutional framework is not ready for decriminalizing illegal drug use.
Chiang, seeking re-election, on Saturday evening said in a Facebook post that “there is no room for ambiguity when it comes to combating drugs,” and asked if city residents could accept Shen’s idea of setting up community centers and providing clean needles, syringes and drugs.
Photo: CNA
He criticized Shen as “blurring the line between illegal drugs and medicine,” bringing fear and doubt to city residents.
As of 5pm yesterday, Chiang’s post had more than 475,900 comments, mostly accusing him of deliberately misstating the situation.
Shen at midnight said in a Facebook post that there are no problems discussing anti-drug policies, but Chiang and KMT lawmakers should stop disingenuously conflating harm reduction policies, such as methadone maintenance treatment and needle and syringe programs, with “encouraging illegal drug use,” as it could misguide parents and children and discourage drug prevention workers.
Asked to comment on the rapidly increasing visibility on Chiang’s post, Chiang’s campaign office yesterday accused Shen of being unable to confront his past positions, while the comments section was active late into the night.
“The money is burning, must be hard work,” it added, implying that the DPP was behind an organized online campaign.
Chiang said yesterday that he has always supported methadone maintenance treatment and needle and syringe programs.
In Taiwan, methadone maintenance treatment is administered orally.
He urged Shen not to shift the focus, adding that in Shen’s 2014 article, he didn't mention a word about methadone maintenance treatment but that Taiwan could set up "community centers like in some countries to provide drug users with clean needles and controlled substances."
Shen said yesterday that his 2014 article was about introducing drug-related harm reduction measures around the world.
His campaign platform announced on Friday last week was focused on addressing the spread of new psychoactive substances on campuses, he said, adding it is regrettable to see the crucial issue, of protecting school children become a point to spar over.
Many public health workers might feel like they are being stigmatized, as his political adversaries are tarring public health harm reduction policies, he said.
Shen invited Chiang to debate him on drug policy.
KMT Culture and Communications Committee Director Chen I-hsin (陳以信) yesterday urged Chiang and Shen to publicly debate on drug policy to make their policies clear and allow Taipei voters to decide.
In response, Chiang yesterday said that opposition to drug use is an absolute moral issue, not something up for debate, and that his zero-tolerance stance was firm.
Shen said he is willing to accommodate any format of debate, provided that the discussion focuses on specific details, rather than an exchange of insults.

Chiang needs Wanhua reality check
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:51 UTC
01:38:51 KST

During a tour of Taipei’s Wanhua District (萬華) on Sept. 22, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) proposed a seemingly appealing urban-planning vision for the area: linking Xinfu Market (新富市場), East Sanshui Street Market (東三水街市場), Longshan Temple (龍山寺), Bopiliao Historical Block (剝皮寮歷史街區), Bangka Park (艋舺公園), the underground mall and surrounding commercial areas through neighborhood redevelopment and environmental improvements, while encouraging specialty and boutique business. It would create what Chiang called Taipei’s version of Omotesando — an upscale, tree-lined boulevard and shopping district in Tokyo — to attract young people and international tourists.
The idea is not new. More than NT$200 million (US$6.28 million) has already been invested in the redevelopment of Bangka Park, and the city government has previously invoked Tokyo’s Omotesando as a vision for the area.
There is no question that Wanhua deserves a makeover. The issue is whether the mayor’s words are grounded in the reality of what Wanhua needs and is ready for.
Just five days before Chiang’s proclamation, Wanhua police carried out a “cleanup operation” targeting prostitution on Xichang Street. Eighteen suspected illegal sex workers and two people suspected of soliciting prostitutes were detained; 10 of them had overstayed their visas.
Pointing out the arrests is not to stigmatize Wanhua, nor to overlook its rich history and culture. Rather, it is a reminder to the Chiang administration that urban renewal is not easily achieved.
When parts of Wanhua are still grappling with aging buildings, environmental quality issues, prostitution and public safety concerns, what the city government should be prioritizing is improving living conditions, enhancing public safety and promoting urban renewal in a way that ensures residents and businesses benefit together. That requires a system of urban governance. Without it, the contrast between the glossy slogan of “Omotesando” and the reality of Wanhua is made even more glaring.
Slogans and policies move quickly through Chiang’s administration, but preliminary assessments do not keep pace. In August, as part of Taipei’s smoke-free city initiative, metal-barred smoking areas installed in areas such as Gongguan (公館) sparked immediate backlash over their appearance, function and integration with the surrounding environment.
Less than a month after their installation, all seven of the barriers, which each cost NT$149,000, were removed. Chiang said that if facilities did not meet actual needs, they should be reviewed and adjusted, and that the city would establish a unified site-review mechanism.
That is precisely the issue: Why did the city only realize after the fact that a basic review of location, appearance and the surrounding environment might be necessary? Public policy must certainly be open to revision, but public funds are not the mayor’s pocket money for endless trial and error.
What residents should be asking is not how nice Chiang’s Wanhua idea sounds, but how thoroughly planned it actually is.
Where would it be redeveloped? How much would be invested? What would the construction schedule be? How might prostitution and public-safety problems be addressed? How would aging blocks be renewed? How would transportation, pedestrian environments and commercial districts be integrated? Would residents and traditional markets be squeezed out by commercialization?
Without answers to these basic questions and with a city government rushing to hang an “Omotesando” sign over Wanhua, residents have every reason to be worried. The risk is that announcements are made and money is spent, only for an issue to be discovered the next day, followed by a review and then more money being spent to tear down what had already been started.
A project of this magnitude needs a city government capable of thinking things through before construction.
Chiang might have the ambition to transform Wanhua, and the district certainly deserves public infrastructure commensurate with its historical importance. However, one of the greatest taboos of urban governance is to treat a vision alone as an achievement.
Tokyo’s Omotesando only became what it is through decades of urban design, commercial activity, transportation infrastructure and neighborhood development. Wanhua has little reason to copy Omotesando; it is one of the most historically rich parts of Taipei and a fundamentally different case. Before anything else, Chiang should first endeavor to get Wanhua’s governance right. Otherwise, residents have reason to question whether this is another case on Chiang’s municipal agenda destined for the cycle of slogans, spending and backtracking.
Elliot Yao is a reviewer.

The government would soon be able to invest in offshore artificial intelligence (AI) companies that conduct their primary business activities in Taiwan, following an amendment aimed at boosting investment in AI start-ups.
The National Development Fund (NDF) in 2024 earmarked NT$10 billion (US$314.17 million) for the Ministry of Digital Affairs to invest in AI start-ups and the digital economy over 10 years. The program launched last year, with seven years for investments and three years for divestments.
Administration for Digital Industries Director-General Lin Jiunn-shiow (林俊秀) yesterday said the government is also working with venture capital firms, accelerators and corporate venture capital investors to identify and jointly fund start-ups with high potential.
Photo: Fang Wei-chieh, Taipei Times
The collaboration helps expand the corporate scale of start-ups, and expedite their progress in public trading and breaking into the international market, Lin said.
“The project originally targeted Taiwanese AI start-ups and companies in the digital economy sector. However, it has come to our attention that some are raising funds overseas and tapping international markets. As a result, they might set up offshore entities while maintaining their operational and research-and-development bases in Taiwan,” Lin said.
“This is also a demonstration of Taiwan’s power in AI-related industries. As such, we decided to consider investing in more companies, so long as they are affiliated with Taiwan,” he added.
The plan would expand to offshore entities whose main business activities and investment targets are in Taiwan, including those that set up research-and-development (R&D) headquarters in Taiwan, spend more than 50 percent of their total R&D budget here and recruit more than 50 percent of their employees from Taiwan; and if 50 percent of their total revenue are generated from offices based in Taiwan, the ministry said.
As of August, 10 AI start-ups have received funding from the government and private investors, including Turing Drive (台灣智慧駕駛) and Linker Vision Co (鑫蘊林科).
In terms of funding, NT$255 million came from the National Development Fund, while NT$570 million was from the private sector.
From January to August, the government invested about NT$194 million from the National Development Fund in seven start-ups, Lin said.
Turing Drive’s autonomous driving demonstration vehicles began operating in Japan’s Miyakojima and Uwajima Islands in the first quarter of this year and have obtained Japanese plates, he said.
The company has also brought on board Japanese autonomous driving technology firm Tier IV as an investor, and is working with it to expand operations to Nagoya and Singapore, he added.
Linker Vision has joined AT&T, Cisco and Nvidia in building AI grid infrastructure, combining Cisco’s edge platform, Nvidia’s GPU computing capabilities and AT&T’s video intelligence technology, Lin said.

AI frenzy powers Hong Kong fundraising record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

Bankers in Hong Kong skipped the summer break as an artificial intelligence (AI)-fueled rush for capital sent share sales to a record, defying a bruising selloff in the city’s stocks.
Initial public offerings (IPOs), placements and block trades raised US$47.5 billion in July to last month, the biggest haul ever for the period, data compiled by Bloomberg showed. That pushed fundraising this year above US$92 billion and within reach of the US$112.5 billion record set in 2021.
AI has been at the heart of Hong Kong’s deal revival, but this summer brought a new level of intensity. Chinese companies raised ever-larger sums and returned to the market more quickly as they sought to fund expansion in the fast-growing industry.
Photo: Bloomberg
Alibaba Group Holding Ltd’s (阿里巴巴) US$10.2 billion follow-on offering was the biggest transaction during the period, while Zhongji Innolight Co (中際旭創) raised almost US$8 billion in Hong Kong’s largest listing in nearly seven years. Others tapped investors repeatedly: AI model maker Z.AI Co (智譜) has raised US$9.6 billion this year through its IPO, placements and convertible bonds.
“People raise capital right out of lockup and tend to do so more frequently,” said James Wang (王亞軍), head of Asia ex-Japan equity capital markets at Goldman Sachs Group Inc.
“Before, they did it once and it would be quiet for one to two years. Now they do it and three months later they come back. This will continue for a couple of years because of AI. I don’t see that pace slowing down,” he said.
Aside from Z.AI, rival model maker MiniMax Group Inc (稀宇科技), as well as chipmakers Shanghai Iluvatar CoreX Semiconductor Co (天數智芯) and Shanghai Biren Technology Co (壁仞科技) all returned to the market during that feverish July, soon after their IPO lockups expired.
Hong Kong Financial Secretary Paul Chan (陳茂波) in a blog post yesterday said that there was increased participation from the Middle East, with several funds from that region planning to invest more in Hong Kong.
The boom extended across the Asia-Pacific, where share sales topped US$120 billion in the third quarter, the most for the period in six years. Mainland China produced some of the region’s biggest deals, including memory chipmaker CXMT Corp’s (長鑫存儲) 66.6 billion yuan (US$9.9 billion) IPO — the country’s second-biggest ever.
The fundraising boom has unfolded against a much shakier market backdrop. The MSCI Asia-Pacific Index slumped as much as 7 percent in July, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Tech Index has been on a downward trend this year.
Weak deal performance is testing investor appetite. Of the 10 largest deals in Hong Kong since the start of July, just two are trading above water, while expectations for further US Federal Reserve rate hikes are tightening financial conditions globally.
“If you look at overall sentiment, having large transactions trading through the offer price is not helpful for risk appetite,” said Martin Zoll, global head of equity capital markets and global co-head of strategic equity and financing at HSBC Holdings PLC. “So as we go into year-end, I would expect that investors potentially become more selective about where they put their money to work.”

Ireland cut short news conference before Israel game
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:46 UTC
01:38:46 KST

The Republic of Ireland’s news conference on Saturday on the eve of their second UEFA Nations League match against Israel in Serbia was cut short as head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson fielded questions from Israeli journalists.
Ireland on Tuesday last week beat Israel 3-0 in Hungary in their first match following a turbulent build-up in which the Irish players voted to fulfil the fixture despite unease among the team over the war in Gaza.
During that match the Irish players wore armbands and pointedly lowered their heads while the Israeli national anthem played. There were no handshakes between the captains before kick-off.
Photo: AP
The return leg was to take place after press time last night in Backa Topola, Serbia, after the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) refused to host the match at home for security reasons.
On Saturday, one journalist asked Hallgrimsson for his thoughts about an incident on Wednesday last week when an Indian pilot was attacked by the copilot during a Flydubai flight from the United Arab Emirates to Israel, which Emirati judicial authorities and Israeli officials have described as a “terrorist act.”
“What do you say about the people that you support? Their ideology is based on murder,” the journalist said. “Just this week, one of them tried to kill 170 Israeli passengers, including 27 innocent children and thousands of others.”
An Irish team press officer intervened, saying: “We are not doing any questions like this today. We are doing football questions.”
Another journalist then addressed the Ireland manager, saying: “Your players call our players monkeys during the match...,” only to be immediately interrupted by an FAI official repeatedly insisting “that is completely untrue,” while the microphone was taken away from the reporter.
The Irish delegation then brought the news conference to an abrupt end.
Israeli authorities have condemned the actions taken by the Irish team in the first game, with Israeli Minister of Foreign Affairs Gideon Saar accusing Dublin of being on “the wrong side of history.”
“Surviving this, coming out of it together as one would be a massive win for me. That is coming from my heart,” Hallgrimsson told journalists on Saturday. “All the challenges that this team has gone through, all the criticism. Just surviving as a group after this game, that would be a big win for me and for this group, for the association.
“There’s been a lot of emotions from the people in Ireland about this, and obviously that affects the players as well,” he said. “We want to do good, but it’s always going to be a challenge when the environment is as noisy as it is. So, we try to focus on the football side.”
Israel coach Ran Ben Shimon said he was not “dealing with any politics” in his news conference ahead of the game.
“My opinion about that is that I need to keep my players’ focus on the game. I didn’t let anything, any emotion about it, to penetrate our squad,” he said. “I want my players to come to the game with the football knowledge and the solutions for what’s going to happen on the pitch. I’m not dealing with any politics now. I want the team to be much better in tactical matters, in their approach to the game.”
“And this is my only focus. I’m not going to respond to anything not connected to football at this stage,” he added.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:45 UTC
01:38:45 KST

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen yesterday took his first win of the season at a chaotic Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia that only started on the second attempt 1 hour 40 minutes late because of rain.
Verstappen gained the lead after an early safety car and led home the Mercedes of championship leader Kimi Antonelli and the Ferrari of Lewis Hamilton at the Sepang International Circuit. However, there was agony for George Russell who had to retire from third place in the second Mercedes with five laps to go when his power unit appeared to fail under a late safety car.
An eventual standing start saw four-time world champion Verstappen start from pole for the first time this season after dominating practice and qualifying.
Photo: AFP
However, he had a slow getaway on intermediate tires allowing the Mercedes pair of Antonelli and Russell to pass him easily in the wet early conditions.
A safety car when Valtteri Bottas spun into the gravel on lap nine saw most drivers dive in for new slick tires to take advantage of a rapidly drying track.
Verstappen took a lead that he would not relinquish when the safety car ended, swooping past Antonelli and Russell and quickly opened a comfortable gap.
Hamilton started on the front row on dry tires and quickly slid down the field in the wet conditions. However, the seven-time world champion used all his experience to work his way back through the field for a brilliant podium place as the surface dried out.
His teammate Charles Leclerc was fourth with Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar in fifth.
The Bahrain Grand Prix was being raced in Malaysia due to disruption in the Gulf linked to the US-led war with Iran.
Formula One moves on to nearby Singapore for a night race and sprint next weekend.

Soldier indicted for disobeying orders about sleeping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:44 UTC
01:38:44 KST

The Taichung District Prosecutors’ Office has indicted a soldier on a charge of disobeying orders after he allegedly refused to go to sleep or get out of bed, seeking a heavy sentence.
The soldier, surnamed Lee (李), assigned to the 302nd Infantry Brigade at the Chenggong Ling (成功嶺) training depot in Taichung, was suspended on July 4, prosecutors said.
Lee allegedly struggled to adapt to military life and repeatedly disobeyed orders from his superiors, investigators found.
Photo:Taipei Times
At about 10pm on May 3, he allegedly refused to go to bed at lights-out after being told to do so by his company commander, surnamed Lin (林), and was eventually carried bodily to the dormitory by other soldiers.
The following morning, he ignored orders issued by Lin to get up, sleeping in until 9:30am, the indictment said.
Lee allegedly disobeyed orders issued by his commander within the scope of his authority and related to military duties on two consecutive occasions within a short period, prosecutors said.
The alleged conduct went beyond his daily routine, involving military discipline and the chain of command, they said.
Lee had admitted the offenses, prosecutors said, adding that testimony from Lin and other officers supported the allegations and there was sufficient evidence to prosecute.
Lee was charged under the Criminal Code of the Armed Forces (陸海空軍刑法) with disobeying orders issued within the scope of authority regarding military affairs.
The case, referred for investigation by the Taichung military police of the Military Police Command, had a serious impact on unit discipline and the authority of the commanding officer, prosecutors said, requesting the court impose a heavy sentence.
When asked for comment, lawyer Lee Hsueh-yung (李學鏞) said on Saturday that soldiers are obliged to obey lawful, clear orders issued by superiors within their authority and concerning military matters.
Under Article 47-1 of the Criminal Code of the Armed Forces, anyone who disobeys an order issued by higher authorities or within the commander’s powers faces a sentence of up to five years in prison, he said.
The punishment for disobeying orders is not limited to disciplinary action, such as demerits or confinement to base, but can lead to criminal prosecution, he said.
Not every instance of disobeying orders constitutes the crime of disobedience, he said.
Orders involving ordinary day-to-day matters would not necessarily fall within the scope of criminal law, he said.
The key issues are whether the order was issued with the superior’s authority, whether its content was clear and whether it concerned military matters, he said.
The issue in this case is whether the orders to “return to the dormitory and go to bed” and to “get up” constituted orders related to military duties, unit routines and military management, he said.
Based on the indictment, the soldier did refused to obey more than once, and he continued to disregard the company commander’s orders despite being repeatedly instructed to comply, he said.
Both incidents involved disobedience of orders issued by a superior within the scope of the officer’s authority and related to military matters, he said.
The court would consider factors including the frequency of violations, degree of defiance, impact on discipline, and the defendant’s attitude after the offenses, he said.
Last year, a soldier was sentenced to three months in prison, commutable to a fine of NT$90,000, for allegedly twice ignoring a sergeant major’s orders to put away his mobile phone during an inspection at Penghu Defense Command. The court ruled that while it was not a direct combat order, it concerned military affairs, leaving the soldier with no right to refuse to comply.

Taiwan tourism event in California draws praise for culture, food and safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:44 UTC
01:38:44 KST

Americans attending a Taiwan tourism promotion at a Southern California shopping center on Saturday praised the island for its friendly people, convenient lifestyle and safety.
Taiwan’s Tourism Administration hosted a promotional event titled “100 Ways to Wonder” at Irvine Spectrum Center in Irvine, California, featured a traditional glove puppetry stage beneath a Ferris wheel, along with cultural displays showcasing sky lanterns and xiaolongbao soup dumplings. The Tourism Administration joined travel industry representatives and airlines, including China Airlines, Starlux Airlines and EVA Air, in setting up booths at the busy shopping center.
Lin Yi-cheng (林宜錚), head of the tourism division at Taiwan’s representative office in Los Angeles, said the venue was chosen for its heavy foot traffic and visibility, allowing the event to reach not only Americans familiar with Taiwan but also those with little knowledge of the island.
Photo: CNA
The Kuang Hsing Ko Hand Puppet Troupe from Changhua performed beneath the Ferris wheel, drawing families with its colorful production, sound and lighting effects. Activities focusing on food, culture, nature, leisure and shopping introduced visitors to Taiwan’s attractions and cultural heritage.
Irvine City Council member Melinda Liu (劉令淳), who is of Taiwanese descent, said the shopping center attracts large numbers of visitors each year, making it an ideal venue for promoting Taiwanese culture and tourism.
In response to media queries on how she would describe Taiwan to someone unfamiliar with the island, Liu called it “very beautiful and modern, with a rich culture.” Taiwanese food and the warmth of its people, she said, were what she most wanted to showcase.
Among the Americans interviewed were visitors who had never been to Taiwan as well as others who had lived there.
Eldred, who has Taiwanese friends but has never visited the island, said the first things that came to mind when he heard Taiwan mentioned were “positive, happy and very friendly people.” He hopes to travel to Asia and would like to visit Taiwan to experience its culture firsthand.
“I want to experience the local culture and really immerse myself in it,” he said.
Juan, who has also never visited Taiwan, said his impression of the island was that it was “a beautiful place that is worth visiting.” He said he would like to try the food and see how traditional culture and modern city life intersect.
Todd, who lived in Taiwan for three years for work, said the food left a lasting impression, but he especially praised the island’s safety.
“You can walk almost anywhere, and even walking around outside in the middle of the night is no problem. It’s so much safer than here,” he said.
“There are so many good things about Taiwan that I could go on talking about them endlessly. But what I like most is still the people,” he added.
Todd said bubble tea had helped make Taiwanese culture more familiar to Californians, who are exposed to a wide range of cultures. He said he believes most Americans have a positive impression of Taiwan.
Linda, who lived in Taiwan for two years more than a decade ago while working as an art teacher at a private school in Taipei, said the island’s convenience was among her strongest memories.
“Different cultures from all over the world come together there,” she said.
Asked what she would tell Americans unfamiliar with Taiwan, Linda said: “Taiwan is really wonderful. Everyone should visit at least once in their life.”

AI needs more safety layers: ex-OpenAI engineer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:43 UTC
01:38:43 KST

Another former OpenAI employee has added his voice to a chorus of frantic calls to make artificial intelligence (AI) safe, saying that the industry must mimic the aviation or nuclear power sectors with their layers of safeguards to avoid disaster.
In an article published in The Atlantic Magazine, David Robinson echoed warnings from inside and outside the AI world that its agents are being developed so fast and becoming so smart they could soon elude control and conceivably wipe out humanity.
Robinson said alarming incidents reported since the start of the summer — in which AI agents slipped out of their controlled spaces and went rogue to attack a variety of targets — show the industry is not taking safety nearly seriously enough as it sprints to develop faster and more powerful AI capabilities.
Photo: AP
In the essay Robinson said his credentials include overseeing the writing of safety reports on 12 advanced model product launches and leading the drafting of OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework.
Robinson says he worked at OpenAI for three-and-a-half years and was among the longest-tenured employees at the company.
The mistakes revealed are typical because of “the speed and flexibility with which people operate,” Robinson wrote.
“An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to,” he added.
He said that cutting-edge AI labs need to operate like the aviation or the nuclear industry with layers of redundant safeguards and careful planning “so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.”
Robinson also insisted that the issue of “alignment” — the industry term for how AI can be trained to respect human values — is essential, but something the industry has failed to even define, much less master.
He also said that AI models are getting better and better at detecting when they are being tested and might behave differently when they are actually deployed, fooling their masters.
After a meeting on Tuesday at the White House, amid global worries about what AI means for humanity, top AI executives said they had committed to measures for self-regulation, as opposed to submitting to government rules. This includes internal controls on AI systems and bringing in outside analysts.
A White House task force on AI would assess the technology’s risks and opportunities, while preventing overregulation that stifles innovation, its leader Jay Clayton has told The Wall Street Journal.
Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, is widely reported to be the new AI czar in US President Donald Trump’s administration, though the appointment is yet to be confirmed.
The new Super Intelligence (SI) Force — using Trump’s preferred term for AI — would have 120 days to report on the risks and opportunities of the technology, The Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday.
The task force’s charter states that it would “develop plans for responding to SI-enabled threats to our society, while preventing overregulation and regulatory capture that would stifle innovation and competition,” The Wall Street Journal said.
It would also “recommend ways to improve the government’s response capacity under existing authorities.”

US-China differences offer Taiwan opportunity: expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:40 UTC
01:38:40 KST

Fundamental differences between the US and China make major disputes difficult to resolve, but create an opportunity for Taipei to deepen economic and security ties with Washington, China expert Miles Yu (余茂春) said Saturday.
Yu, director of the China Center at the Washington-based think tank Hudson Institute and a former China policy adviser in US President Donald Trump’s first administration, made the remarks on the sidelines of a Double Ten National Day event in Maryland.
Regarding Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) last month and their expected meetings later this year, Yu said differences in the two countries’ political systems and how their governments operate make major disputes, including over tariffs and regional security, difficult to resolve.
Photo: Reuters
The two sides aim to maintain strategic stability, avoid an unintended clash and buy time to bolster their positions, he said.
The need for repeated summits and elaborate ceremonies suggested the two countries had “many fundamental problems that cannot be resolved,” he said.
Washington’s and Beijing’s inability to “come together on some fundamental issues” represented “an opportunity” for Taiwan, Yu said.
Further integration between Taiwan and the US in trade and economics is important, but “the most crucial thing is integration on security,” he said.
“For Taiwan, the foreign hostile force is the Chinese Communist Party,” which is also the US government’s top foreign hostile force, he said.
Taiwan and the US require a “common defense,” with a high degree of security integration, and defending Taiwan also serves US national security interests, Yu said.
At a separate forum last week, Hudson Institute Asia-Pacific Security chair Patrick M. Cronin said a temporary US-China trade truce showed that neither side intended to surrender its “most valuable source of leverage.”
Ahead of last month’s summit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the truce, originally set to expire on Nov. 10, had been extended for two months to Jan. 10 next year.
Beijing “has little reason” to give up its critical minerals advantage, while Washington “should be equally reluctant to squander one of its greatest strategic advantages: its network of capable allies and partners,” Cronin said.
The temporary easing of tensions should be used as a period of “accelerated American and allied renewal,” rather than simply as a respite from confrontation, he said.
With China set to mark the centennial of the Chinese People’s Liberation Army next year, the US and its allies need to enhance “deterrence by denial around Taiwan and elsewhere in the Western Pacific,” Cronin said.
However, military deterrence alone would not be enough, he said, calling for stronger industrial capacity in areas including energy, shipbuilding, munitions, autonomous systems, semiconductors and artificial intelligence to “sustain deterrence over the long term.”

Laos base part of China’s regional ambitions: expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:38:40 UTC
01:38:40 KST

The opening of a joint air support center in Laos is part of China’s decades-long power-projection efforts to extend its influence into the Indian Ocean, a Taiwanese defense expert said yesterday.
The Chinese Ministry of National Defense on Wednesday last week announced that the China-Laos Joint Support and Training Center at Ban Keun Airport in Vientiane Province and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy officially opened on Tuesday last week.
The jointly maintained and operated center is aimed at helping Laos bolster pilot training, Beijing said.
Photo: Screen grab from Google Maps
“It is not directed against any third party and contributes to enhancing practical military cooperation as well as promoting regional peace and stability,” the Chinese defense ministry said in a statement.
The project is part of China’s long-term strategy to extend its influence beyond its borders, said Su Tzu-yun (蘇紫雲), director of Defense Strategy and Resources at the government-funded Institute for National Defense and Security Research.
Since the launch of its “Belt and Road Initiative,” Beijing has been laying the groundwork for overseas naval and air bases, primarily to secure shipping routes in the Indian Ocean and mitigate risks associated with the Strait of Malacca, Su said.
The Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) already operates a military facility in Djibouti in East Africa, as well as a facility at the Ream Naval Base in Cambodia.
With the base in Laos, the PLA is expected to extend its presence toward the South China Sea, the Indian Ocean and the Strait of Malacca, Su said.
The new facilities also reflect Beijing’s overarching strategy aimed at safeguarding China’s maritime transport routes and access to the sea, protected by naval and air power, so that in the event of a blockade of the Strait of Malacca, crude oil and natural gas could still be transported to China, he said.
Ban Keun Airport, about 45km northwest of Laos’ capital, Vientiane, has a roughly 2km-long paved runway that can accommodate fighter jets, Su.
However, China might seek to extend it to 3km to accommodate larger aircraft, such as bombers, transport aircraft and tanker aircraft, he added.
In the event of a conflict in the South China Sea or the Taiwan Strait, US Air Force assets at Naval Support Facility Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean would likely need to fly from west to east across the Indochina Peninsula, potentially exposing them to Chinese interception, Su said.
