Air strike in Sudan kills UN aid truck driver: WFP
WFP food aid truck attacked in Sudan’s South Kordofan, killing one driver as violence escalates in the region.
An air strike on United Nations trucks has killed a driver in Sudan’s South Kordofan, according to the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP).
The WFP said in a statement released on Sunday that the trucks, carrying food aid, were “clearly marked as humanitarian vehicles” as they came under attack. The agency did not identify those responsible.
The strike hit the convoy on Saturday as it was travelling between two cities controlled by the government’s Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) in South Kordofan state.
Fighting in the Kordofan region intensified in late 2025, turning the territory into a strategic battleground between the SAF and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The two have been fighting for control of Sudan in a civil war that has now lasted more than three years.
The extent of the damage and additional details regarding the attack on WFP aid trucks are still being assessed. The UN agency said that it has called for an investigation.
“These incidents underscore the increasingly challenging security environment in Sudan and the risks that aid workers face when delivering life-saving assistance to communities in need,” the statement reads.
Since the war began in April 2023, one in five attacks in Sudan has occurred in the Kordofan region. The army has the upper hand in the north, having made a series of recent gains, while the RSF maintains control over much of the west. South Kordofan remains contested.
Both the SAF and RSF have increasingly deployed drones in their war, with attacks on towns in North Kordofan growing more frequent and deadly, and civilian infrastructure coming under attack across the region.
The civil war has forcibly displaced 14 million people, plunging the country into one of the worst modern food crises and killing tens of thousands of people.
Nearly 19.5 million people – about 41 percent of Sudan’s population – were struggling with acute food crises between February and May, according to an Integrated Food Security Phase Classification assessment, a leading authority on global hunger. More than five million faced extreme, life-threatening food shortages, and 135,000 were at risk of famine.

Saeidi Brothers release reimagined folk single “Sar-e Dast-e Yarom”
TEHRAN- Iranian traditional vocalist brothers Ali and Mohammad Saeidi have released their latest single, “Sar-e Dast-e Yarom” (“My Beloved’s Cuff”), a reimagined version of an old Iranian folk song.
The piece, performed by the Saeidi brothers, draws on a traditional folk composition attributed to Hossein Kouhi Kermani, and is based on the rendition of maestro Mohammad-Taghi Saeidi.
According to the artists, the song is rooted in a folk narrative associated with fashion and the period when modern fashion began making its way into Iranian society. The brothers have sought to preserve the character of the old folk material while developing it through a contemporary musical arrangement, and the track is presented as an expanded reinterpretation rather than a straightforward revival of the original.
In the new release, Mojtaba Mojtaba Abolqasempour is credited with playing santur and electronic instruments, as well as arranging, mixing and mastering the piece, while Majid Mazaheri plays the kamancheh.
Ali and Mohammad Saeidi, born in Isfahan in 1981, are twin traditional Iranian singers who studied Persian vocal techniques and the radif repertoire with masters including Mohammad-Taghi Saeidi, Mohammad Ali Kianinejad and Fazlollah Shahzamani. Their work has included concerts in Iran and abroad as well as recordings drawing on traditional Iranian music.
The brothers previously launched a short-song project aimed at introducing Iranian traditional music and art to audiences with limited time, producing brief musical videos based on selections from the Persian traditional repertoire.
Their collaboration with internationally known Iranian composer and conductor Ali Rahbari has also included the orchestral project “Persian Nightingales.”

Iran’s “The Long Winter” wins award at Eurasia documentary festival
TEHRAN- Iranian documentary “The Long Winter”, directed by Hassan Jafari, won the Best Film Award at the 10th International Documentary Film Festival of CIS Countries “Eurasia.Doc,” which concluded in Minsk, Belarus, on October 2.
The film was among the winners announced at the festival’s closing ceremony, receiving the Prize of the 10th CIS Documentary Film Festival “Eurasia.Doc” in the Best Film category, Mehr reported on Sunday.
“The Long Winter”, a 44-minute documentary, tells the story of an elderly couple living in a village in northern Iran. The film follows the couple as they confront the difficulties of rural life and the wife’s illness, while facing a difficult decision over whether to remain in their village or move to the city.
Jafari directed the film, with Farzaneh Fathi as screenwriter, Farahbakhsh Farhadnia as cinematographer, Yasser Talebi as editor and Yasser Faryadras as producer.
The documentary was produced by the Nehzat Media Arts Center and the Documentary, Experimental and Animation Cinema Center.
Jafari has directed several documentary works, including “Forty Years of Love”, “Kijakarchal”, “Paradise”, and “Last Breaths”.
The 10th edition of Eurasia.Doc was held from September 28 to October 2 in Smolensk, Russia, and Minsk, Belarus. According to the festival’s official website, 361 films from 14 countries were submitted to the main competition, with 34 works eventually selected for the final competition.
The festival brought together documentary filmmakers, journalists, experts and audiences from several countries, with films addressing historical events, contemporary social issues, human experiences and developments in different societies.
The festival’s Grand Prix was awarded to the Russian documentary “39th Medical Unit: The Battle for Life”, directed by Anastasia Mikhailovskaya and Artem Somov. Key Biden aide recalls "draconian measures" being considered against Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:25:34 UTC
01:25:34 KST

Key Biden aide Brett McGurk on Hamas, Iran, Saudi Arabia and why U.S. nearly took "draconian measures" against Israel
President Joe Biden was on the verge of taking "draconian measures" after an Israeli military drone strike killed seven World Central Kitchen aid workers in the Gaza Strip in April 2024, but U.S. intelligence that Iran was about to launch an "unprecedented" aerial attack on Israel prevented Biden from moving forward, according to Brett McGurk, a top Middle East adviser to four presidents.
In an interview with "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" taped Thursday, McGurk described Biden as "fed up" with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's handling of the war in Gaza.
"At that moment, if not for that impending missile attack, which we then had to deploy military forces … I think we would have taken some pretty draconian measures against Israel," he said, adding that cutting off U.S. weapons to Israel "was very much on the table."
The U.S. and its Arab and European partners helped protect Israel from the Iranian attack, which McGurk said included 120 ballistic missiles, 170 drones and 30 cruise missiles that were "all launched to land at the same time."
In his new memoir titled "Brink," which is set to be published Tuesday, McGurk recalled a tense conversation between Biden and Netanyahu around that time in which the U.S. leader warned the prime minister he could end the weapons supply. At the time, the Israeli government said it believed there were more than 130 hostages in Gaza and around 34,000 Gazan deaths, according to the Hamas-run Gaza Ministry of Health.
"You think I'm Santa Claus? No Santa in Israel, pal," McGurk quotes Biden as saying.
In McGurk's interview with CBS News, the longtime foreign policy aide recounted the Biden administration's initial reaction to Hamas' Oct. 7 terror attack on Israel, its handling of Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza, the efforts to secure an Israel-Hamas ceasefire and hostage release deal, the role of Iran and — starting years earlier — a long-sought push to normalize relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia.
McGurk is no longer working with the Bidens and is currently a CNN contributor.
McGurk: "If you just stop American support for Israel, that is not going to end the crisis"
Biden's handling of the Israel-Hamas war has drawn years of scrutiny — including from within his own party. During the 2024 presidential campaign, the administration faced intense pressure to stop military aid to Israel amid the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.
The U.S. is the largest weapons supplier to Israel, and provides billions in aid. A 2023 State Department review of Israel's conduct found that it was "reasonable to assess" that Israeli security forces have used U.S.-made weapons in ways "inconsistent with" international humanitarian law obligations. Casualties in Gaza, "including high levels of civilian casualties," raised "substantial questions as to whether the IDF is using" U.S.-made weapons "effectively in all cases," the report said.
Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen told "Face the Nation" in November 2024 that Biden didn't use U.S. leverage effectively, arguing he sent Israel "more bombs and more money" after Netaynahu disregarded his requests, and pointed to U.S. laws blocking arms shipments to military units that violated human rights.
Since then, debates over the future of U.S.-Israel relations have continued to rage. Some of the criticism that the Biden administration was not strong enough in its response to Israeli actions in Gaza has been directed at McGurk, who was the White House National Security Council's coordinator for the Middle East and North Africa and one of his most influential advisers.
McGurk noted that the Biden administration did pause some weapons transfers to Israel, including 2,000-pound bombs but never instituted a weapons halt. He believes some of the calls to go further may not have been effective.
"Israel also has one of the largest arms industries in the world, so the idea that had Biden gone further on a step on that course, it would have stopped the war, I just think the record does not support that," McGurk said.
McGurk also argued that exerting too much public pressure on Israel could have hardened Hamas' stance, ultimately setting back the negotiations to end the war in Gaza and release the hostages.
"I come back to the question: How do you end this crisis?" he said. "And I think the record shows: If you just stop American support for Israel, that is not going to end the crisis, it's going to make it worse."
At the same time as the Israel-Hamas war, attacks on U.S. forces by Iranian-backed proxy groups surged. McGurk pushed Biden to punish Iran in an effort to deter the attacks, and expressed some frustration with Biden administration colleagues who were wary of striking Iranian officials in response.
What would've happened if Iran "made a dash" toward weapons-grade uranium
McGurk said part of Biden's goal was to prevent the outbreak of a broader regional war. Meanwhile, periodic aerial attacks between Iran and Israel continued.
In December 2024, McGurk traveled to Israel with national security adviser Jake Sullivan as they worked toward a deal with Hamas to release the remaining Israeli hostages.
During the visit, according to McGurk, Netanyahu talked about taking out nuclear sites in Iran, including at Fordow, a facility built inside a mountain that processed and stored highly enriched uranium. Fordow was one of the three Iranian nuclear sites that President Trump ordered to be bombed in June 2025, eight months before the Trump administration and Israeli forces launched a wider war against Iran.
McGurk said the Biden administration was concerned in late 2024 that Iran "might make a dash" toward making weapons-grade uranium, and officials were open to carrying out strikes if there were evidence obtained that showed Iran was making a bomb. Netanyahu urged the US not to wait for that step. Iran had been building up a stockpile of 60%-enriched uranium, which is a short step from the material required to build a bomb.
"We actually had a principals committee meeting — that's everybody around the table — what would we do if we see that?" McGurk said. "And as I recall, unanimity on: We would do the strike in Fordow. We didn't see that. We sent a message to Iran, don't even think about it. But yet Netanyahu was clearly contemplating that."
Hamas and Israel struck a ceasefire deal that led to the release of some hostages a month after that, just days before President Trump was inaugurated and the Biden national security team left the White House. McGurk said he and Mr. Trump's Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff "agreed we're going to work in lockstep." He described how the Biden and Trump teams put pressure on both Hamas and Israel.
Hamas released the last living hostages in October 2025, as part of another ceasefire agreement.
U.S. saw no "warning or indicator" of Oct. 7 attack
The circumstances leading up to the Oct. 7 attack have drawn renewed attention in recent weeks, as The New York Times, The Atlantic and the Israeli newspaper Haaretz report on warnings that officials in Egypt and the United Arab Emirates allegedly delivered to Israel that Hamas was planning a major attack. Netanyahu has strongly denied that there were any warnings, but his opponents in Israel's election later this month have expressed outrage.
CBS has confirmed via a former US official and a diplomatic source that Emirati Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed al Nahyan, President of the UAE, did share a warning with Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu in the weeks leading up to the attack. The UAE had learned that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a major attack but did not have specific intelligence such as a date, time or location.
McGurk told CBS News the U.S. had no intelligence that could have warned about Hamas' Oct. 7 attack.
"We did not have anything in our system that would have been a warning and indicator," he said. "No U.S. intelligence of a warning or indicator."
But he said Israel should launch an official inquiry that probes its own security establishment and political leadership, much like the U.S. did after the 9/11 attacks.
"I think they had an assumption that was deeply ingrained that Hamas was deterred, assuaged, and was not about to do something massive on any scale like this," McGurk said. "I think that was a false assumption in their system, a failure of imagination, and it was tragic."
McGurk on the Biden-MBS fist bump: "I encouraged the president to just shake his hand"
Hours before the Oct. 7 2023 attack, McGurk said he met with the Saudi Arabian Ambassador to the U.S., Princess Reema Bandar, to discuss a different issue — a potential pathway for Israel and Saudi Arabia to normalize relations.
MB SUGGESTIONED INSERT: Just weeks prior, Prime Minister Netanyahu had stood at the UN General Assembly in New York and predicted a new Middle East to include normalization between the Jewish State and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, birthplace of Islam.
"I believe that we are at the cusp of an even more dramatic breakthrough: an historic peace with Saudi Arabia," Netanyahu said.
The idea of Saudi Arabia establishing formal diplomatic ties with Israel had been floated to McGurk by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman nearly two years earlier, in January 2021, shortly after Biden took office, McGurk said, a deal that would have included a pathway to a Palestinian peace agreement. McGurk said he reported that extraordinary offer back to the President, but the U.S. did not act on it.
Biden was skeptical of Saudi Arabia, vowing in the 2020 Democratic primaries to treat the kingdom as a "pariah" due to U.S. intelligence indicating that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was linked to the murder of Washington Post columnist Jamal Khashoggi.
McGurk also explained that Biden did not want to focus on the Middle East, and only reached out to the Gulf States after the chaotic August 2021 U.S. exit from Afghanistan caused the emergency need for the U.S. to ask those governments to take in Afghan allies fleeing the Taliban. The U.S. needed another favor in 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine, and turned again to the Gulf states, specifically Saudi Arabia, asking them to pump more oil to alleviate a spike in prices.
Rebuilding frayed relations because a necessity for U.S. national security. McGurk said it was a "mistake" that administration officials did not engage with Saudi Arabia more frequently early in Biden's term. He convinced him to visit in 2022.
McGurk offered rare criticism of Biden over his 2022 visit to Saudi Arabia, which came during a global spike in energy prices. He recounts that for 18 minutes Air Force One sat on the tarmac in the Kingdom as Biden argued with aides over how he would greet the Crown Price at his palace.
Rather than shaking bin Salman's hand, Biden famously gave him a fist bump.
"He was concerned about the optics and the imagery," McGurk told CBS News, and "I encouraged the president to just shake his hand." He later said: "We were asking some very hard things to the Saudis that we needed for our core interests, and so I think the fist bump set us back."
By 2023, the U.S., Israel and Saudi Arabia were working toward a normalization agreement, a complicated deal that likely would have involved the U.S. offering Saudi Arabia a civil nuclear program and Israel agreeing to concessions around the Palestinian territories. The Oct. 7 attack derailed those talks — and President Biden often openly theorized that Hamas may have sought to prevent normalization.
McGurk said he "never saw anything to tie a direct connection," but didn't rule out that idea.
"Hamas, of course, does not recognize Israel, wants to destroy Israel, and I would not be surprised if one of the motivations on October 7th was to knock this agenda off the table," McGurk said, calling the prospect of Saudi-Israeli normalization "one of the biggest deals since the Cold War."
President Trump has revived the terms of that U.S.-Saudi arrangement, including the pledge to develop a civil nuclear program. However, the current Israel government has refused to discuss a Palestinian state in the wake of Oct 7 attacks, and the civilian death toll in Gaza from the war makes normalization more politically difficult for Saudi leaders.

The Guardian view on nurseries: some things are going right for under-fives | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:25:32 UTC
01:25:32 KST

Recognition of the importance of babyhood and early childhood continues to grow. It is widely understood by many ordinary people, as well as experts, that what happens to us when we are very small, and our brains are at their most malleable, has lasting effects. As the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) put it in a study of early years education, “the first five years of a child’s life represent a window of opportunity, but also of vulnerability”.
New Labour’s grasp of this underpinned its pioneering Sure Start programme. Much of this was dismantled under the Tory-Liberal Democrat austerity programme. But despite that loss, England’s results in this year’s OECD Early Learning and Child Well‑being Study were strong. This study does not have the high profile of the programme for international student assessment (Pisa) comparing the academic performance of 15-year-olds. It is newer and relies on a far smaller sample size. But while its findings should not be treated as gospel, it is heartening that England’s five-year‑olds were found to be thriving. On a social-emotional development measure, they came out on top.
Concerns about school readiness, with a rising number of children in England arriving in reception classes without basic skills such as climbing stairs, must continue to be taken seriously. So must the attainment gap between economically disadvantaged children and those from wealthier backgrounds. The recent announcement by the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, that the Healthy Babies programme will be extended to more family hubs should be warmly welcomed as one means of tackling these problems.
But as well as addressing the inequalities that restrict children’s chances, ministers should focus on the early years sector’s strengths – which are a legacy of Sure Start and all the investment that went in. While less often discussed than the national curriculum, England’s early years framework is admired internationally.
Early years funding has expanded massively, with eligible working parents entitled to 30 hours’ childcare weekly for children from nine months until school age. The Tories now propose removing the £100,000 earnings ceiling: a £700m policy that rewards richer families. The model sees public money follows working parental demand rather than building universal provision. Families without working parents remain less well supported, while private providers gravitate towards wealthier areas, where extra hours and charges are more affordable.
The Competition and Markets Authority found that private providers were making excess profits in the children’s social care market. A study into their role as childcare providers requested by the former education secretary Bridget Phillipson should establish whether something similar is going on in nurseries, and assist ministers in finding ways to target low-income areas. Alan Milburn’s review of young people and work is expected to highlight the role of early years in getting toddlers on track for school.
The OECD was right to acknowledge the vulnerability, as well as the potential, of the youngest children. The horrific abuse of toddlers by Vincent Chan at a nursery in London was a grim reminder of what can go wrong. Safeguarding must continue to be strengthened; the switch to more frequent inspections by Ofsted was a good move. But as well as facing up to failures, ministers should embrace past successes – and work out how they can be built on.

Iran rejects Axios report on expulsion of diplomats from US

Iran rejects Axios report on expulsion of diplomats from US
TEHRAN — Iran has rejected a report by the US news website Axios claiming that two members of its delegation to the United Nations General Assembly left New York after failing to comply with a US State Department request to leave the country, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi describing the alleged “expulsion” as a sign of “desperation and defeat.”
Axios reported that two Iranian diplomats were “kicked out” of the US on Saturday, several days after the State Department had ordered the Iranian mission to the UN to have its entire delegation leave the country. According to the report, the two diplomats had not complied with the US request issued on Monday.
Araghchi rejected the account in a post on X on Sunday, saying that Iranian diplomats who had attended the UN General Assembly had left the US according to schedule.
“All Iranian diplomats who attended UNGA, except one who departed earlier, left as scheduled,” Araghchi said.
He added that taking pride in what he described as a fake diplomatic “expulsion” was inappropriate for the head of any diplomatic corps.
“It oozes of desperation and defeat, and is inconsistent with UN host nation obligations,” he said.
Axios had earlier reported that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered the Iranian delegation to leave the country after diplomatic negotiations between Washington and Tehran reached a stalemate. The report said the move was an unusual diplomatic rebuke, although the Iranian delegation was likely to leave soon in any case because the General Assembly had concluded.
Baghaei: ‘A pure lie’
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei also rejected the Axios report during his weekly press conference on Sunday, describing it as an attempt to manufacture an achievement through false claims.
“In my view, they are trying to manufacture an achievement through lies,” Baghaei said. “What they claimed is an absolute falsehood.”
He said the Iranian delegation’s travel plans, including both its arrival in and departure from the United States, had been communicated in advance.
“It was clear from the outset on what date the honorable foreign minister’s delegation would leave New York,” Baghaei said.
Addressing Axios’ reference to two other Iranian diplomats, he said one of them had originally been scheduled to remain in New York for several more days to carry out his duties.
“Because of the pressure they exerted, yes, that diplomat left New York,” Baghaei said. “But in all other respects, we left New York according to the plans that had been made in advance.”
US violating host-nation obligations
Baghaei said that, regardless of the circumstances surrounding the diplomats’ departure, the US account itself amounted to an admission that Washington had failed to meet its obligations as the host country of the United Nations.
“This is itself an admission of a violation of the obligations by the host country,” he said.
“There is absolutely nothing to be proud of in the US boasting about violating its commitments as the host country,” the spokesman added, arguing that such conduct merely demonstrated that the US was not a worthy host for the United Nations.
Araghchi made a similar argument in his X post, saying that the alleged expulsion was inconsistent with the obligations of the country hosting the UN.
US failed to isolate Tehran
Baghaei further argued that the controversy over the diplomats came after Washington failed to prevent the Iranian delegation from attending the UN General Assembly and failed to achieve what Tehran described as an attempt to portray Iran as internationally isolated.
“It seems that after the US failed to prevent the participation of the Iranian delegation in the United Nations and could not implement its plan to portray Iran as isolated, it has resorted to such very low-level news-making,” he said.
“In my view, it is not even worth giving much attention to.”
The Iranian delegation took part in the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, where Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian addressed the assembly and Foreign Minister Araghchi held a series of diplomatic meetings, including contacts related to efforts to end the ongoing conflict between Iran and the United States. American Marine arrested over brutal murder of Japanese woman in Okinawa

The murder lays bare an enduring history of foreign troop violence on the island.
Okinawa accounts for less than one percent of Japanese territory yet hosts roughly 70 percent of all American military bases in the country alongside 30,000 active-duty personnel.
For eight decades, local residents have endured toxic pollution, jet noise, and a relentless sequence of violent offenses.
Prefectural police recorded 101 criminal charges against base-affiliated personnel in 2025 alone, marking a 22-year high.
In 2017, former Marine Kenneth Franklin Shinzato received a life sentence for raping and murdering 20-year-old Rina Shimabukuro.
In 1995, the gang rape of a 12-year-old girl by three American servicemen brought 85,000 protesters into the streets.
Legal scholars and Okinawan leaders have pointed to the Status of Forces Agreement as the structural mechanism shielding American forces from genuine accountability.
Under the 1960 pact, U.S. authorities retain primary jurisdiction over service members accused of crimes before formal indictment, creating a framework of extraterritorial impunity.
This structural protection is replicated across Washington’s global network of around 750 known military installations in 80 countries.
From Latin America to East Asia and West Asia, overseas bases function as sovereign enclaves that generate local insecurity while enabling imperial power projection.
The tragedy coincides with shifting domestic politics in Naha. Newly elected governor Genta Koja has aligned with Takaichi to accelerate base expansion in Henoko, dismantling local administrative bodies that previously resisted foreign military infrastructure.
Tokyo’s drive to expand base infrastructure leaves the safety of local civilians subordinated to the demands of the American military presence.

====================================================================================================

France faces record debt as €54B cuts fuel protests and school unrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:20:27 UTC
01:20:27 KST

About 400 high schools across France, roughly one in 10, were shut down on Friday at the end of a week in which more than 1,200 schools were blocked, disrupted or set on fire. As students burned trash bins in Toulouse and Lille, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s government submitted a 2027 budget to parliament calling for 54 billion euros in “efficiency measures,” or cuts.
The timing is no coincidence. The unrest and the budget fight are different manifestations of the same macroeconomic crisis that has been building in France for years and repeatedly erupts in new places. At its core is a widening gap between the level and quality of public services French citizens expect, including education, and what the state can still afford to provide.
France’s public debt is projected to reach 119.3% of gross domestic product this year, an all-time high, and rise further to 121.7% next year, according to Finance Ministry estimates submitted to the country’s independent fiscal watchdog.
Successive French governments have failed to bring the deficit under control. It currently stands at 5.4% of GDP, among the highest levels in the European Union and far above the bloc’s standard ceiling of 3%.
Financial markets have already registered the deterioration. On the day the budget was presented, the yield on France’s 10-year government bond climbed to 4.96%, its highest level in 24 years.
Interest becomes France’s biggest bill
Finance Minister Roland Lescure acknowledged that interest payments alone will account for more than half of next year’s deficit and could reach 100 billion euros by the end of the decade.
In 2027, France is expected to spend 74 billion euros simply servicing its debt, more than the 65 billion euros allocated to education and the 63 billion euros earmarked for defense, despite defense receiving the largest budget increase. Debt interest would therefore become the government’s single largest spending item.
The imbalance is not the result of one unusually wasteful year. It reflects a structural gap between what the French state promises and what its economy produces.
The European Commission estimates that without new measures the deficit will widen to 5.7% next year. Lecornu has said that without the proposed cuts it would exceed 6.5% of GDP. Even with the measures, Lescure has acknowledged that France is not expected to return to the 3% threshold until 2029.
When economic growth remains below the cost of borrowing, governments eventually have to decide what to cut, tax or reform. Those choices have repeatedly destabilized French governments over the past two years.
A bond yield approaching 5% for a sluggish economy is not simply a punishment from markets but a price attached to risk. France has lost two prime ministers in less than a year, both amid budget disputes, while successive governments have struggled to explain to voters which parts of the existing social model they are prepared to scale back.
Schools expose the fiscal trap
France’s education system illustrates the dilemma particularly clearly.
In 2026 recruitment drives, 24,351 of 25,000 teaching positions were filled, while 20 million hours of instruction went undelivered over the past year.
According to France’s national audit office, roughly one-tenth of scheduled teaching hours in public middle schools are lost because of teacher shortages despite billions of euros in additional government spending.
Against that backdrop, the new budget proposes freezing teachers’ salaries as part of a wider freeze on public-sector pay.
French classrooms also remain crowded despite a 20% decline in births since 2010. Rather than using that demographic contraction primarily to reduce class sizes, governments have also used it to cut teaching positions.
Another protest movement, the same underlying problem
France has repeatedly seen economic and fiscal disputes spill into the streets.
In 2018, a fuel tax helped trigger the Yellow Vest movement. In 2023, raising the retirement age brought millions of people out to protest. Last year, a government budget sparked mass demonstrations that ultimately contributed to the fall of François Bayrou’s government.
Now the education system has become the latest flashpoint. Combined with diesel prices climbing to new highs, public anger is once again rising.
France’s political crisis reflects a country caught between increasingly rigid political blocs. The left opposes spending cuts, the far right rejects tax increases, while the center has repeatedly tried to promise fiscal restraint without fully confronting the political cost of either approach.
The next eruption may come over a different issue, but the underlying bill will be the same: France must somehow reconcile the public services its citizens expect with a debt burden, deficit and interest bill that leave governments with steadily less room to maneuver.

His comments came as India continued to explore ways to preserve its interests in the port following the expiration of the US waiver.
The Chabahar issue has become even more complicated by Washington’s latest economic pressure campaign against Iran. For New Delhi, the challenge is to preserve a project it regards as strategically important for regional connectivity while navigating an increasingly restrictive US sanctions environment. The ambassador’s emphasis on the long-term nature of India-Iran relations and his outlook about Chabahar therefore point to New Delhi’s continued interest in the project, even as its future operational framework remains subject to the wider geopolitical situation.

While US midterm elections are often seen as a key factor, the newspaper suggested that events in Israel may be even more important. India successfully demonstrates its first free-space quantum-secure communication link for over 5.5 km
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:17:21 UTC
01:17:21 KST

NEW DELHI: Indian deep-tech startup QNu Labs, in collaboration with Bhaskaracharya National Institute for Space Applications and Geo-informatics (BISAG-N) and IIT Gandhinagar, has successfully demonstrated India’s first free-space quantum key distribution (QKD) link for over 5.56 km.A free-space QKD link is an ultra-secure way to share secret digital passwords using particles of light travelling through open air or space instead of a physical fibre-optic cable. It uses quantum mechanics principles, and any attempt by an outsider to intercept or measure the photons changes their state; therefore, it is the most secure form of sending data. Traditional QKD is limited by signal loss inside fibre-optic cables, whereas free-space links allow communication across open terrain, water or obstacles where laying cables is difficult. Free-space optics form the foundational bridge for transmitting keys between Earth and orbiting satellites and create the backbone for a global, quantum-secure internet network.“The field trial, conducted on the night of Sept 27–28, established a secure quantum communication channel between BISAG-N and IIT-G,” the IT and electronics ministry said in a statement on Saturday.Using QNu Labs’ pointing, acquisition and tracking system, the trial achieved a stable quantum bit error rate below 5% and generated secure keys at a rate of 230–260 bps.
These keys were integrated with BISAG-N’s post-quantum cryptography-enabled Vedic Kavach platform, enabling successful end-to-end encryption and decryption of test messages.Vinay Thakur, director general, BISAG-N, said the integration of Vedic Kavach with QNu Labs’ QKD technology marks a significant step towards practical quantum-resilient communication systems. Sunil Gupta, co-founder and CEO, QNu Labs, emphasised that the successful 5.56 km demonstration paves the way for longer-distance quantum-secure networks and satellite-based quantum communication.
Cmde Manish Tripathi (Retd.), In-charge, ISTF, IIT Gandhinagar, said the demonstration provides a valuable field environment for advancing practical quantum communication technologies and showcases how academia, indigenous technology and real-world experimentation can be integrated to meet emerging secure communication requirements. The trial provides a foundation for advancing India’s capabilities in secure communication infrastructure, strengthening resilience against emerging quantum-era security threats.

Australia probes flydubai co-pilot's links to the country, police say

The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team – which comprises federal police, Victorian state police and the ASIO intelligence agency – were "investigating the man's links to Australia," the Australian Federal Police spokesperson said.
Two sources briefed on the investigation said the co-pilot studied at a university in Melbourne, the capital of the Australian state of Victoria. A third source said he studied at RMIT University around a decade ago. RMIT declined to comment.
The co-pilot of the flydubai flight FZ1073, which was bound for Israel from Dubai on Wednesday, attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday, calling the incident a "terrorist attack".
Flight FZ1073 would have felt like a "vertical roller coaster", when it plunged 16,000 feet in about 30 seconds before being levelled out and landing safely, according to an aviation instructor who recreated the descent in a flight simulator for Reuters.
Co-pilot in custody in UAE
Two sources have said the co-pilot is an Omani national named Hamam Al-Hamami. Israeli officials have not named the co-pilot but said that he is from Oman. UAE authorities and flydubai have not publicly disclosed the co-pilot's identity.
Reuters could not independently reach Al-Hamami, who is in UAE custody, for comment. The UAE has not announced any formal charges against him and it is not known if he has appointed legal counsel. Oman has not commented on the incident.
Disaster on board flight FZ1073 was averted after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, who had attacked the captain in what Israeli officials said was an attempt to crash the plane carrying more than 170 passengers and crew. The UAE public prosecutor has said the co-pilot had attempted to take control of the plane.
Radical mosques and extremist websites
Most of the passengers on board were Israeli nationals.
A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities and later transferred to the UAE on Thursday.
The Financial Times reported on Sunday that Al-Hamami had allegedly visited what it described as radical mosques and extremist websites while in Australia, citing two people familiar with the investigation. Australian intelligence services held a file on the individual, according to the FT.
Reuters could not immediately verify the FT report. The government of Australia did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside normal business hours.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the co-pilot had undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was clearly suicidal, although he has not said when or where that indoctrination allegedly occurred.
Israel does not have official diplomatic relations with Oman, and Netanyahu has also said pilots from such countries were not permitted to operate flights to Israel. It is not clear how the co-pilot came to be assigned to the flight to Tel Aviv.

UK Green party adopts ‘Zionism is racism’ policy
LONDON - The UK’s left-wing Green party on Oct 4 voted to define Zionism as racism at the party’s annual get-together, drawing sharp backlash from British Jewish groups and the Israeli government.
Members of the Green party, which has five MPs in Britain’s 650-seat Parliament and which enjoyed a boost in recent local and special elections, backed the motion at the party’s conference, with 1,022 votes in favour and 813 against.
According to the motion, Zionism would be “treated as any other form of racism” and the party supports the establishment of a “single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine”.
“This has been a serious and deeply felt debate within our membership,” a Green spokesperson said.
The Greens have enjoyed a surge in popularity under the charismatic leadership of Zack Polanski, attracting voters dissatisfied with the centre-left Labour government’s stance on the Israel-Hamas war.
However, Polanski’s popularity has taken a hit in recent months, polls show, following several missteps.
“This motion would make the Green Party the first electorally significant UK political party in living memory to adopt what appears to be an overtly antisemitic political platform,” three Jewish community groups said in a letter to the party ahead of the vote.
“We also emphasised the implications for the safety and welfare of all British Jews,” the heads of the Board of Deputies, Community Security Trust and Jewish Leadership Council warned.
Israel’s anger
Israel’s foreign ministry said the policy went “far beyond the boundaries of legitimate political debate”.
“Every political party in Britain, first and foremost the governing Labour Party, must unequivocally reject this twisted resolution,” Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.
Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, called the Green party’s decision “a disgrace”.
“Zionism is the national liberation movement of the Jewish people, and it forms the basis for the Jewish people’s right to a state and a national home in the Land of Israel,” Herzog said on X.
Bridget Phillipson, chair of the ruling Labour Party and Minister for Women and Equalities, also condemned the Green Party’s conference decision.
“It is shameful to vote against a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine and to condemn the vast majority of British Jews and Jews around the world as racist for supporting Israel’s right to exist,” she said in a party statement.
The motion laid bare divisions in the party with Polanski – who is currently running to become an MP in former prime minister Keir Starmer’s London constituency – skipping the vote.
Despite at least three out of five Green MPs opposing the motion, Polanski said earlier this week that the “displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people” was “clearly racism”.
United Nations investigators have accused Israel of committing “genocide” in the war in Gaza, a finding that Israel has rejected. AFP

Iran vows stronger response to military attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:01:41 UTC

Iran vows stronger response to military attack
Araghchi says Iran remains ready for a diplomatic solution to US conflict
TEHRAN — Iran is ready for a diplomatic solution to its conflict with the US, but if Washington again chooses a military course, Tehran is more prepared than before to defend itself and will deliver a stronger response, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday.
Addressing ambassadors and representatives of foreign countries based in Tehran at the Foreign Ministry, Araghchi said Iran remained firm and serious on both fronts — defending itself and pursuing diplomacy.
“If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, they will receive a stronger response than before, and we will defend ourselves more powerfully than before,” he said. “And if they are seeking diplomatic avenues, we remain ready to reach a just and dignified solution to end this war through diplomacy.”
Araghchi said Iran hoped the US would choose “the path of wisdom and rationality,” stressing that there was no military or sanctions-based solution to the conflict.
“The only solution that can work is a negotiated solution based on justice and fairness, and a dignified and diplomatic solution,” he said, adding that such an approach could provide a final way out of what he described as the “illegal and unjust aggression” launched against Iran.
Diplomatic outreach remains strong
Araghchi also highlighted Iran’s diplomatic activity during the recent UN General Assembly meetings in New York, saying the Iranian delegation had played a strong and effective role.
“I met with 42 foreign ministers, and the president met with 10 heads of state in New York,” he said.
He said Iran had clearly explained its positions in New York and that the level of interest shown by different countries in meeting with Iranian officials, learning about Tehran’s views and hearing its proposals had been “very significant.”
Araghchi said this had demonstrated the failure of what he described as an attempt by some in the US to isolate Iran.
“The perception that some people in the US may have had that they could turn Iran into an isolated country had completely failed,” he said, adding that Iran had acted in New York as “a powerful country respected by the international community” and demonstrated that it continued to have “rational positions” and solutions for both war and peace.
Iranian diplomats, he said, had been highly active at the General Assembly and had conveyed the voice of the Iranian people to the international community.
“We were present in all fields and conveyed the voice of the Iranian people to the world,” Araghchi said, adding that Iran had delivered its people's message in favor of peace and rational solutions.
He also said Tehran had clearly explained its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, stressing that all of those conditions were consistent with commitments that the US must accept.
Tehran dismisses US claim over Iranian delegation
Araghchi also rejected a claim from the US that the Iranian delegation had been expelled from the country.
“Regardless of whether this claim is true or not, since we went and returned according to our own pre-planned schedule, the claim made by the Americans is truly strange,” he said.
He argued that the claim was contradictory because, on the one hand, it amounted to an admission that the US had violated its obligations as the host country of the United Nations, while on the other hand it demonstrated how angry Washington had become over the presence of the
Iranian delegation in the US.
‘No solution through more sanctions’
Araghchi said the US had already failed both militarily and diplomatically and would gain nothing from imposing additional sanctions.
“The US has lost both in war and in diplomacy in the past,” he said. “Trying new sanctions will also be of no benefit to them. There is no military solution and no solution based on more sanctions.”
He reiterated that Tehran remained prepared for both military defense and diplomacy.
“We remain firm and serious in both areas of defending ourselves and advancing diplomacy,” he said.
Calls on Europe to reconsider its position
Araghchi said he had also held extensive discussions with European countries and described those talks as “very frank.”
“We hope that European countries will reconsider their approach toward the Islamic Republic of Iran,” he said.
He referred to what he described as a significant admission by the NATO secretary-general regarding European involvement in the US war against Iran.
“The admission by the NATO secretary-general that European countries participated in the US war against Iran was a serious admission,” Araghchi said.
According to Araghchi, the NATO chief had explicitly said that more than 5,000 US fighter jets had taken off from bases in Europe to attack Iran.
“We are still waiting for European countries to answer this question: Why did they play an effective role in this war against Iran?” he said.
Despite his criticism, Araghchi said Iran's proposal to European countries was to establish dialogue with Tehran and avoid any participation in renewed efforts by the US and Israel to escalate the conflict.
“Our proposal to these countries is to establish dialogue with the Islamic Republic of Iran and avoid any participation in renewed warmongering by the US and the Zionist regime,” he said.
Seven-day plan could reopen Hormuz
Araghchi said Iran's most important diplomatic initiative was a proposal it had presented for resolving the disputes between Iran and the US and ending the ongoing war.
He referred to the initiative as the seven-day plan, saying that acceptance of the proposal would allow the Strait of Hormuz to be reopened within seven days.
“The most important of all these issues is the plan that the Islamic Republic of Iran has presented for resolving the existing disputes and the ongoing war between Iran and the US,” he said.
“This plan is known as the seven-day plan, and if it is accepted, the Strait of Hormuz will be reopened within seven days.”
Araghchi's remarks came as Tehran reiterated that it remained open to diplomacy while warning that any renewed military action would be met with a stronger response.

Green Party recognizes Zionism as a form of racism
The Green Party of England and Wales has voted to declare Zionism a form of racism in an unprecedented move at its party conference in Brighton, Middle East Eye has learnt.
The vote by party members on Sunday makes it the first major party in the UK to recognize Zionism as a form of racism - and to back a single democratic Palestinian state with equal rights for all ethnic and religious groups, rather than a two-state solution.
1,022 members voted for the motion while 813 voted against it.
Co-Deputy Leader Mothin Ali told Middle East Eye on Sunday that he was strongly in favor of the motion, unlike Green MPs Carla Denyer and Adrian Ramsay, who criticized[as1] it.
"As defined in the motion," Ali said, "Zionism is an ethno-nationalist state. Zionism is resulting in ethnic cleansing, in the belief that one group of people is superior to another."

"The belief that one group of people is superior to another, I just can't accept that."
Green members voted against an amendment to the motion saying it "shall not be used to pressure, proscribe or discipline members based on affiliation with Jewish community institutions, such as synagogues, community centers or denominational groups, that describe themselves as Zionist or used to discipline or sanction Jewish members for expressing views that would be non-sanctionable if expressed by non-Jewish members (such as support for a binational state, or two state solution)."
But members voted for an amendment supporting the "inalienable right to self-determination" for Palestinians, party insiders told MEE.
Ali told MEE on Sunday morning he believed the motion would shift political discourse in Britain. "In 2024 the Green Party recognised the genocide that was taking place in Gaza, before any other major political party.

'Motion safeguards Jewish people'
Before the start of the conference, it was widely reported that Jewish members of the Green Party who belong to synagogues that identified as Zionist could face internal disciplinary procedures.
Lubna Speitan, a British Palestinian and the lead author of the motion, told MEE on Saturday this was wrong. She explained the motion is an "E-Motion," meaning it concerns external matters and has no bearing on internal processes.
"We've made explicitly clear in the motion that not all Jews are Zionist and not all Zionists are Jewish," she said.
The motion was endorsed by prominent Holocaust survivor and activist Stephen Kapos, who said he believed that "Zionism both as an ideology and practice is harmful and has no legitimacy and must be rejected."

Problematic pornography use is linked to craving, shame, depression, and loneliness, meta-analysis finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
16:00:55 UTC
01:00:55 KST

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 111 samples found that problematic pornography use tends to be higher among people who report stronger cravings, more sexual shame, depression, loneliness, emotion dysregulation, and moral disapproval of pornography. The strength of these links varied widely across studies and may partly depend on how problematic use was measured. The paper was published in Addictive Behaviors Reports.
In modern times, pornography is widely accessible through the internet. Many people worldwide use it without problems in their daily lives. However, for some individuals, pornography use becomes difficult to control and begins to interfere with relationships, work, sexual functioning, or emotional well-being. This pattern is often called problematic pornography use.
Problematic pornography use is not a formal psychiatric diagnosis. Rather, it is an umbrella term for a range of self-reported difficulties, such as feeling unable to control one’s use, being preoccupied with pornography, or feeling distressed about it. It is less about how often pornography is viewed than about whether use feels compulsive or causes significant distress or impairment.
Researchers have examined a range of factors linked to problematic pornography use. These include impulsivity, difficulties with emotion regulation, loneliness, stress, anxiety, depression, and a tendency to use pornography as a way of coping with negative emotions. Sexual factors, such as high sexual desire or dissatisfaction with one’s sex life, also seem to play a role for some people.
In addition, moral or religious conflict about pornography can intensify feelings of guilt and distress, sometimes making people perceive their use as more problematic than its behavioral pattern alone would suggest. Easy availability, privacy, novelty, and the virtually unlimited variety of online sexual content may further reinforce repeated use in susceptible individuals.
These different perspectives are reflected in the questionnaires researchers use. Some measures focus mainly on loss of control, such as unsuccessful attempts to cut back, compulsive use, or continued use despite negative consequences. These are known as dysregulation-oriented measures. Others focus more on the emotional distress associated with pornography use, such as guilt, shame, worry, or moral conflict, and are known as distress-oriented measures.
Study author Sonay Sheikhi and colleagues at Kharazmi University in Tehran, Iran, conducted a systematic review of existing studies to identify psychological characteristics associated with problematic pornography use. They also conducted a meta-analysis, a statistical technique that combines results across studies, to estimate how strong these associations are. In addition, they examined whether the strength of these associations depended on which kind of measure a study had used.
The researchers searched the PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science databases, and supplemented the results with searches of Google Scholar, Iranian databases (SID, Magiran, and Noormags), and gray literature sources such as the Open Access Theses and Dissertations database. They included studies published in English or Persian between 2012 and 2025.
In the search, they used keywords related to problematic pornography use (e.g., problematic pornography use, pornography addiction, compulsive pornography use, problematic online pornography use, cyber pornography) combined with terms referring to psychological correlates (e.g., impulsivity, emotion regulation, attachment, craving, moral incongruence, depression, anxiety, and personality).
The search identified over 38,000 unique records, from which the authors selected 925 full-text documents for review. Of these, 97 articles met the inclusion criteria. Together, they described 111 independent samples totaling 121,728 participants. The average participant age was about 27.5 years, and around 46% of participants were women.
The studies were published between 2012 and 2025, with about 85% of participants coming from studies published between 2017 and 2025. Nearly all of the data were collected online.
The psychological characteristics most strongly associated with problematic pornography use were craving (a strong desire to view pornography) and sexual shame, each with an average correlation of 0.54. Correlations range from −1 to 1, with values near zero indicating no relationship. The weakest associations were with the personality trait of extraversion and with indicators of family environment, both close to zero.
Problematic pornography use was also associated with depression (0.32), emotion dysregulation (0.29), moral disapproval, meaning the belief that pornography is morally wrong (0.27), and loneliness (0.23). The craving and sexual shame estimates, however, were each based on only four or five studies, compared with 12 to 21 studies for these other characteristics.
Results also varied widely from study to study. For most characteristics, the range in which future studies’ results would be expected to fall was wide and often included values near zero, meaning a given study could find a much weaker association or none at all. The authors therefore describe the pooled results as average tendencies rather than effects that apply equally across all populations.
The authors also examined whether the type of measure mattered. Studies using dysregulation-oriented measures tended to show stronger associations with impulsivity and craving, whereas studies using distress-oriented measures tended to show stronger associations with shame and moral disapproval. However, the authors describe these patterns as descriptive, and formal statistical tests found few reliable differences between the two kinds of measures.
In one case, the subgroup results ran against this pattern: religiousness was more strongly associated with problematic use in studies using dysregulation-oriented measures than in those using distress-oriented ones. The authors conclude that measurement differences may account for some, but not all, of the variation across studies.
“Across the available evidence, PPU [problematic pornography use] was associated with a broad range of psychological variables spanning behavioral self-regulation, emotional functioning, interpersonal processes, and evaluative distress. However, the magnitude of these associations varied considerably across psychological domains and across studies, indicating that PPU cannot be adequately characterized as a single, homogeneous construct,” the study authors concluded.
The study sheds light on the psychological characteristics linked to problematic pornography use. However, the authors note that the studies they analyzed were predominantly cross-sectional, meaning they measured everything at a single point in time, which rules out conclusions about cause and effect or about which came first. Additionally, most studies relied on self-report questionnaires for both pornography use and psychological characteristics, which the authors say may have inflated some of the observed associations.
The authors also note that their two categories of measures are rough groupings, since many questionnaires capture both loss of control and distress. The differences between them should not be read as evidence of distinct types of problematic pornography use.
The paper, “Psychological correlates of problematic pornography use: A systematic review and meta-analysis of measurement and conceptualization differences,” was authored by Sonay Sheikhi, Shahram Mohammadkhani, and Mehdi Akbari.

Philippines arrests 244 suspects in online scam crackdown

Philippines arrests 244 suspects in online scam crackdown
Criminal gangs accused of using Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs) as cover for human trafficking, fraud, murder.
Philippine authorities have arrested more than 200 foreign workers, mostly Chinese, in their biggest crackdown this year on illegal offshore gaming operators.
The country’s Immigration Bureau reported late on Saturday that military and other law enforcement agencies had raided two addresses on the southern Philippine island of Mindanao on Friday. Criminal gangs are accused of using Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs) as cover for various crimes.
The raid on one site resulted in the arrest of 110 Chinese citizens, two Cambodians and a Hong Kong resident, according to the bureau’s statement.
A further 131 foreign citizens were arrested at the second site. Again, the majority were Chinese, alongside citizens of Malaysia, Indonesia and Myanmar, according to the statement.
Authorities seized large quantities of computer equipment, mobile phones, laptops and SIM cards.
Manila banned POGOs in 2024 on the grounds that crime groups use them as a cover for human trafficking, money laundering, kidnappings, fraud and murder.
A 2023 United Nations report noted that in recent years hundreds of thousands of people have been trafficked by gangs and forced to work in scam centres and other illegal online operations across Southeast Asia.
The UN report estimated that at least 120,000 people across Myanmar and approximately 100,000 in Cambodia may be trapped in scam operations, with other criminal-owned enterprises in Laos, the Philippines and Thailand ranging from crypto-fraud to online gambling.
The Philippine government is investigating potential human trafficking-related offences by several of those arrested in the latest raids, while the rest will be deported.
International concern has grown in recent years over similar scam operations in other Asian nations, where trafficking victims are tricked or coerced into promoting bogus cryptocurrency investments and other cons.
“We will continue to enforce our immigration laws against foreign nationals who violate the conditions of their stay and ensure that the Philippines is not used as a base for illegal activities,” immigration chief Joel Viado said in the statement.
Chinese embassy spokesperson Ji Lingpeng told the AFP news agency that they are “reaching out to the Philippine law enforcement agencies on the details of this case”.
“Chinese law prohibits any form of gambling, including Chinese nationals gambling overseas or working for gambling companies,” he added.

Hong Kong builders take three WorldSkills honours in best CIC haul

Hong Kong builders take three WorldSkills honours in best CIC haul
Nine young competitors represented Hong Kong across eight construction trades in Shanghai, with concrete construction work earning its first honour and welding its third in succession
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
Nine young construction competitors from the Construction Industry Council returned from WorldSkills Shanghai with three Medallions for Excellence, the strongest finish the CIC has recorded at the competition.
The honours went to Law Chak-sum in painting and decorating, Tse Yu-lok in welding, and the concrete construction work team of Huang To-kong and Wan Tsz-ho.
It was Hong Kong’s first WorldSkills honour in concrete construction work, while welding delivered a third successive Medallion for Excellence for CIC.
Construction companies should give skilled tradespeople clearer positions on their grade charts, allowing a young welder, joiner or other craftsperson to see a path towards supervisory and leadership roles without assuming that a university degree is the only way forward, he said.
The four-day concrete competition provided perhaps the squad’s most dramatic turnaround.
Huang and Wan said they had been among the fastest competitors over the first two days. But one of the pair became unwell on the second day, forcing them to discuss tactics with their expert before the next session.
Then, on the third afternoon, their concrete pour failed. Wet concrete spilled across the slab. “The whole floor was concrete,” one of the pair said. “We wanted to cry. We did not pack it in.”
They rebuilt the work layer by layer and recovered sufficiently to record the highest mark in the steel-fixing section. They finished fourth overall and secured a Medallion for Excellence, about 13 points behind first place.
Their expert, James Li, had previously described the pair as having contrasting temperaments, with trust between them becoming particularly important during the competition.
The concrete module also demanded skills across several areas. Cheng said competitors had to work with aluminium, steel and timber formwork as well as steel fixing and concrete pouring.
Tse’s welding competition produced another CIC honour.
Unlike most members of the squad, he joined from paid welding work rather than as a Hong Kong Institute of Construction student.
Before Shanghai, Tse had identified pipework and X-ray inspection as areas where marks could be lost. He said afterwards that all three of his X-ray inspections exceeded the standard he had set himself.
Cheng said Tse also performed well in both X-ray and pressure testing.
Official results put Tse on 716 points, placing him 11th on the same score as another competitor. The gold medallist scored 735.
Tse said he hoped to return to the Institute to pass on what he had learned, while also gaining experience on construction sites.
The CIC has now won welding honours at three successive WorldSkills competitions, in 2022, 2024 and 2026.
Law completed the trio of Medallion winners in painting and decorating.
He said the four-day competition had presented difficulties along the way, but he had worked through them and intended to continue in the trade.
Other competitors said their performances had surpassed what they had achieved in training.
Huang Tsz-ho, who had paused a social-science degree to train, represented Hong Kong in joinery. He said he found a wood course online and that some practice days ran to more than ten hours.
The squad later trained with partner institutes in Beijing, Zhejiang, Guangdong, Chongqing and Shanghai.
Some training days ran from early morning until 10pm or 11pm. The CIC also uses each WorldSkills cycle to study overseas techniques, equipment and standards and feed relevant lessons back into HKIC training.
Competitors who want to enter the industry will be helped to find work, while further training is available in areas including BIM and robot operation.
Cheng added that the two years of preparation had also changed the nine competitors, who returned from Shanghai speaking more readily and with greater confidence than when they were selected.
The 49th WorldSkills Competition will be held in Aichi Prefecture, Japan, in November 2028.

They could be planning an October surprise before the U.S. midterms. We are still seeing Iranian attacks on ships now. I mean, how can you be so confident prices are headed down?
SEC. WRIGHT: Well, because we've got increasing supplies coming out of the Strait of Hormuz and they've continued to rise over the last months, over the last recent weeks. Diesel's mostly been infected by the Russia-Ukraine war and also by China's decision not to export diesel or gasoline into the marketplace. And of course, we're living with two refineries that were recently closed, large refineries in California that Gavin Newsom forced the closure of. And frankly, 15 years of Democrat policies that have been energy subtraction, trying to close coal plants, close refineries, and shrink our capacity. Which means when you get in crisis, we're just less resilient than we should be.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you still think that in the next four weeks prices are going to go down?
SEC. WRIGHT: Absolutely. Diesel prices have been going down. Gasoline prices have been going down. I expect that to continue.

They've got a lot of diesel in stores. Why not release some of that? This is what you store diesel for. When all the Russian exports of diesel are shut down, when the Chinese have said we're not going to deliver any more diesel, and you still have a reduction of diesel flows coming out of the Gulf, but we're restoring those, but that takes time. This is just common sense. This lowers diesel prices, not just in the United States, but it lowers them in Europe and around the world. But it will drive diesel prices down as those releases come. It'll drive diesel down through the winter in the United States and around the world. And- and by then we'll be in another place. We'll have more refining capacity online. I- I suspect we'll continue to see diesel decline as we go into next spring as well.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So below six bucks? Which is where it is.
SEC. WRIGHT: Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah. By post-midterms?
[CROSSTALK]
SEC. WRIGHT: It's- it's down a little over 20 cents so far.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
SEC. WRIGHT: I think you'll see it continue to go down. Yeah, you should see it below $6 before too long. But exactly when, I certainly don't know that.

SEC. WRIGHT: I--

SEC. WRIGHT: Again, I won't get in front of the president on that. We're trying to have the best relations we can--
MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm sure you've looked at the projections on what it would do for pricing.
SEC. WRIGHT: Of course, we're trying to have great relations with China and move that ball forward. I think things are going reasonably well there. But then the flip side is you've got to look at every leverage you've got to bring a murderous conflict to an end.

SEC. WRIGHT: He- he was well aware of- of the risk to energy flows that were coming out of the Persian Gulf region. He said, "I simply cannot. The world cannot sustain a nuclear-armed Iran, and I'm not going to do it."

SEC. WRIGHT: Thank you, Margaret.

“We don't feel a sense of worry” in Europe, says the head of the Muslim World League
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:56:54 UTC
00:56:54 KST

While in Brussels to meet with political and religious leaders, Sheikh Dr Mohammad bin Abdulkarim Al-Issa stressed the need to deepen dialogue in order to confront the turmoil facing the world and that Europe's "civilised constitutions" will prevent political excesses.
Dialogue. That was the word repeated by the Secretary-General of the Muslim World League, Sheikh Dr Mohammad bin Abdulkarim Al-Issa, during his visit to Brussels on Friday.
During his stay in the Belgian capital, the Saudi religious leader met political figures and representatives of the country’s religious communities and civil society who gathered for a high-level meeting on dialogue and social cohesion.
Al-Issa stressed the importance of dialogue in resolving conflicts, saying it needed sincere intentions and effective leadership.
“Of course, we always believe in dialogue and place great faith in it,” he said, adding that “dialogue is the language of reason and wisdom.”
Established in 1962, the Muslim World League is a Mecca-based Islamic organisation that describes its mission as promoting Islam, tolerance and friendship among peoples.
Europe’s far-right rise and containing its dangers
His visit came after the far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD, finished first in state elections in both Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in September.
France is due to hold a presidential election in 2027, while parliamentary elections are expected in Italy, Poland and Greece.
Despite the rise of the hardline right in some European countries, Al-Issa expressed confidence in national constitutions, European institutions and societal values.
“As for talk of a hardline right emerging in some European countries, we are generally not worried. Each European country has a civilised constitution that no one can override. There are also societal values that everyone must respect,” he explained.
“Any departure from the constitution and these civilised societal values will prompt society to speak out and put things right,” he said.
He also pointed to the possibility of challenging legislation before constitutional courts.
Al-Issa said similar questions had arisen in other countries because of certain governments. Things had turned out as he had hoped, he said, where there was constitutional oversight and an active public conscience.
Religious freedom is protected by national constitutions
He also called for respect for religious practices within the framework of national constitutions.
The issue comes amid debate over restrictions on religious clothing in Europe. Italy’s government has approved a decree banning face coverings during school activities, with exceptions for certified medical reasons and educational activities.
The decree does not explicitly mention the burqa or niqab, although Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni referred to both when announcing the measure, saying that in Italy “no one should force a girl to hide herself”.
“We always call for respect for each religion’s distinctive practices, provided they do not conflict with the constitution,” Al-Issa said.
“There is no doubt that civilised constitutions, particularly European ones, respect those practices and the observance of religious rituals.”

Ukraine and Germany sign series of defence and energy agreements
Ukraine and Germany signed a number of documents covering defence, security, energy and rescue technologies at the Ukrainian-German Business Forum on Sunday 4 October.
Source: European Pravda
Details: Key agreements include the procurement of thousands of IRIS-T missiles, new firing modules and radars, alongside joint development of interceptor drones and expanded energy sector cooperation.
Ukraine's Ministry of Defence concluded three memorandums with the German company Diehl Defence, which provide for the procurement and delivery of thousands of IRIS-T missiles, IRIS-T firing modules and additional missiles and joint work on high-precision artillery ammunition.
A separate memorandum with the company Hensoldt concerns the procurement of tactical radars and surveillance systems.
Another document – a letter of intent with Quantum Systems – provides for the testing and procurement of interceptor drones designed to counter jet-powered Shahed-type loitering munitions.
In addition, the National Guard of Ukraine agreed with Quantum Systems and Ukraine's Frontline Robotics on the localisation of Ukrainian drone production in Germany.
A separate memorandum between the State Emergency Service of Ukraine and Alpha Robotics Germany relates to cooperation in unmanned systems for firefighting and rescue operations.
In the energy sector, Siemens Energy signed two memorandums with Ukrainian counterparts: one with the Ministry of Energy and another with Naftogaz of Ukraine NJSC.
Another document was concluded by German operators 50Hertz Transmission and Amprion with Ukrenergo, Ukraine's state-owned electricity transmission operator. The agreements are aimed at further cooperation in the energy sector and strengthening Ukraine's energy security.
The signing of the documents was part of high-level Ukrainian-German meetings on 4 October.
Background:
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the total value of the agreements with Germany exceeds €8.5 billion.
- On the same day, it was announced that Germany will provide Ukraine with a new assistance package worth more than €1 billion.

Ukraine to Begin Using Small Air Defense Missiles Against Russian Drones in October — Zelensky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:51:00 UTC
00:51:00 KST

Small air defense missiles are expected to begin being used against Russian jet-powered drones in the second half of October.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced this during a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv.
“There are several types of them. Obviously, we will see the result this month. At the end of the month, in the second half of this month, we expect to see the result. So, you asked about their use and how widespread it is. For now, there is no such use. It will only happen,” the President said in response to journalists’ questions.
At the same time, he noted that if these systems show strong interception results, production could be rapidly scaled up.
In February 2025, 19 Ukrainian companies joined the Brave1 grant program to develop missile weapons.
In August 2025, Brave1 announced four grant competitions to develop explosives, autonomous drones, tactical ballistic missiles, and air defense systems to counter UAVs. Developers could apply for grants ranging from UAH 100 million to UAH 150 million.
In January 2026, it became known that eight of the 18 companies that had submitted applications for the competition received grant funding from Brave1 to develop tactical ballistic missiles and low-cost air defense missiles. Brave1 CEO Andrii Hrytseniuk shared this at the time on Militarnyi’s “Do zbroi!” (To arms!) program.
All 18 companies submitted proposals for developing air defense systems to counter UAVs. Four of them also submitted their tactical ballistic missile projects for funding.
“How does it work? First, a military commission reviews all applications to determine the winners, and the teams pitch their projects. There is a second stage — independent experts also review them. There are several levels of decision-making. Then the Brave1 supervisory board makes a decision, analyzes the evaluation results and projects, and after that the winners are selected. The winners then receive funding,” Andrii Hrytseniuk said.
According to the Brave1 CEO, funding is usually provided in tranches, with developers receiving payments in stages as they reach certain development milestones.
In addition to funding assistance, Brave1 also conducts technical reviews of developments and, when necessary, can connect a company with a supplier of specific components or a research institution with the required laboratory equipment.
Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, five new Ukrainian air defense systems have become publicly known.
These include the upgraded Koral air defense system for medium- to long-range use and the Shershen air defense system for short- to medium-range use.
The list also includes the Desna and Rif air defense systems with RK-2PZ missiles for short-range use, as well as the short-range DRAGON air defense system, which currently uses R-73 and AIM-9 air-to-air missiles and for which the ST-100 small air defense missile is being developed. Ukraine has also developed the new RK-19 missile for Soviet Osa-AKM systems.
