Japan summons US envoy as marine arrested over Okinawa murder
Japan has summoned the United States envoy after a US marine was arrested on suspicion of robbing and murdering a woman.
US ambassador to Japan George Glass pledged “full cooperation” on Sunday. Lance-Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard is accused of killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi on the southern island of Okinawa, where thousands of US servicemen are stationed.
“The occurrence of such an extremely brutal and heinous incident is a matter of profound regret,” Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi wrote on social media. “As the Government of Japan, we have lodged a strong protest with the US side, while firmly demanding maximum cooperation with the investigation.”
Glass stated that the US “confirmed our policy of providing full cooperation with the investigation” while sharing his condolences on social media. The 20-year-old marine has denied the charges.
CCTV footage, according to local Japanese media, showed a non-Japanese man going into a hotel room with the Japanese woman in the city of Naha. Later on, the footage shows the man leaving by himself, with what appear to be the woman’s belongings, reports the AFP news agency.
“Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause significant anxiety to the local community and must never occur,” Japan’s Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi wrote on social media.
Japan hosts about 54,000 US military personnel, including 18,000 marines. The majority of these forces are based in Okinawa, a Japanese island that came under US administrative control at the end of World War II and was returned to Japan in 1972.
Since the handover, about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested in Japan, according to the local newspaper Yomiuri Shimbun.

Russia strikes data center and logistics hub in Ukraine – MOD (VIDEO)
The Russian military has struck a data center and a logistics hub in Ukraine, the Defense Ministry in Moscow said on Sunday.
The ministry said that Geran drones targeted a Nova Poshta logistics center in Chernomorsk and a data center in Odessa. Footage released by the MOD shows direct hits on both facilities. Russia has increasingly targeted Ukrainian data centers in recent strikes, with internet and mobile providers reporting damage and connectivity disruptions.
Additionally, Russian forces struck two dry-cargo vessels carrying military supplies to the port of Odessa, hit a drone command post, destroyed an air-surveillance radar, and struck military-used transport infrastructure, weapons depots, drone storage sites, and positions housing Ukrainian troops and foreign mercenaries across 147 locations. It later added that its forces struck Kiev’s Severny road bridge across the Dnieper, which it said was used to move troops and military cargo.
The ministry also reported that its air defenses downed four guided bombs, three US-made HIMARS rockets, and 1,222 fixed-wing drones over the past 24 hours. The ministry further said Russian forces tightened an encirclement in northeastern Kharkov Region and advanced elsewhere, including in northern and central Dobropolye.
Both Kiev and Moscow have ramped up long-range strikes in recent weeks following Ukraine’s botched “pressure campaign,” which saw Kiev intensify drone attacks on Russian civilian and energy infrastructure amid battlefield setbacks. The attacks hit energy facilities, civilian warehouses and logistics hubs, residential buildings, and resort areas, as well as polling stations during last month’s parliamentary elections.
Russia has retaliated by sharply expanding strikes on Ukraine’s military-industrial facilities, shipping, and key ports handling military-related imports. The campaign has severely disrupted Ukrainian Black Sea shipping and logistics. Moscow maintains that it targets only infrastructure supporting Ukraine’s war effort.
President Vladimir Putin recently warned that Ukraine faces a “catastrophic scenario” after “opening Pandora’s box” by attacking Russian economic and civilian infrastructure, which ultimately failed to alter the course of the conflict. Putin also warned that with its “provocative actions,” Kiev was only hindering a peaceful settlement rather than bringing one closer.
Despite the mounting toll, Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky vowed on Saturday to further intensify strikes on Russian oil facilities. The Russian Defense Ministry responded on Sunday by pledging to step up its own campaign. The ministry said Ukrainians “should blame only the head of the Kiev regime” for any further escalation, adding that his threats meant he “bears full personal and political responsibility for it.”

The flydubai incident: A miracle or a story of resourcefulness? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:37:43 UTC
00:37:43 KST

I do not believe in miracles. Alleged miracles are frequently the result of human intuition and resourcefulness, just like many catastrophes frequently result from human failures, misjudgments, and arrogance.
In my opinion, what happened last Wednesday in the case of flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai International Airport to Ben-Gurion Airport in Israel was an event of the former type, even though many reactions in Israel gave God full credit for it. My answer: “Ish ish be’emunato yichyeh” (Each person shall live within his faith).
The immediate culprit in this story was the Omani co-pilot on the flight, Hamam al-Hammami, who stabbed the plane’s Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, who was its main hero. Hammami’s intention was apparently to cause the plane, in which the majority of the 174 passengers were Israeli, to crash, possibly over Israeli territory.
Of course, beyond Hammami’s personal responsibility, there is that of the Dubai authorities who allowed the Omani pilot to co-pilot the flight to Tel Aviv, even though he had a record of extreme Islamic expressions and activities and had been removed from Oman Air, and Royal Air Maroc training courses, for the same reason.
At the time of writing, it is not yet known whether any terrorist organization or country stood behind Hammami, or whether he acted as a lone fanatic.
Nevertheless, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who seems eager to take credit for any successes associated with the event for reasons connected to the upcoming elections in Israel, announced on Friday in Hebrew that “whoever sent the pilot will pay a very heavy price.”
On CNN and Fox News, Netanyahu insinuated (in English) that Iran might well be involved but did not indicate whether this is merely speculation based on self-interest or a reflection of reality based on Israeli intelligence information.
Another question to which there is no definitive answer at present is whether Israel’s mutual flight agreements with the UAE in general and Dubai in particular contain reference to Israel’s requirement that pilots flying the planes of foreign companies to Israel should hold the citizenship of a country that maintains diplomatic relations with it.
If such a stipulation does exist (and at least one Israeli source quoted in the media has claimed that it does not), then Israel is at fault for not checking whether it is upheld on all flights of UAE airlines that land in Israel.
The hero of the story
As mentioned at the outset, the main hero of this episode was the plane’s Indian captain, Machchhar, without whom the plane and its passengers would not have come out intact or alive.
Despite his severe wounds and loss of blood, Machchhar managed to send two distress codes: Squawk 7700 (general emergency) and Squawk 7500 (unlawful interference/hijacking), and to verbally alert air traffic control about the ongoing physical attack against him inside the cockpit.
Most importantly, he managed to open the locked door into the cockpit, which cannot be opened from the outside. Once the door was open, four Israeli passengers managed to enter, overcome the co-pilot, who not only kept stabbing the captain but also tried to destroy equipment in the cockpit, and provide first aid to the pilot.
In addition to the four Israelis, two off-duty flydubai pilots who were on the flight (according to reports, they were supposed to fly the plane back to Dubai after the disembarkation of the passengers at Ben-Gurion Airport) entered the cockpit.
One of the two (apparently a British national) took control of the plane, after one of the Israelis – a plumber by the name of Yaniv Hayoun – attempted to stop the plane diving down at great speed (there was no one in control of the plane at the time) by pulling up the aircraft’s control yoke and thus managing to temporarily lift the plane from its dive.
Hayoun, who had never flown a plane in his life, had learned that pulling up the yoke was what had to be done in such a situation from a Canadian TV documentary series, Mayday, which deals with true cases of serious airplane accidents.
Hayoun’s act saved the plane and its passengers from a certain immediate crash, but it might also have been responsible for the plane losing the blades of the rotor in its tail, which could have caused the plane to fall apart midair. That this did not happen was due to exceptional good luck, though again, some might count it as a miracle.
At any rate, not only was the plane saved, but the two off-duty pilots managed to fly the plane to safety and land at the airport of Tabuk in southwestern Saudi Arabia, close to the Saudi border with Jordan. If the two off-duty pilots had not been on the plane, the plane and its passengers would have been doomed.
Incidentally, the Israeli who saved Machchhar’s life by stopping his profuse bleeding was a dentist of Georgian origin called Shota Musayev. The other three Israelis involved in detaining the co-pilot and saving the captain were Asaf Rajuan (the owner of an insurance brokerage), Zvika Manes (the CEO of Barak Capital), and his wife, Tali, who was the first to discover what was going on in the cockpit. The plane’s stewards (all men) are reported to have been in total confusion, not knowing what to do.
Conclusions from the incident
My conclusions from this extraordinary story are, firstly, that with low-cost airlines (and flydubai is officially in that category) the chances of something going extremely wrong seem greater, especially because of manpower issues.
Secondly, since many Israelis have active and diverse military experience, accompanied by a propensity to improvise, one is safer being part of a random Israeli group of people than part of a random group of people of any other nationality, if one gets into a messy situation.
In my opinion, it has nothing to do with our allegedly being “God’s chosen people” but rather with the very long history of the Jewish people in the Diaspora and its need to survive under difficult circumstances, and the Israeli ethos and self-confidence (at times an exaggerated and annoying self-confidence).
Though the catastrophe of October 7, 2023, threatened to severely damage this ethos and self-confidence, the flydubai incident has undoubtedly given both a boost.
Nevertheless, some irritation in Dubai concerning what they see as Israeli audacity regarding the role played by Israeli citizens in last Wednesday’s incident suggests that a measure of hatzne’ah lechet (walking humbly) might be called for.
The writer has written journalistic and academic articles, as well as several books, on international relations, Zionism, Israeli politics, and parliamentarism. From 1994 to 2010, she worked at the Knesset Library and the Knesset Research and Information Center.

Over 25 NYC Jewish groups oppose Mamdani antisemitism plan, demand new one
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:37:28 UTC
00:37:28 KST

More than 25 grassroots organizations, local school groups, and neighborhood nonprofits signed an open letter criticizing Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s newly released municipal strategy to combat antisemitism, arguing that it “falls dangerously short” and ignores the primary threats facing Jewish residents on the ground.
The coalition, consisting of over 25 New York City-based entities including the BridgeBuilders Grassroots Coalition, the New York Jewish Alliance, JewBelong, and End Jewish Hatred, stated that they represent “everyday New Yorkers across the city” who deal with antisemitism daily in schools, workplaces, cultural institutions, and neighborhoods.
The signatories said that the administration’s plan largely overlooks contemporary anti-Jewish hostility tied to Middle East politics, noting that the document “reaches back eight years to highlight right-wing terrorist attacks in other cities, while failing to discuss, or even mention, a single anti-Jewish incident that occurred in New York in the past three years.”
The letter, signed on Friday, said that “our community generally isn’t encountering Charlottesville-style white supremacists in our neighborhoods” but is instead facing “anti-Zionist animus that too often veers into anti-Jewish harassment, exclusion, and even violence”.
Groups state Mamdani's plan ignores biggest threat to NY Jews
While noting that some of the proposed measures may have value, the groups said that “they largely sidestep the biggest threat Jewish New Yorkers are dealing with today: anti-Jewish exclusion and violence cloaked as anti-Israel activism.”
The group also said that the “omission isn’t incidental. It’s the central failure of the report.”
Detailing the daily reality on city streets, the coalition said that “anti-Zionist harassment has become normalized in our city and the violence it inspires is completely unsurprising,” pointing out that Jewish New Yorkers are targeted due to events in the Middle East and Israel.
The letter noted that “‘Free Palestine’ is yelled at Jewish performers in derisive tones” and residents “are called ‘babykillers’, ‘rapists’, and ‘genocidaires’ as we walk the street or shop for groceries,” alongside acts of physical violence such as “stabbings, car rammings, bomb threats and assaults.”
The letter criticized the administration’s framework for omitting a definitive stance, stating that the report “explicitly declines to adopt a definition of antisemitism and provides little concrete guidance for perhaps the hardest and most pertinent questions institutions are confronting: When is conduct framed as anti-Zionist political expression simply anti-Jewish targeting or discrimination?”
Groups demand new plan
Concluding that “how can we solve a problem if we refuse to even acknowledge the cause?” The groups demanded a new plan, stating that “a strategy to combat antisemitism in New York City must address antisemitism as Jewish New Yorkers are experiencing it today, and must not deny their agency to identify and define the hate they encounter.”
The letter’s release comes in direct response to the municipal strategy report titled “Tackling Hate: The Mamdani Administration’s Strategy to Combat Antisemitism,” published by the Office of the Mayor and led by the newly reestablished Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism under Executive Director Phylisa Wisdom.
The administration’s report outlines a whole-of-government approach across seven strategic objectives, including a nearly ninefold budget increase for the Office for Prevention of Hate Crimes to $26 million.
This features $7.4 million designated for nonprofit physical security and doubled funding for Partners Against the Hate grants, alongside enhanced educational curricula through New York City Public Schools, expanded cultural competency training via the NYC Commission on Human Rights, and increased support from the NYPD Hate Crimes Task Force.

Netanyahu can keep posing for photos with heroic survivors while ignoring the fact that they were forced to save themselves because he failed – for the hundredth time – to do his job.

Within Israel’s security establishment, that incident was logged and classified as a successful attack – an event that actually took place, resulting in the deaths of 260 Israeli passengers and crew members (in a best-case scenario).

Attacks on oil infrastructure endangering marine life in Persian Gulf, research finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:36:59 UTC
00:36:59 KST

The Iran war has severely threatened sensitive marine and coastal ecosystems across the Persian Gulf, with oil spills, military strikes and damage to coastal infrastructure threatening coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds, wetlands and marine life, according to an analysis published in the International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science.
The study found that the conflict has compounded existing pressures from climate change, coastal development and unsustainable exploitation, warning that the resulting ecological damage has also undermined fisheries, aquaculture, desalination and ecotourism.
The Persian Gulf is estimated to be home to more than 700 fish species and provides critical habitats for dugongs, dolphins, whales, sea turtles, sharks and migratory birds, many of which have been put at risk as a result of Iran’s attacks on oil and energy infrastructure in the region.
<strong>The conflict's compounding risks for marine life</strong><a href="https://www.jpost.com/environment-and-climate-change"></a>
Global warming and pollution have already put pressure on the region’s marine life, while the conflict has added further risks to species that depend on the Gulf’s waters, the researchers stressed.
Oil released into the water after attacks on tankers and other infrastructure can damage the cardiac, respiratory and immune systems of marine animals, while its neurotoxic effects can disrupt navigation and sensory processing in species such as dolphins and turtles.
A central example offered is the Iranian vessel Shahid Bagheri, which was confirmed to have been leaking heavy oil into the Khuran Strait for at least a month after being struck in March.
The vessel is grounded in shallow waters approximately five kilometers off Qeshm Island, and the study predicted that prevailing currents were carrying contamination westward toward the Hara wetlands and the protected Hara Biosphere Reserve.
The UNESCO-recognized reserve, the largest mangrove forest in the Persian Gulf and an important habitat for migratory birds, fish, and endangered turtles, has not been cleaned up despite the temporary ceasefire, according to the researchers, as a result of maritime tensions and the interference of GPS and AIS signals, which have obstructed coordination among international environmental response groups.
Additionally, nearly 2,000 ships stranded by the attacks and ongoing blockade are carrying an estimated 21 billion liters of oil, raising the risk of further environmental damage. The Strait of Hormuz is not only a vital route for global oil shipments but also a habitat for dolphins, whale sharks and critically endangered Arabian humpback whales, all of which could be harmed by oil spills or attacks on vessels.
Kharg Island, which has critical coral reefs surrounding it, is also in danger, given that it is Iran’s primary oil export hub and a significant military target, the researchers noted, especially given that dredging and land reclamation have already reduced the resilience of coral reefs.
Violations of environmental laws, agreements
Beyond the ecological damage, the analysis argues that the conflict has resulted in violations of international, regional and national environmental laws and agreements, including the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, Convention on Biological Diversity, Ramsar Convention, Convention on Migratory Species, Agreement on the Conservation of African-Eurasian Migratory Waterbirds and International Maritime Organization conventions.
The researchers advised that there were several key steps that could be taken to either mitigate the damage already done and prevent future harm.
Theorizing that the Gulf’s ecosystems can recover through targeted restoration and regional cooperation, it recommended expanding coral transplantation through nurseries and transplantation projects, including initiatives around Kuwait’s Kubbar and Qaru islands, Oman’s Musandam and Muscat, and reef patches near Kharg Island and the Strait of Hormuz.
The study also recommended restoring seagrass through transplantation and sediment stabilization, particularly in Qatar’s Ras Laffan, Abu Dhabi’s seagrass meadows and Bahrain’s pearl oyster beds.
It was also recommended that a regional biodiversity monitoring program conduct regular health assessments of dugongs, dolphins and whale sharks, including veterinary interventions by marine biologists to detect stress, disease and injury, and that a Gulf-wide oil spill response system be developed.
To ensure regional cooperation, despite the tensions, it suggested that the United Nations oversee the establishment and running of a Gulf ecological union to coordinate ecological restoration, resilience planning, monitoring and conflict-sensitive environmental governance across the Gulf.
The Environment and Climate Change portal is produced in cooperation with the Goldman Sonnenfeldt School of Sustainability and Climate Change at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev. The Jerusalem Post maintains all editorial decisions related to the content.

‘Punishment for the crime of being female’: Sexual assault crisis at US colleges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:36:31 UTC
00:36:31 KST

In 2013, Emma Sulkowicz, then an art student at Columbia University, filed a formal complaint with the university administration alleging that she had been raped in her campus dorm room by a fellow student, Paul Nungesser. The two knew each other and had previously had consensual sexual relations, but Sulkowicz said this encounter was nonconsensual and violent, including choking. Nungesser denied the allegations and maintained that the entire encounter was consensual.
Columbia conducted an internal investigation that found Nungesser “not responsible” and decided not to take action against him. Sulkowicz’s appeal was rejected. Three additional complaints filed against Nungesser by other female students were also dismissed or dropped. Sulkowicz filed a complaint with the New York Police Department, but authorities determined there was insufficient evidence to bring criminal charges.
Sulkowicz then decided to turn her trauma into a performance piece that also served as her senior art project. During her final year at Columbia, she carried a dorm-room mattress with her everywhere she went on campus. The mattress was intended as a physical representation of the weight of trauma that survivors of sexual assault are forced to carry every day.
Before her 2015 graduation ceremony, the university asked Sulkowicz not to bring the mattress, but she refused and walked across the stage accompanied by friends who helped her carry it. Two years later, Columbia reached a financial settlement with Nungesser and issued a statement expressing regret for “the damage to his reputation.” Sulkowicz received nothing from the university.
Sexual assault on college campuses across the United States is a long-running epidemic that has never been resolved. Cornell University became the latest flashpoint this week, but it is only another example in a broader pattern involving elite institutions, political systems and American society at large that protects men accused of sexually assaulting women.
The numbers are staggering. According to data from the National Sexual Violence Resource Center, one in five female students experiences sexual assault while in college. Nearly 90% of campus perpetrators are known to the victim. Alcohol or other substances are involved in about 70% of reported assaults, and perpetrators sometimes deliberately use them to incapacitate victims, leaving them unable to resist and, of course, unable to consent.
More than 90% of campus sexual assaults are not reported to law enforcement or the appropriate university authorities because of fear, social stigma or a lack of confidence that anything will be done. At Cornell alone, more than 1,200 reports and complaints of sexual assault were filed between 2018 and 2024. According to a USA Today investigation, the university brought disciplinary charges in just 162 cases. Of the 51 students found responsible, only 14 cases resulted in suspension and just seven resulted in permanent expulsion.
As in many other areas, the political winds blowing from Washington have a significant impact here as well. During the first half of the previous decade, universities appeared to make substantial progress in addressing the issue. In 2011, the Obama administration reminded institutions of higher education that Title IX — the landmark 1972 law prohibiting sex-based discrimination at any educational institution receiving federal funding — required them to address sexual violence and instructed them to step up investigations. Colleges and universities responded with major educational initiatives and strengthened their Title IX offices, creating an environment that led to more reports and more women coming forward.
Critics, however, argued that the Obama-era guidelines went too far. The first Trump administration rescinded those guidelines in 2017, the Biden administration reinstated them and the Trump administration has now rolled them back again — coincidentally or not, just this week.
“In a deeply misogynistic society, groups of boys and men routinely bond over humiliating and exploiting women,” Kate Manne, a professor of philosophy at Cornell University, wrote in New York Magazine this week. “As a professor at Cornell, I have had many, many victims in my office, confiding in me their experiences of sexual assault and harassment. Many didn’t even try to report them to the police or the university, and, for those who did, the experiences and the outcomes have rarely been positive.”
In the case of “Jane Doe,” who has alleged for two years that she was raped by seven Cornell students, the district attorney declined to bring charges after relying on an investigation conducted by campus police. Investigators did not even interview the men involved.
The university allowed five of the seven students to complete their studies and graduate. Meanwhile, “Jane Doe” was forced to leave Cornell, and her request for a tuition refund so she could transfer to another university was denied. Only the lawsuit she filed against the university last week prompted authorities to reopen the investigation and thrust the issue of campus sexual assault back into the headlines.
In her article, Manne argued that U.S. universities often take a much tougher approach and impose far harsher penalties on students who participate in political protests or are accused of academic cheating than on students accused and found responsible for sexual assault.
“She ['Jane Doe'] hence,” she wrote, “faced more severe consequences than most of the men who she alleges gang-raped her. And rape can effectively be a punishment for the crime of being female..”

Over 800 Palestinian teachers killed in Israeli attacks since Gaza genocidal war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:35:39 UTC
00:35:39 KST

Israel has killed more than 800 Palestinian teachers and injured over 3,300 others since the start of its war on Gaza in October 2023, the Palestinian Education Ministry said on Sunday.
In a statement ahead of World Teachers’ Day, observed annually on October 5, the ministry said educators across the occupied Palestinian territories are fighting “a real battle for survival” to protect the right to education amid systematic targeting.
The education sector in Gaza and the West Bank has suffered “comprehensive genocide” since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, the ministry said.
The ministry said more than 170 teachers remain detained “in harsh conditions.”
It said movement restrictions and harassment at hundreds of checkpoints have compounded educators’ daily suffering, particularly in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, the village of al-Mughayyir in the central West Bank, the Jordan Valley and areas classified as Area C.
Under the 1995 Oslo II agreement, intended as an interim arrangement, the West Bank was divided into Areas A, B and C.
Area A is under Palestinian civil and security control, while Area B is under Palestinian civil administration and Israeli security control. Area C, which accounts for about 60 percent of the West Bank, remains under full Israeli control.
The ministry said abuses against Palestinian teachers have been accompanied by severe financial hardship, undermining their material and psychological stability as Israel withholds Palestinian tax revenues.
Known as clearance revenues, the funds are taxes collected by Israel on behalf of the Palestinian Authority on imported goods and transferred under the 1994 Paris Protocol.
Israel began deducting sums from these revenues in 2019 and subsequently halted transfers, worsening the Palestinian Authority’s financial crisis and its ability to pay public employees’ salaries in full.
Clearance revenues account for approximately 56 percent of total Palestinian public revenues, making their withholding a major obstacle to paying salaries, providing public services and meeting government obligations.
The ministry urged the international community, the UN, and education and human rights organisations to take urgent action to curb violations and provide international protection for students and education personnel.
It also called on unions worldwide to press for the release of detained teachers and withheld financial entitlements to ensure educators can live with dignity.

Strike on UN aid trucks in Sudan kills one
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:26:04 UTC
00:26:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Strike on UN aid trucks in Sudan kills one
A strike on two United Nations food aid trucks in Sudan's South Kordofan state killed one of their drivers, the World Food Programme (WFP) said on Sunday, without specifying who was behind the attack.
The attack comes as fighting intensifies in Kordofan, a strategically important region where Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) are battling for territory more than three years into a war that has devastated much of the country.
The WFP trucks were travelling between the two army-controlled cities of Dilling and Kadugli on Saturday when they came under attack, despite being "clearly marked as humanitarian vehicles", WFP said.
The agency said it was assessing the damage and called for a prompt investigation into the incident.
It added that just the day before, a WFP truck had struck an explosive device in Dilling after delivering lifesaving food assistance.
The WFP did specify the munition used in the latest attack, but both the army and the RSF have increasingly deployed drones in recent months, with the high-tech weapons killing more than 1,100 people in the first half of the year alone, according to UN figures.
The war between Sudan's army and the RSF has killed more than 200,000 people, aid workers estimate, displaced more than 11 million and created the world's largest hunger and displacement crises.
Famine was confirmed last year in South Kordofan's Kadugli, and in El-Fasher in the western Darfur region, as fighting and access restrictions continue to hamper aid deliveries.

Student protests in France: 400–500 schools fully or partially closed Monday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:24:12 UTC
00:24:12 KST

Another day of mobilisation is planned for Tuesday. By then, 400 to 500 secondary schools are expected to remain fully or partially closed, including 24 that have been “burned or vandalised”. The ministry also reports that 78 education staff have been injured since the movement began.
Up to 500 secondary schools in France are expected to be fully or partially closed on Monday as a new day of mobilisation by pupils gets under way, following several days of protests marked by clashes with police, damage to schools and street violence.
The demonstrations, which have spread across several major cities, have seen rubbish bins and other objects set on fire, projectiles thrown at security forces and damage to school buildings and street furniture.
The Ministry of Education said on Sunday that classes would be "totally or partially" suspended in 400 to 500 secondary schools where security conditions "are not met".
There were "between 400 and 500 suspended classes" on Friday, and "there will probably be just as many on Monday, but with a gradual, partial resumption of classes", Education Minister Édouard Geffray said in interviews with TV channel France 2 and radio station France Inter.
Twenty-four of the 735 schools affected by the protests have been "set on fire or ransacked", the minister said. Geffray also said that "78 staff members" from the Ministry of Education have been injured "since the start of the events".
Interior Minister denies any disproportionate intervention
The Interior Ministry said that the unrest has led to nearly 5,000 arrests since Monday.
Rubbish bins and other objects have been set on fire, while projectiles have been thrown at security forces. Police have intervened to disperse some demonstrators, using tear gas, rubber bullets and defensive ball launchers (LBDs), as well as batons
On Sunday morning, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez defended the actions of the security forces, rejecting claims that the response was "disproportionate".
Nuñez insisted that "the police do not repress young people", but "protect" pupils and students who wish to "advance their demands peacefully". He nonetheless warned that they intervene "firmly and without delay" to put an end to "damage, violence [and] abuses" committed by troublemakers.
He also denied that the security forces are specifically targeting "racialised young people from working-class neighbourhoods", condemning what he called a "blaming narrative totally disconnected from the real world".
Unsafe buildings, overcrowded classes and absent teachers
The movement began two weeks ago at the Saint-Exupéry secondary school in Créteil, in the Paris suburbs, in support of striking teachers who were denouncing a lack of staff and resources.
It then gathered pace and gradually spread across the country over the past week.
Pupils are denouncing, among other things, unsafe and insanitary buildings, overcrowded classes, timetables they say are impossible to cope with and a shortage of staff, with teacher absences that are not systematically covered. Some are also challenging the ban on mobile phones in schools.
On Friday morning, the Minister of Education, Édouard Geffray, met representatives of the pupils. After the meeting, they said they had not obtained any "concrete measures" and called for the movement to continue next week.
An "act III" planned for Tuesday
After two nationwide days of mobilisation, on 29 September and 1 October, an "act III" is planned for Tuesday.
All the teachers' unions said on Sunday that they would join the pupils' protest. "Their demands are legitimate, and we support them all the more because they are at the heart of our own mobilisations denouncing the lack of resources for several years now," they stated in a press release.
The unions also criticise a government response to the mobilisation that they say has been limited to the intervention of the security forces. "Reports from pupils who have been injured, assaulted and threatened are increasing by the day. This is unacceptable," they argue.
A mobilisation marked by several serious incidents
Several serious incidents have also been recorded on the fringes of the mobilisation.
In Tours, in central France, a young man who was injured lost sight in his right eye after clashes between pupils and police on Wednesday, according to the local prosecutor.
In La Ciotat, in Provence, a 59-year-old teacher was doused in petrol and beaten during a pupils' demonstration. A 16-year-old boy, suspected of carrying out the attack, was arrested in Marseille on Sunday morning and taken into police custody.
Police officers have also been targeted. In Belfort, in the east of the country, one officer was chased, beaten and repeatedly kicked by a group of young people. Two people were taken into custody following this attack.
According to information from Le Parisien, faced with the widespread damage around schools and in public spaces, the government intends to bring forward the timetable for the "casseurs-payeurs" bill. The aim is to make people who take part in violent gatherings contribute to the cost of repairs, even when they are not directly responsible for the damage.
The Senate is due to examine the bill at the end of October

‘Did he know?’: Why Israel is rejecting an October 7 reckoning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:22:25 UTC
00:22:25 KST

‘Did he know?’: Why Israel is rejecting an October 7 reckoning
The fixation on Netanyahu’s failures allows Israel to avoid confronting what it has done in Gaza.
As Israel prepares to mark three years since the October 7 attacks and with less than a month to go to parliamentary elections, one topic is dominating the electoral agenda.
Media reports that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was warned by the United Arab Emirates before the attacks have put his alleged responsibility back in the spotlight.
“Did he know?” is the question on everyone’s lips.
Listening to the accusatory choir, one might think that Israeli society finally is acknowledging the real meaning of October 7. Yet the opposite is true.
Instead of giving a platform to a reckoning, the elections function to scapegoat Netanyahu for his alleged role in facilitating Hamas’s attack while absolving Israeli society and the Zionist movement of its collective responsibility for the preceding violence and ensuing genocidal aggression.
For example, it does not insist on investigating whether the “Hannibal Directive” was deployed as part of the Israeli military response on October 7 and whether it killed Israeli citizens and how many.
It does not scrutinise subsequent Israeli military operations or whether they put the Israeli hostages in danger or how many were killed by Israeli bombs.
There is no questioning of why key Palestinian negotiators were attacked during ceasefire and hostage negotiations, including Ismail Haniyeh, Hamas’s chief negotiator, in July 2024 in Tehran and Hamas’s negotiating delegation in September 2025 in Doha.
There is no debate about why the Israeli government repeatedly rejected ceasefire proposals that could have brought the hostages back much earlier.
There is little attention paid to the fact that Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant face arrest warrants from the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity.
None of these made the cut. Why?
The answer lies in the psychological state of Israeli society. For many Israelis, October 7 became a psychological rupture, making it difficult to reconcile their sense of humanity with their complicity in the criminal reality that followed.
The problem, then, is not that Israelis are in denial or misinformed. It is that a large portion of the society is complicit in criminality and actively avoids reckoning with it.
The absence of Gaza and Palestinians more broadly from Israeli political discourse is because of their complete dehumanisation by Israeli society.
How else could one explain the absence from the election rhetoric of questions about, and subsequent accountability for, actions against the Palestinian people?
Why has the Israeli military killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, the vast majority of them civilians? Why has it carried out mass and arbitrary detentions, torture and enforced disappearances of Palestinians?
Why has it targeted journalists, medical workers and academics? Destroyed and occupied hospitals? Wiped out ancient landmarks and irreplaceable cultural heritage sites?
Why has the sadistic and often sexually deviant celebration of destruction, subjugation, ethnic cleansing and death by Israeli soldiers been allowed?
What’s more, there is also little interrogation of the consequences of bombing and invading Lebanon, killing nearly 9,000 people since October 2023. Or bombing Syria and Yemen.
These are not isolated abuses. They are symptoms of a system of theft and domination driven by greed and sustained through psychological conditioning, segregation, fear and rewards for aggression. In line with the “Wired to Steal” model, dehumanisation helps produce consent for aggression while escalation following acts of resistance leads to normalisation of further expansion and robbery.
Thus, this election is not about a reckoning with October 7 or its horrifying aftermath. It is a lens onto a fascistic settler society engaged in denial and dehumanisation of an Indigenous “other” as a means of evading and normalising its own ongoing genocidal actions. Although Netanyahu may become the scapegoat, replacing him does not address the underlying machinery of domination and may instead serve to entrench it further.
That machinery remains firmly in place. The continuity between the violence unleashed since October 7 and the longer history of Zionist colonial expansionism is striking, with no lessons learned other than how to improve and grease the machinations of genocide. Fear, victimhood and the construction of a permanently besieged “us” against a dehumanised “them” continue to produce consent for further aggression and expansion.
October 7, therefore, has become not an occasion for genuine reckoning but another means of avoiding one. Netanyahu seeks to focus responsibility for the attacks on questions of what he knew and when while leaving the much broader record of what Israel has done since largely outside the electoral debate. His opponents, meanwhile, have their own complicity and ambitions to answer for. Thus, there is little political interest in a genuine reckoning with October 7. The fixation on Netanyahu allows the wider political establishment and Israeli society to avoid confronting the system of domination in which they remain invested.

Xinhua Headlines: China's new generation shines at Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
23:19:03 CST
00:19:03 KST

* China reaffirmed its continental dominance by topping the gold medal table for a record 12th straight Asian Games, securing 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals - its best-ever haul at an overseas Asiad.
* The Games signaled a changing of the guard, with 548 of China's 815 athletes making their Asiad debuts and over a quarter born in 2005 or later.
* Beyond traditional disciplines, young Chinese athletes broke new ground in skateboarding, sport climbing, surfing and BMX freestyle-sports aligned with the Olympic program's youth-oriented shift.
NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games came to a close Sunday, with China topping the gold medal table for the 12th consecutive edition, and finishing with 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals, its best haul at an overseas Asiad.
Beyond the medal count, the Games offered a glimpse of the next generation of Chinese athletes. Young competitors rose up across a spectrum of sports -- strengthening China's traditional powerhouses, breaking new ground in emerging disciplines and signaling ambitions that extend well beyond Nagoya.
DEPTH ON DISPLAY
China's dominance in its traditional strength events was evident throughout the Games.
Diving once again provided the clearest example. With Lian Junjie winning the men's 10m platform title, China swept all 10 diving gold medals on offer at the Games. Since making its Asiad debut in 1974, China has never missed out on a diving gold medal, and the latest title was the team's 100th diving gold in Asian Games history.
That dominance extended across the water. Chinese swimmers won 30 gold, 13 silver and 11 bronze medals, their best-ever haul at the Games. They also swept all seven relay titles for the first time, while setting five Asian records and 17 Games records.
On the track and field, China continued to turn depth into medals. The team won 17 gold, 14 silver and eight bronze medals, its best show at an Asiad held outside China since Bangkok 1998, to finish atop the athletics medal table.
The momentum also extended to other medal-rich events. China claimed 16 of the overall 28 shooting titles and set five world records.
"The Asiad gave us an opportunity to test our preparations for Los Angeles 2028," said Wang Lian, an official with China's shooting and archery administration. "It was also an important step in developing our team, particularly our promising young athletes."
Weightlifting and gymnastics further underscored China's strength in established events. Yang Liuyue broke world records in the snatch and total in the women's 61kg category, while the men's gymnastics team captured its 13th consecutive Games title and the women's team extended its winning streak to 14 editions.
YOUTH TAKES FLIGHT
China's delegation had a distinctly youthful look at the Asiad. Of its 815 athletes, 548 were making their Asian Games debuts, while 27 percent were born in 2005 or later.
In the women's 400m individual medley, 13-year-old Yu Zidi and 15-year-old Ke Wenxi took gold and silver.
Yu won three golds, setting Asian Games records in the 200m butterfly and 400m individual medley, as well as an Asian record in the 200m individual medley. Her performances earned her the women's Most Valuable Player award, announced by the Olympic Council of Asia on Sunday.
They arrived with talent, but talent alone was not enough. Behind their breakthroughs were years of repetition, training and persistence.
"Only I know how much I went through this year. But I got through it all. I hope I can keep getting better and better," Yu said.
19-year-old Zhang Zhanshuo won seven gold medals, the most of any athlete at the Games. His celebration of counting the golds on his fingers in the pool became one of the memorable images.
That confidence was on display in the field, too. 18-year-old javelin thrower Yan Ziyi made an immediate impact, launching 70.46 meters with her first attempt to improve the Games record by 4.37 meters.
"I plan to save my chance to break the world record for the 2027 World Championships in Beijing," Yan said.
The emergence of young athletes such as teenage sprinter Chen Yujie offers a glimpse of what could lie ahead for Asian athletics.
The 17-year-old competed in four events and won three golds and a silver, including a gold in the women's 100m in a Games-record 11.06 seconds.
Off the track, her confidence was just as striking. A photo that she took a nap in the athletes' lounge before the final became a hit on Chinese social media.
"These Asian Games have given me a lot of motivation. Now that it's over, I'm already looking ahead to the next challenge," Chen said. "I hope that one day I can represent China and Asian women on the world stage and showcase our strength at the Olympics."
BREAKING NEW GROUND
Young athletes are opening up new possibilities for Chinese sports.
After years of struggling to regain the footing, China's men's football team beat Uzbekistan in a penalty shootout on Saturday to win a bronze medal, its first in 28 years at the Games. The result gave Chinese fans something more to celebrate during the National Day holiday.
"This is the most valuable medal of my career," said 21-year-old center back Peng Xiao. "But I would rather see it as a starting point. I hope the generation that comes after us can one day stand higher on the podium."
As the Olympic program embraces younger, more urban sports, skateboarding, sport climbing, surfing and BMX freestyle have become regular features at the Asian Games. Chinese athletes are making their mark in these events, chasing results while gaining recognition on the world stage.
China's climbers made their presence felt on National Day, sweeping the women's boulder and men's speed titles to claim the country's first Asian Games gold medals in Olympic events. With Olympic and world champions in the field, both victories were hard-earned.
For 17-year-old Yang Siqi, reaching the Asiad surfing final and winning women's shortboard silver turned what once seemed out of reach into reality. The teenager from the mountainous region of southwestern China secured the country's first Asian Games surfing medal.
Her dedication in training even caught the attention of Song Min, a coach with South Korea's surfing team, who said he believed Yang could one day make it to the Olympics.
"I have never been afraid of surfing since I first started," Yang said. "The next step is to keep improving, one step at a time."
China's skateboarders also came out on top against the host nation Japan, taking gold and bronze in the women's street event with composed performances when it mattered most.
21-year-old Sun Sibei made history by winning China's first gold in the cycling BMX freestyle, which made its Asian Games debut.
"I hope this niche sport can reach a wider audience, so more people can see the twists and turns in the air, and more children can have the chance to try BMX at facilities close to home," Sun said.
The younger athletes are telling a different story, a story of confidence, exploration and willingness to step into unfamiliar territory. To some extent, these Games left behind more than medals: they opened up a new path for Chinese sport. ■

Across China: China's island province Hainan offers diverse tourism experiences to holidaymakers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
23:18:55 CST
00:18:55 KST

HAIKOU, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- China's southernmost province of Hainan has more to offer than beaches and coconut trees.
During the first National Day holiday since the launch of the island-wide special customs operations at Hainan Free Trade Port (FTP), the tropical island has offered visitors from home and abroad a diverse range of experiences -- from duty-free shopping and local food to historic neighborhoods and the distinctive lifestyle of fishing communities.
In the seaside resort city of Sanya, the Sanya International Duty-Free Shopping Complex has drawn a steady stream of visitors during the holiday. The sprawling mall offers a wide selection of international brands, attractive duty-free prices and convenient pickup services.
"The shopping mall is huge and nice," said Alina, a Russian tourist. "There are many international brands and the prices are good. I enjoy shopping here very much."
Visiting China for the first time, Alina said she had enjoyed her trip to Hainan, where tropical coastal scenery was complemented by a world-class shopping experience.
Since Hainan expanded its duty-free shopping access to departing tourists last November, a growing number of overseas visitors like Alina have been seen at the island's major duty-free shopping centers.
For domestic tourists, duty-free shopping has long been a popular part of a Hainan itinerary.
Li Tian, a tourist from central China's Henan Province, purchased perfumes and cosmetics during her visit.
"Duty-free shopping is a must-do for me every time I visit Hainan. The prices are attractive, and the wide range of products meets my one-stop shopping needs," she said.
But the island's appeal goes well beyond its glossy shopping malls. Across Hainan, old streets, traditional neighborhoods and fishing ports offer visitors a chance to slow down and experience a different side of the island -- one rooted in local history and everyday life.
At Qilou Old Street in Haikou, the provincial capital, century-old arcade buildings line the historic streets, where tourists wander through narrow lanes, sample local snacks and soak up the atmosphere.
A local tea house on the street was packed with guests during the National Day holiday. "I came here to experience the local way of life. It's bustling and has a very authentic feel," said a tourist surnamed Xu from east China's Zhejiang Province.
At Xincun Port in Lingshui Li Autonomous County, hundreds of Tanka fish rafts are lined up across the blue waters, forming a unique "village on the sea." Shuttle boats ferry tourists back and forth, offering them a close-up look at the traditional culture and way of life of the Tanka people.
The Tanka people, or boat dwellers, are those who have traditionally lived on sampans and made their living by fishing in coastal waters. Over generations, they have developed a distinctive culture.
"I have never seen such a large cluster of fish rafts before, and I've never had a meal on one either. Today's experience is truly unique," said Gao Chen, a tourist from Beijing who enjoyed a seafood meal on a floating raft for the first time.
During the day, tourists here engage in fun activities like beachcombing and sea angling, harvesting fresh seafood. As night falls, Xincun night market comes alive with bustling crowds as people gather around stalls serving grilled seafood, tropical fruits and local snacks.
Sanya's Xidao Island, home to a fishing village with more than 400 years of history, offers yet another glimpse into the island's traditional coastal life. Visitors can explore its winding lanes on foot or rent electric scooters to get around.
"Cycling around the village makes me feel totally relaxed and at ease," said a tourist surnamed Zhang from north China's Hebei Province.
Hainan is at the forefront of a broader national effort to upgrade tourism offerings. The latest five-year tourism development plan, approved by the State Council and released in July, calls for nurturing new drivers of tourism growth and enriching the supply of high-quality tourism experiences.
The Hainan FTP officially launched island-wide special customs operations in December last year. According to plans, China aims to build Hainan into a globally influential tourism and consumption destination by 2035. ■

Trump announces new federal task force to coordinate AI efforts

23:18:50 CST
00:18:50 KST

WASHINGTON, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday announced a new federal task force to coordinate the government's efforts on artificial intelligence (AI).
Trump said in a Truth Social post that the task force, named the "Super Intelligence Force," will coordinate federal efforts to ensure the United States continues to lead the world in AI.
It will also coordinate the government's engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers and AI companies, according to the post.
According to the post, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will lead the task force.
Trump also named Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor among the officials leading the group, which will report to Trump and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.
The announcement followed a White House meeting on Tuesday between Trump and executives from major AI companies, who signed a voluntary accord calling for stronger internal controls and reviews of AI models.
On the same day, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to use the terms "Super Intelligence" and "SI" instead of "Artificial Intelligence" and "AI," read a fact sheet released Tuesday by the White House. ■

Defense Forces Managed to Deliver Second Batch of Humanitarian Aid to Occupied Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:16:28 UTC
00:16:28 KST

Units of the 11th Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine and the 34th Kherson Regiment of the National Guard, in cooperation with the 30th Marine Corps, the 34th Borysfen Marine Brigade and the 79th Border Guard Detachment of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine, delivered a second batch of humanitarian aid to Oleshky.
Ukrainian Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi reported this.
During the second operation, the military delivered a total of 400 packages weighing nearly 4 tons. The humanitarian aid included food, medicines, and children’s kits.
“I thank everyone who directly took part in this operation: those who delivered the aid, provided cover, ensured engineering support, and handled logistics. Special recognition goes to the crew of the Perun UAV, which during this operation not only delivered food but also rescued six animals from the occupied territory. We also thank communities, educational institutions, benefactors, and volunteers from across the country who collected the humanitarian aid and made this operation possible,” the minister said.
Last night, guardsmen from the 11th Mykhailo Hrushevskyi Brigade of the National Guard and the 34th Kherson Regiment of the National Guard of Ukraine carried out their second successful operation to deliver humanitarian aid to the town of Oleshky. https://t.co/h4YjcPxgic
— Ivan Vyhivskyi (@IvanVyhivskyi) October 4, 2026
The previous batch of food, weighing about 4 tons, was delivered to occupied Oleshky in late September. However, Russian military personnel are attempting to shoot down the drones carrying the supplies.
The invaders detain Oleshky residents for receiving humanitarian packages, hold them in basements, beat them severely, and subject them to violence.
According to estimates by the regional administration, Russian forces are holding about 2,000 people hostage in occupied Oleshky, including nearly 50 children. They are forced to survive without food, electricity or water.
The city has been on the brink of a humanitarian catastrophe for almost a year, since late 2025. The last time food was delivered to Oleshky by road was in late May, when local entrepreneurs managed to enter the city in two commercial vehicles.
Subsequent road delivery attempts failed. During one such attempt, four vehicles hit mines on June 2, killing two people.
Since then, supply has been irregular, and after stocks and garden produce ran out, residents were left on the verge of starvation.
Journalists identified Russian military personnel, including their commanders, who were involved in creating the humanitarian catastrophe in the occupied Oleshky, Kherson region.
The blockade of the city and the deprivation of civilians of food and medicine have been linked to personnel of the 126th Coastal Defense Brigade and the 331st Guards Air Assault Regiment of the Russian Armed Forces.
According to the journalists’ investigation, the brigade is commanded by either Col. Oleg Oleksandrov or 43-year-old Konstantin Kochetkov, while the 331st Regiment is commanded by 40-year-old Oleg Morozov, known by the call sign “Kholod.”
