Transcript: Brett McGurk on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 4, 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:16:20 UTC
00:16:20 KST

Transcript: Brett McGurk on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 4, 2026
The following is the full transcript of the interview with Brett McGurk, who served as a top Middle East adviser to former Preident Joe Biden, a portion of which aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 4, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, October 6th, 2023, Saudi Princess Reema Bandar shakes hands with you on a deal meant to normalize relations, or start normalizing relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia, create a pathway for the Palestinians, give Saudi the civilian nuclear deal, and within hours this incredible attack happens in Israel. Why, in the book, do you argue that those two things are connected?
BRETT MCGURK: Well, first, Margaret, it's great to be here. And I try to just tell this history. It's chronological, but I really try to bring the reader into the room. And the book starts about three days into the Biden administration, President Biden asked me to go see the Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia about some significant changes we were going to make in Saudi policy, including cutting off various weapons systems and a number of steps. And the Crown Prince in that meeting kind of put on the table the possibility of recognizing Israel, a kind of big, you know, breakthrough possible deal. And we didn't really pick that up until about a year and a half into the administration, and I describe, I think, that was lost time and unfortunate. But once we did pick it up, we made some real progress on it, and we had a package of agreements, including the Palestinian Authority was working with us on this deal. And on October 6, you're right, I had a Saudi delegation in my office with Princess Reema. Tony Blinken was about to go to the Middle East. And we had mapped out- I still can't say if not for what happened a few hours later, we definitely would have gotten the deal. But it was definitely- it was moving in that direction, and we were quite confident. And Reema and I shook hands on by the end of the year, really, to have this in place, and then talk about the- the rollout of it in the first quarter of 2024. What happened just a few hours later obviously knocked that issue off- off the agenda and everything else. I think it's- it's tragic because I think that deal, when you step back, if you look at what was happening just a few weeks before the events of October 7th, we're now the third anniversary, you had things happening that had not happened in 55 years. You had a senior Saudi official visiting Ramallah in the West Bank to see the Palestinian Authority, first time since 1967. You had Israeli officials in Israel- or Israeli officials in Saudi Arabia, and- and I think a package that would have set the foundation for what is now in a UN Security Council resolution, Margaret, a credible pathway to Palestinian state determination and statehood. That's what we were talking about. Hamas, of course, does not recognize Israel, wants to destroy Israel, and I would not be surprised if one of the motivations on October 7th was to knock this agenda off the table.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Do you believe that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar knew that there were these plans for a Palestinian pathway and normalization between Israel and Saudi Arabia, and that factored into his thinking?
BRETT MCGURK: We never saw anything to tie a direct connection.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay.
BRETT MCGURK: I never saw anything to tie a direct connection, but certainly it was known that this deal was moving in that direction. Mohammed bin Salman said it in September. It's like a- one of the biggest deals that- could be one of the biggest deals since the Cold War--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --Transform the Middle East if it had happened.
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, so it was very much in the- But I think October 7th had been planned, from what we later learned, for a period of years, and this was not something that just suddenly put together. But I learned about the attack that night around midnight from Mike Herzog, the Israeli ambassador. I got a call from the Situation Room, also. It was rocket attacks and then cross-border attacks, and, you know, events kind of unfold- I describe it in the book of, as a crisis unfolds, you- you learn and you- you see jagged pieces. And it still wasn't clear even by daybreak, when I was at the White House, and eventually saw President Biden later that morning, just the scope of the scale of- of what was underway.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, you wrote that the U.S. "had no clear warnings; nor did the Israelis, from what they told us." But you leave open the idea that there were missed signals. Was this a total intelligence failure?
BRETT MCGURK: I think, Margaret- So we have really looked, we did not have any- anything in our system that would have been a warning and indicator.
MARGARET BRENNAN: No U.S. intelligence.
BRETT MCGURK: No U.S. intelligence of a warning or indicator. I can't speak to whether the Israelis- the Israelis still have to this day not had a commission of inquiry. We had a 9/11 commission that I think made a number of reforms that have helped keep our country safe since 9/11. The Israelis still have not done that. I think they have to, they should do that. But from what I, in dealing with all these guys in Israel, security echelon, political echelon, I think they had an assumption that was deeply ingrained that Hamas was deterred, assuaged, and was not about to do something massive on any- any scale like this. I think that was a false assumption in their system, a failure of imagination, and it was tragic. I can't speak to whether or not there was a specific warning. We did not, we did not know of any.
MARGARET BRENNAN: The U.S. didn't know, and the U.S. didn't warn. But there has been recent reporting in the New York Times, in the Israeli paper Ha'aretz, in the Atlantic, about multiple sort of heads up from other regional leaders. Emirati leader Sheikh Mohammed apparently reported to Israel's Prime Minister Hamas was planning a major attack. The Atlantic said Egypt's intel chief also came to Israel in late September and warned Hamas was mobilizing for an attack. He didn't have a date, he didn't have the specifics, but he had a warning. Why wasn't that taken more seriously?
BRETT MCGURK: So again, I- I know Sheikh Mohammed quite well. When something on- is on his mind, he'll call. He called me at the White House once. Great respect for him. But we- we did not- we were not aware of- of a phone call. And Abbas Kamal, the Egyptian intel chief, is a main character in the book, we're with him all the time. Again, I also I just never- I had not- I did not hear–and I've checked with a number of my- my colleagues on this–of a pre-warning of October 7 from those two individuals. So I can't- Again, this is why I think Israel should have a clear investigation of what was known, what was missed at the very top, and also, you know, what intelligence analysts might have been seeing things that others weren't, why that information wasn't passed up. That's what has to happen in a situation like this. Again, we went through it, and I think Israel should do the same.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But just days after the attack, on Capitol Hill, you know, the head of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Mike McCaul, said Egypt did give a heads up. Diplomatic sources said that there were messages conveyed in late summer and September, including a warning from Yahya Sinwar that he was going to do something. But you say it's just a failure of imagination, that as to what that something was.
BRETT MCGURK: I think, I suspect when you look back, you will find similar to the types of warnings that were in our intelligence system before 9/11. Nothing of a, kind of, an actionable nature. And remember, Hamas and Israel before October 7th, they were in a negotiation, this kind of ties into the theme of the book, Margaret, a hostage negotiation, because Hamas had been holding two Israeli hostages: [Avera] Mengistu and Hisham al-Sayed. Two- one Arab Israeli, one Ethiopian Israeli, who were mentally ill, found their way in Gaza, and Hamas have been holding them for 10 years, and the remains of some Israeli soldiers from- from an earlier war. That negotiation had been going on. Again, this just gets to Hamas. They hold hostages for- to exceed maximum leverage and concessions. And I think in the course of putting a new demand on the table, Hamas saying it's either this or else, given the assumptions that were in the Israeli system, it probably would have been a warning would have been read in that--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --In that context.
BRETT MCGURK: --this is Hamas trying to play for that negotiation. But again, I have to say, I don't- I don't know what was in the Israeli system and what was known in the Israeli side. I think that's why they have to, you know, they're going to have an election soon, and everything before an election, particularly in Israel, can get a little crazy. But once there's a new government, I think having a serious commission of inquiry for what happened and making any reforms to ensure nothing like this can ever happen again is very important.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Because you believe there should be accountability from the top down?
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, I believe that- what was--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Or there is culpability?
BRETT MCGURK: --what was missed. Clearly, what- what was missed. I think it's very important for any country to go through something like that after a horrific incident like this.
MARGARET BRENNAN: In talking about Hamas, you write extensively about the country of Qatar and their centrality to the deal-making with Hamas because you weren't talking directly to the terror group, you were speaking through this country as an intermediary in order to get the hostages out. And you reveal that the Emir of Qatar told you Hamas was a burden to them, one he'd shed if only the U.S. asked. Do you mean to say Hamas is still only in Qatar because America wants them there? That we want that way to get in touch with the terror group?
BRETT MCGURK: Well, Qatar- and I go through this in- in the book. When you're- we're in this awful, horrific, awful crisis in every dimension and how do you- you can't just say stop the war release the hostages, you have to actually make that happen using diplomacy, leverage. And Qatar is the key mediator with Hamas leadership, and that is something that we inherited in our administration. It's been that way, they've been in Doha since the outbreak of the Syrian Civil War when they moved from Damascus to Doha, again, with the basically tacit agreement of Israel and also the agreement of, then, the Obama administration. So what the Qataris will say is, look, they're- they're here, they have their offices here partially for your benefit. So do you want us to get rid of them? Sometimes they would say that to us, and sometimes I said in peak of frustration, yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Kick them out?
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, the question is then: where are they going to be, and how do you actually get something done? I mean, this is what was so tragic, Margaret. I mean, here- here we have the worst day in Israel since the Holocaust. We have about 1,200 people dead. We have the largest mass hostage attack in- or hostage crisis in modern history, and Hamas knew that by taking hostages on this scale, they will be treated as, basically, statesmen in a negotiation. I mean, that's kind of how it- how it plays out, and the asymmetry there is incredibly frustrating, obviously, to the Israelis, it's frustrating to me throughout the process, but Qatar plays a critical role. And Sheikh Mohammed, who's a character in the book, the Prime Minister and Foreign Minister of Qatar also, was a key intermediary. I don't think we could have gotten this done without him.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, it's a point in the context of the Israeli elections that's interesting because you know some of the candidates who are running to replace Netanyahu are saying Qatar's an enemy state. They're funding terrorism, and they need to go after them.
BRETT MCGURK: I have a chapter in the book where I lay out the the kind of enigma in dealing with Qatar, and, you know, the Gulf states are very often very divided because- you mentioned Sheikh Mohammed and UAE, and this gets into relations with- the relation between the state and political Islam with the Muslim Brotherhood, and countries like Egypt, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, UAE completely banned, for example, the Muslim Brotherhood. Whereas Qatar has a very different philosophy. Their philosophy is we have to deal with everybody. Of course, we have one of our largest military bases in Qatar. Qatar also has Al Jazeera. I was in the Bush administration, I remember President Bush railing on the Qataris about what was being played on Al Jazeera. So it is a chronic issue and something I think we raise with Qatar very strongly. But when it comes to these deals, Qatar plays a central role. It's just- it's just a fact of it, and I talk about this in the book. When you're in the middle of the crisis, we're trying to get hostages home, we're trying to manage what could be a broader regional war. We're constantly- one reason it's titled "Brink," we are constantly on the brink of a broader regional war, and without Qatar, we would not have had some very critical channels to try to keep things under- under control.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Let me ask you about the Israeli Prime Minister. You dealt with him quite directly. Throughout the book you document that. And in February 2024, you talk about a meeting you had with him. You were very focused on these hostages and trying to get them out. You said "for more than thirty minutes he never mentioned the hostages…Netanyahu was animated in discussing the military campaign and far less so when discussing the hostages–when he chose to discuss them at all."
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Why? Why do you think that is?
BRETT MCGURK: Well, first of all, I describe Netanyahu, I spent a lot of time with him, he's kind of– As a negotiator, there's a term of art in the book called a ZOPA, Zone of Possible Agreement. And if you- if you just kind of line this up, where was the- you have Hamas saying, their core demand is they have to stay in power, go back to October 6th status quo, they stay in power, they will reconstitute, they'll be on Israel's border, they want all Palestinian prisoners released, and then we can release the hostages. Israel's core demand after October 7th is that Hamas can no longer be in power in Gaza, ever. Completely irreconcilable. And the hostages are such a central piece of this because you're never going to actually stop the war without- without the hostages. And there's a continuum in a hostage negotiation, and I've done them before, even outside this context, with Iran in particular, in which the hostage negotiator sets a price. And Maimonides, who was a 12th-century Jewish legal theorist, and he has a, kind of a commandment, and I have it in the book. There's no higher commandment for a state, for a government, than the redemption, he says, of hostages, of captives. But he also says there's a- the price cannot be so high to basically put the rest of society in jeopardy. And this is the- this is the tension, the- the demand to- to bring the hostages home, and ensuring that the price is one that doesn't encourage further hostage taking or set the conditions for the next war. Okay. So, and this- this is a debate, Margaret, that goes through Israeli society and went through the highest echelons of the Israeli government. It plays throughout this book. It went into this- Keith and Aviva Siegel, who were taken hostage on October 7th, in their home, they have a sticker–and they're very cooperative for this book–it says, "Gilad is alive." That was Gilad Shalit, an Amer- an Israeli soldier, held by Hamas for five years, released after five years for 1,000 Palestinian prisoners, hardcore Hamas operatives, including Yahya Sinwar, and like many Israelis, they supported that deal. And on October 7th, on Yahya Sinwar's orders, the elite units of Hamas are approaching Kfar Aza, their kibbutz, and eventually entering their home, taking them hostage. So where do you draw this line? And Netanyahu was- was focused far more on the military campaign and ensuring Hamas can never retain power in Gaza, believing the military campaign and the pressure on Hamas would lead to a deal that released all the hostages, whereas we were trying to focus on a phased deal. At least let's get some of the hostages out first. And Netanyahu always believed that more military pressure will actually deliver a better deal, whereas Sinwar believed more time would put more pressure on the U.S. and others to deliver him a better deal. So it makes this almost an impossible situation to deal with.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But it also reveals your frustration in that, that you felt the U.S. was putting more value on those lives than the Israeli government did?
BRETT MCGURK: I feel- I think the- the U.S. role in this, in all dimensions, we're trying to stop a war and- and get the hostages home, and the two were- the two are completely linked, and to reduce human suffering as much as possible in Gaza. You know Netanyahu, I describe him as obviously very confident in his assumptions–and he has a brother who was killed in the Entebbe raid–very confident in terms of his belief in how to deal with these groups, and yet I believe a lot of times there were miscalculations. This is also very very difficult. Yeah, but I describe my meetings with him- again, I bring readers inside the room. You're sitting there with Bibi Netanyahu. You're with intelligence chief of Egypt when Hamas is on another floor. You're- you kind of get a sense of what this is like in the day- in the day-to-day.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, it's an interesting dynamic because now, since the end of the Biden administration, there continues to be, sort of, debate about this strategy. And National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan has publicly suggested that the U.S. focus was so much on the hostages that it was almost a "trap," as he put it, "in thinking that we can get to a ceasefire and a hostage deal," and other things were sublimated to that objective. I mean, in hindsight, do you share that feeling?
BRETT MCGURK: I do not, and no- no one's been able to point to me to a moment in which we could have ended this war without the hostages. The war would not have stopped without the hostages. I don't- I don't believe that. And I think it's important to kind of really go through the history, as the book does. And if I could just pause on- on when we did have a hostage deal. About a month into the war, we had- we had a deal with Hamas–not easy, I described what it was like to get it–for all women and children. It's very clear, all women and children hostages are going to come out, and- in exchange for a number of Palestinian prisoners. And we had a ceasefire for eight days, and about 100 hostages came out. I'm talking about this with you here, Margaret, because three of those women that did not come out, because on the eighth day, Hamas said, "we're not going to release the younger women, actually. We'll release the young toddlers like Abigail, the young American girl. We'll release the 80-year-old grandmothers. We're going to hold on to the younger women." They said "We can't find them," which was completely untrue.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Wasn't part of the excuse that they were of military age too?
BRETT MCGURK: No, they said some- they claimed that, but they said let's- let's keep the ceasefire and talk about the older men. And in the book, I go through this night, midnight here in Washington, December 1st, and it's a moral quandary, and this is what a hostage-taker does. Hamas is good at this- Iran is- this is- they're masters at this. They put the moral onus on the other side. Do you skip the younger women, start talking about older men, keep the ceasefire, or say no, you broke the deal. Three of those women, Romi, Doron, and Emily, Margaret, came out on January 19th. I was actually on your program and I broke the news--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --I remember.
BRETT MCGURK: --I learned that- I learned about it–because I'd been up all night, they came out–in the green room here. One was taken from Nova Festival. Two were taken from their home in Kafr Aza. Late 20's, one is 31 years old. They should have come out in that November deal. Carmel and- and Eden, two other women, were later killed in a tunnel under Rafah together with six hostages, including the American, Hersh Goldberg, which I still- So, and I'm very clear in the book–when that deal broke down in November, because Hamas would not release those younger women, I thought we would be able to get to another deal sooner. One reason we didn't is that we came under massive attack, and I go through that in the book. In the next two months, we're consumed with that, and I go see the Iranians in Oman. But no, I do not think that there was a way to stop this war without the hostages. It had to be a hostage deal, and it took a lot to get there. I go through it in the- in the book.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Just on that point of those women. Some of them, after they were released, talked about the sexual assaults--
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: --that they experienced in captivity. Is that why the women, those young women, were held for so long?
BRETT MCGURK: Well, this got- that- that moment, and if you read the book, you're there. And I let readers make judgments. What would you do in this moment? We have a ceasefire. Eight days, the guns are silent. You have humanitarian aid flowing throughout Gaza. We have a deal for all women and children. Hamas says we're going to hold on to the younger women, and let's talk about the older men. Some of the older men were in their 80's. Do you say, okay, okay, let's- let's skip over the younger women and move to the men? Israel was unanimous that they cannot do that because it'll- it'll be the death sentence for the women, and given how some of the younger women were believed to have been treated, as you just referred to. Why did they want to hold on to the younger women? I think Hamas thought they were their- they were their, as Hamas would put it sometimes in the negotiation, their most precious cards, and--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Why?
BRETT MCGURK: I don't want to think about how they were being treated. I mean, there are many many testimonials now. Hamas wanted to hold on to them, and they thought they could get the highest price for some of them. I mean, ultimately, for women soldiers, it was 50- the keys, the nomenclature is: this is the keys, an exchange ratio for women soldiers [was] 50 life sentence Hamas, life sentence Palestinian prisoners, often who have killed many Israelis. They got the most- they got the most keys for the women.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Just to clarify that, there were literally, like, mathematical equations there of what one Israeli was worth in terms of Palestinians who could be released from detention, not necessarily from prisons, but from detention.
BRETT MCGURK: Both.
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's the key. From both places.
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, this negotiation was- I mean, I- I don't think it has been--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --It was a ratio.
BRETT MCGURK: --so tedious and negotiated down to the individual names, and a ratio for how many prisoners for an older man, how many prisoners for a female soldier, and Hamas played with this all the time, all the way down to the very end of the negotiation, where they threw in a wrench at the end for even civilian, sick and wounded hostages. They put a new demand on the table for 300 life sentence prisoners, which had never been- those are all- life sentence prisoners were- was the key for soldiers, and Hamas changed that at the end. But I bring this- I bring it back to this because I think some of these facts have been lost in the horrific nature of this crisis, which is so polarizing and so difficult. But Romi, Emily, and Doron should have come out in November. The deal was unequivocal. And they didn't. Carmel and Eden should have come out, and they were later killed by Hamas in a tunnel under Rafah. And I go back to that November deal a lot, and- and could we have done something differently to keep that on track? And it's very tragic. But to your question, I- no, I do not think there was a way to end this crisis without- without the hostages. And- and I've told some of the hostages that have come out, Keith and others, I think Hamas intended to hold on to hostages for- for many years.
MARGARET BRENNAN: In order to stay in power.
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, definitely.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Which ultimately they still are, just Yahya Sinwar and his family are not. But let's- let's talk about- you mentioned how polarizing this issue is. You have worked for both Republicans and Democrats. BRETT MCGURK: Yeah.

Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:16:03 UTC
00:16:03 KST

An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms.
Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days.
On Sunday, Egyptian authorities charged Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, according to a statement by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, a NGO. The charges came after an interrogation that lasted from 10pm to 8am and focused exclusively on material published by Matsadaash, the rights group said.
Ashraf was to be held for 15 days, pending investigation, while the whereabouts of the other five journalists were still unknown.
Abdelrahman Mansour, the co-founder of the platform, denied having any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational movement that was designated a terrorist organisation by Egypt in 2013 after the former president Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, was ousted in a coup. Mansour called the arrests “one of the gravest attacks on journalism in Egypt’s modern history”.
“My colleagues were doing what journalists should do: asking difficult questions, uncovering facts, and reporting on issues that affect people’s lives. They deserve recognition for their work. Instead, their homes were raided, and all six were taken away,” he said. “The government must answer this question: why have you arrested six journalists? What have they done beyond doing their jobs?”
The Guardian contacted the Egyptian State Information Service for a comment but did not receive a reply by the time of publishing.
Dozens of journalists staged a sit-in outside the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate (EJS) in Cairo on Saturday, demanding the release of the Matsadaash staff. Members said they would keep the sit-in open ended until the journalists were released, and the EJS said it would convene an emergency meeting on Monday.
The EJS had filed a request with the ministry of interior and public prosecutor for the release of the journalists, as well as for information on their whereabouts.
More than 80 rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, condemned the arrests as a violation of freedoms, and demanded the immediate release of the Matsadaash staff.
The arrests came little over a week after the US government waived its human rights conditions on $320m (£242m) in military aid to Egypt, citing Cairo’s “helpful role” to US national security after the US-Iran war.
The US gives about $1.3bn in aid to Egypt annually, but a portion is contingent upon the Egyptian government meeting certain human rights and democracy-related requirements. The US has withheld portions of aid several times since the 2013 coup owing to Egypt’s poor human rights record, but has largely kept funds flowing.
This year, Washington waived the human rights requirement in total, as doing so was “essential for the US-Egypt relationship and US national security priorities”, according to a state department memo revealed by Reuters.
While saying that he was unsure whether the arrests were linked to the recent waiver, Mansour said: “The use of the national security waiver on human rights conditions by the US by many years, a willingness by other states to look the other way on Egypt’s human rights record … certainly enables violations like this to occur more easily.”
Cairo has for years faced criticism for its human rights abuses, with the rights monitor Freedom House saying Egyptian security forces “engage in human rights abuses and extrajudicial killing with impunity”.
Since the Egyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi took power in the coup that ousted Morsi, civil liberties have been curbed and domestic political opposition has been violently crushed.
Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries on the Reporters Without Borders Press freedom index. Freedom of the press is tightly restricted in the country and independent platforms such as Matsadaash are rare. About 26 journalists are held in Egyptian prisons, according to the EJS.

Ukraine’s New FP-9 Ballistic Missile With Moscow in Range to Be Ready This Fall, Zelenskyy Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:10:37 UTC
00:10:37 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s New FP-9 Ballistic Missile With Moscow in Range to Be Ready This Fall, Zelenskyy Says
Ukraine expects its domestically developed FP-9 ballistic missile, a longer-range weapon that its manufacturer says is capable of reaching Moscow, to be ready this fall, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Reuters on October 3, Zelenskyy said he had personally contacted Ukrainian defense company Fire Point and urged the manufacturer to accelerate work on the FP-9 following the first combat deployment of Ukraine’s shorter-range FP-7 ballistic missile.
“I said to them, where is my FP-9?” Zelenskyy told Reuters. “We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be (ready) this autumn, I’m sure.”
The FP-9 is being developed as a significantly longer-range ballistic system than the FP-7. Fire Point has previously said the missile would have sufficient range to reach Moscow from Ukrainian territory.
The missile has a stated range of up to 855 kilometers and is designed to carry a warhead weighing up to 800 kilograms. The ground-launched system is intended to give Ukraine a domestically produced capability for striking targets deep behind Russian lines.
Zelenskyy’s comments came days after Ukraine announced the first combat use of the domestically produced FP-7 tactical ballistic missile. Reuters reported that the FP-7 has a range of approximately 250 kilometers.
The deployment marked another step in Ukraine’s effort to expand its domestic long-range strike capabilities as Kyiv seeks to reduce its dependence on foreign-supplied missile systems.
In the same interview, Zelenskyy told Reuters that Ukraine plans to intensify strikes against Russian oil refineries in response to Moscow’s expanding attacks against Ukrainian energy, transport, and other infrastructure. He said Kyiv would focus on facilities supporting Russia’s war effort rather than indiscriminately targeting civilian infrastructure.
“We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners etc: what gives money to them for this war,” Zelenskyy said. “But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects.”
Ukraine has increasingly invested in domestically developed missiles and long-range drones as restrictions, limited inventories, and dependence on foreign partners have constrained the availability of Western long-range weapons.
Earlier, Fire Point CEO and CTO Iryna Terekh said the FP-9 had entered the final stage of development and was expected to be completed by the end of fall 2026. The missile is designed for a range of about 850 kilometers, sufficient to reach Moscow from Ukrainian territory.

More than 400 schools in France to be closed on Monday as more protests planned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:08:23 UTC
00:08:23 KST

More than 400 schools in France will be closed or partly closed on Monday as authorities brace for another week of student protests.
Lessons will be totally or partly suspended in 400 to 500 schools because security conditions “have not been fulfilled”, the education minister, Édouard Geffray, said on Sunday.
The minister said 24 schools had been burnt or ransacked and 78 education staff members injured. The number of school closures on Monday would be comparable to Friday’s but the government envisaged a “partial, progressive return to lessons”, said Geffray.
Thousands of teenagers staged widespread demonstrations and erected barricades last week to protest against what they said was underfunding and neglect of the education system.
Clashes with riot police left hundreds of people injured, led to more than 5,000 arrests, mostly of minors, and jolted President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist administration.
There was a lull at the weekend, but protest organisers called for renewed demonstrations on Tuesday because the government had failed to produce “concrete measures”.
Authorities say political agitators have infiltrated the protest, which started at a Paris school on 17 September and spread across the capital and the rest of France.
“There are activists – particularly from the far left – who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence,” said Geffray. “Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students.”
The injured education staff members were deliberately targeted, “something we have never seen before”, said Geffray.
The protests caught the government by surprise and confronted Macron with his worst crisis in months. Images of burning barricades and police using teargas, batons and other methods to disperse protests have dominated TV news.
Student grievances include overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success. Other factors are an opaque and difficult online system for university applications as well as the sweltering temperatures in classrooms during heatwaves.
Protesters have accused the state of disengaging from secondary education and cited difficult conditions such as leaks, cockroaches, collapsed ceilings and decayed buildings. Others have complained about excessively long school days and a lack of teaching staff.
The government said the grievances were legitimate but condemned what it called “urban violence”. On Sunday, police detained a 16-year-old in relation to an assault of a teacher in La Ciotat, a town on the southern coast between Marseille and Toulon. The teacher, 59, was doused with gasoline and struck during a protest on Friday.
The government is also under pressure from trade unions that called a day of strikes last week to compel the new prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, to rethink budget cuts and consider a form of wealth tax on the super-rich. The CGT trade union exhorted workers to sustain the pressure with demonstrations this week.

Has plague returned to Siberia? Panic in Russia after death of lab worker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:07:54 UTC
00:07:54 KST

A female staff member at an anti-plague institute in the Irkutsk region who died amid rumours of a "black death" outbreak was diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown origin". Rospotrebnadzor insists that the situation in the region is "stable".
Residents of Russia's Irkutsk region are deeply worried by rumours of a possible outbreak of pneumonic plague in this Siberian area. Speculation began to spread rapidly after the death of an employee of the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute.
Darya Shipilova died in the early hours of 2 October in the intensive care unit of the district hospital in the town of Shelekhov. According to local media, she broke a test tube containing the plague pathogen.
The incident prompted authorities to introduce quarantine measures: around 200 people have been placed under strict medical observation. The outlet "Baikal People" (source in Russian) reports that several Irkutsk hospitals were immediately closed and placed under quarantine, due to last three weeks. On Saturday, masks were made compulsory as a preventive measure at the Irkutsk aluminium plant in Shelekhov.
Residents of Shelekhov have seen people on the streets wearing protective suits, masks and gloves. Local parents also say masks were handed out in kindergartens.
Where did the plague come from?
The deceased, a 28-year-old laboratory assistant, specialised in research on dangerous pathogens. According to the main account reported by her colleagues and independent media, on 25 September, while working with live biological material in the laboratory, she accidentally smashed a test tube containing the dangerous bacterium Yersinia pestis.
Two days later Shipilova's condition suddenly worsened. She was rushed to Shelekhov district hospital. At first doctors, unaware of what had happened, suspected a severe case of coronavirus and admitted her to a specialised Covid unit. However, the rapid deterioration and the clinical picture forced them to carry out rapid tests for highly dangerous infections. The patient was put on a ventilator, but her life could not be saved.
The pulmonary form of plague develops extremely fast and, without prompt and targeted antibiotic treatment, is almost invariably fatal.
Are the authorities hiding information?
The authorities' immediate response underlined how serious the situation was. The head of Rospotrebnadzor, Anna Popova, urgently arrived at Shelekhov hospital and took part in an emergency meeting of the sanitary and anti-epidemic commission chaired by regional governor Igor Kobzev.
After the incident, officials initially restricted the information they released. During the first 24 hours, authorities in the Irkutsk region and Governor Igor Kobzev avoided using the word "plague". On 2 October Kobzev spoke of "a particularly dangerous infection" and said that "the situation is under strict control". The next day the authorities in Baikalsk urged residents not to travel to Shelekhov because of plague, but deleted the post a few hours later.
The head of Buryatia, Alexey Tsydenov, also commented on the situation. Citing Rospotrebnadzor and the republican government, he said the woman's death was linked to plague infection, but later his statement was amended to a more cautious wording.
This lack of clarity has fuelled panic on social networks in Irkutsk and neighbouring regions.
Well-known Russian epidemiologist Gennady Onishchenko tried to reassure local residents, saying that plague carriers - rodents and fleas - in Siberia usually go into winter dormancy by early October. But that did not dispel people's fears.
"Pneumonia of unknown aetiology"
On Sunday, Rospotrebnadzor said that the sanitary and epidemiological situation in Irkutsk region was stable, and that the woman had died from "pneumonia of unknown aetiology". The agency insists that further testing of samples taken from the patient did not reveal any micro-organisms related to her professional work.
"The sanitary and epidemiological situation in Irkutsk region, in the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov, is stable," the press service of Rospotrebnadzor said. "A special package of measures has been organised and carried out in connection with the illness of an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, diagnosis: 'Pneumonia of unknown aetiology'."
Rospotrebnadzor also stated that no incidents involving pathogenic microorganismshad been recorded at the institute and that "no staff member has sought medical help for infectious diseases in the past 10 days".

Yemen government launches major ground offensive as Houthis advance on Taiz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:05:48 UTC
00:05:48 KST

Yemen's internationally recognized government announced Sunday the start of a large-scale ground offensive against the Iran-backed Houthis, as fighting escalated across the country and reports indicated the rebels were continuing to advance in southwestern Yemen.
The operation comes amid repeated Saudi airstrikes against Houthi positions and follows a Houthi offensive last month that gave the group control of strategically important areas overlooking the Bab el-Mandab Strait, a vital shipping route linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and, through the Suez Canal, Europe and Asia.
"We have moved from the preparation phase to the action phase," Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, said in announcing the operation.
"We declare the battle for the state, until Yemen is liberated from the Houthis," he said. "Our position today is to assume national responsibility for confronting the Houthis, after all opportunities to calm the situation have been exhausted. This is not a war against our people in Sanaa, Saada or any other province, and it is not directed against any tribe."
Reports over the weekend said the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia were preparing a broad campaign aimed at pushing back the Houthis and restoring pro-Saudi forces' control of the Bab el-Mandab Strait.
Reuters reported that the plan calls for about 100,000 Yemeni troops to take part in the operation under Saudi supervision and with support from Saudi airstrikes.
The announcement came as the Houthis appeared to be making further gains on the ground. The group surprised pro-Saudi Yemeni forces last month with a ground offensive that seized large areas of southwestern Yemen, including territory commanding the Bab el-Mandab Strait.
The strait's importance to the global economy has grown further since the Strait of Hormuz was blocked during the war with Iran.
As the government announced its new offensive, several international news organizations reported that Houthi forces were either close to encircling or had already encircled Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city and a major stronghold of government forces.
Military officials told Reuters on Sunday that the Houthis had made gains over the previous 48 hours in fighting for strategic hills near Taiz and were advancing toward the last route connecting the city with Aden, Yemen's second-largest city and the seat of the internationally recognized government since it was driven from the capital, Sanaa, early in the country's civil war in 2014.
Houthi control of the road would allow the group to cut off reinforcements and supplies to Taiz, a city with hundreds of thousands of civilians and large numbers of fighters, effectively placing it under siege.
AFP, meanwhile, cited security officials as saying the road between Taiz and Aden had already been blocked by the Houthis, meaning the city was effectively surrounded.
"We were told that the Houthis seized the al-Safiya area, cut the main road and took control of the police station," a local police official told AFP.
Three other sources from Yemeni government forces also confirmed that the Houthis had seized the area and the supply route south of Taiz. Witnesses reported hearing heavy fighting in al-Safiya and al-Samsara, two communities along the route between Taiz and Aden.
Mohammed al-Qadhi, a veteran Yemeni journalist and analyst from Taiz, told Reuters that the Houthi advance would further consolidate the group's grip over areas farther west along the coast overlooking Bab el-Mandab by giving it control of mountainous territory in the countryside west of Taiz.
"This will help them protect their back in case of any operation against the coastline, and make recapturing those areas much more difficult," he said.
The Houthis had not immediately responded to the government's announcement of a new ground offensive. Their military spokesman, Yahya Saree, however, said Sunday afternoon that Houthi forces had repelled what he described as an attempt by Saudi-backed forces to advance toward their positions in the northern province of al-Jawf.
Saree said the operation resulted in the destruction of vehicles belonging to what he called the "Saudi enemy," as well as deaths and injuries among Saudi-aligned forces. He said Houthi forces pursued the retreating troops and attacked enemy concentrations with ballistic missiles and drones.
Saree later claimed responsibility for missile and drone attacks targeting facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in the capital, Riyadh, and the Khurais area.
"The forces will continue to strike the bases and oil facilities of the Saudi enemy using Yemeni-made missiles and drones, weapons that have proven their ability to hit targets with great precision and successfully penetrate Western defense and interception systems," he said.
Civil war reignites after four-year truce
Yemen's civil war erupted in 2014 following years of political turmoil that grew out of the Arab Spring protests. Those demonstrations led in 2011 to the removal of longtime President Ali Abdullah Saleh, who had ruled the country for decades.
Three years later, exploiting the weakness of Yemen's new government, the Houthis launched a major offensive and seized Sanaa.
Saudi Arabia viewed the Houthi takeover as a direct threat to its security and regional influence. In 2015, Riyadh assembled a coalition of Arab states and launched a military intervention that included thousands of airstrikes, a naval and air blockade and support for Yemeni government forces.
Although the Saudi-led coalition prevented the Houthis from taking control of the entire country, it failed to defeat them. The group maintained control over northwestern Yemen and over the years launched missiles and drones at Saudi cities, airports and oil installations.
The conflict also produced one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, while the Saudi-led coalition faced intense international criticism over civilian casualties and damage to infrastructure.
Against that backdrop, Saudi Arabia changed course and reached a ceasefire with the Houthis in 2022. The truce remained largely stable for four years before collapsing in July amid the war with Iran, when the Houthis sought to break an air and naval blockade imposed on them by the Saudi-led coalition.
Bab el-Mandab becomes key battleground
During the renewed fighting, the Houthis also declared what they called a "naval blockade" against Saudi Arabia and attacked Saudi tankers and ships attempting to pass through the Bab el-Mandab Strait.
Their territorial gains in southwestern Yemen last month, which tightened their control over the strategically critical waterway, were therefore seen as a major setback for Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia has sought international support in recent weeks for its renewed campaign against the Houthis. But U.S. President Donald Trump, seeking to avoid another military entanglement in the Middle East, rejected appeals from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for the United States to join strikes against the rebels.
U.S. representatives have also met with the Houthis and received assurances that American vessels would not be attacked.
Meanwhile, the so-called Mecca Alliance signed in August by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan has so far produced no direct military intervention. Under the agreement, the three countries pledged that an attack on one would be considered an attack on all. Turkey and Pakistan, however, have so far limited their responses to condemning Houthi attacks.

Nigel Farage questioned by standards commissioner over £5m gift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:04:34 UTC
00:04:34 KST

Nigel Farage has been interviewed by the standards commissioner for an investigation into whether he should have declared a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.
The Reform UK leader spent about half an hour being questioned over the money, the Sunday Times reported. Farage maintains the gift was for his personal security.
The interview conducted last month is a sign the process is nearing a conclusion, although Reform UK is not believed to have been informed that the report is finished.
An MP under investigation is usually notified before the conclusion of the process. If the commissioner finds that there has been a serious breach of the rules, the matter is passed to the standards committee of MPs and lay members, which can ask for further evidence.
The committee can recommend a sanction or override the report.
If it suggests more than a 10-day suspension from the Commons – and parliament agrees – the Reform UK leader could find himself facing a recall petition and second byelection in his Clacton constituency.
Farage has been under investigation over the gift since shortly after the Guardian revealed in May that Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024.
The Reform leader has said it was a personal matter, not political, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament.
After a slide in the polls over the summer, Reform is about to embark on a major reorganisation at its headquarters to try to revive its fortunes.
Insiders said it would involve a big shake-up of staffing, in addition to the suspensions of James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, Farage’s close aide. The pair are facing an internal investigation into whether they encouraged illegal foreign donations during an undercover investigation by reporters from Verbatim.
The inquiry is being carried out by lawyers who are expected to reach their conclusions soon. The matter is also the subject of a police inquiry.
The party is working out how to spend £72m in donations from Harborne and another crypto billionaire, Ben Delo. The huge sums have prompted calls from political rivals for a donation cap.
A possible use of the money is the relaunch of a TV channel that produces Reform-related video coverage and a show fronted by Farage.
Farage told the Sunday Times he thought the reaction to the donations would be “far worse” but had produced “some grudging respect – the fact that I managed to pull off a coup of that magnitude, I think people were quite impressed”.
It is not clear whether the donations fall within the rules because the government is putting forward legislation to ban overseas donors from giving more than £100,000 in a calendar year – backdated to March this year.
Harborne joined the UK electoral register only this summer and Delo has been largely based in Hong Kong, although on the register for some years.
If the donations are ruled impermissible, Reform could have to hand them back, a prospect that is likely to lead to court action.

Thousands of child-on-child sexual offences reported at schools in England and Wales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:00:31 UTC
00:00:31 KST

Lawyers and campaigners have condemned the “horrifying” scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools after a Guardian investigation revealed thousands of sexual offences against under-13s, including multiple rapes, are reported to police every year.
Close to five sexual crimes against children aged 12 and younger were recorded on average by police every day in primary and secondary schools in England and Wales, according to Guardian analysis of police data for 2021-25.
The figures include reports of almost 2,000 rapes and attempted rapes, which is equivalent to an average of one allegation of rape at a school received by the police every single day. More than a third of the rape victims were children under 13.
The new data showed at least 8,500 sexual offences against under-13s were recorded by police as having occurred on school premises or nearby between 2021 and 2025 – equivalent to 4.7 offences reported each day.
While most of the police reports did not specify the age of the alleged perpetrator, they are likely to be fellow pupils, and in at least 1,890 of the offences reported as being committed against under-13s the offender was described as under 18.
Girls are more likely to be victims of sexual offences than boys, according to the analysis, which found that close to two-thirds of reported crimes affecting under-13s where the sex of the victim was documented had involved female victims.
Responding to the figures, the children’s commissioner for England, Dame Rachel de Souza, described peer-on-peer abuse in schools as “widespread, normalised and too often brushed under the carpet”.
“We have taken important steps in the last few years,” she said. “But as these figures show we have a long way to go. This is not simply a school or college issue, it is a societal one.”
The data, obtained via freedom of information requests, also includes reports of a further 6,140 crimes involving the possession, taking, making or distribution of indecent or prohibited images of children under 18.
This has become a significant problem in schools, particularly with the introduction of AI and deepfakes, but headteachers are hoping phone bans and social media restrictions will help to turn the tide.
Andrew Lord, a partner with Leigh Day solicitors who represents survivors of sexual abuse, said: “This new dataset evidences clearly the horrifying true scale of sexual abuse of children within schools.
“Those in authority can no longer claim that they were not aware of how prevalent an issue this is. Parents deserve to know that their children are safe while undertaking their education, and anything short of concrete action to tackle this problem is simply not good enough.”
The data also detailed reports of at least 2,300 sexual crimes against children aged 13 to 16 and a further 9,100 sexual crimes against those aged 13 or over recorded by police as having happened in or in the vicinity of schools between 2021 and 2025. Three-quarters of these involved a female victim.
The true figure is likely to be significantly higher, since the analysis is based on data provided by 33 police forces that replied to FoI requests, out of a total of 43 in England and Wales. There may also be variation in the ways forces collect data.
Janaya Walker, interim director of the End Violence Against Women (EVAW) campaign, said: “This data is shocking but sadly not surprising, and underlines the urgent need to protect children from sexual violence at school.
“We’ve long raised the alarm about this national crisis in schools. However, despite what should have been numerous watershed moments, young people continue to be harmed en masse.”
Excluding 2021, when schools were closed between January and March due to the Covid-19 pandemic, the rate of sexual offences increased by 4% outside London, with 26.6 offences per 100,000 children under 13 in 2022, rising to 27.6 in 2025.
A government spokesperson described the figures as appalling. “No child should be unsafe at school, and no child should have to carry this alone. That is why schools’ duty to respond to sexual violence and harassment is now statutory, and why staff are trained to spot concerns early and support victims.
“As part of our strategy to halve violence against women and girls, we have pledged to make sure all young people are taught about healthy relationships and consent from an early age – and we’ve forced tech companies to tackle harmful content and protect young people online through the Online Safety Act.”
Acting chief constable Becky Riggs, who leads on child protection and abuse investigation for the National Police Chiefs’ Council, said the number of sexual offences reported in school settings was “deeply concerning”, but might also reflect growing awareness and greater confidence among child victims to come forward and report what has happened to them.
“These findings underline the urgent need for a stronger focus on prevention through age-appropriate education, digital resilience, effective safeguarding measures and greater support for parents, schools and professionals to identify concerns early and intervene before harm occurs,” she said.
“Tackling child sexual abuse requires a whole-system response, with policing, education, social care, health services, technology companies and communities working together to prevent harm, protect children and hold offenders to account.”
Soma Sara is the chief executive and founder of the Everyone’s Invited campaign, which has played a key role in highlighting sexual violence in schools. She now runs education programmes for young people. “When we first launched [in 2020], people refused to even refer to rape culture,” she said.
“It is now accepted as an issue both in wider society and within our schools. But we cannot expect schools to tackle it alone, particularly when the online world is changing so rapidly.
“The proliferation of violent pornography and the increasing harms young people are exposed to online are creating challenges that are incredibly difficult for teachers to keep pace with.”
Pepe Di’Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said: “The prevalence of these incidents is simply appalling and a source of great concern for everyone working in education.
“We hope measures being taken by the government to better protect children online will improve matters but ministers must be prepared to go further in regulating online platforms.”
Figures from some forces were taken from keyword searches of police summary notes, so may include cases that mentioned schools but happened outside school premises. Some other forces recorded schools as a location for crimes both on and nearby school premises.

From unwanted touching to rape: the scale of child-on-child abuse in English and Welsh schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:00:30 UTC
00:00:30 KST

It is 10 years since a report first revealed the epic scale of sexual bullying, harassment and abuse girls faced in England’s schools on a daily basis.
The report, by MPs on the women and equalities committee, showed the horrifying normality of child-on-child abuse in schools. The need for government action was “overwhelming”, said the committee chair, Maria Miller. Ofsted duly investigated, recommendations were written, promises were made and a new sex education curriculum was rolled out.
A decade later, and six years after the Everyone’s Invited movement began to collect anonymous testimonies from victims, a Guardian investigation has shown the problem persists unabated at schools in England and Wales. In many ways it may be more pernicious as a result of the rise of social media, misogyny and the mass consumption of online pornography by teenage boys.
The freedom of information investigation captures only the most serious incidents; those reported to and recorded by police. Interviews with experts, lawyers and campaigners suggest many more cases never get reported, often because the children involved are under the age of criminal responsibility and the assault is dismissed as “age-related exploration”.
Andrew Lord, a partner with Leigh Day solicitors and a specialist in abuse claims, has dealt with cases of child-on-child sexual abuse in private and state schools, inner-city schools, rural schools, primary, secondary and boarding schools for more than a decade. He says the impact on victims can endure for years and many suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder.
“From my own cases I can see it’s happening up and down the country to children of all ages,” he said. In many instances, however, schools were still struggling to deal with it appropriately. “If you have children in a physical fight, schools know exactly how to react. When you are talking about sexual assault, it’s a different matter.”
Lord is currently representing a secondary school pupil who reported being subjected to a number of sexual and physical assaults by fellow pupils in a changing room. The family is seeking a claim for negligence and breach of human rights against the school for its failure to protect the child.
“Schools do have a duty to ensure that both children [involved in an incident] receive their education, but I am aware of situations where the children continue at the same school and the victim has felt that they have not received adequate support to enable them to engage safely with their studies after disclosing incidents of sexual violence.
“Victims can find themselves being ostracised, which may represent a breach of the Human Rights Act,” he added.
Lord also represents a number of primary school children, including a boy who reported being seriously sexually assaulted by another child on school premises. He was scared he would be hit if he did not comply.
“The biggest issue for me with primary-age cases, when children are below the age of criminal responsibility, is there is often no real statutory investigation and there’s an overreliance on ‘age-related exploration’.”
What typically happens on primary school premises, Lord said, is that a child is taken to a more hidden area by fellow pupils – behind a shed, climbing frame or bushes – is forced to undress and is assaulted, often under threat of being excluded from play and friendship groups.
While most victims of sexual abuse in schools are girls, boys are also targeted. Bethany’s* eight-year-old son was sexually abused on three occasions by a classmate during play dates at her home.
She only discovered what had happened when he began crying at bedtime. She reported it to the school but claims it tried to dismiss what happened as relationship difficulties. “This was not a relationship difficulty. This was sexual assault,” she said. “No one was taking it seriously.”
Her son was never interviewed. There was no proper investigation into what happened and no appropriate safety plan was drawn up to protect her son. “They wanted to sweep it all under the carpet, and that’s not good enough. It was like he was not believed.” In the end, he moved to another school. The other boy remained.
“My son was never treated as a victim in any sense. They offered him no real support. What was worse than the incident itself was how the school dealt with it. It was just appalling. We both felt very, very let down,” said Bethany.
Richard Scorer is another lawyer who deals with civil claims arising from sexual abuse and receives regular approaches from parents, and in some cases teenagers who have suffered child-on-child sexual abuse of various kinds in school.
“We see a lot more of it now than we would have done even a few years ago. As well as a greater awareness, it’s also possible there’s a greater underlying level of abuse and that may have something to do with the pervasiveness of online pornography, particularly in the lives of teenage boys.
“It’s the full range of sexual assault, ranging from unwanted touching to rape. Some of that will take place on school premises, some of it will be off-site. Boys are overwhelmingly the perpetrators. There’s obviously all of the issues around revenge porn and the sharing of intimate photographs – that’s a big issue as well.
“My sense is that schools in some instances are struggling to know how to respond because of the extent of what’s going on and because safeguarding is quite resource intensive. Schools are forced into a bit of a social work role, picking up the pieces from things that are going wrong in society at large.”
Tony Hartney, a school improvement consultant and former headteacher, said awareness around child-on-child sexual abuse was much better in schools and there was a greater willingness to tackle such issues, but they remained “tricky” to handle.
“When there are allegations made like this, schools are very sensitive to the needs of both young people involved to try and make it as viable as possible for them to continue with their education in schools.
“The difficulty of course is things take time. Whilst investigations are going on, you ideally want them to be in schools and to have as normal an education as they can. It’s tricky for schools to manage these situations.”
When she became children’s commissioner for England in 2021, Rachel de Souza knew from her time as a headteacher about sexual harassment and abuse in schools.
“But what I heard as I listened to young people shocked me. Children were viewing violent pornography, it was changing behaviour and peer-on-peer abuse was widespread, normalised and too often brushed under the carpet.
“We have taken important steps in the last few years – from work to bring highly skilled professionals together under one roof to care for child victims of abuse, to action to prevent children from accessing pornography, and a focus on evidence-based relationships education that addresses the realities of teenagers’ lives.
“But as these figures show, we have a long way to go. This is not simply a school or college issue, it is a societal one. We need to address the causes – harmful sexual behaviours are increasingly shaped by the content and cultures that children are exposed to online.
“And we need to urgently improve what happens when young victims of sexual assault speak out and their experience of the justice system, and make sure they get the support they need.”
* Name has been changed for reasons of anonymity

Stop holding only one man accountable for Oct. 7 – opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

If we presumed this election period for the 26th Knesset would be dominated by the memory of October 7, 2023’s debacle, and that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would be pilloried by the slogan: “You were in charge, you are responsible,” that’s not quite the current case.
A new spin has emerged seeking to frame Netanyahu’s “responsibility” more narrowly. The new conseptzia (Hebrew for a “fixed notion”) in public discourse is that there definitely were warnings of the Hamas invasion.
However, they weren’t negligently missed and overlooked by the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), IDF intelligence units, the Mossad, or any other section and/or officer in charge, as we have read in various reports.
Those warnings, the new motif is, were passed on to Netanyahu and stayed with him. He did not reveal them. He did not pass them on.
The current memes on social media read: “You knew and hid it.” And what did Netanyahu know? The left-wing version of the conspiracy theory framework surrounding the events of October 7 has erupted.
According to an exposé in Haaretz, based on a forthcoming book by Shlomi Eldar and Ruthie Yuval, Emirati President Mohamed bin Zayed called Netanyahu about a week and a half before October 7 to warn that Hamas was planning a major operation against Israel. Netanyahu, however, remained unperturbed.
A purported second warning was then revealed. The Atlantic reported that Egypt’s intelligence chief Abbas Kamel arrived in Israel 11 days before October 7.
He also warned that the armed group in Gaza was preparing a major attack. Kamel, it emerged, sought to pressure Israel to award Hamas further economic concessions.
The revelations are literally flooding the social discourse platforms and the media.
Unfortunately for the anti-Bibists, logic dictates that if Netanyahu was responsible for the October 7 debacle, he also must be responsible for the ultimate results of Israel’s quite successful post-October 7 operations.
Even if this were true, can it be that the heads of the various services bear no responsibility for the lead-up to October 7? The order not to approach the fence? The decision not to wake Netanyahu when there were genuine warnings?
Of course, there were warnings. The female field scouts’ reports were dismissed out of hand, as well as warnings of a different type – one that the anti-Bibists would prefer to be forgotten.
And in 2023, amid the judicial reforms controversy, were central figures opposed to Netanyahu impressing upon Hamas, or warning Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar, that Israel was crumbling from within?
Israel’s security network often clashes with any given governing body
While this is very relevant to Israel’s internal political struggles, the real conseptzia that should be considered is that ever since the Oslo Accords, Israel’s security establishment has been in conflict with the country’s elected political leadership.
That leadership has mainly been critical of, and disbelieving in, the wisdom of those agreements.
The conflict brought them, as Efraim Karsh wrote in an article for the Begin-Sadat Center for Strategic Studies – “How the 30-year peace delusion led to the October 7 Hamas massacres” – to adopt a conception that the century-old Arab conflict with Zionism and Israel paved the way for Hamas’s invasion.
Karash wrote: “The failure to prevent Hamas’s slaughter … is a direct result of [those who] decided to do nothing despite acute warning signals, and failed to alert the Gaza division commander and the political echelon to the imminent attack.”
He asserts that there was an underlying mindset to this blunder that can be traced to what the “Oslo peace delusion” brought upon the thinking of the security establishment. He views Oslo as “a grand strategic deception” that aimed at the “emasculation of the IDF’s military capabilities and combative/offensive ethos.”
Former defense minister Yoav Gallant has now said that Israel was warned ahead of the October 7 massacre. He confirmed that the Shin Bet received a message that Hamas leader Sinwar would “shake the prisons.” Israeli security officials interpreted the threat as Hamas’s intention to take dramatic actions to compel Israel to release thousands of Palestinian prisoners.
But that message was thought not to focus on Gaza. Was that because the thinking was that Hamas was deterred?
A conseptzia overrides normative reason and critical analysis. Only a conseptzia could have thought that the July 6, 2023, warning from a veteran Israeli signals intelligence analyst, that Hamas was holding large-scale training exercises, to be dismissed by her superior as an “imaginary scenario.”
Likewise, only a conseptzia could have convinced those specialists who provided situation analyses to Netanyahu, and to then-head of the National Security Council, Tzachi Hanegbi, that Hamas was in a state of deterrence.
Journalist Amit Segal, criticizing Eldar’s and Yuval’s claims, notes: “Tragically, Netanyahu and [Shin Bet head Ronen] Bar adopted the Yuval-Eldar approach: economic concessions are preferred in the hope that these would appease” Hamas, and that they would choose money over ideology.
More importantly, Segal writes further that “Netanyahu and his subordinates operated in line with the prevailing approach of the media, think tanks, academia, and the High Court of Justice – always offer a carrot, never a stick – or if a stick is unavoidable, make it as small as possible.”
As we approach the October 27 elections, we cannot allow another conseptzia – the “he-was-warned” charge – to take hold.
The writer is a researcher, analyst, and commentator on political, cultural, and media issues.
