Reaching the core: could Russia cut Ukrainians off from the internet and mobile communications?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
17:59:00 EEST
23:59:00 KST

Reaching the core: could Russia cut Ukrainians off from the internet and mobile communications?
Over the past week, the Kremlin has been expanding its campaign of terror to include new targets. In addition to hitting energy infrastructure and logistics hubs, Russia is now attacking the data centres that house equipment used by internet service providers, government services, banks and other digital systems, launching a wave of strikes on buildings where vital telecoms infrastructure is concentrated.
Telecoms industry representatives say it is not possible to cut Kyiv or Ukraine off from the internet by hitting data centres. There is no single facility whose destruction would take the country offline. But the objective of these attacks is not merely to carry out acts of terror. The goal is not the total destruction of the internet, but to degrade internet quality and overload backup routes, which could increase latency and destabilise networks.
And that may not be the worst-case scenario. The Russians have also started targeting mobile operator infrastructure, which may have more far-reaching consequences. Could these attacks disrupt communications across Ukraine? Where are the weak points in the country's telecoms infrastructure, and why is it that mobile networks could turn out to be significantly more vulnerable? Read on to find out.
From data centres to mobile network operators
On 23 September, Russian drones attacked a building in central Kyiv that housed one of the capital's data centres. A business centre was hit by several jet-powered Shahed drones in the course of an hour, and a fire then broke out.
Later that day, drones struck a similar data centre in another part of the city, and that evening, Russian forces hit yet another facility housing a data centre.
In one day, Russia had attacked at least three data centres in different parts of Kyiv. All housed equipment belonging to internet service providers. Some, notably the cloud service Fex.net, reported disruptions to their services. Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Transformation said around 100,000 users had problems accessing the internet.
Ekonomichna Pravda estimates that at least nine data centres in Kyiv may have been targeted since September, some of them more than once. The Protasiv Yar business centre, which housed the Cosmonova data centre, has been hit twice. Cosmonova suspended operations at the site as a result.
Four days later, the Russians turned their attention to mobile operators' infrastructure. Kyivstar, Ukraine's largest mobile operator, reported that a drone had struck one of its buildings, and Russia's Defence Ministry claimed that equipment belonging to Vodafone Ukraine had been damaged.
Internet service providers and mobile operators have suffered attacks to their networks before, but since 23 September the attacks have been on a different scale. Several data centres were hit within a few days, including some facilities that are critical to the telecoms industry.
For instance, a Russian attack destroyed a data centre that housed infrastructure belonging to hosting provider MiroHost. Founder Oleksandr Olshanskyi said MiroHost won't be able to bring its Ukraine-based infrastructure back online for at least the next three months.
Government digital services have also been disrupted, including state registries and electronic registration at centres run by Ukraine's Ministry of Internal Affairs that provide administrative services related to vehicles and driving licences.
The attacks on data centres have affected television broadcasts too. Disruptions have been reported by Army TV, Novyny.Live, We Are Ukraine, Pershyi, STB, 1+1, Channel 5, Suspilne Sport and Suspilne Culture.
Further evidence of the attacks is contained in a video posted by the Varyag Brigade, which is regarded as one of Russia's elite drone units alongside the better-known Rubicon unit. In the footage, Russian military personnel claim to have struck at least 11 data centres in Kyiv.
The exact dates of the strikes shown in the video cannot be established, but some appear to have taken place between 23 and 27 September. The footage clearly shows a strike on the Datagroup data centre on 25 September.
Read more: Fahrenheit 451: Russia has destroyed one-third of the books printed in Ukraine this year
The Ukrainian authorities had to respond. Following a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said specific decisions had been taken to protect data centres and other critical communications infrastructure. The government is preparing for the worst. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said the risk of widespread internet disruptions will persist for as long as Russia continues its strikes.
There is no one-size-fits-all way to protect this infrastructure. Some equipment can be moved underground; some can migrate to cloud environments or be relocated abroad. For some systems, a combination of these approaches may be used.
The government has allocated UAH 518.3 million (about US$11.5 million) to establish backup environments at separate locations, cloud infrastructure, and additional sites for state information systems. The funds will also be used to purchase server equipment, software, and data backup and recovery systems.
What happens if a data centre is attacked?
Much of the digital infrastructure Ukrainians rely on every day is built around data centres. The servers and storage systems they house keep websites, apps, state registers and banking services running.
Data centres are critical for internet service providers, as they house essential resources such as web, email and Domain Name System (DNS) servers, cloud infrastructure, and equipment belonging to providers and their clients.
Dmytro Kokhmaniuk, an expert on internet infrastructure and DNS, says some companies rent capacity in several data centres, others have their own facilities, and some combine both approaches. Spreading infrastructure across multiple sites helps make networks more resilient.
Repairing a data centre after an attack is a complex and lengthy process. "It's not just a room full of servers," Kokhmaniuk says. "It's a vast engineering system that includes a power supply, generators, cooling systems, ventilation, physical access control and network infrastructure. Damage to one or more of these elements can render the entire facility inoperable."
Consequently, a strike on a data centre can disrupt its operations even if the servers themselves escape damage. That does not necessarily mean, however, that the data stored there would be lost.
If up-to-date backups are stored at another independent site, the data can be restored. But getting everything back up and running requires computing resources, system configuration, and time. The impact of an attack therefore depends on how the particular service is set up and operated.
Since the start of Russia's full-scale war, a significant proportion of Ukraine's state registers and digital infrastructure has been moved to cloud services and backup environments in other countries.
So even if Russia destroys a Ukrainian data centre, the resulting outage may not last long. The attack may, however, cause temporary disruptions, loss of access and damage to equipment, and make it necessary to repair or relocate infrastructure.
Internet connectivity must also be restored separately. Damage to routers or an internet provider's cables can cut users off even when the service itself continues to operate. In that case, access can be restored using backup routes and equipment that survived intact, or by repairing the damaged network.
Internet speeds may drop
The events of 23 September offer some insight into what Russia may be trying to achieve by targeting Ukrainian network infrastructure.
One of the organisations affected that day was the internet service provider Pavutyna, which notified users of disruptions to its network. Co-owner and director Oleksandr Arutiunian said it was the third strike on the company's infrastructure, but the latest attack hit equipment at several locations almost simultaneously.
"The first two attacks were less disruptive because the backup systems worked better and the damage didn't all happen at the same time," Arutiunian says. "During the third attack, two locations were hit at once. The network could not recover automatically, so some users were left without a connection for between one and two hours. Repair crews then brought the network back online."
It appears that the Russians' target is not so much individual government services as the infrastructure that provides internet access. To this end, they are striking large data centres that house equipment used by several providers.
The telecoms industry representatives interviewed by Ekonomichna Pravda say these attacks cannot cut Ukrainians off from the internet entirely, because providers' network nodes are not only located in data centres.
"Networks have become much more decentralised in recent years," Arutiunian explains. "An operator can have far more than just one, two or five nodes. If necessary, backup equipment can be deployed at another site. In many cases this happens automatically, and engineers only need to step in when the damage is more serious."
If Ukrainian networks have numerous connections and backup routes, then what can Russia realistically achieve by attacking data centres?
Ekonomichna Pravda's sources say providers' network nodes and internet exchange points (IXPs) could potentially be targets. Network nodes support the operation of providers' networks, while IXPs allow different networks to exchange data. There are around 20 IXPs in Ukraine, and their equipment can be located at a single site or several.
The destruction of some of these facilities would not result in a nationwide internet blackout. As long as alternative connections are intact, internet service providers could reroute traffic through other operators, direct connections and international IXPs, just as traffic is diverted when a road is closed. Networks without an alternative route, however, could lose connectivity if their infrastructure is damaged.
The problem may lie elsewhere. Backup routes often have less capacity and are not set up to handle additional traffic. This could result in slower internet speeds and dropped connections for users.
That is what happened to internet provider Fiberlink after Russian attacks damaged the infrastructure of one of its backbone partners. The company rerouted traffic through a backup channel and warned users that internet speeds could temporarily drop. Further damage could lead to more significant disruptions.
According to Kokhmaniuk, poorer connection quality and slower data transfer speeds could be likely. In any event, operators will also have to absorb the additional cost of repairing infrastructure, deploying emergency repair crews and constructing backup lines. If the attacks continue, this could ultimately drive up the cost of broadband for subscribers.
"Operators will need to decentralise their networks further and expand the number of nodes and backup sites, which will increase the cost of providing services," Arutiunian says. "They will need more equipment, more staff and more resources to maintain and support this infrastructure."
Mobile network operator infrastructure
Mobile communications are another area of concern. If Russia continues to hit facilities belonging to mobile network operators, as it did on 27 September, this could have more serious consequences than attacks on data centres.
The Russians would not need to strike tens of thousands of base stations. The mobile core network, which manages subscriber registration, calls, text messages and mobile internet access, may be a far more vulnerable target.
If attacks were to disrupt critical functions of a core network beyond what its backup systems can handle, the consequences could be similar to those of the cyberattack on Kyivstar, which left millions of subscribers without access to calls, text messages or mobile internet.
Operators maintain backup infrastructure, but a fully-fledged mobile core network cannot simply be replicated by installing spare equipment at another node. Ekonomichna Pravda's sources estimate that building an additional core could cost each operator US$40-50 million. How many layers of redundancy would be needed if attacks on this infrastructure became sustained is an open question.
Ekonomichna Pravda's sources say the state and operators are taking steps to build more redundancy into critical network components. Some of these measures have been introduced only recently and will take time to implement. Russian attacks on mobile infrastructure could therefore pose a greater risk to communications.
What does this mean for users? In a critical situation, it's best to have more than one way of accessing the internet – for example, broadband from one provider and mobile internet from another. The more independent connections there are, the lower the risk of losing access during a large-scale attack.

What is Sisi's emerging 'anti-Ethiopia bloc'?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:53:38 UTC
23:53:38 KST

Breadcrumb
What is Sisi's emerging 'anti-Ethiopia bloc'?
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi called for "dialogue, not confrontation" over Africa's cross-border disputes on Sunday, as he prepared to meet three leaders whose countries share increasingly strained relations with Ethiopia.
Sisi was due to hold talks at El Alamein with Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, alongside an African Union summit hosted by Egypt.
The Egyptian presidency says the four-way meeting is intended for "consultation and coordination on regional issues of mutual interest".
But the gathering comes amid renewed war in northern Ethiopia and rapidly deteriorating relations between Addis Ababa and several of the countries attending, raising questions over whether an informal anti-Ethiopia alignment is emerging in the Horn of Africa.
What is the 'anti-Ethiopia bloc'?
There is no formal anti-Ethiopia alliance. The term instead describes the growing convergence between four countries with separate but increasingly overlapping disputes with Addis Ababa.
Egyptian officials have rejected suggestions that their regional cooperation amounts to an alliance against Ethiopia.
But Cairo, Asmara, Mogadishu and Sudan's army-led authorities have strengthened ties amid growing tensions over the Nile, access to the Red Sea, disputed territory and the wars in Ethiopia and Sudan.
Those tensions have become particularly acute in recent days, with Ethiopia accusing Egypt, Eritrea and Sudan of supporting the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) in renewed fighting against the federal government. All three countries deny the accusation.
Why do Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan oppose Ethiopia?
For Egypt, the central dispute is the Nile.
Ethiopia has built the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), Africa's largest hydroelectric project, on the Blue Nile, which supplies most of the water eventually reaching Egypt.
Cairo fears Ethiopia's control over the dam could threaten its water security, particularly during drought, and has unsuccessfully sought a binding agreement governing its operation. Ethiopia says GERD is vital to its development and rejects restrictions it believes would unfairly constrain its use of the Nile.
Eritrea's relationship with Ethiopia has meanwhile undergone a dramatic reversal.
The neighbours fought a bloody border war between 1998 and 2000 before Afwerki and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reconciled in 2018. Eritrean forces later fought alongside Ethiopia's army against the TPLF during the devastating 2020-22 Tigray war.
Relations have since collapsed, however, amid disputes over the aftermath of that war and Ethiopia's increasingly vocal pursuit of access to the Red Sea.
The two countries severed diplomatic relations last week after Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of backing the TPLF-led opposition.
Somalia has its own dispute with Ethiopia over the sea.
Landlocked Ethiopia angered Mogadishu in 2024 by signing an agreement with the breakaway territory of Somaliland that could have given it access to the Red Sea in return for possible recognition of Somaliland.
Although Ethiopia and Somalia subsequently agreed through Turkish mediation to pursue Ethiopian sea access under Somali sovereignty, Addis Ababa's maritime ambitions remain a sensitive regional issue.
Sudan's relationship with Ethiopia is more complicated.
The neighbours have long disputed ownership of the fertile al-Fashaga border region, while Sudan is also directly affected by GERD as the other downstream country on the Blue Nile.
Sudan's civil war has added another source of tension, with the army-led government accusing Ethiopia of facilitating support for the rival Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Ethiopia denies the allegation.
Why is Tigray bringing the tensions to a head?
The immediate backdrop to Sunday's gathering is the renewed war in northern Ethiopia.
The TPLF fought Abiy's government in a devastating conflict between 2020 and 2022, before a peace agreement halted the fighting without resolving many of the disputes behind it.
Large-scale fighting erupted again last month, with TPLF-led forces launching an offensive before Ethiopian government troops and allied militias counter-attacked.
Federal forces have now retaken Mekelle, the Tigray regional capital, although the TPLF has vowed to continue fighting.
The conflict has also become entangled with Ethiopia's deteriorating relations with its neighbours. Addis Ababa has accused Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan of supporting the rebels, while Eritrea has severed diplomatic relations with Ethiopia and Egypt and Ethiopia have expelled each other's diplomats.
That does not make the four countries gathered at El Alamein a formal anti-Ethiopia alliance, and their interests are far from identical.
But it does mean Ethiopia now faces an unusual convergence of disputes with several important neighbours at the same time.
Sisi's appeal on Sunday for cross-border challenges to be met with "cooperation, not competition, and dialogue, not confrontation" may therefore be directed at one of the most volatile regional rivalries facing Africa.

Nicaragua announces withdrawal from Central American Parliament

Nicaragua announces withdrawal from Central American Parliament
MEXICO CITY, Oct 4 - Nicaragua is withdrawing from the Central American Parliament, furthering its isolation on the international stage as the country is accused of rampant human rights abuses.
In a statement on Saturday, the foreign ministry said that it had decided to denounce the 1987 treaty establishing the six-country parliament "in the full exercise of its sovereignty". It said the move would take immediate effect.
The government of Nicaragua did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.
The action followed a resolution on Friday from the Organization of American States that called on Nicaraguan authorities to free political prisoners and restore civil liberties. Nicaragua left the OAS in 2023, saying the diplomatic organization had become a tool for US interventionism.
In 2025, Nicaragua also said it would withdraw from the United Nations Human Rights Council following a UN report that urged the international community to address human rights violations by Nicaragua.
Nicaragua has been in the grip of a political crisis since April 2018, when social protests that were suppressed by police resulted in more than 350 deaths, 2,000 injuries and thousands of detentions and people fleeing the country.
Last July, the government run by Daniel Ortega and his wife, Rosario Murillo, announced the country would no longer hold elections. Ortega has continuously held power since 2007 following an earlier presidential term in the 1980s. REUTERS

Israeli children's psychiatric ER visits surge 121% since Oct. 7, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:51:13 UTC
23:51:13 KST

Children and teenagers in Israel made 121 percent more visits to psychiatric emergency departments after the outbreak of the war on October 7, 2023, than in the two years before it, according to a report released Sunday, highlighting the war's growing toll on the country's mental health.
A report by Clalit Health Services, Israel's largest healthcare provider, examined changes in health and medical service use during the three years of war and found a 45.5 percent increase in anxiety disorder diagnoses and a doubling in diagnoses of post-traumatic stress disorder, with both increases persisting throughout the war.
The increases were particularly pronounced among people displaced from communities in southern and northern Israel. In the first year of the war, the number of PTSD diagnoses among residents evacuated from communities near the Gaza border was 18 times higher than before the war. The rate remained 11 times higher in the second year and six times higher in the third year, the report found.
The report also pointed to worsening physical health among Israelis, including increases in high blood pressure and cholesterol.
Dr. Yarden Levinsky, director of Clalit's mental health division, said the figures do not necessarily mean that the trauma occurred shortly before the diagnosis. A new PTSD diagnosis can relate to an event that happened six months earlier or five years earlier, he told Haaretz.
"People don't go to seek diagnoses at the height of the fighting," Levinsky said. "They try to cope because they're worried about their children and having a roof over their heads."
Levinsky said some of those seeking treatment may be suffering from trauma directly related to the October 7 massacre. But if that were the case for all those affected, he said, new diagnoses would be expected to decline steadily over time.
Instead, he said, new diagnoses rose sharply after the war began and have remained high, as repeated traumatic events have prevented much of the public from returning to normal. The prolonged war means the strain on mental health is likely to remain high for the foreseeable future, he said.
Levinsky said the rise in PTSD cases has far-reaching consequences for Israeli society, with many sufferers struggling to function as they did before.
He said the effects are unlikely to ease soon. One of the report's key findings, he noted, was that people who reported being in distress two years ago are still reporting distress. Unlike someone who contracts pneumonia and recovers, these people are not managing to recover from their trauma, Levinsky said, adding that policymakers need to recognize that the burden on the health system is growing and is unlikely to return to prewar levels.
The report found a similar increase in anxiety diagnoses among children, with new diagnoses rising by about 45 percent. Among children evacuated from southern Israel, prescriptions for medication to treat bed-wetting rose by 47.8 percent.
The war's effects extended beyond mental health. Across the population, new diagnoses of high cholesterol and other blood lipid disorders rose by 20 percent, while among people evacuated from northern Israel, they increased by 60 percent.
Evacuees from southern Israel also experienced a significant and sustained worsening in blood pressure control, while use of smoking-cessation medications rose sharply. At the same time, evacuees were less likely to seek routine preventive medical care, the report found.
Dr. Avital Margalit, a senior physician in Clalit's Northern District, said the disruption in chronic disease management among northern evacuees was largely linked to their time in hotels, where their diets and daily routines changed significantly amid stress and unemployment.

'China plays active role at recent G20 meeting'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:50:51 UTC
23:50:51 KST

China played an active role in promoting dialogue and cooperation with other G20 members while upholding principles during the recent G20 trade ministers' meeting, the country's Ministry of Commerce said on Sunday.
The ministry spokesperson made the remarks in response to a media question about the meeting, which was held on September 30 and October 1 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, the United States.
Members exchanged views on issues proposed by the US G20 presidency, including opposing the weaponisation of food, addressing overcapacity, eliminating forced labour and adjusting the Most-Favoured-Nation (MFN) principle.
Members reached a joint statement opposing the weaponisation of food, while no outcome documents were issued on the remaining matters, according to the ministry.
During the meeting, the Chinese side consistently upheld an attitude of openness and cooperation, constructively participated in discussions and maintained close communication with other members, fully playing its role in promoting dialogue and cooperation, said the spokesperson.
At the same time, China adhered to its principles, resolutely safeguarded the common interests of China and other developing countries, and worked to promote unity and cooperation within the G20, the ministry added.
Regarding the food issue, many emerging market and developing members, including China, put forward the view that food-importing and food-exporting countries should jointly safeguard the stability of food supply chains, and that all parties have the right to take measures for domestic public policy objectives and to safeguard food security, the spokesperson said.
The presidency gave positive consideration to these views, which were also fully reflected in the joint statement, the spokesperson said, adding that the outcome was the result of consensus-building and the joint efforts of all G20 members.
Issues such as overcapacity and forced labour were highly controversial from the outset, said the ministry. The ministry said that at present, G20 members are generally subject to additional Section 301 tariffs under the pretext of so-called "forced labour" and are mostly targets of Section 301 investigations over the so-called "overcapacity" issue.
Against this backdrop, many members put forward different views on the issues set by the presidency, and the meeting ultimately failed to produce outcome documents on these matters, the ministry said.
The spokesperson also noted that, after the meeting, the US side issued a chair's statement mentioning that it had released a statement on forced labour with two other G20 countries outside the G20 framework.
On the issue of reforming the MFN treatment principle, the vast majority of members, including China, emphasised that the principle is the cornerstone of the multilateral trading system, providing stability and predictability for global trade, and that any undermining of this principle would seriously damage the foundation of the multilateral trading system, said the ministry.
In light of the views expressed by the members, the presidency did not propose an outcome document on this topic, the ministry revealed.
Looking ahead to the G20 Leaders' Summit in December 2026, the spokesperson said that China is ready to work with the G20 presidency and all members to uphold consensus-building, and jointly contribute positive and practical economic and trade outcomes to the summit. (Xinhua)

geoffrey bawa and the materialization of an architect’s gaze on his country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:45:07 UTC
23:45:07 KST

geoffrey bawa and the materialization of an architect’s gaze on his country
from the lunuganga garden to the sri lankan parliament, the retrospective at the vitra design museum reflects a shifting relationship between history, modernity, and place.
Geoffrey Bawa: Architecture for the Senses at Vitra
At the Vitra Design Museum, the exhibition Geoffrey Bawa: Architecture for the Senses explores the dynamic world of the renowned Sri Lankan architect. Born on the island country, Bawa spent much of his early years traveling the world, particularly in Europe. Although tempted to stay in Italy, Bawa returned to his place of birth and decided to become an architect, a move that closely followed Sri Lanka’s independence from British rule.
It could be argued that perhaps Bawa was one of the key spectators of the historical circumstances he found himself in. In the essay, In Time: The Architecture of Geoffrey Bawa, for the exhibition catalogue, Shayari De Silva writes, ‘In the tropical heat and humidity of Sri Lanka, the progression of decay over time is palpable and indefatigable. Bawa realized this early in his career,’ going on to describe how, even in his early works, the architect’s structures responded to the rain and humidity in the country. There’s parallel movement between his work and Sri Lanka’s path toward redefining itself in the face of colonial rule. In his buildings, homes, and hotels, there’s a certain gaze that Bawa places on his country, one that is watching how the nation shifts in response to political factions, foreign influence, and a desire to move forward.
‘tropical modernism’ and its European history
Bawa (1919–2003) is widely considered a steward of the ‘Tropical Modernism’ movement, which came to blend traditional forms indigenous to the country with the prevailing aesthetics of modernism that were first popularized in the 1920s during the era of the Bauhaus – the exhibition at Vitra gives nuance to this. Pre-liberation, Sri Lanka was populated with hulking English-style colonial buildings, recognizable by their extremely ornate decoration and light-colored facades—a style imported by the occupying power. The wake of their withdrawal left space for a new kind of architectural style.
It should be noted, though, that Tropical Modernism wasn’t imported to Sri Lanka, or any of the other countries in the so-called ‘Tropics.’ It was an adaptation of the modernist architectural style first popularized in Europe and diffused throughout these countries by Maxwell Fry and his wife Jane Drew. The V&A adeptly notes that ‘The Tropics’ as a has its own problematics as it was, ‘a broad geographical zone spanning the equator and covering 40 percent of the world’s surface. It was a colonial definition that encompassed most of the territories of the British Empire, but ignored regional variations in climate as well as local cultures and traditions.’
Bawa’s contribution to the movement
In Sri Lanka’s new post-independent state, the architect took the qualities that worked, like rejection of Eurocentric ornamentation, while furthering this approach with methodologies that worked for his geographic context. A notable thread throughout the exhibition is Bawa’s continual collaboration with creatives who practiced and disseminated local craft, like Ena de Silva, Laki Senanayake, and Barbara Sansoni. Throughout the exhibition, colorful batik works can be found, echoing their presence in Bawa’s work, like in the expansive, technicolor ceilings of the Bentota Beach Hotel.
The link between environment and structure
In a large-scale three-channel video installation by Kavindu Sivaraj, which moves through the environment around Bawa’s projects, the viewer becomes immersed in the lush landscapes that would have become inextricable from his design language. It is said that, upon coming back to Sri Lanka, Bawa wanted to create a garden on his property. When he realized that he lacked the technical expertise to execute it, he had made up his mind to formally pursue architecture. The first part of the exhibition, showing his country estate and personal home, Lunuganga in Bentota (1948–2003), and his Colombo home Number 11 (1958–1969), allows one to see the way that he was able to merge historical influence, local context, and his personal style into these laboratories for his practice.
The Sri Lankan Parliamentary Building
During his lifetime, Bawa received an honor that few architects get in their lifetime: he led the construction of his nation’s parliamentary building. Near the capital city of Colombo, the building was completed in 1982 and looks out onto a man-made body of water. It largely references both modern styles and vernacular architecture, with the exhibition catalogue describing it as, ‘a floating ensemble of pavilions that appear to rise from the water.’ Thinking back on De Silva’s essay, a line jumps out: ‘Bawa is not precious about what was existing or historical and seamlessly marries the language of the past with the needs of the present.’ It is with this fluid view on time, the past, and the future that, in his lifetime, Bawa was able to use his architecture to crystallize a view on Sri Lanka’s position in the wider world in the second half of the 20th century.
project info:
exhibition: Geoffrey Bawa: Architecture for the Senses
architect: Geoffrey Bawa
dates: September 26, 2026–February 28, 2027
institution: Vitra Design Museum | @vitradesignmuseum
organizing bodies: Vitra Design Museum, M+, and the Wüstenrot Foundation, in collaboration with the Geoffrey Bawa Trust.
location: Charles-Eames-Str. 2, D-79576 Weil am Rhein

Farm groups protest low Rabi MSP hike, call it an insult
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:39:19 UTC
23:39:19 KST

NEW DELHI: A number of farmer organisations, joining hands under umbrella outfit, Samyukta Kisan Morcha (SKM), have rejected the new minimum support prices (MSPs) for Rabi crops for 2027-28, announced by the govt on Sept 30, saying that the Rs 25-per-quintal hike in the MSP for wheat—equivalent to just 25 paise per kilogram—is an insult.The farm group also called for an immediate revision of the MSPs for all Rabi crops, including wheat, and demanded that states be given full freedom to provide bonuses.Referring to the hike, the farm group said, “25 paise a kilo is not a price it is an insult…Yet the government calls it a 106% profit (return over the cost of production).”Alleging that the states’ price recommendations were bulldozed by the Centre and the Commission for Agricultural Costs & Prices (CACP), the SKM flagged that the increase in the diesel prices and other input costs were ignored while arriving at the cost of production.Noting that the price of diesel, which powers every tractor and pump set, was hiked four times in ten days in May, by about Rs 7.50 a litre, the SKM also demanded a rollback of the increase in diesel prices.Factoring in the deficient monsoon rainfall this year, the Centre last Wednesday announced new MSPs with focus on better hike to low water-consuming oilseeds, pulses and coarse grain so that farmers may opt for these crops over the most popular winter crop, wheat, whose new MSP at Rs 2,610 per quintal for 2027-28 got an increase of less than 1% over the existing support price of Rs 2,585 per quintal in 2026-27.
The absolute highest increase in MSP was announced for Safflower (oilseeds) at Rs 675 per quintal followed by Rapeseed & Mustard (oilseeds) at Rs 413 per quintal. For Lentil (Masur), barley (coarse grain), and gram, there is an increase of Rs 390 per quintal, Rs 136 per quintal and Rs 83 per quintal, respectively.The Union agriculture ministry noted that the expected margin over cost of production, as calculated by the CACP, is the highest (106%) for wheat, followed by 96% for rapeseed & mustard; 92% for lentil; 59% for gram; 58% for barley; and 50% for safflower.Agriculture expert and former member of the Uttar Pradesh Planning Commission, Sudhir Panwar, however, questioned the hike, saying it is lower than inflation in input costs. “This suggests that the govt rejected the norm of providing a 50% profit on input costs under the guise of diversification,” he said.The new MSP for the Rabi marketing season, beginning April 1 next year, will give a signal to farmers for their choice of crops during the upcoming sowing season, which is expected to face challenges of low moisture content in the soil and less water availability for irrigation due to deficient monsoon rainfall.The govt claimed that the increase in MSPs of all six Rabi crops is in sync with the Union Budget 2018-19 announcement of fixing the support price at a level of at least 1.5 times of the All-India weighted average Cost of Production, ensuring minimum 50% return over the cost of production.
The cost, as calculated by the CACP, includes all paid out costs such as those incurred on account of hired human labour, bullock labour/machine labour, rent paid for leased in land, expenses incurred on use of material inputs like seeds, fertilizers, manures, irrigation charges, depreciation on implements and farm buildings, interest on working capital, diesel/electricity for operation of pump sets etc., miscellaneous expenses and imputed value of family labour. It is called A2+FL methodology, which means paid-out cost of cultivation plus the imputed value of family labour.SKM, however, has been demanding the comprehensive cost (C2 methodology) that should also include the rental value of the family's own land and the interest on its own capital, and a legally guaranteed MSP at C2+50%.Giving a call for protests against the new MSP, the SKM on Saturday urged farmers and youth of rural India to burn copies of the recent order on the hike in every village, saying it will go on until a legal MSP at C2+50% is won.
Vishwa Mohan is Senior Editor at The Times of India. He writes on environment, climate change, agriculture, water resources and clean energy, tracking policy issues and climate diplomacy. He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

The government bodies responsible for monitoring and checking foreign flight crews landing in Israel are the Transportation Ministry's Security Department and the Mossad, security sources told Haaretz.
Both bodies are supposed to receive, according to the sources, the list of foreign flight crews arriving in Israel and to issue warnings if there are suspicions about any of them.
On Wednesday, a co-pilot attempted to attack the crew of a flydubai plane en route to Israel. The co-pilot, an Omani citizen, stabbed the Indian captain and tried to crash the plane in Jordanian territory. According to passenger accounts, the wounded captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing several passengers to enter, intervene and overpower the assailant. Two pilots who were among the passengers then landed the plane in Saudi Arabia, and the passengers were subsequently flown to Israel.
The attacking pilot was identified as 29-year-old Humam al-Humami, CNN and Saudi state media reported Saturday. Al-Humami's LinkedIn account, which has since been deleted, showed that he worked for Oman Air for seven years, and in 2025 flew for Royal Air Maroc for about seven months.
He had worked for flydubai for about eight months. An Omani citizen and native of the United Arab Emirates, he was born to a Syrian mother and an Omani father. Sources told The Wall Street Journal that Oman had previously barred al-Hammami from flying over concerns that he had adopted "extreme ideological views."
Captain Smith Machhar, the captain seriously wounded in the hijacking attempt, spoke on Saturday with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. During their conversation, Machhar recounted that he used his remaining strength to open the cockpit door, only to have the co-pilot close it behind him several times.
"Call it a personal matter or call it doing it for others, but let's just say I did it knowing that if I didn't, I was going to die," he said. "I summoned all the strength I had, gave it everything I had, and simply charged toward the door and opened it. Luckily, people were waiting to rush inside."

In Kyiv, a driver fled from the police and attacked patrol officers: he was shot
Kyiv • UNN
The driver of a Ford fled from patrol officers, crashed into a utility pole, and attacked police officers with a entrenching shovel. He was wounded in the leg.
In Kyiv, a Ford driver failed to stop when ordered to do so by patrol officers and attempted to flee. As a result, he crashed into a utility pole, after which he attacked the police officers with a sapper shovel. One of the patrol officers used his weapon and shot the man in the leg. The Patrol Police of Ukraine reports this, according to UNN.
Details
We detained a driver who was fleeing from the police and attacked inspectors. Today in Kyiv, patrol officers received an alert regarding a Ford whose driver had ignored a police order to stop. After locating the vehicle, the inspectors ordered the driver to stop. However, he ignored the order and continued driving. We began pursuing the vehicle
According to the available information, the driver left Kyiv and, in the village of Sofiivska Borshchahivka, lost control and crashed into a utility pole.
After that, the man got out of the vehicle and attacked the police officers while holding a sapper shovel. As a result of the attack, two of our colleagues sustained bodily injuries. The man did not respond to the police officers’ repeated demands to stop his unlawful actions and put down the shovel. He also ignored repeated warnings about the possible use of firearms and did not stop the attack
To repel the attack and eliminate the threat to the lives and health of the police officers, in accordance with Article 46 of the Law of Ukraine "On the National Police," one of the inspectors used his service firearm, shooting the attacker in the leg.
Medics were called to the scene. The injured individuals are receiving the necessary medical assistance. There is no threat to the lives of the attacker or the police officers. Investigators detained the man in accordance with Article 208 of the Criminal Procedure Code of Ukraine and initiated criminal proceedings under Article 345 (Threat or violence against a law enforcement officer) of the Criminal Code of Ukraine
We would like to remind you
Police detained a 36-year-old man in Kyiv who attempted to flee during a document check. He was taken to a territorial recruitment and social support center, and a report was drawn up.

An Iranian strike severely damaged an RE-3A surveillance aircraft of the Royal Saudi Air Force.

The strike on the air base took place in March 2026 during the intense phase of the U.S. Operation Epic Fury.
The satellite imagery also shows traces of fires at the sites where U.S. aircraft were destroyed. In addition, several U.S. military infrastructure facilities at the base were damaged.
The RE-3A is a specialized Royal Saudi Air Force surveillance aircraft based on the Boeing 707 and used for surveillance missions.
Saudi Arabia is known to have only one such aircraft.
The post’s author also noted that the damaged Saudi aircraft was at the same air base where U.S. E-3G Sentry and KC-135R aircraft were destroyed during the Iranian strike.
Overall, during Operation Epic Fury and after its official conclusion, the United States lost about 50 aircraft.
These included two KC-135s, four F-15Es, two MC-130Js, four MH-6s, one E-3G Sentry, and one A-10C that was effectively written off after sustaining combat damage. Several other aircraft were damaged, including an F-35A and an A-10C.
Unmanned aviation suffered the largest losses: according to the Pentagon, up to 30 MQ-9A Reapers were destroyed during the operation.

The additional aircraft will provide aerial refueling for Saudi fighter jets involved in repelling missile and drone attacks.

Novak Djokovic produced a trademark comeback to defeat top seed Alexander Zverev 4-6, 6-4, 6-4 and reach the China Open semifinals on Sunday, extending his unbeaten record in the tournament.
Playing the ATP 500 event in Beijing for the first time since 2015, the six-time champion was pushed to the limit by reigning French Open and US Open champion Zverev.
Meeting for the first time in nearly 16 months, Djokovic struggled to contain the German's power in the early stages as Zverev claimed the opening set, but the Serb gradually worked his way into the match and refused to let his opponent pull away.

In the women's draw, Aryna Sabalenka crashed out in the third round following a 6-4, 6-3 defeat by Czech Nikola Bartunkova, the latest setback in a frustrating season for the world number two.

UK justice secretary unable to say how many early release prisoners have been tagged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:35:25 UTC
23:35:25 KST

Alex Norris has been unable to say how many prisoners freed early from jail this week have been tagged, despite previous reassurances from the justice department.
In an interview on Sunday, the justice secretary said it was “too soon” to say how many of the roughly 700 male prisoners let out on Thursday had been fitted with monitoring devices.
The government has introduced a “presumption of electronic tagging” for offenders released early from prisons in England and Wales to help manage severe overcrowding.
The first wave of releases began on Thursday, with nearly 5,000 prisoners due to be freed in stages over the next year as the Sentencing Act 2026 comes into force.
Asked how many of those released so far had been tagged, Norris told the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg programme: “I don’t have that figure today, it only happened on Thursday. You know, there can be a bit of a lag.
“We don’t have that number. But you know, we’re very candid about who’s leaving prison and when they do.”
Asked if he knew if released domestic abusers have been tagged or not, he said: “It would be too soon to know that, as it was only on Thursday. We’ve been talking to every victim to offer them the chance to say what controls they’d like to see over that individual.
“I’m well aware of the past in tagging. Over the last year, performance has increased significantly.”
Several prisoners released last week told the Guardian that they had not been tagged.
Michael Bogle, a former bus driver who left HMP Wandsworth on Thursday having served 78 days in prison after breaching a 32-week suspended sentence for shoplifting, said he had no idea when he was going to be tagged. “I have an appointment with probation officers on Thursday, but as far I know it could take months before I actually get given a tag,” he said.
Bogle, who is taking anti-psychotic drugs and has more than 100 convictions including for common assault and drug possession, was told in prison that he would be housed in a bail hostel and had been promised a place in south-east London. However, he said he had instead been housed in a bed and breakfast facility in north-west London.
“I am running out of money, and if I have to shoplift a sandwich to stop being hungry, I will just have to do it,” he said. “I won’t have a choice. But I really do not want to go back to prison – it is a pigeon-infested, rat-infested place and people are dying in the conditions there.”
Prisoners thanked the prime minister as they celebrated walking free from jail on Thursday. One told the press as he left HMP Durham: “Justice system, what justice system? Thank you, Andy Burnham.”
A prisoner released from HMP Cardiff after being jailed for burglary said he would “probably be back in the next month or two”.
Ministers intervened to exclude rapists and the most serious child sexual offenders from early release, after criticism of the policy over the summer.
The rules will also not apply to those guilty of manslaughter, such as the killers of PC Andrew Harper, who died in the line of duty in 2019.
Almost half of electronic tags used to track offenders’ movements are not fitted on time, with significant delays putting victims in England and Wales at risk, a report found last month. 
HM Inspectorate of Probation said some criminals waited up to five months to be fitted with a tag, leading to repeated breaches of court and prison orders.

Polling stations open in Brazil for some 160 million voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:32:06 UTC
23:32:06 KST

Nearly 160 million Brazilians were eligible to vote in Sunday's presidential election. Polls close at 17:00 Brasília time. With voting conducted digitally, the first results are expected about three hours later, overnight in Europe
Brazilians headed to the polls on Sunday in the first round of the presidential election, in which President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party (PT) is seeking re-election against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party and son of Jair Bolsonaro.
The election is attracting international attention, as it will determine whether this Latin American economic powerhouse remains under left-wing rule or joins the rightward shift sweeping South America, championed by US President Donald Trump.
Soon to turn 81, veteran leftist Lula da Silva is running for a fourth and final term, warning voters that Brazil's sovereignty is at risk because of pressure exerted by Trump. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, is making his debut in the presidential race, in which he aims to follow in his father's footsteps, Jair Bolsonaro who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence, who governed the country between 2019 and 2022 and pursued policies of close alignment with the United States.
According to opinion polls, which put the two leading candidates in a statistical tie, Lula da Silva (45% of voting intentions) faces a tough battle against the right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro (43%), aged 45, who has been emphasising his proximity to the White House and insisting that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, particularly when it comes to the economy of rare minerals.
Polls also suggest that neither candidate will cross the 50% threshold needed for an outright victory this Sunday. A second round of voting is therefore expected on 25 October.
Almost 160 million citizens are eligible to vote in these elections. According to the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), 158 745 463 voters are expected to cast their ballots this Sunday. Voting is compulsory and those who do not vote must provide a justification.
Brazilians will also elect 27 state governors, state deputies, all 513 federal deputies in the Chamber of Deputies and 54 of the country's 81 senators in Sunday's vote.
Overseas, voting is only for the President and Vice-President, and around 918 000 registered voters scattered around the world are expected to take part.
In some places, voting has been under way for several hours, as is the case in Portugal, home to the second-largest Brazilian electoral constituency abroad, while in others polls have already closed.
According to provisional results published so far, Lula da Silva is ahead in Malaysia, Singapore, China, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand. Flávio Bolsonaro is winning in the Philippines and Japan.
The final results will be released by the TSE from 17:00 in Brasília (22:00 CET).

Demining Syria: How Not to Let Word Games Bury the Work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

On Sept. 22, 2015, the infantry fighting vehicle I was driving hit an anti-tank mine. It felt strange to spend the 11th anniversary of my injury standing among ruins in a country far from home that had also been devastated by Russian mines and shells.
As members of a Ukrainian delegation on an official visit to Syria, we were discussing with local colleagues how to bring areas destroyed by war back to life. For me, the connection between these experiences felt very real. The effects of attacks on civilian infrastructure by Russian and Assad forces have long been documented, but seeing the destruction and working among the ruins is a different experience.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Two days earlier, on Sunday, Sept. 20, we signed an intergovernmental agreement on mine action cooperation in Damascus. Next came Idlib and Aleppo: local response teams, destroyed neighborhoods, and tests of Ukrainian technologies.
Two days of field visits is not much, and I do not claim to fully understand the situation across the country. But I had seen enough to spend the long journey home thinking about issues I know well from Ukraine’s experience.
In my March column after my first visit, I wrote that Ukraine could help Syrians build a mine action system by sharing our own solutions and mistakes. This time, I was more concerned about the gap between what people say about building such systems, what they believe those systems can achieve, and what they actually do.
Ukraine’s Science Under Fire: Russia Is Targeting Knowledge, People and the Future
Start with the foundations
In Aleppo, we visited a district in ruins, where people were already clearing the area and trying to rebuild what can still be saved.
The Syrian government’s goal is to move people from tents back into homes. Standing amid a mix of concrete, steel, bricks, and household waste, I thought about what I usually say in meetings: how we are building a mine action system, which approaches we use, and what experience we draw on.
But here, I found it hard to see how everything we talk about would allow us to clear these areas within realistic limits of time and resources.
In Ukraine, I see how expensive and slow humanitarian demining can be, even in much simpler conditions. The level of complexity here is different, and using familiar approaches seems likely to cost even more and take even longer. I may be wrong in this assessment. But it is Ukraine’s experience that makes me question whether consistently following standards is enough to deliver results within a reasonable timeframe.
My first thought was to use remotely operated equipment much more widely. Mechanized methods are already covered by international standards. But I wonder whether all the requirements for carrying out the work remain justified given the technology available today. How far can robotics allow us to rethink procedures? We must demonstrate that the work is safe and that the land will be safe to use afterwards.
At the same time, when another way to achieve a safe outcome becomes available, we must also examine whether a particular requirement is still necessary. This question applies both to operators’ procedures and to the standards themselves. Years of experience in applying them should not make them untouchable or beyond question.
What worries me most is that we may agree on all the right words, build a system around them, and still not answer whether it can do the job it was created for. If clearance requires money that cannot be raised and timelines that leave people’s return home an uncertain prospect, then the practical value of the proposed approach comes into question.
Who is responsible?
Another related question is how much influence the country itself can have over the choice of approaches and the planning of the work.
Syrian colleagues are expanding response teams, looking for equipment, and working to ensure that the national center can fully coordinate the sector. International programs are being rolled out in parallel, with their own budgets, procedures, and priorities. According to the information we received, government approvals are being obtained and work is being carried out in response to government requests. For now, however, it appears that operators largely agree among themselves on who will work where, while the national center has a limited role in these particular decisions.
I understand why organizations make arrangements among themselves: work must continue, duplication needs to be avoided, and a state institution’s capacity does not develop overnight.
But I want to understand how this practice will grow into a system that the country itself can coordinate.
Syrians are making efforts to take on more responsibility. To what extent does the way partners work help them gradually gain a corresponding say in decisions? If we wait until the center has enough capacity while continuing to coordinate the main operations among ourselves, where is that capacity supposed to come from?
Supporting a national institution also requires changes in the way its partners work. It means involving the local team in planning while decisions can still be changed, explaining the constraints of our own programs and working together to align them with the country’s needs. Sometimes this will be harder than reaching an agreement among a few experienced international organizations.
But it is difficult to learn how to coordinate a sector if your role remains largely limited to approving plans developed by others. Training and advice are needed, but they do not replace participation in the decisions themselves.
The same applies to separate arrangements with farmers, the energy sector, and other government bodies. They all have urgent needs, and helping them is necessary. The question is how these arrangements fit into an overall plan and what role the institution being built has in that process.
I do not expect the Syrian center to decide on every deployment or determine how every task should be carried out. Operators have their own areas of expertise and responsibilities. But any discussion of national leadership must also include partners’ willingness to reconsider their own plans when the country proposes a different sequence of actions.
Word games
In Syria, I recognized another familiar situation: a local team puts a great deal of effort into earning donors’ trust and securing resources for its own work. It needs to demonstrate capacity that it is still largely trying to build. An international organization enters the same discussion with a reputation built over many years, established procedures, and existing relationships with donors.
I understand this difference. But when a lack of capacity becomes an argument for working mainly through an external system, I struggle to see how the local system is supposed to grow stronger.
Enthusiasm and a desire to rebuild the country are not enough to manage large programs. Skilled staff, financial controls, and accountability are needed. The Syrian team must meet these requirements too, even in difficult conditions. But an international organization’s reputation does not automatically prove that its work is effective in a particular country either. Trust in procedures does not tell us how efficiently resources have been used or what the country itself will be able to do afterwards.
This is why it feels to me like a game of saying the right words. The country’s representatives learn how to describe their needs to secure support. In meetings, they talk about the future system, then return to searching for the machines, equipment, and people they need today. Partners talk about national leadership but continue to work within the boundaries of their own projects.
Building a system must go hand in hand with urgent work. The problem arises when this work continues but the national team’s involvement in joint planning does not grow. Under these conditions, even effective individual projects do not necessarily add up to the system everyone agreed to build.
Ukraine’s experience makes me particularly sensitive to this. We too were discussing the future model for mine action while expanding state units capable of responding to hazards. Now I was seeing a familiar situation from the outside.
Our own solutions also need to be adapted. We came to the site of a destroyed factory after a local resident reported a suspicious object. The Ukrainian operators launched a drone equipped with a standard high-resolution camera, collected images, and tried to analyze them.
A neural network trained in Ukraine produced too many false positives: Syrian rocks and debris proved challenging for it. We continued processing the data later at the hotel. Eventually, the images revealed a 152 mm artillery munition and a cluster munition. During a ground survey, the Syrian team found those same items.
This is a good start to our joint work, but more effort is needed before we have a solution ready for Syrian conditions. We saw the limitations of our own technology, and we will work on them. What I find difficult to understand is why the same approach is sometimes missing when it comes to transferring governance models. Knowledge brought from another country needs to be tested against local realities, even when it is backed by decades of experience.
Among the Syrians we worked with are people who have returned from Europe and elsewhere. They have a great deal of energy and experience, and a strong desire to rebuild their own country. They have to put teams together, restore connections, and make decisions in conditions that are hard to understand without speaking to people in person. Staffing problems, local culture, and who can reach agreement with whom all matter. Arriving with a ready-made model is much easier than understanding how it will work for the people involved.
I keep telling my Syrian colleagues that I did not come here to teach them how to build their own country. I share what we have tried, where we made mistakes, and what we had to redesign. If I see that a Ukrainian solution may not work in local conditions, we say so immediately. I want us to be able to speak just as openly within international partnerships, without first having to agree with every proposed approach in order to earn the right to receive support.
After this trip, I have a clearer understanding of what I expect from our cooperation: assistance should leave Syrians with greater capacity to solve their own problems themselves. Teaching them to work according to our rules is not enough. We ourselves will have to align our work with the institution we are encouraging them to build, explain our decisions to it, and be prepared to change those decisions after discussion. Otherwise, we may build any number of things, but certainly not a national system.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

Separately, an investigation by Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera said on Sunday that the co-pilot, identified as 29-year-old Omani national Hammam al-Hammami, had planned to kill the captain without alerting authorities and crash the aircraft into skyscrapers in Tel Aviv before Israeli fighter jets could intercept it.
Flydubai flight FZ 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv made an emergency landing in the Saudi city of Tabuk on Wednesday. United Arab Emirates authorities said the co-pilot attacked the captain with an emergency axe during the flight before passengers and crew subdued him.
The injured captain, Smit Machchhar, told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday that he had used his remaining strength to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to intervene. Feature: A taste of Yunnan finds its way into Vietnam's coffee landscape
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
22:28:28 CST
23:28:28 KST

HANOI, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- After finishing a 150-gram box of Yunnan coffee, Nguyen Ngoc Ly cut out the beans' flavor profile to add to her collection, a habit reflecting her fascination with specialty coffee from different origins.
The Hanoi coffee lover told Xinhua that she had ordered the box out of curiosity after members of specialty coffee groups on social media praised the beans from China's southwestern province.
She brewed the coffee using the pour-over method and sometimes served it with cold milk, finding its flavor so lively that it made a latte unlike any she had tasted before.
"The Yunnan beans have a very rich flavor, not the dark chocolate or bitter taste people usually expect from coffee," Ly said, adding that their fruity flavor and cooling qualities make them well suited to iced coffee on hot days.
Hanoi coffee specialist Pham Duy Anh said Yunnan beans are attracting interest among Vietnamese consumers, with many specialty cafes and roasters in the country now selling them.
He attributed their appeal to noticeably improving quality with each harvest and a range of processing methods that suit Vietnamese drinkers looking for new experiences.
"Diverse processing methods like washed, natural, honey and anaerobic have kept the beans from being boxed into a single flavor profile, giving drinkers notes such as mild wine, raisin, guava, tea and watermelon," Anh said, describing this as an advantage in a market that values diversity and personalization in the coffee experience.
In the northern port city of Hai Phong, Nguyen Minh Ngoc, owner of the Unbranded. café and roastery, began selling Yunnan beans in July 2024 after seeing how much their quality and processing had improved.
Ngoc said she brought in two batches of green beans, each weighing about 10 kilograms, and both sold out quickly. The first had jasmine notes, while the second had notes of watermelon, melon, peach and rose.
"Many customers return for a third and fourth time," Ngoc said, adding that Yunnan beans account for between 20 and 30 percent of customers' coffee selections at her small café, which also serves beans from Ethiopia, Kenya and Colombia.
Ly, too, has bought Yunnan beans again, saying the flavor is consistent, with one batch tasting no different from the next. She credits this consistency to Yunnan roasters' good control of anaerobic fermentation.
The local market remains largely limited to specialty coffee fans, but interest in Yunnan beans is rising fast in bigger cities, she told Xinhua.
From a market perspective, Anh said Yunnan beans stand at an interesting intersection: close enough to offer advantages in price and logistics, and new enough to spark discovery.
"If their quality keeps improving and the coffee is promoted through its flavors, the beans could well reach beyond today's circle of specialty coffee drinkers," he said. ■

Two people have died in Catalonia as the region is hit by torrential rain and flooding

14:23:57 UTC
23:23:57 KST

On Sunday, Spanish Civil Protection sent a new Es-Alert to five Catalan counties reminding residents of travel restrictions, after Barcelona saw its wettest day in at least 20 years and the Besòs river passed the danger threshold.
Two people have died and another is missing after heavy rain and flooding hit Catalonia, in north-eastern Spain, authorities said on Sunday.
Catalan regional president Salvador Illa confirmed the second death in a social media post on Sunday.
Firefighters said the missing person had been swept away by a stream in Pineda de Mar, a town north of Barcelona.
Catalan Civil Protection has sent a new Es-Alert on Sunday to the mobile phones of residents in Vallès Oriental, Maresme, la Selva, Baix Empordà and Gironès.
The message urges people to comply with travel restrictions while the torrential rain continues. Residents in the affected counties are advised to avoid all non-essential journeys.
At 16:48 on Saturday, another Es-Alert was sent to 20 Catalan counties, recommending that all activities and travel be suspended from 20:00. The alert warned that the severe weather could persist until 14:00 on Sunday.
Heavy rain has been falling since midday on Saturday along a stretch of the Catalan coast, which remains under an emergency alert due to the formation of a convective mesoscale system over the Mediterranean.
By midnight on Sunday, between 100 and 200 litres of rain per square metre had fallen across Barcelonès. Meteocat recorded 190.8 litres in the Raval, 170.3 in the University Zone on Diagonal Avenue — the highest total in 18 years — and 152 around the Badalona Museum, (highest figure in 21 years).
In the Raval, 3.4 litres fell in a single minute and 36.1 litres in just half an hour. According to Meteocat, the total was almost double the 95.4 litres recorded in the neighbourhood on 24 March 2017.
The agency said heavy and torrential rain continued into the early hours of Sunday, with bands of showers slowly moving northwards across Catalonia.
"We still have hours to go," Meteocat warned on social media, adding that rainfall totals would be exceptional both in terms of volume and geographical extent.
The president of the Government of Catalonia, Salvador Illa, has urged citizens "not to let their guard down". He spoke of "a complicated night" and an episode that "has not yet come to an end".
Rivers on alert, rescues and trains halted
The Catalan Water Agency (ACA) has reported that the final stretch of the Besòs has exceeded the danger threshold, with an imminent risk of flooding. At 03:00 the river was flowing through Santa Coloma de Gramenet with a discharge of 520 cubic metres per second, and the ACA issued a hydrological risk warning.
By three in the morning, Catalonia's fire service had received 682 calls, most of them about flooding, and had not yet dealt with incidents involving serious injuries. Barcelona's Bombers logged a total of 910 calls and 145 operations related to the storm by 7:20.
At 05:10 firefighters were called to Granollers because of a violent downpour and the sudden swelling of streams. They are working to rescue several people trapped in their cars at the approaches to a flooded roundabout, some of them standing on the roofs of their vehicles.
Heavy rain overnight in Biscay as well
On Saturday the storm also affected northern Spain. The Basque country emergency centre recorded a total of 150 rain-related incidents in the province of Biscay by 20:30, 137 of them in Bilbao, with flooding and pools of water on the roads. In some parts of the Old Town the water reached knee height, and several residents were unable to get into their homes. Some businesses put up wooden boards to keep the water out.
Traffic through the La Avanzada tunnels in Leioa was cut off, and similar incidents were reported in Getxo, Basauri, Laudio, Galdakao, Sestao and Erandio. Euskalmet kept the orange alert in place until 00:00, when the rain was expected to ease, before switching to a yellow advisory until 06:00 on Sunday.

Yemeni presidency announces offensive to retake all Houthi territory
Yemen's leader announced on Sunday the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by the Houthis, even as the group made fresh gains on the ground, effectively encircling a government-held city.
The announcement sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost large swathes of the country's Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab Strait - a chokepoint for international shipping - after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemen's government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia, where the Houthis said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital yet again on Sunday.
"I announce today the start of military operations to retake the remaining territories of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory," Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen's presidential council, said in a statement.
Alimi called on all the armed forces "to begin carrying out their assigned missions, in accordance with the approved plans, until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia".
The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government's interim capital Aden, according to four security sources.
The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.
"We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station," a police source in the area told AFP.
Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city.
The military sources added that fighting in the area was ongoing.
Taiz itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen's long-running civil war.
"They've achieved the military objective of isolating Taiz from Aden, even if they haven't fully taken control of it," Farea Al-Muslimi, research fellow at the Chatham House think-tank, told AFP.
Muslimi also downplayed expectations over what the coming government offensive might accomplish.
"In my opinion, it's meaningless, he added.
Saudi attacks
Following several years of relative calm, Yemen's civil war reignited in July against the backdrop of the wider conflict in the Middle East.
It has also drawn in Saudi Arabia - leader of an anti-Houthi military coalition since 2015 - with the group regularly claiming attacks on the kingdom's territory in recent weeks and declaring a blockade of its ships in the Red Sea.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree on Sunday said the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi energy giant Aramco's sites in Riyadh and in the oil-rich Khurais area in the east.
"The strikes were precise, causing large fires at the targeted sites," Saree said on X.
Saudi oil exports were already under pressure thanks to Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
The Houthi's Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.
They came a day after Yemen's government said its forces struck Houthi targets around the country, including in the capital Sanaa, the northwestern governorate of Saada and the group's positions near Taiz in the southwest.
The Yemeni government's air capabilities, however, are limited, and the Saudi-led coalition has long been the primary force carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis.
Experts believe the recent operations have most likely been conducted by Saudi warplanes as well.
Yemen is one of the poorest countries in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis that has unspooled since the civil war broke out in 2014.
That year the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa from the Saudi-backed government, before going on to take control of much of the country's north, with Riyadh's international coalition intervening the following year.

Dodik declared Bosnia ‘dead’. Irrelevant rhetoric or serious threat?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:21:20 UTC
23:21:20 KST

Dodik declared Bosnia ‘dead’. Irrelevant rhetoric or serious threat?
Bosnian Serb leader’s controversial comments ahead of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s high-stakes elections.
Speaking at the final rally of his right-wing alliance ahead of Bosnia’s October 4 election, Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik delivered a predictably controversial statement.
“Bosnia-Herzegovina is dead. It is an impossible country, it makes no sense,” Dodik told supporters of the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) party in Banja Luka on Friday.
“It is now nothing more than an empty shell … for those who are trying to keep it alive, so they can prove themselves right about something,” said the former president of Republika Srpska, who is known for frequent separatist threats and for challenging the country’s constitution.
Dodik’s comments came as Bosnia remains deeply divided over its political future more than three decades since the 1995 Dayton peace agreement. It split the country into two semi-autonomous parts – the Serb-majority Republika Srpska entity and the Federation entity, where most Bosniaks and Croats live.
The agreement ended the 1992–95 Bosnian War and established a political framework for power-sharing among Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats.
On Sunday, voters across the country cast ballots to elect the three members of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s multiethnic presidency, representatives to the national parliament and leaders of institutions in the country’s two entities.
Dodik himself is not on the ballot after being stripped of his post last year, following his conviction for refusing to carry out decisions issued by Christian Schmidt, the international peace envoy who oversees the implementation of the Dayton peace agreement.
‘No political relevance’
Elvis Fejzic, a professor at the Faculty of Political Science in Sarajevo, said attempts by figures such as Dodik to dismantle Bosnia and Herzegovina amount to “populist rhetoric”.
“Politicians and political parties that act unconstitutionally do not determine the fate of Bosnia and Herzegovina,” Fejzic told Al Jazeera, arguing that Bosnia and Herzegovina’s status as a UN member and internationally recognised state is secure.
“Bosnia and Herzegovina … will outlive all those who, through inflammatory statements, seek to obstruct its path towards integration and development,” he said. “Their statements have no political relevance whatsoever.”
Political analyst Tanja Topic said that while Dodik was not officially a candidate, he remained a central figure in the campaign and sought to present himself as a “senior official in international relations”.
Topic told Al Jazeera that the election result could produce several political scenarios in Bosnia and Herzegovina, from “cohabitation in Republika Srpska”, through the formation of a grand coalition, to a “blockage at the state level and the Council of Ministers continuing to operate in a caretaker capacity”.
Dodik’s rhetoric marks ‘long escalation’
Expert Adnan Cerimagic said Dodik’s rhetoric should be taken “seriously” and viewed as part of a “long escalation” rather than a reflection of the country’s current reality.
“For the past four years, his moves against the Dayton order and against Bosnia’s EU and NATO path have reached a new and dangerous level: in March 2025 the country came close to an armed standoff between Republika Srpska and state police,” Cerimagic, a senior analyst at the European Stability Initiative, told Al Jazeera.
“Casting Bosnia as a front-line in a supposed war between Christianity and Islam, and himself as a defender of Christian Europe, is aimed at the one people in Europe against whom a genocide has been committed since the Second World War and recognised as such by two international courts,” he added.
Cerimagic added that Dodik’s rhetoric may reflect uncertainty over the electoral prospects of his preferred candidate, as well as a belief that the European Union has less leverage over Bosnia than it once did.
Initial results are customarily released by the Central Election Commission late on election night and then refreshed every few hours.
In the days that follow, the commission progressively inputs votes from polling stations that remain outstanding, mobile voting teams, as well as ballots sent by mail and those cast at diplomatic and consular missions.
The final, official results must be published by November 20 at the latest.
