Yemen’s Saudi-backed forces earlier confirmed the strikes but said they were targeting vital Houthi positions, claiming 700 fighters were killed or wounded in 24 hours.
The latest exchange marks a sharp escalation after four years of relative calm between the Iranian-backed Houthis and Riyadh following a UN-brokered truce in 2022. The Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led intervention in support of the Yemeni government the following year.
Tensions reignited in July after government forces struck Sanaa Airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia, declared the de-escalation over, and announced a naval blockade of the kingdom. By mid-August, they were launching coordinated missile and drone attacks on Saudi-backed government forces, prompting counteroffensives across several provinces.
Fighting escalated last month as the Houthis struck energy infrastructure in southern Saudi Arabia, including Saudi Aramco facilities and the East-West Pipeline. The group has also made major territorial gains, seizing Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the strategic Bab el-Mandeb shipping chokepoint.
Houthi forces are now pushing toward Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city and a crucial crossroads between the Houthi-held north, government-controlled south, and Red Sea coast. Its capture would open a direct route south toward Aden, the seat of the Yemeni government.
Saudi Arabia is preparing an offensive to reverse the Houthi gains, Reuters reported on Friday, citing officials and diplomats. Riyadh could mobilize more than 100,000 Yemeni government troops backed by Saudi airstrikes, the report said, with Western allies providing intelligence and material support but staying out of combat. Plans reportedly range from retaking the strategic Bab el-Mandeb coast to a broader multi-front assault across Houthi-held provinces.
The renewed fighting has worsened Yemen’s already dire humanitarian crisis. The UN World Food Program warned on Friday that three-quarters of the population is unable to meet its basic food needs.
The fighting has also collided with the US war against Iran, which has disrupted the Strait of Hormuz – the conduit for around 20% of global oil supplies. The Houthi seizure of Bab el-Mandeb, a key alternative, coupled with their blockade of Saudi oil exports and attacks on tankers and energy infrastructure, has put both shipping arteries under pressure and jolted energy markets. Brent crude has remained above $100 a barrel for weeks, closing at around $102 on Friday.
UPDATE: Yemen later on Sunday announced the launch of large-scale military operations to retake Houthi-held territory.
Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi said the government had exhausted all possibilities for de-escalation and was moving “from the preparation phase to action” to restore state control.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,750 Troops, 49 Artillery Systems, 1,742 UAVs in One Day
Russia lost an estimated 1,750 troops, 49 artillery systems, and 1,742 operational-tactical UAVs over the past 24 hours, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 4.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the latest Ukrainian military estimate, Russia’s total personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, have reached approximately 1,540,700. Russian forces also lost six armored combat vehicles, bringing the cumulative total to 25,483, while estimated tank losses remained unchanged at 12,391.
Another 49 artillery systems were added to the tally, bringing Russia’s estimated cumulative losses in the category to 50,686. Ukraine also reported one additional multiple-launch rocket system, raising the overall total to 2,179.
Russia lost three air defense systems over the past day, bringing the cumulative figure to 1,686, while estimated aviation losses remained unchanged at 443 aircraft and 356 helicopters.
The General Staff also recorded 13 ground robotic systems lost over the past day, raising the cumulative total to 2,837. Another 1,742 operational-tactical UAVs were added to the tally, bringing the total to approximately 546,240.
Russia’s estimated cruise missile losses remained unchanged at 5,126, while naval losses stayed at 35 ships and boats and two submarines. Another 527 vehicles and fuel tankers were recorded as lost, bringing the cumulative figure to 157,258. Ukraine also reported five additional pieces of special equipment, raising that total to 4,788.
Fighting remained intense across the front, with Ukrainian forces recording 204 combat engagements over the latest reporting period.
According to the General Staff, the Pokrovsk sector saw the heaviest fighting, with Ukrainian forces stopping 31 Russian attacks. Another 16 attacks were recorded in the Kostiantynivka sector, while Ukrainian forces repelled 13 attacks in the South Slobozhanskyi sector.
Russian forces also launched nine attacks in the Lyman sector, seven in the Sloviansk sector, five in the Huliaipole sector, four each in the North Slobozhanskyi and Kupiansk sectors, three in the Oleksandrivka sector, and two in the Kramatorsk sector.
No active Russian offensive operations were recorded in the Orikhiv and Prydniprovskyi sectors, while the situation in the Volyn and Polissia sectors remained largely unchanged, with no signs of Russian offensive formations being established.
Earlier, the Institute for the Study of War said Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s claims of major battlefield gains in September “border on hallucinations,” as Russian forces actually ended the month with a net territorial loss of about 81 square kilometers.

Green party votes to adopt policy that equates Zionism with racism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:15:31 UTC
23:15:31 KST

The Greens have formally adopted a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state, a move opposed by the bulk of the party’s MPs and which is expected to face legal challenge.
Zack Polanski, who heads the Greens in England and Wales and missed the vote at the party’s conference in Brighton to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, has faced criticism for a perceived lack of leadership on a hugely divisive issue.
There have also been concerns that the policy change was pushed largely by newcomers who have little interest in the rest of the party’s platform.
Four of the party’s five MPs opposed the motion. Adrian Ramsay and Ellie Chowns said they were “deeply saddened” while Siân Berry and Carla Denyer said they would support any Jewish members who believed they were being targeted as a result of the policy change.
The binding policy motion, passed by 1,022 votes to 813, says Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – should be “treated as any other form of racism”. It calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state “with equal rights for all”.
Israel’s foreign ministry said the resolution “constitutes a clear antisemitic text according to the IHRA (International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance) definition, as it denies the Jewish people’s right to self-determination”.
Foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar decided to declare Green party leader Zack Polanski barred from entering Israel, the ministry said, adding the decision had been coordinated with the relevant authorities.
While opinion among Jewish Green members is split, some have expressed worry that this will mean they could face disciplinary action for belonging to Jewish organisations that officially support Zionism, even synagogues.
After the vote, one backer of the motion, Salma Yaqoob, a former member of George Galloway’s Respect party who is now a Green, insisted this would not happen, saying: “Nobody will be removed, challenged, disciplined, suspended because they put forward or articulate their belief in Zionism.”
However, an amendment put forward saying the motion should not be used to “pressure, proscribe or discipline members based on affiliation with Jewish community institutions” was voted down.
It is understood that some Green members are consulting lawyers over whether the policy could be challenged for breaching equalities legislation.
Adam Wagner KC, the barrister who led a case that concluded Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour broke equalities laws over antisemitism, said such a case would have a good chance of success.
“I think there is a strong risk that the motion as passed contravenes the Equality Act 2010, which applies to political parties, as it will discriminate against and harass people who hold Zionist beliefs and Jewish people more generally,” he said.
Zionism when defined in the broad sense of supporting a Jewish nation state “is likely to be a protected belief” under the act, he said.
The motion argues that Zionism is necessarily racist as it “privileges one ethnic group on the basis of the subjugation of others”. It adds: “This motion is aimed at the political ideology and practice of Zionism, as defined, and not at the religious or ethnic background of those who may identify as Zionists. Not all Jews are Zionists and not all Zionists are Jews …
“Zionism, as defined above, will be treated as any other form of racism, and this motion will be implemented by the anti-racism policy working group as appropriate and in accordance with its ordinary practice.”
According to the Institute for Jewish Policy Research, about two-thirds of British Jews consider themselves Zionists.
During the lengthy debate, which was for members only, Chowns and Caroline Lucas, the former leader who was the Greens’ first MP, argued against the plan.
The motion had been pushed by a group called Greens for Palestine, which encouraged non-party members to sign up to the party to make sure the policy was debated and adopted. After it was passed, supporters came to the front of the hall to hug and cheer.
One member who opposed the motion said: “There are now two Green parties – the everyday members, and those who have joined for just one reason, Palestine, and who have no interest in anything else.”
There is considerable disquiet among some senior Greens who feel that Polanski, who is Jewish, could have taken a stronger stance on the issue. The party leader has justified the motion’s broad argument by pointing to the death toll in Gaza during Israel’s assault on the territory.
Asked on Saturday if he believed Zionism was racist, Polanski told the BBC: “Well, in the motion, it is defined as the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people. I think that is clearly racism.”
After the vote, the party’s five MPs, plus Polanski and his two co-deputy leaders, released a joint statement saying the party “will never tolerate any form of discrimination or harassment”, adding: “We know there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people.”
However, Ramsay, Chowns, Berry and Denyer all posted this on social media with messages noting their opposition to the motion.
The Movement for Progressive Judaism, one of the main Jewish denominations in the UK, condemned the vote, saying: “The motion is antisemitic in its formulation and intention. By adopting it, the Green party has made antisemitism party policy and become a racist party.
“Jewish self-determination is a right. Declaring it racist is an attack on Jews. The Green party has chosen to brand Jews who hold this belief as racists and make their equal participation in the party conditional on renouncing it.”
Adam Langleben, who coordinated complaints from the Jewish Labour Movement to the Equality and Human Rights Commission, said: “This is without doubt the most antisemitic and racist motion brought before a mainstream political party in my lifetime. It is Corbynism on steroids, and would seem even more open to legal challenge.”

Switzerland’s heaviest pumpkin weighs in at 651kgs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:15:02 UTC
23:15:02 KST

Switzerland’s heaviest pumpkin weighs in at 651kgs
The heaviest pumpkin in Switzerland, weighing 651.5 kilos, was grown in a private garden in canton Zurich.
This marks the third consecutive year that the same grower has won the Swiss championship.
This exceptional specimen belongs to the Atlantic Giant variety. Florian Isler set three Swiss records: the heaviest specimen of the Bushel Gourd variety weighing 136.6 kg, the tallest sunflower (7.695 metres) and the heaviest watermelon (97.2 kg).
Other Swiss and world records for giant vegetables were also broken. The Meier family, from Dättlikon, now hold the world record for the heaviest sweet potato (single tuber) at 13.6 kg. Jürg Wiesli, from Dozwil, broke the world record for the longest chilli, measuring 54.3 centimetres.
A total of 18 giant pumpkins were weighed at the Bächlihof farm. Sixteen teams had registered for the event, including two teams of growers and two families.
Among the 18 specimens weighed were 14 orange pumpkins of the Atlantic Giant variety and four green squash.
The current Swiss record for a pumpkin stands at 1,054 kilograms. The world record is 1,278.8 kilograms.
During Saturday’s competition, the various vegetables were transported to the scales using a forklift truck.

After Ukrainian drone attacks, demand for electric vehicles in Russia nearly doubled - NYT
Kyiv • UNN
Sales of electric vehicles and hybrids in Russia rose to 83,000 in January–August. The reason was a gasoline shortage following attacks by Ukrainian drones.
Demand for electric vehicles in Russia has nearly doubled after Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries. This is reported by The New York Times, reports UNN.
Details
According to the publication, Russian automotive expert Sergey Tselikov owned more than 20 cars, but in July he bought a Chinese electric hatchback after experiencing problems with the availability of gasoline at filling stations.
I tried to refuel one of my cars and drove to the five nearest filling stations, but they had only diesel fuel or lower-quality gasoline
According to available data, the number of electric vehicles sold in Russia, including hybrids, rose from 43,000 between January and August 2025 to more than 83,000 over the same period this year.
As Ukraine increasingly brings the war to Russia, the consequences may be most visible on the roads. Since the end of June, Russia’s electric vehicle market has more than doubled. Most electric vehicles sold in the country are Chinese, signaling an economic shift. Russia is trying to catch up
According to the publication, Tselikov had to act quickly, as the price of a vehicle manufactured by Great Wall Motor rose by approximately $2,000 within a few days due to a sharp increase in demand.
According to Avtostat, an automotive industry research agency headed by Mr. Tselikov, by the end of September, the share of fully electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid cars that can operate without gasoline had reached 11.5% of the Russian automotive market, compared with approximately 5% at the beginning of the year. Russia’s electric vehicle market share is now slightly higher than that of the United States, but it is only a small fraction of China’s share, which stands at 45%. Although the surge in the popularity of electric vehicles in Russia is driven by a specific factor — Ukrainian attacks — this shift is the latest example there of how war and supply disruptions can quickly alter car-buying decisions
We remind you
In many regions of Russia, the shortage of gasoline and diesel fuel is deepening. Drivers are complaining of a critical shortage and recording appeals to Putin.

Little more than an hour after the drama began aboard a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, claims were already spreading online that Israel had staged the incident.
According to research by CAM’s antisemitism research center, 2,963 posts on X within 12 hours attributed the incident to Israel, Mossad, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Zionists or Jews. A post by Jackson Hinkle, a far-right American influencer associated with conspiracy theories, disinformation and strongly anti-Israel content, portrayed the incident as a staged operation and drew more than 2.4 million views.
From there, the theory expanded rapidly: Netanyahu supposedly knew in advance; Israeli security personnel had allegedly been planted on the plane; the flight number supposedly concealed an Oct. 7 message; and the absence of deployed oxygen masks, even a cup of water that did not spill, was presented as proof that the entire incident had been staged.
At the same time, a fabricated video made to resemble a BBC report circulated online, alleging involvement by Mossad and Indian intelligence officials.
But information that emerged in the days after the incident did not come only from Israel. Flydubai confirmed there had been a confrontation in the cockpit, and on Saturday the United Arab Emirates’ attorney general said the co-pilot had attempted to carry out a “terrorist act,” attacked the captain with an emergency axe and tried to seize control of the aircraft.
The investigation into his motive and any possible connections is continuing.
So what lies behind the claims circulating online, what has already been disproved and what questions remain unanswered?
‘Israel staged the incident’
This is the central conspiracy theory from which most of the others stem: that the attempted hijacking did not happen as described, but was instead a “false flag” operation intended to benefit Israel, whether by strengthening Netanyahu before the election, creating justification for action against Iran or portraying Israel as a victim of terrorism.
During the first hours after the incident, there was a genuine gap between the dramatic details being reported in Israel and Flydubai’s highly cautious initial wording. The airline at first confirmed only that an “incident” had occurred during the flight and that the aircraft had landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
It later confirmed that a confrontation had taken place in the cockpit and that members of its crew secured the aircraft and landed it safely.
Then, on Oct. 3, a source that could hardly be described as part of an Israeli narrative entered the picture: the UAE attorney general.
He said the investigation had found that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a “terrorist act,” attacked the captain with an emergency axe and tried to take control of the aircraft.
That announcement still does not answer what motivated him, whether he acted alone or whether he had ties to any organization. But it contradicts the claim that the cockpit attack itself was an Israeli fabrication.
‘Netanyahu warned about it a day earlier, then it happened’
This is one of the most effective details in the conspiracy theory because its underlying premise is real.
A day before the incident, Netanyahu said Israel had “indications” that its enemies might try to attack it ahead of the Oct. 27 election. He did not specify the nature of the threat.
The following morning, the drama aboard flight FZ1073 unfolded.
The coincidence can prompt questions, but it is not evidence that Netanyahu knew in advance about the flight, let alone that Israel organized the incident.
No evidence published so far has linked Netanyahu’s warning to the Flydubai flight.
‘The plane plunged, so why didn’t the oxygen masks drop?’
This is one of the most frequently repeated technical claims.
Flight-tracking data showed an unusually sharp descent. The aircraft, which had been cruising at about 34,000 feet, descended to roughly 16,600 feet in about a minute and a half. During part of that descent, it lost nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds.
But passenger oxygen masks are not triggered simply because the aircraft itself falls below a certain altitude, nor because it descends rapidly.
The system responds to pressure inside the cabin. On Boeing 737 aircraft, the oxygen system is automatically activated when the “cabin altitude,” the equivalent altitude produced by cabin pressure, rises above roughly 14,000 feet.
An aircraft can descend rapidly from cruising altitude while the cabin remains pressurized. In that situation, there would be no reason for the oxygen masks to deploy.
No cabin-pressure data from the incident has been released, so it is not possible to determine precisely what happened to the pressurization system.
But the absence of dangling oxygen masks in passenger videos does not prove the aircraft did not lose altitude.
‘What about the cup of water that didn’t spill?’
A cup of water also became a centerpiece of the conspiracy claims.
Posts circulating online highlighted a cup standing on a tray table inside the aircraft, arguing that if the plane had really “fallen” thousands of feet, the cup could not possibly have remained in place.
There is, however, no evidence that the image was taken during the precise tens of seconds in which the aircraft underwent its unusual loss of altitude.
And descending thousands of feet per minute does not necessarily mean an aircraft is in free fall. Flight-tracking data shows altitude and vertical speed, but by itself does not reveal the G-forces acting on passengers and objects at every moment.
Without flight-recorder data and an exact timestamp for the image, the cup cannot be used to reconstruct the aircraft’s motion, much less prove that the descent did not happen.
One of the countless social-media posts focusing on the cup drew 5.2 million views.
‘But the videos were filmed on two different planes’
Here, conspiracy theorists noticed something real: the two videos they compared do show different aircraft.
The problem is that one of them had nothing to do with the incident.
One video showed passengers aboard the Flydubai aircraft. Another, circulated as footage of FZ1073 passengers celebrating after the plane was secured, showed Israelis dancing aboard an aircraft while one carried a large speaker.
Online users compared the ceilings, seats and overhead bins and concluded that the footage came from two different cabins, supposedly proving the event was staged.
A fact-check by Lead Stories found that the second video was filmed in August 2025, more than a year before the Flydubai incident, and showed Israel’s national basketball team traveling to EuroBasket.
So the observation that the videos show two different aircraft was correct. The claim that both videos depicted the same flight was not.
Contrary to claims online, this is not footage from the hijacked flight
‘BBC exposed a Mossad link to Indian intelligence’
After the incident, a video began circulating that at first glance appeared to be a BBC News report.
It featured BBC presenter Sally Bundock and purported to link an Indian citizen to the incident while raising allegations about Indian intelligence and Mossad involvement.
The video was fabricated.
The BBC confirmed to fact-checking organization Full Fact that it was not genuine, while ABC Verify found that authentic footage of Bundock had been paired with a fabricated voice track and script.
The video also mixed footage unrelated to the Flydubai flight with genuine images from the incident. According to ABC, it was viewed hundreds of thousands of times.
This was no longer simply a competing interpretation of a real event. The purported “evidence” itself had been manufactured.
‘1073 really means 10/7/3’
Even the flight number was drawn into the conspiracy theories.
Online posts suggested reading FZ1073 as 10/7/3, a reference to Oct. 7 and three years since the Hamas attack, and presented the supposed code as evidence that the incident had been planned in advance.
But FZ1073 was not a flight number assigned specifically for Sept. 30.
Plane Finder flight history shows the number was already being used for Flydubai’s Dubai-Tel Aviv route between Sept. 11 and 17, weeks before the incident.
The fact that the flight number existed beforehand turns the supposed code into a numerical coincidence, not evidence of advance planning.
‘How did there happen to be more pilots on board?’
Another detail presented as suspicious was the presence of additional crew members aboard the aircraft who were capable of flying it after the cockpit confrontation.
Some posts went further, describing them as Israeli “special forces” operatives planted on the flight in advance.
But Flydubai itself directly confirmed the presence of its crew members.
The airline said the aircraft was “successfully secured” by Flydubai personnel traveling on the flight, who diverted it and landed safely in Tabuk.
The company’s CEO later thanked the captain, “the pilots who secured the aircraft and landed it safely,” the cabin crew and passengers who assisted.
Transporting airline crew as passengers between destinations is a routine part of commercial aviation.
Flydubai has not publicly explained in detail why those particular crew members were aboard that flight, so there is no basis for drawing conclusions beyond the airline’s account.
But no evidence has been published showing they were Israeli security personnel planted on the aircraft.
There are real questions, too
None of this means every detail of the affair has been explained.
On the contrary, information that emerged after the incident has raised serious questions about the co-pilot and the background checks he underwent.
AP reported that the suspect, identified by three sources as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani citizen, had previously been removed from flying duties at Oman Air because of concerns over extremist views and transferred to an administrative role. He was later hired by Flydubai.
A Gulf diplomat quoted by AP said al-Hammami underwent standard security checks before he was hired, but in the diplomat’s assessment those checks focused on whether he had criminal convictions and did not include a deeper examination for possible signs of radicalization.
The diplomat said the continuing investigation had so far found no link between al-Hammami and a terrorist organization. The UAE attorney general has also said possible connections remain under investigation.
CNN reported that social-media accounts linked to al-Hammami contained extremist material, including a video featuring images of former al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri and Humam Khalil Abu-Mulal al-Balawi, the suicide bomber who carried out the 2009 attack on a CIA base in Afghanistan.
However, the video was posted about nine hours after the Flydubai incident, meaning it remains unclear who uploaded it or whether it had been scheduled for publication beforehand.
Another question concerns how al-Hammami came to be assigned to a flight to Israel.
According to a document obtained by ynet, Flydubai had committed as early as 2020 to implementing restrictions in its crew-scheduling system designed to comply with “nationality restrictions for flights to Israel,” as required by Israel’s Transportation Ministry.
After the incident, ministry officials said the assignment of the Omani pilot apparently violated that commitment.
The affair also exposed a broader problem: Israel currently has no mechanism for individually screening in advance the identity and background of every crew member aboard commercial flights operated by foreign airlines.
Transportation Ministry officials acknowledged that Israel relies heavily on declarations by foreign airlines and on security systems in the countries where those airlines are based.
The question, therefore, is not only how al-Hammami came to be assigned to an Israel-bound flight, but who was supposed to identify the problem before the aircraft took off.
UAE authorities also have yet to present a final picture.
The attorney general said the investigation is continuing and is examining, among other issues, the motive, the full circumstances of the incident, possible connections and physical and digital evidence.
That may be the most important distinction between fact-checking and conspiracy theory: an unexplained detail is a reason to keep asking questions. It is not proof that the entire event was staged.
Questions remain surrounding FZ1073. But so far, no evidence has been presented that the incident was fabricated.
What does exist are flight-tracking data, official Flydubai statements and an explicit finding from UAE authorities that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a terrorist act.

What next after Iraq’s sovereignty day?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:08:53 UTC
23:08:53 KST

What next after Iraq’s sovereignty day?
TEHRAN – Will Baghdad truly be able to make its own decisions? This is the question many Iraqis are asking following the September 30 celebration of what is known as “sovereignty day.”
Has Iraq escaped the restrictions of foreign military presence only to enter another form of control that is less obvious and may last even longer? This matter can no longer be delayed, especially after U.S. forces, under a coalition of about 82 countries, completed their withdrawal from their last bases at the end of September 2026.
This marked a victory for those who fought in the battles of dignity, honor, and resistance. At the same time, Iraq and Turkey reached an understanding to gradually transfer the Bashiqa-Zilkan base to the Iraqi government. Several other steps to strengthen Iraqi state sovereignty are also waiting to be settled through national and foreign negotiations that lie ahead.
This event has closed a difficult chapter that, in many different forms, began in 2003. But it does not answer the harder question: Will Iraqis truly have the power to make their own decisions?
Sovereignty cannot simply be measured by the absence of foreign soldiers. That is only partial sovereignty. Real sovereignty is measured by a state’s ability to make decisions, carry them out, and accept the cost of those decisions. Only then does it truly deserve to be called sovereign.
As a matter of principle, even before considering the facts on the ground, neither the legal nor the geographical answer is sufficient. A state recognized by the international community must have institutions with the power and independence necessary to exercise full sovereignty in practice. Only then can sovereignty move from being a formal principle written into the constitution to something real on the ground.
For this reason, a distinction must be made between formal sovereignty and effective sovereignty. Formal sovereignty means that the state is legally independent and free from foreign authority. Effective sovereignty, by contrast, means that the state itself possesses the capacity to exercise that independence in practice, making and enforcing its own decisions across the country.
What has been achieved at the first level is not a small thing. It would not be reasonable to call for state sovereignty while ignoring the departure of a foreign military force that had been the subject of deep political and legal disagreement in the country for more than two decades. But the first step, important as it is, is only the beginning. What comes next is much harder.
What has been achieved at the first level is not a small thing. It would not be reasonable to call for state sovereignty while ignoring the departure of a foreign military force that had been at the center of deep political and legal disagreement in the country for more than two decades. But the first step, important as it is, is only the beginning. What comes next is much harder.
The Iraqi contradiction that has emerged in reactions to the withdrawal itself is difficult to ignore. Some groups see it as a political and security victory for themselves, while others warn of possible security gaps and the return of Daesh cells, in a different form, to vulnerable areas following the end of the U.S. military occupation.
This shows the difference between independence and capacity. A country may be legally independent while remaining weak in practice. It may have the right to make its own decisions in theory while lacking the means to carry them out. Modern states do not simply declare themselves sovereign; they must build the power and capacity necessary to protect and exercise that sovereignty.
This requires a state built on institutions rather than competing centers of power that share control, influence, and resources.
What Iraq needs is an independent national will based on the country’s interests, security, laws, and the needs of its people. Through its legitimate institutions, Iraq itself should determine the nature of its relations with Washington, Ankara, Riyadh, Tehran, Cairo, Amman, and every other capital.
This does not mean calling for isolation. A sovereign state can form alliances, draw on the experience of other countries, sign security and economic agreements, and develop broad strategic partnerships. The important distinction is that it does so according to its own decisions and to strengthen its own capabilities, rather than out of a lack of those capabilities.
Relations with Iraq should be based on equal treatment and shared interests, not on what can be taken from it while it is busy dealing with its own wounds.
Sovereignty is a combination of many kinds of power, and they cannot be separated. A state that does not have a strong economy, a reliable financial system, reasonably independent technology and infrastructure, highly capable institutions, and international relationships that give it room to act will remain open to pressure and control, especially when that pressure comes from Washington.
When it comes to economic sovereignty, Iraq has spent the past two decades receiving more than nine-tenths of its government budget from oil sales. The income from this oil is deposited in an account connected to the U.S. financial system. Sending dollars abroad is also subject to compliance and checking rules imposed by correspondent banks. As a result, Iraq’s banking sector itself has become unable to fully depend on the world’s trust in it.
Iraq has become a country that pays the salaries of millions of employees from one main source of income, sells that resource in one currency, and yet cannot honestly say that its economy is free.
When it comes to energy and water sovereignty, Iraq imports gas, oil products, and electricity. At the same time, its Turkish neighbor controls much of the water flowing from the upper Tigris and Euphrates rivers in the north. These rivers are a lifeline for central and southern Iraq, leaving Iraqi summers dependent on decisions made in Ankara.
This weakness is the fault of the state, diplomacy, poor planning and absence of a national strategy for governing the country. Neighbors have watched Iraq’s great natural wealth become a burden instead of being turned into industry, agriculture, refineries, and transportation networks. This makes no sense and cannot be accepted as normal. As a result, control over shared resources has become a bargaining tool rather than the basis for cooperation and partnership.
In the area of digital sovereignty, Iraqis live their daily lives using platforms, services, and computer servers that they do not control. Their personal information, messages, and family photographs are stored in data centers far across the seas. The state sometimes even shuts down the entire internet during exam periods because it has no other way to stop cheating. In doing so, it punishes an entire society because one institution cannot solve a problem.
In education and culture, sovereignty also faces difficult questions about school programs, universities, and scientific research. Who is shaping the minds of the next generation? Who is giving them the tools to understand the region and the world and produce something useful? Do universities graduate students who will build the country, or people who look for a way to leave it?
As for military sovereignty on land, at sea, and in the air, it requires an army and a Popular Mobilization Force with a unified command and military doctrine. It also requires an air defense system capable of protecting Iraqi airspace, most of which is still exposed. Iraq also needs its own military industry, even if it is modest, to reduce its complete dependence on one source for weapons, spare parts, and training.
Every oil revenue that, over the past decades, failed to become a school, factory, university, power station, bank, or national company represents part of the national strength Iraq lost. When the moment comes to make an important decision, Baghdad suddenly discovers that the wealth it consumed was never turned into real power.
The experiences of other nations can show Iraq a possible path, without suggesting that their models should simply be copied. For instance, nations that came out of war were among the poorest countries in the world. They invested in education and industry and eventually became able to negotiate with powerful countries because they had something of their own to offer.
These countries succeeded because they understood that sovereignty is built through long-term work, not through loud slogans. Iraq has enough resources, a good geographical position, and talented people. What it lacks is something that cannot simply be bought in a market: a united political will that puts the state above the political party and public interest above personal gain.
Recognizing how difficult the task is does not justify delaying it. The period after the U.S.-led forces leave Iraq could make the cost of reform much higher if there is no banking reform, economic diversification, or rebuilding of the country’s security and education institutions.
From the point of view of the people, who matter most, sovereignty is not a privilege for those in power or a decoration used in political speeches. It is a guarantee of a citizen’s everyday life. It means electricity that does not disappear because of a decision made outside Iraq. It means water reaching Basra is safe to drink. It means a salary that does not depend on changes in the mood of the U.S. Federal Reserve.
The departure of the U.S.-led forces is a major event in Iraq’s modern history. It is a legitimate step toward recovering some of the sovereignty lost because of direct U.S. intervention in Iraqi affairs, as well as what followed from the Israeli regime’s involvement in different forms: military, ideological, political, social, cultural, and geographical terrorism, targeting both Iraq’s democratic experience and its society.
The question before was: When will the foreign forces leave? The question now is: What comes after sovereignty? It is time for those who hold the power to govern and make decisions. From now on, there will be no one else to blame for failures in running the state.

The Green Party has become the first mainstream party in Europe to declare itself openly anti-Zionist after voting in the controversial "Zionism is Racism" motion at its party conference in Brighton, UK, on Sunday, passing the motion 1,022 votes to 813.
Amendment III - which would have protected Jewish people from being expelled if they belong to synagogues that define themselves as Zionist - also failed to pass, with 684 votes in support and 1,026 against.
Israel's Foreign Ministry issued a statement on social media in response to the resolution on Sunday, claiming that the Green Party was "legitimising armed struggle against Israel, and calling for the establishment of a Palestinian state “from the river to the sea” - meaning the destruction of the State of Israel."
"The resolution constitutes a clear antisemitic text according to the IHRA definition," the Foreign Ministry added, "as it denies the Jewish people’s right to self-determination."
The Green Party previously planned to vote on the motion at its Spring Conference in March; however, multiple no-confidence votes were submitted, creating delays and meaning it was never heard or debated.
The motion recognizes Zionism as Israel’s foundational ideology that has created and maintains an apartheid regime between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea.
It further affirms the right to self-determination and liberation of the Palestinian people and supports the establishment of a “single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine, with Jerusalem as its capital.” This would effectively eradicate the State of Israel.
On Saturday, Zack Polanski told the conference, "We stand with one voice now as we say: 'Drop the charges. End the genocide. Deproscribe Palestine Action.'"
However, according to The Telegraph, Polanski did not vote on the motion, as he was on the campaign trail in north London ahead of Thursday's Holborn and St Pancras by-election.
Polanski, who is Jewish, has nevertheless failed to condemn the motion.
Jewish Greens remain split on motion
The Jewish Greens - a Jewish group within the party - remain split on the Zionism is Racism motion. Ahead of the conference, the group answered a survey about key conference issues.
On a 0–10 scale measuring whether Jewish Greens should collectively oppose the motion, the average was 5.1, indicating an almost exact split. Consequently, Jewish Greens said it will not take an official position on the motion.
Most Jewish Greens (81%) identify as anti-Zionist or non-Zionist. Of the Zionist respondents, 80% of Zionist respondents oppose the Zionism as Racism motion. Interestingly, however, the anti-Zionist Greens were divided on the motion too.
A majority of 70% strongly support de-proscribing Palestine Action, and 64% strongly support Palestinians' right to "resist apartheid, occupation and genocide through all available means within international law.”
Exactly half support criminal prosecution of UK citizens who fight with the Israeli military.
'Safe-rooms' designated for Jews during the conference
Another shocking revelation came when Jewish members of the party told the Mail on Sunday that a designated 'safe-room' has been set aside during the conference for Jewish members who feel they are in danger.
“We have been given a ‘safe room’ for Jewish members to use in an emergency,” a member told the Mail on Sunday.
“It was used on the first day of the conference to host a meeting between a rabbi and some Jewish members. It’s a deeply upsetting situation, but that’s the reality.”
Rabbi Charley Baginsky and Rabbi Josh Levy, Co-Leads of the Movement for Progressive Judaism, told The Jerusalem Post Sunday that the motion is "antisemitic in its formulation and intention."
"By adopting it, the Green Party has made antisemitism party policy and become a racist party," the two said.
"Jewish self-determination is a right. Declaring it racist is an attack on Jews. The Green Party has chosen to brand Jews who hold this belief as racists and make their equal participation in the party conditional on renouncing it."
Baginsky and Levy said Jews should not have to justify their connections to Israel to be entitled to equal treatment, nor should they have to disown their communities to participate in British politics.
"Support for this motion from some Jewish members does not excuse discrimination against other Jews."
"We stand with Jewish members and our communities. We will challenge this policy and hold the Green Party’s leadership accountable for the discrimination it has endorsed."
Yaakov Hagoel, the Chairman of the World Zionist Organization, told the Post that the Green Party of England and Wales's decision to adopt a resolution defining Zionism as racism is a "shameful, scandalous resolution tainted with severe antisemitism."
"Zionism is the national movement of the Jewish people and expresses its historical, legal, and moral right to self-determination in its homeland. The attempt to portray it as racist is a recycling of modern blood libels and dark UN resolutions (such as Resolution 3379), which have long since been repealed and thrown into the dustbin of history," he said.
Israel's Foreign Ministry said that, with the vote, the Green Party in Britain has "ceased to act as a political party and became a body that gives legitimacy to terrorism."
"The Greens have adopted not only the green of Hamas, but also its ideology: the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle."
The shocking resolution adopted today legitimizes armed struggle, calls for a Palestinian state “from the river to the sea” - meaning the destruction of the State of Israel - and labels as “racist” the aspiration of the Jewish people for self-determination.
"Every political party in Britain, first and foremost the governing Labour Party, must unequivocally reject this twisted resolution," the ministry added.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

High Court rejects Democrats’ bid to bar Otzma Yehudit from election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:08:18 UTC
23:08:18 KST

The High Court of Justice on Sunday rejected The Democrats’ petition to remove Otzma Yehudit from the October 27 election.
The Election Law did not give the party the right to appeal the Central Elections Committee’s decision, the court ruled, adding that the circumstances did not justify making an exception.
The judges also rejected The Democrats’ appeal to disqualify National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and MK Tally Gotliv individually. They ruled that it had not been signed by the required one-third of the committee’s members.
The ruling leaves the party and both candidates in the race. It does not, however, decide whether The Democrats’ allegations that Otzma Yehudit undermines Israel’s democratic character and incites racism are correct.
The court dismissed the case on procedural grounds without examining those claims on their merits.
Justice Ofer Grosskopf wrote the decision, which was joined by Justices Dafna Barak-Erez and Khaled Kabub.
The dispute began with two separate decisions by the Central Elections Committee last month.
Democrats argue Otzma Yehudit incited racism and negated Israel as a democratic state
On September 24, the committee voted 19-10, with one abstention, to reject requests by The Democrats and the Zulat Institute, an Israeli left-wing research institute, to disqualify the entire Otzma Yehudit slate. The party’s actions negated Israel’s existence as a democratic state and amounted to incitement to racism, they said.
Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara opposed disqualifying the slate. Her position described the evidence as deeply troubling and said it brought Otzma Yehudit very close to the prohibited line. Nevertheless, she concluded that it did not meet the exceptionally high evidentiary threshold required to remove an entire party from an election.
The Democrats had also sought to disqualify Ben-Gvir and Gotliv individually. Justice Noam Sohlberg, chairman of the Central Elections Committee, dismissed that request on September 14 because it was not supported by the signatures of at least one-third of the committee’s members, as required by law.
Election Law allows only the attorney-general, the Central Elections Committee chairman, or at least one-third of the committee’s members to appeal a decision allowing a party to run, and The Democrats did not fall into any of those categories.
A request to disqualify an individual candidate must similarly carry the signatures of one-third of the committee before it can be considered. Because the Democrats did not obtain those signatures, the requests concerning Ben-Gvir and Gotliv were never properly placed before the full committee.
The Democrats acknowledged those obstacles but argued that the High Court retains broad constitutional authority to intervene in exceptional circumstances. They said the evidence against Otzma Yehudit and its leading candidates was so extreme that the judges should hear the case despite the procedural failures.
The judges said they still had the power to intervene, but The Democrats needed to show a compelling reason to depart from the appeal process set by law. They had not done so, particularly given the compressed election timetable.
The judges said much of the petition had focused on Ben-Gvir and Gotliv and relied partly on the attorney-general’s position concerning Otzma Yehudit. Yet The Democrats had not approached the attorney-general and asked her to exercise her own authority to appeal the committee’s approval of the slate.
Petition against Ben-Gvir and Gotliv was filed too late
The court also found that the challenge concerning Ben-Gvir and Gotliv had been filed too late. The petition was submitted on Tuesday, more than two weeks after Sohlberg rejected the individual disqualification requests.
Candidate and party approvals must be completed quickly enough for the election to proceed on schedule, Grosskopf said.
The Democrats said senior Otzma Yehudit figures had acted against the rule of law, judicial independence, separation of powers, and equal protection of citizens. Their petition cited Ben-Gvir’s alleged interference in police operations and appointments, Gotliv’s statements concerning compliance with court rulings, and the conduct of other candidates whom the party accused of promoting racist views.
The petition also cited expressions of support by party candidates for Amiram Ben Uliel, who was convicted of murdering three members of the Dawabshe family in the 2015 Duma arson attack and allegedly identified with the ideology of the outlawed Kach movement.
Otzma Yehudit opposed the original disqualification requests and argued that they should be rejected on their merits.
Baharav-Miara, while sharply criticizing aspects of Ben-Gvir’s conduct as national security minister, said misconduct that could justify judicial intervention in his ministerial role did not necessarily satisfy the substantially higher test for barring an entire party from an election.

“And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president. And it really is a form of protection,” he added.

US President Donald Trump on Sunday confirmed national intelligence chief Jay Clayton as head of a new White House task force on artificial intelligence, amid increasingly vocal warnings from researchers about the technology's potential dangers.
Under Clayton, the new Super Intelligence Force -- Trump's preferred term for artificial intelligence -- will ensure that the United States "continue to lead the world" in AI development, the president posted on his Truth Social platform.
Trump said the force had also been tasked to "protect the interests, and improve the lives of all Americans."
Clayton will become the second person to hold the informal title after venture capitalist David Sacks, who held the role at the start of Trump's second term before stepping down.
Sacks continues to advise the president on AI, as does Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
Coordinating federal efforts
Trump said last month he would create an AI force modeled on the Space Force he established during his first term, and name a czar to coordinate federal efforts.
A longtime Wall Street lawyer, Clayton represented Goldman Sachs during the 2008 financial crisis and Barclays in its purchase of Lehman Brothers' assets.
He chaired the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump's first term, where he largely took a pro-business stance but brought enforcement cases against the nascent crypto industry.
Crypto entrepreneurs have since become major Trump backers.
Trump tapped Clayton to lead federal prosecutors in Manhattan at the start of his second term, and the Senate confirmed him as intelligence chief in July.
AI potential dangers
The appointment would come as AI researchers warn of the technology's potential dangers, following cases of AI systems going rogue and hacking outside systems.
Trump has resisted tighter AI regulation, arguing a slowdown could hand Chinese firms an advantage and that federal law enforcement can deal with bad actors misusing the technology.

Those concerns gained force from a run of incidents in which tech giant OpenAI's autonomous systems slipped out of their constraints, beginning with a July breach of Hugging Face -- a widely used platform for sharing AI models.

"The risk of not being first is high," Clayton told the Journal.
"Not being first increases the identified and unidentified risks, particularly from our adversaries. Being first will better enable us to address those risks on behalf of the American people."

London Exhibition Reclaims Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra Treasures as Ukrainian Heritage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:03:00 UTC
23:03:00 KST

The Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) in London has opened “Sacred Treasures from Kyiv,” presenting seven sacred works from the collection of the National Preserve “Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra” in the UK for the first time. The display also brings the Lavra works together with Holy Gates already held by the V&A on a long-term loan, accompanied by updated historical and artistic interpretation.
The display opened in mid-September at V&A South Kensington and will run until Sept. 17, 2027. The seven works represent Ukrainian Baroque sacred art and include pieces created by Kyiv goldsmiths in the 17th and 18th centuries. They include an icon, a silver-bound altar Gospel, a diskos, a silver-gilt chalice depicting the Crucifixion, a cross, and other liturgical objects.
The display builds on a multi-year partnership between the V&A and the National Preserve “Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra,” including research into the provenance and history of two pairs of rare silver-gilt Holy Gates from the Lavra.
During the Soviet period, the Gates were removed from the monastery and later passed through several private collections abroad. For decades, their origins and history were described through a Russian imperial framework. Research by the V&A in collaboration with Ukrainian specialists has helped establish a more accurate historical context and connection to the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra.
Ukraine’s Science Under Fire: Russia Is Targeting Knowledge, People and the Future
The Holy Gates are now held by the V&A on a long-term loan from the Gilbert Trust for the Arts. Some of the seven works lent by the Lavra were made by the same craftsmen who worked on the Gates. Displaying the objects together helps clarify their connections within a shared Ukrainian artistic tradition.
Ukraine’s Deputy Prime Minister for Humanitarian Policy and Minister of Culture Tetyana Berezhna said the presentation marks a significant change in how Ukrainian heritage is represented at one of Britain’s major museums.
“For the first time, these seven important objects, as well as our Lavra Gates, are presented at the Victoria and Albert Museum, one of the most visited and largest museums in the United Kingdom, as Ukrainian artifacts. That is, as objects representing the history of Ukraine.”
According to Berezhna, the objects had long been held by the museum, but their information had previously presented them as belonging to or being connected with Russia and Russian history.
She said: “We are very grateful to the museum team and to the team of Ukrainian historians and researchers who were able to show the museum the true history, open the genuine archives, and connect these artefacts – the cross, the icon, and the Gospel – with Ukraine, with the Ukrainian Lavra, and with our history. This is a process of decolonisation that we, as a country that for a long time was under the occupation of different empires, have to go through.”
Berezhnа noted that the Lavra objects will remain at the V&A until September 2027.
“We very much hope that one day these treasures will return to Ukraine, but for now, being in one of the world’s largest museums, they fulfil a dual purpose. First, these treasures, as the name of the display itself suggests, tell the world about Ukraine. And secondly, they are genuinely safe here at the moment,” she added.
V&A Director Tristram Hunt highlighted the artistic significance of the works and the importance of further international cooperation.
“These national treasures showcase the exceptional skill of Ukrainian silversmiths and illuminate the rich artistic heritage preserved by the Lavra. We hope that the display and conference this September will inspire greater appreciation of Ukraine’s unique heritage and foster collaboration across the cultural sector to uncover and share the country’s remarkable story.”
Founded in the 11th century, Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra has been an important centre of spiritual life, learning, art, and patronage for nearly a millennium. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The V&A display opened in a year marking the 975th anniversary of the Lavra and the centenary of the National Preserve “Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra.”
The project is supported by the British Council, Gilbert Trust for the Arts, the Ukrainian Institute, Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture, Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Embassy in the United Kingdom. It is also part of the wider cultural cooperation under the UK-Ukraine 100 Year Partnership.

Russia Nears Completion of Hangars Likely Intended for Tu-22M3, Tu-95, and Tu-160 at Ramenskoye Airfield Near Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:01:16 UTC
23:01:16 KST

Satellite imagery shows that Russia is nearing completion of hangars at Ramenskoye airfield near Moscow. They are likely intended for testing Tu-22M3, Tu-95, and Tu-160 bombers.
Analysts from the AviVector group published recent imagery of the airfield.
The new construction was first identified in March 2026. The first building measures 100 × 230 × 33 meters and contains three separate hangars, each about 77 meters wide. Its annex measures 17 × 220 × 8 meters, while the second building measures 90 × 220 meters.
For simply housing bombers, the dimensions of the first building appear excessive. Each section, about 77 meters wide, exceeds the maximum wingspan of even the Tu-160 by approximately 21 meters, while its 100-meter depth exceeds the aircraft’s length by almost 46 meters.
The structure is 33 meters high, approximately 2.5 times the height of the largest missile-carrying aircraft. This extra space may be needed for repair and modernization work using cranes, work platforms, and other equipment.
A road connects the construction site with the Gromov Flight Research Institute, but there is no connection allowing aircraft to reach the runway.
The imagery also shows hangars made of conventional metal structures with lightweight roofs. These structures do not protect against potential drone or missile attacks.
Ramenskoye airfield is located in Zhukovsky town, Moscow region, and is part of the test infrastructure of the Mikhail Gromov Flight Research Institute. It serves experimental, government, and civil aviation. The same airfield is also home to Zhukovsky International Airport, which opened in May 2016.
Aircraft manufacturers also use the airfield for flight testing. In particular, Sukhoi’s base in Zhukovsky participated in tests of the Su-57, while Yakovlev’s facility conducts certification tests of the MC-21 and the new Superjet with Russian engines and systems. Meanwhile, a branch of the Tupolev company, which has its own production, laboratory, and testing facilities, conducts tests of experimental and upgraded Tu-160M, Tu-95MS, and Tu-22M3 aircraft.
Another hypothesis is that the new structures could be part of an expansion of the exhibition facility, whose pavilions are located directly next to the construction site. The MAKS International Aviation and Space Exhibition was held here. It was established in Zhukovsky in 1993 and was traditionally held every two years on the Gromov Flight Research Institute’s airfield.
Russia’s Ministry of Industry and Trade and the state corporation Rostec organized the exhibition, while Aviasalon handled preparations. For Russian manufacturers, it served as a platform for presenting new developments to potential customers.
The airfield featured a permanent exhibition facility for the salon, covering more than 42 hectares. More than 40,000 square meters were allocated for pavilions and exhibition chalets, while more than 45,000 square meters were designated for outdoor equipment displays. The new structures’ location next to the exhibition area suggests they could be part of its expansion.

Women and underrepresented minorities have higher tenure-track placement rates in the political science job market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:00:35 UTC
23:00:35 KST

Getting a tenure-track faculty position is often the primary goal for doctoral students, but the odds of landing one are notoriously low. A recent analysis of the political science job market suggests that while the prestige of a candidate’s university is linked to the type of academic institution they end up at, it does not actually predict whether they will secure a professorship. The research, published in PS: Political Science & Politics, indicates that having a strong publication record, studying a high-demand field, and being a female or an underrepresented minority candidate are stronger predictors of finding a tenure-track academic job.
A tenure-track professorship is a university teaching and research position that can eventually lead to a permanent, lifelong appointment. In many academic fields, the competition for these roles is intense, with far more new graduates than available openings.
Past research analyzing this system has pointed to a rigid prestige hierarchy. For instance, a 2022 study of faculty hiring across the United States found that a small minority of elite universities supply the vast majority of professors. Similarly, a 2025 analysis of political science departments indicated that the top 20 percent of programs produced 75 percent of tenure-track faculty at U.S. doctoral departments, while the bottom half produced less than 5 percent.
These past studies tend to imply that graduating from a top-tier university is the only reliable way to get a job in academia. But that approach relies on looking backward at the people who already secured positions at major research universities. This method can introduce bias.
First, it ignores the fact that elite universities often have much larger graduate programs, meaning they naturally produce more job applicants. Second, it overlooks professorships at the thousands of colleges and universities that only offer bachelor’s or master’s degrees. About 17,000 people teach political science in the United States, but only about 3,000 work at doctoral departments, meaning studies that look only at those departments miss more than 80 percent of faculty jobs.
“Existing work has claimed that where one earns the PhD is critical to whether they find a professor job, and some even suggested closing more than half of PhD programs,” Scott W. Desposato, the Simón Bolívar Chair of Latin American Studies and a professor of political science at the University of California, San Diego, told PsyPost.
“But this body of work assesses placements by looking at professors at PhD-granting programs. Thus, they don’t control for the size of the PhD program (bigger programs should have more placements, even if their training is the same as smaller programs) and they ignore the many professor jobs at small liberal arts colleges, community colleges, and other universities that don’t have phD programs.”
“As I write in the paper, it’s like studying fitness by seeing which country won the most medals in the Olympics and concluding that the best way to be healthy is to move to that country,” Desposato continued. “That would be a crazy way to study fitness, and it’s the wrong way to study the academic labor market.”
“Faculty are full of advice about what students should do to succeed on the job market,” he said. “But their recommendations are based on anecdotal observations. We try to be systematic and scientific in our research – so why wouldn’t we want some real evidence from which to make recommendations to our PhD students?”
To get a more accurate picture of how hiring works, Desposato identified a group of active job seekers and checked on their outcomes a year later. The researcher collected data on 413 political science candidates who were actively on the academic job market during the 2023 to 2024 hiring cycle. The candidates were identified from the “Job Market Candidate” pages on various university websites in the fall of 2023. The sample only included candidates who were either finalizing their dissertations or had recently graduated, excluding anyone who already held a tenure-track job or had graduated before 2023.
Using the candidates’ websites and resumes, the researcher recorded a variety of details. These included the rank of their university, their specific field of study, their teaching experience, any awards they had won, and their publication record. To assess publications, the study tracked both the number of articles and the prestige of the journals in which they were published.
The researcher also coded the candidates’ perceived gender and underrepresented minority (URM) status based on names, pronouns, identity-specific awards, personal statements, and appearance. Candidates perceived as Black, Latino, or Native American were classified as URM, a measure meant to approximate how hiring committees might see them.
In the fall of 2024, the researcher checked back to see what types of jobs the candidates had secured. By that time, about 26 percent of the candidates had accepted tenure-track professorships. Surprisingly, the prestige of the university where a candidate earned their degree had virtually no bearing on whether they secured one of these positions.
Placement rates showed no consistent pattern by rank: the top 10 departments placed 25 percent of their candidates, while departments ranked 71st or lower placed 35 percent. The results suggest that graduating from an elite institution does not guarantee a job, nor does graduating from a lower-ranked program automatically disqualify a candidate. However, lower-ranked programs were thinly represented in the data, as only 13 of the 60 lower-ranked departments listed candidates online. The lowest-ranked group’s 35 percent placement rate largely reflected the University of Missouri, which placed nine of its 16 candidates; the rest of that group placed just five of 24 candidates.
While institutional rank did not predict if a candidate got a job, it did predict what kind of job they got. Candidates from top-ranked programs were much more likely to secure postdoctoral fellowships, which are temporary research positions that often serve as stepping stones to tenure-track jobs. When elite candidates did land tenure-track roles, they mostly went to universities that also grant doctoral degrees. By contrast, candidates from lower-ranked programs were more likely to find tenure-track positions at smaller colleges and universities that do not have doctoral programs, or they took temporary teaching positions.
More than 70 percent of candidates held some kind of academic job a year later. Among candidates who were already postdoctoral fellows when the study began, 30 percent landed tenure-track jobs, compared with 15 percent of those working as visiting lecturers.
Publishing was among the strongest predictors of landing a tenure-track job. Candidates without any published research had a placement rate of just 16 percent, compared with 32 percent for those with one to three publications. In statistical models, the researcher compared hypothetical candidates to a baseline: a non-minority man studying American politics at the 30th-ranked department who had not yet finished his degree and had no publications. That baseline candidate had an estimated 27 percent probability of landing a professorship.
If that same candidate had co-authored an article in the American Political Science Review, a top journal, the probability rose to 41 percent. A solo-authored article in that journal was associated with a probability of roughly 52 percent, nearly double the baseline, though this estimate was less statistically certain. Only about 5 percent of candidates had published in a top journal at all. Teaching experience, on the other hand, did not seem to help: candidates with seven or more teaching roles had a lower placement rate of 18 percent.
The candidate’s field of study and demographic identity were also linked to their job market outcomes. Applicants specializing in American politics were the most successful, with nearly 40 percent finding a tenure-track position, compared with 20 to 24 percent in other fields. That year, there were about as many job listings in American politics (118) as American politics candidates (118), whereas comparative politics had 189 candidates for 71 listings.
When looking at demographics, the study found no evidence that female or URM candidates faced hiring disadvantages. In fact, these identities were associated with higher placement rates. The raw placement rates for tenure-track jobs were 19 percent for non-minority men, 32 percent for non-minority women, 36 percent for URM women, and 39 percent for URM men. In the researcher’s statistical models, a baseline non-minority male candidate had a 27 percent probability of securing a tenure-track job.
By comparison, a URM male candidate had a 47 percent probability, and female candidates sat at roughly 44 percent. However, this advantage only appeared for positions at doctoral universities; for jobs at colleges without doctoral programs, gender and minority status were not significantly linked to placement. These findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that women applying for tenure-track faculty positions in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics disciplines experienced hiring equality or advantages compared to men with matching qualifications. Desposato’s own analysis of the American Political Science Association’s placement survey data from 2017 to 2025 found the same advantages for female, minority, and American politics candidates.
“The effect sizes for URM/female were particularly large,” Desposato pointed out. “Members of those identities had a much higher placement rate than white/Asian males.”
“The most striking finding was that departmental rank had so little effect on placements, whereas both female gender and minority status had such large effects compared to the other predictors,” Artur Nilsson, a professor of personality psychology at the University of Bergen who was not involved in the study, told PsyPost. “That publications and research topics matter too is not surprising.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The study provides an observational snapshot of a single hiring cycle, meaning it cannot demonstrate that specific factors directly caused people to be hired. For example, a strong publication record might improve a candidate’s chances by impressing a search committee, or it might simply be a byproduct of writing a very good dissertation, which the committee also recognizes.
The models accounted for broad subfields, such as American or comparative politics, but not for narrower research specialties that might have been in higher demand. “These are observational data with tons of selection issues,” the researcher explained. “For example, why are URM candidates placed at double the rate of non-URM males? This might simply be that those candidates were studying more popular fields.”
“Or, it may be that non-URM candidates have better alternatives to academia and are leaving for those positions,” he continued. “Or, it may be that there is discrimination based on identity. It could be all of these! This is just one year’s worth of data, from a unique moment of racial reckoning, but it deserves some consideration.”
There are also many unmeasured variables that influence hiring decisions, such as a candidate’s interview skills, the strength of their recommendation letters, and the overall quality of their research. Additionally, the data collection relied on which candidates academic departments chose to list on their public websites. This means some job seekers were likely missed, especially those from programs outside the United States or those whose departments do not maintain such directories.
It is also unclear whether the hiring trends apply to other countries or disciplines. “The main caveat is that these findings represent a specific job market at a particular point in time, subject to the idiosyncrasies of the U.S. system,” Nilsson said. “Their generalizability is difficult to estimate.”
Because the academic job search often takes several years, tracking outcomes after a single year may not capture the full trajectory of a candidate’s career. Looking ahead, Desposato hopes to apply the same approach to other fields and follow candidates for several years. He noted that upcoming experimental studies on hiring by other scholars will also help address these limitations.
He argued that graduate programs should release hard numbers on how their students fare, since many advertise an “excellent placement record” to prospective students without backing it up. “It’s not clear what ‘excellent placement record’ can mean when 75% of candidates did not have professor jobs after a year on the job market,” he added. “We owe it to our PhD students and prospective students to be honest about the job market and what they are signing up for when they start a PhD program, and we should make sure there are non-academic pathways for our PhD students.”
“This is especially true given demographic change,” Desposato concluded. “Many small colleges are going to close as enrollments decline. Most of those colleges offer political science or government as a major, and those professor jobs just won’t exist anymore. I expect a difficult academic job market for PhD candidates for the foreseeable future.”
The study, “Where You Go, What You Do, Who You Are: Predictors of Political Science Job-Market Outcomes, 2023–2024,” was authored by Scott W. Desposato.

====================================================================================================

It’s never been so easy to find answers. But sitting with uncertainty can ultimately bring wisdom | Muhammad Abdulsater
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:00:30 UTC
23:00:30 KST

We live in an age that has become profoundly uncomfortable with not knowing.
A delayed email reply becomes a source of anxiety. A medical symptom is immediately searched online. We refresh news feeds, ask AI for instant explanations, and expect the answers to life’s biggest questions to arrive at the same speed as food deliveries.
Modernity has conditioned us to believe that uncertainty is a dilemma to be solved.
Perhaps that is why one of the Qur’an’s most remarkable stories, involving Prophet Moses and al-Khidr, feels so unexpectedly relevant today.
In the story, Prophet Moses embarks on a journey to learn from a mysterious servant of God known as al-Khidr, otherwise known as the “Green One” or “Green Man” . Before the journey even begins, al-Khidr warns him: “You will never be able to remain patient with me.” It is a curious statement. Moses is one of the greatest prophets, a man of extraordinary faith and wisdom. If anyone should possess patience, surely it is him.
But the lesson is not about Moses’s character. It is about the limits of human understanding. As they travel together, Moses witnesses some deeply troubling events. Among them, al-Khidr deliberately damages a boat belonging to poor fishers. He repairs a crumbling wall for a town whose people had refused them hospitality, without asking for any payment.
Each time, Moses objects. Each time, he judges what he sees according to justice, compassion and reason. Each time, he is gently reminded that he does not yet possess understanding of the whole story.
Only at the end of this story are the hidden reasons revealed. The damaged boat was saved from confiscation by a tyrannical king. The wall protected an inheritance belonging to orphaned children.
The story is not asking us to suspend thinking or rational inquiry. Rather, the narrative exposes something far more subtle: our tendency to mistake partial knowledge for complete understanding.
That tendency feels particularly familiar today.
Our lives are increasingly shaped by technologies that promise certainty. Artificial intelligence summarises complex subjects instantly. We have become accustomed to immediate explanations, immediate diagnoses and immediate conclusions.
The great paradox of our age is that although information has become ubiquitous, our tolerance for uncertainty has never been lower. We increasingly expect life itself to function like a search engine with immediate output in response to our input.
The Quranic story of Prophet Moses and al-Khidr gently suggests that reality does not work that way.
One of the most overlooked aspects of this story is that understanding arrives only after patience. The explanations are deliberately delayed. Had al-Khidr explained each event before it occurred, there would have been no lesson at all. The transformation lies precisely in learning to remain faithful before understanding appears.
This challenges one of modernity’s deepest assumptions, that peace comes from having all the answers.
The Islamic spiritual tradition proposes something different. Peace is not born from eliminating uncertainty but from learning how to inhabit it without despair.
This is not an invitation to passive resignation or to explain away suffering. What the story offers is humility about the limits of our own knowledge and perspective.
Most of us are living somewhere in the middle of our own stories. We judge our lives from chapter three without knowing chapter 20. We interpret delays as failures and endings as defeats. We rarely consider that we may simply lack the vantage point from which the full picture can be seen.
That is why the story continues to resonate across centuries. It reminds us that there is a profound difference between something that is meaningless and something whose meaning has not yet become apparent.
In a culture that rewards instant opinions and relentless certainty, perhaps one of the most radical spiritual practices is learning to say: “I do not yet understand.”
Not because reason has failed. But because wisdom sometimes arrives more slowly than information.
And perhaps faith begins, not when every question has been answered, but when we discover the courage to keep walking before the explanation arrives.

Evolution of the Resistance: three phases since Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:57:53 UTC
