Evolution of the Resistance: three phases since Oct. 7
LONDON - Phase one of the resistance is divided into two parts, the first is the war of supporting Gaza until the many resistance leaders were eliminated. It was then followed by the “battle of determination” where the comprehensive confrontation took place, which was the attempt to completely eliminate the resistance.
This phase began on October 8, 2023, following the October 7 Al-Aqsa operation and continued until November 27, 2024, lasting approximately one year and one month. Its general character was a confrontation between the Israeli occupation entity and the resistance forces in the region. The basis of the confrontation was initially the response to the October 7 operation, followed by the involvement of the resistance in Lebanon in support of Gaza.
The primary objective of the resistance in Lebanon was to support Gaza. During this phase, it achieved a very important objective, which was paralyzing the north of the Israeli occupation entity. For the entity, the phase began with an attempt to contain the resistance in Lebanon while focusing on Gaza. It ended, however, with a shift towards seeking to eliminate the resistance in Lebanon altogether, through the killing of its leaders and the destruction of parts of its military infrastructure.
The Israeli occupation entity was unable to achieve its ultimate objectives during this phase despite the severe blows it inflicted on the resistance. This is despite the fact that the leader of the resistance and a large number of other leaders were killed, and parts of the resistance’s infrastructure were struck. Had it not been for the strength of the resistance, its institutions, its spirit, and its determination, it would not have been able to withstand this confrontation. The imbalance in capabilities, the scale of the penetration that had taken place, and the extensive use of technology created conditions under which the confrontation could have ended with the elimination of any other resistance. Therefore, the resistance’s very ability to withstand the confrontation constitutes an important asset for it. During this phase, Israel was unable to advance beyond the front line more than approximately two to three kilometers.
The second phase began on November 27, 2024 and continued until March 2, 2026. It was a nominal ceasefire phase, while the Israeli occupation entity retained five positions and continued attempting to expand. The most significant development during this phase was the elimination of the Syrian government as part of an international and regional conspiracy, in cooperation with Turkey and the United States, and the installation of a new regime. This resulted in the loss of the strategic depth on which the resistance had relied on Syria and completely complicated its logistical operations, particularly its supply, equipment, weapons, protection and support lines.
The second phase was one of the most difficult phases for the resistance, psychologically and organizationally, because the decision was to remain silent on the ground. There was an urgent need for restoration, repair, restructuring and rebuilding, as well as for learning from the lessons of the first phase. The resistance used this period to rebuild itself and adapt its organizational, military and security structures, while learning from the lessons of the first phase, which had exposed significant vulnerabilities. It also had to adapt to the reality of the second phase, in which the resistance no longer had a strategic rear in Syria.
It was difficult for the Lebanese resistance to remain silent in the face of Israeli transgressions, attacks and violations without responding. However, the balance of power, the political circumstances, and the need for restructuring and reorganization compelled it to maintain this silence. The November 27 agreement, and its provision for the handover of resistance positions to the Lebanese authorities, reduced the resistance’s presence during the second phase.
 
This negatively affected the confrontation in southern Lebanon and made it easier for the Israeli occupation entity to expand.
The Lebanese resistance entered the third phase on March 2, 2026, which is considered the most important phase, when it seized the appropriate regional moment to connect itself to the broader conflict in the region. After the objective had been to contain, exclude, besiege and eliminate it, the resistance entered the battle through the widest possible gateway when the Israeli occupation entity and the United States’ level of aggression reached the point of attempting to topple the Islamic Republic of Iran.
The Lebanese resistance’s greatest drive was to contribute to preserving the Resistance Front. It therefore entered the battle and transformed the conflict in Lebanon from a local sphere into a regional and international one. The same applied to the Israeli occupation entity, as the results of this war would impose consequences on both sides. Its ultimate outcome therefore became linked to the outcome of the larger battle, a battle that the resistance believes will ultimately favor the Resistance Front led by the Islamic Republic.
The Lebanese resistance entered a war in support of the Islamic Republic of Iran and a battle to restore the standing of the resistance in Lebanon. It employed new means that it had spent fifteen months developing during the period when it had reluctantly remained silent in the face of Israeli attacks, which included the use of fiber-optic drones. These had a significant impact in terms of Israeli casualties and equipment losses, thereby slowing the entity’s ability to advance. It should not be overlooked that every advance by the enemy in Lebanon occurred during periods of ceasefire, rather than during periods of direct confrontation.

After three days of silence, the National Rally's French presidential candidate has responded to Mediapart's release of new alleged evidence of antisemitic remarks by the party leader.
Marine Le Pen has broken her silence to publicly renew her support for Jordan Bardella, who is now in turmoil after fresh revelations about antisemitic and conspiracist messages attributed to him.
Three days after investigative website Mediapart published a second article on the affair, the presidential hopeful told La Tribune Dimanche she has "total confidence" in the man tipped to become her prime minister if she wins the 2027 presidential election.
Le Pen had already defended Bardella when Mediapart first published the allegations on Monday. "You won't get anyone to believe that," she told reporters during a walkabout at a trade fair, cutting the exchange short. "It's not that it's not an issue (...) it's just madness," she added.
What are the allegations?
Mediapart, which says it preserved the grammatical and spelling mistakes of the original messages, reports that Bardella, then 17 or 18, railed in one conversation against the supposed desire of "the Jew" to "dominate" other peoples, to "crush" and "rob" them, adding that "a Zionist is necessarily Jewish, deep down".
He is also said to have accused several ministers from François Hollande's presidency of putting Israel and banking interests ahead of French interests.
The article also highlights the alleged influence of Alain Soral on Bardella's political thinking. Soral is a far-right ideologue repeatedly convicted of inciting racial hatred, antisemitic insults, homophobia and Holocaust denial.
Bardella dismisses the messages as "crude fakes" and says they mark "the beginnings of a total war" meant to derail the National Rally's presidential campaign. He has announced two legal complaints, one for defamation and one for forgery and use of forgeries.
Mediapart presents its second article as a response to what it calls a "violent challenge" to its work. It accuses Bardella of having "lied to the whole of France" by refusing to acknowledge authorship of his own texts.
It publishes screenshots that sources described as coming from Bardella's entourage are said to have supplied and says Meta authenticated the messages, which date from 2013, through a Facebook archive extraction.
A row with no impact on voting intentions
According to an investigation by Le Parisien, Marine Le Pen "is not necessarily convinced of her protégé's good faith".
The French newspaper says it has interviewed a member of the RN candidate's campaign team, who told it that "in her view, it is quite likely that the exchanges are real. They are the words of a 17-year-old kid intoxicated by Soral, who is no longer the same person today."
A version that stands in stark contrast to the brief comment made by Marine Le Pen in La Tribune Dimanche.
The weekly also points out that, according to a source within the campaign team, "these controversies do not in any way dent the 30% to 35% of voting intentions in favour of Marine Le Pen". "If our electorate paid attention to what the press says about us, we'd be on 2%," she dismisses.
These accusations against Jordan Bardella come as Marine Le Pen is currently credited with 31% to 36% of first-round voting intentions in the presidential election, according to opinion polls, ahead of former prime minister Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the France Unbowed candidate, who are vying for second place.
According to several media reports, Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella are due to appear together on Tuesday at a joint press conference to present an alternative budget put forward by the RN candidate, just as the government unveiled its budget plans on Thursday.
Le Journal du Dimanche (JDD) wonders, quoting an RN MP, whether the controversy could lead the party not to seek to censure the government if it pushes its bill through using article 49.3, which allows a text to be adopted without a vote unless a motion of censure secures a majority. Resorting to this constitutional tool is deemed likely by an expert interviewed by Euronews.
"Even if we consider that Jordan is innocent of the acts of which he is accused, the controversy is there, whether we like it or not. Perhaps we should avoid adding further disorder to the bad press," the JDD writes.

US marine arrested in Japan on suspicion of killing woman, police say

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:46:19 UTC
22:46:19 KST

A US marine stationed on Japan’s southern island of Okinawa is accused of murdering a Japanese woman and has been arrested on suspicion of murder, police said on Sunday.
The suspect allegedly “killed [a] 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Naha and stole her wallet” as well as her backpack, local police told news media outlets.
Citing police, NBC News reported that the suspect charged in the case was identified as Lance Cpl Devin Jacob Ballard, 20. Anna Yagi was identified as the victim.
Ballard denied the allegations, police said, according to NBC.
Crimes including rape, assault, hit-and-run and drunk driving by US personnel have long sparked protests on Okinawa. The island bears a disproportionate burden of hosting about 70% of US military facilities in Japan.
US ambassador George Glass posted on social media that he had spoken with Japan’s foreign ministry and Okinawa’s governor, offering “sincere condolences to the victim’s family” and pledging cooperation into the investigation of her death.
The Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said Japan had lodged a protest with US authorities and called the crime “exceptionally brutal and vicious”.
The government has urged the US “to provide maximum cooperation with the investigation, enforce stricter discipline among US military personnel, and take thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of similar crimes”, Takaichi said.
Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.
Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage and asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station, where he was arrested, NHK reported.
“We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened,” Yagi’s brother said through local police, according to the Asahi Shimbun daily newspaper. “My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter.”
The US has about 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.
Crimes committed by US personnel in Japan have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.
“Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen,” Japan’s defense minister Shinjiro Koizumi said.
In June 2025, a Japanese court sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton – then 22 – to seven years in prison after being convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.
Earlier, in 2017, former US marine and civilian military base worker Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The same year, US forces in Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated American marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.
According to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper, about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since Okinawa was returned to Japan from the US in 1972 after the second world war.
The number of arrests in a year hit 80 in 2024, the highest in 20 years.

How was Flydubai co-pilot cleared despite being deemed a security risk?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:42:16 UTC
22:42:16 KST

How was Flydubai co-pilot cleared despite being deemed a security risk?
Aviation security protocols under scrutiny after co-pilot accused of attempted axe attack aboard Flydubai flight.
A Flydubai co-pilot accused of attacking his captain with an emergency axe and attempting to seize control of the flight bound for Israel had previously been barred from flying over concerns about alleged “extremist” views, raising questions about how he was allowed to fly to Tel Aviv.
The co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national, according to multiple media reports.
The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has described the September 30 incident aboard Flight FZ1073 as an attempted “terrorist” operation.
But investigators are still working to establish the motive and whether anyone else was connected to the attack, which has raised concerns about pilot vetting and aviation security.
So, what security checks do pilots have to go through and how al-Hammami may have evaded background checks?
How did al-Hammami apparently pass the checks?
That is now one of the central questions facing investigators.
Al-Hammami had previously been barred from flying in Oman because of concerns that he had adopted “extremist” views and was instead moved to an administrative role at Oman Air, according to sources who spoke to the AP news agency.
He was subsequently hired by Flydubai.
A Gulf diplomat told AP that al-Hammami had undergone standard security checks before being hired. It wasn’t immediately clear to what extent the co-pilot was vetted.
The US-based network CNN reported that a LinkedIn profile bearing al-Hammami’s name said he had spent seven years at Oman Air before leaving in February 2025. The profile said he joined Royal Air Maroc in June 2025 and left in January this year.
It is unclear what those alleged views were or whether Oman informed other countries or airlines about its concerns.
What background checks do commercial pilots go through?
Background checks for commercial pilots vary by airline and country, with no single global standard governing the process, an airline pilot and instructor told Al Jazeera.
The captain with an international airline who chose to remain anonymous said pilots are generally required to obtain aviation medical certification from the regulator in the country where they are licensed to fly.
In the UAE, that is overseen by the General Civil Aviation Authority (GCAA), he said.
Some airlines also require prospective pilots to provide police clearance certificates from their country of residence as part of pre-employment screening, the pilot added.
One type of check is a Class 1 medical assessment, which typically examines areas including vision, hearing, cardiovascular and neurological health, as well as conditions that could cause sudden incapacitation.
When it comes to security checks, aviation rules require background checks for personnel who have unescorted access to security-restricted areas.
Psychological assessments, drug and alcohol testing and other evaluations may be required depending on the jurisdiction.
How did Israel allow him to fly?
Israel has some of the world’s toughest aviation security measures.
As a result, questions have been raised over how the alleged attacker was allowed to operate a flight to Israel, despite reportedly being an Omani national and Oman having no diplomatic relations with Israel.
According to the Haaretz newspaper, Israeli authorities received the Flydubai flight’s crew and passenger lists before it departed. Under a law passed in 2023, airlines are required to provide information about passengers and crew members, including their names and nationalities, to Israel up to 48 hours before a flight.
The Israel Tax Authority confirmed to Haaretz that it had received the lists for the Flydubai flight. The media outlet reported that the information is also supposed to be available to Israeli security bodies, including the Mossad, police and Shin Bet, to identify people who may pose a security risk.
According to security sources who spoke to Haaretz, the Transportation Ministry’s Security Department and the Mossad are responsible for checking foreign flight crews and issuing alerts if concerns arise.
However, two security sources told Haaretz that while the Transportation Ministry holds responsibility “on paper”, it does not have its own intelligence capacity.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that Israel has longstanding arrangements with foreign airlines aimed at preventing pilots who are nationals of countries without diplomatic relations with Israel from flying there.
Netanyahu has described what happened as a “loophole” and Israel says it will now strengthen its checks.
The UAE has not yet publicly established a motive or announced whether investigators believe al-Hammami acted alone.
UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said on Saturday that the latest ‘terrorist’ attack is a new warning that the region’s fight against “extremism” is not over.
“This underscores the importance of the UAE’s early and firm stance: no tolerance for extremism and no leniency towards its rhetoric. Security begins with confronting hatred and drying up the sources of extremism,” he posted on X.

ULAN BATOR, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Mongolia has planted a total of 140 million trees across the country since launching a national tree-planting campaign in 2021, according to the presidential press office on Sunday.
The national campaign, which aims to plant at least 1 billion trees by 2030, was officially launched in October 2021, when Mongolian President Ukhnaa Khurelsukh addressed the UN General Assembly and announced the country's goal of combating desertification and climate change.
As part of efforts to accelerate tree planting nationwide, Mongolia organizes tree-planting campaigns twice a year, in spring and autumn, encouraging government institutions, businesses and citizens to take part.
The latest autumn tree-planting campaign began last week. On Saturday alone, more than 1,000 people from 42 organizations planted 3,000 trees of eight species at the International Garden of Mongolia in the capital, Ulan Bator, the presidential press office said in a statement.
An exhibition providing tree seedlings and saplings to individuals and organizations interested in planting trees will also be held from Oct. 5 to 18, it said.
Under the "Billion Trees" national campaign, Mongolia is also taking measures to protect its forests from pests, diseases and degradation.
A survey conducted this year to assess the spread of forest pests across 2.4 million hectares in 16 provinces found pest outbreaks covering 256,500 hectares.
Based on the findings, pest-control measures have been carried out across 133,500 hectares using aircraft, backpack sprayers, light traps, mechanical methods and drones.
Environmental experts have noted that Mongolia is among the countries most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change. Due to its geographical location and changing climate conditions, the Asian country has experienced an increasing frequency and severity of natural hazards, including forest and steppe fires, desertification, land degradation and yellow dust storms.
According to the latest national assessment released by Mongolia's Ministry of Environment and Climate Change in August, at least 81.9 percent of Mongolia's total land area has been affected to some extent by desertification and land degradation. ■

NAIROBI, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- A joint initiative by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and Chinese coding teaching platform Codemao is making progress in integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into schools across Africa.
According to Mary Nyasimi, national program specialist at the UNESCO Regional Office for Eastern Africa, AI and digital tools are transforming teaching and learning across the continent, equipping students with essential skills for future careers and innovation.
"Accelerating AI education is essential to bridge the digital divide, strengthen human capital, and improve the global competitiveness of both Kenya and the broader African continent," she said during a recent meeting in Nairobi, the Kenyan capital.
Launched in 2021, the youth coding initiative by UNESCO and Codemao promotes inclusive, safe and equitable AI and coding education across Africa and Asia.
The program focuses on delivering hands-on training, establishing cross-continental educational networks, and raising awareness of digital empowerment.
"Between 2021 and 2022, over 200 teachers from the Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Namibia and Thailand, including 45 percent women, completed UNESCO's initial international coding training program," Nyasimi said.
The initiative operates on a train-the-trainer model, with newly trained educators cascading coding and digital skills to thousands of their peers and students across the region, she added.
Augustine Nzuki, a teacher at Tala Township Primary School in Machakos County, eastern Kenya, shared how a recent trip to Shenzhen, China, sponsored by the initiative, transformed his approach to teaching.
Although Nzuki had previously taught robotics theoretically, his visit in July marked the first time he operated a real drone and interacted with a robot in person.
"I saw practically what robots and drones are, gaining hands-on knowledge of AI and coding," Nzuki said.
He was among eight Kenyans -- four teachers and four students -- who traveled to China to see firsthand how the Fourth Industrial Revolution is reshaping education.
Looking ahead, Nzuki plans to visit 20 neighboring schools to share his insights and mentor the next generation of educators.
In Kenya, 20 schools across Kiambu, Nairobi, Kajiado and Machakos counties have been incorporated into the project since 2025.
To date, the program has trained more than 1,200 Kenyan students and established dedicated school coding clubs to foster continuous peer-to-peer learning. ■

Poland and Romania have rejected appeals by Ukraine to expand agricultural transit corridors and provide financial subsidies to export millions of metric tons of trapped grain through Europe, Politico reported.
The refusal follows a diplomatic mission to Brussels earlier in the week by Ukrainian Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi, who met directly with EU counterparts to request transit authorization for larger cargo volumes alongside €1.1 billion ($1.2 billion) in financial assistance to offset elevated freight costs.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It’s very, very critical,” Vysotskyi told Politico, warning that Russian kinetic strikes against Ukrainian Black Sea ports and commercial vessels, now entering their third consecutive month, have paralyzed conventional maritime export routes.
Vysotskyi stated that harvested grain and oilseed stockpiles are accumulating rapidly inside domestic storage silos, depriving Ukrainian agricultural enterprises of the working capital necessary to purchase seeds, fuel, and fertilizers for the upcoming planting season.
“If the situation remains like this until spring, it could mean a reduction in sown areas next year of even 35 to 40 percent,” Vysotskyi cautioned, pointing to the risk of compounded harvest contractions in 2027.
Domestic farm protections
Neighboring Central and Eastern European governments maintain that their regional transport networks and maritime terminals cannot absorb additional Ukrainian freight without displacing domestic producers.
Kulbergs’ Pro-Ukraine Party Wins Latvian Election
Romanian Agriculture Minister Barna Tánczos confirmed that Bucharest will not accommodate higher Ukrainian export volumes, emphasizing that protecting local agricultural markets remains the Romanian government’s core priority.
Tánczos explained that existing transit volumes, combined with seasonal low water levels along the Danube River, have already overwhelmed Romanian ports such as Constanța, leaving domestic farmers unable to offload and market their own harvests.
“The interest for our own farmers remains a priority,” Tánczos told Politico. “Everyone knows that we cannot double the number of trains, we cannot double the capacity of roads, railways, and ports.”
Poland’s Ministry of Infrastructure delivered an identical rebuff, informing reporters that the Polish government is “not planning any changes aimed at increasing the transit of Ukrainian agricultural products.”
Black Sea maritime blockade
The transit impasse coincides with sustained Russian strikes targeting Ukrainian maritime hubs and commercial shipping across the northwestern Black Sea.
Over recent months, Russian missile and drone bombardments have repeatedly hit port elevators, container berths, and civilian cargo vessels docked across Odesa, Chornomorsk, and Pivdennyi, increasing maritime freight insurance premiums and constraining commercial navigation through Ukraine’s unilateral coastal corridor.
The mounting operational hazards were underscored in recent diplomatic representations. Since late June, at least 25 Turkish-owned or Turkish-operated merchant vessels have been damaged or caught in crossfire in the Black Sea, prompting Ankara to launch a multilateral mediation initiative.
A Turkish diplomat confirmed that Ankara transmitted a draft memorandum of understanding to both Kyiv and Moscow seeking a formal cessation of kinetic strikes directed at commercial maritime traffic and civilian port installations.
The diplomatic proposal is modeled partially on the Black Sea Grain Initiative, the wartime agreement brokered in July 2022 by Turkey and the UN that facilitated the export of nearly 33 million metric tons of Ukrainian foodstuffs through a protected maritime corridor before Russia unilaterally abandoned the arrangement in July 2023.

Trump names AI czar to head White House task force

Trump names AI czar to head White House task force
October 4, 2026
US President Donald Trump on Sunday announced a White House task force to coordinate the administration's response to artificial intelligence (AI).
The group will be led by director of national intelligence Jay Clayton, chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon chief technology officer Emil Michael and director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor.
The task force, named the "Super Intelligence Force" or SI, in accordance with the term that the president prefers over AI.
"The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies," Trump said in Truth Social post on Sunday.
Trump under pressure to regulate AI
Trump in September said he would create a new AI force to oversee the development of the fast-moving technology, but has so far opposed any strict regulation that codifies pillars of AI safety into law.
"We will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth of this incredible industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump said in the September post where he announced he was going to choose an AI czar.
Leading up to the midterm elections in November, Trump has been under pressure to address concerns about AI risks. AI researchers and tech CEOs have sounded the alarm about the existential threat that the technology can pose.
Anthropic's chief executive Dario Amodei, for example, published an essay last month in which he called for a global slowdown in the race to develop AI. His call was met with agreement from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
Trump, AI CEOs sign safety pact
The US president hosted a White House lunch for nearly 20 tech titans at the end of September, where he said there was an agreement in the room that there should be "tremendous self-regulation" by tech companies.
The tech leaders signed onto a one-page document that relies on companies to voluntarily follow through on their safety commitments. But the accord is largely symbolic since it is not an official order.

Why is fighting intensifying in Yemen’s Taiz governorate?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:31:15 UTC
22:31:15 KST

Why is fighting intensifying in Yemen’s Taiz governorate?
Government forces fend off waves of Houthi attacks as civilians in the populous province are imperiled.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Iran-backed Houthis are engaged in a fierce struggle for the Taiz governorate, a key strategic area in the southwest of the country.
Rashad al-Alimi, chief of the Saudi Arabia-backed Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), announced on Sunday the start of a major offensive against the Houthis to regain lost territory. It is expected that this will result in more battles around Taiz, already the site of some of the most recent fighting.
Observers and analysts say that the Houthis are trying to consolidate their gains after seizing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast last month. For the government, the battle for Taiz represents a strategic and existential struggle for control of the country.
Here’s what we know.
Why is Taiz important?
Taiz governorate is Yemen’s most populous region, with nearly 4.5 million people. The flat western coastal region sits on the Red Sea and includes the port city of Mocha and the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb strait.
These coastal regions were captured by the Houthis in a surprise and lightning campaign in early September, raising fears the group could choke off international shipping through the strait. They were also key supply routes for Taiz.
Much of the governorate lies within Yemen’s highlands and remains contested between the two sides. The region’s capital, Taiz City, is nestled between a number of mountains and is under government control. It is one of Yemen’s most populous cities and a key source of legitimacy for the Yemeni government.
The governorate sits between Yemen’s Houthi-controlled north and the government-held south. The Houthi advance threatens to isolate government forces from Aden, the southern coastal town where key state institutions are based.
Ibrahim Jalal, a senior researcher and policy adviser, told Al Jazeera that Taiz is a city of huge social, political, economic and military importance for the whole of Yemen.
“The Houthi attempt to isolate and constrict the city seeks to secure their coastal Red Sea gains up to Bab al-Mandeb, as well as double down on pressure on Lahij, Aden and much of the south,” said Jalal.
“The Houthis seek to expand their territorial control at the moment along the former boundaries of northern Yemen, or to say, that they want to remove all little pockets of resistance to consolidate control.”
Taiz has been one of the most heavily contested cities in the war, beginning shortly after Houthi forces captured the capital Sanaa in September 2014.
Thousands of civilians have been killed in a devastating Houthi siege and assault on the city, with government forces driving back repeated assaults between 2015 and 2022.
Fighting has been focused on Jabal Han, a mountain overlooking Taiz from the west, as well as a key road into the city.
Control over this mountain would allow the Houthis to attack people and supplies entering Taiz City from the southwest, Saeed Thabet, head of Al Jazeera’s bureau in Yemen, said.
Who has the upper hand?
There has been no clear winner in the battle for Taiz so far, which observers have described as a stalemate.
Al Jazeera’s Mohammed al-Qadi, reporting from the city, said government forces have launched dozens of air strikes on Houthi bases and positions across Taiz in recent days.
Houthi fighters are trying to advance under cover of intense artillery, tank, mortar and Katyusha rocket fire into the city.
Artillery fire could be heard around Taiz as residents appealed to be evacuated, Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali, reporting from Taiz City, said on Sunday.
On that day, local authorities reported that a shell had hit a residential area in Dhubab, killing a 14-day-old infant. Other attacks have wounded civilians.
Government forces are also shelling Houthi forces positioned around the city.
Face-to-face fighting has now reached the countryside on the outskirts of Taiz City. Residents are fighting on their own initiative against Houthi attempts to infiltrate villages and mountain areas around Taiz, a local source said.
The heaviest fighting is taking place at the western axis of the city, where government forces have mounted a fierce defence at Jabal Han.
On Sunday, Yemen’s government forces announced gains against the Houthis, saying they had captured several areas, including a fort in Samaa.
The military command in Taiz also claimed its forces had repelled Houthi attacks on Jabal Han, Hazran and other points west of Taiz City.
Yemeni military spokesman Majed al-Nuzaili said government forces had carried out dozens of operations using aircraft, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers, resulting in hundreds of Houthi casualties. Al Jazeera could not verify these claims.
In early September, the Houthis managed to expand their control over Yemen’s Red Sea coast with unexpected speed and limited resistance.
However, they have faced much fiercer fighting from government forces in Taiz.
One key reason for this is the cohesion between government forces and the local tribes. Al Jazeera’s Yasser Hassan reports that tribesmen took part in Sunday’s capture of the Samaa Fort.
How are civilians in Taiz being impacted?
The humanitarian cost of the renewed fighting in Taiz has already manifested in a refugee crisis with limited access to humanitarian goods and services.
There has also been an increase in civilian casualties. Since fighting escalated in early September, nearly 200,000 people have been displaced in Yemen, most of them from Taiz governorate, according to Yemen’s Executive Unit for IDP Camps Management.
The closure of some major roads into Taiz City has raised fears of an impending humanitarian disaster.
The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and the World Health Organization (WHO) have both warned that the fighting was putting Yemen’s fragile healthcare system in peril.
Al Jazeera’s Hassan described the humanitarian situation as “very difficult” after government forces decided to shut down all roads leading into the city out of fear of Houthi infiltration.
Before Mocha was taken over by Houthis, its port was a critical supply line from which food and aid were delivered to Taiz City.
The ongoing war has also devastated the country. Nearly half of Yemen’s 34 million population face acute food insecurity, according to the UN, with about half a million people suffering severe malnutrition.

Lessons will be “totally or partly suspended” in some “400-500” high schools as the security conditions “have not been fulfilled”, said Education Minister Edouard Geffray on Oct 4, adding that 24 schools had been “burned or ransacked” since the start of the movement.
He described the closures as chiefly a security precaution ahead of large-scale protests that the leaders of the movement have called for Oct 6.
The teens at French high schools, known as lycees, say that their studies are being ruined by high teacher absences, overlong school days and dilapidated facilities, as well as other grievances.
Geffray said the number of schools affected on Oct 5 would be comparable to the figure from Oct 2 but vowed there would be a “partial, progressive return to lessons”.
More than a third of the 468 schools in the wider Ile-de-France region surrounding the capital will be shut on Oct 5 as a result of the protests, Valerie Pecresse, the right-wing president of the region, told broadcaster Franceinfo.
The movement began at a Paris school on Sept 17 but grew last week into nationwide protests marked in places by outbursts of violence involving teenagers and the security forces, which have used tear gas and truncheons against the students.
‘Deliberately targeted’
At Saint-Denis, just north of Paris, students took turns expressing their grievances at an open-air meeting on Oct 4.
When you are a student from one of the deprived districts, said one student, “The violence is unleashed.”
She referred in particular to one student who had lost his teeth to a police rubber bullet and another who had been hit in the eye.
One 16-year-old boy, Campion, held a placard that read: “They say they are listening to us but prefer to gas us”.
“I don’t understand why the government deploys so much force against a case that is valid: our education, our future,” he told AFP.
Geffray, in his statement, spoke of far-left infiltrators who had “hijacked” the movement “and engaged in extreme violence”.
“Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students,” he said, adding that 78 education staff members had been injured.
“They were deliberately targeted because they were employees of the national education system,” Geffray said.
Organisers have called for the protests to continue on Oct 6, citing a lack of “concrete measures” from the government.
In a bid to address the protesters’ concerns, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu set out a timetable on Oct 4 urging local authorities to prioritise filling gaps left by long-term absences and unfilled posts.
He also called a meeting for Oct 6 with regional presidents to discuss overhauling the country’s often-dilapidated school buildings.
Violent incidents
More than 5,000 people, 85 per cent of them minors, have been arrested since the start of the movement.
A 16-year-old was detained on Oct 4 over the assault of a teacher in the southern town of La Ciotat. The teacher, 59, was struck and doused with gasoline on the sidelines of a high school student protest on Oct 2.
A group of youths were last week filmed beating and kicking a policeman on the ground in Belfort in eastern France in images that caused an outcry among officials.
Two youths, Bulgarian nationals aged 15 and 17, have been arrested and investigated for suspected aggravated violence, the prosecutor said.
One of the youths, whom the policeman had tried to arrest before being beaten, has now filed his own attempted murder complaint, his lawyer said.
The France branch of Amnesty last week slammed “disproportionate police violence” in tackling the demonstrations and said students must be allowed to express their grievances.
“Authorities must allow young people to exercise these rights without fear of being hit by tear gas grenades or batons, or being arbitrarily taken into police custody,” said Amnesty France president Anne Savinel-Barras.
But Interior Minister Laurent Nunez stated that security forces “are not cracking down on young people” but rather “protecting” school and university students wishing to “peacefully voice their demands”. AFP

SBU Drones Strike Su-35 and Su-34 Jets at Russian Airfield

Long-range strike drones operated by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) struck advanced Russian Su-35 and Su-34 combat aircraft alongside an ammunition depot at the Khanskaya military airfield in Russia’s Republic of Adygea early Sunday morning, Oct. 4.
According to an official dispatch from the SBU, operators from the service’s “Alpha” Special Operations Center carried out the overnight strike against the air base, located approximately six kilometers outside the regional capital of Maykop and roughly 500 kilometers from Ukrainian-controlled territory.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The security service confirmed direct hits on an Su-35 multi-role air superiority fighter – one of the Russian Aerospace Forces’ most advanced frontline combat aircraft, carrying an estimated export valuation of $100 million – and an Su-34 fighter-bomber, which serves as Moscow’s primary tactical strike aircraft for launching standoff guided aerial bombs, valued at approximately $50 million.
In addition to targeting the combat aircraft, Ukrainian strike drones detonated an on-site ammunition storage facility within the airfield perimeter.
“Last night, the Security Service of Ukraine successfully attacked the military airfield Khanskaya in the Republic of Adygea, Russian Federation,” the SBU stated. “The distance to the target is about 500 kilometers.”
The operation confirms earlier reports from regional monitoring channels and eyewitnesses in Maykop, who reported drone engine sounds and active Russian air defense fire beginning around 1:00 a.m. local time on Sunday, followed by loud secondary explosions and large blazes visible across the airfield complex.
Ukraine to Deploy Small Missiles, Turrets Against Jet Drones, Zelensky Says
Deep-strike campaign
The Khanskaya facility serves as the permanent home station for the Russian Aerospace Forces’ 272nd Training Aviation Base.
Despite its primary instructional designation, Russian military planners have integrated the installation into active combat logistics, utilizing its runways, hangars, and fuel reservoirs as a dispersed forward staging post to support tactical air units.
Satellite reconnaissance recorded in recent months showed a substantial concentration of military aircraft deployed across the installation, including Su-24 bombers, Su-30, Su-34, and Su-35S multi-role fighters, L-39 jet trainers, Mi-8 transport helicopters, and heavy military cargo planes.
The airfield previously came under Ukrainian deep-strike bombardment in December.
The precision strike against Khanskaya marks the second consecutive night of coordinated Ukrainian operations targeting Russian air assets and unmanned aviation nodes.
Overnight into Saturday, Oct. 3, Ukrainian strike drones struck the Tsymbulovo droneport in Russia’s Oryol region, sparking multiple fires across workshops and launch pads used to deploy turbojet-powered loitering munitions toward Kyiv.

Hero passengers on Fly Dubai flight speak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:27:34 UTC
22:27:34 KST

Hero passenger on FlyDubai flight: "I decided that we are going to survive"
This past Wednesday, they were strangers on a plane. By Friday, they were family. It was the first time hero passengers Daniel Schlichter, Zvika Manes, Tal Samuel and Asaf Rajuan had seen each other since those terrifying moments on FlyDubai's Flight 1073.
"That minute is probably the longest minute of my life," said Schlichter about the plane's terrifying freefall. "And the first thing that went up is actually 9/11. And I said, 'How can it be? How can we end this life like that?' You see all your life and you think about what is important. And just holding my wife's hand and saying, 'If we have to go, we have to go.'"
Their Boeing 737 Max was nosediving into the Arabian Desert nearly at the speed of sound. The co-pilot from Oman had stabbed the captain, grabbed the controls, and tried to crash the plane full of Israeli passengers. The jet plummeted 14,000 feet in seconds. They were less than 30 seconds from crashing, with G-forces Manes described as being "like a roller coaster."
What they couldn't have known was that inside the locked cockpit, Captain Smit Machchhar was fighting for his life, as he told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday: "The co-pilot, he wanted to pray. And suddenly there was a big blow to the back of my head," Machchhar said. "I did try to stop him, and that's when I gave everything that I had, and just went for the door and opened the door and thankfully people were waiting."
Manes and his family were sitting in the first row. His wife had just taken his daughter to the bathroom. "I heard my daughter shouting, 'He's stabbing the pilot. He's stabbing the pilot.' She was shouting like animal," he said.
At that moment, Rajuan said they thought they were going to die.
Schlichter, holding his wife's hand, thought to himself, "'If I have to go, I'll hold her hand as tight as possible, and we'll go together.' That's it."
Almost simultaneously, these passengers decided they had to take action.
"I saw my daughter and my wife, and I understand that I must run. I turn, switch to an animal switch, and I feel really like an animal. … I decided that we are going to survive, try to survive, to save my family," Manes said.
Tal Samuel said, "Everyone here, on the day-to-day, are super decent and polite people. But when you watch the situation, you didn't see a finance person, and you didn't see an insurance guy. It was something different. It was like lions that are in a killing mode."
Along with an Israeli plumber named Yaniv Hayoun, they ran toward the bleeding captain, whom they called a hero.
"Not just because he opened the door. Because he had amazing fight with the terrorist. He really fight him," said Rajuan.
Then, they piled onto the co-pilot, Hamam al Hamami, who we've now learned had been banned from flying in his home country, Oman, because of concerns he'd adopted extremist views. And Israeli investigators say they've uncovered social media posts where he talked about killing Jews. Officials in the United Arab Emirates now say he'd committed a "terrorist act."
"I was jumping on him, punching," said Manes. "He tried to resist, and we didn't know if he has a knife."
With a pack of men struggling at the entrance to the cockpit, just then, Tal Samuel looked up and saw the cockpit was empty. He remembered he had been sitting next to two off-duty pilots.
"And the other pilot that came from his seat, because they are blocking the entrance to the cockpit, so that's why he jumped," Samuel said.
According to Rajuan, the pilot leaned over the chair to grab the controls and right the plane.
They were out of freefall. But the captain was bleeding out. "And we are shouting, if there is a doctor in the plane," Manes said.
Shota Musaev, a dentist, said to his wife, "'I need to go,' and, 'I love you.' That's it."
Musaev got up and began treating stab wounds on Machchhar's head and hands. Musaev was afraid he could die from the wounds.
"Yes, I think we have not more time. I check everything, of course, I said to the steward, 'We have no time – land the plane,'" he said.
But the nearest airport was in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, a country that has no diplomatic relations with Israel.
"I was worried that maybe they will arrest us," Manes said, "because they will see blood all over."
But they were not arrested — they were welcomed.
The captain was whisked to a hospital where he's recovering, but at night Dr. Musaev remains with his heroic patient. He said that he can see his face when he closes his eyes: "Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. I think from this time we are a very big family, you know."
And then, in Hebrew, Musaev said, "If he hadn't been smart and heroic, we would not be alive. On the other hand, if we had not been heroes, he would not be alive."

'Russia stood by us when our territorial integrity was under threat': Jaishankar in Munich
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:26:51 UTC
22:26:51 KST

Jaishankar said India and Russia had maintained strong relations since the 1950s.
NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Sunday highlighted India's longstanding ties with Russia, saying the country had stood by us when New Delhi's security and territorial integrity faced threats and much of the world preferred backing a military regime.Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi, Jaishankar said India and Russia had maintained strong relations since the 1950s and that the legacy of those ties continued to shape the relationship.“India and Russia have historically very good relations, particularly since the 1950s. That history is not forgotten,” Jaishankar said.He added that Russia which was Soviet Union before “stood by us in many ways when our security, when our territorial integrity was under threat”.“At a time when much of the world preferred backing a military regime (Pakistan) next to us, Russia was a country with which our relations were very good, and we are shaped in many ways by that legacy,” he said.
“Today, the relationship has widened beyond that... It is very much more today an economic relationship as well. So there is a military component, there are nuclear component, there is space issues, but there is a significant amount of trade and investment between the two countries and energy and resources as well...
India's experience has been quite positive and consistently positive” he added.Jaishankar also said India had moved beyond simply advocating dialogue and diplomacy to taking a more active role in efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict.He said India had held conversations with both Kyiv and Moscow in recent months and was trying to address some immediate concerns arising from the conflict.“Our position on that conflict has been very clear, which is that we would like to see an end to this conflict. This will require dialogue and diplomacy. There has to be negotiations in this regard,” he said.“We have been advocating it for many years, and in recent months we have got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy. We have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard. We are trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping issue,” he added.
Jaishankar said India's efforts were focused initially on ensuring the safety of shipping in the Black Sea, while also addressing issues related to grain and energy exports.“India is going beyond that to cover some immediate concerns which both of them (Russia and Ukraine) have on grain exports, energy exports, non-attack possibilities. Those are ongoing conversations right now,” he said.His remarks came days after Russian President Vladimir Putin said Prime Minister Narendra Modi had “good ideas” for finding a mutually acceptable solution to the conflict.Ukraine foreign minister Andrii Sybiha had also said on Friday that Kyiv received separate proposals from India and three other countries on a possible ceasefire. India has for more than four years maintained that the Ukraine conflict should be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy, PTI reported.PM Modi held wide-ranging talks with Putin in Bishkek on August 31. During the meeting, the Prime Minister stated that “endless war must now give way to end of war”.
Kanchan Yadav is a writer at The Times of India, where she covers business, politics, international affairs and social issues. Her reporting also focuses on policy, governance and economic developments, with a close lens on how decisions in corridors of power affect everyday lives and community well-being.

Azerbaijani Bayraktar Company Unveils KASIRGA Loitering Munition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:26:37 UTC
22:26:37 KST

Bayraktar Teknoloji Azerbaijan has presented the KASIRGA loitering munition at the ADEX 2026 defense exhibition in Baku.
Baykar announced this, calling it the first product of its Azerbaijani enterprise.
KASIRGA can take off and land autonomously on various terrain and wheeled vehicles without a runway.
The system has four electric motors and can perform strike or reconnaissance missions. In the reconnaissance configuration, it can return to its base.
KASIRGA can also serve as a communications relay through Bayraktar TB2, AKINCI, or Bayraktar TB3 drones.
This allows the system to be controlled at greater distances and when terrain obstructs the communications link.
According to Azerbaijan’s state news agency AZERTAC, the platform has a maximum takeoff weight of 33 kilograms and a payload capacity of 6 kilograms. The strike configuration carries a 5-kilogram warhead.
The unmanned system is equipped with an electro-optical camera with artificial intelligence capabilities.
It also features resistance to electronic interference, visual positioning, and autonomous flight using data from multiple sensors.
KASIRGA has an operational radius of 60 kilometers for strike missions and 90 kilometers for reconnaissance missions. Its communications range exceeds 80 kilometers.
Militarnyi previously reported on the appearance in Azerbaijan’s arsenal of another Baykar loitering munition, SİVRİSİNEK. It was shown during President Ilham Aliyev’s visit to the city of Nakhchivan.
SİVRİSİNEK is launched from a catapult and uses an internal combustion engine. According to the specifications provided in the article, its versions can carry warheads weighing up to 20 kilograms and have a flight range of 900-1,000 kilometers.

OK, comrade: The American AI dream sounds a lot like digital communism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:24:35 UTC
22:24:35 KST

OK, comrade: The American AI dream sounds a lot like digital communism
Donald Trump and major tech leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and other tech companies gathered for a meeting at the White House to reach a deal on what Trump described as an “AI constitution” to ensure that frontier models do not pose catastrophic, unintended risks.
In the course of the meeting a “morally binding” voluntary accord was signed in order to “win safely,” as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei put it.
Beyond this self-regulation pact, the Trump administration will additionally set up a governmental board to oversee the safety of AI tools.
Another big change emerging from the meeting is not surprising, given Trump’s affinity for the naming of names. From now on, executive departments and agencies “shall use ‘Super Intelligence’ or SI” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” in official correspondence, reports, and policy documents within the executive branch.
Trump’s rationale is that the word “artificial” makes the technology sound “fake.” So this new White House executive order seeks to implement the change, stating that the name “Super Intelligence” more appropriately captures the promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies.
All of this signals that the American government is actively looking to pivot away from the current doomsday public narrative surrounding AI, aiming instead to focus public attention on the positive outcomes of its development.
So, with this new name, we can all finally breathe a sigh of relief and put to rest all those spooks of evil, fake intelligence agents escaping their sandboxes to hack Mark knows what. The looming AI apocalypse has taken a raincheck, and we can happily prepare for the dawn of a golden-age paradise ushered in by this new, real Super intelligence. Right? Well…
Broadly speaking, experts remain skeptical about what genuine safety regulations will actually come out of the pact, given that the executives signing it are likely to be the very ones who will get to define the term “safety.” So at least in this regard, the meeting is largely symbolic.
It is primarily aimed at cooling public heat around apocalyptic AI narratives and the growing discontent over data centers, exactly what you would expect from an administration whose 2024 campaign was heavily bankrolled by tech elites such as Elon Musk, Greg Brockman, and others eager to promote their own corporate agendas.
But if we zoom past the end-times scenarios that the administration and these billionaires are trying to dampen, there is one critical thread left out of the conversation, which is the inherently collectivist nature of the Super Intelligence shaping this future “Golden Age of America.”
From each according to his ability
Since the beginning of his term, Trump and the Republican Party have been championing AI as an individualistic enterprise, framing it as a tool to amplify personal intellectual capabilities and boost American rugged individualism on a new technological frontier. That certainly has a pleasant Americana ring to it, especially if the bell that it’s ringing is Republican.
However, not even all the tech billionaires bankrolling the party see it the same way. A notable example is venture capitalist and Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, who has drawn parallels between AI and collectivism. Thiel previously argued that unlike crypto, which he believes promotes libertarianism, AI is, at its core, communist.
If you look closely at what kind of future artificial intelligence has to offer, Thiel’s claim no longer seems so far-fetched. There is indeed a deep, structural similarity between the growth of AI systems and core Marxist ideals.
Firstly, building a powerful AI model requires massive centralization, which is what Thiel apparently has the biggest problem with as a libertarian. Developing more powerful AI models requires harvesting billions of gigabytes of data into massive data centers, controlled by only a handful of corporate entities with the necessary capital and computing power.
That means your private intellectual ownership is effectively cast out of the window. For good. Whatever you write on the internet, post on YouTube, or even the books you published way before the age of AI, all of it turns into AI food, constantly fed in chunks into a data center to train a model, which in its turn redistributes the results of your work to anyone who uses AI.
That inherently builds a top-down, centralized system of information redistribution, which is reminiscent of how a collectivist state functions.
To each according to his needs
Silicon Valley leaders are increasingly using the rise of AI to push for heavily socialist economic frameworks as part of their public relations strategy. Because advanced AI systems are automating millions of human jobs, tech leaders believe they need to pacify the public by advertising AI as a structural safety net to keep society stable when human labor is no longer economically viable.
Open AI CEO Sam Altman, for instance, advocated for universal basic income, a classic socialist economic concept. If that sounds too good to be true, well, it’s because it is. Even Altman eventually walked back the idea, replacing it with a concept he calls “universal basic compute.”
Comparing AI to public utilities like water or electricity, Altman argues that every human being should be given an equal, baseline slice of a centralized supercomputer’s output in the form of AI tokens, which people can use, share, or sell.
A remarkably similar philosophy underpins Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s public manifesto, “the future is for everyone,” in which he argues that computational power and advanced data models should be distributed equally to give the power back to people.
In Marxist terms, these tech billionaires are basically advocating for the redistribution of the means of production to the masses, pushing the idea of collective ownership over the very personal data they seized from you. The “empowering everyone” rhetoric surely sounds nice when reading the utopian visions of Altman and Zuckerberg and it conveniently keeps you from thinking about how those same tech lords acquired your data in the first place by making off with your intellectual property.
Intellectual communism
In the 20th century, Soviet ideologists spent decades trying to engineer what they called the “New Soviet Man.” This was a theoretical ideal of a uniform, selfless citizen who would completely dissolve their individual desires, beliefs, and identity into one collective entity striving for the common good.
This experiment became a major concern for dystopian writers like George Orwell, who saw one of the vices of collectivism in making everyone the same, and it is the very same concept actively criticized by Republicans today as a totalitarian manifestation of communism.
Yet, this totalitarian equality of thought is an inherent design feature of AI operational systems we use every day.
In an interview with journalist Tucker Carlson, Sam Altman explicitly admitted that they train their AI models “to be like the collective of all of humanity.” This means that instead of amplifying unique human perspectives or protecting individual thought, the core goal of leading AI development seems to be building a machine that represents the mathematical average of everyone at once – not highlighting individualism, but eroding it.
Furthermore, AI models by design always favor strict neutrality and highly balanced answers. They are taught to avoid taking strong, polarizing ideological stances, which you may have noticed whenever an AI chatbot answers a controversial question. It automatically forces a framework of mutual understanding and polite compromise, which makes the answer lack individuality or any personal edge.
On the surface, this design seems very helpful and positive. It can defuse toxic political arguments and depoliticize intense cultural conflicts by conditioning users to look at both sides of an issue, leading to a “More Perfect Union,” as Barack Obama would call it.
However, this forced neutrality and conformity has a dangerous dark side to it. By constantly pushing users toward a safe, mass-approved middle ground, AI slowly rewires your individual reasoning patterns and causes you to adopt a safer, collective intellectual framework and a common morality shared by the majority – essentially turning you into a Clockwork Orange.
If one relies on AI to write, think, and make decisions, which is incredibly convenient and tempting in modern, fast-paced society, their unique worldview and ideological standing are gradually lobotomized. Over time, it creates a synthetic collective unconscious where individual dissent is softly phased out in favor of a group consensus, or rather, a group consensus approved by the Superintelligent Equalizer that AI is.
Republican AI paradox
All of this creates a paradox for Donald Trump and his conservative base. Anti-communist rhetoric, warnings of a “socialist takeover,” and the defense of American individualism are the absolute core fixtures of Trump’s political speeches.
Yet, by demanding the rapid, acceleration of the domestic AI industry, Trump is championing the exact technology intentionally or unintentionally designed to dissolve individual identity into a massive collective pool, strip citizens of private data ownership and centralize technological power. And Republicans, knowingly or unknowingly, are actively building the infrastructure for the ultimate collectivist system, all while preaching the virtues of the free market.
So, while GOP members continue to manufacture a new Red Scare to rally voters in the culture wars, they are simultaneously subsidizing a technological framework, which upon closer examination, looks very much like a textbook caricature of some dystopian totalitarian collectivism run by a party of techlords.
And even though Trump says “America will never be communist,” even some of his billionaire donors don’t seem to buy it.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.
