Iran has the attractions, the challenge is turning them into tourism: Javad Gharaei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:24:23 UTC
22:24:23 KST

Iran has the attractions, the challenge is turning them into tourism: Javad Gharaei
TEHRAN - Iran does not lack tourism attractions. What it has struggled to do, says Iranian traveler and documentary filmmaker Javad Gharaei, is turn the country’s extraordinary natural and cultural diversity into a tourism industry capable of attracting visitors, generating revenue and properly introducing the ancient country to the world.
After decades of traveling across Iran, from the Hyrcanian forests and Zagros Mountains to the Lut Desert and the Makran coast, Gharaei has seen a country where landscapes, climates, cultures and traditions can change dramatically within relatively short distances. He considers that diversity one of Iran’s greatest national assets, but an asset that remains underused.
For Gharaei, the challenge is not simply building more hotels, roads or other tourism infrastructure. Promotion, investment, education and infrastructure must advance together, he argues, while the authenticity of destinations must be protected from the pressures of tourism itself.
In a conversation with the Tehran Times on the Tehran Talks program, Gharaei reflects on more than two decades of travel and documentary-making, the tourism potential of Iran’s diverse landscapes and communities, the role of documentaries in putting little-known destinations on the map, and the need to develop tourism without destroying the very authenticity that makes places worth visiting.
Below is an edited selection of the interview:
Where did your fascination with Iran’s nature begin?
Well, I fell in love with nature when I was about 17 or 18. I began mountaineering in the mountains of Shemiran, in northern Tehran. Gradually, I moved on to other mountains and took mountaineering and skiing courses at different clubs.
The more I traveled through the mountains, the more I realized that there was much more than the peaks themselves. There were plains, deserts, valleys and completely different environments along the routes.
That was when I gradually became familiar with Iran’s extraordinary natural diversity.
Iran has almost all of the world’s major climates. Apart from tropical and polar climates, we have almost every major type of climate in one country.
And this climatic diversity has produced cultural diversity as well.
If the entire planet had one climate, cultures would probably be far more similar. But climate affects almost everything: architecture, food, clothing, music, customs, ceremonies, rituals, beliefs and even, to some extent, people’s ways of life and temperaments.
For me, this is one of the most fascinating things about Iran.
So your journey began with nature, but eventually took you toward culture and history as well?
Exactly. As I became familiar with different natural environments, I also encountered different ethnic groups and communities. That made me increasingly interested in Iran’s history and culture.
I began studying them more seriously and became fascinated by the depth of Iranian civilization.
Eventually, alongside my filmmaking education at the Iranian Youth Cinema Society, I studied tourism management at university. During my studies, I became even more interested in the enormous number and diversity of tourism attractions in Iran.
I began asking myself a very simple question: If we possess such an extraordinary range of attractions, why have we not made better use of them?
Iranian traveler and documentary filmmaker Javad Gharaei speaks to the Tehran Times at the newspaper’s studio.
Iran has not only natural attractions. We have ethnic and cultural diversity, history, architecture and a civilization that has developed over thousands of years.
In my view, these attractions are national assets, just as oil, gas, mineral resources, agricultural land and our territory are national assets.
Yet we have not used this particular asset as effectively as we could have.
We have not generated the foreign-exchange earnings that tourism could potentially provide, and we have not attracted the number of international visitors that a country with this level of diversity might expect.
That realization was one of the reasons I entered the tourism field.
I wanted to portray these attractions as well as I could, because of my love for Iran, for Iranian people and for the country’s civilization.
I also felt that some people inside the country, including some officials, had not fully recognized the importance of these attractions, either as things that need to be protected or as assets that can create economic opportunities and introduce Iran to the world.
You have described tourism attractions as a national asset. Why do you think Iran has struggled to turn that asset into a successful tourism industry?
One of the biggest weaknesses is that we have not properly introduced our attractions to the world.
For about eight years, I have been pursuing a project called Journey to the Land of Dreams. My objective has been to introduce Iran beyond its borders.
But the project has not yet come to fruition because, in my view, officials have not fully recognized the extent to which tourism can contribute to the country, economically, politically, culturally and even spiritually.
Think about the situation: a country with this geographical position, cultural diversity and history has still not been able to introduce itself to the world as effectively as it could.
That is one of the major weaknesses of our tourism industry.
You have emphasized promotion. But many people argue that Iran must first develop its tourism infrastructure before it can seriously compete with countries such as Turkey or Malaysia. Do you agree?
I think infrastructure, promotion, education and investment must develop together.
When I was studying tourism at university, I researched Malaysia. Malaysia has a very successful tourism industry, but in terms of the diversity of attractions, I believe Iran has a much greater range.
What happened in Malaysia was interesting. At first, officials focused heavily on infrastructure. They invested for years and developed very good infrastructure. But then they realized that tourists were still not arriving in sufficient numbers.
They understood that infrastructure alone was not enough. They also needed to advertise the country and introduce its attractions to the world.
I think we can learn from that experience.
Sometimes we say, “First we need infrastructure. Then, perhaps 10 years later, we can promote tourism.”
I do not think that is economically sensible.
Imagine spending billions of dollars over 10 years on infrastructure and only then beginning to expect revenue. Why not develop infrastructure while simultaneously promoting destinations, educating people and attracting investment?
We already have a certain level of infrastructure. We have hotels, hostels and inns. We have extremely hospitable people, which is a very important tourism asset.
We also have aviation infrastructure, although aviation has faced serious difficulties, including the attacks on passenger aircraft during the recent war.
The important point is that we should not wait for everything to become perfect before we begin.
Tourists themselves generate demand. Demand attracts investors. Investment creates more infrastructure.
You have a practical example of that process in Sistan-Baluchestan province.
Yes. Sistan-Baluchestan is a very good example.
In 2009, I went there and began producing my first documentary series in the region. I worked along the Makran (aka Makkoran) coast, from Gwatar Bay toward the borders of Sistan-Baluchestan and Hormozgan.
At that time, around 2010, Chabahar had only three hotels. Along the coastal strip there were essentially no hostels, eco-lodges or guesthouses. Those hotels were mainly used by a limited number of business travelers, and there were only one or two flights a week.
We produced several documentary segments and they were broadcast on television.
After the programs were broadcast, many tourists began traveling to the region.
Today, there are more than 15 four- and five-star hotels in Chabahar, and more than 150 eco-lodges along the coastal strip alone.
The change was remarkable.
What does that tell us?
Tourists bring investors. They create demand for infrastructure. They create demand for training and services.
If you promote a destination properly and bring people there, you can identify what is needed. Then government authorities, investors and local communities can respond.
Infrastructure can develop very quickly when there is real demand.
In that region, a great deal changed within two or three years.
So I believe tourism development is not as complicated as we sometimes make it.
You mentioned the extraordinary experience of moving between different climates. One place that illustrates this particularly well is Opert, on the border between Semnan and Mazandaran. What makes it special?
Opert is extraordinary because of the dramatic change that takes place within a very short distance.
It lies on the border between Semnan and Mazandaran. Imagine starting in a dry landscape, with little water and vegetation, and then moving toward the mountains.
At one point, the temperature below was around 35 degrees Celsius. I was traveling in short sleeves. That same night, it snowed in the higher elevations and the temperature fell to around minus 14 degrees.
That is a difference of roughly 45 degrees within a very small geographical area.
And the climatic change brings cultural and ecological changes with it.
As you travel, dialects change. Clothing changes. Food changes. Music changes. The landscape changes. You encounter different communities and different ways of life.
From the dry landscapes of Semnan, you can eventually look toward Mazandaran and see the dense Hyrcanian forests.
Within perhaps 30 kilometers, you can move from camels, saxaul and desert vegetation to snow-covered mountains and forested landscapes.
Further up, you enter habitats associated with species such as the Persian leopard, golden eagle and brown bear.
Every few dozen kilometers, it can feel as if you have entered a completely different world.
It can also be difficult.
On one trip, we planned to return the next day, but everything froze and became covered in snow. Our vehicles could not reach the higher elevations.
The Red Crescent came to our assistance and sent specialized vehicles. A journey that would normally have taken perhaps half an hour or an hour took about six hours.
So Iran’s diversity is not simply beautiful. Sometimes it is also physically demanding.
You have spent years documenting such places. What makes a tourism documentary successful? How can it encourage people to travel rather than simply watch?
The first requirement is honesty.
A documentary should be something people can rely on. It should not create a false picture.
Of course, we should show beauty. But we should also show challenges, opportunities and realities.
The audience should see different dimensions of the place, person or subject and then make an informed decision.
That is particularly important in tourism documentaries.
Let me give you an example.
I once visited a village in Sistan-Baluchestan, between Zahedan and Chabahar, where people were living in a very traditional way.
Their houses were handmade from the branches and leaves of a wild date palm found in the region.
There was no electricity. They obtained water from a mountain spring. When I arrived, I felt as though I had gone back hundreds of years.
Someone else might have looked at the same place and said, “How difficult and terrible these people’s lives are.”
But I did not see it that way.
I saw an extraordinary example of adaptation and traditional knowledge.
The people had preserved handmade architecture over generations. The women wore clothing with elaborate handmade embroidery. They had developed ways of coping with their environment without modern technology.
They even had what you might call a handmade refrigerator.
They dug a hole about a meter deep, lined it with palm fibers and leaves, kept the material wet and placed food inside. In an environment where the outside temperature could reach around 40 degrees Celsius, this simple system kept food considerably cooler.
When I arrived, a wedding ceremony was taking place. Families had gathered and were celebrating.
For me, this was not simply a story about poverty or a lack of modern facilities. It was a story about authenticity, traditional knowledge and a way of life that had survived for generations.
And that authenticity itself has value.
What happened after the documentary was broadcast?
Something very interesting happened.
After the film was published on YouTube and elsewhere, tourists from Finland, Japan, China and several European countries visited the area.
The local headman later sent me a photograph of his son. He had gone to a place where there was mobile reception and contacted me through WhatsApp. He told me that foreign tourists had come because of the film.
The journey was not easy. The area could be reached only by motorcycle, horseback or on foot. Visitors had to travel for two or three hours through the mountains.
Interestingly, the local governor once asked me, “Where did you find this place?” Even he had never been there.
That experience showed me the power of documentary filmmaking.
A film can introduce a place that even local officials may not know well.
But it also raises an important question: What happens to authenticity when tourists begin arriving?
Exactly. If tourism brings visitors to pristine communities, how do we make sure that the very authenticity attracting those visitors is not destroyed?
That is where the concept of authenticity becomes extremely important.
In my view, countries that want to succeed in tourism must preserve their authenticity.
Much of the modern world has become similar. People in different countries have access to similar hotels, shopping malls, restaurants, hospitals, parks and entertainment.
People do not necessarily travel thousands of kilometers simply to see things they can find at home.
They want to see something that does not exist in their own environment.
That is why Iran’s traditional lifestyles, cultural diversity and ancient heritage are so valuable.
But these authentic elements are becoming weaker or disappearing.
If we want tourism to succeed, we have to protect them.
We must respect authenticity, preserve it and present it carefully to visitors.
At the same time, we have to understand carrying capacity.
Every attraction and every destination has a limit.
Before developing tourism, we should understand the attraction, understand its sensitivity and learn how to manage it.
Then we must protect it.
If we ignore carrying capacity, large numbers of tourists can damage natural, historical, rural and ethnographic attractions.
This is not only about foreign tourists. It also applies to domestic tourism.
I also went to Shirz Valley in Lorestan and introduced it through my work. It is an extraordinary and spectacular valley, particularly at certain times of the year.
Local people had already been visiting, but there were environmental problems, including litter.
I tried to raise awareness about those problems.
The important point is that carrying capacity does not depend on nationality.
An Iranian tourist can damage an attraction just as a foreign tourist can.
The question is whether visitors understand how to use a destination responsibly.
We should not allow mass tourism to destroy local communities, nature or heritage.
If I ask you to choose just one Iranian landscape that has impressed you more than all the others, what would you choose?
I cannot choose only one.
I have traveled abroad, and I have deliberately tried not to let patriotic feelings influence my judgment. I wanted to compare things rationally.
And when I did that, I still reached the conclusion that Iran is genuinely unique in many respects.
Take the Hyrcanian forests.
These ancient forests stretch across Gilan, Mazandaran and Golestan and continue toward the border with Azerbaijan. They are among the world’s ancient forest ecosystems and have been recognized on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
Then there is the Lut Desert, which is also a World Heritage site.
When I first entered the Lut about 17 years ago, I did not imagine that a desert could be so fascinating.
People sometimes say the desert is fascinating because of its silence.
For me, it was more than silence.
There are no trees, rivers or mountains in the way you normally experience them. There may be almost no vegetation. But the absence itself becomes beautiful.
The curved lines of the land disappear into the horizon. At sunrise and sunset, the colors can change dramatically.
And then there is the night sky.
When you stand in the desert at night, you can see an extraordinary number of stars. They seem incredibly close.
Because of light pollution, this experience has become increasingly rare around the world.
The night sky is itself an environmental asset, and light pollution is a growing problem. As cities and villages expand, we lose the natural darkness required to see the stars.
I have even produced a multi-part documentary about the Lut.
And beyond the forests and deserts?
The Zagros is another extraordinary world.
When you enter the Zagros, you encounter oak forests, nomadic communities and the cultures of the Lurs, Qashqai and Kurds.
The mountain range stretches across a huge part of western and southern Iran, from Kurdistan through Lorestan and Fars toward Bushehr and Hormozgan.
It is rugged and sometimes difficult, but I love it very much.
Then there is Iran’s southern coastline.
In parts of Bushehr and Hormozgan, you travel through mountainous landscapes and suddenly look down into deep valleys extending toward the Persian Gulf.
Further east, you reach the Makran coast and the Sea of Oman.
There are blue waters, golden beaches and sand dunes beside the sea.
In parts of Sistan-Baluchestan, you can see sand dunes almost next to the sea, with palm groves between them.
Such combinations are rare.
You can find comparable landscapes in parts of Namibia, Chile and some Arab countries, but Iran has its own version of this extraordinary combination.
That is why I say that almost every part of Iran has something unique.
You have spoken at length about Iran’s beauty. But your documentaries also address environmental and social problems. How important is it for a filmmaker to show those problems?
It is essential. A documentary filmmaker must be honest and deeply committed to the work.
Over roughly 20 years, I believe I have produced around 140 documentary episodes. My focus has been Iran, its beauty and attractions, but also its challenges and problems.
In almost every program, alongside the beauty, I have tried to show problems affecting the environment, nature or local communities.
But I do not want simply to point at a problem.
Where possible, I consult scientists and specialists and try to present solutions.
I want the presence of the documentary team to have a positive effect.
In many places where we documented problems, those problems were later addressed or improved.
That is very important to me.
A documentary should not merely observe a problem. If possible, it should help people understand it and encourage a solution.
Today, however, audiences are increasingly consuming very short content on Instagram and other social-media platforms. Younger people may not sit through a long documentary. Does this mean documentaries themselves have to become shorter?
What you have described is a serious problem.
Very short content cannot go deeply into an issue.
It cannot adequately explore a complex environmental, historical, political or social question.
Social media has encouraged people to seek faster and shorter content. As a result, patience has declined, and people can become superficial in the way they approach complex subjects.
Someone hears one sentence and immediately reaches a conclusion.
That is dangerous.
At the same time, I do not completely agree that people will no longer watch long-form content.
Look at cinema. Films can last one, two or even three hours, and people still watch them.
Television and streaming series can contain dozens of episodes, each lasting 45 or 50 minutes, and audiences continue to follow them.
So we have to find a balance.
Personally, I think documentaries generally should not be longer than around 40 or 45 minutes.
Within that time, we should tell the story properly and bring it to a conclusion.
But the rhythm has to be engaging.
We need to understand today’s audience and make programs that move at an appropriate pace.
What we must not do, however, is sacrifice depth simply because the audience has become accustomed to superficial content.
If we completely adapt ourselves to superficial thinking, we will have betrayed our responsibility to society and future generations.
We should make documentaries more engaging, but we should not reduce the depth of research, investigation and writing.
Instead of following the audience into superficiality, we should try to take the audience toward greater depth.
If you put on your critical glasses and compare your documentaries with international productions, what would you change if you had the opportunity to make them again?
I would certainly change things.
But many of the things I would change are connected to the conditions under which we work.
My biggest limitations are time and budget.
Let me give you an example.
There was a BBC documentary, I believe the title was something like ‘human and nature”, although I may not remember the exact title, that consisted of eight episodes of around 50 minutes each.
According to what I remember, they spent about five years producing it. They had a strong team and a budget of more than $25 million.
Do we have such conditions in Iran?
We do not even have one-tenth of those resources.
If I were given a year and a half or two years to produce 26 one-hour episodes, I would do it.
That is roughly the kind of time I am usually given for such work.
But if you told me, “You have five years to make eight highly professional documentary episodes,” I would still need a budget that is not normally available.
So my two major problems are time and budget.
We have equipment. We have facilities. We have professional and highly skilled crews. We have extraordinary attractions and infrastructure.
But we do not have enough time and money to produce at the level I would like.
Much of the criticism I have of my own work comes back to those limitations.
What are the physical challenges of documentary production?
There are many, far more than people see on television.
And limited budgets make those challenges even greater.
I remember hearing about one of Sir David Attenborough’s productions in Africa. Several vehicles belonging to his team became stuck in mud, and the crew spent one or two hours trying to get them out.
He said the British Army supported their productions in different parts of the world so that they could complete their work under difficult circumstances.
We do not have that kind of support.
Wherever we go, it is essentially just us.
Imagine producing documentaries across a country as geographically diverse as Iran, with deserts, high mountains, forests, remote villages, snow, extreme heat and difficult roads, and doing it with limited resources.
The challenges are enormous.
But we love Iran.
That love is one of the reasons we continue.
We have tried, despite all these difficulties, to maintain international professional standards.
I am not saying that we have produced perfect or extraordinary programs every time.
I am saying that we have tried to stay within professional standards and not compromise the fundamental principles of documentary filmmaking.
Maintaining those standards under difficult circumstances, in such a vast country with such extraordinary climatic diversity, is not easy.

Israel attempts to frame Gaza reporters it killed as 'militants'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:22:30 UTC
22:22:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel compounds pain of slain Gaza journalists' families with 'militant' claims
For nearly three years of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, Palestinian journalists have worked under the constant threat of Israeli targeting and bombardment.
Now, even in death, some are being targeted by accusations seeking to recast them as members of armed groups rather than journalists.
On Thursday, the Israeli army claimed that 170 Palestinian media workers and journalists killed in Gaza were, in fact, members of armed factions.
The army claimed that 118 of those named were affiliated with Hamas' military wing and 49 with Palestinian Islamic Jihad, while two allegedly belonged to the Popular Resistance Committees and one to the Mujahideen Brigades. It also claimed that 17 had participated in the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.
The army posted names on a website along with documents and visuals as alleged evidence of the individuals' affiliations and roles.
It also appeared to try to drive a wedge between reporters in Gaza international media outlets, highlighting that some of those named had worked with Reuters, CNN, the BBC, Agence France-Presse, the Associated Press, and Le Monde.
According to the Israeli army, this demonstrated a discrepancy between how they were presented internationally and what it described as their "reality on the ground".
The claims have been flatly rejected by Palestinian media organisations, which say Israeli military allegations cannot by themselves determine whether a deceased journalist was involved in military activity.
'A journalist until the very end'
Among those named by the Israeli army was Palestinian journalist Adam Abu Harbid, who was killed in Gaza on 25 July 2025.
His family said the attempt to reclassify him after his death amounts to an effort to erase his professional identity and cast doubt on the circumstances of his killing.
"Adam was a journalist; that is how we knew him throughout his life," his relative told The New Arab.
"He carried his work tools and went to places where people needed to know what was happening. He did not carry a weapon, nor did he conceal any military affiliation, as the occupation is now trying to portray," he said.
"The allegations were particularly painful because Adam could no longer respond to them," he added.
"It is difficult for his family to hear, after his death, that he was anything other than who we knew him to be," he said. "If Israel has clear evidence that he was a fighter, why doesn't it publish independent, verifiable proof? We know our son, and we know his work."
"Adam died a journalist, and that is how we know him," he continued. "We want nothing more than for him to be remembered as he was, and for his profession and work to be kept separate from these accusations."
Families of other Palestinian journalists killed during the war have similarly expressed concern that accusations made after their deaths could damage their reputations while leaving them unable to defend themselves.
'We report what we see'
Palestinian journalists in Gaza have worked under extraordinary conditions since the genocidal war began, with hundreds killed according to Palestinian authorities and media organisations.
At the same time, foreign journalists have largely been prevented by Israel from entering the enclave independently.
A Palestinian field journalist, speaking anonymously for security reasons, said local reporters had effectively become "the world's eyes inside Gaza".
"We do not go to a location because we want to be a party to the war," he told TNA. "We go because there is an event the public needs to know about. When a bomb hits a home, our mission is to document what happened and report the names of the victims, not to participate in the fighting."
"Sometimes we work without knowing if we will return home," he said. "A journalist in Gaza carries a camera, a phone and a notebook, attempting to convey what is happening amid fear. Yet after all that, someone might claim you were a combatant simply because you were present at the site of a bombing."
He said the absence of foreign journalists had placed an even greater burden on Palestinian reporters.
"If foreign journalists were here with us, they could see for themselves how we work and how we reach targeted areas, gather information and interview people," he added. "Yet while the world relies on Palestinian journalists, the occupation turns around and claims that these very people are not journalists."
He said reporters understood the risks involved but continued working, because stopping would mean many stories would never reach the outside world.
"We do not ask anyone to believe us simply because we are Palestinian," he explained. "We ask that our work be judged by journalistic standards and that accusations be investigated independently. If a journalist participated in military action, let the evidence be presented. But a journalist killed in Gaza cannot simply be labelled a combatant because the Israeli army says so."
Journalists' syndicate rejects Israeli claims
Tahseen al-Astal, deputy head of the Palestinian Journalists' Syndicate in Gaza, condemned the Israeli claims as part of what he described as a "systematic campaign" to undermine the professional standing of Palestinian journalists killed during the war.
He told TNA that the journalists and media workers killed in Gaza had been engaged in documented journalistic work, working for local, Arab and international organisations or as independent reporters.
"These baseless allegations are part of a systematic campaign aimed at targeting the truth, tarnishing the image of Palestinian journalists and undermining their professional and national standing," al-Astal said.
He added that the syndicate was the Palestinian professional body responsible for representing journalists and documenting violations against them.
The Gaza Government Media Office said the number of Palestinian journalists killed since the beginning of the war had reached 263 following the death of media worker Mohammed Abdul Aziz al-Najjar in recent days.
It accused Israel of systematically targeting Palestinian journalists and called on international and Arab press organisations to condemn what it described as crimes against media workers.
For Palestinian journalists, the Israeli list has added another layer to the dangers of reporting from Gaza: not only the possibility of being killed while working, but the prospect that their professional identity could be challenged after death.
The journalists' work has provided much of the imagery, testimony and reporting reaching audiences around the world during the war, amid restrictions on the entry of foreign media.
Their families and colleagues now say that allegations made after their deaths should not be accepted as established fact without independent verification.
For those still reporting from Gaza, the concern is not only what may happen while they are alive, but also how they could be portrayed once they are gone.

UK Greens vote on motion critics say backs Israel’s destruction; Jewish leader to abstain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:21:43 UTC
22:21:43 KST

Britain’s Green Party convened Sunday to vote on a highly contentious motion that would define Zionism as a form of racism and call for the creation of a single Palestinian state across all of what it describes as “historic Palestine,” wording critics say would effectively mean the end of Israel as a Jewish state.
The motion has proved too far-reaching even for some of the party’s most outspoken critics of Israel, including Green Party leader Zack Polanski, who is Jewish and describes himself as anti-Zionist. Polanski is expected to abstain.
The vote is taking place at the party’s annual conference in Brighton, against the backdrop of the Greens’ sharp rise in British opinion polls in recent years. Once a marginal political force, the party now ranks fourth or fifth in several recent surveys.
The proposal would add to official Green Party policy the position that Zionism is a form of racism because it supports what the motion calls an “ethno-national Jewish state.”
British media noted that, if approved, the measure could make the Greens the only mainstream European political party to define itself explicitly as anti-Zionist.
The motion also calls for the establishment of “one democratic Palestinian state across all of historic Palestine, with Jerusalem as its capital” and demands sweeping boycotts and sanctions against Israel similar to those imposed on apartheid-era South Africa.
It argues that “Zionism has created, and seeks to maintain and, where possible, expand, a system of apartheid between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea.”
Green Party deputy leader Mothin Ali, who has become one of the party’s most prominent anti-Israel voices over the past year, became the most senior party figure to endorse the motion.
Speaking to the BBC on Saturday, Ali said he supported it “absolutely,” arguing that it addressed “ethnic cleansing and ethno-nationalism.”
“Anyone who believes in that, I think, believes in a racist ideology,” he said.
In an interview with Sky News, Ali added: “The ultimate form of racism is genocide, and therefore anyone who believes in carrying out genocide against human beings simply so that they themselves can live freely, that is racism.”
Polanski, meanwhile, said he plans to abstain from the vote but again declined in a BBC interview to say whether Israel has a right to exist.
Asked whether the call for a single Palestinian state amounted in practice to a demand for the elimination of Israel, Polanski said that was precisely why he wanted the motion amended.
“What I want to see is equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians,” he said. “I don’t think we, as the Green Party of England and Wales, or even the British government, should determine what a future settlement looks like.”
Pressed on whether Israel has a right to exist, he replied: “I believe human beings have a right to exist. Israelis have a right to exist, and Palestinians have a right to exist. I think our job as political parties is to protect the rights of human beings, not to protect the rights of states.”
The Daily Mail, a right-leaning British tabloid frequently critical of the radical left, noted that three former Green leaders, Caroline Lucas, Adrian Ramsay and Carla Denyer, had publicly opposed the motion.
Lucas, who in 2010 became Britain’s first Green member of Parliament, said she would not support it because of the risk that it would deepen divisions and be seen as signaling that Jews were not welcome in the party.
Denyer wrote on social media that adopting the proposal could “set us back” in efforts to support Palestinians and could alienate a large part of Britain’s Jewish community, including people who strongly oppose the Israeli government, support the BDS movement and advocate for Palestinian rights.
Amid claims that the issue was tearing the party apart, Polanski told the BBC that the Greens were “completely united” on the Palestinian issue.
He cited Palestinian casualty figures in Gaza and said the party agreed on the need to “stop the genocide” and halt British arms sales to Israel.
This year’s Green Party conference includes a series of events focused on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Among them was a panel titled “Palestine: The Golden Thread That Unravelled Britain,” moderated by an activist who took part in a Gaza flotilla and was detained by Israeli forces, as well as an event titled “Justice for Palestine” and a discussion on claims of Israeli “sportswashing.”
Pro-Palestinian and pro-Israel demonstrations were also held outside the conference venue.
The Daily Mail reported Sunday that, amid tensions inside the party, conference organizers had designated a “safe room” for Jewish members who might feel threatened.
A Jewish party member described the situation as “disturbing and deeply upsetting, but this is the reality.”
A senior Jewish figure in the party said: “I’ve been a member of the Green Party for years, but never, ever, have Jewish Greens had to endure a situation like this.”

Putin’s Claims of Russian Battlefield Gains “Border on Hallucinations,” ISW Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:21:19 UTC
22:21:19 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Putin’s Claims of Russian Battlefield Gains “Border on Hallucinations,” ISW Says
Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s claims of major Russian battlefield gains in Ukraine in September “border on hallucinations,” according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), which assessed that Russian forces actually ended the month with a net territorial loss.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to ISW on October 2, Putin claimed that Russian forces captured 1,301 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory in September. ISW’s battlefield data, however, showed that Russian forces suffered a net territorial loss of 80.81 square kilometers during the same period.
Putin made the claim during a meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club on October 1, saying Russian forces had brought 1,301 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory under their control in September—roughly 2.5 times more than in previous months.
ISW’s geolocated battlefield data showed a substantially different picture. The institute assessed that Russian forces captured 175.54 square kilometers during September, while Ukrainian forces regained 256.35 square kilometers.
That resulted in a net Russian territorial loss of 80.81 square kilometers over the course of the month, rather than the large territorial gain described by Putin.
The discrepancy becomes even larger when areas where Russian troops infiltrated but failed to establish control are included. Under that calculation, ISW assessed Russia’s net territorial losses in September at 175.18 square kilometers.
ISW said Putin’s claims about Russian battlefield progress were so disconnected from observed developments that they “border on hallucinations.”
The institute assessed that Putin’s statements are consistent with the Kremlin’s broader cognitive warfare efforts to portray Russian forces as advancing rapidly across the front and Ukrainian defenses as deteriorating.
ISW noted that it remains unclear whether Putin is aware of the discrepancy between the figures he publicly presents and observed battlefield developments.
The institute has previously assessed that senior Russian military officials have exaggerated territorial gains when reporting battlefield developments.
ISW has linked such discrepancies to what it describes as a deeply rooted practice within the Russian military command of concealing setbacks and presenting senior leadership with inflated reports of battlefield success.
During his Valdai remarks, Putin also claimed that Russian forces could seize the remaining Ukrainian-held areas of the Donetsk region sooner than Ukraine and European countries expect.
Earlier in September, ISW assessed that at Russia’s then-current rate of advance, its forces would need more than six years to capture the remaining Ukrainian-controlled territory in the Donetsk region, pushing the timeline to October 2032—well beyond Moscow’s stated goal of taking the entire region by the end of 2026.

The SBU urges Ukrainians not to publish photos and videos of enemy shelling
Kyiv • UNN
The SBU urged people not to share footage of attacks, air defense operations, or military facilities, as the enemy could use it to launch repeat strikes. This is punishable by up to 12 years in prison.
Sharing footage from the sites of Russian strikes could help the Russian military prepare follow-up attacks. The Security Service of Ukraine calls on citizens not to publish such materials online, UNN reports.
Details
The Security Service of Ukraine calls on citizens not to film or share photos and videos of enemy attacks. In particular, people should not publish content documenting the occupiers’ strikes on military facilities and critical infrastructure, the operation of air defense systems, and so on. These recordings may be used not only by Russian propagandists, but also by the Russian military, which monitors and analyzes such materials in order to adjust its follow-up strikes
In addition, the agency emphasizes that law enforcement authorities may regard the publication of such content as a crime, which carries severe punishment.
Depending on the accompanying circumstances, such actions may be classified under Article 114-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. In particular, this concerns the unauthorized dissemination of information about the movement of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and the provision of information to a state carrying out armed aggression against Ukraine (punishable by up to 12 years in prison)
According to the available information, the Service’s operational units are systematically investigating cases involving the dissemination of such recordings online and bringing their authors to justice.
We call on Ukrainians to act responsibly, not to help the enemy, and not to endanger other citizens!
We remind you
A survey by Active Group showed that 56.1% of Ukrainians support European standards for content removal, although support has declined from 67.2% in May. At the same time, 53.9% of respondents do not feel protected from dangerous content online.

Shocking report: 121% rise in psychiatric ER visits among children and teens since Oct. 7th
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:18:26 UTC
22:18:26 KST

Shocking report: 121% rise in psychiatric ER visits among children and teens since Oct. 7th
Southern evacuees continued to record a PTSD diagnosis rate six times higher in the war’s third year, according to a report publish by Clalit
Three years into the war, a health snapshot released by Clalit, based on data from approximately five million members, highlights a continuing burden on mental and physical health, with notable increases among children, adolescents and residents evacuated from southern and northern Israel.
The findings span psychiatric emergency care, post-traumatic stress disorder, blood pressure, high cholesterol and medication use for childhood bedwetting. Together, they point to health needs extending well beyond the immediate period of displacement.
Clalit reported a 121% increase in psychiatric emergency room visits by children and adolescents, more than double the comparison level.
The finding concerns visits rather than the number of individual patients. The figures provided do not indicate how many young people sought emergency care, whether some attended more than once, or which conditions accounted for the increase.
Nevertheless, the rise highlights the scale of demand for urgent psychiatric care among young people during the war.
Among residents evacuated from the South, the rate of PTSD diagnoses remained six times higher even in the war’s third year, Clalit reported.
The persistence of that elevated rate suggests that the mental health burden has continued long after the initial evacuation. However, the information released here does not specify the comparison population or baseline used to calculate the sixfold difference.
Diagnosis rates also reflect conditions identified and recorded within the healthcare system; they do not necessarily capture everyone experiencing symptoms.
Among southern evacuees, Clalit reported a 53.7% increase in the rate of uncontrolled blood pressure. Among northern evacuees, the rate of diagnoses of hyperlipidemia, high levels of fats in the blood, including cholesterol—rose by approximately 60%.
Among children from the South, the use of medication for bedwetting increased by 47.8%, according to Clalit.
The figure measures medication use, rather than the overall prevalence of bedwetting. Without additional information about prescribing patterns and the children receiving treatment, it cannot establish how much the condition itself increased or how directly the change was connected to wartime experiences.
Clalit’s approximately five million members provide a substantial basis for examining health trends. But the headline findings supplied do not include absolute patient numbers, the precise comparison periods, age breakdowns or details of the statistical methodology.
The reported percentage increases are relative changes, not percentage-point increases. Their full scale therefore depends on the underlying rates: a large relative increase can represent different numbers of patients depending on how common a condition or service was at the outset.
The snapshot also documents changes occurring during the war; the figures alone cannot establish that the war caused every increase.
Even with those limitations, the findings highlight a sustained burden across several areas of health.
Three years into the war, the elevated rates of psychiatric emergency visits, PTSD diagnoses and physical health concerns underscore the continuing care needs of young people and communities displaced from their homes.

Dmitri Moskovtsev: Citizenship carries deeply personal meaning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:14:00 UTC
22:14:00 KST

Dmitri Moskovtsev: Citizenship carries deeply personal meaning
The meaning of citizenship is deeply personal. For some, it is important that the entire family share the same citizenship; for others, it is about having the opportunity to participate more actively in Estonia's social and political life, Dmitri Moskovtsev writes.
It is easy for us to ask why a person who has lived in Estonia for 10, 20 or more years is still not an Estonian citizen. From the outside, the path may seem simple: learn the language, pass the exams, submit the documents and become a citizen. In reality, it can mean years of studying, paperwork and waiting, as well as significant costs in many cases.
We can see this particularly clearly now in the case of permanent residents of Estonia who are citizens of the Russian Federation and want to become Estonian citizens. In August, the cost of renouncing Russian citizenship rose sharply. While the cost associated with the process could until recently be just over €300, it now costs €2,376.
ERR recently reported on the experience of one new Estonian citizen whose path to Estonian citizenship took nearly three and a half years, with renouncing Russian citizenship taking the most time. They had to wait months for a consular appointment and some of the required documents expired in the meantime.
The high fee, long waits and complicated process are increasingly giving people the impression that renouncing Russian citizenship has been made so difficult that it seems almost insurmountable and that there is no point in even starting the journey toward Estonian citizenship. Our task is to counter this discouraging narrative by showing that, alongside the obstacles, there are also concrete opportunities and support available for applying for Estonian citizenship.
For many people, €2,376 represents several years of savings or simply a sum their family budget cannot afford. Of course, Estonia did not impose this fee. We cannot influence another country's procedures, waiting times or state fees, but that does not make the obstacle any smaller for the person involved. When we discuss why someone is not yet an Estonian citizen, we must also take into account circumstances that depend neither on the Estonian state nor on the applicant's own will.
Not everything can be explained by a lack of desire
In public debate, we occasionally hear that if someone had really wanted Estonian citizenship, they would have obtained it long ago. That may be true for some people, as citizenship is a conscious choice and not all noncitizens living in Estonia want Estonian citizenship. Research shows, however, that the situation cannot be explained simply by a lack of desire.
According to the 2023 Estonian Integration Monitoring survey, 48 percent of permanent residents surveyed who did not have Estonian citizenship wanted to obtain it. Among Russian citizens, the figure was 50 percent. Among residents with undetermined citizenship, it was 60 percent at the time.
A comprehensive study of residents with undetermined citizenship published in 2025 showed an even greater willingness to obtain Estonian citizenship. Given the opportunity, 79 percent of respondents would choose Estonian citizenship, while 65 percent said they were prepared to apply for it. The study also clearly highlighted the obstacles. The most frequently cited barrier was attaining the required B1 level of proficiency in Estonian, but a lack of money and time, age and limited awareness of the process also pose problems.
These figures do not mean that all these people will submit citizenship applications tomorrow, but the desire is not confined to survey responses. Russian citizens submitted 465 applications for Estonian citizenship to the Police and Border Guard Board in 2025, followed by another 217 in the first seven months of 2026.
Next to requirements, we must talk about what citizenship provides
There are specific requirements for applying for Estonian citizenship. Applicants must know Estonian, be familiar with the Constitution and the Citizenship Act and meet the other conditions established by law. Citizenship is a legal relationship between an individual and the state that entails both rights and obligations.
Alongside these requirements, it is also important to talk about what being a citizen means to people personally. In the latest Integration Monitoring survey, people who wanted Estonian citizenship cited the opportunity to participate in Estonian public life and vote in elections as one of its main benefits.
In our work at the Integration Foundation, we see that the meaning of citizenship is deeply personal. For some, it is important that the entire family share the same citizenship; for others, it is about having the opportunity to participate more actively in Estonia's social and political life.
For some, Estonian citizenship provides greater legal certainty as well as the rights and opportunities that come with EU citizenship. For others, becoming an Estonian citizen represents long-awaited confirmation that their legal status finally reflects the reality of their lives: their family, work, home and future are in Estonia.
If we talk more as a society about the value of Estonian citizenship and what it means to be a citizen, it may also give some people an additional incentive to take concrete steps toward citizenship.
Support does not mean lowering the bar
We cannot take the exam for someone or make the decision for them. Nor can we arrange for them to renounce another country's citizenship. What we can do is help them understand the next step in applying for citizenship and what support the Estonian state provides along the way.
It is important to us that people do not give up on the path to citizenship simply because they do not know where to start or what to do next or because the entire process has been portrayed as hopelessly complicated.
The Integration Foundation's role is to make the path to Estonian citizenship as clear and manageable as possible. People can come to us even with beginner-level Estonian and work step by step toward the required proficiency level, receive support in preparing for the citizenship exam and get advice throughout the process. In cooperation with the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Culture, we provide free language courses, opportunities to practice Estonian and civic education.
In my view, we need to pay more attention to civic education than we have in the past so that residents whose native language is not Estonian have a better understanding of how the Estonian state and society function, the shared information space, national defense and opportunities to participate and have a say in public life.
Behind the requirements, services and statistics, however, we must see the individual: the person who goes to Estonian classes after a day at work, the person preparing for the B1 exam, perhaps not for the first time, the person gathering documents and waiting months for a response from another country's consulate and perhaps also the person who has to find more than €2,000 to renounce their current citizenship.
These efforts should not be taken for granted. When someone becomes an Estonian citizen after a journey lasting years, that choice deserves to be noticed and recognized. Instead of asking, "Why only now?" perhaps we should say: "Welcome to the ranks of Estonian citizens!"
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

What are the five questions being asked regarding the Flydubai attack?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:11:27 UTC
22:11:27 KST

What are the five questions being asked regarding the Flydubai attack?
As investigations are conducted, official versions of the incident have come under scrutiny.
An attack by the copilot on the pilot during a Flydubai flight has raised many questions regarding aviation security, and some of the official versions of the incident have come under scrutiny from online commentators and aviation enthusiasts.
About two and a half hours after Flight FZ1073 departed from Dubai International Airport on Wednesday, it went into a sharp descent before eventually making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Media reports said the copilot attacked Captain Smit Machchhar. Passengers were able to overpower the copilot, identified by media as Hamam al-Hammami, after Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door during the attack, which the prosecutor general of the United Arab Emirates said was carried out with the cockpit’s crash axe.
While investigators continue working to establish a motive for the attack, several questions have arisen about the incident more generally across social media.
Here are five questions that are being asked:
Why was al-Hammami allowed to fly despite being flagged over security concerns?
Al-Hammami has been identified as an Omani national, according to media reports.
On Friday, The Wall Street Journal quoted unnamed sources as saying that Omani authorities previously blocked the suspect from flying in the country due to concerns over his ideological views.
On Saturday, CNN reported, quoting a regional diplomatic source, that the copilot had also been removed from flight training over similar concerns and was later reassigned to another position.
It added, quoting two sources familiar with the matter, that the pilot was removed from a job at Oman’s national airline last year over concerns about his views.
It remains unclear how al-Hammami managed to get the Flydubai route despite these security concerns.
The possibility of a plumber stabilising plane before reserve pilots stepped in
Reports have emerged that Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door while covered in blood, allowing passengers to subdue the copilot.
One of those who subdued al-Hammami was Yaniv Hayoun, whom Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu described as a plumber.
In a video with Netanyahu, who met him at the airport, Hayoun, 50, was asked how he knew what to do at the plane’s controls before another pilot took control. He said: “I watch Air Crash Investigation, Mr Prime Minister.”
“I jumped back, grabbed the controls and started pulling back the handles” the way he had seen in the Canadian investigation show, in which experts analyse plane crashes.
People on social media have questioned how a plumber could have handled an aircraft in the air.
No report of mass injuries despite fall of 5,180 metres
According to the flight-tracking website Flightradar24, the Flydubai flight rapidly descended about two and a half hours after takeoff, dropping more than 5,180 metres (17,000ft) in less than two minutes.
While the midair drop caused mass panic among passengers, no one was reportedly harmed, according to the publicly available information about the incident. An Air India flight that dropped 90 metres (300ft) during turbulence in August injured at least 17 passengers.
A flight instructor, who recreated the Flydubai jet’s near-vertical dive in a simulator, said the plane would have exceeded its maximum structural speed and anything unsecured would have flown all over the cabin during the recovery’s negative G-forces.
Why was the copilot allowed to fly despite being an Omani national?
Israel does not have official diplomatic relations with Oman, and Netanyahu has previously said such countries were not generally allowed to operate flights to Israel.
On Friday, Netanyahu said Israel was looking into whether the copilot had acted under anyone’s direction, warning that anyone involved would pay a “heavy price”.
On Saturday, the Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that government officials had received in advance the list of crew members and passengers who were on the flight, including the Omani copilot.
Security sources told Haaretz that the government bodies responsible for monitoring and checking foreign flight crews landing in Israel are the Ministry of Transport and Road Safety’s Security Department and the security agency Mossad.
Copilot prayed before attack
According to The Times of Israel, Machchhar spoke to Netanyahu on Saturday. He told the prime minister that al-Hammami had asked to pray before the attack. Four or five minutes later, Machchhar was hit with “a big blow” to the back of his head, he said.
The flight departed from the UAE at 7:05am (03:05 GMT). The attack reportedly took place about two and a half hours later (05:35 GMT).
The predawn prayer time in the Emirates on Wednesday was 04:51am (12:51 GMT), which would mean al-Hammami’s prayer did not align with Islamic prayer times.
However, al-Hammami could also have been performing a different personal prayer before the attack.

Palestinian Christians face persecution, discrimination: Serbian Orthodox Church
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:09:42 UTC
22:09:42 KST

The Serbian Orthodox Church said on Saturday that Christians in Palestine face persecution and discrimination, warning against attempts to marginalise their historical presence.
In a letter to Palestinian official Ramzi Khouri, Serbian Patriarch Porfirije expressed solidarity with the Palestinian people, as well as concern on worsening conditions facing Christians and other residents in the region.
The church said the community was facing “suffering, persecution and discrimination,” stressing that the suffering of civilians regardless of their faith or background was incompatible with human dignity.
It urged the protection of Christian communities, noting that Christians have maintained a continuous presence in the region for more than 2,000 years and remain an integral part of its history and heritage.
The church also warned that excluding or marginalising any religious or ethnic community risked damaging the region’s social and religious fabric, and urged respect for international law and religious rights.
Israeli restrictions on religious sites
Porfirije said the church would continue raising the protection of Christian communities and efforts for peace in the Middle East in meetings with political leaders and international institutions.
Khouri is a member of the Palestine Liberation Organisation’s Executive Committee, and heads the Higher Presidential Committee for Church Affairs in Palestine.
The Palestinian committee has repeatedly raised concerns about attacks on Christian communities and institutions in the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, as well as restrictions affecting worship, education and access to religious sites.
The effect has also extended to Gaza, where five Palestinians were killed early Saturday, including four women, two of whom were Christians.

Russia Pretends to Negotiate: Washington Must Change Moscow’s Calculation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:09:00 UTC
22:09:00 KST

Russia continues to tell Washington that it is open to peace even as its demands remain unchanged and its military campaign against Ukraine intensifies. That contradiction should shape the next stage of diplomacy. If Moscow still believes that continued attacks and the passage of time can produce better terms at the negotiating table, diplomatic contact alone is not evidence that Russia is moving toward ending the war.
On Sept. 5, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner spent more than three hours with Vladimir Putin in Moscow before traveling to Kyiv with proposals to narrow the gap. Although the Kremlin called the meeting “highly useful,” it produced no breakthrough. Moscow continued to demand that Ukraine surrender four regions Russia does not fully control and abandon its NATO aspirations – asking diplomacy to deliver concessions it has not secured militarily.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
After Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in New York on Sept. 23, Rubio said Russia and Ukraine had expressed interest in a limited ceasefire involving energy and grain. The talks produced no agreement, while Lavrov said Moscow would not pause military operations during negotiations in any format.
A limited ceasefire would not end the war. It would, however, show whether Russia is prepared to reduce – and eventually end – the force it uses while peace is discussed. Instead, the night after the Rubio-Lavrov talks, Russia launched 282 drones and other weapons, including ballistic and hypersonic missiles. Eight people were killed: two in Kyiv, where a maternity hospital was damaged, and six agricultural workers at a farm in the Kharkiv region.
Kulbergs’ Pro-Ukraine Party Wins Latvian Election
Those attacks were not isolated. In the first three weeks of September, Russia launched roughly 2,100 jet-powered Shahed-type drones and 136 missiles, killing 288 people, including children. The jet-powered drones fly faster and higher than older variants, while Ukraine’s interception rate against them has fallen to about 60%, versus roughly 90% for propeller-driven models. The shift matters because Russia is adapting its air campaign to make the pressure harder for Ukraine to absorb.
Taken together, unchanged demands, refusal to pause hostilities, continued attacks, and investment in weapons that make a prolonged strike campaign more sustainable form a pattern that is difficult to dismiss. Moscow still appears to believe that time and military force can improve its negotiating position.
Access to Washington gives Moscow another route to press territorial and political terms it has not achieved on the battlefield, seek sanctions relief and renewed economic ties, and encourage US pressure on Kyiv to accept conditions closer to Russia’s demands. Russia does not need diplomacy to end the war; it needs diplomacy to advance Russian interests.
The Trump administration has invited Putin to the December G20 summit in Miami. A bipartisan group of 14 senators urged the president to rescind the invitation, warning that admitting Putin while Russia continues attacking Ukrainian civilians risks legitimizing and normalizing the Kremlin without corresponding changes in its conduct. That invitation makes the next question immediate: what should Washington do if Moscow’s conduct does not change?
Washington now has a concrete instrument to test whether leverage can change Moscow’s calculation. On Sept. 18, President Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The Senate passed it 86-11 and the House 262-159. The law expands sanctions, tariffs, and prohibitions on Russia and reaches financial, energy, and commercial channels that sustain its war economy. It also targets sanctions evasion, including transactions involving Russian-origin oil and shadow-fleet vessels.
Passage is only the beginning. Russia has built networks designed to preserve wartime revenue despite restrictions. Strategic and decisive implementation should reduce the revenues and commercial channels that make a prolonged war sustainable and make clear that economic relief follows measurable movement toward ending the war, not merely another round of talks.
Economic pressure should be reinforced by military support that prevents Moscow from assuming Ukraine will become easier to coerce with time. The administration has now committed most of the $400 million Congress approved through the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative, and that assistance should reach Ukraine as quickly as possible. Combined with US licensing for Patriot-interceptor production in Ukraine, immediate military assistance would add leverage by limiting what Russia can achieve through continued attacks and reducing Moscow’s incentive to wait for better terms.
Reagan’s “peace through strength” principle was not that strength replaces diplomacy, but that strength gives diplomacy credibility. President Trump now has the authority to apply that principle. The administration should implement the new sanctions law strategically and decisively, while sustaining the military support necessary to strengthen Washington’s leverage and Ukraine’s position at the negotiating table. The goal is straightforward: confront Moscow with a reality it can no longer postpone – continuing the war must become more costly than ending it.

The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:00:29 UTC
22:00:29 KST

There’s a common fear among people who work in Silicon Valley: snag one of the fast-growing, high-paying jobs in artificial intelligence, or get trapped in the “permanent underclass”, a phrase describing the fate of those who won’t have upward mobility in the age of AI.
The phrase usually describes a future in which AI automates human jobs. But for women in tech, it’s starting to look like the present.
“A lot of people say: ‘Oh, AI is lowering barriers, it’s equalizing the playing field for women,’” said Urvashi Batra, co-founder and CEO of Prioriwise, an AI platform for IT service providers. “I actually think it’s the opposite.”
Batra said people take her less seriously as the founder of an AI company than her male co-founder. When pitching investors, she and her co-founder have learned that they are more likely to get an investment if he does the pitching.
Women made up only about a quarter of new hires in AI roles in the last year, compared to 50% of new hires in non-AI roles, according to a recent report from LinkedIn. In executive roles, that number drops to just 13%. At the same time, LinkedIn’s research shows that women are more likely to work in roles with high exposure to AI disruption, like customer service, meaning they are also at higher risk for job loss due to AI.
AI jobs, whose postings have doubled since 2023, come with a salary premium, on average paying more than twice as much as roles that don’t involve working with AI, according to LinkedIn’s research. But women who do have jobs in AI are disproportionately concentrated in low-paying roles, like data annotators, said Sarah Steinberg, the head of global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn. Across all AI occupations, men have $45,000 higher median pay than women, partly due to the types of jobs they are likelier to have.
“AI is creating some of the fastest growing, highest paying and most consequential jobs in the global economy,” said Steinberg. “Women are just strikingly underrepresented.”
The ongoing trend could produce the greatest gender pay gap in generations and leave women out of building a technology that shaped the economy, advocates for women in tech said.
“What we’re witnessing is a sort of backsliding,” said Brenda Darden Wilkerson, president of AnitaB.org, a non-profit devoted to advancing women in tech jobs.
Initiatives to promote women in the tech industry have been ongoing for years, with mixed results. Women now hold about one-third of tech jobs in the US. But research has found that women leave the tech industry at a much higher rate than their male counterparts, citing factors like non-inclusive cultures and barriers to advancement.
‘I’ve seen so many women fall through the cracks’
Women working in AI may face even greater challenges. “AI moves extremely fast, and the pressure to keep up is immense,” said Jayeeta Putatunda, an AI engineering lead at investment firm Turing. “I have seen throughout my career so many amazing women I know kind of fall through the cracks.”
Putatunda said it’s not uncommon to be the only female engineer on a team, and that when women are outnumbered, they have to speak up louder to make their ideas known. Mentorship in the AI field, especially by other women, can be hard to come by. And the breakneck pace of AI advancements means anyone working in the field should expect to put in long hours in order to keep up.
“If you have very ambitious career goals in this field, there will be seasons when you work beyond normal hours,” she said, noting that a culture of working 12-hour days to keep up was not uncommon. “I don’t think there is always a neat shortcut around that than to put in the hours.”
Those kinds of work expectations can make it impossible for everyone to stay in the field. “I went on maternity leave for four months, and by the time I came back, there were completely different frameworks and levels of models,” Putatunda said. Getting caught back up was overwhelming. She said it was only possible with the help of supportive co-workers and a husband who equitably split childcare.
“That is one way women get pushed out of AI,” she said. “They don’t lack the interest or ability to keep up. They may lack the infrastructure that makes keeping up possible.”
The AI industry is so new and fast-moving that it should in theory be more meritocratic. No one has a decade of experience working with a model developed one year ago, which should mean everyone has a level playing field. But instead the field has indexed more on personal networks and other loose signals, according to some women who work in AI.
“Companies are hiring at a breakneck speed, but they’re finding people through the same networks, the same referrals, the same filters that they’ve always used,” Wilkerson said. “Generally, that’s not given women the same sort of exposure they should have.”
When people have tried to address these tech industry problems in the past, the solutions have largely come down to giving women more mentorship and implementing diversity programs with goals around representation. But in recent years, companies have aggressively scaled back their diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs, largely in response to a political climate that discourages them. That has left fewer companies with institutional programs to hire and promote women.
The political climate has made it more challenging to get AI companies to support initiatives focused on women, said Felicia Newhouse, founder of AI Powered Women, an organization that promotes women’s participation and leadership in AI. Newhouse, a product marketer who has worked in technology companies for two decades, points to the Department of Justice targeting corporations with DEI programs, claiming the initiatives violate anti-discrimination laws. Companies like Accenture, Deloitte, IBM and PayPal have all agreed to pay multimillion-dollar settlements under this enforcement.
“It is getting harder to go into companies being called AI Powered Women,” Newhouse said. “And our advocates inside those companies are also struggling with having women-focused initiatives.”
Still, she said the risk that women are left behind in the AI workforce was something that kept her up at night. “We’re talking about who captures a major new source of economic mobility,” she said. “The deepest risk is that a participation gap becomes a power gap.”
