Oat of this world: cooks descend on Scotland for ultimate porridge making contest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:00:28 UTC
22:00:28 KST

There are many varieties of spurtle. The traditional Scottish cooking implement, designed for stirring porridge without forming lumps, comes in a range of sizes, can be formed from cherry wood, beech, or maple, and might be topped with a decorative finial or smoothed out at its end for a more modern finish. But on Saturday in Carrbridge, in the Scottish Highlands, only one spurtle mattered: the Golden Spurtle, awarded annually to the winner of the World Porridge Making championship, which have been hosted here since 1994.
The sun shone on the picturesque village as almost 40 competitors lined up in the village hall for six heats across the day. Tasked with producing a traditional porridge – made only from untreated oatmeal, water and salt – and a speciality dish where additional ingredients and flourishes were permitted, entrants had travelled from across Scotland and as far afield as Australia and the US for a shot at the Golden Spurtle.
As the first heat kicked off, technical difficulties beset some contestants when the provided induction hobs, new this year after a long tradition of gas, failed to heat. But the reigning champion, Norway’s Sven Seljom, was unaffected, serenely stirring Norwegian mutton into oats and filtered water he had brought with him especially for the competition. He had planned to bring Norwegian cheese, too, he said, but import rules meant he had to make do with something more local. A sizeable entourage watched on in traditional Scandinavian dress as he measured, stirred and tasted, boisterous chants of “SVEN, SVEN, SVEN” breaking out at each mention of his name.
The first of the day’s many whisky breaks came 10 minutes into proceedings at 10.40am, with shots of a lowland malt distributed throughout the exuberant crowd as competitors did well to retain their focus. The drams’ effects meant nobody seemed to mind too much when the crucial timer was accidentally reset just moments from the heat’s tense final countdown.
Any initial teething problems were quickly ironed out as the day settled into a well-oiled rhythm. In a separate “judging chamber”, a trio of judges from Scotland’s culinary scene blind-tasted each batch, assessing primarily for taste, texture and colour. Among the speciality porridges on offer throughout the day were a “Granola Espanola”, a porridge cannoli from the Australian national champion, Robert Reid, and a recipe featuring soft-boiled quail eggs.
“The first thing I did was burn my oats,” lamented Switzerland’s Jeremy McTeague after a heat that didn’t quite go to plan. But he remained upbeat: “It gave them a distinctive toastiness – maybe the judges will like it.”
Hundreds of spectators showed up for the day’s spectacle, from Carrbridge residents who turn out each year to support the community-powered event, to tourists such as Joe, 43, and Tina, 39, who were visiting from England and had overheard a conversation about the championship in a local pub the previous night.
“We looked it up and decided straight away we’d be here,” said Joe. “It’s Scotland, it’s porridge, someone said there would be whisky … it was a no-brainer.” The pair said they were making a beeline for the tasting room to sample the produce left over from judging.
The event proved so popular that the village hall had to operate a one-in, one-out policy. Those who couldn’t fit inside were decanted into a merch tent bursting with oats, spurtles and “always stir clockwise” tote bags, while local cafes and tourist centres screened a live stream of the competition. There was plenty of action to be found around the village, from competitors spotted calming their nerves with pints in the local hotel, to an American visitor who accidentally caused controversy by dressing as a box of Scott’s Porage Oats – rolled oats of the kind not allowed in competition, and a rival to the event’s sponsors, Hamlyns.
By the afternoon, the hall was full of cooking aromas and the crowd full of whisky and porridge as they took their seats once more to see who would walk away victorious. There was a minor upset when the reigning champion, Seljom, missed out on the final, but a surprise win for McTeague saw him through to the cook-off despite his earlier woes.
Once the top six had taken to the hob one last time, though, it was the Netherlands national champion, Gina Saarberg, who emerged victorious in the traditional competition, with the speciality prize going to Reid for his cannoli.
“I’m at a loss for words,” Saarberg said as she clutched her Golden Spurtle. “To be here was already such a win in the first place. This is a beautiful community, so of course I’m very happy I won, but it’s also just a pleasure to be here.”

====================================================================================================

New study links sexual objectification at home to young women’s difficulty saying no to unwanted sex
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:00:18 UTC
22:00:18 KST

New research suggests that women who received sexually objectifying messages from their families while growing up tend to view themselves more as objects as young adults, a mindset that was in turn linked to more difficulty refusing unwanted sex, communicating sexual desires, and experiencing orgasm. The authors propose that these early family experiences may lead women to internalize an outsider’s view of their bodies, which could make it harder to assert their sexual needs. The study was published in Psychology of Women Quarterly.
Sexual objectification occurs when a person is valued primarily for their physical appearance and treated as an object of sexual desire rather than a complete human being. While this is often discussed as a broader cultural issue, many women first encounter these pressures within their own homes. Sexual objectification in the family of origin involves hearing comments from relatives about body shape, receiving pressure to look attractive, or witnessing family members make sexualized comments about other women.
“Women are subjected to chronic and multiple forms of sexual objectification throughout their lives, in which their bodies are valued for their physical appearance and sexual appeal and treated as sexual objects,” Dawn M. Szymanski, a professor in the Department of Psychology and Neuroscience at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and Greta Hacker, a doctoral student at the university, told PsyPost, summarizing the theory their work builds on. “Sexual objectification experienced early in life can be especially impactful.”
According to objectification theory, a framework the study draws on, women who are repeatedly exposed to these attitudes often begin to view themselves through the same critical lens, a process known as self-objectification. Instead of focusing on how they feel or what they are capable of, individuals who self-objectify tend to constantly monitor their own physical appearance from an outsider’s perspective.
Previous research has documented the negative mental health outcomes of being treated as a sexual object. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2017, which was also led by Szymanski, indicated that women working in sexually objectifying restaurant environments experienced higher levels of anxiety and disordered eating.
Less is known about how objectifying experiences within the family shape a woman’s sexual well-being later in life. The research team aimed to explore how early family messages might translate into young women’s sexual experiences. Specifically, the authors wanted to see if these experiences influenced sexual agency, which is the ability to freely communicate sexual desires to a partner and refuse unwanted sexual activities.
“Previous research indicates gender disparities in sexual functioning,” the researchers explained. “For example, heterosexual women are less likely to report experiencing orgasm during sexual activity with another person than heterosexual men.” The authors cite a 2018 national survey in which 65% of heterosexual women said they usually or always orgasm during partnered sex, compared with 86% of lesbian women and 95% of heterosexual men.
“Past research also indicates that psychosocial factors are more important in understanding these disparities than physiological factors,” the researchers noted. “Our study extends this line of research by applying objectification theory and research on the importance of early family environments to increasing our understanding of factors associated with sex-related outcomes in young adult college women.”
The researchers also looked at orgasm, an important component of sexual pleasure and a strong predictor of sexual satisfaction. The psychological and relational aspects of sex play an important role in whether women experience orgasm. Supporting this, a 2026 study of Italian adults indicated that women’s orgasms are heavily tied to relationship dimensions like emotional closeness and how much partners agree on important matters in their relationship.
Szymanski and her team suspected that by fostering self-objectification, early family experiences might interrupt a woman’s ability to focus on her own pleasure and communicate her needs, setting the stage for fewer orgasms.
To investigate these associations, the researchers surveyed 700 young adult women at a university, recruited through a psychology research pool in exchange for course credit. The participants had an average age of about 19, and the vast majority identified as White and heterosexual. Sixty-two percent were first-year students, 56% were in a romantic relationship, and all had prior partnered sexual experience. They completed a series of online questionnaires assessing their past and current experiences.
The survey included a measure asking how often family members made comments about their appearance or the bodies of other women while they were growing up. The questionnaire also measured the women’s current levels of self-objectification, their anxiety about how their bodies look during sex, and their ability to assert their sexual boundaries and desires. A subset of 533 women who had engaged in sexual activity over the previous month answered questions about how frequently, easily, and with how much satisfaction they experienced orgasms. The researchers controlled for relationship status in their analysis, as being in a committed relationship often influences sexual communication and satisfaction.
The findings point to a pattern connecting early family messages to current sexual behaviors. Women who reported more sexual objectification in their families tended to report more self-objectification as young adults, a moderate association. The links described below, from family experiences to sexual agency and orgasm, were smaller.
Self-objectification also statistically linked family experiences to lower sexual agency. Women who reported more family objectification tended to self-objectify more, and that was in turn associated with more difficulty refusing unwanted sex and communicating their sexual desires to partners. Family objectification was also directly linked to more difficulty refusing unwanted sex, even after accounting for self-objectification.
When looking at the women who had recently engaged in sexual activity, the researchers found that sexual objectification in the family was indirectly linked to lower rates of orgasm. This connection operated through a chain of psychological and behavioral factors. Higher self-objectification was linked to less ability to refuse unwanted sex and communicate sexual desires, which was in turn associated with fewer orgasms, less satisfaction with orgasms, and greater difficulty reaching climax. Overall, the full statistical model explained 21% of the variation in the women’s orgasm scores.
“Our findings suggest that experiencing sexual objectification in one’s family of origin is important in understanding women’s sexual experiences and sexual functioning in young adulthood,” the authors concluded.
Self-objectification was linked to more anxiety about body image during sex, but this anxiety was not a statistically significant predictor of orgasm once the women’s ability to communicate and to refuse sex was taken into account. The authors called this surprising, since earlier studies had pointed to body self-consciousness as a key link, and suggested that what a woman does during sex, such as voicing what she needs, may matter more for orgasm than how she feels about her body.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on the women’s own reports, including recollections of family experiences from years earlier, which may not always be accurate. Because the data was collected at a single point in time, the results cannot establish a timeline of cause and effect. It is possible that other unmeasured factors play a role in these dynamics.
The sample also consisted primarily of young, White, heterosexual women attending a university. The findings might not apply to women from different cultural backgrounds, sexual orientations, or age groups. Future studies tracking individuals over several years could provide evidence for how family messages shape sexual development over time.
The study, “Sexual Objectification in Family of Origin, Self-Objectification, Sexual Agency, and Young Adult College Women’s Orgasm,” was authored by Dawn M. Szymanski and Greta Hacker.

Yemen's government declares counter-offensive as Houthis cut vital route to besieged city
The leader of Yemen's Saudi-backed government announced the beginning of a major military operation against the Iran-backed Houthis on Sunday aimed at recapturing territory under their control. The announcement came as Houthi forces cut off a vital supply route to the besieged government-held city of Taiz, according to several security sources.
The head of Yemen's presidential council on Sunday announced the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by Iran-backed Houthi fighters.
"I announce today the start of military operations to retake the remaining territories of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory," Rashad al-Alimi said in a statement.
Alimi called on "the armed forces, security forces and all military formations to begin carrying out their assigned missions, in accordance with the approved plans, until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia".
The announcement marks the latest major escalation in the war against the Houthis following a rapid offensive by the Iran-backed group last month that saw them seize large swaths of the Red Sea coastline.
Read moreYemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels seize strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha
Earlier Sunday, several security sources also told AFP that the group had effectively encircled Taiz after cutting the main supply route to the government-held city.
The Houthi advance follows days of heavy fighting in and around the city of Taiz between the group and government forces.
"We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station," a police source in the area told AFP.
Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and supply route, with the group effectively encircling Taiz city.
The military sources added that the Houthis had also halted traffic on the main road linking Taiz to Aden, with fighting in the area ongoing.
The city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen's civil war.
"They've achieved the military objective of isolating Taiz from Aden, even if they haven't fully taken control of it," Farea Al-Muslimi, research fellow at the Chatham House think-tank, told AFP.
Saudi support
Elsewhere in Yemen, the Houthi's Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.
The strikes come a day after Yemen's government said its forces hit Houthi targets around the country, including in the capital Sanaa, the northwestern governorate of Saada and the group's positions near Taiz in the southwest.

Experts believe the recent operations have most likely been conducted by Saudi warplanes rather than the Yemeni air force.
Following several years of relative calm, Yemen's war reignited in July against the backdrop of the widening Middle East war.
The country is one of the poorest in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis.
Fighting intensified in September as the Houthis launched a lightning offensive that saw them seize Yemen's entire Red Sea coast, including the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital shipping lane.
The Houthis have in parallel launched a blockade on Saudi energy exports, already squeezed by Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Southern cities jolted by moderate tremors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:58:04 UTC
21:58:04 KST

People who were frightened by the earthquakes rushed outside. (AA Photo)
Türkiye’s southern provinces of Adana and Osmaniye were jolted by a series of moderate earthquakes on Oct. 4, with authorities reporting no immediate adverse developments.
A magnitude 4.8 earthquake struck Adana’s Saimbeyli district at 2:19 p.m., according to the Disaster and Emergency Management Presidency (AFAD).
The tremor occurred at a depth of 7.9 kilometers (4.9 miles), followed 17 minutes later by another earthquake measuring 4.9.
A magnitude 5.2 earthquake subsequently struck Osmaniye province at 2:43 p.m., with its epicenter in the Sumbas district. The quake occurred at a depth of 7 kilometers.
In separate statements, the governors’ offices of Adana and Osmaniye said no adverse incidents had been reported so far, adding that authorities were continuing to assess all reports received from the affected areas.
Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi said in a statement following the earthquakes that all AFAD and relevant agency teams had immediately begun field assessments to check for any damage or other developments.
Speaking to the media following the consecutive earthquakes, geologist Professor Dr. Okan Tüysüz said the region had remained under stress since the Feb. 6, 2023, earthquakes that killed more than 53,000 people in the region.
“These earthquakes are likely to continue. It is possible to say that a significant proportion of these earthquakes have emerged as a result of the effects of the Feb. 6 earthquakes,” Tüysüz said.
He added that the area was not dominated by a single major fault, but rather consisted of numerous smaller faults, with the Savrun Fault being the largest among them.
“My expectation is therefore that an earthquake exceeding magnitude 7 is not likely to occur in this region. A major, destructive earthquake is not expected,” Tüysüz said.

Drug-use offenders fall to 24.8% of Taiwan prison population
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:56:33 UTC
21:56:33 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — People imprisoned for drug use accounted for 24.8% of Taiwan’s prison population at the end of June, down from 35.1% in 2022, as the government increasingly used deferred prosecution and addiction treatment for less serious cases, per CNA.
The Ministry of Justice’s Agency of Corrections said the government’s New Generation Anti-Drug Strategy follows approaches used in other developed countries that emphasize case diversion, differentiated treatment and multiple forms of rehabilitation.
People involved in less serious drug-use cases who primarily require medical care may receive mandatory addiction treatment as a condition of deferred prosecution, allowing them to remain in the community. Those involved in violence, serious crimes or other offenses are more likely to enter correctional institutions, the agency said.
The approach aims to provide treatment suited to individual circumstances while reducing unnecessary incarceration, easing overcrowding and limiting contact between people imprisoned for drug use and drug dealers inside prisons.
The Justice Ministry’s anti-drug strategy for 2025 through 2028 has four goals: cutting drug supply and demand, reducing drug-related harm, supporting reintegration into society, and reducing recidivism. The government has allocated NT$15 billion (US$471 million) for the program, per the MOJ.
Since 2019, the agency has expanded its psychological and social-work staff and used interdisciplinary teams to connect prisoners with resources inside and outside correctional institutions, particularly those assessed as having a greater need for addiction treatment.
Research by the Judicial Academy’s Crime Prevention Research Center found that people who completed mandatory addiction treatment under deferred prosecution had a 66.3% lower risk of relapse than those who did not complete treatment, per CNA.
The agency said medical, psychological, social-work and community resources should be coordinated whether treatment takes place in the community or a correctional institution. Continued support after release is intended to help people reintegrate into society and avoid reoffending.

Yoseph Haddad rejects past support for Palestinian state after old interview resurfaces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04

21:56:32 KST

People of Israel member Yoseph Haddad rejected his past support for the establishment of a Palestinian state on Sunday after an old interview resurfaced showing him endorsing a two-state solution, triggering a new political dispute weeks before Israel’s election.
Journalist Mohammad Magadli circulated footage from an interview Haddad gave to Al-Arabiya more than five years ago, in which the Arab-Israeli public diplomacy activist said the eventual solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict should include a Palestinian state alongside Israel.
The comments stand in sharp contrast to the current platform of People of Israel, the right-wing party led by Brig.-Gen. (res.) Ofer Winter, which has explicitly rejected the establishment of a Palestinian state. Haddad is running in the second slot on the party’s Knesset list.
In the old interview, Haddad argued that greater integration of Arab-Israelis into the country’s decision-making institutions could eventually help advance Israeli-Palestinian peace.
“The final solution is the State of Israel alongside the State of Palestine. Of course, this is something that has to happen. There is no denying it,” Haddad said in the interview.
Haddad, who joined Winter’s party in August and announced his ambition to become Israel’s public diplomacy minister, responded to the resurfaced video by saying his position had changed following the May 2021 riots during Operation Guardian of the Walls.
“When I saw the unity between Palestinians and Arabs from within who were setting mixed cities on fire, I changed my mind and understood that this was not the solution,” Haddad said.
He later expanded on his current position, saying that his shift regarding the Palestinians and the possibility of peace began during Guardian of the Walls.
“That was when I understood that there would be no peace with them and that they must not be given a state,” Haddad said. “As public diplomacy minister, I will expose the Palestinian lie to the world to make sure that no one remains who believes them and to finally kill the idea of a Palestinian state.”
People of Israel party leader Winter defends Haddad
People of Israel party leader Ofer Winter defended Haddad, calling him "my brother" and "the State of Israel's strongest public diplomacy fighter."
"I saw the things Yoseph Haddad said in past interviews before October 7," Winter said. "People write to me, go after him, remove him, throw Yoseph out, what hypocrisy, what a disgrace. You've lost the plot."
Winter also defended Haddad's character, saying, "A person who has done and continues to do so much for the State of Israel, who pays prices you would not believe for you, for us."
He argued that people should be able to change their views when circumstances change, particularly when they believe they are moving in the "right direction," and said he supported Haddad's shift in position.
"Friends, anyone who did not change his views after October 7 is ignorant and foolish," Winter said.
Winter also reaffirmed his party's opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state and reiterated a hardline position on Gaza, calling for a decisive victory, saying that "trucks will not enter Gaza," and pledging to ensure "voluntary migration."
Haddad's past statement used as political ammunition
Haddad’s political evolution quickly became ammunition for Winter’s rivals.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party attacked Winter and his slate, arguing that the resurfaced remarks exposed contradictions within the new right-wing party.
“Ofer Winter and his opposite,” the party said in a statement.
“Pro-conscription, but supports a draft-evasion government.
“Pro-‘responsibility,’ but supports the prime minister of October 7 and opposes a state commission of inquiry.
“Pro-‘settlement,’ but members of his party support a Palestinian state, and to this moment Winter has not even thought to call them to order or clarify the matter.”
Yashar accused Winter’s party of lacking “a value-based backbone and a path,” and claimed its objective was “to confuse the serving public and crawl into Netanyahu’s draft-evasion government.”
The attack follows previous criticism of Winter from Eisenkot’s camp. Eisenkot has argued that Winter’s positions contain contradictions, particularly because Winter has conditioned his participation in a future government on passage of a broad conscription law while remaining politically aligned with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Winter has publicly said that his party would not join a government unless legislation ending draft exemptions was passed first.
Show of support from Channel 14's Abuhatzira
The resurfaced interview also prompted an unusual intervention from inside Channel 14.
Yitzhak Abuhatzira, editor of Channel 14’s website, published an article defending Haddad and accusing Likud and Religious Zionist Party chairman Bezalel Smotrich of turning against a figure they had previously praised because he now posed an electoral threat.
“Just two months ago, the Right was furious when Eisenkot compared Yoseph Haddad to Mansour Abbas, and Netanyahu was still showering him with praise,” Abuhatzira wrote. “Now, when he threatens to take votes from them, Likud and Smotrich have already turned the public diplomacy hero into a target.”
“The Israeli political system proves once again: Values end where the mandates begin,” he added.
The dispute comes as People of Israel seeks to establish itself as an independent force on the Right. Likud officials have previously expressed concern that Winter and Haddad could draw votes from established right-wing parties, particularly if their slate hovers around the electoral threshold. Political sources have estimated that part of Winter’s support is coming directly from Likud voters.
Haddad, meanwhile, has increasingly emphasized a political platform that combines strong Israeli national identification with greater integration of Arab Israelis. In a recent interview, he described his goal as building an Arab-Israeli “partnership” rather than “coexistence,” while drawing firm political red lines following October 7. He has described that approach as central to his bid to enter the Knesset.
The old Al-Arabiya footage nevertheless gives Winter’s opponents a new line of attack as the campaign enters its final weeks, while Haddad maintains that the views expressed in the interview no longer represent his position.
One point worth flagging for the desk: a second video was being circulated later Sunday that Magadli reportedly said was recorded after Operation Guardian of the Walls, potentially challenging Haddad’s stated timeline for his change of position. I left that development out of the copy because it wasn't in your supplied material, and the available reporting had not yet established the recording date conclusively.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

Iran-backed militias in Iraq determined to retain arms after US withdrawal - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:56:07 UTC
21:56:07 KST

The United States’ planned withdrawal from Iraq on Wednesday has been celebrated by Iraqi militias as an “incomplete victory,” emboldening them to continue to resist disarmament beyond the previous deadline, according to Dr. Ronen Zeidel, an Iraq specialist at Tel Aviv University’s Moshe Dayan Center for Middle Eastern and African Studies.
The extension will likely be pushed back again, he told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday.
With US forces fully withdrawn and Turkey expected to leave the strategic Bashiqa-Zilkan military base in northern Iraq by the end of 2026, Baghdad has projected a celebratory sense of “sovereignty” despite Iranian and Houthi military elements remaining unofficially present in the country.
Iraqi militias have shared videos of themselves driving over American flags to demonstrate their sense of accomplishment.
Since Iran is maintaining a physical presence in Iraq, much of Washington’s remaining leverage over Baghdad would come through economic pressure, including potentially halting transfers from the Federal Reserve, Zeidel said.
Iraq's military escalation dilemma
Since 2003, Washington has held Iraq’s oil revenues, giving it significant leverage over Iraq’s affairs and helping prevent it from fully aligning with the Iranian axis, he said.
If Washington concluded that Baghdad was not committed to disarming the militias or was testing the limits of its patience, the US could threaten Iraq’s entire economy, although it has so far shown patience, Zeidel said.
Even though Baghdad is aware of such a threat, it still has a “dilemma” over whether to risk military escalation against the Iranian-backed groups, he added.
Iraq’s apparent reluctance to confront the militias, as shown by the deadline extension, and America’s withdrawal have resulted in a sense of confidence that will see the militias continue to resist and influence Iraqi legislation, Zeidel said.
Baghdad postpones militias' disarmament
Last Thursday, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said the original September 30 deadline for militias to disarm would be pushed back to June 30. Statements from the militias, however, have indicated that they may disregard the extended timeline as well.
Kataeb Hezbollah military spokesman Jaafar al-Husseini said Baghdad had not yet responded to his group’s negotiations to “regulate” its weapons.
As a result, he said, “the Islamic Resistance declares that it is not bound by any timetable or agreement that any governmental or political party has spoken of or may speak of.”
Zeidel said the development was not surprising. The militias would likely cite the continued presence of armed Kurdish groups in the semiautonomous Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq as an excuse for refusing to disarm, he said, as well as continued American military flights over Iraq.
The militias would continue to “bluff” in negotiations, finding new ways to delay disarmament, Zeidel said, adding that their terminology had increasingly shifted away from disarmament and toward the “regulation” of weapons.
Any new “eruption,” whether a return to active conflict between the US and Iran or an escalation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, would likely see the groups abandon all their commitments, he said, citing militia demands to retain missiles and drones capable of striking Israel and Saudi Arabia.
“They make a distinction between small arms or light arms and strategic arms,” he added. “Under strategic arms, they include long-range missiles and long-range drones that can hit Saudi Arabia, Israel, or any other country in the region. So, they are ready to deliver some of the small arms, and probably some of the short-range drones, but not the strategic arms.”
Beyond the issue of arms, Zeidel said the US withdrawal had altered the psychological state of the militias. Leaders aligned with the militias had pressured the Iraqi cabinet to finally approve the new Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) Law, controversial legislation that would formally recognize the Iranian-backed paramilitary network as a permanent national security institution.
Legislation to integrate the PMF into Iraq’s armed forces under a unified military hierarchy was pulled last year, following both internal strife and pressure from Washington.
“It’s not going to be voted on this week, but it’s very close to being put on the agenda of the Iraqi Parliament, and they might have their way by having this law approved,” Zeidel said.

Head of Yemen's presidential council announces military operations to retake territory
Unknown

2026-10-04

The Saudi-backed head of Yemen's Presidential Council, Rashad al-Alimi, announced on Sunday the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory held by Iran-backed Houthis terrorists and restore state authority across the country.
"Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory," Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address.
Regional and western officials had previously told Reuters that Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies were planning to launch an assault on the Houthis, with the Saudis leading aerial combat and Yemeni forces fighting on the ground.
Saudi Arabia entered neighboring Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition in support of the internationally recognized government, which the Houthis had driven out of the capital Sanaa.
A truce agreed between the warring parties in 2022 largely held until this year, when the Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi shipping and oil infrastructure in a spillover from the Iran war.
Alimi said the decision to launch the counteroffensive came after all opportunities for de-escalation had been exhausted, accusing the Houthis of responding to efforts to calm the conflict with further mobilization and escalation.
"Our position today is to assume the national responsibility of confronting the Houthi terrorists, after all opportunities for de-escalation have been exhausted," he said.
Alimi said he had ordered the armed forces, security forces and all military formations to begin carrying out their assigned tasks under approved plans.
Houthis continue to hold territory seized in ground offensive
Despite the preparations for a counteroffensive, the Houthis have so far maintained the initiative on the ground, weeks after seizing the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait in a lightning offensive down the coast that saw government forces collapse.
Bab al-Mandab is the southern exit passage of the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia that has assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed by the Iran conflict.
In the last 48 hours, the Houthis have made gains against government and local forces on strategic hilltops near Yemen's Taiz, military sources said, advancing on the last road between the city and Aden, where the Saudi-backed Yemeni government is based.
Houthi control over the Taiz-Aden road would lead to an effective siege of the city, Yemen's third-largest, inhabited by hundreds of thousands of civilians and where thousands of government forces are also stationed.
Houthis seek control of mountains overlooking Bab al-Mandab coastal area
It would also consolidate control of that flat coastal Bab al-Mandab area by seizing the rugged mountains overlooking it in the western Taiz countryside, according to Mohammed al-Qadhi, a veteran Yemeni journalist from Taiz now working as a political analyst.
"This will help them protect their back in case of any operation against the coastline, and make recapturing those areas much more difficult," he said.
The city is important not just for its strategic location. Alimi is from the region, and a siege of Taiz would amplify an already-dire humanitarian situation in the country.
Three-in-four families in parts of Yemen are going hungry from the impact of the surge in fighting, which has displaced tens of thousands of people and disrupted supplies to millions, the World Food Programme said last week.
Houthis claim missile, drone attacks on Saudi Aramco sites after coalition strikes
The Houthis, meanwhile, said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco sites in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia, claiming the attacks caused major fires, in response to what they said were 50 Saudi-led air and missile strikes on Yemen in the past 12 hours.
Saudi Arabia did not immediately confirm the attacks.

High Court to weigh direct Shin Bet protection over private security for Democrats chair Yair Golan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:55:56 UTC

The High Court of Justice is scheduled to hear arguments Tuesday over whether intelligence monitoring and armed private guards are enough to protect The Democrats chairman Yair Golan, or whether the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) must guard him during the final three weeks of the election campaign.
Supreme Court President Isaac Amit and Justices Ofer Grosskopf and Ruth Ronnen are scheduled to hear the petition at 1 p.m.
Golan and The Democrats petitioned the court on September 29, asking it to order immediate Shin Bet protection at least until the October 27 election results are published and afterward according to an updated threat assessment.
Last Thursday, the state said it had already begun implementing a new security framework for party leaders. It did not, however, commit to providing Golan with a Shin Bet protection detail.
The framework followed a top-secret decision adopted by the Ministerial Committee for Shin Bet Affairs on September 16, nearly two weeks before the petition was filed.
Following that decision, the Shin Bet reviewed the available intelligence and security measures and devised a response tailored to the threat facing each party leader, the state said.
The plan applies to party leaders contesting the election who are not cabinet ministers or MKs and are not already protected because of a previous position. Relevant Shin Bet officials intend to contact Golan shortly, the state said.
Under the arrangements announced publicly by the agency, Shin Bet intelligence units will monitor threats against all party leaders and help build an updated picture of the danger surrounding each of them.
Democrats argue state responsible for protecting politicians
Party leaders who want physical protection will be able to hire private security companies, whose guards may carry weapons even without specific intelligence pointing to a concrete threat. The Shin Bet will coordinate with those private teams and conduct periodic assessments to determine the appropriate level of protection.
The Democrats rejected that model when it was announced, saying the state was shifting responsibility for protecting threatened political leaders to private companies.
The dispute now before the court is whether the measures offered by the Shin Bet are sufficient, or whether the circumstances require direct Shin Bet protection.
Petition documents dozens of threats
According to the petition, the head of the Israel Police unit responsible for threatened individuals informed Golan’s office about a month before the filing that the threat level against him had been raised to four on a six-point scale.
The petition documents dozens of threats posted between July and late September, including calls to shoot or hang Golan and messages threatening members of his family.
It also says Golan’s name appeared in a death-threat letter attached to a brick thrown at Channel 12’s studios on July 27. According to the petition, he was the only party leader named as a target in the letter.
The petitioners said they had made three written approaches seeking state protection. Letters dated August 25 and September 2 were sent to the chairman of the Central Elections Committee, and copies were sent to security and legal officials.
A third request was sent directly to Shin Bet Director David Zini on September 22. It sought a response by September 27 and warned that the party would petition the High Court if no decision was received.
None of the three approaches had been answered by the time the petition was filed, according to The Democrats.
The state’s response indicates that officials had begun addressing the broader question of protecting party leaders before the petition. It does not say, however, that the September 16 decision or its practical implications had been communicated to Golan.
Under Section 7 of the Shin Bet Law, the agency is responsible for protecting people designated by the government. Golan says the threats against him, his position as a party leader, and the public demands of an election campaign require state protection rather than reliance primarily on a privately hired company.
The petition also argues that leaving a threatened candidate without state protection restricts his ability to appear before voters and campaign on equal terms.
The state said the exact measures approved for party leaders are classified and can be presented to the judges only behind closed doors, without Golan or his lawyers present.
Grosskopf declined to order immediate protection when the petition was filed. “The respondents can be expected to keep the need to protect Golan under ongoing review, in accordance with the latest threat assessment in his case,” he wrote.

Israeli spy Eli Cohen may have been buried near Damascus barracks, Syrian official claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:55:51 UTC
21:55:51 KST

Legendary Israeli spy Eli Cohen may have been buried near unidentified military barracks outside Damascus, Syrian security officer Saeed Jawish claimed in an interview with the Saudi-owned Al Majalla on Saturday.
Cohen, a Mossad agent best known for his work in Syria, operated under the alias Kamel Amin Thabet, posing as a wealthy Syrian businessman who had returned to Damascus after years in Argentina. His cover was ultimately blown in January 1965, when Syrian counterintelligence caught him transmitting messages to Israel. He was arrested, tried for espionage and publicly hanged in Damascus on May 18, 1965.
Jawish, who claims to have been involved in the operation that led to Cohen’s arrest, explained that he and five other Syrian officers heavily debated the matter of where to bury the spy the night before his execution.
“We said the Israelis would not let the matter go and would try to obtain his remains, so each of us began suggesting a place where he could be buried,” Jawish told Al Majalla.
According to Jawish, another Syrian official named Adnan Tayara suggested burying Cohen at the entrance to a military barracks that already had permanent security.
That way, Tayara had explained at the time, “the grave would not need special guarding.”
“There were several barracks, and I do not know which one was chosen,” Jawish said in the interview. “The person who knows is [Syrian Warrant Officer] Melhem Qassem, who attended the burial.”
Since Cohen’s execution, Syria has refused to return his remains, which have allegedly been buried multiple times to prevent Israel from finding and returning them.
Nearly a year ago, Saudi state-run news outlet Al-Hadath reported that Cohen’s remains could be returned to Israel in a deal with Syria.
The report followed the Mossad's seizure of 2,500 documents on Cohen. Additionally, Reuters reported at the time that Syria's leadership approved the handover of the remains to Israel in a bid to ease Israeli hostility and show goodwill to US President Donald Trump.
Israel seeks return of Jewish remains buried in Lebanon as part of prisoner talks
More recently, Hezbollah-linked Lebanese newspaper Al-Akhbar reported that Israel and Lebanon discussed what was referred to as a "civilian prisoner exchange deal" during recent negotiations, with Israeli officials raising the possibility of transferring the remains of Jews buried in Lebanese cemeteries to Israel.
According to the report, the issue was raised during discussions over Lebanese prisoners and detainees held by Israel. The discussions focused on individuals classified by Israel as civilians whose ties to Hezbollah were unclear, but who Israel said nevertheless posed a threat to IDF troops and were detained on those grounds.
The Israeli representatives specifically referred to what Al-Akhbar described as a significant number of remains buried in Jewish cemeteries in Beirut and Sidon.
The report came after Israel and Lebanon's recent round of talks in Rome, which a source speaking to The Jerusalem Post at the time described as "positive."
Shir Perets and Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

Up to 500 French schools to be totally or partly closed Monday amid student protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:50:45 UTC
21:50:45 KST

Hundreds of schools to shut Monday as France braces for more student protests
France's education minister said lessons would be "totally or partly suspended" at up to 500 high schools on Monday after several days of sometimes violent protests against teacher shortages, dilapidated school buildings and overcrowding in classrooms. The minister said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the start of the protest movement.
Up to 500 schools across France will be totally or partly closed on Monday due to the protests by teenage pupils that have shaken the country, the education minister said.
Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some "400-500" high schools as the security conditions "have not been fulfilled", said Education Minister Edouard Geffray on Sunday, adding that 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the start of the movement.
Read moreHundreds of French schools remain closed as riot police clash with student protesters
The teens at French high schools, known as lycées, say that their studies are being ruined by high teacher absences, overlong school days and dilapidated facilities, as well as other grievances.
Geffray said the number of schools affected on Monday would be comparable to the figure from Friday but vowed there would be a "partial, progressive return to lessons".
More than a third of the 468 schools in the wider Ile-de-France region surrounding the capital will be shut on Monday as a result of the protests, Valerie Pecresse, the right-wing president of the region, told broadcaster Franceinfo.
The movement began at a Paris school on September 17 but grew last week into nationwide protests marked in places by outbursts of violence involving teenagers and security forces, which sometimes used tear gas and batons to disperse the children.
'Deliberately targeted'
At Saint-Denis, just north of Paris, students took turns expressing their grievances at an open-air meeting Sunday.
When you are a student from one of the deprived districts, said one student, "The violence is unleashed."
She referred in particular to one student who had lost his teeth to a police rubber bullet and another who had been hit in the eye.
One 16-year-old boy, Campion, held a placard that read: "They say they are listening to us but prefer to gas us".
"I don't understand why the government deploys so much force against a case that is valid: our education, our future," he told AFP.
Geffray, in his statement, spoke of far-left infiltrators who had "hijacked' the movement "and engaged in extreme violence".
"Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he alleged, adding that 78 education staff members had been wounded – "something we have never seen before".
"They were deliberately targeted because they were employees of the national education system," Geffray claimed.
Watch moreFrench Unrest: Are we witnessing a new 'Yellow Vests' movement?
Organisers have called for the protests to continue on Tuesday, citing a lack of "concrete measures" from the government.
In a bid to address the protesters' concerns, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu set out a timetable on Sunday urging local authorities to prioritise filling gaps left by long-term absences and unfilled posts.
He also called a meeting for Tuesday with regional presidents to discuss overhauling the country's often-dilapidated school buildings.
Violent incidents
More than 5,000 people, 85 percent of them minors, have been arrested since the start of the movement.
A 16-year-old was detained on Sunday over the assault of a teacher in the southern town of La Ciotat. The teacher, 59, was struck and doused with gasoline on the sidelines of a high school student protest on Friday.
A group of youths were last week filmed beating and kicking a policeman on the ground in Belfort in eastern France in images that caused an outcry among officials.
Two youths, Bulgarian nationals aged 15 and 17, have been arrested and investigated for suspected aggravated violence, the prosecutor said.
One of the youths, whom the policeman had tried to arrest before being beaten, has now filed his own attempted murder complaint, his lawyer said.

The France branch of Amnesty last week slammed "disproportionate police violence" in tackling the demonstrations and said students must be allowed to express their grievances.
"Authorities must allow young people to exercise these rights without fear of being hit by tear gas grenades or batons, or being arbitrarily taken into police custody," said Amnesty France president Anne Savinel-Barras.
But Interior Minister Laurent Nunez stated that security forces "are not cracking down on young people" but rather "protecting" school and university students wishing to "peacefully voice their demands".
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Russia Deploys Shturm Heavy Robotic System During Military Exercises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:49:44 UTC
21:49:44 KST

Russia demonstrated the Shturm heavy assault robotic system, based on the T-72B3M tank, during the Center-2026 strategic command-and-staff exercises.
Uralvagonzavod published footage from the exercises.
The demonstration took place on October 2 at the Chebarkulsky training range in the Chelyabinsk region. According to the manufacturer, the military used unmanned vehicles equipped with tank turrets and BMPT modules to provide fire support for assault units.
According to tank history researcher Andriy Tarasenko, Shturm is a long-standing project based on the development of a remotely controlled mine-clearing vehicle. He criticizes applying this approach to a combat vehicle because it depends on a direct line of sight between the vehicle and the control station.
“As far as I know, the vehicle loses the connection behind folds in the terrain; it requires a direct line of sight. It only makes sense if Starlink or whatever it is called — ‘Rassvet’ — is used,” Tarasenko said.
According to Defence Blog, which cited Russian sources, the Shturm robotic vehicle repeatedly lost its radio link with the control vehicle during the exercises.
The publication claims that, for the demonstration in front of Vladimir Putin, remote control of the vehicle was not used due to concerns about a technical failure, and a driver was placed inside the vehicle.
Despite this, the Shturm robotic vehicle became stuck in a muddy ditch beside an unpaved road during the demonstration. In addition, the vehicle lacked additional anti-drone protection, and its turret roof and engine-transmission compartment were not reinforced.
Uralvagonzavod CEO Alexander Potapov said in 2018 on the sidelines of the ADEX exhibition that the corporation was developing a robotic system based on the T-72B3 at the request of Russia’s Defense Ministry.
Among the main requirements for the T-72-based robotic system was an extremely high level of all-around protection capable of keeping the vehicle operational after hits from 10-15 hand-held anti-tank grenade launchers and detonation on an anti-tank mine.
Based on footage from the exercises, a standard T-72B3 tank was used to build the Shturm robotic tank, with remote-control mechanisms added but no changes to the internal compartment. This allows a standard tank crew to operate the vehicle.
Four types of combat vehicles with different weapons were planned:
The Shturm robotic tanks are controlled from a remote-control station, also built on a T-72B3 chassis and equipped with all-around protection against shaped-charge anti-tank weapons. During development, it was planned that each control station would be capable of controlling a platoon of combat vehicles within a 3-kilometer radius.

Yemen’s leader announces military operation to retake Houthi-held territory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:48:50 UTC
21:48:50 KST

Yemen’s leader announces military operation to retake Houthi-held territory
Rashad al-Alimi says the campaign aims to restore state authority throughout Yemen.
The Saudi Arabia-backed chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, has announced the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory held by the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), and restore state authority across the country.
In a televised address, al-Alimi said on Sunday that the internationally recognised government’s forces would extend “the authority of the state and its institutions over the entire national territory”.
“We have instructed the armed forces, security forces and all military formations to begin carrying out their assigned tasks under an approved plan until the country is liberated from the Houthis,” he said.
Al-Alimi added that all state institutions will be placed on full alert “until the mission is completed and victory is achieved”.
Hundreds killed
The development comes after the Yemeni government army and forces loyal to it “executed 257 precision targeting operations” against Houthi sites, movements and military capabilities on Saturday, according to the spokesman for Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces, Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili.
He added that initial estimates indicate that the operations killed at least 700 Houthi rebels.
The spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition supporting the government, Turki al-Malik, said on Saturday that the Houthis’ “ties to external agendas” have brought “chaos and devastation to Yemen”.
Early on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition said its armed forces carried out 97 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi reinforcements on the Tor al-Baha front and the Taiz axis, using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers.
Later in the day, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claimed the group’s forces had fired ballistic missiles and drones at two Saudi Aramco sites in Saudi Arabia – one in Riyadh and the other in the area of Khurais, 150km (93 miles) north-east of the capital.
There was no immediate comment by Saudi Arabia.
‘New calculus’
London-based defence analyst Ibrahim Jalal told Al Jazeera the internationally recognised government’s new “full-scale” operation against the Houthis has brought the conflict into a “new phase”.
“Peace and de-escalation processes have failed because there’s an obvious imbalance of power that has been hanging in the balance for about six years now at least. In order to break the stalemate, there must be a decisive battle,” said Jalal, who specialises in regional security and armed groups.
The fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces has intensified since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July, displacing hundreds of thousands of people since.
In mid-September, the Houthis seized the port city of Mocha and strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital route for global oil shipments, before anti-Houthi forces stabilised front lines.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, forcing the Yemeni government to retreat to Aden.

Ukraine to Deploy Small Missiles, Turrets Against Jet Drones, Zelensky Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:47:00 UTC
21:47:00 KST

Ukraine will begin deploying domestically produced small missiles by late October to counter Russian jet-powered strike drones, alongside expanding networks of automated gun turrets around the capital region, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced during a joint press briefing with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on Sunday, Oct. 4.
According to Ukringrom, Zelensky confirmed that Ukrainian defense enterprises have developed several types of specialized, lower-cost interceptor missiles engineered to neutralize high-speed unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), with initial combat deployments anticipated during the second half of the month.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The small missile program – I will not state the name now, there are several types – we will evidently see results in the second half of this month. We expect to see results,” Zelensky said.
While the missiles are not yet in serial mass production, the president stated that manufacturing can be scaled up rapidly once operational performance is confirmed.
Zelensky noted that Ukrainian forces currently intercept roughly 50 to 60 percent of incoming turbojet Shahed drones, with combat aviation demonstrating the highest efficacy against high-velocity targets.
“Right now, high-quality interception of [jet UAVs] is about 50 percent, 55 percent, sometimes 60 percent – that is our aviation,” Zelensky said.
“F-16s are helping very significantly, and 20mm ammunition is working well.”
Germany Pledges €1.3B Defense Package During Merz Kyiv Visit
Automated defensive turrets in Kyiv
To reinforce ground-level interception networks, Zelensky announced that Ukrainian defense units have installed more than 12 automated counter-drone turrets across the capital, with plans to deploy eight additional systems in the surrounding Kyiv region.
The automated modules are configured to fire 50-caliber (12.7mm) ammunition to destroy incoming loitering munitions on terminal approach vectors. Zelensky explained that the installations form part of a layered, combined defense posture required to address Moscow’s evolving air assault doctrine.
“The Russians will now focus precisely on jet-powered drones and ballistics,” Zelensky observed. “Regarding mass strikes similar to what we are seeing now, I believe they will move toward quality rather than quantity, transitioning from conventional Shaheds to maximum utilization of jet variants.”
The technological adaptation arrives as Russian forces have increasingly paired high-speed loitering munitions with ballistic missile salvos to overwhelm mobile air defense fire teams and deplete inventories of high-end surface-to-air guided missiles.
Bilateral drone agreement
The technical announcements coincided with the formal conclusion of a bilateral agreement between Ukraine and Germany to deepen operational cooperation in counter-drone warfare, enabling German defense manufacturers to integrate Ukrainian combat lessons directly into joint production ventures.
Chancellor Merz emphasized that defense cooperation between Berlin and Kyiv functions as a reciprocal partnership, noting that German corporate representatives accompanying his delegation are studying Ukrainian battlefield adaptations while establishing joint high-tech industrial facilities.
Merz referenced a thwarted Russian-directed sabotage plot at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4 as a clear demonstration of why counter-drone technologies are critical for Germany’s own domestic security.
Addressing Russian rhetoric, Merz stated that public threats issued by the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs warning foreign diplomats of “mortal danger” in Kyiv did not influence his decision to visit the Ukrainian capital.
“Despite the threats that reached us from Moscow in recent days, I came today. Together with me came a colleague from the government, Federal Minister for Economic Affairs Katharina Reiche, a large delegation from my government, and a major economic delegation,” Merz said.
“This shows: we will not allow ourselves to be intimidated.”
The chancellor added that ongoing Russian drone attacks on the capital during his visit underscored Moscow’s conduct, reaffirming that Berlin’s solidarity remains steadfast on his second visit to Kyiv as head of government and fourth overall.
Diplomatic resilience
Merz’s presence in Kyiv follows public assurances from EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová, who confirmed that no EU member state embassy is preparing to evacuate the capital despite Moscow’s threats and infrastructure strikes.
Mathernová confirmed regular coordination with the diplomatic missions of 25 EU member states based in Kyiv, stating that both the EU Delegation and the EU Advisory Mission (EUAM) Ukraine remain fully operational.
The ambassador characterized Moscow’s escalatory statements as an attempt to compensate for military setbacks on the battlefield, echoing statements by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine that standard diplomatic protocols mandate prior notification and that zero relocation requests have been received.

No EU Embassies Leaving Kyiv Despite Russian Threats, Envoy Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:42:00 UTC
21:42:00 KST

No EU member state embassy is preparing to evacuate the Ukrainian capital despite Russian aerial bombardments and threats directed at foreign missions, EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová confirmed in an interview with state news agency Ukrinform.
Mathernová stated that she maintains continuous coordination with the diplomatic representations of 25 EU member states based in the capital, rejecting reports in foreign media alleging that Western embassies were preparing contingency withdrawals to western Ukraine or Poland.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I am not aware of any embassy that is leaving – and certainly not embassies of EU countries,” Mathernová told Ukrinform. “I do not know what sources The Guardian used, but I am not aware of any embassy currently leaving; quite the contrary.”
The ambassador confirmed that both the EU Delegation to Ukraine and the European Union Advisory Mission (EUAM) Ukraine, alongside national embassies representing EU member states, remain fully operational on the ground in Kyiv.
While security personnel continuously evaluate operational hazards, Mathernová emphasized that the latest public threats from Russia have not altered their operational posture.
Mathernová framed Moscow’s escalatory rhetoric as an attempt to compensate for military setbacks on the battlefield.
“I think [Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s rhetoric is a consequence of the lack of success on the battlefield,” Mathernová observed.
Ukraine’s Science Under Fire: Russia Is Targeting Knowledge, People and the Future
“He is escalating rhetoric and threats – both regarding the civilian population and diplomats, and regarding EU countries. I believe this is a sign of frustration over failing in his strategic goals – to conquer Ukraine in a few weeks.”
Diplomatic coordination
Mathernová‘s public clarification directly addresses reporting published earlier in the week by The Guardian, which cited anonymous Western diplomats claiming that contingency plans were being drafted to relocate staff to the western city of Lviv or eastern Poland if the Kremlin began deliberately targeting foreign diplomatic compounds.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine (MFA) previously refuted the report on Friday, with spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi noting that established international diplomatic conventions mandate formal notification to the host nation prior to any mission transfer, confirming that zero relocation requests had been received by Ukrainian authorities.
The ambassador’s comments also reinforce statements made by European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand, who dismissed threats issued on Saturday, Oct. 3, by the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
In an official dispatch, Moscow had warned foreign citizens and accredited diplomats in Kyiv of “mortal danger,” pledging to sustain mass aerial strikes across the capital. Wigand reaffirmed that the EU would not be intimidated into reducing its diplomatic footprint or scaling back defense assistance.

A meteor hit Oklahoma 100 million years later than scientists thought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:41:43 UTC
21:41:43 KST

A meteor hit Oklahoma 100 million years later than scientists thought
- Date:
- October 4, 2026
- Source:
- University of Texas at Austin
- Summary:
- A meteor crater buried beneath Oklahoma has turned out to be nearly 100 million years younger than scientists thought. Zircon crystals show the Ames impact occurred about 370 million years ago, meaning it was not part of the mysterious Ordovician bombardment once linked to a possible ring of debris around Earth. Instead, the impact coincided closely with a major mass extinction that devastated marine life.
- Share:
Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin have revised a key piece of Oklahoma's geologic history, with possible implications for how scientists interpret major events in the history of life on Earth.
Beneath the town of Ames, Oklahoma, lies a meteor impact structure that stretches for miles underground. Layers of sediment now cover the crater, but it remains significant both scientifically and economically. The Ames impact structure is also a major producer of oil and gas.
A Crater Long Linked to an Ancient Meteor Event
For years, the Ames crater was thought to belong to a cluster of major meteor impacts across North America dating to roughly 467.5 million years ago. That period is known as the Ordovician Meteor Event.
Because so many impact structures appear to date from around the same time, some researchers have proposed that Earth may once have been surrounded by a Saturn-like ring of asteroid debris during the Middle Ordovician.
New work from UT researchers now shows that the Ames impact does not belong to that episode.
By dating zircon crystals taken from granite altered by the impact, the team determined that the meteorite struck about 370 million years ago during the Late Devonian. That makes the crater nearly 100 million years younger than previously believed.
"No matter what technique we used, it was coming back to this younger signal," said lead author Elizabeth Catlos, associate professor at UT's Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences.
The research was published in July in Meteoritics & Planetary Science.
Why the Earlier Date Was Misleading
Before this study, the Ames impact had only been dated using biological evidence. Researchers had found teeth from an ancient eel-like animal called a conodont preserved in the rock. Those fossils came from organisms that lived during the older Ordovician period.
But Catlos said the teeth were probably already millions of years old by the time the asteroid struck. The impact likely churned up older material and mixed the fossils into the rocks while still preserving them.
The zircon dating provides a very different timeline. It shows that the Ames crater could not have formed during the Ordovician Meteor Event.
Instead, its new age places it close to the Frasnian-Famennian mass extinction event, which occurred about 372 million years ago and wiped out a large proportion of marine life on Earth.
Tiny Zircon Crystals Preserve the Impact
Danny Stockli, dean of the Jackson School of Geosciences and a co-author of the study, said zircon U-Pb dating offers one of the most accurate ways to determine when events occurred deep in Earth's past.
Zircon crystals can also preserve microscopic structures created by the intense pressures generated during an impact.
"These small crystals allow us to go back in time and learn about the major changes to Earth's ancient landscapes," Stockli said. "It would be great to do this for more of the meteor impact sites across the continent so we could get a more accurate timeline for these major events."
To confirm that the zircons had actually been affected by the meteor strike, the team worked with NASA to image the crystals using cathodoluminescence and electron backscatter diffraction.
When zircon experiences the extreme conditions of an impact, it recrystallizes in a distinctive way. Those changes can be detected with these imaging techniques, allowing researchers to verify that the crystals recorded the collision itself.
A New Piece of a Mass Extinction Puzzle
According to Catlos, establishing more precise dates for mass extinctions and other major events is essential for understanding how Earth has changed over time.
One key question is whether extinction events were triggered primarily by forces from space, such as meteor impacts, or by processes within Earth, including episodes of massive volcanic activity.
"With this research, we're basically taking a major pawn out of the Ordovician Meteor Event and dumping it into the Frasnian-Famennian event, and saying, 'This is where this impact belongs,'" she said.
The project was initiated by former Jackson School of Geosciences graduate student Andrew Parisi, who graduated in 2018 and has since passed away. Parisi traveled to Oklahoma to obtain the Ames rock core from the Oklahoma Geological Survey, extracted zircon crystals from the material, and helped determine their ages.
Co-author Michael Brookfield, an affiliated researcher at the school, also passed away before the paper was published.
Research Professor Sean Gulick and Professor Emeritus Mark Cloos at the Jackson School also contributed to the research.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Texas at Austin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Elizabeth J. Catlos, Andrew F. Parisi, Michael E. Brookfield, Timmons Erickson, Sean P.S. Gulick, Axel K. Schmitt, Daniel F. Stockli, Daniel P. Miggins, Ben Ruchte, Mark Cloos. The Ames impact structure, Oklahoma: New radioisotopic constraints and implications for North American impact chronology. Meteoritics, 2026; 61 (8): 2103 DOI: 10.1111/maps.70191

Iran shines brighter in Nagoya with 19 gold medals

Iran shines brighter in Nagoya with 19 gold medals
TEHRAN - Iran’s delegation concluded its campaign at the 20th Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya with an improved gold-medal tally compared with the previous edition in Hangzhou.
The Nagoya Asian Games came to an end with Iran finishing sixth in the overall medal standings after winning 19 gold, 18 silver and 15 bronze medals for a total of 52 medals.
Iran sent a delegation of 304 athletes to Nagoya, competing across 38 sports. The number of athletes was higher than at the previous Asian Games in Hangzhou.
Iran also climbed one place in the overall standings compared with the 2022 Asian Games, moving up to sixth. The country had previously finished sixth at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta as well.
Although Iran’s overall medal haul fell short of the 54 medals won at the Hangzhou Games, the number of gold medals increased significantly. Iran won 13 gold medals in Hangzhou, compared with 19 in Nagoya — an increase of six golds.
The performance of Iran’s women was another notable highlight of the Games. While Iranian women failed to win a gold medal in Hangzhou, they claimed three golds in Nagoya.
Overall, the Nagoya campaign marked a significant improvement in Iran’s performance at the top end of the medal table, with the delegation combining a higher gold-medal tally with a one-place rise in the overall standings.

‘Russia is not our enemy’: Hundreds rally in Paris against Ukraine aid (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:39:38 UTC
21:39:38 KST

‘Russia is not our enemy’: Hundreds rally in Paris against Ukraine aid (VIDEO)
Hundreds of anti-government protesters took to the streets of Paris on Saturday to rally against continued aid to Ukraine as part of a nationwide protest organized by former MEP Florian Philippot, who is running in France’s 2027 presidential election.
The protesters called on French President Emmanuel Macron to halt aid to Ukraine and pushed for France’s withdrawal from the EU and all supranational institutions, including NATO. Apart from Paris, the right-wing Les Patriotes party, led by Philippot, organized rallies in Aubiere, Annecy, Grenoble, Perigueux and Chaumont, highlighting issues such as fuel costs, freedom of expression and peace.
The demonstration comes after a series of mass protests has gripped France in recent weeks, with students taking to the streets alongside broader labor actions over wages, public spending, working conditions and the government’s budget plans.
Philippot, a prominent Eurosceptic, marched through Paris with supporters, who waved French flags, as well as banners reading “Russia is not our enemy,” and calling for France to stay out of the Ukraine conflict.
“We must leave NATO, we must stop funding the war in Ukraine and stop arming it as well,” he stressed. “Instead of putting money over there, it must be put into lowering taxes on petrol, for example, because people can’t take it anymore.”
A Philippot supporter argued that “war efforts don’t achieve much,” calling for greater spending on “hospitals, education, and a whole range of budgets that are humane.”
The nationwide unrest comes as the French government unveiled its proposed 2027 budget earlier this week, targeting €54 billion in measures to bring the budget deficit to 5% of GDP, including spending cuts and freezes affecting public services, pensions and social benefits.
Philippot tore up an EU flag in front of demonstrators, saying, “This blue-starred rag is not our flag and never will be. So today, we are obviously going to get rid of it, because our fight is to get out of this horror through Frexit.”
Earlier this week, the EU reiterated its commitment to the €90 billion ($101 billion) loan aimed at covering the Ukrainian government’s budgetary and military financing needs for 2026 and 2027.

Bernie Sanders rallies for billionaire tax ahead of midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:31:02 UTC
21:31:02 KST

Breadcrumb
Bernie Sanders rallies for first-ever billionaire tax ahead of midterms
If a billionaire tax passes in California, it would be the first of its kind in the world, which advocates hope will give momentum for similar measures elsewhere.
On Saturday, one month ahead of the midterms, Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and other progressives held a rally in San Francisco to advocate for Proposition 40, a measure that would impose a 5% wealth tax on billionaires, who account for a fraction of a percentage of the population, but who hold an estimated 45% of the state’s household wealth. The tax would go toward the healthcare of residents.
Opponents of Proposition 40 say that the measure risks pushing businesses and jobs out of the state.
“I say to California billionaires and billionaires all over this country: Show a little concern for your fellow Americans. You and your class have never ever had it so good, but you cannot have it all,” Sanders said to a cheering crowd.
“Instead of spending over $225 million on TV ads, we have a better idea. Start paying your fair share of taxes,” he said.
“Once California passes Proposition 40, trust me that will not be the end. We’ll enact a national wealth tax,” Sanders added. He likened the fight for a billionaire tax to the right for democracy, saying there can be democracy or extreme wealth inequality -- but not both.
The 85-year-old senator was met by a standing ovation and roaring applause as he took the stage at the Curran Theatre, an intricately designed French revivalist structure near the city’s downtown.
He was introduced by Representative Ro Khanna, whose district makes up a large swath of Silicon Valley (home to a high proportion of the state’s billionaires), and who is rumoured to be considering a 2028 presidential bid.
“We’re here to do something very important. It’s the first time in the history of the world that there is a billionaire tax on the ballot,” he told a cheering crowd. “The whole world, the whole nation, is watching. And you know what they’re asking us? They’re asking us: Will the Democratic Party stand with the donor class or are they gonna stand with the working class?”
He described Proposition 40 as a choice between 250 billionaires or giving poor children healthcare and keeping the jobs of 150,000 healthcare providers. He noted that the billionaires who oppose the tax are spending $200 million to oppose it. He called out politicians who oppose the tax. He also challenged his colleagues to call Israel's actions in Gaza a genocide.
Another headline speaker was Jane Kim, who is running for the state’s Insurance Commissioner, a position she describes as the most important job you’ve never heard of.
In her speech, she vowed to lower monthly premiums and develop a system in which insurance is used for protection rather than profit.
Audience members, many of whom were healthcare workers, held signs reading “Yes on 40, No-41-42, Save Lives, Tax Billionaires” and raised them in the air after speakers made rousing statements.
“We’re trying to hold the billionaires accountable. They have made millions off of regular people for years. This one-time five percent emergency tax will not even put a dent in what they are making,” Savonnda Blaylock, a healthcare worker, told The New Arab prior to the rally.
“They are still making trillions of dollars. Some of them are becoming trillionaires, whereas regular people can’t even afford basic needs like gas and food. We’re here to make sure voters know, that communities know, that we’re going to fight this to the very last day – November 3rd,” she said.
“I’m excited about all of us seeing Bernie, because he brings hope. His vision and the hope he brings is what we need right now to be able to bring this home,” she said.
Saturday’s rally was part of a multi-day tour across California by progressives to encourage voter turnout and advocate for Proposition 40.
