Putin Hugged the Man Behind Russia’s Jet-Powered Shahed Program—OSINT Identifies Him
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:30:46 UTC
21:30:46 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Putin Hugged the Man Behind Russia’s Jet-Powered Shahed Program—OSINT Identifies Him
Ukrainian OSINT researchers have identified a senior executive at Russia’s Alabuga Special Economic Zone as the man who presented the new jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 attack drones to Vladimir Putin during Russia’s Center-2026 military exercises.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Evocation.info on October 3, the man seen briefing Putin was Ildar Tazutdinov, a senior executive at Alabuga, the Russian industrial complex involved in producing Iranian-designed Shahed-type attack drones.
The identification followed the publication of footage from the Chebarkulsky training ground in Russia’s Chelyabinsk region, where Putin inspected new Russian weapons on October 2.
In the video, Tazutdinov described the capabilities of the Geran-4 and Geran-5 before concluding: “We are ready to continue striking the enemy in the same way. That concludes my report!” Putin then shook his hand and embraced him, according to footage analyzed by Evocation.info.
Interfax reported on October 2 that Putin had been shown both jet-powered Geran variants during his visit to the training ground. According to the presentation, the Geran-4 uses a jet engine allowing it to reach approximately 350 km/h, carry a 50-kilogram warhead, and operate at a range of around 750 to 800 kilometers.
The larger Geran-5 was described as having a speed of up to 450 km/h, a 90-kilogram warhead, and a maximum range of roughly 900 kilometers. Evocation.info identified Tazutdinov as one of the executives connected to Alabuga’s drone program.
His involvement with the facility has previously been documented by the US government. In February 2024, the US Treasury Department sanctioned Ildar Rashitovich Tazutdinov, identifying him at the time as Alabuga’s deputy director general of corporate affairs.
Treasury said he had been involved in the shipment and import of materials and disassembled Iranian UAVs to Russia in connection with drone production at Alabuga.
The US Treasury said Alabuga officials were involved in producing Iranian-designed UAVs, including the Shahed-136 and its Russian Geran-2 variant, as well as importing components from Iran for the program.
The Geran-4 and Geran-5 represent newer jet-powered additions to Russia’s expanding family of long-range attack drones. Their higher speeds make interception more difficult than with earlier propeller-driven Shahed-type UAVs, prompting Ukraine to develop and deploy faster drone interceptors designed specifically to engage such targets.
Earlier, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence identified 20 pieces of foreign-made industrial equipment being used at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone to produce various Geran drone modifications, including machinery from China, Germany, Japan, Switzerland, and Iran.

Few people thought I could win gold: Emami
TEHRAN - Iranian freestyle wrestler Yones Emami, competing in the 74kg weight class, spoke about the difficulty of the competition, the high level of his opponents and his determination to win gold after claiming the title at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya.
Emami, who also won gold at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, secured his second consecutive Asian Games title with another impressive performance.
“Everything went well and I was able to win the gold medal. I’m happy that I can return home with a gold medal, and I hope I have not disappointed my family, the federation or my dear people. It was really difficult, and few people thought I could win the gold medal, but thankfully I was able to achieve this success.”
“The level of the competition was really high. There were world champions and many highly regarded wrestlers in my weight class, and I faced all of them. I managed to defeat my opponents and win the gold medal.”
The Iranian champion also reflected on his victory over Olympic champion Razambek Zhamalov, a match that many observers had expected to be particularly challenging.
“The reality was that many people did not think I could beat Zhamalov. Even before the competition, some people were worried that I might have problems in the early rounds. But, I was able to manage the competition well from the very beginning and eventually win the gold medal.”
Emami also admitted that winning two consecutive Asian Games gold medals was not something he had previously imagined.
Asked about the feeling of winning his second Asian Games gold after his triumph in Hangzhou, he said: “I honestly hadn’t thought about winning two Asian Games gold medals. My entire focus was on these competitions in Nagoya. I wanted to be in the best possible condition, wrestle my best matches and ultimately win the gold medal.”

How the ‘G2’ effect of Trump-Xi summit is reverberating through Asia
When the world’s two biggest powers speak of respecting each other and swap stories about a war against Japan, the message is clear
4-MIN READ4-MIN
2
 Listen
Wang Xiangwei is a senior visiting scholar (2026-27) at the Rajawali Foundation Institute for Asia, Harvard Kennedy School, and a former editor-in-chief of the South China Morning Post. 
For American and Chinese people interested in the outcome of the latest summit between China’s President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump, their conclusions could not be more different if they turn to the media and pundits for guidance.
Chinese state media spared no superlative, echoing the official description of the summit as: forging the right way for the major powers to get along and writing a new chapter in ties. It played up the fact that Trump gave Xi the highest-level reception and met him at the airport, the first time since 1962 that a US president has done so for a visiting leader other than a pope.
By contrast, US media and pundits were almost united in dismissing the summit as heavy on symbolism and light on substance, noting that both leaders played down their stark differences and delivered little more than a two-month extension of the trade truce and a new dialogue on artificial intelligence.

OPEC+ Agrees to Keep November Oil Output Targets Steady
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:29:00 UTC
21:29:00 KST

OPEC+ agreed to keep oil production targets steady for November at a meeting on Sunday, the producer group said, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments are unlikely until next year.
Seven core members of the group comprising the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia made the decision for November in a brief online meeting on Sunday. The core members are Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman.
Gulf OPEC+ producers have been pumping well below output targets in the face of continuing export disruptions from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, with exports fluctuating at 60% to 80% of normal levels in recent months.
“The OPEC+ group of seven kept their production ceilings unchanged, in line with market expectations. That said, despite rising flows through the Strait of Hormuz, their output levels remain well below quota,” said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo.
“Consequently, the oil market remains tight.”
Oil prices had dropped on Friday after European leaders agreed to U.S. President Donald Trump's request to release diesel reserves. Even so, Brent crude remains above $100 a barrel, up from about $73 before the Iran war started in late February.
OUTPUT HIKES HAVE BEEN LARGELY ON PAPER THIS YEAR
The Iran war has also delayed the group's output capacity review — crucial to determine members’ 2027 output quotas — because it has thrown estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, industry sources told Reuters last week.
OPEC+ has been raising output targets for much of 2026 after years of production cuts, but most of the increases stayed on paper because of the Middle East conflict.
The seven core OPEC+ members pumped 25 million barrels per day in August, up 630,000 bpd from July, yet still roughly 5 million bpd below prewar levels in February, OPEC data shows.
The seven hold their next meeting on Nov. 1.
OPEC+ still has about 2 million bpd of output cuts in place covering most members. It needs the result of the capacity review to decide how to distribute increases and any changes to output are unlikely before 2027, sources have said.
A separate OPEC+ ministerial group called the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee (JMMC), which does not decide policy, also met on Sunday to review the market.

Kyiv’s Green Line metro is once again transporting passengers across the Dnipro during the yellow threat level
Kyiv • UNN
During the yellow level, trains will transport passengers between the banks of the Dnipro. At the red level, service on the above-ground section will be suspended.
In Kyiv, the green metro line will now operate during a yellow alert. Before passenger services began, trains made test runs in both directions. This was reported by the Kyiv City State Administration, according to UNN.
Details
As of today, trains on the "green" line operate during an alert: during the yellow threat level, they carry passengers between the right and left banks of the Dnipro; if a red threat level is announced, service on the above-ground section is suspended
At the same time, according to the information available, during a red threat level, trains will operate on two sections: "Syrets" - "Vydubychi" and "Osokorky" - "Chervonyi Khutir".
We urge passengers to carefully monitor announcements in the carriages and at stations and to follow the instructions of metro staff

Ten stories of Ukraine’s defenders
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

From a drone-downing pastry chef to the company commander who carried a wounded soldier for miles on foot: 10 stories of Ukraine's defenders
2026 has been a year of victories great and small for the Ukrainian military, and the whole country has celebrated along with them.
Nazar Daletskyi, a serviceman believed to have been killed three years ago – a funeral had even been held for him – came home alive from captivity.
Vladyslav Polskyi, a company commander in the 475th Assault Regiment (Code 9.2), single-handedly evacuated two wounded soldiers in a civilian pickup truck as Russian drones circled overhead.
The National Guard awarded the title of Hero of Ukraine to a woman for the first time – machine gunner Oleksandra Davydenko.
Ukraine's defence forces in the south reclaimed up to 435 sq km of territory. The 3rd Army Corps stunned the public with the successful Operation Vivaldi counteroffensive in Donetsk Oblast.
Ahead of Defenders' Day, Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life) looks back to 10 of this year's most interesting stories about our defenders. Read them all – you won't regret it!
"Four of them couldn't walk": how a Special Operations Forces company commander evacuated a wounded soldier on foot, then went back for his comrade's body
"Eighteen", a company commander in the Special Operations Forces (SOF), would normally have been expected to coordinate the evacuation from the command post. But when four of his soldiers were no longer able to walk independently after a battle and an encounter with an improvised explosive device, he went into the area himself.
"The guys all had leg wounds. There were two uninjured operators left in the group, plus one medic.
That was when I realised I had to go into the area and get my people out. Nobody could have imagined that out of a group of eight we'd end up with four seriously wounded men and one slightly wounded. Four of them couldn't walk," Eighteen recalls.
It took 15 hours to carry the most seriously wounded soldier, Malyi (Little One), to the medics. The young man had severe injuries to his arm and abdomen and a ruptured liver.
"There were moments when he couldn't take it any more and lost heart. He'd say: 'I don't want to. You don't need to carry me anywhere.' But painkillers make all the difference. Obviously he was in a lot of pain. But he did well and held on," Eighteen says.
As soon as Malyi had been handed over to the doctors, Eighteen went back for the body of his fallen comrade, Sava. The rescue operation took five days in all, and the soldiers covered more than 50 km. All but Sava survived.
This remarkable operation proved once again that even in the era of ground robots, those who operate on their own two feet still have the decisive say in battle.
"I thought about tightening the tourniquets and bleeding to death so I wouldn't suffer": how a badly wounded infantryman hunted by six drones was rescued
Herodotus is a private first class in the 3rd Mountain Assault Battalion of the 128th Separate Mountain Assault Brigade. After 18 months fighting in an assault unit, he miraculously survived being hunted down by six Russian drones.
Herodotus was alone in a wooded area. He had already lost a foot, and as he was being evacuated, a Russian drone destroyed the ground robot and mangled his other leg.
He crawled, hid from FPV drones, and even played "cat and mouse" with one of them around a dugout, moving in such a way as to stay out of the Russians' line of sight. His comrades watched him from a drone throughout, dropping water, painkillers and food and trying to find a way to get him out.
Eventually three soldiers came to retrieve him and carried him for about 2.5 km. Herodotus lost both legs, but he survived. He says that in his darkest moments he remembered that he had promised his family he would return.
"There, look at what I've got now instead of legs. Ta-da! What am I supposed to do now – cry? It's already happened... I'm alive, so everything should be all right. Life can be a complete pile of shit sometimes, but we'll get through it," he says cheerily.
"We accepted that we were going to die": the military anaesthesiologist who volunteered to go to the besieged Azovstal steelworks
In spring 2022, military anaesthetist Oleksandr Demchenko volunteered to fly to the besieged Azovstal steelworks in Mariupol by helicopter. He realised that it could be a one-way trip. He later learned that the helicopter was shot down on its return journey.
At Azovstal, Oleksandr operated on wounded soldiers in an underground hospital, in cold and damp conditions and with a dwindling supply of medicines: even amputations had to be performed under local anaesthetic.
After one airstrike, five floors of the building above the medics collapsed while hundreds of people were inside.
"We all accepted that we were going to die there, because, essentially, there were no other options," Oleksandr recalls. But he was lucky – he made it out of there.
He survived Azovstal, Russian captivity and the Olenivka prison camp. When he returned home, he went back to medicine.
"I returned to the profession because I love it. I genuinely love my work," he admits.
"I'd serve for another six years, as long as my son never sees all this": the nurse who swapped her uniform for combat fatigues
Before joining the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Tamila had worked as a nurse at a district hospital for 15 years. Then she swapped her uniform for combat fatigues, eventually becoming head of the medical station of the 3rd Mountain Assault Battalion of the 128th Separate Mountain Assault Brigade.
In autumn 2022, when the brigade was conducting a counteroffensive in Kherson Oblast, Tamila was constantly going out to evacuate the wounded.
"I provided first aid in the vehicle. I had to stop the bleeding from severed arms and legs, apply tourniquets and administer painkillers. The brigade was carrying out assault operations, and guys were dying both on the battlefield and in front of me," she recalls.
Once, two years later, she happened to meet a soldier whom she had once evacuated with a severed arm. He recognised her first: "You were the one who evacuated me back then. Thank you."
Tamila's first contract ended long ago and she could have left the military, but she stayed. She still goes out on evacuations sometimes, even though her current position does not require her to.
She says she is ready to serve for as long as necessary, as long as her 16-year-old son never has to follow in her footsteps.
"I've been in the Armed Forces of Ukraine for six years now, and they haven't been easy years for me – they've been really hard. Because war is the worst nightmare there can be. But I'm ready to serve for another six years, as long as my son never sees all this, as long as he never has to fight," Tamila admits.
"Several times we had enemy infantry jumping into our trenches": the company commander who spent 343 consecutive days on the front line
Three hundred and forty-three days is enough time to celebrate Christmas, New Year and Easter. But for company commander Oleksii, aka Botanik (Nerd), it was the length of time he spent at positions on the Orikhiv front without rotation.
About half of the soldiers in Botanik's company are over 50, and many suffer from chronic health problems. This makes normal rotations almost impossible, so they have to remain on the line of contact for long periods.
Oleksii's longest combat deployment took place in June 2025. The Russians would attack the Ukrainian positions using infantry fighting vehicles, motorcycles and quad bikes and on foot. When they managed to reach the trenches, machine gunners and drone operators would join the fighting. Evacuation crews collected the wounded under fire.
"I tried to make the fighters' time at the combat positions as bearable as possible. I made sure everyone had a chance to talk to their families every day – that helps a lot," the company commander says.
Oleksii finally left the line of contact on 8 March 2026 and immediately went on leave to celebrate his daughter's 10th birthday. Then it was back to the front line.
"I see my primary role as a commander as minimising personnel losses – ideally ensuring there are none at all," he says.
Pastry chef by day, air defence operator by night: the woman from Bucha shooting down Russian drones
Liudmyla, from Bucha, isn't your typical volunteer. By day she makes exquisite cakes and pastries, but after dark, she protects the skies over Kyiv Oblast.
It all began in 2024, when an acquaintance told Liudmyla about the Bucha Witches – a women's unit of mobile air-defence fire groups established as part of the Bucha Volunteer Formation of the Territorial Community. Liudmyla couldn't stand idly by.
The first time she shot down a Russian Shahed drone, the adrenaline rush was overwhelming. Two years ago she knew almost nothing about the military – now she commands a mobile fire group.
Liudmyla does all this as a volunteer and receives no pay. After a night shift, she returns home, puts down her weapon, and gets back to making cakes.
"It can be difficult at times – exhausting night shifts and winter cold when your hands quite literally freeze to the machine gun – but I love this work. Now I see safety in a completely different way and always silently thank those who protect my sleep when I am off duty," the defender says.
"It was eating away at me that my country was at war while I was here": the Mariupol surgeon who returned from abroad to serve in the army
In March 2022, urological surgeon Dmytro Hetmanov was operating on wounded civilians in besieged Mariupol. The hardest moment came when a father carried in his wounded teenage son. The injury looked minor from the outside, but the boy's heart and blood vessels had been virtually torn apart. The boy could not be saved.
On 16 March, Dmytro decided to try to escape the city with his parents and neighbours. On the way, he saw the bombed-out Drama Theatre still smouldering. It took him a long time to get through the Russian checkpoints.
Two years later, Dmytro was working as a surgeon at the University Hospital in Katowice, Poland. He had a job and his life was gradually getting back on track, but thoughts of his homeland never left him.
"It was eating away at me that my country was at war while I was here. Some of my friends had joined the Armed Forces, while I was sitting here enjoying life," he admitted.
Dmytro resigned and left Poland to return to Ukraine. He completed basic military training, signed a contract and joined the Unmanned Systems Forces. Six months later, he realised that he was missing surgery.
Now Dmytro is serving as a surgeon once again, this time with the 4th Medical Battalion of the 3rd Army Corps. He deals with combat injuries, assists with amputations, and has even tried his hand at neurosurgery for the first time.
Although Dmytro's daughter lives in the United States and rarely sees her dad, he does not regret his decision to join the military.
"They actually listed me among the dead": Azov fighter Web on the Olenivka terrorist attack and rehabilitation after three years in captivity
Dmytro "Web" Tishchenko was listed among the dead after the Russian terrorist attack on the Olenivka prison camp. When he came to, he was lying in a pile of metal and concrete, with a punctured lung and a bleeding arm. He crawled out of the destroyed barracks by himself.
"We asked the Russians for at least some medical supplies, but all they brought us was a bag of army sheets. We tore the fabric into pieces and used them to dress our wounds," the Azov fighter recalls.
When he was finally taken to hospital, one of the Russians was surprised to hear his name called out: "You're alive? I'd already got a body bag ready for you."
Web was only 21 at the time of the terrorist attack on Olenivka. He became a soldier at 18, took part in the defence of Mariupol, was wounded in the leg, made it to Azovstal, and from there he was taken into Russian captivity.
Dmytro spent another two months in hospital after the attack, and then he was moved from one penal colony to another. He had to endure torture, cold, hunger, and being made to stand for hours on end.
Because of a shrapnel wound, his leg became so badly infected that the wound simply opened up. In order to be admitted to hospital and avoid losing the limb, he had to pretend to faint.
Dmytro spent almost three years in captivity. In April 2025, he was suddenly taken out of his cell, given clean clothes and driven to an unknown destination. It was a prisoner swap. Web came home on the eve of Easter – exactly when he had dreamed of returning.
Now Web is undergoing treatment for his injuries and the effects of captivity, while also helping other young soldiers who have returned from Russian captivity.
"Sometimes I forget I'm missing a leg": two Khartiia infantrymen who've returned to service after suffering severe injuries
Assault trooper "Bilyi" stepped on a mine 15-20 metres from his position. He applied a tourniquet himself and waited to be evacuated, but the team that set off to retrieve him was attacked by a drone. When dawn broke, he realised that help might not come in time, so he started crawling on his own.
Bilyi crawled for nearly a whole day before two reconnaissance soldiers found him. By then the tourniquet had been on his leg for about two days. Bilyi had realised immediately after the explosion that his leg would have to be amputated.
"Terry" went through a similar ordeal. During his third combat deployment, he stepped on a petal mine hidden in the grass.
"It didn't hurt, I didn't lose consciousness. I opened my eyes and saw these toes lying around. Only the heel was left. I thought, 'That's it. I've had my run,'" Terry recalls.
It took 25 hours to evacuate him. Along the way, the wounded man and the soldiers carrying him were pursued by Russian FPV drones. One drone missed them, but another exploded near the group, injuring all three of the soldiers who were carrying Terry. Despite their own injuries, however, they managed to carry him to shelter.
Both Terry and Bilyi had their legs amputated. Months of surgery, rehabilitation and prosthetic fittings lay ahead of them. Terry recalls that after receiving a temporary prosthesis, he started walking the very next day and soon left his crutches behind. Bilyi was also quick to learn how to use his prosthesis.
"After they cut off my leg, there were moments when I felt a bit down. Then I'd lie there and think: it's all good. I'm alive, I can eat and get around on my own, go to the toilet and have a shower – I can do all of that," Terry says.
Bilyi is equally convinced: "Life goes on. The main thing is that I'm alive."
Their service didn't end there. Less than a year after being wounded, Bilyi got a call from the company's senior sergeant, who offered him a new position. On 12 May, he rejoined the Khartiia Brigade. Terry later joined him.
The two former infantrymen began learning an entirely different role – they became ISTAR dispatchers at a command and observation post. Instead of going out on combat missions, they now monitor the battlefield through screens, work with reconnaissance personnel and drone operators, and pass on information about targets.
"If I sat at home, what would I do? At least this way I can help out here," Bilyi says.
For now, the Khartiia soldiers have no plans to return to civilian life.
Olena Barsukova

Germany Pledges €1.3B Defense Package During Merz Kyiv Visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:22:00 UTC
21:22:00 KST

Germany has committed a comprehensive military and energy assistance package valued at more than €1.3 billion ($1.5 billion) to Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced in Kyiv on Sunday, Oct. 4.
According to Ukrinform, the newly allocated assistance package comprises roughly €1 billion ($1.13 billion) in military aid focused on air defense, long-range strike capabilities, combat drones, and satellite communications, alongside approximately €350 million ($396 million) to reinforce Ukrainian power substations and emergency generation ahead of winter.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Speaking during a joint press briefing in the capital, Zelensky stressed that the agreements combine emergency battlefield deliveries with sustainable industrial integration.
“There is a new support package for Ukraine – a comprehensive package of more than €1.3 billion,” Zelensky stated. “This is weapons that will help right now, as well as support for our energy sector ahead of winter – an important energy package. Naturally, we discussed the need for air defense, which is crucial at this time.”
In parallel with the emergency assistance, the two governments and corporate partners concluded 15 bilateral agreements and industrial documents valued at more than €8.5 billion ($9.6 billion), focusing on long-term arms manufacturing, joint defense ventures on Ukrainian soil, and direct state orders for German industrial manufacturers.
No EU Embassies Leaving Kyiv Despite Russian Threats, Envoy Says
“To date, we have 15 agreements and documents, and most of them concern security cooperation, manufacturing, corresponding procurement, our orders for German industry, and joint projects in Ukraine,” Zelensky said.
“The total weight of today’s agreements is more than €8.5 billion.”
Military breakdown, long-range systems, and winter energy aid
Details outlined by Chancellor Merz during the briefing confirmed that the €1 billion ($1.13 billion) military component prioritizes long-range standoff capabilities and advanced communications to allow Ukrainian forces to target Russian launch installations directly.
“We are launching another military support package worth around one billion euros,” Merz said, noting that Berlin will supply long-range strike weapons, combat drones, and satellite technologies.
“Regarding the details of the military support, I ask for understanding that we do not wish to disclose them in detail.”
Merz emphasized that German military assistance is concentrating on two foundational capabilities: expanding layered air defense and reinforcing space-based satellite communications to ensure Ukrainian units receive real-time operational data.
The chancellor added that German funding is accelerating serial assembly lines for newly developed interceptors engineered to neutralize jet-powered strike drones following recent technological breakthroughs.
Addressing the civilian heating sector, Merz announced approximately €350 million ($396 million) in targeted energy assistance to procure mobile generators, repair damaged electrical substations, and restore transmission infrastructure battered by Russian aerial strikes.
“We are facing what may be a very difficult winter. Moscow is deliberately targeting energy supply infrastructure – thermal power plants, substations, fuel stations, and railway infrastructure,” Merz said.
“The goal is entirely obvious: to break the morale of Ukrainians. Despite the attack that occurred this morning, I see here a determined people and a determined government.”
Industrial ventures and Berlin winter summit
A core component of the newly finalized accords is a dedicated bilateral agreement on joint counter-drone operations, established to counter Russia’s accelerating use of turbojet-powered loitering munitions against Ukrainian urban centers and power generation facilities.
The agreement aligns with Chancellor Merz’s pledge, announced upon his arrival in the capital, that Berlin intends to ensure the expedited transfer of 1,000 newly developed interceptor systems designed specifically to defeat turbojet-powered Shahed drones directly from German production lines.
Merz traveled to Kyiv accompanied by German Minister for Economic Affairs Katharina Reiche alongside a 10-member delegation of chief executives and senior managers representing Germany’s defense and energy industries.
The corporate representatives conducted working sessions with Ukrainian defense officials to advance collaborative assembly lines, technology transfers, and resilient industrial supply chains.
The industrial focus comes as German defense planners and corporate partners seek to deploy lower-cost interceptors capable of neutralizing fast-moving strike drones without depleting high-end surface-to-air missile stockpiles such as the IRIS-T or Patriot.
Looking ahead to multilateral diplomatic coordination, Merz announced that Germany intends to convene a high-level summit in Berlin this winter alongside France and the UK.
“Together with France and Great Britain, we want to hold a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin this winter, particularly to coordinate further assistance,” Merz confirmed, though specific calendar dates and formal agendas remain under development.
Academy of Sciences visit
Following their formal talks, Zelensky and Merz traveled together to inspect the site of a recent Russian drone strike on the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv.
The strike on the academic institution killed two people and injured seven others, causing severe structural damage to the historic scientific complex.
Zelensky stated that video records confirmed the facility was deliberately targeted by Russian loitering munitions, characterizing the strike as an intentional effort to destroy Ukrainian scientific infrastructure.
The joint inspection took place against the backdrop of recurrent air raid sirens and ongoing drone strikes across the capital on Sunday morning, which included a repeat strike that damaged the road deck of Kyiv’s North Bridge.
Zelensky commended the German chancellor for maintaining his itinerary and visiting the damaged research complex despite operational security warnings, describing the gesture as an important signal of personal and national solidarity from Berlin.
Merz’s visit follows statements delivered in Berlin on Sept. 29, in which the German leader identified territorial air defense as Ukraine’s “weakest point” ahead of the winter heating season, confirming that Germany is coordinating with EU partners to finalize additional military aid packages ahead of the European Council summit in Brussels on Oct. 15–16.

The demands of Welsh devolution are simple: just give us what Scotland has | Will Hayward
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:21:16 UTC
21:21:16 KST

As I sat in the first Plaid Cymru conference since the party won the Welsh election and started leading the Welsh government, I heard things I had never heard before. I have been to a lot of Plaid conferences and not once have I heard people being really positive about a UK Labour leader. But there was no mistaking it: the Welsh nationalist party feels that Andy Burnham is a man it can work with.
When I interviewed Welsh first minister Rhun ap Iorwerth, he indicated he was hopeful – in a way he never was under Keir Starmer – that there was a prime minister who had a genuine desire to give Wales meaningful concessions when it comes to additional powers.
In his speech in Llandudno, the first minister said that the prime minister had “looked me in the eyes and promised he would not [bypass the Senedd]”. He said he had written to Burnham with a “formal ask” for “a new deal for Wales”.
There were five demands from the Welsh government to Westminster: powers over policing and justice, powers over rail infrastructure, control over the crown estate, “fiscal fairness” and control of welfare. Seems like a pretty long shopping list, right? Well, it can actually be summarised in just five words: “Give us what Scotland has.”
The Scots have control of the crown estate, a better funding settlement, with more money through the Barnett formula, heavy rail is devolved, and the Scottish government controls policing and justice, as well as having partial control of welfare spending.
When you look at it from that perspective, it’s not as if the Welsh government is asking for something unprecedented. The UK government only has to look north to see the precedent.
You don’t have to be a Welsh nationalist to think it’s unfair that Wales’s government is equipped with fewer tools than its Scottish counterparts to meaningfully tackle Wales’s challenges. Wales has less borrowing capacity than a local council and, as mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham had more power over policing in his area than the first minister of Wales does.
The stars are aligning for Wales to get more parity with Scotland. If Burnham follows his own devolution logic – that decisions should be taken closer to the people they impact –then how could he defend a region of England getting more autonomy than a nation?
Though figures within Plaid clearly believe that Burnham is genuinely open to giving Wales more powers, they have real concerns that the more devo-sceptic figures within both the UK Labour party and the civil service will hinder their attempts. These fears are not unfounded. A leaked memo from Starmer revealed that he warned his cabinet against being “overly deferential” to devolved governments. In December 2025, 11 Labour Senedd members wrote to the then PM accusing him of “rolling back” devolution.
This fear led to one of the better lines in ap Iorwerth’s speech, where he said that if Burnham fails to give Cymru concessions: “Wales will know again that our best interests will never be served by Westminster, and that it matters little whether who lives in No 10 Downing Street is an Evertonian or an Old Etonian.”
With all the talk of “the Burnham bounce”, one thing that I think is being missed in the wider media is the total collapse of Labour’s status in Wales. Before the Senedd election in May, Welsh Labour was the most successful democratic party in history, having been the largest party in Wales at every general and Senedd election since 1922.
When Labour was struggling in England and Scotland against the Tories, led by both David Cameron and Boris Johnson, Welsh Labour was winning election after election. But now Labour’s dominance in Wales is over. In a 96-seat Welsh parliament, Labour now has just nine seats.
At Labour conference in Liverpool, speaking to people on both the Welsh and UK sides of the party, it was clear to me that they were facing very different trajectories. UK Labour members were full of hope, optimism and excitement for what is to come: the conference was like an engagement party, to celebrate a union with their new partner.
Meanwhile, Welsh Labour members had just broken up with their partner of 27 years and were totally cut up about the divorce. They were at the engagement party, trying to keep a stiff upper lip while nursing a can of strong lager and wondering how they were going to afford to furnish their new one-bed flat.
But this is a very bad time for Welsh Labour to have an identity crisis. All of the demands made by Plaid to Burnham are longstanding Welsh Labour policies. For so long, Welsh Labour and devolution were synonymous with each other, but now the mood music is very different. Welsh Labour’s new leader, Ken Skates, has actively criticised Plaid for pursuing the very policies Labour previously sought around more devolution.
There is a chance for the people of Wales to get more direct tools to improve their own prosperity, but to do so they need all their representatives to understand the value of devolution and be united in their fight for it, regardless of the party they represent.
- Will Hayward is a Guardian columnist. He publishes a regular newsletter on Welsh politics

In Southern Brazil, a Ukrainian Community Flourishes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:15:00 UTC
21:15:00 KST

Ukraine has had a tumultuous history and has featured prominently in many of Europe’s major events over the past few centuries, including both World Wars. With each upheaval came waves of Ukrainian migration to other continents, as people sought economic opportunities while others fled war and political repression. Many went to North America, where Canada and the United States developed established Ukrainian diasporas. But Ukrainians also migrated to South America, including Argentina and Brazil.
The strongest concentration is in Prudentópolis, a municipality of roughly 50,000 people sometimes called “Little Ukraine.” More than three-quarters of its residents speak at least some Ukrainian, according to Anderson Prado, a historian at the Federal University of Paraná who has studied the community.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukrainian is taught in public schools in some parts of the Paraná region. There are over 100 Greek Catholic parish centers in Prudentópolis. Brazil is home to 600,000 people of Ukrainian descent, with roughly 80 percent living in Paraná. Many are descended from immigrants who arrived more than a century ago, creating one of the largest Ukrainian communities outside of eastern Europe.
                                                                                                                                                                         The Church of Our Lady of Patronage in Prudentópolis. (Photo: Facebook page of Igreja Nossa Senhora do Patrocínio – Linha Esperança.)                             
A Kyivan Elegy – Babyn Yar
A community takes root
The first organized group of Ukrainian immigrants arrived in Paraná in 1891. Roughly 1,500 families settled around Prudentópolis in the 1890s, many coming from villages around present-day Ternopil in western Ukraine, which was then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.
The Ukrainian outlet RBC-Ukraine wrote: “People from Galicia, Ternopil, and Ivano-Frankivsk regions sought a better life and migrated to South America. The Brazilian government offered land for settlement, so thousands of Ukrainian families settled here.”
Cláudia Serathiuk’s family was among those early immigrants. Her paternal ancestors, Simão and Eufrosina Serotiuk, arrived from Vertelka, in the Ternopil region, in 1895 with nine children. They initially settled in a forested area near the Serra do Mar, where Simão died. Eufrosina continued inland with her children and eventually settled in Prudentópolis.
Serathiuk, who was born and lives in Curitiba, traces all sides of her family to Ukrainian immigrants. “All my ancestors are Ukrainian,” she said.
“Most Ukrainian émigrés were peasants who came there in the late 19th and early 20th century, or their descendants,” said Nataliia Rudnytska, a scholar at Volodymyr Dahl East Ukrainian National University who has studied Brazil’s Ukrainian diaspora. Unlike Ukrainian communities in the United States, Canada and West Germany, “where many Ukrainians who were opposed to the Soviet regime decided to stay after World War II,” she said, many of those who came to Brazil were seeking economic opportunity.
According to research from the Lviv University of Business and Law, Ukrainian migration to Brazil occurred in several distinct waves: between 1872-1914, 1917-39, and 1947-51.
Unlike Ukrainian communities in North America, however, Brazil’s diaspora received relatively little new immigration in the decades that followed. Augusto Harmatiuk, a Ukrainian-Brazilian who lives in Curitiba and whose ancestors arrived from Halychyna [Galicia] between 1896 and 1909, describes it as an “ancient diaspora.”
“We were not ‘renewed,’” Harmatiuk said. “We are largely the descendants of immigrants who self-identified as ‘Ruthenians,’” which the Encyclopedia of Ukraine notes as “a historical name for Ukrainians corresponding to the Ukrainian.” It was historically associated with Ukrainians who lived in western Ukraine under the Habsburg monarchy.
Harmatiuk added, “There are language classes, pysanka classes, bandura classes, and dance classes. There are those who write, those who translate books, those who make movies, those who embroider, those who do crafts, those who play instruments, those who sing.”
The earliest communities were largely agricultural, but the immigrants quickly built institutions that helped preserve their identity.
Historian Serge Cipko, citing an account of Ukrainian settlements from 1922 by Petro Karmansky, notes that the Prudentópolis area had 23 schools run by the Basilian Fathers, nine Ukrainian churches and chapels, and 10 branches of the secular organization Soyuz.
By 1920, Ukrainians may have represented roughly 5 to 6 percent of Paraná’s population.
Later waves brought political refugees and members of the Ukrainian intelligentsia, adding to communities that had initially been dominated by farmers. In 1934, Ukrainians established the Ukrainian Union in Brazil, which became another center of cultural life.
Ukrainian Greek Catholic and Orthodox churches were also important, serving as centers for both worship and community life.
In January 2025, a new Ukrainian Greek Catholic church dedicated to St. Nicholas was consecrated in Joinville, in neighboring Santa Catarina, after years of work by the local Ukrainian community.
                                                                                                                                                                         Demonstration against Russia’s invasion of Ukraine at Ukraine Square in Curitiba, 2025. (Photo: Augusto Harmatiuk)                             
Keeping a culture alive
The communities’ relative isolation helped preserve those traditions. Many of the early immigrants settled in rural areas, where generations of families lived alongside other Ukrainians.
Researchers John Lehr and Serge Cipko found that aspects of traditional Ukrainian culture survived longer in Brazil than among Ukrainian communities in Canada, even though many of the immigrants came from the same areas of western Ukraine.
Ukrainian-Canadian historian Orest Subtelny described the settlements as the closest surviving approximation of a 19th-century Galician village.
The Ukrainian spoken around Prudentópolis developed differently from the language spoken in Ukraine. This is because generations were separated from their ancestral homeland, meaning residents preserved older forms of Ukrainian brought by immigrants in the late 19th century, even as the language in Ukraine continued to develop.
Many are now fifth-generation Brazilians who have never visited Ukraine but continue to speak the language.
Serathiuk grew up speaking both Ukrainian and Portuguese and was baptized in the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church. She lived with her grandparents for decades, while the family continued many of the traditions brought from Ukraine.
“My great-grandmother Teodosia Petryk lived in Brazil for 52 years without ever speaking a word of Portuguese,” Serathiuk said. “She never needed to, because in her family, in the neighborhood, at the market and at church, everyone spoke Ukrainian.”
Brazilian filmmaker Guto Pasko is another example. A fifth-generation descendant of Ukrainian immigrants who grew up near Prudentópolis, Pasko reportedly spoke only Ukrainian until he was 11. He later directed several documentaries about the Ukrainian community in Brazil, including “Made in Ucrania: Os Ucranianos no Paraná.”
But maintaining the language has become more difficult with each generation. Harmatiuk said Ukrainian is becoming less common among descendants, even as community groups offer language classes, including online.
“Maintaining the language among young people is a constant challenge,” he said, particularly for a small community surrounded by Portuguese speakers.
In 2021, Prudentópolis made Ukrainian its second official language, more than 125 years after the first large Ukrainian settlements were established there. The neighboring municipality of Mallet followed in 2022.
In Curitiba, Paraná’s capital, the Ukrainian Society of Brazil operates the Lesia Ukrainka Ukrainian Saturday School alongside Ukrainian dance and choir ensembles.
Ukrainian-Brazilian writer and translator Vira Selianska, better known as Vira Vovk, became central to that effort. In 1959, she helped publish an anthology introducing Brazilian readers to Ukrainian literature spanning centuries.
According to Rudnytska, nearly all literary translations from and into Ukrainian produced by the community were made either by Selianska or with her participation, including dozens of journals and more than 40 books. “It is really the case when one person’s dedication and commitment brings real changes,” Rudnytska said.
The community has pushed for recognition of Ukrainian history as well. Paraná recognized the Holodomor, the Soviet-engineered famine that killed millions of Ukrainians in 1932 and 1933, as genocide in 2007. Curitiba and Prudentópolis followed in 2008, Maringá in 2019 and Roncador in 2021. Roncador’s city council pointed to the Ukrainian roots of local families and the continued preservation of their culture when adopting the measure.
                                                                                                                                                                         Members of the Grupo Folclórico Ucraniano Poltava, which is a traditional Ukrainian folk group based in Curitiba, Brazil, founded in 1981. (Photo: Facebook of Grupo Folclórico Ucraniano Poltava)                             
The war renews old ties
Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine has helped revitalize historical ties.
In May 2024, a delegation from the Ukrainian Council of Churches and Religious Organizations traveled to Brazil, meeting Presbyterian, Baptist, Adventist and Pentecostal leaders in São Paulo before continuing to Curitiba. The delegation’s mission was to raise awareness about Russia’s invasion and encourage Brazilian churches to support Ukraine.
According to researcher Nataliya Shevchenko of the Foreign Policy Council “Ukrainian Prism,” lawmakers from Paraná make up a noticeable share of the Brazilian congressional friendship groups with Ukraine. Before President Jair Bolsonaro traveled to Moscow just days before Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, the Ukrainian diaspora appealed to him to support Ukraine and visit Kyiv.
However, that influence has not always translated into support from Brasília. Brazil recognized Ukrainian independence in December 1991, and the two countries later developed a strategic partnership. But relations cooled following Russia’s seizure of Crimea in 2014. Brazil abstained from a United Nations resolution affirming Ukraine’s territorial integrity, creating a divide between a Ukrainian community with strong cultural ties to its ancestral homeland and a national government reluctant to oppose Russia.
The Brazilian diaspora’s relationship with Ukraine itself has not always been as strong. Ola Hnatiuk, a professor at the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy who has researched the role of the Ukrainian diaspora in advancing Ukraine’s interests abroad, said diaspora communities have built extensive ties with one another, with Ukrainian Americans providing substantial support to the community in Brazil. But she said the Ukrainian government could have done more to engage those communities.
“Ukraine as a state should have done much more to support the diaspora,” Hnatiuk said. While the war has made that more difficult, she added, money is not necessarily the most important part. “The financial dimension is not crucial, the symbolic dimension is much more vital.”
Similar communities took root elsewhere in South America. Argentina also became home to a sizable Ukrainian diaspora beginning in the late 19th century. Many of the first immigrants were peasants from Galicia who settled in the northern province of Misiones, where they established farming communities and churches. Later waves brought Ukrainians fleeing political repression and war.
“In Argentina alone, before Russia’s invasion, there was a Ukrainian diaspora of over 400,000 people, one of the largest in both Americas,” Ukraine’s first lady, Olena Zelenska, said in 2024.
Chile developed a much smaller community. Its first significant wave arrived after World War II, when roughly 300 Ukrainian refugees came from displaced-person camps in Europe in 1948 and 1949. However, the degree to which Ukrainian culture survived in southern Brazil is unusual.
Russia’s full-scale invasion brought some descendants closer to Ukraine. “We have become much more patriotic as we connect with the stories of wars, famines and invasions that our ancestors suffered,” Serathiuk said. “The ideal of a free and sovereign Ukraine remains.”
Harmatiuk has noticed another change. He said more descendants are researching their family histories, learning about Ukraine and taking a greater interest in their ancestry.
“I see more descendants interested in their ancestry than I realized a decade ago,” he said, adding that a longing for the ancestral land “has been rekindled.”
For some Brazilian Ukrainians, the war has made that relationship more direct. Father Makariy, an Orthodox priest who grew up in Brazil’s Ukrainian community, traveled to Ukraine and became a chaplain with the 2nd International Legion of Defense of Ukraine.
Today, a piece of Galicia remains somewhat frozen in time in southern Brazil. In some places, it can feel like Ukraine itself, only from another era. The traditions run deep, even as familiarity with the homeland has faded over generations. “Being Ukrainian is part of my life,” Serathiuk added. “It is important for our community because it keeps our history and the history of Ukraine alive.”

Norway Jails Conscription Offender for First Time Since 2006
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:14:51 UTC
21:14:51 KST

A Norwegian court has sentenced a 25-year-old man to two weeks in prison for failing to report for compulsory military service, citing the war in Ukraine and the security situation in Europe as reasons for the custodial sentence.
Norway’s public broadcaster NRK reported this.
Norway has mandatory military service for both men and women, but not everyone serves. Conscripts are selected based on medical examinations and test results. The man had been selected and called up for service but failed to report by the specified date.
The Haugaland and Sunnhordland District Court found that the man was required to report to a military camp in spring 2023. He was aware of this obligation but failed to appear. At the same time, there was no evidence that he intended to evade military service permanently.
The prosecution sought a 30-day prison sentence. The court imposed two weeks in prison as an appropriate punishment, citing the war in Ukraine and the changing security situation in Europe.
This approach differs from Norway’s Supreme Court practice since 2006, when similar cases generally resulted in suspended sentences.
Militarnyi reported in August 2023 that the length of compulsory military service in several Norwegian units had been increased from 12 to 15 months. Depending on the assignment, it can now last from six to 18 months.

China Focus: Ancient temple draws visitors as cultural tourism booms in Shanxi
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:10:45 CST
12:10:45 KST

TAIYUAN, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- For years, Yang Liangen saw strangers as a threat.
After a series of break-in attempts at a 900-year-old temple in north China's Shanxi Province, Yang moved into the compound in 1997, sleeping behind its gates and guarding its rare sculptures and wooden structures.
Nearly three decades later, he eagerly waits for strangers to arrive. "We used to be afraid when people came," Yang said. "Now we hope they will come."
Located in Xiaonan Village in Jincheng City, Erxian Temple fully opened to the public in 2024 as interest in Shanxi's ancient architecture surged following the release of "Black Myth: Wukong," a blockbuster Chinese video game.
During China's National Day holiday that year, Yang counted 1,280 visitors in a single day -- a record for a site whose gates had long been kept mostly shut. The crowds have continued to grow, with more than 4,300 people visiting the temple from Oct. 1 to 3 this year.
The change at Erxian Temple reflects a broader shift across China, as growing interest in cultural tourism brings new attention to historic buildings that for decades were little known beyond their local communities.
Built in 1097, Erxian Temple is a major national cultural heritage site. Its main hall is known for rare Song Dynasty (960-1279) painted sculptures and an exceptionally well-preserved miniature wooden architectural structure known locally as the "sky bridge."
Dubbed China's "above-ground cultural relics museum," Shanxi is home to over 28,000 ancient structures. The province also preserves more than 12,000 painted sculptures and 24,000 square meters of murals from the Tang Dynasty (618-907) onward.
PRESERVED BEHIND THE GATES
For Yang, the new attention marks a dramatic change from the late 1990s.
Facing growing risks to the temple in 1997, Yang, then the village Party secretary, took responsibility for Erxian Temple and moved in with his wife.
The couple kept watch day and night. On one occasion, Yang's wife rushed outside with a flashlight after two people were spotted apparently chiseling through a wall, sending them fleeing.
No theft has occurred since Yang became its caretaker.
A major restoration completed in 2014 repaired the compound and revived its two-courtyard layout. Surveillance cameras were installed, giving the couple what Yang described as their first truly restful sleep in years. But the gates largely remained closed.
Visits by preservation experts became important opportunities for Yang. He followed them around, learning about Song Dynasty construction and the temple's rare architectural features.
As architecture enthusiasts began making their way to the village, Yang sometimes made exceptions to let them inside and shared what he had learned.
"They had come such a long way," Yang said. "Maybe they would only come once in their lives. How could I not let them see it?"
Over time, Yang turned himself from a guard into an unofficial guide.
FINDING NEW AUDIENCES
Years of restoration and improved security eventually made it possible for more people to see what Yang had spent decades protecting.
In late 2022, an upgrade of Erxian Temple's security system was launched. Around the same time, local heritage enthusiasts formed a volunteer association in Jincheng City to support heritage site caretakers, organize educational visits and train volunteer guides.
In August 2024, Jincheng began opening 18 nationally and provincially protected heritage sites to the public on Sundays on a trial basis before fully opening them in October. Erxian Temple was included.
"The temple didn't become popular overnight," said Zhang Jianjun, one of the association's founders. "Without all those years of preparation, we wouldn't have been ready when the crowds came."
The association now has more than 400 members, including Zhang Jie, a local charter driver who first visited Erxian Temple while taking customers around Shanxi in 2024. Standing among centuries-old sculptures and elaborate woodwork, he realized how little he knew about the heritage of his own home province.
"I felt ashamed, but also curious," he said. He began studying traditional architecture, joined the volunteer association and now shares what he has learned with tourists.
At the Hanging Temple in Datong City, Chen Ruiyan recalled a recent road trip she and her husband had taken from Guangdong Province to Shanxi, visiting more than a dozen historic sites across the province. Inspired by films and animations featuring Shanxi's ancient architecture, they had studied traditional architectural features before setting out.
"Beyond their aesthetic impact, ancient wooden buildings have a sense of quietness and vitality," Chen said.
Beyond Shanxi, efforts to preserve historic architecture are also bringing old buildings closer to contemporary life. In Fujian Province, traditional Tulou, or earthen buildings, are being preserved and given new uses, while in Guizhou Province, more than 12,000 endangered traditional buildings have undergone emergency restoration.
China's latest five-year plan for cultural heritage calls for stronger systematic protection while making preservation efforts more accessible and beneficial to the public.
Wang Chunbo, a researcher specializing in ancient architecture, sculptures and murals in Shanxi, said the growing interest in historic architecture reflects a deeper engagement with traditional culture among younger Chinese.
"Young people are no longer satisfied with simply checking a destination off their list," Wang said. "Historic buildings are becoming cultural spaces they can experience, engage with and share."
Li Junda, a university student studying anthropology in London, traveled to Shanxi after encountering Yang's story online. What struck him was how the temple's history was still carried by the people around it.
"At the British Museum, I saw many Chinese artifacts on display, identified simply by their dynasties," Li said. "Here in Shanxi, the heritage is still 'alive,' because villagers like Yang are here to tell the stories behind it." ■

Brazil's Lula, Flavio Bolsonaro head to presidential runoff
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:10:17 CST
12:10:17 KST

BRASILIA, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Brazil will hold a presidential runoff on Oct. 25 as official results showed Sunday that no candidate secured a majority of valid votes in the first round.
According to results released by the Superior Electoral Court, with over 99 percent of the ballots counted, Flavio Bolsonaro, presidential candidate of Brazil's Liberal Party, garnered about 47 percent of valid votes while incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party came in second with about 45 percent.
Under Brazil's electoral rules, a presidential candidate must secure more than half of the valid votes to win outright in the first round. Otherwise, the two candidates with the most votes advance to a runoff.
Following the announcement of the first-round results, both candidates made remarks on Sunday night.
Bolsonaro said at a press conference in Brasilia that he was satisfied with the election result and hoped to have the opportunity to serve Brazil and its people.
"Brazil wants change. I just need a mandate to put Brazilians at the center of my government, to tackle and solve Brazil's real problems," he said.
Speaking in Sao Paulo, Lula acknowledged that he had expected to win in the first round but described the result as a lesson from voters.
He pledged to campaign on economic development and social inclusion, and urged those who abstained in the first round to vote in the runoff.
"We have a second round, and it's time for the test, time to show the true picture of Brazil," Lula said. ■

300 students take on AI, deepfake fraud challenges at BIT Mesra hackathon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:13:18 UTC
21:13:18 KST

RANCHI: More than 300 students from Birla Institute of Technology (BIT) Mesra took part in in a 24-hour hackathon focused on some of the most pressing challenges emerging from the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence, including high-precision generative AI systems, deepfake-driven insurance fraud and agentic AI applications.The event, Adrosonic Build, organised by technology company Adrosonic, has attracted 106 teams comprising around three students each. Twenty-one teams have been shortlisted for the final round, which began on October 3 and will conclude with the announcement of results on October 4.Unlike conventional coding competitions, the hackathon is centred on real-world industry problems. Participants are developing solutions for high-precision Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, AI-powered detection of synthetic identities and deepfake-based insurance claims, and agentic Statement of Values (SOV) intelligence systems for the insurance sector.Highlighting the broader objective of the initiative, Mayank, founder, CEO and MD of Adrosonic, said the idea was to bring practical industry knowledge, real-world use cases and access to technology leaders into the academic ecosystem so that students can work on problems that mirror actual business and societal challenges.Faculty members say such platforms are becoming increasingly important as employers seek graduates who can apply technical knowledge to complex situations rather than merely demonstrate theoretical understanding.
“The gap is not in knowledge. It is in applying that knowledge to real-life scenarios, which are more uncertain and complex,” said Dr Manish Kumar Pandey, head of the Digital Innovation Lab and Department of Quantitative Economics and Data Science at BIT Mesra.The hackathon is part of a wider industry-academia partnership between Adrosonic and BIT Mesra that has been underway since 2022. The collaboration led to the establishment of the Digital Innovation Lab (DIL) in 2024, with an investment of around Rs 5 crore. The facility provides students access to infrastructure and technologies spanning artificial intelligence, machine learning, large language models and data science.Over the past two years, the partnership has expanded through fellowship programmes, industry-led initiatives and mentorship opportunities, allowing students to engage with professionals and gain exposure to practical technology applications beyond the classroom.
“A hackathon gives students the opportunity to test their theories against real challenges, while building teamwork, problem-solving and execution skills,” said Kamlesh Yadav, head of innovation at Adrosonic.The event was inaugurated on October 2 in the presence of senior faculty members, including Prof Vishal H Shah, associate dean, alumni and international relations, and Dr Kishore Kumar Sinapati, along with representatives from Adrosonic. As teams race against time to build and present working solutions, the hackathon offers a glimpse into how institutes are preparing students for an AI-driven future.

Russia strikes Kyiv bridges with drones as Putin escalates attacks on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:12:30 UTC
21:12:30 KST

Russia continued its extensive assault on bridges in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv on Sunday, first-person view (FPV) drones on roads crossing the Dnipro River for a fourth straight day. The bridges connect the eastern and western parts of the city, and the attacks appear aimed at sowing panic among Ukrainians and disrupting supply routes while causing massive traffic jams. At least four air raid alerts sounded in Kyiv Sunday morning, and a Russian drone exploded on the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro as vehicles were crossing it. No injuries have been reported so far in that incident.
Russia began attacking Kyiv’s bridges on Thursday, saying it was seeking to sever supply routes to the Ukrainian military from central Ukraine to the east. On Thursday and Friday, it repeatedly attacked the city’s Southern Bridge with drones, forcing its closure and causing massive traffic jams across the Kyiv metropolitan area, home to about 3 million people.
The strikes were Russia’s first significant attacks on a major bridge in Kyiv since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. On Saturday, it also attacked the Northern Bridge, which it struck again Sunday. Ukraine has now been forced to partially or fully close three of the six bridges over the Dnipro that carry vehicle traffic, causing severe congestion across large parts of the city throughout the weekend.
Russia is attacking Kyiv’s bridges with domestically produced jet-powered drones, which it has increasingly deployed in recent weeks. The drones are fast and relatively inexpensive, and their speed makes them more difficult for Ukrainian air defense systems to intercept. Russia has used them to strike not only bridges but also residential buildings, supermarket warehouses, gas stations and server farms.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky acknowledged in an interview with Reuters on Saturday that his country is managing to intercept only about 60% of the drones and has been forced to rely heavily on its F-16 and MiG fighter jets, whose ammunition stocks are running low. He said Kyiv is urgently seeking other solutions, including upgrades to its electronic jamming capabilities. Ukraine is expected to receive its first shipment of small, inexpensive air defense missiles capable of striking the new drones in the second half of October.
Russia describes its broad assault on Ukraine in recent days as a campaign of retaliation. On Saturday, it urged diplomats and foreign nationals in Kyiv to leave the city ahead of further “mass retaliatory strikes,” which it said would target military sites in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities. Russia says it is seeking to make Ukraine pay for its repeated drone attacks in recent months against oil refineries and storage facilities deep inside Russia, strikes that caused a Russian fuel crisis over the summer, as well as attacks on warehouses belonging to Russian e-commerce giants Wildberries and Ozon, which caused significant disruptions for Russian consumers. The strikes on Russian refineries have also repeatedly drawn criticism from U.S. President Donald Trump, who argues that they are worsening the global diesel shortage.
Zelensky defies Trump: We will double attacks on oil refineries
Russia’s retaliatory attacks in recent weeks have included almost daily drone strikes. On Friday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko described the situation in the capital as “extremely dramatic,” saying Moscow was “destroying” the city by systematically targeting its infrastructure and logistics. Nevertheless, Zelensky said in his Reuters interview Saturday that the Ukrainian military would double its attacks on oil refineries in Russia.
Zelensky said Ukrainian intelligence services had obtained documents indicating that Russian President Vladimir Putin had formulated a “new doctrine” for military attacks against a far broader range of civilian targets ahead of the coming winter. According to Zelensky, the doctrine is intended to pressure Ukrainians to leave the capital and other cities. Zelensky attributed the shift to what he described as Putin’s battlefield setbacks, particularly in “Operation Vivaldi,” in which he said Ukraine recaptured about 140 square kilometers (54 square miles) of territory in the eastern Donbas region that had previously been seized by Russia.
Despite Russia’s call Saturday for diplomats to leave Kyiv, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the Ukrainian capital Sunday morning. Merz traveled to Kyiv by train and was greeted upon stepping off the train by Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. The chancellor said he had come to demonstrate his support for Ukraine because it “needs all our support in the coming weeks.” He warned: “If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will be turned against us.”
Merz, whose country is among Ukraine’s largest supporters in its war against Russia, arrived in Kyiv accompanied by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and senior business executives. He is expected to announce a new military aid package for Ukraine worth about 1 billion euros, specifically intended to help counter Russia’s jet-powered drones. He is also expected to pledge 350 million euros in assistance for Ukrainian infrastructure ahead of winter, a critical period in which Ukraine fears massive Russian attacks on its power plants, similar to those in 2025 that repeatedly left millions of people without electricity or heating in freezing temperatures.
Merz, who is deeply unpopular at home, arrives in Ukraine after stinging defeats in regional elections to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which advocates ending aid to Kyiv and normalizing relations with Moscow. Polls show that nationwide, the AfD is currently Germany’s most popular party.

Chick-fil-A wants to stay a family business even as it expands in the U.S. and abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:08:54 UTC
21:08:54 KST

With restaurants as far-flung as Singapore, Chick-fil-A has expanded far beyond its Southeastern stronghold in recent years, but CEO Andrew Cathy still wants the family-owned business to stay true to its roots.
Nearly five years ago, Cathy succeeded his father, Dan, as chief executive of the chicken chain his grandfather, S. Truett, founded. He took the reins as elevated inflation rocked the restaurant industry and a bevy of new chicken rivals looked to challenge Chick-fil-A's dominance. Since then, not much has changed — except for sluggish traffic across the industry as consumers have become more selective about their dining choices.
The challenging conditions have led to disappointing results for McDonald's, Popeyes, KFC and other restaurant competitors. While Chick-fil-A is not immune to these headaches, Cathy told CNBC that the chain's restaurants have not seen the same downturn.
"This has been a good year," the Atlanta-based Cathy said in downtown Manhattan before a planned activation to raise awareness for the chain's Shared Table hunger relief program.
"Our operators have done such a good job executing on the fundamentals and adding the hospitality to it," he added.
As a privately held business, Chick-fil-A does not report quarterly results. However, franchise disclosures reveal that the company's revenue in 2025 rose 14% to $10.3 billion, while its net income ticked up 1% to $1.05 billion. Its roughly 3,000 locations generated $23.92 billion in system sales last year, making it the third-largest U.S. restaurant by sales, trailing only McDonald's and Starbucks.
Chick-fil-A has no plans for an initial public offering or any other opportunities for outside investment. Cathy said the company plans to stick with its "calculated" and "conservative" growth.
But he may be underselling Chick-fil-A's recent expansion. It opened 179 restaurants last year and has launched in international markets like Canada, Singapore and the United Kingdom in recent years.
Staying private also has advantages, particularly as restaurant stocks have broadly struggled this year. Shares of Jersey Mike's have fallen nearly 28% since its initial public offering in July, while Dunkin' owner Inspire Brands is reportedly unlikely to go public this year unless the sector's performance improves.
"We're able to plan for the quarter century, and we don't have to plan for the quarter," Cathy said.
Balancing Chick-fil-A's past and future
During Cathy's tenure so far, Chick-fil-A has pursued bold ideas for future growth, like a $1 billion international expansion plan and Daybright, a new beverage-focused restaurant concept created by its venture arm.
But the company is trying to balance those new strategies with its existing traditions.
"I look at driving this business like driving a race car — there's a reason that the windshield's bigger than the rearview mirror," Cathy said. "It's important for the rear view to be grounded on where you are, and there are things that we think about our purpose, our mission, that won't change, but everything else we have to be able to evolve and change."
Some tenets, like staying closed on Sundays, will never change. Others, like its restaurants' signature Southern hospitality, will evolve as diners change their ordering and eating habits.
Cathy said that Chick-fil-A takes a "human plus" approach to technology in its restaurants.
"We think about all these new things into the future, about how will people want to receive food in the future?" he said. "As you think about drone delivery and all the other kind of things that could be coming, it's a fun time in the industry, to think about all the possibilities of what we can do to make a better experience for our guests."
While Chick-fil-A is exploring opportunities to use artificial intelligence behind the scenes, he said that its restaurants will not pursue AI voice ordering in its drive-thru lanes, unlike many of its industry rivals. McDonald's, for example, said at its investor day in September that it plans to test Archy, its voice AI tech, to take orders in both English and Spanish.
"From our experience, we really want that hospitality to be human to human," Cathy said. "We're not gonna substitute that interaction with technology, because we feel like that hospitality is so important to create that warm environment for consumers."
Other restaurants are also refocusing on hospitality, hoping that the extra effort from employees will encourage customers to come back. Starbucks bought around 200,000 Sharpie markers so its baristas could write friendly messages on customers' coffee cups. Burger King has redefined its restaurant manager role into a "Your Way Champion," who greets diners and fixes botched orders. And starting Monday, McDonald's will begin its "Make It Golden" training program for franchisees and employees, which focuses on hospitality as well as food quality.
Chick-fil-A's long-standing focus on service has made it the fast-food leader in customer satisfaction for more than a decade, according to the annual American Customer Satisfaction Index. That reputation can also help the chain stand out from other dining options as consumers have grown more choosy about how they spend their money. Jersey Mike's recently toppled Chick-fil-A in the 2026 study, although Chick-fil-A's score was unchanged from a year ago.
Waffles and pimento
Another enduring element of Chick-fil-A is its famously simple menu. But the chain has even been carefully expanding its offerings, typically through seasonal limited-time items like chicken and waffles or its Honey Pepper Pimento Chicken Sandwich. If a menu item is a "home run," as Cathy calls it, then Chick-fil-A might add it permanently, like its Pineapple Dragonfruit drink line.
"We're very careful about what we want to do, because we want to keep it really focused on unique Chick-fil-A items that they can only get at Chick-fil-A," Cathy said. "But we do want to bring in new flavors and profiles, and that's what we'll do with a lot of our seasonal items that we do, and we learn a lot from our customers about trying those things."
Other fast-food chains are trying to edge into Chick-fil-A's territory. In 2019, Restaurant Brands International's Popeyes sparked the "chicken sandwich wars" by releasing its own version. Chick-fil-A remains the dominant chicken chain in the U.S., with roughly a 43% market share as of 2024, according to Barclays. However, the chicken sandwich helped catapult Popeyes to the No. 2 spot, with about 11% share.
McDonald's could reignite the battle as it prepares to test hand-breaded chicken strips and sandwiches.
But Cathy said that he loves the competition.
"I'm grateful that there's competition in the chicken space, because that means we're in a good space to be," Cathy said. "Competition just makes us better .... What little details can we do to make that environment even more welcoming for customers?"
Red Wagon Ventures
Chick-fil-A has also innovated outside its restaurants.
In 2017, the company created Red Wagon Ventures, named for the vehicle Truett used to sell bottles of Coca-Cola in his first entrepreneurial gambit at age 6.
"The lion's share of our time and effort is continuing to make sure that we're getting better and better at Chick-fil-A, but we do have a small team that's working and incubating some of these new ideas and thinking about what could be some things that could help us grow into the future," Andrew Cathy said.
Some of those ventures are based in the restaurant industry. Its experimental Little Blue Menu concept served traditional Chick-fil-A menu items along with burgers, pizza and onion rings; the chain will convert its final location into a traditional Chick-fil-A next year. More recently, the subsidiary opened Daybright, which serves coffees, smoothies, juices and doughnuts — but no chicken sandwiches or waffle fries.
Another Red Wagon Ventures bet is even further from Chick-fil-A. Last year, it launched Acrew Home Professionals, a home repair and maintenance business that nodded to the Chick-fil-A ties by promoting "service with a smile," according to its website.
"I think from a family business standpoint, we've got to build off of our core competencies and look at other types of things that we can get into, so we can continue to serve customers in unique ways," Cathy said.
Cathy said that he studies family businesses, and those that have been around for more than 100 years still have to think about innovation and think ahead. At 80 years old, Chick-fil-A still has a few more decades to go before it hits the century mark.
"My grandfather was entrepreneurial to the core. He died at 93, and he opened a new business at 92 years old that he created himself," Cathy said, referring to Truett's Luau, a Hawaiian-themed restaurant concept that opened during the same month that Truett handed over the reins of the family business to his son.
In addition to starting its own brands, Red Wagon Ventures will explore acquisitions of family businesses, Cathy said. Most likely, those will be companies without a succession plan or just looking to sell — in other words, very different from Chick-fil-A.
