Scientists find a surprising clue to why the universe’s expansion doesn’t add up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:05:54 UTC
21:05:54 KST

Scientists find a surprising clue to why the universe’s expansion doesn’t add up
- Date:
- October 4, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- Tiny magnetic fields created shortly after the Big Bang may help explain the long-running disagreement over how fast the universe is expanding. Detailed simulations show that these primordial fields could have changed the formation of hydrogen in the early universe, affecting the cosmic microwave background and the expansion rate inferred from it.
- Share:
It’s well established that the universe is expanding, but there’s serious disagreement among scientists over how fast it’s happening.
Two of our best ways of measuring the cosmic expansion rate, the Hubble constant, give answers that are stubbornly at odds. This presents a major problem in modern cosmology known as the Hubble tension.
However, we wondered if an idea originally proposed to solve another cosmic mystery — the origin of cosmic magnetic fields — could help us unlock the mystery of the Hubble tension.
Our recently published research explores whether extremely weak magnetic fields left over from the earliest moments after the Big Bang might help us unpack the Hubble tension, while offering a glimpse into physics at energies far beyond anything achievable on Earth.
The Hubble constant and tension
Astronomers use the Hubble constant as a measure of how fast the universe is expanding. It is named after the American astronomer Edwin Hubble who first discovered that the universe is expanding.
There are two conceptually different approaches to measuring the Hubble constant. One is indirect, based on predictions of our cosmological model tuned to match the patterns in the cosmic microwave background, the faint afterglow of the Big Bang.
Telescopes such as the Planck Space Telescope have measured tiny fluctuations in this ancient light, predicting a Hubble constant of about 67 kilometers per second per megaparsec (km/s/Mpc). A parsec is a unit of distance used in astronomy equal to about 3.26 light years, or 30.9 trillion kilometers. A megaparsec is one million parsecs.
The second method is more direct, similar to the one used by Hubble in the 1920s when he first demonstrated that the universe is expanding.
It measures how fast distant galaxies are moving away from our home galaxy, the Milky Way, by observing the brightness of supernovae explosions in these far away galaxies.
Type Ia supernovae are known to be “standard candles” because we know that their luminosity is the same wherever they are. That means we can judge the distance to them from how dim they appear to us.
To determine their intrinsic brightness, astronomers use other standard candles, such as Cepheid stars, in the galaxies nearby. These observations, which use the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes, give a higher value of around 73 km/s/Mpc.
This difference between the two measurements is called the Hubble tension. The difference between 67 and 73 may seem small, but it is statistically highly significant. If both methods are correct, then our standard model of cosmology must be missing something important.
Where did cosmic magnetic fields come from?
Magnetic fields are everywhere in the universe. Planets and stars generate their own fields, but gaps in our understanding emerge when we attempt to explain the much larger scale magnetic fields threading galaxies and clusters, and possibly even cosmic voids.
One long-studied possibility is that magnetism first arose in the very early universe, long before the first stars or galaxies formed. These so-called primordial magnetic fields have been studied for decades, and searching for their imprints in the cosmic microwave background and other data offers a way to probe the early universe and the extreme energies that would have generated these fields.
In 2011, two of us (Karsten and Tom) pointed out that primordial magnetic fields would influence recombination — when electrons and protons first combined to form neutral hydrogen — and the universe turned from opaque to transparent. The first light able to travel freely from that moment on is what we now observe as the cosmic microwave background.
If present, primordial magnetic fields would speed up recombination by pushing and pulling on charged particles, making matter slightly clumpy. Where particles are more crowded, they are more likely to meet and form hydrogen.
Shifting the moment when the universe becomes transparent changes the size of the observed patterns in the cosmic microwave background. This effectively alters the cosmic ruler used to measure distances and, in turn, the value of the Hubble constant inferred from the model, helping to ease the Hubble tension. Two of us (Karsten and Levon) demonstrated this effect in 2020 using a simplified model of recombination.
A breakthrough: What we found
In our new paper, we used the first full three-dimensional simulations of the primordial plasma with magnetic fields embedded in it, tracking how hydrogen forms.
We used the hydrogen formation history found through these simulations to compute predictions for how cosmic microwave background should appear if there were primordial magnetic fields, and tested these predictions against observations of the background.
The cosmic microwave background is extraordinarily sensitive to changes in recombination. If primordial magnetic fields altered it in a way that disagreed with observations, the idea could be ruled out. Instead, the data showed that our proposal remains viable.
Across multiple combinations of datasets, we find a consistent, mild preference for primordial magnetic fields, ranging from about 1.5 to three standard deviations. This is not yet a discovery, but a meaningful hint that they exist.
Equally important, the field strengths favored by the data, about five to 10 pico-Gauss today, are close to what would be needed for galaxy and cluster magnetic fields to originate from primordial seeds alone. A pico-Gauss is a unit used to measure the strength of magnetic fields.
Aside from helping ease the Hubble tension, if primordial magnetic fields are confirmed, they would open a new window into how the universe was when it was only split seconds old, perhaps offering a glimpse into important events such as the Big Bang itself.
Our results show that the proposal survives the most detailed test available today and provides clear targets for future observations. Over the next several years, we will learn whether tiny magnetic fields from the dawn of time helped shape the universe we see today and whether they hold the key to resolving the Hubble tension.

Hong Kong woman loses HK$21.5 million in cryptocurrency scam
Clerk, 60, was duped by a fraudster posing as an investment expert she met online
A 60-year-old Hong Kong woman has lost more than HK$21 million (US$2.7 million) in a cryptocurrency scam after a fraudster posing as an investment expert she met online duped her.
The clerk reported the case to police on Saturday, saying she had befriended an individual claiming to be an investment specialist on “Baby Kingdom”, a popular online parenting forum and community website, on March 15 this year, a source said.
The fraudster duped her into investing on a fake cryptocurrency platform that promised high returns. Believing the pitch, she remitted HK$19 million to the fake website.
Subsequently, an accomplice posing as a platform compliance officer contacted her, claiming that her account had been involved in money laundering and demanding funds to clear her name.
Acting on the instructions, the victim transferred an additional HK$1.2 million.

West Bank: Palestinians ‘harassed’ by settlers’ increasing use of drones
Palestinians and activists report an increased use of drones in the occupied West Bank, particularly by the army and settlers, to whom the government supplies the drones directly. The drones are used to intimidate, monitor, demolish and make daily life unbearable.
Issued on:
Four men strike a pose, each holding a drone and smiling at the camera. This photo was posted on X on September 3, 2026 by Israeli settler Elisha Yered, a member of the Frontline Hills Administration, a settler organisation in the occupied West Bank whose aim is to establish and strengthen illegal settlements. In the caption, he claims to have distributed the drones to four settlements in the West Bank – a territory occupied by Israel since 1967.
“Drones are an essential tool on the ground: both for monitoring attacks and arson in real time, and for documenting events and refuting blood libel allegations,” he writes. He adds: “And above all: a huge thank you to the Jewish people who contributed to the purchase of this security equipment and who have enabled us to support our activists.”

Elisha Yered is also a member of the “Hilltop Youth”, a movement of young settlers who regularly commit acts of violence against Palestinians and their villages in the occupied West Bank. He is accused of being part of a group of armed settlers who killed a 19-year-old Palestinian, Qusai Jammal Mi’tan, in August 2023 in the Palestinian village of Burqa. He has been under European sanctions since April 2024.
To display this content from , you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
'They started sending drones over us at night, during the day, in the morning – at any time'
The use of drones by the Frontline Hills group is symptomatic of a policy of increasingly widespread use of these devices by various actors in the occupied West Bank. The drones are sent to fly over Palestinian homes and crops.
This harassment is all too familiar to Abdel (an alias), a Bedouin cattle farmer who lives near Jericho, northwest of the Dead Sea. He says he and his family were forced to leave their village of Shalal al-Auja in January 2026 following numerous attacks by settlers.
He attests that the same settlers followed them to their new home and are prolonging their suffering. He and his wife sent us several videos of drones flying overhead, usually late in the evening. He says intimidation attempts occur almost daily:
 "I was displaced from Shalal al-Auja; my family and I settled 10 kilometres away. Two and a half months after I arrived, they [the settlers] set up an outpost about 500 metres from my home. This outpost has nothing; it simply launches drones to harass people.
After that, they started sending drones over us at night, during the day, in the morning, at any time…
At first, it was every day, but recently it’s been two or three days a week.
Every time a car drives into your property, or if you go out to feed the sheep or do anything else, they immediately send a drone after you.
And then, one day, they came right up to my house. They were the same settlers who had driven me out of my first home in Shalal al-Auja. They followed me all the way home and beat me up in my new house. They attacked me right in the heart of my home and beat me up."

'Drones are used to monitor whether new buildings are constructed'
Shai Gortler is a research associate at the Centre for Humanities Research at the University of the Western Cape in Cape Town. He specialises in surveillance, incarceration and colonisation. Shai states that four entities use drones in the occupied West Bank, for various reasons:
 "The first group are the settlers. They use drones to intimidate and gather information.
Next, there are the regional councils [government bodies in the occupied West Bank comprising several illegal settlements] which monitor new construction [by Palestinians].
The third group consists of NGOs. The most significant is Regavim, which means ‘clods of earth’ in Hebrew [an Israeli NGO subject to European sanctions, co-founded by the Israeli Finance Minister, the Jewish supremacist Bezalel Smotrich]. It uses drones for the same reasons as the regional councils: to monitor the presence of new constructions. It then calls on the Civil Administration [an Israeli government body in the occupied West Bank] to have them demolished.
Finally, the last group is the Israeli army, which uses its drones for surveillance and demolition.
There is one final major use that has been documented in the West Bank, which involves scaring away Palestinians’ flocks of sheep or goats.”
'They even infringe on your privacy, right inside your own home.'
Faris (an alias) is a farmer in the village of Burqa in the Ramallah Governorate. According to the NGO Peace Now, Burqa is situated near 12 Israeli settlements. Faris says he has witnessed drones flying over the area to scatter the sheep.
 “Some shepherds who were grazing their sheep on the outskirts of the village have encountered drones. The settlers use drones to scare the sheep away: they fly them very close to the flock and the noise disturbs the animals immensely, causing them to scatter in all directions. The aim is notably to create a situation that makes it easier to steal the sheep.
We had already noticed the presence of drones after October 7, 2023, but not with this frequency. Those who used them most were mainly the army or the police.
The problem with drones is serious. They even infringe on your privacy, right inside your own home. Sometimes, you only spot the drone when it’s already close to your window.
We’ve gone from seeing them once a month, or even less frequently, to an almost constant presence. The drones hardly ever seem to leave the village skies, day or night.”

 “Generally speaking, when settlers want to launch an attack or carry out a robbery without being spotted by the locals — who might try to stop them — they send up a drone. The drone can then quietly survey the whole area, identifying the routes they can use to enter and those they can use to leave. In this way, they map out their itinerary and plan their operation.”

Government support
Since its formation in 2022, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has accelerated the establishment of new settlements in the occupied West Bank, and has approved the creation of 103 of them.
In 2026, the Israeli government allocated 50 million shekels (more than €14 million) to fund “security equipment”, including drones, and infrastructure for outposts and illegal settlements in the West Bank.
Nonetheless, the government and the Ministry of Settlement and National Missions do not confine themselves to providing financial and legislative support: they personally deliver supplies to the colonies and take part in “security equipment” handover ceremonies.

The previous year, in July 2025, the Benyamin Regional Council, which comprises 17 illegal settlements in the West Bank, had welcomed the latest distribution of equipment, which it claimed included 20 off-road vehicles, night-vision devices and drones.
In its report “The Elimination Project”, B’Tselem, an Israeli organisation fighting for Palestinian rights, notes that the Ministry of Settlements had allocated 20 million shekels (equivalent to over €5 million) to regional councils in the West Bank so that they could monitor the construction of new Palestinian buildings. These councils could therefore apply to the Ministry for funds to purchase surveillance equipment and aerial photography, including drones. The Israeli army’s use of drones in the West Bank has also been documented since that same year.
Israeli settlements and outposts in the West Bank are considered illegal by the United Nations. In March of 2026, the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights expressed concern about “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank following “the intensification of attacks, the systematic destruction of entire neighbourhoods, the denial of humanitarian aid and forced transfers”. New underground Tainan Station receives approval to open
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:00:47 UTC
21:00:47 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Passengers will begin using the new underground Tainan Station on Oct. 17, a day earlier than planned.
The Railway Bureau announced the date Sunday after the Ministry of Transportation and Communications approved operations, per UDN. Seven issues from Sept. 19–20 inspections were addressed, covering fire safety signage, track checks, central monitoring, station and platform facilities and equipment, electromechanical systems, and independent verification and validation.
The station’s four tracks and two island platforms will enter service with the first phase of the 8.23-kilometer railway undergrounding project.
The bureau plans to reduce the railway’s longstanding disruption to road traffic by gradually removing 23 underpasses, overpasses, and railroad crossings, per CNA.
Twelve services face cancellations or shorter routes, including 10 local trains and two reserved-seat services. One track will close at 10 p.m. on Oct. 16, followed by a full closure from 11 p.m. until 6 a.m. on Oct. 17.
Replacement buses will link Tainan with Shalun on the Shalun Line and Shanhua with Baoan on the Western Trunk Line. Staff will guide passengers at stations, and travelers should check station notices or Taiwan Railways Corp.’s website and allow extra transfer time.

Virtual reality can induce mystical experiences, new study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:00:33 UTC
21:00:33 KST

Virtual reality headsets might offer a reliable way to induce profound feelings of unity and awe typically associated with deep spiritual practices or psychedelics. A recent experiment found that viewing both fantastical imagery and realistic meditation exercises through virtual reality led many people to report complete mystical experiences, whereas viewing the exact same exercises on a standard computer screen did not. The findings were published in the journal Psychology of Consciousness: Theory, Research, and Practice.
Psychologists define a mystical experience as a profound mental event characterized by a sense of deep connection with the universe, an altered perception of time and space, and intense positive emotions. Early psychological theorists proposed that these experiences are defined by their ineffability, meaning they defy expression in standard language. Later researchers emphasized a sense of nonduality, a state where the ordinary sense of oneself as an independently conscious being dissolves. In this state, personal boundaries blur and the individual feels a sense of oneness with all of existence.
While these profound states can occur spontaneously in daily life, researchers have historically struggled to trigger them reliably in laboratory settings using psychological methods alone. Only a small fraction of people typically achieve a complete mystical state through standard meditation, fasting, or hypnosis. Modern studies have heavily relied on psychedelic substances to reliably evoke these states. Finding non-pharmacological methods to trigger self-transcendent experiences remains an ongoing challenge for scientists studying human consciousness.
In recent years, scientists have found that immersive virtual reality can sometimes trigger these profound states at higher rates than traditional psychological methods. Western University psychologists Rebekka Miller, Tallulah Nyland, and Paul Frewen wanted to know what specific types of digital environments are best suited to create these feelings. They aimed to test whether virtual reality required highly imaginative, fantastical elements to trigger mystical states, or if simply practicing a standard breathing meditation in a realistic virtual nature setting would work just as well.
The research team also wanted to move beyond relying solely on subjective surveys. Previous studies on virtual reality and mysticism only asked participants how they felt after the simulation ended. To gain a deeper understanding of how the body reacts to these immersive environments, the investigators decided to measure the physical brain and body changes that happen during these digital encounters. This physiological data could help cross-validate the self-reported emotional outcomes.
The researchers recruited 80 young adults and divided them into two groups. Both groups viewed their respective experiences using a program called Nature Treks: Together, which simulates interactive, three-dimensional natural environments like islands and underwater landscapes. Within this digital world, users appear as bodiless spirits wearing tribal masks and gloves, floating through the space. The software allows users to relax and explore lush vegetation, fossilized rocks, and ocean life.
One group listened to a guided imagery script describing a fantastical encounter. During the first five minutes, this script guided users through normal daytime activities like walking down a path. In the second half, the narration shifted to nighttime and introduced surreal elements, such as watching animal spirits emerge from a campfire and viewing a black hole in the sky. The other group listened to a standard breath-focused guided meditation, which replaced the magical elements with a mindfulness practice focusing on internal physical sensations.
To see how the delivery method affected the participants, the researchers had everyone complete their assigned exercise twice in a counterbalanced order. Participants experienced the simulation once while wearing a fully immersive virtual reality headset, which allowed them to turn their heads and look around the environment. They also completed the exact same audio script and visual environment while watching it on a standard, flat computer monitor, keeping their eyes open and facing forward.
While the participants underwent the exercises, the researchers recorded their brain waves using wearable sensors placed on the forehead and behind the ears. This electroencephalography equipment measures the electrical activity of the central nervous system. The team also tracked heart rates and heart rate variability using chest straps. After each viewing, the participants answered extensive survey questions about their emotional states, their sense of being present in the digital environment, and the intensity of any mystical feelings.
The researchers found that the viewing format drastically changed how people responded to the exercises. Among the participants who used the virtual reality headset, 28 percent of the guided imagery group and 18 percent of the guided meditation group reported having a complete mystical experience. To meet this threshold, participants had to score at least 60 percent of the maximum possible score on each of four dimensions: feelings of unity, transcendence of time and space, intense positive mood, and ineffability. In contrast, not a single participant achieved a complete mystical experience when viewing the exact same environments on a standard computer monitor.
The virtual reality format also produced much higher ratings for specific positive emotions. Participants reported stronger feelings of awe, serenity, interest, and the perception of beauty while wearing the headsets. They also felt a much stronger sense of being physically and temporally present inside the digital world. Conversely, the standard flat-screen viewing format was associated with higher ratings of boredom and fatigue, indicating that the two-dimensional screen failed to captivate the participants’ attention in the same way.
The physical measurements aligned with the survey responses, showing a physiological shift when participants entered the immersive environment. When participants used the virtual reality headsets, their brain wave activity increased across all measured frequencies, including theta, alpha, beta, and gamma waves. This elevated electrical activity suggests a heightened state of cognitive and emotional engagement. The standard monitor viewing resulted in much lower brain wave amplitudes across the board.
The heart rate data revealed a similar pattern of heightened physiological arousal. During the second half of the virtual reality exercises, participants experienced higher overall heart rates and lower heart rate variability compared to the standard monitor viewing. A decrease in heart rate variability often indicates that the nervous system is highly stimulated or engaged by external events. These physical changes indicate that the immersive digital world provoked a stronger bodily response than the flat screen.
When comparing the fantastical imagery to the realistic meditation, the researchers found remarkably few differences. Participants in virtual reality reported similar levels of mystical feelings and positive emotions regardless of whether they were imagining a magical encounter or simply focusing on their breath. The brain wave and heart rate data during the virtual reality sessions were also nearly identical between the two groups. It appears that the immersive nature of the technology itself drives the profound feelings, rather than the specific presence of magic or fantasy.
One detail to keep in mind is that the meditation group still rated their supposedly realistic virtual environment as highly dreamlike and surreal. Floating as a bodiless spirit in a pristine digital landscape might be so inherently unusual that it blurs the line between fantasy and reality. This overlap could explain why the realistic meditation script produced results so similar to the fantastical imagery script. The basic visual beauty of the digital world might be powerful enough to trigger awe on its own.
The study’s physical measurements also come with technical caveats. Because the virtual reality format allowed participants to move their heads and bodies to look around, this physical movement might have introduced electrical noise into the sensor data. In the standard monitor condition, participants remained seated and were instructed to look directly at the screen. Future studies will need to account for this physical movement to ensure that the brain wave and heart rate differences are entirely due to the psychological experience rather than simple muscle activity.
Finally, having participants complete the identical scripted exercises twice might have diluted the overall intensity of their emotional responses. The extent to which an experience feels miraculous or beyond words typically decreases once a person knows exactly what to expect. Researchers will need to explore how people respond to these environments upon their very first viewing to capture the full potential of digital mysticism. Testing these experiences on diverse populations with different spiritual backgrounds could also reveal how cultural expectations shape these digital encounters.
The study, “Mystical experiences in virtual reality 2: Fantasy versus realism and psychophysiological correlates,” was authored by Rebekka Miller, Tallulah Nyland, and Paul Frewen. The research was supervised by Frewen at Western University.

Iran secures third consecutive world title with five golds at IOAA 2026

Unknown Publisher

Iran secures third consecutive world title with five golds at IOAA 2026
TEHRAN – Iran’s national Astronomy and Astrophysics Olympiad team has been crowned world champion for the third consecutive year after winning five gold medals at the 19th International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics (IOAA 2026).
Iranian students secured five gold medals at the international competition, which was held in Hanoi, Vietnam, from September 25 to October 5, 2026.
More than 320 students from over 66 countries took part in this year’s Olympiad. Sarina Elmpour, Mohammad-Hossein Hosseini, Hirbod Foudazi, Hossein Masoumi, and Arshia Mirshamsi-Kakhaki won gold medals for Iran.
IOAA is an annual competition in astronomy and astrophysics for high school students worldwide to strengthen ties between different nations and promote the exchange of knowledge.
The main goal of the IOAA is to promote the growing interest in astronomy and related STEM subjects, especially through the general education of young people, and to enhance the development of international contacts among different countries in promoting astronomy and astrophysics in schools.
It is expected that, through events like the IOAA, brighter high-school students will be eager to study astronomy at the university level to become the next generation of astronomy and astrophysics professionals.
The IOAA is one of the twelve International Science Olympiads. Established in 2006 by five nations—Iran, Thailand, Indonesia, China, and Poland—the IOAA was created with a shared vision: to inspire the next generation of astronomers, astrophysicists, and space enthusiasts, while fostering international friendship through scientific collaboration.
The Iranian students grabbed five gold medals at the 18th IOAA, marking the country’s second consecutive world championship.
The event was held from August 11 to 21, 2025, in Mumbai, India, attracting over 300 high school students from 64 countries.
The 17th IOAA was held from August 17 to 27, 2024, in Vassouras, state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
Over 250 students from 57 countries participated in the event; Iranian students won five gold medals, ranking first globally.
In 2023, Iranian students grabbed three gold medals and two silver medals, ranking third in the 16th IOAA.
Iran ranked first in the world in the 15th IOAA 2022, held in Georgia from August 14 to 22.
The Iranian team won first place in the tournament by winning 9 gold medals and 1 silver medal. 250 students from 45 countries participated in this competition.
In IOAA 2021, the Iranian delegation won 2 gold medals, 5 silver medals, 2 bronze medals, and an honorary diploma at the competition, held in Colombia on November 14-21.

How to make the perfect zuppa di cozze – recipe | Felicity Cloake's How to make the perfect …
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:00:27 UTC
21:00:27 KST

Abundant, good value and ready in minutes, mussels are one of my favourite seafoods, but when it comes to preparing them, I rarely look farther than northern France. Italians, of course, also eat mussels, and this tomato-rich recipe is a particular favourite in the south – Neapolitans traditionally tuck into zuppa di cozze on Maundy Thursday but it’s found on menus all year round. With its bold flavours and oily, garlicky sauce, it’s a great alternative to creamy moules marinières, and similarly needs no accompaniment but a hunk of bread to make a meal, though chips, of course, are rarely unwelcome.
The mussels
There’s not much to say about the main ingredient, except to bemoan the increasing difficulty in getting hold of live mussels due to the disappearance of so many fresh fish vendors, and the subsequent closure of supermarket fish counters (another rant for another day). Any remaining fishmongers should have British mussels, or they can easily be bought online. Don’t wash them until you’re ready to cook, when you should dump them in the sink and sort through them, discarding any with broken shells or that don’t close when you give them a sharp tap. Rinse with cold water; most mussels on the market are farmed, and rope-grown, so should be pretty clean, and I’ve never seen the point of scrubbing away at barnacles for hours when you’re not going to be eating the shells anyway (though please do enlighten me as to why I should bother). Remove any remaining trailing beards, though – I do have some standards!
The Silver Spoon dry-fries the mussels, then shells them to add to the soup later, while the Giallo Zafferano website steams them in garlicky oil and a little white wine, then removes them from the pot to be returned to the finished soup. It makes more sense to me to eat them as freshly cooked as possible – as Elizabeth David cautions in Italian Food, these “final operations must be carried out only immediately before serving”. Not only does this leave less chance of the shellfish overcooking, but necessarily ensures that every last drop of that delicious mussel liquor makes it into the sauce; tipping it back and forth, as in the Zafferano recipe, risks sacrificing a little, and when there’s not a lot to start with, that’s a gamble I’m not prepared to take.
Zafferano, whose recipe is specifically Neapolitan, includes octopus, squid and prawns alongside the mussels. Delicious as all those things are, we find the squid and prawns are overcooked and rubbery once they’ve been fried and then simmered in tomato sauce for 15 minutes. If you’d like to include them, I’d fry them briefly first, then return them to the pan right at the end (and buy the octopus ready-cooked, if you can).
The base
David and the Silver Spoon are the only ones to use onions as the base of their dishes, with the former also including celery. More common is garlic in more or less generous amounts – Zafferano simply uses it to flavour the oil, while Marcella Hazan, perhaps reflecting the more Italian-American milieu in which she was writing The Essentials of Classic Italian Cuisine, sticks in a whole teaspoon and a half of the stuff, finely minced. I like the fiery flavour, especially alongside the chilli she also includes, plus this feels like a dish that should pack a punch.
And that also applies when it comes to the tomatoes. Hazan uses tinned, and reduces them to a jammy, oily sauce before adding the bivalves, a similar approach to David, but the latter’s more watery fresh fruit (and seeded summer san marzano plum tomatoes are about as far from watery as you’re likely to get) yields a lighter, fresher flavour. My favourites, however, are the cherry tomatoes suggested by Benedetta Rossi of the Fatto di Casa da Benedetta website, because they strike a good balance between the intensity of the tinned variety and the zingy acidity of plum tomatoes. My recipe uses a few more than Rossi’s, though, because we find her version a bit light on sauce, and cooks them for a little longer, in homage to Hazan.
The Silver Spoon flavours the base with saffron, Hazan chilli and parsley (Rossi adds the stalks, reserving the leaves as a garnish), and David suggests fresh marjoram, thyme or basil. I really like the echoes of Mediterranean French fish soups that the saffron brings with it, but my testers are ambivalent as to its merits, so I’ll leave that one up to you. Herbs, I think, are better used on top; not only do they look pretty against the glossy black shells and vivid sauce, but the peppery flavour of the parsley gets lost in the heat.
The liquid
Not all recipes add extra liquid – the mussels give off enough to make a sauce, but it’s fairly scanty, so it makes sense to dilute it a little so everyone gets a decent spoonful alongside the shells. Wine is popular, used by David (who also adds a little water), Zafferano and Edinburgh’s Contini, while the Silver Spoon, whose recipe is more of a mussel soup garnished with a few actual bivalves than a pot of mussels, goes for fish stock. If you don’t drink, then this, with a spritz of lemon juice, is a decent substitute, but the zesty acidity of a crisp white is the ideal, not least because you can then drink it as an accompaniment.
Serving suggestion
Peppery parsley looks good, and tastes great, according to those who like it better than I do (if you share my aversion, you might like to experiment with mint, thyme or basil), and the garlicky toasts that pop up in the Silver Spoon, Hazan and Zafferano’s recipes are the perfect accompaniment, whether you want to spoon the mussels on top, so the bread soaks up their liquid, or serve it on the side to mop up the end of the sauce.
Perfect zuppa di cozze
Prep 10 min
Cook 15 min
Serves 2
2 garlic cloves
500g cherry tomatoes
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, plus extra to serve
1 pinch dried chilli flakes (optional)
1 pinch saffron (optional)
Salt
800g live mussels
2 tbsp white wine, or dry vermouth or fish stock
2 thick slices crusty bread
1 small bunch flat-leaf parsley, to serve
Finely chop one and a half cloves of garlic. Cut the tomatoes in half. Heat the oil on a medium flame in a saucepan large enough eventually to hold all the mussels, then fry the garlic and chilli, if using, until pale golden.
Stir in the tomatoes, saffron, if using, and a pinch of salt, then turn down the heat a little and cook until soft and pulpy. You can prepare the dish ahead up to this point if needed.
For this recipe, I’m assuming you’ve bought your mussels; should you have gathered them yourself, however, you’ll need to purge them in salt water overnight first, to get rid of any grit (have a look online for specific instructions).
Either way, just before cooking, tip the mussels into a large colander and give them a good rinse with cold water. Sort through them, discarding any with broken shells or that don’t close when given a sharp tap (unless you can see the creature moving within). Scrub off any dirty patches (and barnacles, if you wish), and give any trailing beards (the weedy bits hanging out of the side of the shell) a sharp tug to pull them off.
Add the wine to the pan, turn up the heat, then tip in the mussels. Cover and leave to cook, shaking the pan occasionally, for five to eight minutes, until most of them have opened (discard any that do not).
Meanwhile, grill or toast the bread, then rub it with the remaining half-clove of raw garlic and drizzle with oil. Finely chop the parsley.
Divide the bread between serving bowls, then use a slotted spoon to scoop out the mussels and arrange on top (or serve the bread on the side). Bring the liquid back to a simmer, reduce slightly, taste for seasoning and ladle on top of the mussels. Sprinkle with parsley and devour immediately.
- Zuppa di cozze – how do you like yours, and can anyone explain the many regional variations that surely exist on Italy’s extensive coastline? And which other mussel recipes would you recommend to anyone wanting an alternative to marinières?
- The Guardian aims to publish recipes for sustainable seafood. Check ratings in your region: UK; Australia; US.

Manhattan ‘mole’ mystery: rumors of lost gold spur clandestine excursions into New York sewers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:00:26 UTC
21:00:26 KST

There’s been one thing in particular that has been intriguing New Yorkers this summer: the existence, and whereabouts, of so-called “mole people” – a mysterious group of individuals who spend at least some of their time wading about in the city’s sewers.
New Yorkers learned a bit more about the phenomenon this week, when two men were caught red – or perhaps another color – handed, after allegedly emerging from a tunnel in Manhattan. Their arrests have shed some light on a slew of instances where people have been witnessed lifting manhole covers and clambering underground.
Samuel Reveron and Kevin Rodriguez were apprehended in Queens after police tracked them down through video footage. The pair were allegedly spotted entering the sewers with four other people, who have yet to be identified.
Both were charged with criminal trespassing, but it is the reason the men gave for their adventure that has proved particularly fascinating.
“We go into the sewer and look for valuables that get stuck in the storm drains and sewers, gold, anything of value,” Reveron, 25, reportedly told police after his arrest.
The gang’s quest fits an apparently misguided pattern of people thinking New York’s sewers are paved with gold. Last year, three men were arrested after they were allegedly seen emerging from a sewer in Brooklyn, one of them telling police: “The reason we went down there is that people lose their gold down there. We got to get it and sell it to make money.”
Despite that vaulting ambition, there is little evidence that sewer foraging is a lucrative trade. Steve Duncan, a former urban explorer who has spent a lot of time in New York’s sewers and subway tunnels, told the New York Times that in more than 100 sewer trips, the most valuable thing he found was an expired credit card.
Still, the penchant for sewer exploration continues. In May this year there were three separate reported incidents of people climbing down into sewers, two of which were captured on video. In footage of the first incident, three people, wearing dungaree-style hip waders and carrying flashlights, walk into the middle of the road in Astoria, Queens. They haul a circular man cover aside, and descend into the darkness of the sewer.
“Three random guys walking around in a strange suit. Open the sewer, go in like the Ninja Turtles,” eyewitness Aki Jakupovic told NBC New York at the time.
Jakupovic isn’t the first to make the comparison to the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, a fictional group of human-turtle hybrids who, across a comic book, cartoon TV show and feature film, are depicted as living in the sewers. Per canon, the turtles mutated into humanoids after being exposed to a toxic green goo. They are subsequently trained in martial arts by a large rat.
The turtles, who are brothers, fight crime, frequently crossing paths with a man called Shredder and his accomplices Bebop, who is a mutant warthog, and Rocksteady, who is a sort of rhino. They also encounter Krang, an alien blob-thing who lives in a robot.
While there appears to have been an increase in sewer incidents this year, this isn’t a new phenomenon. In 2015, a trainee at the New York department of environmental protection was arrested after being caught in the sewers, and last year three men were arrested after entering the sewer system in Brooklyn, allegedly in an attempt to find gold.
“God knows what they were looking for. I know for damn sure I wouldn’t be crawling through the sewers of New York, but these three were evidently looking for something,” the then New York police commissioner, Bill Bratton, told journalists at the time.
Reveron and Rodriguez’s September sojourn might have been written off as a bit of a hoot, but police were seemingly extra interested because it coincided with world leaders gathering at the UN, some of them staying at swanky hotels close to where the two men went underground.
Brian Kennedy, an attorney for Reveron, dismissed those concerns when he spoke to NBC News.
“It seems like not much of a case,” Kennedy told NBC News. “I understand that it is strange that it’s alleged he went [into the sewer]. But there’s no connection to the UN or the appearance of Netanyahu or any other kind of nefarious scheme.”
It’s both strange and dangerous, Rob Wolejsza, a spokesperson for New York’s department of environmental protection, previously told the Guardian. Wolejsza said it was “both illegal and extremely dangerous” to go into the sewers, adding: “Sewers can contain numerous hazards, including noxious and potentially deadly gases, unstable surfaces, flooding risks and confined spaces. For these reasons, members of the public should never enter a pipe, drain, catch basin, manhole or outfall.”
Whether people will listen remains to be seen. On the same day Reveron and Rodriguez were arrested, another three men were spotted climbing out of a sewer at 4.30am in Bensonhurst, south Brooklyn.
ABC7NY reported that police found a shovel in the sewer, but the men got away.

‘He felt heard’: How a film brought a UN report to life in Xochimilco
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

‘He felt heard’: How a film brought a UN report to life in Xochimilco
A documentary drawn from United Nations University research was screened at the COP30 climate conference and film festivals across Europe. Its most important journey, though, was the one back to the Mexico City canals where it was filmed.
Scientific reports rarely leave the shelf. Sometimes, though, the research itself becomes a real story that sparks conversations far beyond academia.
That is what happened in Xochimilco, in Mexico City.
In 2025, the UN University Institute for Environment and Human Security (UNU-EHS) published a report on interconnected risks.
It asked why societies struggle to make the changes needed to tackle climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution. One conclusion: societies must think beyond the short term and weigh the wellbeing of future generations.
To bring that idea to life, the researchers turned to Xochimilco. For centuries, its chinamperos have cultivated chinampas – fertile plots built on wetlands that produce food while preserving knowledge handed down through generations.
Today that living heritage faces urbanization, environmental degradation, climate change and a shifting relationship between young people and the land.
The result was a documentary, Chinamperos: Preserving Ancestral Farming Practices in Mexico City, directed by Mexican filmmaker Rodrigo Jardón Galeana and shot in San Gregorio Atlapulco.
The aim was simple – take a scientific report off the page and show what it means for people at the centre of it in real terms.
A call that reverberated
Mariana Páez, one of those featured, shared the film on social media expecting family, friends and neighbours to watch. Instead, she also heard from people she had not spoken to in years.
Among them were Karen Ramírez and Abel Bastida, former schoolmates on different career paths who shared a fascination with the place where they grew up. A video call planned for 20 or 30 minutes ran to nearly two hours – farming, food, traditions, water, the problems they saw around them.
“We couldn’t stop talking,” Ms. Páez recalls.
That conversation led the three to found the Permanent Seminar on Xochimilco Studies, or SEPEX, to open up dialogue about the territory and its culture. A film meant to communicate research had sparked a local conversation nobody had seen coming.
Heard at last
The documentary has since been screened at COP30 in Brazil and at festivals in Spain, Greece, Türkiye and the Czech Republic. Our colleagues in the UN News Spanish team also told the chinamperos’ story in April 2025.
For Ms. Páez, though, the most important effects were closer to home. In her own family, the film brought greater recognition to work and Indigenous knowledge that had not always been valued like other professions.
One of those featured, chinampero Samuel Avelino, died earlier this year. Ms. Páez later discovered that a screenshot of the UN News story carrying his testimony was among the last things he shared on Facebook.
“He felt heard,” she says.
That matters, she explains, because the everyday lives of chinamperos rarely reach beyond their own circles. Outsiders rarely ask what a day working the land is like.
Coming home
More than a year on, the film returned to Mexico. SEPEX helped organize a visit to Xochimilco for representatives of the University and the UN in Mexico, and screenings followed at the National Centre for the Arts and the Metropolitan Autonomous University.
Residents, researchers, students, UN staff and city officials came together. The aim was not just to show a film, but to let the community speak directly to researchers and decision makers.
“Xochimilco is a living territory,” said Allegra Baiocchi, the UN Resident Coordinator in Mexico – a place where biodiversity, water management, climate adaptation, food security and ancestral knowledge all converge.
For Shen Xiaomeng, Vice-Rector of the University in Europe and Director of UNU-EHS, the trip was a chance to give something back.
Meeting chinampero Eric Enríquez, she noted the pride with which he spoke about his work. Farmers’ survival, she said, depends on how much society values them – but everyone else depends on those who grow our food.
A window, not a solution
Ms. Ramírez sees the film not as a solution but as a “window”. It’s a way of looking at what may lie ahead before deciding what to do. She wants it screened in more neighbourhoods and public spaces across Xochimilco, with children joining the conversations.
Mr. Bastida stresses that Xochimilco is not simply a landscape in need of preservation. People live there, with different needs and different visions of its future.
The documentary does not resolve those differences. But it has done something less visible, and perhaps necessary before any solution can emerge: created a place where people can meet on common ground and talk about them.

Beyond the Moon: Space Week around the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Beyond the Moon: Space Week around the world
Right after the Soviet Union launched Sputnik in 1957, UNOOSA, the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs, was established and has since been monitoring developments across more than 77 successful lunar missions and other journeys while also taking a lead role in the annual World Space Week, which runs from 4 to 10 October.
What you need to know
- This year’s theme, Rocket revolution, focuses on the rapid transformation of how we reach space – now expanding through commercial launch providers, reusable rockets, university teams, and other innovators
- More than 50,000 events are planned in more than 100 countries
- The week represents the world’s largest space event
What’s the UN doing in space?
Early this year, the UN hosted four astronauts who just returned from outer space, carrying out the farthest human spaceflight in history when they travelled beyond the far side of the Moon.
But, the UN has been involved in space affairs for decades. The General Assembly created a committee in 1959 to govern the exploration and use of space for the benefit of all – focused around peace, security and development.
Instrumental in creating the five treaties and principles governing outer space, the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) has mandated duties that include keeping pace with rapid technological advances.
Since then, space science and technology and their applications are increasingly being used to support a wide range of UN activities. At least 25 UN entities use them.
Here are some examples:
Cosmic crops: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) sent seeds to the International Space Station in November 2022 to test how harsh space conditions alter plant genetics for climate resilience on Earth
Satellite tele-medicine: The World Health Organization (WHO) collaborated with UNOOSA to apply space science and satellite technology to help solve global health challenges
Space junk: The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) helps to promote long-term sustainability in Earth’s orbit given the 130 million pieces of debris in circulation – from satellite fragments to abandoned spacecraft
Learn more about World Space Week here.
What’s it like being in outer space?
“Like entering a dream state,” one astronaut recalled.
In 1990, 17 astronauts shared their out-of-this-world experiences in Our Planet Earth, a timeless documentary produced for the UN by Lemle Pictures, Inc. with cooperation of the Association for Space Explorers and the Canadian International Development Agency.
“It was the greatest feeling I ever had in my entire life,” said one astronaut. “Seeing the black sky and the bright sun. This is really impossible, but I saw it.”
Another said he tried clumsily manoeuvring in a state of weightlessness, finding himself awkwardly jammed against a window when he was awestruck by both the view and the magnificence of Earth.
One summed up a commonly shared feeling among the space travellers.
“I felt a love for all the inhabitants of the Earth,” he said. “I just wanted to love them all.”

The unannounced visit, marked by the sound of air sirens and explosions, came on Sunday to underscore Germany’s support for the nation at a time when Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities are increasing.
In a written statement, Merz said he “travelled to Kyiv today because Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks”.
“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said.
Merz and Zelenskyy met at the National Academy of Sciences, which was struck by a Russian drone on September 28.

Merz was accompanied by his economy minister, as well as executives from several large German companies, such as Siemens Energy and Diehl Defence.
Ukraine and Germany are also expected to finalise a deal to produce drones and other weapons together that can travel more than 600 miles (965.6km) in an effort to strike deeper into Russia.
Germany has been one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters. In April, the two countries signed a military pact worth more than $4bn. On Sunday, a $1.1bn military aid package is set to be announced, alongside $394m to repair damage to Ukraine’s energy sector.
Merz’s visit comes a day after Russia warned foreign diplomats and nationals to leave the capital to avoid getting hurt.

Russia’s all-out war on Ukraine is in its fifth year. Both sides have increased the number of drone and missile attacks on infrastructure, logistics and military sites in recent months.

China upholds principles, promotes dialogue at G20 trade ministers' meeting: commerce ministry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
19:56:42 CST
20:56:42 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- China played an active role in promoting dialogue and cooperation with other G20 members while upholding principles during the recent G20 trade ministers' meeting, the country's Ministry of Commerce said on Sunday.
The ministry spokesperson made the remarks in response to a media question about the meeting, which was held on Sept. 30 and Oct. 1 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, the United States.
Members exchanged views on issues proposed by the U.S. G20 presidency, including opposing the weaponization of food, addressing overcapacity, eliminating forced labor, and adjusting the Most-Favored-Nation (MFN) principle.
Members reached a joint statement opposing the weaponization of food, while no outcome documents were issued on the remaining matters, according to the ministry.
During the meeting, the Chinese side consistently upheld an attitude of openness and cooperation, constructively participated in discussions and maintained close communication with other members, fully playing its role in promoting dialogue and cooperation, said the spokesperson.
At the same time, China adhered to its principles, resolutely safeguarded the common interests of China and other developing countries, and worked to promote unity and cooperation within the G20, the ministry added.
Regarding the food issue, many emerging market and developing members, including China, put forward the view that food-importing and food-exporting countries should jointly safeguard the stability of food supply chains, and that all parties have the right to take measures for domestic public policy objectives and to safeguard food security, the spokesperson said.
The presidency gave positive consideration to these views, which were also fully reflected in the joint statement, the spokesperson said, adding that the outcome was the result of consensus-building and the joint efforts of all G20 members.
Issues such as overcapacity and forced labor were highly controversial from the outset, said the ministry. The ministry said that at present, G20 members are generally subject to additional Section 301 tariffs under the pretext of so-called "forced labor" and are mostly targets of Section 301 investigations over the so-called "overcapacity" issue.
Against this backdrop, many members put forward different views on the issues set by the presidency, and the meeting ultimately failed to produce outcome documents on these matters, the ministry said.
The spokesperson also noted that, after the meeting, the U.S. side issued a chair's statement mentioning that it had released a statement on forced labor with two other G20 countries outside the G20 framework.
On the issue of reforming the MFN treatment principle, the vast majority of members, including China, emphasized that the principle is the cornerstone of the multilateral trading system, providing stability and predictability for global trade, and that any undermining of this principle would seriously damage the foundation of the multilateral trading system, said the ministry.
In light of the views expressed by the members, the presidency did not propose an outcome document on this topic, the ministry revealed.
Looking ahead to the G20 Leaders' Summit in December 2026, the spokesperson said that China is ready to work with the G20 presidency and all members to uphold consensus-building, and jointly contribute positive and practical economic and trade outcomes to the summit. ■

Mozambican president calls for stronger agricultural cooperation with China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
19:56:42 CST
20:56:42 KST

Mozambican President Daniel Chapo (C, front) is briefed on the wheat cultivation during a wheat harvesting ceremony at the Wanbao rice farm in the southern province of Gaza, Mozambique, Oct. 3, 2026. Chapo has called for stronger agricultural cooperation between Mozambique and China and expressed hope that the cooperation model of the Chinese-invested Wanbao rice farm could be expanded to other parts of the country. Chapo made the remarks Saturday while attending the ceremony at the farm. (Photo by Mendes Mondlane/Xinhua)
MAPUTO, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Mozambican President Daniel Chapo has called for stronger agricultural cooperation between Mozambique and China and expressed hope that the cooperation model of the Chinese-invested Wanbao rice farm could be expanded to other parts of the country.
Chapo made the remarks Saturday while attending a wheat harvesting ceremony at the Wanbao rice farm in the southern province of Gaza.
During the event, Chapo viewed displays of crops and seeds, including rice, wheat and maize, and learned about the farm's cooperation with local farmers.
Agriculture is of great importance to Mozambique, Chapo said, calling on the two countries to further strengthen capacity building and cooperation to enhance Mozambique's food production capacity.
Shao Jiayun, general manager of the Wanbao rice farm, said the farm plants about 3,500 hectares of rice annually, including around 1,000 hectares cultivated in cooperation with local farmers, producing about 20,000 tonnes of paddy rice and 12,000 tonnes of processed rice each year.
This year, following small-scale trial planting last year, the company planted about 667 hectares of wheat and achieved a good harvest, he said.
Shao said the farm currently works with about 350 to 400 local farming households each year. By introducing improved crop varieties, promoting agricultural technologies, providing machinery and offering production guidance, the project has helped participating farmers increase their yields.
Some farmers working with the farm have seen grain yields rise from about one to 1.5 tonnes per hectare in the past to between five and seven tonnes per hectare, he said.
Adriano Francisco Bila is one of the local farmers cooperating with the Wanbao rice farm. He joined the project in 2020, starting with one hectare of farmland.
Bila said the income generated from farming has gradually improved his family's living conditions, enabling him to secure access to water and electricity at home and support his children's education.
"Things that once seemed beyond my reach have now become possible through farming," Bila said, hoping to continue cooperating with Wanbao and receive further support for agricultural production. ■

Homegrown robots to enhance IRCS rescue operations in crises
TEHRAN – Domestically made rescue robots make search and rescue missions faster and more accurate, lower risks, and enhance the safety of rescuers by collecting efficient data and helping rescuers identify potential threats before they enter dangerous zones.
Equipped with cameras, thermal sensors, sound and gas detectors, robot rescuers will be used to assess and analyze the hazardous environment, locate survivors, and send pictures to operational teams, helping them to make the best decision for each scenario, IRNA quoted Babak Mahmoudi, the chief of the Iranian Red Crescent Society’s rescue and relief organization, as saying.
Rescue robots will be used to navigate mountainous areas, forests, and insurmountable locations that are dangerous for humans to collect images and data and transmit them to rescuers and enhance field operations, Mahmoudi added.
The official went on to say that rescue robots will not replace human forces; they serve as tools that assist rescuers in search and rescue operations, enabling them to operate remotely in high-risk environments.
The number of manufactured rescue robots in the country will soon reach 100, which will play a key role in enhancing preparedness, response speed, and safety in search and rescue operations.
Skilled IRCS rescuers will benefit from drones, life detection devices, search and rescue dogs, and robots to carry out rescue missions with greater safety, higher speed and precision, he further noted.
IFRC: IRCS serves as a model of excellence in crisis management
In July, Jagan Chapagain, the Secretary General of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), in a letter to Pirhossein Kolivand, the head of the IRCS, lauded the IRCS efforts during the 40-day US-Israeli war against Iran, noting that relief and medical services, search and rescue operations, and dedication of the IRCS volunteers showcase the outstanding capabilities of a strong national society in crisis management.
Highlighting the immense operational, logistical, and humanitarian challenges, Chapagain stated, “The Iranian Red Crescent Society has demonstrated decisive and effective leadership by acting as the country’s primary humanitarian player,” IRIB reported.
“On behalf of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, I wish to extend our appreciation and recognition for the extraordinary humanitarian response led by the Iranian Red Crescent Society in the context of the current conflict situation in the Islamic Republic of Iran,” the letter reads.
“Your swift mobilization of volunteers and staff, the scale and effectiveness of life-saving assistance, and the steadfast commitment to our fundamental principles have ensured that those in need of urgent assistance have received timely and dignified support.
The coordination of emergency health services, round-the-clock relief operations, psychosocial assistance, and community outreach, as well as the courageous and highly professional search and rescue operations, reflect not only technical excellence but also deep-rooted trust within communities. Such trust is the cornerstone of effective humanitarian action and underscores the unique auxiliary role of IRCS and its footprint in the wide Iranian territory.
We are deeply saddened by the loss of four dedicated IRCS volunteers who tragically lost their lives in the line of duty. Their selfless commitment to saving lives stands as a powerful testament to our values. On behalf of the IFRC, I wish to express our heartfelt solidarity with the IRCS, as well as our deepest condolences to the families, friends, and colleagues of these selfless individuals. Their sacrifice will not be forgotten.
 
Your response stands as a powerful example of what a strong National Society can deliver in times of crisis- saving lives, alleviating suffering, and preserving human dignity.
The IFRC remains fully committed to supporting IRCS in its ongoing efforts and in addressing the evolving humanitarian needs. We stand in solidarity with you, your dedicated staff, and your vast network of volunteers, whose courage and commitment continue to inspire the entire IFRC network.”
Also, Hossam Elsharkawi, the IFRC Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), in a letter to Kolivand lauded the IRCS for its significant achievements, highlighting that the IFRC seeks to strengthen strategic partnership with the IRCS to turn agreements into action.
The official also commended the IRCS’s constructive role in the expansion of humanitarian efforts, describing the IRCS as a role model for other societies, the IRCS website reported.

ICC weakened by ‘impotence’ over Netanyahu arrest warrant – attorney (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:56:05 UTC
20:56:05 KST

ICC weakened by ‘impotence’ over Netanyahu arrest warrant – attorney (VIDEO)
The International Criminal Court (ICC) is being weakened by the “impotence” of its member states and the UN, renowned American criminal-defense and human-rights attorney Stanley L. Cohen has told RT.
“Unless the international signatories to the Rome Statute and the UN begin to take action against those countries that are seeking to silence, if not end, the call to justice from the ICC, then its power is obviously going to be weakened,” Cohen said in an interview on Friday.
Cohen pointed to the freedom of movement Western nations have afforded Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, despite an outstanding ICC warrant for his arrest. In 2024, the Hague-based court issued warrants for Netanyahu and his former defense minister, Yoav Gallant, over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the Gaza war.
The fact that Netanyahu who’s a fugitive, who’s a wanted fugitive and war criminal, can fly to New York, could go in front of the UN, who’s wanted for genocide, and go on to speak in furtherance of genocide without any accountability from the UN, really sums up the problem, the impotence, and apparently the indifference of most of the UN.
Israel and the US are not parties to the ICC’s founding treaty, the Rome Statute. However, even Western nations that do recognize the court’s authority have allowed Netanyahu to pass through their airspace despite the arrest warrant. Last February, Washington imposed sanctions on ICC officials for pursuing cases against American soldiers, Netanyahu, and other Israeli officials.
Cohen also argued that as global power shifts toward a new generation of leaders in the Global South and Western “violations of international law” are exposed, future leaders will be less willing to tolerate efforts to undermine or constrain the ICC.
Established in 2002 under the Rome Statute, the court is tasked with prosecuting genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression, and relies heavily on the cooperation of its 125 members. However, some of the world’s most powerful states, including the US, China, India or Russia, reject its authority.
The court has long faced accusations from some governments of selective justice and political bias. The tensions intensified in the past year, with Venezuela and Chad joining Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger in moving to withdraw.

OSLO, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Two people were killed and one was seriously injured in a shooting in Halden, southeastern Norway, on Sunday morning, local police said.
The shooting occurred around 7:30 a.m. (0530 GMT) in a wooded area east of Halden. The three victims belonged to the same hunting party, police incident commander Wilhelm Bjolseth told Norwegian news agency NTB.
A male suspect was detained by witnesses and handed over to police when officers arrived. Police said preliminary information indicated that he was not a member of the hunting party and that they did not suspect any other perpetrators.
The injured person was airlifted to a hospital. The motive and the relationship between those involved remained unclear.
Norway's National Criminal Investigation Service, known as Kripos, told NTB that it would assist the investigation following a request from the local police district.
A large emergency response was mobilized, including police officers, ambulances and helicopters.
Halden Mayor Fredrik Holm said local authorities were working to establish a full picture of the situation and arrange support for the relatives of the victims. ■

Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games close amid logistical snags, organizational criticism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
19:55:54 CST
20:55:54 KST

by sportswriter Li Jia
NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games came to a close Sunday, wrapping up 16 days of competition marked by record-breaking performances but marred by logistical snags and criticism over its organization.
More than 17,000 athletes and officials from 45 countries and regions took part in the Games while over 50 world records have been broken.
President of the Olympic Council of Asia, Sheikh Joaan Bin Hamad Al Thani announced the closing of the Games.
"Tonight, we close the Games that will shape the next generation of Asian Sport," he said. "From the first competition to the very last, Asia's finest athletes captivated us with their performances. You created a legacy that reaches far beyond sport and Japan, touching every corner of our great continent."
China topped the gold medal table for the 12th consecutive edition, collecting 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals for its best haul at an overseas Asian Games. Sailor Bi Kun carried the Chinese delegation's flag at the closing ceremony.
Japan finished second with 83 gold, 95 silver and 91 bronze medals, its most gold medal tally at an Asian Games. South Korea placed third with 39 gold, 43 silver and 68 bronze medals.
Thai sprinter Puripol Boonson and Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi were named the men's and women's Most Valuable Players of the Games, respectively.
Boonson won the men's 100m and 200m titles and took silver in the mixed 4x100m relay. The 20-year-old clocked an Asian Games record of 9.90 seconds in the 100m, becoming the only finalist to break the 10-second barrier.
Yu, 13, claimed three gold medals, setting an Asian record in the women's 200m individual medley and Asian Games records in the 200m butterfly and 400m individual medley.
Throughout the 16-day competition, the Aichi-Nagoya Games were plagued by problems, including a shortage of beds and transportation failures. Organizers encountered accusations of poor management.
Games organizing committee president Hideaki Omura apologized Sunday for a series of logistical glitches, including delays in accommodation check-ins and transportation.
Omura said organizers had faced "unforeseen challenges" and responded to them on a day-to-day basis.
The Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) acknowledged that the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games had faced various operational challenges, but said the Games had ultimately provided athletes with the necessary conditions to compete and perform at their best.
"There is no Games without challenges," said Mohammad Tayyab Ikram, chair of the OCA Coordination Committee for the 2026 Asian Games, at a press conference on the final day of the Games. "The way we handled the challenges should be more important to highlight."
The Aichi-Nagoya Games adopted a distributed accommodation model, with athletes staying in container-style huts, cruise ship and hotels rather than in a purpose-built village. "It was difficult to understand when this model was proposed, but we now have a good practice. Maybe other Games will look at it," he said.
The OCA flag was passed from Aichi-Nagoya to Doha, the host of the 21st Asian Games. However, the date of the event has not been decided yet. There has been speculation that the Games could be pushed back by a year, but organizing committee CEO Ahmed Abdullah Al Buainain of Doha Asian Games said "it remains undecided". ■

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei speaks at a weekly press conference in Tehran, Iran, Oct. 4, 2026. Baghaei said Sunday the country has conveyed its positions through the Qatari mediator regarding the U.S. response to its proposed plan to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.(Xinhua/Shadati)
TEHRAN, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Sunday the country has conveyed its positions through the Qatari mediator regarding the U.S. response to its proposed plan to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran conveyed a proposed seven-day plan to the United States on Sept. 22 to cease hostilities and reopen the waterway to the United States, through mediators on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
"We conveyed our positions to the mediator during the brief stopover we made in Doha on our way back (from New York)," Baghaei said at a weekly press conference in Tehran. "The Americans' proposals are more or less in line with their previous positions, and specifically concern the nuclear issues."
He stressed that Iran has explicitly said its current focus is the Strait of Hormuz, noting that restoring security there requires Washington to take certain steps, including ceasing disruptions to Iran's commercial shipping, lifting sanctions, and ending other meddlesome actions.
"We will conduct the necessary reviews regarding certain details (of the U.S. proposals) and convey our additional points to the other party," Baghaei added.
Also at the press conference, Baghaei said the United Arab Emirates (UAE) released a number of Iranian nationals imprisoned in the Arab state the night before.
He appreciated the UAE officials' cooperation in that regard, though he did not specify the number of inmates released or their charges.
On Feb. 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.
A ceasefire was achieved between the warring parties on April 8. On June 18, Iran and the United States signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on ending the war in the region on all fronts.
Under the MoU, the two countries were scheduled to hold negotiations within 60 days, ending on Aug. 17, to reach a final agreement. However, the two sides failed to make sufficient progress toward a deal as tensions continued to escalate. ■

Government forces seize capital of Ethiopia's Tigray region from rebels
Ethiopian government forces and allied militias have regained control of the capital of Tigray, three sources told Reuters on Sunday, dealing a major setback to the opposition alliance that rules the northern region.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which leads the opposition alliance, said in a statement posted on Facebook it had retreated from the capital and that the regional government would be "temporarily moved out of Mekelle and operate from somewhere else."

Loss of Mekelle a major blow for TPLF
The taking of Mekelle by pro-government forces is a major loss for the opposition alliance led by the TPLF, which launched a big offensive on 23 September against the Ethiopian military.
Ethiopian federal forces and allied fighters have made a quick counterattack into Tigray, but analysts say the fighting - the worst escalation since the 2020- 2022 civil war - threatens to escalate into a wider regional conflict.
The federal government in Addis Ababa severed diplomatic ties with Eritrea last week, accusing it of supporting the rebel alliance alongside Sudan and Egypt. The three countries deny this.

Tehran to host 7th Iran Smart City Exhibition and Conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04

Tehran to host 7th Iran Smart City Exhibition and Conference
TEHRAN – The seventh Iran Smart City Exhibition and Conference is set to open in Tehran on October 31, coinciding with World Cities Day, bringing together stakeholders and experts in the field of smart urban development. The three-day event will continue through November 2.
This year’s conference focuses on artificial intelligence (AI) in urban management, AI in urban security and crisis management, AI in citizen health and well-being, AI-driven governance and smart economy, AI in environment and sustainable energy, citizens’ participation and smart public services, IRNA reported.
The exhibition aims to improve the quality of urban and rural life, support sustainable smart city development, showcase the latest cutting-edge innovations in the smart city sector, introduce new concepts in structures, design, and smart cities, examine challenges of construction and propose scientific solutions, as well as develop cooperation with other countries and benefit from the achievements and successful experiences of smart cities.
The event will serve as a great platform for experts in smart cities, urban managers, industrialists, scholars, and knowledge-based companies to boost their interactions.
Moreover, the deadline for the submission of the articles is October 20.
World Cities Day
World Cities Day is marked on October 31 each year and was first celebrated in 2014. As with World Habitat Day, a global observance is held in a different city each year, and the day focuses on a specific theme.
 
It aims to raise international awareness of urbanization trends, challenges, and visions for sustainable urban development, promote international cooperation, and contribute to global efforts to build equitable, prosperous, sustainable, and inclusive cities that provide their communities with better living environments and quality of life.
On October 31, the Global Observance of World Cities Day takes place in Fuzhou, China, under the theme “Regenerating the City: Adequate Housing for All.” The 2026 observance focuses on urban regeneration as a catalyst for achieving adequate housing for all and on how area-based regeneration, combined with housing and informal-settlement strategies, can create more inclusive and climate-resilient neighborhoods.
Cities around the world are confronting interconnected pressures, including housing affordability challenges, ageing neighborhoods and infrastructure, underutilized urban land, climate-related risks and widening social inequalities. According to the World Cities Day 2026 Concept Note, up to 3.4 billion people lack access to adequate housing, secure tenure, basic services or affordable living conditions. Urban regeneration offers an opportunity to address these challenges by improving existing urban areas while expanding access to adequate housing and ensuring that no one is left behind.
The 2026 theme emphasizes integrated approaches that connect affordable housing with improvements to public space, infrastructure, connectivity and climate resilience. It also places particular importance on participatory and community-led regeneration, together with safeguards that can prevent displacement and ensure that existing residents benefit from improvements to their homes and neighborhoods.
World Cities Day 2026 will provide a platform for national and local governments, United Nations entities, international organizations, academia, the private sector and communities to exchange experiences, showcase innovative practices and identify practical solutions. The official 2026 program framework runs from 31 October to 2 November 2026 at the Fuzhou Strait International Conference and Exhibition Center and includes an opening ceremony, thematic forums, side events, exhibitions and city tours.
