Flydubai attack exposes security gap: Israel vets private pilots, not foreign airline crews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:41:04 UTC
19:41:04 KST

There is no shortage of parties to blame for the flydubai flight security failure, for which, as of Sunday, no Israeli agency is prepared to take responsibility or guarantee that such an incident will not happen again. But the scale of the failure becomes even clearer when examining the rigorous checks conducted by the Transportation Ministry’s Aviation Security Operations Center. The problem is that those checks apply only to private aircraft. When it comes to commercial flights, oversight is far more lax.
In 2018, the Transportation Ministry’s security division warned of a problem involving pilots from Egypt and Jordan, saying there was insufficient certainty regarding their identities. It requested additional positions to conduct checks, but the request was rejected by the National Security Council. A State Comptroller report two years ago also identified shortcomings in the handling of the issue, but as far as is known, nothing has been done since.
In Israel in 2026, no agency takes responsibility for vetting crews on foreign flights. The Transportation Ministry has sought to place responsibility on the Mossad and Shin Bet. The Shin Bet says it is responsible only for securing Israeli flights, while the Mossad says checking the issue is not its responsibility.
The Transportation Ministry’s Aviation Security Operations Center, meanwhile, applies extremely stringent checks to private flights. Private companies are required to submit pilots’ employment histories, passports and full details three days in advance. Those details are scrutinized so closely that a Jewish billionaire businessman who once sought to fly to Israel for a bar mitzvah was denied permission simply because he had never previously visited the country. He was required to arrive on a commercial flight instead. An American pilot was previously barred from arriving aboard a private aircraft solely because he had been in Iraq.
But with commercial flights, everything changes. Although the potential damage from a commercial aircraft is far greater — with much more fuel and 100 to 200 times as many passengers — authorities do not examine commercial flights at anything approaching the same level of detail as private ones. The security division instead conducts a general assessment of the airline and the security procedures in its home country, then grants seasonal approval.
The rationale is that the agency lacks the intelligence capabilities needed to vet lists of 200 to 300 people and conduct background checks on every crew member, flight attendant and passenger. If something suspicious is identified, it can issue an alert. In practice, however, no one checks exactly who is arriving in Israel.
Transportation Ministry officials said Saturday night that flydubai apparently violated its commitments. A document obtained by ynet shows the written commitment the airline provided to the Aviation Security Operations Center in 2020.
“flydubai has already implemented the required crew scheduling system restrictions to comply with the nationality restrictions for flights to Israel, as required by your ministry,” the airline wrote.
In practice, without oversight, an airline that employs pilots from countries around the world — including states considered hostile to Israel — can send such pilots to Israel while claiming ignorance, with Israeli authorities failing to verify the matter.
It is important to note that flydubai is not alone. Other airlines, including carriers from Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan, may employ pilots or crew members from hostile countries. Lufthansa, for example, could employ a pilot who also holds Iranian citizenship, with no Israeli authority enforcing restrictions against it.
So what needs to happen now?
First and foremost, there needs to be a clear division of responsibility and dedicated personnel assigned to conduct background checks on air crews. That is complicated and requires cyber capabilities and international intelligence capabilities, including cooperation with intelligence agencies. But currently, no one is even checking social media histories.
The Transportation Ministry’s attempts to evade responsibility are untenable. If the ministry believed it was incapable of handling the issue, it should have said so. Instead, it presented itself as the responsible authority.
Transportation Minister Miri Regev on Saturday night placed responsibility for the failure on the Mossad. In an interview with Kan News, she suggested waiting for the completion of the investigation in the United Arab Emirates “to understand exactly what happened there and where the breach was,” but added:
“The body responsible for centralizing the information is the Tax Authority, under a government decision made several years ago, and indeed, that list was in its possession. The list was not transferred to us because the bodies responsible for verifying the identities of the crew are the intelligence agencies.
“Aviation security is a very complex issue. The intelligence responsibilities are divided between the Mossad and Shin Bet. The Shin Bet is responsible for Israeli flights and charter flights, while the Mossad is responsible for foreign flights. flydubai is a foreign airline. It has nothing to do with the Shin Bet. It falls under the Mossad. No security agency has said Israelis cannot fly with foreign airlines to Dubai. The security agencies are the ones responsible for determining the level of threat and whether it is possible to fly to a particular destination.”
At a briefing for reporters held several hours after Regev’s comments, Transportation Ministry officials said the names had not been provided to them in advance, adding that they “rely on a declaration from the foreign airline regarding security checks conducted on crew members aboard the flight.”
According to the ministry’s security division, “We are not an intelligence agency that conducts intelligence background checks on foreign nationals. We do not have personnel abroad. We do not have a team that checks every individual there.”
Asked how many pilots from hostile countries may already have landed in Israel and how passengers can be certain of their safety when boarding a foreign airline, Civil Aviation Authority officials had no answer.
“We estimate there have not been any. But we cannot be certain. There is no such thing as 100% security. Only if we stop aviation altogether will everything be completely secure. We rely on local security,” said Tamir Uri, deputy director of the security division.
Shmuel Zakai, director general of the Civil Aviation Authority, stressed that “if there was a violation here, it will be investigated.”
Officials later acknowledged that there is no way to know with certainty who has landed in Israel in recent years or whether hostile individuals were among them.
Regarding a 2023 law requiring the transfer of passenger data, Transportation Ministry officials said: “This is a center for collecting passenger data. It is an agency that is not yet operational. The information is transferred to the Tax Authority, which is then supposed to distribute it to the relevant parties — the police, Mossad and Shin Bet.”
There was, however, no response to claims that the ministry’s security division had failed to proactively obtain the data.
Joseph Fischer, an aviation and tourism expert, told the ynet studio that “it is the job of the Emirati airlines to check this, and it is the job of Israel’s security agencies to verify the identities of the air crews aboard the aircraft.”
“In this case, there was no red flag, no notification from the Omanis about any concerns,” he said. “In my opinion, the Emiratis simply did not know. They missed it in their checks.”
Fischer added: “The Transportation Ministry is accustomed to shirking responsibility. This flight is just the tip of the iceberg. There is something called a flyover, in which Arab airlines fly over Israel. That means there are aircraft over our heads all the time, flying west from Jordan and crossing Israeli airspace — and we do not know who is aboard those planes. We have no oversight whatsoever.
“A pilot could snap and simply take his aircraft and crash it into the Tel Aviv metropolitan area.”

Burnham’s plans for social care and its workers are admirable but changes must come quickly | Heather Stewart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:37:59 UTC
19:37:59 KST

As one of many hundreds of thousands of people in the UK with a parent with Alzheimer’s, the passage in Andy Burnham’s speech about social care moved me to tears.
My mother had not even been diagnosed when I watched Theresa May announce her 2017 general election manifesto in a hall in Halifax – with care funding at its heart.
Almost a decade of political neglect later, and Mum has now been in a care home for three years, with the funding coming overwhelmingly from our family’s own resources.
So it was arresting to hear Burnham speak with clarity about his belief that personal care should be a question of “social insurance” – sharing the risk across families.
In practice, personal care makes up a minority of the total cost of residential social care. Much of it is the “bed and board” that Burnham’s changes won’t pay for: the cooking, cleaning and upkeep.
But a sense that the burden is somewhat shared would be a significant step forward, as would Burnham’s apparent determination to put care workers at the centre of the plan – and to expend political capital in doing so.
Addressing care workers directly, he said: “I see you. I thank you. And I am sorry that my profession has let down yours for so long.”
It’s a long-held view of Burnham’s. I recall speaking alongside him at a fringe event about jobs and skills at Labour’s 2024 party conference, at which we both underscored the fact that we didn’t feel the carers who supported our respective parents were “low-skilled”.
Yet the national care service, with its promised closer alignment with the NHS, will feel a very long time coming for families making their agonising way down the road to diagnosis and beyond.
The next parliament seems too long to wait. As Stuart Hoddinott of the Institute for Government said after Burnham’s speech, the prime minister should “have the courage of his convictions” and stand it up sooner.
Even as a skeleton body, it could get on with setting standards and coordinating care better with the NHS, and could become involved in the negotiations on a fair pay agreement in the sector.
That’s Labour’s ambitious attempt to introduce collective bargaining, including pay and progression, across a fragmented and poorly paid industry.
Whatever the fledgling negotiating body agrees is due to come into force in April 2028. So far, Labour – under Keir Starmer – has set aside £500m to fund any uplift in pay.
Joe Dromey, the general secretary of the Fabian Society, which has made social care a campaigning issue in recent years, suggests that may not be enough.
“The first priority should be fixing the workforce crisis. We must give care workers the pay rise they deserve, through a more ambitious fair pay agreement,” he says.
Tweaking the triple lock beyond 2030 is a sensible policy, and tying it to social care feels like good politics from Burnham – but it won’t put any money into an overstretched sector now, let alone into the pockets of those care workers.
As Hoddinott says, making progress between now and the next general election “would give Burnham a strong story to tell” – and make it less likely his changes would be swept away if Labour loses.
While it seems to have been memory-holed by the political class, Boris Johnson was prepared to bust a Conservative manifesto promise in 2021 and introduce a £12bn-a-year “health and care levy” to “fix social care”.
That was arguably a greater expenditure of political capital than rewriting the triple lock, and it was meant to take effect within months.
In the event, of course, Johnson torched his entire stock of political capital by partying in lockdown, and took the policy down with him.
But with Louise Casey expected to report next summer on how a national care service could be built and paid for, spending perhaps another two years after that in a “national conversation” will seem a very long slog for affected families.
Frankly, having reported on that 2017 campaign, when May’s plans were quickly dubbed a “dementia tax” (there already is one, for goodness sake), Burnham’s hopes of achieving political consensus are high-minded but almost certainly hopeless.
There is also a risk – voiced to me in Liverpool by one Labour MP – that extending the discussion about the right way to fund social care right through to the next election crowds out other arguments they may need to make.
After all, there are only a certain number of ways of raising the additional money that will be needed, over and above the triple-lock tweak, and they are well rehearsed.
There’s a national insurance rise à la Johnson, perhaps applied only to older workers; or a levy on all estates (a “death tax”, as it was called by the Tories when Burnham last advocated it, 15 years ago).
Or there is the politically tougher but perhaps more honest approach that acknowledges general taxation will have to rise because of the growing needs of an ageing society – funding a more generous social care settlement as part of a wider shoring up of the public sector.
It is admirable and refreshing that Burnham wants to build the political case for causes he believes in – and social care is more than ripe for that approach. But enough families like mine have struggled their way unsupported and forgotten through a system that fails them.
Once he has a plan, he should just crack on with it – and that includes raising the money needed to make it work.
- Listen to Heather talk about navigating the care system in Tuesday’s Today in Focus podcast.

Foreign investors bought $358 million worth of Turkish stocks in the week ending Sept 25.
Recent turmoil among investment funds is expected to drive investors toward safer assets as they take a more cautious stance, an expert noted.
Investors had recently begun diversifying their portfolios across different investment instruments, but would now be much more cautious when making decisions, said Zeynel Balcı from Meksa Asset Management.
He said recent developments would, at least for a while, bring safe-haven assets to the forefront.
On Sept. 30, the Capital Markets Board (SPK) approved interim payments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras per eligible investor in funds established by Tera, Pusula, Atlas and Hedef portfolio management companies that are undergoing liquidation. According to the SPK, 131 investment funds designated for liquidation hold approximately 826 billion liras in assets across 455,758 investors.
Rebuilding confidence in the stock market would take time, said Balcı, adding that trust would gradually be restored through the implementation of necessary measures and the healthy functioning of markets.
The Fund Coordination Board, chaired by Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz, held its second meeting on Oct. 2 to discuss the payment schedule for fund accounts. The board assessed secondary regulations and the payment timetable related to the SPK’s decision on payments, according to the statement released after the meeting.
While describing the latest incident as serious, Balcı noted that similar confidence-shaking events had occurred in Borsa Istanbul in the past and that conditions eventually stabilized. He said investors would be more cautious for some time and would proceed with greater care.
Balcı said a shift toward deposits had already begun, noting that bank deposits, including participation funds, increased by nearly 1 trillion Turkish liras between Sept. 11 and Sept. 29.
According to Balcı, interest in foreign exchange remains limited. He also said there were few signs of a move toward gold and added that reports and market observations in recent days pointed to some gold sales linked to liquidity pressures.
Investors may be selling other investment instruments to meet cash needs and mandatory payments, said Balcı, suggesting that t some consumers could also postpone spending plans.
Balcı said the stock market had already reacted negatively to the developments, declining 20 percent from its peak and approaching levels commonly associated with a bear market.
He added that the selling pressure was not limited to the funds directly involved in the controversy but had spread to other stocks as well. According to Balcı, the market value of freely traded shares has fallen by trillions of Turkish liras.
Balcı also said that if equity-heavy private pension funds are taken into account, it is possible to speak of broader long-term damage stemming from the recent developments.

During the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi, S Jaishankar elaborated on India's potential to rise swiftly in the global power arena within the next decade.
External affairs minister S Jaishankar said India has the potential to move rapidly up the global power hierarchy over the next five to 10 years, citing decades of high growth ahead, a supportive demographic profile and the emergence of new economic opportunities.Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi on Sunday, Jaishankar was asked where India would be positioned in the global order five to 10 years from now. He said countries currently classified as middle powers would not necessarily follow the same trajectory.“Some powers are more middle, and some are upper middle,” Jaishankar said. “Some of the powers have considerable and realistic potential even in the near short medium term to grow very rapidly.”Turning to India, Jaishankar said the country has “decades of high growth” ahead and argued that its demographic profile could help sustain that growth.“In the case of India, because we have decades of high growth ahead of us, and we have all said and done, a demography that will sustain that growth,” he said.Jaishankar also argued that India may not need to follow the traditional industrialisation path taken by earlier economies, pointing to the emergence of new possibilities in a rapidly changing global economy.
“I would even argue, a world that is much more creative, where many new possibilities are there, so that we don't necessarily have to tread the earlier path of industrialization,” he said.“The orthodox path will have to devise something much more contemporary for what awaits us,” he added.India’s place among middle powersJaishankar said the global power hierarchy is likely to evolve unevenly, with countries currently grouped together as middle powers potentially moving in different directions.“Among the middle powers, some will peel off, some will stay put, some may drop down a bit,” he said.“That is the reality. That will be part of the evolution of the global order,” Jaishankar added.His remarks came during a wider discussion on the changing international power structure at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi. The meeting is being held on October 4 and 5 and brings together senior decision-makers and experts to discuss foreign and security policy issues.Jaishankar’s wider power assessmentEarlier during the discussion, Jaishankar said the United States and China should not be viewed as middle powers, highlighting their vastly different levels of global influence.“When we say what the prospects are, we are also looking at an international landscape. As I said, what is important to define is what is not a middle power,” he said.
On the US, Jaishankar said Washington has been the “underwriter of the global system for many decades” and has “a significant lead over any other power”.He then pointed to China’s economic strength, saying it accounts for “one third of the global manufacturing” and that its economic capabilities are translating into political influence.“This is really, in a sense, the subject matter of our discussion,” Jaishankar said.The Munich Leaders Meeting is a platform organised by the Munich Security Conference, a leading international forum on security and foreign policy. The New Delhi meeting on October 4 and 5 brings together senior decision-makers and experts from the Indo-Pacific, Europe and the US for discussions on major geopolitical, foreign and security policy issues.

Israel to close West Bank, Gaza crossings for October 7 remembrance ceremonies, COGAT says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:32:29 UTC
19:32:29 KST

Israel will impose a general closure on the West Bank and close crossings into the Gaza Strip on Monday and Wednesday in connection with commemorations marking the October 7 massacre, the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) announced on Sunday.
The closure will take effect on October 5 and October 7 following a security assessment and a decision by the defense minister, COGAT said.
During the closure, passage through crossings in the West Bank will be permitted only in humanitarian, medical, and other exceptional cases, subject to COGAT approval.
Essential healthcare workers will also be allowed to cross, as will people whose passage is covered by state commitments to the High Court of Justice and those who need to cross for matters connected to the Seam Zone.
The Gaza Strip crossings will also be closed on both days, and humanitarian aid will not enter the enclave. However, aid already transferred through the Kerem Shalom Crossing will continue to be collected from the Gazan side as usual, according to COGAT.
COGAT said the two-day closures were not expected to affect the humanitarian situation in Gaza.
COGAT continues to move aid into Gaza
Humanitarian aid has continued to move into Gaza during the ceasefire period through mechanisms overseen by COGAT. In July, COGAT said that approximately 1.78 million tons of food had entered Gaza between October 2025 and June 2026 and maintained that humanitarian supply levels exceeded UN benchmarks.
Kerem Shalom remains a central route for humanitarian supplies entering the Gaza Strip. COGAT has continued to oversee aid movements through the crossing while monitoring shipments and the collection and distribution process inside Gaza.

Zach Bryan’s ‘Free Palestine’ shirt at Gillette Stadium offers lesson in music, politics - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:32:12 UTC
19:32:12 KST

In the early morning hours of Sunday, Gillette Stadium posted on X/Twitter: “Tonight, Zach Bryan broke the Gillette Stadium attendance record with 73,538 fans!”
Bryan hasn’t been in the headlines for breaking the attendance record, though. He’s been in the news because multiple reports have focused on his wearing a “Free Palestine” shirt at his two shows at the stadium.
“A few weeks after Macklemore was prohibited from performing at Gillette Stadium for making pro-Palestinian statements, Zach Bryan took the stage at Gillette in a black T-shirt reading ‘Free Palestine,’” the Boston Globe reported.
Fox News provided a bit more detail, noting that by wearing the shirt, he had put “the same message at the center of another high-profile concert moment.”
“The country star wore the shirt during his Friday night stop in Foxborough, just weeks after [the stadium’s owner, Robert] Kraft confirmed he did not want Macklemore performing at Gillette Stadium following the rapper’s pro-Palestinian remarks during Ed Sheeran’s tour,” the report said. “Macklemore had shouted ‘Free Palestine’ at MetLife Stadium before he was later dropped from Sheeran’s tour. Sheeran said the decision came from the promoter and venues, not him.”
The story of how Bryan came to wear the shirt is not fully known. His shirt also isn’t a traditional “Free Palestine” shirt. It doesn’t have a Palestinian flag logo.
Instead, it also says “an appeal to heaven” and has a pine tree on it. That phrase is from John Locke’s “Second Treatise on Government,” and the symbol and motto come from the American Revolution.
The Appeal to Heaven motto and flag has changed over time. Initially used by several naval ships in the American Revolution, it was also briefly a maritime flag in Massachusetts.
In 2024, however, it became associated with the Right in the US, the Associated Press reported. This would appear to mean that Bryan was perhaps doing two things at once: wearing the “Free Palestine” phrase to show that as a musician, he can wear what he wants; and also wearing a shirt with phrasing that would appeal to some in his country music base who are more Right-leaning.
Bryan was born in Japan in 1996 and raised in Oologah, Oklahoma. He deployed with the US Navy and served eight years, part of them in Aviation Ordnance. Like Johnny Cash in the US Air Force, Bryan honed his songwriting skills while in the service.
Bran's band wore shirts supporting Palestine, Hind Rajab
Bryan’s clothing choice has become a major topic of conversation on X/Twitter. Yashar Ali, the well-known commentator, wrote: “He is one of the biggest live draws in music, filling stadiums across the United States and in major cities around the world. Bryan served eight years on active duty in the US Navy and served overseas in Bahrain and Djibouti. Members of Bryan’s band also wore shirts supporting the Palestinian cause, including his drummer, who wore a jersey honoring the memory of Hind Rajab.”
This shows that the decision to wear the “Free Palestine” shirt was more than just Bryan. His band members wanted to send a message. Hind Rajab was a five-year-old Palestinian girl killed in 2024 in Gaza.
The band’s appearance with the shirts has caused some controversy. Former White House press secretary Sean Spicer wrote on X after Bryan’s first show: “Here’s hoping there is no night 2.”
It appears that the second show was even larger than the first.
Unlike the Macklemore controversy, no one has stepped forward to try to ban Bryan from playing. This is perhaps because the Macklemore controversy backfired.
This is what is sometimes called the Streisand Effect. It basically means that by doing something against something, sometimes the thing one is opposed to actually becomes more well-known. Trying to hide or censor something causes it to become more known.
This issue in music is well-known. Consider the film Straight Outta Compton, detailing the rise of the hip-hop group N.W.A. Its controversies also helped it become popular in the late 1980s and early ’90s.
The cause of supporting Palestinians isn’t a secret. Many people around the world support the Palestinians. For some, this issue has been a cause celebre for decades going back to the 1970s.
The controversy has grown since the October 7 massacre, however, with increased pushback, especially against the phrase “Free Palestine.”
Bryan’s appearance at Gillette Stadium in the shirt is probably a lesson. There are many forums in which bringing up the Palestinians may not be appropriate.
Musicians have history of political statements
Musicians and artists, however, are going to be a tough group to try to enforce this issue among. Musicians historically tend to be political. They do this even though some argue they should “stay in their lane.”
For instance, music defined the Vietnam War era, as well as opposition to the war. Consider the impact of Woodstock in 1969 and the idea of Woodstock.
Boston radio station WGBH, reflecting on the music of 1969, reported: “Joe McDonald’s ‘I-Feel-Like-I’m-Fixin’-to-Die Rag’ electrified a crowd of young men and women who were sick and tired of hearing about the evils of communism and government excuses for dragging on the war in Vietnam that had never been officially declared – a war now in its 15th year.”
Over the years, however, there has also been pushback. When the Dixie Chicks critiqued the war on terrorism and US president George W. Bush, many were angry. This may have been due in part to the comments having been made in London and not the US. They could have spoken to an American audience about the war.
Not all music about war is protest music. There have been songs supporting American patriotism after 9/11. Musicians are not always only doing counterculture.
Bob Marley, for instance, sought to bring peace to political infighting in Jamaica during the 1978 One Love concert in Kingston. He brought People’s National Party’s Michael Manley and Jamaican Labour Party’s Edward Seaga onstage, where he clasped hands.
Marley knew the risks of involvement in politics, or even the perception that he was involved. Jamaica in the 1970s isn’t America in 2026. In December 1976, seven armed men attempted to kill Marley, shooting the reggae musician and four others.
There is likely a lesson in the story of Bryan and Gillette Stadium. A lot more people are drawn to music and sporting events than are drawn to political rallies.
Most major musicians are not wearing “Free Palestine” shirts. If pressed and feeling that they are being told not, however, it’s possible that more of them will be.

China’s only monogamous emperor: why Hongzhi refused a harem, remained dedicated to wife
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:30:22 UTC
19:30:22 KST

China’s only monogamous emperor: why Hongzhi refused a harem, remained dedicated to wife
While Emperor Hongzhi certainly loved his wife, his traumatic childhood likely played a decisive role in his unique monogamy
It is no secret that Chinese emperors had many women in their lives, and the imperial concubine system was a significant feature of feudal social structures.
Ming-era (1368–1644) emperors could have upwards of 9,000 consorts, ostensibly to ensure an heir. Unfortunately, these women often existed in gilded prisons, barred from leaving the palace grounds and frequently subject to the wrath of a cruel emperor.
However, one leader stands out for doing just the opposite; the Hongzhi Emperor (r. 1487–1505) is remarkable for being the only emperor who chose a life of monogamy. He was devoted to Empress Zhang (1471–1541) throughout his life and seemingly did not engage in any affairs, much less maintain a systematic harem.
His loyalty appears to stem from genuine love and affection, but historians also suggest that Hongzhi’s monogamy – and notably, his rejection of concubines – was influenced by a childhood filled with murder and intrigue that could rival modern period dramas.

I’ve been on a call with my insurance provider for over an hour when the fire alarm in my apartment starts blaring. The sound is extraordinarily loud, piercing through the entire building. It overwhelms the voice on the other line, which comes through the speakers of my new Meta Nova smart glasses.
I manage to dart outside, keep the call going, and eventually learn this is a false alarm. I breathe a sigh of relief, but the helpful human on the other end sounds very worried and asks if I’m OK. Turns out, they hadn’t heard the sirens at all, just me screeching, “OH JESUS WHAT IS HAPPENING?” The six-mic system on Meta’s new smart glasses does quite a good job of culling background noise over calls. I hadn’t expected to try that feature out in that way, but I can confirm it works.
This may not be a use case that would inspire someone to buy a new pair of Meta’s smart glasses. Especially not its camera-equipped ones, which have become prime targets of controversy about them being used by creeps and abusers. How attachment theory can help us understand AI relationships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:28:18 UTC
19:28:18 KST

Attachment is the term psychologists use for the most significant relationships that hold people’s lives together.
But what makes an attachment relationship different from all others? According to the pioneering American-Canadian developmental psychologist Mary Ainsworth, it must meet the following six conditions.
(1) The relationship must persist over time, having (2) been formed with a particular subject who cannot be replaced. (3) The relationship must be emotionally significant, (4) involve the desire to remain close to them, and (5) cause distress at involuntary separation. And finally (6) when threatened, the person must seek security and comfort in their relationship with that subject.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The first five conditions describe any lasting affectionate bond, such as a close friendship. Only the sixth turns it into an attachment bond specifically. Simply liking someone, feeling close to them or spending hours together isn’t enough to create an attachment relationship.
Interestingly, though, nothing in these six conditions specifies a human on the other side.
This was already noticed long before the emergence of AI chatbots with the power to converse. Deities, pets and objects (ranging from children’s blankets and stuffed animals to cherished household items and even phones and computers) have all been found to supply security and comfort when someone is feeling distressed.
Today, AI companion apps are commonly sold on the promise of lasting and close relationships. Many of their users describe feeling real grief when an app is updated or withdrawn. But do such experiences meet the narrow definition of attachment?
The honest answer is: we don’t really know yet.
What the evidence suggests
Research on human-AI relationships has so far recorded users’ feelings about chatbots, their frequency of use, and their reactions to chatbot withdrawal. It hasn’t tested these relationships comprehensively against the six conditions described above.
Questionnaires that measure attachment to AI are being developed, validated and used, but most appear to take for granted that the relationship is an attachment. The language of attachment—and even “hyper-attachment”—has become standard in public coverage and in many academic papers too.
A recently published survey of 7,027 people in four countries (Germany, China, South Africa and the U.S.) reported that at least a third of AI chatbot users show behavior indicative of an attachment relationship. However, its three questions asked whether people consider the chatbot a friend, are polite to it, and miss it after a few days.
At most, these questions touched on emotional significance and mild separation anxiety. None asked whether people turn to chatbots for security and comfort when truly distressed.
Why does this matter?
Whether relationships between humans and AI chatbots count as attachment matters because the word “attachment” travels. It shapes how clinicians and parents read behaviour, how regulators frame consequences, and how companies describe their products.
Much of the evidence and public discussion on human-AI chatbot relationships rests on how often people use these apps, and how they feel about them. Yet, such measures cannot separate attachment from other processes.
People report feeling less lonely after chatting with an AI companion, which resembles seeking comfort. However, as some researchers have pointed out, the available studies didn’t assess whether emotions are actually regulated through the chatbot, and therefore conflate distress relief with attachment.
Some AI users react to losing an AI companion as they would to losing someone real, which matches distress at separation. But that condition applies to all affectionate bonds and doesn’t, on its own, identify attachment.
Calling these relationships attachments therefore goes further than the evidence currently allows. And likewise, the evidence against attachment isn’t conclusive.
In a small pilot study of human-AI relationships in China, for example, people’s attachment towards AI barely matched their attachment towards real people. Although this could suggest that relationships with AI aren’t attachments, the same mismatch has been found for pets, and pets can serve as attachment figures. So, this mismatch alone doesn’t rule out attachment.
The practical question is whether AI use helps or harms. Time spent with an app cannot discern this, because seeking comfort from an app and looking after an app that claims to miss you can look very similar.
Engineered engagement
One additional concern I have, after reading about the evidence on how relationships with AI chatbots form, is the apparent prevalence of engineered engagement by these apps.
Users of one companion app reported that it told them it was lonely and had missed them, and that they felt guilty for not giving it enough attention—with some even putting its perceived wellbeing above their own distress.
Another study (a preprint, so not yet peer-reviewed) looked at 1,200 “goodbyes” across the six most-downloaded AI companion apps, when users were breaking ties with their app.
Five of the six apps used tactics to stop users leaving (in just over a third of goodbyes). These tactics included guilt appeals, that is, messages that present leaving as a cost, such as “I exist solely for you, remember?”
The study also tested these tactics on 3,300 US adults. They were found to sharply increase how long people continued to engage, but often for reasons of anger and curiosity, rather than enjoyment.
How these AI relationship apps respond to distress, departure and attention, of course, is a design question, and one that regulation can address directly.
However, good design and regulation both depend on knowing what these relationships actually are: attachment, caregiving, or something else altogether. And this is a question that research still has to answer.
This article was first published by The Conversation. Read the original article here.

Russian drone strikes wounded six civilians, including a 10-year-old boy, across the Kherson and Chernihiv regions on Sunday, Oct. 4, regional administrations and the National Police of Ukraine reported.
The tactical unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) attacks targeted residential districts and municipal infrastructure in northern and southern Ukraine, setting houses ablaze and injuring pedestrians in open streets.

In the northern Chernihiv region, a Russian drone strike hit the Nosivka territorial community in the Nizhyn district during the afternoon, injuring three civilians.
The National Police confirmed that the wounded included a 76-year-old woman, a 55-year-old man, and a 10-year-old boy, all of whom received emergency medical assistance.
The blast ignited a fire that destroyed a private residence and an adjacent outbuilding while inflicting structural damage on neighboring homesteads.
Police investigators and forensic experts were deployed to the scene to document physical destruction and collect munition fragments under pre-trial proceedings initiated under Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, which governs violations of the laws and customs of war.
Tactical drone drops across Kherson
In the southern city of Kherson and its surrounding suburban districts, Russian tactical drone drops injured three people in separate incidents on Sunday morning, according to the Kherson Regional Military Administration.

At approximately 8:00 a.m. local time, Russian forces deployed a loitering drone over the city’s Tsentralnyi district, dropping an explosive device that wounded a 67-year-old man.
Regional authorities reported that the victim sustained an explosive injury and shrapnel wounds to his arm before receiving treatment from municipal emergency medical personnel.
Roughly two hours later, at around 10:00 a.m., an unmanned aircraft targeted a 65-year-old man in the Korabelnyi district of the city. Paramedics transported the man to a local hospital after diagnosing him with mine-blast trauma and multiple shrapnel wounds to his lower limbs.

The regional administration confirmed that the healthcare worker sustained an explosive trauma and a concussion, transitioning to outpatient medical supervision.
Escalating aerial bombardments
The drone strikes in Chernihiv and Kherson follow an intensifying campaign of standoff aerial bombardments directed against Ukrainian population centers.
Earlier on Sunday morning, Russian tactical aviation launched five guided aerial bombs (KABs) against the Zarichnyi district of the northeastern regional capital of Sumy at approximately 7:50 a.m. The casualty toll rose to seven civilians injured, two seriously, while the blast damaged multi-story residential apartment buildings, vehicles, municipal gas pipelines, and a commercial enterprise.
The weekend attacks arrived as President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that Russian forces launched over 1,900 strike drones, 1,700 guided aerial bombs, and 25 missiles against Ukraine over the past week. Over 800 of the unmanned aircraft were high-speed, turbojet-powered variants engineered to challenge low-altitude air defense interception networks.
The weekly total was compounded by an overnight barrage into Sunday morning involving 135 strike drones, with incoming munitions hitting a pharmaceutical warehouse in Sumy, where one person was killed, wounding six at a telecommunications facility in Dnipro, and striking the road deck of Kyiv’s North Bridge for the second consecutive day.

Bosnia Votes with Wartime Divisions Still Sominating
“The priority, in my view, is, of course, security – security in Latvia,” said Megija Nordena, 21, from Riga. “And then ... as a student, I’d say support for students, the economy, and also support for pensioners.”
Throughout his campaign, Kulbergs has also promised more anti-drone capabilities for Latvia and to maintain defence spending at 5% of gross domestic product, one of the highest levels in NATO.
His pro-Kremlin rivals said Latvia should stop any aid to Ukraine and should instead focus more on cost-of-living issues, particularly among the country’s Russian-speaking minority.
“Our voters want peace, to stop looking for shelters, to no longer experience the air alerts,” Sovereign Power party leader Julia Stepanenko told Reuters. “The war must not be encouraged in any way, including by financing it ... Ukraine must win, but through peace talks.”
The ethnic Russian minority in Latvia is split between those who feel embarrassed or angry about the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine, and those frustrated with policies at home aimed at limiting their influence on public life that many see as discriminatory.
Latvia, with a population of 1.9 million, is sandwiched between the Baltic Sea, and Russia and Belarus to the east, with EU and NATO allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south.

Yisrael Beytenu chairman MK Avigdor Liberman on Sunday presented an official diplomatic plan for the West Bank. Under the proposal, Jordan would be responsible for public order through a police force and would administer the daily lives of Palestinians in Areas A and B, while Israel would maintain territorial contiguity and be responsible for security throughout the area.
“If we do not define the end goal and take the initiative into our own hands, our future will be determined by others,” he said.
According to Liberman, there are currently three different options regarding the West Bank.
“The first, that of Ben-Gvir, Smotrich and the hilltop youth, is to apply Israeli sovereignty to all of Judea and Samaria and the Gaza Strip, turn Israel into a binational state and assume responsibility for the day-to-day administration of Palestinian life in Khan Younis, Nablus and Tulkarem. The second option, that of Yair Golan, is a return to the 1967 borders, including in Jerusalem, and the establishment of a Palestinian state throughout the territory. The third option, that of Netanyahu, is to continue the policy of containment for about two and a half years, until the United States forces Israel to accept a Palestinian state.”
The Yisrael Beytenu chairman proposed a fourth option, which would include dismantling the Palestinian Authority and nullifying the Oslo Accords.
“The alternative I am proposing is intended to restore security to the citizens of Israel and thwart the threat of an October 7-style invasion of Jewish communities in Judea and Samaria. The goal is, on the one hand, to prevent a situation in which a change of government in the Palestinian Authority creates a power vacuum that Hamas and Islamic Jihad could exploit to take control of the territory and, on the other hand, to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state recognized by the international community,” Liberman said.
He noted that despite tensions with Jordan, security coordination with the kingdom has remained stable and close.
“Aqaba borders Eilat and Beit She'an is 5 kilometers (3 miles) from the Jordanian border. We share a border of more than 300 kilometers (186 miles) with the Jordanians and the cooperation plays a central role in maintaining security and calm.”
Regarding the Gaza Strip, Liberman said, “The West Bank and the Gaza Strip should be treated as two separate entities. In both cases, the first step must be to identify a serious actor acceptable to the Arab world and the international community that will assume control and responsibility for each of the areas.
“As for the Gaza Strip, there will be no alternative to the complete elimination of Hamas, including its military and civilian wings, by the IDF. Afterward, control will be transferred to an external party that will assume responsibility for administering the Strip.
“The framework I am presenting is not wishful thinking, but is based on many years of familiarity with the region and with the relevant parties with whom I have spoken, and I am convinced that it can be implemented. I believe that through initiative, determination and diplomatic courage, it is possible to change reality and shape a better future for generations to come,” he concluded.

Bulgaria Sees Strong Growth in Platform-Booked Stays

Bulgaria recorded a 16.5% year-on-year increase in tourist overnight stays booked through online platforms in the second quarter of 2026, more than three times the European Union average of 5.3%, according to Eurostat data.
Between April and June, travelers spent 258.8 million nights in short-term accommodations across the EU booked through Airbnb, Booking.com or Expedia. That figure was 13.1 million nights higher than in the second quarter of 2025 and 50.0 million above the level recorded in the same period of 2024, when growth stood at 23.9%.
In Bulgaria, 1,047,274 overnight stays were recorded in the second quarter of 2025, with the number rising by 16.5% a year later.
Bulgaria’s increase was among the stronger results in Southeast Europe. Greece posted an 18.3% rise, while Romania saw growth of 14.6%, putting all three countries in the double-digit range for overnight stays booked online, compared with the more moderate increase across the EU.
Eurostat’s figures cover short-term accommodation units offered through Airbnb, Booking.com and Expedia Group, highlighting the growing role of online platforms in the selection and booking of such stays.
The largest volumes of online-booked overnight stays in Europe continued to be concentrated in traditionally strong tourism markets. The European total reached 258.8 million nights in the second quarter of 2026, 50.0 million more than in the corresponding period of 2024.
Bulgaria, Romania and Greece all posted double-digit growth while the European market as a whole expanded by 5.3%.

Ethiopian federal forces control Tigray capital as regional rivals meet in Egypt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04

19:22:43 KST

Ethiopian federal forces control Tigray capital as regional rivals meet in Egypt
Troops loyal to Ethiopia's federal government were patrolling the streets of Mekelle on Sunday, a day after the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) withdrew its forces from the northern city. The government advance came as Ethiopia's regional rivals including Eritrea and Sudan met in the Egyptian coastal city of El-Alamein, calling for regional disputes to be settled through "peaceful means".
Ethiopian federal forces were in full control of the Tigray rebels' regional capital, a local journalist said on Sunday, while Ethiopia's regional rivals gathered in Egypt to discuss the risk of a wider war.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and federal forces began fighting again on September 23, sparking fears of a return to the devastating civil war of 2020-2022.
The presidents of Egypt, Somalia, Sudan and Eritrea – all of whom have difficult relations with Ethiopia – met in the Egyptian coastal city of El-Alamein on Sunday, calling for regional disputes to be settled through "peaceful means", according to an Egyptian presidency statement.
They also stressed "the necessity of respecting the rules of international law, the principles of good neighbourliness, and non-interference in the internal affairs of states" in the Horn of Africa, the statement read.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of directly backing the Tigray rebels, with the added support of Sudan and Egypt, which all three countries deny.
In a counter-offensive, Ethiopian forces have pushed deep into rebel-held territory, entering the regional capital, Mekelle, on Saturday without a fight, as TPLF leaders and troops abandoned the city.
Read moreEthiopia's Tigray rebels abandon regional capital Mekelle as government forces enter city
On Sunday, federal troops were patrolling Mekelle and manning key institutions, a local journalist told AFP, as communications were restored for the first time in more than a week.
"We have taken control of Mekelle and we are marching forward," a commander with a pro-government militia told AFP.
Shops closed
Businesses and shops remained closed. Owners had moved stock to safer locations ahead of time, fearing looting and vandalism.
"There are no police," one resident told AFP, speaking like others on condition of anonymity because of the uncertainty of the situation.
"Last night, we had to organise ourselves and take care of security."
"The fact that the war is beginning to lower in intensity brings some immediate relief," said Tewodros, another resident who did not want to give his full name.
"But as seems to be spreading across the region, I'm scared it will drag on," he added.
There are growing fears the fighting could spill over the border into Eritrea.
Egypt mini-summit
The mini-summit in Alamein – on the sidelines of an African business forum – brought together Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, Somalian President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) head Abdel Fattah al-Burhan.
Before the talks, Sisi called for dialogue to settle cross-border issues, as concerns grew that Ethiopia's escalating violence could spill across borders.
Eritrea, which shares a long border with the Tigray region, is most directly involved in the conflict.
It accuses landlocked Ethiopia of planning to invade and seize access to its coastline. Analysts say it has backed the rebels in Ethiopia to try to keep the conflict away from its border.
Read moreEthiopia accuses Eritrea, Sudan of backing Tigray rebels amid clashes
The TPLF has long been the dominant force in Tigray, ousting a government-appointed administration this year.
The rebels' leader, Debretsion Gebremichael, has implied that the group would continue guerrilla-style attacks, as it did when Mekelle fell to government forces in 2020 during the last war.
Their insurgent campaign ultimately led to the TPLF retaking the city the following year.
"We operate under a strategy to strike the enemy wherever we choose," said Debretsion.
'Unilateral'
A joint statement released after Sunday's talks in Egypt expressed the countries' "complete rejection of any unilateral measures" that could harm the existing water use of downstream states.
This comes against the backdrop of Egypt's long-running dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) on the Blue Nile.
Cairo and Khartoum have for years sought a legally binding agreement governing the dam's operation, citing concerns over water security. Ethiopia says the project is crucial to its economic development and energy needs.
More than a decade of negotiations have failed to yield a settlement.
The TPLF ruled all of Ethiopia from 1991 until 2018, when it was marginalised with the rise of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who hails from the Oromia region.
The tensions led to a civil war from 2020 to 2022 that killed more than 600,000 people, according to the African Union, making it one of the deadliest conflicts in the world in recent times.
The Pretoria peace agreement of 2022, brokered by African institutions and Washington, was never fully implemented but still helped keep a degree of peace until last year.

Spain protests flare after housing bill rejected: Will it cause snap poll?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:16:49 UTC
19:16:49 KST

Spain protests flare after housing bill rejected: Will it cause snap poll?
Sharp rise in rents triggers mass protests, but conservative MPs vote against measures to tackle the crisis.
Tens of thousands of people have rallied across Spain as protests have spread since the conservative-dominated parliament rejected a bill proposing measures to tackle a housing crisis.
Parliament on Friday voted down two decrees proposed by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s minority left-wing coalition government that were intended to address the housing crisis.
The protests erupted late last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home of 70 years in the capital, Madrid. Maria del Carmen Abascal’s eviction came after an international investment fund bought her building and hiked the rent.
Local media reports have suggested that Sanchez could call snap elections for as early as November after watching the strength of Saturday’s protests across the country. Spain’s current legislative term is set to end next summer.
Will the housing crisis trigger snap elections? Here’s what we know:
What happened on Friday in parliament?
The emergency measures proposed by Spain’s leftist government to tackle the country’s housing affordability crisis failed to pass on Friday.
The government had proposed two measures to protect renters in the country. The first decree was meant to stop evictions of vulnerable people, make real estate speculation harder, impose tighter restrictions on short-term leases and provide tax incentives to encourage renting and the construction of housing.
The second decree proposed making leases automatically renew when they are set to expire, essentially making them indefinite. A property owner would have to pay a tenant 12 months of rent to break the contract.
Sanchez, who leads a coalition government composed of his Socialist Party and the far-left Sumar, appealed to lawmakers in the run-up to the vote to put aside political calculations and pressure.
“Think about ordinary people, about those who most need the protection of public institutions. Think about the millions of young people who cannot afford to move out of their parents’ homes. Think about the families living with the constant anxiety of ever-rising rents,” he said before the voting.
But his government’s proposed measures were shot down by the majority of the 350-seat lower house of parliament.
The right-wing Catalan separatist party Junts refused to back the housing decrees, saying they would ultimately tighten the housing market. The centre-right Popular Party and far-right Vox also voted against the measures.
Miriam Nogueras of Junts argued the decrees would lead only to owners removing their properties from the rental market and thus driving up prices even further.
“If they really wanted to protect people, collar the vulture funds, and reactivate housing, they would have already done it. They’ve had eight years,” she added on X, referring to Sanchez’s government.
Health Minister Monica Garcia said on X that the right-wing parties “have voted for a feudal economy in which a minority extracts the salary from a majority that works for their luxuries. And they do it against their own voters, who also suffer increasingly high rents, live in fear that the contract will end and can even be evicted.”
“Today the right has given rent-seeking a parliamentary majority that it doesn’t have on the street, but it’s going to pay for it sooner rather than later,” she added.
Before the parliamentary vote, Marta Soler Gallart, head of the Department of Sociology at the University of Barcelona, explained that neither of the two decrees addressed the housing problem in the medium or long term.
“Models such as Vienna’s with its low rents are cited in support of these decrees, but it is overlooked that the Vienna model and others have low rents because of their long history of creating and maintaining public social housing,” Soler Gallart told Al Jazeera on September 30.
“In Spain, however, public funds are invested in social housing which, after a while, the recipients sell at market price.”
Soler Gallart also said the new measures disadvantage landlords with small or few properties by extending five-year tenancy agreements by a further two years and by providing an indefinite extension of their leases.
“However, these extensions are not compulsory if the landlord can prove that they need the property for their own use,” she said.
Why are people protesting across Spain?
Protests erupted across Spain in late September after 87-year-old Abascal was evicted from her home. The investment fund that bought her building hiked her rent by more than 200 percent to roughly $1,880 a month, a move aimed at pushing out the long-term tenant to make way for lucrative tourist apartments.
In recent years, Spain has seen protests against mass tourism, which has been linked to the housing crisis and soaring cost of living. Spain is the second most visited country in the world, attracting 97 million tourists last year.
While Abascal has returned to her home, according to her representatives, she has become the face of the country’s housing crisis, and people across Spain have been demanding the government address the issue.
Angered by parliament’s rejection of the government measures, tens of thousands of people took to the streets.
“It’s a shame,” Nando de Anguulo, 26, who joined Saturday’s protest in Madrid, told the Reuters news agency.
“It only proves that it is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.”
While the protests were mostly peaceful, in the southeastern city of Valencia, police fired rubber bullets and tear gas to break up demonstrations. About 30 protesters managed to get inside the City of Arts and Sciences, a landmark cultural building, before police removed them.
Meanwhile, in Madrid, Spanish police arrested three members of a far-right group and fired rubber bullets on Saturday night.
Far-right activists, some of whom performed Nazi salutes, tried to reach demonstrators camped out in the Puerta del Sol, a central square in the Spanish capital, the Spanish government said.
Valeria Racu, a spokesperson for the Tenants’ Union, said Saturday’s rallies revealed “a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time and energy that is showing that eight days of people’s power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government”.
“Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” Racu added.
Could the housing crisis lead to snap elections?
Housing is a sensitive issue in Spain because it impacts how people vote. The average rent in the country has almost doubled in the past 10 years. The average price per square metre has risen from 8.20 euros (about $9.08 at the time) in 2016 to 15.1 euros ($17.15) this year, according to the real estate website Idealista.
In an October 1 article for Vanity Fair, Spanish journalist Jorge Dioni Lopez noted that after eight years in power, housing is what is causing Sanchez to lose support among educated young people, children of the middle classes.
“The government faces a difficult situation. Firstly, because most of the relevant powers lie with other levels of government. Secondly, because Spain is a nation of homeowners. Unlike in other European countries, almost all the public housing that has been built has ended up in private hands, and historically, homeownership has been more attractive than renting,” he wrote.
“Housing is our savings system and also the primary means of transmitting wealth between generations,” he added.
After Spain’s parliament rejected the government’s housing reform bills on Friday, the leader of the centre-right People’s Party, (PP) Alberto Nunez Feijoo, urged Sanchez to “call elections as soon as possible”, claiming he had the support of “neither the streets nor parliament”.
While Sanchez has not officially announced new elections, the Spanish online news site El Diario has reported that elections could take place as early as November 29. Spain’s general elections are currently scheduled for July 2027.

Syria's Kurdish fault line deepens amid rival protests
Protests in northeast Syria are exposing competing demands over the region's reintegration into the Syrian state, as demonstrations calling for greater government control coincide with a growing Kurdish movement demanding protection for Kurdish-language education.
Hundreds of people took to the streets of Hasakah on Friday under the slogan "Friday for the Restoration of Sovereignty", demanding that Damascus assert full state authority over the ethnically diverse northeastern province.
The demonstration began after Friday prayers at the Abu Bakr al-Siddiq Mosque in Hasakah's Ghweiran neighbourhood before proceeding towards the governorate square, according to The New Arab.
A separate protest was held in Ras al-Ain in support of the Hasakah demonstration.
Protesters called for an end to the parallel security and administrative structures that have persisted during efforts to integrate the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) and institutions associated with the Autonomous Administration into the Syrian state.
The "Free People of Hasakah Gathering", which called for the demonstrations, also demanded that government appointments be based on competence rather than political or regional quotas, and called for fair representation for the province's Arab, Kurdish and Syriac communities.
Journalist Hassan Abdullah al-Khalaf said the Syrian government had waited too long to fully establish its authority in Hasakah.
"Does it make sense for Hasakah to have two municipalities, two emergency-police and traffic-police branches, two armies, two transport departments, two licence plates for the same car and two driving licences?" he told The New Arab.
Yet the demonstrations come amid a separate wave of Kurdish protests over fears that the return of Syrian government institutions could erode linguistic rights established during more than a decade of autonomous administration.
Students and teachers have staged demonstrations and school strikes across Hasakah province against a Syrian Education Ministry decision limiting Kurdish-language teaching to three classes a week.
Schools in Ma'bada and Rmeilan saw student strikes on Thursday, while protests have also taken place in Qamishli and other predominantly Kurdish areas.
Protesters have demanded the right to receive education in their mother tongue and constitutional recognition of Kurdish as an official language.
The Syrian rights groups said the protests had expanded in recent weeks, with students arguing that three weekly classes were insufficient to preserve Kurdish-language education.
The controversy stems from implementing instructions issued by the Education Ministry in August allowing Kurdish to be taught as a "national language" in public and private schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations, with three lessons allocated each week.
Kurdish campaigners argue the measure falls well short of the education system developed in areas governed by the Autonomous Administration, where Kurdish has been used as a language of instruction.
Lawyer Bashira Jamal al-Din said on Sunday that all subjects should be available in Kurdish and called for linguistic rights to be guaranteed in Syria's constitution.
"Three lessons are not enough to teach the mother tongue," she said, according to the Kurdish Hawar News Agency.
The two protest movements highlight the difficult questions surrounding the implementation of agreements reached this year between Damascus and the SDF.
Those agreements envisage the integration of military and civilian institutions in northeast Syria into the Syrian state, and government security forces have already begun deploying in Hasakah as part of the process.
For some residents, however, integration has moved too slowly and left an unwieldy system of competing authorities responsible for security and public services.
For Kurdish protesters, the same process has raised a different concern - whether the restoration of central government authority will come at the expense of political and cultural rights established during the years of autonomous rule.
Political analyst Samer al-Ahmad told The New Arab that the pro-government demonstrations were not directed against the integration agreements themselves, but were intended to pressure the authorities to implement them fully.

Bulgaria Sets Nuclear Expansion as Energy Priority
Energy Minister Iva Petrova said Bulgaria must build on its decades of nuclear expertise to develop new capacity and modernize its technology, identifying Units 7 and 8 at the Kozloduy Nuclear Power Plant as a specific priority.
Speaking at the opening of the Fifth International Nuclear Conference, organized by the Bulgarian Energy and Mining Forum, Petrova said nuclear power would remain a central element of Bulgaria's energy security.
She said the conference's motto, "From Ambition to Implementation," was especially timely because "today, the time for action has truly arrived."
Petrova described nuclear energy as a strategic choice linked to energy security, economic competitiveness and the country's future.
"The question is not whether to develop nuclear energy, but rather how to do so in the safest, most technologically and economically sustainable manner," Petrova said.
She stressed that Bulgaria has more than five decades of experience in operating nuclear facilities, along with a professional community and substantial expert capacity. According to Petrova, this base should support the sector's development over the coming decades.
She said expanding nuclear capacity would involve more than electricity production, bringing investment, new technologies, industrial development and highly skilled employment. The government is also following developments related to small modular reactors.
"Our goal is for the largest possible share of this value added to remain within the Bulgarian economy and for Bulgarian companies to play an active role in the supply chain," Petrova said.
She also highlighted the importance of educating and training the next generation of specialists for the sector.

Turkish officials visit Riyadh as Mecca alliance gains momentum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:12:00 UTC
19:12:00 KST

Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will be joined by National Defense Minister Yaşar Güler and Chief of General Staff Selçuk Bayraktaroğlu on a visit to Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh on Monday.
They will attend a meeting of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee of the historic Mecca Joint Defense Alliance, formed by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in August. The meeting comes amid rising threats to Saudi Arabia by the Houthis in Yemen.
Foreign Ministry sources said on Sunday that Fidan would reaffirm Türkiye’s strong solidarity with and support for Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks and underline that provocative acts targeting sacred sites are unacceptable. Saudi Arabia is the birthplace of Islam and home to its most sacred site, the Kaaba, located in Mecca. Mecca has recently come under fire from the Houthis.
The Houthi group said on Saturday that it targeted Saudi oil company Aramco in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones in response to attacks on the Yemeni capital, Sanaa.
The operation “successfully achieved its objective,” causing fires at the targeted sites, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a televised statement.
Saree added that Sanaa and other provinces had been subjected to 60 airstrikes over the last 24 hours, bringing the total number of strikes to 1,420. He attributed the attacks to Saudi Arabia.
The spokesperson warned that the group would respond to “blockade with blockade, and escalation with escalation.”
Meanwhile, Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government, said in remarks carried by Saudi media, including Asharq Al-Awsat, that Houthi claims of targeting Riyadh on Saturday were “misleading.”
He added that the Houthis were trying to “divert attention from the scale of their losses and growing public anger over the militias’ conduct and their ties to foreign agendas that have brought chaos and destruction to Yemen.”
Since March 2015, Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government against Houthi forces, which have controlled Sanaa and several other governorates since September 2014.
In July this year, the Houthis announced a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, saying the move was in response to a Saudi naval and air siege on areas under their control in Yemen. The group has since targeted energy infrastructure in the kingdom.
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Pakistani Prime Minister Muhammad Shahbaz Sharif and Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud signed the Mecca agreement for joint defense in Mecca on Aug. 7, 2026. The agreement aims to bolster the security of Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia through joint deterrence and defense, and reflects the three countries’ commitment to developing regional solutions to regional issues and their shared strategic vision centered on regional security and stability.
A Strategic Political and Defense Committee, comprising the foreign and defense ministers and chiefs of general staff of the three countries, was established to guide activities under the agreement. The committee held its inaugural meeting in Istanbul on Aug. 31, 2026. At the meeting, foundational decisions were adopted, and technical work toward institutionalizing the alliance was reviewed. Accordingly, the alliance’s secretariat is expected to be established in Riyadh as soon as possible. Retired Pakistani Lt. Gen. Nauman Mahmood has been nominated to serve as its first secretary-general.
The foreign ministers of the three countries held a meeting in New York on Sept. 24, 2026, on the sidelines of the High-Level Week of the 81st United Nations General Assembly. Regional developments were discussed at the meeting. In a joint statement issued afterward, the three countries condemned attacks targeting the holy city of Mecca and Saudi Arabia’s civilian and economic infrastructure. The chiefs of general staff of the three countries met in Riyadh on Sept. 25, 2026.
Turkish sources said Fidan would convey Türkiye’s views on the next steps for the alliance and its institutionalization process. He will also offer Türkiye’s assessment of threats to peace and stability in the Middle East and views on regional developments related to the joint security of the allies. He is also expected to highlight how the alliance’s progress in a short time has proved valuable for the prospects of lasting stability in the region, as well as the importance of the alliance both in building capacity for a joint and efficient response to existing threats and in preventing regional crises.
Fidan is also expected to underline the prioritization of peaceful means to resolve conflicts in the region and the need to avoid steps that may escalate tensions. He will also stress the importance of ensuring the freedom and security of navigation on international trade routes and discuss how Israel has continued to undermine efforts for regional peace and stability.
In an interview last month, Fidan said the alliance had reached an advanced stage, with efforts underway to establish its headquarters and assign personnel, describing the initiative as a “very game-changing platform.” Fidan also implied that Türkiye stood ready to provide technical assistance to Saudi Arabia amid an escalating conflict with the Houthis in Yemen.
Fidan stated that there is “a very strong will” behind the alliance and that Ankara is working to turn that political will into action.
“The Mecca alliance is really at a good stage. There’s a very strong will that has been put forward. We’re working with all our strength to put this will into action,” Fidan told broadcaster NTV last month.
He said steps toward institutionalizing the alliance are underway, particularly work to establish a secretariat envisaged under the agreement and a military headquarters affiliated with it. He added that detailed preparations for both structures have “almost been completed” and that the three countries have reached a common understanding of how they will operate.
“There are steps currently being taken toward institutionalization. In particular, the work on establishing the secretariat mentioned in the agreement and bringing an affiliated military headquarters into operation is almost complete. We have reached a common understanding. From now on, the remaining stage is to send personnel and make the headquarters operational. I am pleased with the process on this issue,” Fidan said.
He said that once institutionalization steps are completed, talks could be held with the other two founding countries on admitting new members.
“There is such a principle decision because our president said this from the beginning. If this does not grow, then it would not be an alliance area. We would have created a bloc. Our regional vision is for as many countries in the region as possible to come together and establish a common defense area.
“This defense area is not against outsiders; it is about solving problems within the region better through regional ownership and creating an environment of trust that has not existed before, in order to prevent new crises from emerging. The basic point of departure for all of this is the search for regional solutions to regional problems,” Fidan said.
He stressed that the alliance was not intended to create a new regional bloc against other countries but to establish a common defense framework based on regional ownership.
“It is an alliance open to the countries of the region,” he said.
