IDF forces dig in for a long winter deep inside southern Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:11:01 UTC
19:11:01 KST

After 100 days of intensive mobilization, including 80 days of determined fighting in Lebanon, the IDF’s 55th Reserve Paratroopers Brigade has completed another significant chapter in a campaign focused primarily on clearing the area between the border and the Yellow Line. 
Security officials explained that capturing the territory was only the first stage, while clearing it was the main phase the forces moved into afterward. The soldiers encountered a complex reality along the Yellow Line and described staggering quantities of weapons uncovered in virtually every house, as well as the resilience of reservists who report for duty time and again despite the heavy personal cost.
The 55th Brigade is now being replaced by forces from the Bislamach Brigade and by troops from the Gefen Battalion of the officers’ course. The forces are preparing for the difficult winter days in southern Lebanon, carrying out drills and improving key positions from which they will be able to maintain observation and fire control deep into the area. This marks a highly significant point, with concern that forces could settle into a routine of securing the defensive line without offensive activity, exposing them to a range of risks, from road and training accidents to erosion in the security of the Yellow Line. Remaining on a defensive line alone could also invite enemy attacks.
Against that backdrop, two operational accidents occurred over the weekend in which IDF soldiers were injured. In one incident, two IDF vehicles operating under the 36th Division collided, leaving several soldiers lightly wounded. In another incident in the western sector under the 91st Division, two soldiers were seriously and moderately wounded as a result of improper handling of a grenade. Such incidents are exceptional, but they also underscore the new reality the forces are entering in southern Lebanon.
After many months of strikes and proactive operations deep inside the territory, the forces are moving into a different mode of operation that they will have to adapt to, focusing now on forward and offensive defense and later on continued clearing of the area. The reservists of the 55th Brigade have completed an 80-day mission in Lebanon, with their main task focused on defending along the Yellow Line in southern Lebanon, where the sector extends up to 12 kilometers from the border.
The most distinctive and challenging feature of the mission was a pocket containing two villages that had not been fully cleared, Majdal Zoun and, in particular, al-Mansouri. According to security officials, the enemy used the period since the ceasefire to prepare the area thoroughly and in a threatening manner against the forces. During the brigade’s operations, more than 600 terror infrastructure sites were destroyed, including eight shafts, dozens of explosive devices and dozens of launchers found in homes and open areas, along with numerous weapons depots.
“Almost every house contained an unusually large stockpile of weapons. Often there were boxes of grenades, vests and helmets, and sometimes actual depots containing 20 to 30 weapons, enough to equip a platoon-size force,” a security official explained. During the operation, the forces employed all the capabilities at their disposal, captured both villages and eliminated many Hezbollah terrorists. At first, the terrorists were documented moving weapons inside homes, after which they were struck.
Another central mission was enforcing the security area after Hezbollah attempted to cross the Yellow Line and enter the zone in which the IDF is stationed. Around 10 terrorists were eliminated through a combination of tanks, the Air Force and drones. The assessment is that Hezbollah will continue trying to infiltrate pockets along the Yellow Line and again attempt to harm IDF soldiers.
The operational concept on the ground has changed fundamentally since Oct. 7, and security officials stress that “the defensive component has become offensive and is based on deep security areas, based on the understanding that the army has learned that you don’t defend from the gate line. You defend Nahariya from Majdal Zoun, 12 kilometers deep, which creates depth in the defense, offensive defense, a large security area and margins that provide breathing room,” the senior official explained.
Regarding emerging threats such as explosive drones or fiber-optic drones, the IDF says they represent a significant operational challenge for the next maneuver. There is still no broad, systematic solution to the threat, and a number of systems are being tested, some of them in the field and some already distributed to soldiers. For the troops, the main focus in dealing with the threat is proper protection, along with timely detection and warning.
Alongside reports of strikes by such drones, many dozens are being successfully intercepted and defeated, while the 91st Division and Northern Command are engaged in a significant learning process. Northern Command officials say the current strategic starting point is particularly favorable for the next maneuver because the IDF is positioned along the deepest section of the Yellow Line and at jumping-off points toward Hezbollah centers of gravity. “Once the order is given, the forces are one night away from Tyre, which makes it far easier to tighten offensive capabilities,” a security official explained.
The challenge: the fighters’ families
Beyond the operational achievements, the heart of the issue remains the people. Some 4,500 soldiers from the reserve paratroopers brigade, many serving their fourth or fifth round of fighting, operated continuously through the holidays. The greatest challenge is on the family home front and in the prolonged strain of 100 days under reserve call-up orders. To provide as much assistance as possible, the brigade established a comprehensive family support system, ranging from activities for family members to contacting university lecturers to seek accommodations for reservist students and sending personal thank-you letters to employers for their consideration.
Ahead of the winter months, the forces prepared in advance to ensure full operational readiness. According to security officials, after the structures were equipped during the summer with generators, air conditioners and sanitation infrastructure, the troops are now staying for the Lebanese winter in protected compounds inside the villages rather than outdoors, while the routes were prepared in advance.
With the current mission complete and the brigade returning to storage readiness, attention is already turning forward, and the forces are aware that they may be called up again in 2027 after debriefing and expectation-setting talks were held with them. Regarding the cumulative strain on the reserve force, security officials say the issue must continue to be managed carefully because the burden is substantial. The central challenge is the private sector, where soldiers called up order after order and the companies bearing the burden face real difficulties.
According to the officials, commanders are doing everything possible to take individual circumstances into account and act according to each soldier’s ability to report for duty. Security officials conclude that a threat cannot be allowed to remain close to the border, and therefore this activity and the continued presence there are absolutely necessary for defense and significantly reduce the threat of raids on northern communities in future rounds.

Effect of research paper mills enough to start affecting LLM query results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:11:00 UTC
19:11:00 KST

Effect of research paper mills enough to start affecting LLM query results
Scientific paper mills and AI-generated content are posing a growing threat to research integrity, while retractions reveal only a fraction of the problem, TalTech researcher Anton Sokolov says.
In early September, a Novaator experiment showed how easily co-authorship of a scientific paper can be purchased on the black market from paper mills. With just a few WhatsApp messages, 20 days and $800, it is possible to become an author of a scientific paper ready for publication. But misconduct involving authorship is only one part of a much broader problem concerning the integrity of scientific literature.
After the experiment was published, Anton Sokolov, a doctoral student at Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) and a researcher at the Tyche Institute, contacted Novaator. As part of his own research, he has taken a closer look at what happens to bogus science once it makes its way into databases. Among the sources Sokolov uses in his research is the Retraction Watch database, which compiles retractions of scientific papers and other cases involving research integrity from around the world.
"If we look at Retraction Watch's public database, there are about 61,000 retracted papers from 2010 to 2025. Currently, about two papers per thousand are retracted each year. The number of retractions shows how much is being cleaned up, not how much garbage remains," Sokolov said.
As part of his research, Sokolov compiled a dataset containing nearly 15,000 retraction records focusing on computer science literature. Analysis of the data showed that violations directly related to authorship accounted for less than 2 percent of cases. "But the small proportion does not mean that authorship is rarely sold. The notice shows what the publisher was able to prove, not how much is actually being sold," he explained.
The latter is precisely what makes the issue difficult for publishers. Such transactions usually take place in private conversations and there is nothing in the published text that unequivocally indicates that authorship was purchased.
For this reason, Sokolov said, retraction notices much more frequently cite problems with peer review. "A single notice usually lists several reasons at once, with peer-review problems cited in about seven out of 10 cases," he added.
Computer-generated content has also become an increasingly serious problem in academia in recent years. According to Sokolov, for example, the most common reason for retractions in computer science and artificial intelligence is computer-generated text, accounting for about one-third of cases.
In 2023, the number of officially retracted scientific papers exceeded 10,000 for the first time. Sokolov said, however, that the figure reveals little about the true prevalence of problematic papers because the vast majority of retracted papers came from large-scale cleanup programs by a handful of academic publishers. "The number of retractions simultaneously measures the problem itself, its detection and classification and a publisher's ability to see cases through to completion — not the actual prevalence of problematic authorship or the use of artificial intelligence," the researcher said.
Cases involving Estonian scientists
Retraction Watch, a website that monitors research integrity, also lists papers co-authored by Estonian researchers. "As of September, there are 13 retractions linked to Estonian institutions and 11 of them involve co-authors from other countries. About half are older cases, involving issues such as duplicate publication or errors in analysis. The rest are more recent, dating from 2023 onward and involve problems with the review of the papers or their data," Sokolov explained.
According to Retraction Watch data, one retraction linked to Estonia is also flagged as involving a paper mill. "But that does not show whether any of the authors here purchased authorship," Sokolov said.
The researcher believes the impact of paper mills could also extend to artificial intelligence systems. Because large language models are trained on material found online and in scientific publications, flawed or manipulated research can also make its way into them. "The risk is real and it has already been measured. In a study published last year, a language model was asked to assess retracted or questionable papers. In more than 6,500 assessments, it did not mention the retraction even once," the researcher said.
The problem is that artificial intelligence may absorb bogus scientific material even before a paper is officially retracted. The publicly available text-screening tool Problematic Paper Screener has flagged tens of thousands of papers as questionable. According to Sokolov's preliminary pilot calculation, more than 20,000 of these papers had not been retracted as of June.
One possible solution, he said, would be to use digital signatures to verify authorship of scientific publications. "At the moment, an author of a scientific paper is simply a name in the text. In Estonia, we use our ID cards to sign contracts and applications; similarly, each author could digitally sign off on their contribution," Sokolov suggested.
He said digital identification of authors and other parties involved in scientific publishing would help increase transparency and make it more difficult to manipulate authorship. "This has not yet been implemented, but we plan to continue this research," he said.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Houthi claims of attack on Saudi capital 'misleading'

Fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is supported by Saudi Arabia, reignited in July, with the group also launching numerous attacks on Saudi territory.

Last month the Houthis also claimed to have attacked an oil facility in the Saudi port city of Yanbu, a major oil terminal on the Red Sea.
After several years of calm, Yemen was plunged back into civil war in July, pitting the Houthis, who control most of northwest Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, against the country's government and its longtime Saudi backers.
The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of Yemen's south and east - a region that is larger but less populated.

Brazil’s Flavio Bolsonaro beats polls in presidential vote, faces incumbent Lula in runoff

- The campaign focused on corruption scandals, economic worries, and accusations of US interference, with voters showing frustration and many undecided ahead of the runoff.
- Economic challenges, rising public debt, and a major fraud investigation involving Bolsonaro and judiciary figures overshadow the election, while legislative races increase political stakes.
AI generated
BRASILIA/SAO PAULO/RIO DE JANEIRO – Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro will face President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the runoff of a presidential election, the country’s electoral authority said on Oct 4.
With just over 97% of the ballots counted, the right-wing challenger took 47.45% of valid votes in the first round, beating the forecasts in most private surveys. 
Leftist Lula received 44.66% of the votes.
The two leading candidates will advance to the second round of voting on Oct 25, beating out a field of 12 candidates in a campaign focused on concerns about the growing cost of living, corruption and insecurity in Brazilians’ daily lives.
Flavio, the 45-year-old son of former president Jair Bolsonaro who hopes to return his father’s right-wing movement to power, led Lula, 80, who is seeking a fourth term, following a campaign dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling.
A candidate must pass 50% in order to win outright in the first round.
The two leading candidates were expected to head into a second round vote, Brazilian pollster Datafolha said. Surveys have shown Lula and Flavio polling roughly even in an Oct 25 run-off.
Early results showed southern states that lean to Bolsonaro reporting faster, while votes from Lula’s north-east stronghold are tallied more slowly.
Analysts told Reuters they believed Flavio was receiving “protest votes” of people voting against Lula rather than for the right-wing senator – votes they had been expected to save until a second round.
A victory for the senator would extend a wave of wins across Latin America by right-wing candidates aligned with US President Donald Trump, while Lula’s reelection could create a headache for Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.
Despite growing worries over Brazil’s public finances and sluggish economic growth, the campaign offered meagre policy debate, as both leading candidates skipped the major TV debates.
Undecided voters
While polls right up until Oct 3 showed Lula would likely lead the first round but not avoid a runoff, Flavio told journalists in Rio de Janeiro he was confident he could win the presidency in the first round, citing voters’ frustration with his chief opponent.
Flavio was counting on “a protest vote from people who would otherwise vote for another candidate but are opposed to Lula”, he said. “I hope it’s enough to secure a victory in the first round.”
Thaise Lima, a 41-year-old lawyer on her way to vote in Sao Paulo, said her main goal was to get Lula’s Workers’ Party out of office.
“I don’t think Flavio is the best candidate, but I might decide to vote for him in the next few minutes,” she said, adding that she wished psychiatrist and author Augusto Cury were a more viable candidate.
Fernando Tempel, 49, a management consultant, told Reuters he was voting for Flavio despite initially planning to vote for Romeu Zema, the former governor of Minas Gerais state.
Outside interference
On the other hand, Lula’s allies have warned that the Trump administration might refuse to recognise election results if he wins, pointing to an aborted effort to send US officials to Brazil.
“What is at stake is the future of Brazil,” Lula said after voting in Sao Bernardo do Campo, in Sao Paulo state.
Trump has not formally endorsed a candidate, though he hosted Senator Flavio Bolsonaro at the White House and praised him publicly.
“I’m a little worried about everything that’s been happening recently, including internationally. I feel this election has had a lot of outside influence, more than in previous elections,” said Cristiano, 34, a doctor in Brasilia who voted for Lula and preferred to withhold his surname.
“We are confident in our President Lula, who will fight for national sovereignty,” said Pedro Palacio, 45, who was voting in Brasilia alongside his wife, Andreia, and their two sons and two dogs, all of whom wore outfits supporting the president.
As at the afternoon of Oct 4, the election was proceeding normally, Brazil’s electoral court chief Kassio Nunes Marques said in a press conference.
“Teams monitoring international risks have not identified any risks whatsoever,” he said.
Reuters reported on Sept 30 that Brazilian intelligence officials briefed a French and German delegation on alleged US and Russian interference before the election. The US has rejected claims of interference in Brazil’s affairs.
Economic headwinds
Despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over voters grappling with high living costs, heavy household debt and the threat of street crime and more pervasive gang activity.
Flavio Bolsonaro has sought to capitalise on cost-of-living concerns, while Lula has moved to ban online gambling and, as the race tightened, expanded welfare and proposed fresh debt relief for families.
Rising spending and public debt above 82% of gross domestic product have stoked fiscal concerns that Brazil’s next president will need to address. The government lowered its economic growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 to just 2.0% and 2.3% respectively.
“I voted for Brazil to start growing again,” said Marciano de Souza e Silva, a 52-year-old public servant in Brasilia and former Lula voter who moved right, voting for Jair Bolsonaro in 2018 and 2022 and Flavio on Oct 4.
“The best social programme is one that encourages people to start businesses, to actually produce real wealth,” he said.
Scandal-plagued campaigns
Overshadowing the policy debate, a scandal surrounding the now-defunct Banco Master has engulfed much of Brazil’s political class and renewed public anger over corruption.
Daniel Vorcaro, who ran the bank, was arrested earlier in 2026 and accused of a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme.
The investigation has probed the banker’s ties to figures from Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes to Flavio Bolsonaro, who is being investigated for money laundering tied to the case by the federal police.
The candidate has denied any wrongdoing, although he confirmed raising millions of dollars from Vorcaro to make a movie about his father.
The banker’s connections to Moraes, widely perceived as a Lula ally, plunged the court into crisis a month before the vote, creating fresh problems for the President.
Moraes has said the case against him is politically motivated for his role in the conviction of the elder Bolsonaro.
On Oct 4, voters will also elect all 513 lower house members and two-thirds of the Senate, where some lawmakers have pushed to impeach Moraes.
Congress has gained greater influence in Brazilian politics since the impeachment of former president Dilma Rousseff, a Lula ally, in 2016, raising the stakes of those legislative races. REUTERS

Poland and Romania refused to increase the transit of grain from Ukraine — media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:05:31 EEST
19:05:31 KST

Poland and Romania refused to increase the transit of grain from Ukraine — media
Kyiv • UNN
Poland and Romania said they cannot increase assistance to Ukraine with grain exports. Due to the blockade, up to 35 million tonnes could remain blocked.
Poland and Romania have said they can no longer do anything to help Ukraine export grain through Europe, as the blockade of the Black Sea continues, UNN reports, citing Politico.
Details
The publication emphasizes that concerns of local farmers outweigh EU solidarity with Kyiv, while the blockade of the Black Sea threatens to deepen the global food crisis and disrupt next year’s harvest in Ukraine.
Ukraine needs help exporting millions of tonnes of grain, as attacks on ports and vessels have been ongoing for the third month already.
This week, Minister of Agrarian Policy Taras Vysotskyi arrived in Brussels to personally appeal to his counterparts from EU countries. Ukraine needs to increase the volume of agricultural products transported through Europe, as well as receive €1.1 billion to cover logistics costs. Without assistance, farmers facing an acute shortage of funds will be unable to begin next season’s sowing campaign, which will only exacerbate the problem.
"The situation is critical, very critical," Vysotskyi told Politico during his visit.
According to the publication, the response was: sorry, but no. The two countries with the most important infrastructure for expanding grain transportation and storage capacity — Poland and Romania — said they could not and would not do anything additional to help.
"The interests of our own farmers remain the priority," Romanian Agriculture Minister Barna Tanchosh told Politico. The surplus of Ukrainian grain, combined with low water levels in the Danube, is already overloading his country’s ports, preventing Romanian farmers from selling their own produce.
The media outlet notes that this refusal demonstrates the persistent gap between the EU’s ambitions to support Ukraine and domestic political realities. As one of the world’s "breadbaskets," Ukraine "poses a real threat to the welfare of European farmers, who are an influential voting bloc in many EU member states." Even before the escalation of hostilities in the Black Sea, Poland, Slovakia, and Hungary banned imports of Ukrainian grain.
According to Vysotskyi, less than half of the export volume can currently be transported through European rail, road, and river routes. If the blockade continues, up to 35 million tonnes of grain could remain blocked in Ukraine this year. Romania is trying to optimize its logistics, Tanchosh emphasized. Last month, Bucharest even signed a memorandum of understanding with Kyiv to simplify border crossings and improve rail connections.
But "everyone understands that we cannot double the number of trains, we cannot double the number of roads, railways, or port capacity," Tanchosh said. — "We have what we have."
In Poland, the Ministry of Infrastructure "does not plan to introduce any changes aimed at increasing the transit of Ukrainian agricultural products," ministry spokesperson Anna Shumanska said.
Although assistance will not arrive immediately, the EU has not ruled out the possibility of collective action. "We need to... resolve this issue," European Commissioner for Agriculture Christophe Hansen said this week, expressing concern about global food security, although he made no specific commitments.
Some capitals are proposing additional support. As Ukraine considers ports in the Netherlands and Germany as new routes for exporting its products, a spokesperson for Germany’s Agriculture Ministry said that Berlin is "making every effort in Europe to ensure the strengthening of alternative export routes."
Additionally
In the interview, Vysotskyi spoke about the harvested grain and oilseeds that are accumulating without buyers, leaving farmers without the funds needed to sow winter crops for next year’s harvest. "If the situation does not change by spring, this could lead to a reduction in sown areas of as much as 35–40%," he said.
The consequences will be felt far beyond Europe. Exchanges of strikes between Russia and Ukraine in the Black Sea could cause exports from both countries to decline, affecting more than 17% of global grain trade, according to a recent report by the Council on Foreign Relations. "The number of people who will find themselves on the brink of acute hunger because of the current crisis in the Black Sea could exceed the total number of battlefield casualties in the war between Russia and Ukraine," the report’s authors warn.

Russia targeted another major bridge in Kyiv Sunday, shortly after Germany’s chancellor arrived in the Ukrainian capital on surprise visit to demonstrate European support amid surge in attacks.

Zelenskyy told him people in Kyiv were suffering "terrible nights and days" from the relentless attacks, and called Ukraine's Russian adversaries "absolute barbarians."
"We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place," Merz said.
"These barbaric attacks on Ukrainian civilians must stop. These are war crimes committed daily here."
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a strike had damaged the road surface on the Northern Bridge – one of several connecting the eastern and western parts of the city over the Dnipro River that have been struck in recent days.
Images posted on social media appeared to show a missile slamming into the structure, sending up a fireball as traffic crossed.
Klitschko said Kyiv – largely spared from the devastation wrought near the frontlines in nearly two years of full-scale conflict – should now be on a war footing due to the surge in attacks.
A spate of round-the-clock attacks has hit residential areas, gas stations, schools, rail and communications infrastructure while near-constant air raid sirens disrupt daily life and put people on edge.
Merz said upon arrival that Ukraine "needs all our support in the coming weeks."
"If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us," he added.
Ukraine wants more Western military support, including advanced interceptors to shoot down Russia's new fast-moving, jet-powered drones.
On Sunday, Zelenskyy promised "important agreements." Government sources in Berlin said they were expected to agree on a new package of military support worth more than $1 billion.
The package includes combat drones and satellite technology to help Ukraine hit Russian launch sites, as well as for the joint production of drones to counter jet-powered drones, the German sources said.
"This support addresses the most significant current gap in Ukraine's air defense system. The impact is expected to be rapid and tangible," a source said.
Merz this week called for unity against Russia within NATO and the European Union as well as his own country, where the far-right, Moscow-friendly AfD opposition is on the rise.
There have been increasing fears in Europe that it could find itself in Russia's crosshairs, including from covert attacks, if Russia is not stopped in Ukraine.
On Saturday, Russia warned foreigners and diplomats to leave Kyiv, saying "massive" new airstrikes would hit the city.
The Russian foreign ministry said in a statement that "responsibility for any potential negative consequences would rest entirely with those who ignore this warning."
Moscow had issued a similar warning in May, but leaders from countries supporting Ukraine have defied the Russian warnings and continued to make visits.
"The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe's support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!" EU Ambassador Katarina Mathernova wrote on X Sunday.
Mathernova told AFP separately "nobody is moving," although European embassies always had contingency plans, including for winter, she added.
Russia has admitted deliberately targeting Ukraine's energy sector as winter approaches. Last year, similar attacks knocked out power and heating for days on end as temperatures plummeted to minus 20 degrees Celsius.
In Kyiv, which is home to some three million people, residents have begun considering what to do if that happens again. The government has also suggested the vulnerable and disabled should consider leaving.
German government sources said Merz's trip was expected to include an announcement of some 350 million euros for generators, transformer stations and grid repairs.

Like a ‘vertical roller coaster’: Simulating flight FZ1073’s sudden plunge

Unknown Publisher

Like a ‘vertical roller coaster’: Simulating flight FZ1073’s sudden plunge
- Flydubai flight FZ1073 plunged over 4,800m in 30 seconds after co-pilot Hammam al-Hammami attacked the pilot, causing a terrifying incident described as a "vertical roller coaster".
- Passengers overpowered the co-pilot, and a reserve crew safely landed the Boeing 737 MAX 8, praised by President Trump for withstanding extreme forces.
- Investigations reveal al-Hammami's background includes rejected airline applications and studies in aviation management, with Australian authorities probing his links to Australia.
AI generated
SHERFIELD ON LODDON, England – Flydubai’s flight FZ1073, which plunged more than 4,800m in about 30 seconds before being levelled out and landing safely, would have felt like a “vertical roller coaster”, according to an aviation instructor who recreated the descent in a flight simulator for Reuters.
The steep fall, after an attack on the captain by the co-pilot during a flight on Sept 30, would have put huge strain on the Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft – as well as the passengers and crew, said Alberto Paduanelli, owner of ALPA Simulation in Sherfield on Loddon, southern England.
The co-pilot of the flydubai jet, which was bound for Israel from Dubai, attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Oct 3, calling the incident a “terrorist attack”.
The co-pilot was identified as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national, two sources with knowledge of the investigation told Reuters.
UAE authorities did not immediately respond to a request for confirmation of his identity. Reuters could not independently reach al-Hammami for comment.
Flydubai says the circumstances surrounding the incident are still under investigation and it cannot comment further. Oman has yet to comment on the incident.
“A plunge of 16,000 feet (4,877 metres) over 30 seconds will feel like you are over on a very, very vertical roller coaster,” Paduanelli said, sitting at the controls of the simulator cockpit.
“The difference is that on the roller coaster, you know what’s happening,” he said, adding that with a sudden drop “you feel the negative g-force on your body”.
For passengers who are not strapped in, “Your body will literally lift from the seat”, he said.
Using a simulator to recreate the incident, Paduanelli said the aircraft’s autopilot disconnected before the plunge began, causing the jet to accelerate rapidly.
US President Donald Trump has praised the Boeing jet for withstanding the severe forces put on it during the incident. The plane was levelled out after passengers overpowered the co-pilot, before a reserve crew of pilots onboard landed the plane.
“It was an amazing show of precise and powerful structural planning and design,” Trump posted on Truth Social, adding that the 737 Max “was able to withstand G Forces and Strain far beyond what it was designed and expected to do”.
Boeing did not respond to a request for comment.
Aircraft are designed and tested to withstand substantial aerodynamic loads, but Paduanelli said a prolonged high-speed dive can place extreme strain on an airframe.
“This was nothing but a miracle that nothing was hurt apart from the captain, unfortunately, and that two pilots were onboard,” Paduanelli said.
Details about al-Hammami’s past have trickled out.
Royal Air Maroc told Reuters he did a three-month training with the airline in 2025 but his application to work there afterwards was rejected.
Buckinghamshire New University in Britain said he did a distance-learning course in aviation management with the institution, but no pilot training.
An Australian Federal Police spokesperson said on Oct 4 that the authorities there were investigating al-Hammami’s “links to Australia”.
A source briefed on the investigation said the co-pilot studied at a university in Melbourne. REUTERS

Off the Record: Teflon Rutte is on a mission to keep NATO together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:02:46 UTC
19:02:46 KST

Every week, Euronews' Chief Europe Editor Maria Tadeo breaks down the stories that made the week in Brussels and beyond. This week: her exclusive interview with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte — a man with Teflon skin.
Welcome back to Off the Record, after a hectic week in our newsroom.
The Brussels media loves to talk about itself, but we prefer to speak with the newsmakers. This week, Euronews hosted its first defence summit -and it made news. That's how I measure success and impact, and it's the only metric I care about. Talking about yourself is fine, but making news is better.
On stage, I sat down with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. I have covered the Dutchman for years, going back to his four terms as prime minister of the Netherlands, when he earned the nickname Teflon Mark.
In the green room, I told him that one of my craziest moments as a journalist in Brussels was a rough doorstep at the height of negotiations over the EU’s 2020 pandemic recovery fund: shaky cameras, people pushing, technicians tripping over each other as we waited for him to return to his hotel.
He remembered it in remarkable detail. He also reminded me that his Brussels hotel was the cheapest used by any of the leaders – others favoured the fancy Amigo – and reminisced about his post-summit walks from the Europa building back to his hotel. No official car, no police escort: the “cheapest and fastest” option.
That’s the thing about Mark Rutte. Most politicians have an ego, but he has always been very effective at pretending he doesn’t. He enjoys self-deprecation and, after a lifetime in politics, knows exactly when to switch on the charming small talk. Not bad for the often blunt Dutchman.
Rutte is approachable and leans into his caricature as a man who is simply there to serve. He understands that managing NATO in the age of Trump means cosying up to the US president – even at the expense of his own image – while preventing Russia’s war from spilling into allied territory.
If, by the end of his tenure, NATO is better funded and Washington is still on board, his “daddy” diplomacy – an unfortunate remark that still haunts him – will have been worth it. My guess is that he genuinely believes this is the right calculus, no matter the cringe.
On stage, he confirmed NATO responded to a provocative Russian letter sent to the alliance threatening to use its full arsenal – including nuclear weapons – if the territory of the Russian Federation came under threat. Moscow mentioned specifically its enclave of Kaliningrad, on the border with Lithuania, and a region where experts say the risk of a false-flag attack is real.
Playing the nuclear card is nothing new for Russia – the West rarely even utters the word – and the Kremlin often reaches for it when the battlefield situation is going badly. But that does not mean it can be ignored.
Rutte was clear: Russia should simply end the war in Ukraine and stop the nuclear threats. He was on a mission to calm nerves after weeks of speculation about a deteriorating security picture on NATO’s eastern flank, particularly in the Baltic states, which have remained on high alert as hybrid attacks linked to Russia multiply. Rutte insisted – and that is part of his job – that there is “no imminent threat” to NATO territory.
This was a secretary-general determined to project an alliance that is strong and united. “So much stronger than Russia. It could never beat us,” he said.
The Kremlin knows it too, hence the sabre-rattling. Nor is the war going well for Russia: the battlefield is largely stuck. A Russia incapable of defeating Ukraine cannot take on NATO. Let’s be clear: it would be wiped out – perhaps we all would – but conventionally, this is not a fight Russia can win.
That doesn’t mean Moscow cannot inflict enormous damage. It has created a climate of paranoia across Europe, while pounding Ukraine in a sharp escalation of the air war. My colleague Sasha Vakulina, who was in Kyiv on assignment, was routinely woken by attacks. During one of our security check-ins, she said it felt worse than at any point this year. Winter is approaching, and Ukraine clearly needs more air defence.
When I pressed Rutte on licensing Patriot systems for Kyiv, he did not give me an answer. The US and Ukraine have been negotiating a deal that would allow Kyiv to produce the system and reduce its dependence on external deliveries. It would not be a game changer in the short term – Rutte is right about that – but this should have been ironed out at the NATO summit in Turkey over the summer.
Rutte is careful not to criticise Donald Trump and is prepared to defend the president’s intervention in Iran at great length – even if the war against the regime in Tehran has also inflicted pain on Ukraine.
Energy prices are surging around the world and the Strait of Hormuz remains shut, despite an agreement three months ago that was supposed to restore freedom of navigation. That promise has yet to materialise.
Trump is also cautioning Ukraine against hitting Russian energy facilities, which are instrumental in financing the war.
He has a point: cutting refinery capacity at a time of acute market stress does not help. But Zelenskyy is not the root cause of the energy squeeze. The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz is.
Rutte is remarkably measured in his words. He won't utter the smallest criticism of Trump. Instead, he calls on Europeans to do more to help unblock the situation.
Europe, he argues, should have been capable of dealing with Iran’s nuclear threat rather than leaving the US to do the heavy lifting. When I asked Rutte, a European, whether he really believed Europe could have done it, his answer was emphatic.
“It should be us doing it. It should be us taking care of the Houthis and the Red Sea, not the Americans.”
Under his watch, NATO allies have committed to spend 5% of gross domestic product on defence, of which 3.5% will go to hard military capabilities. It is an accomplishment, and let's be honest, it's in large part due to Trump’s return to the White House.
But as Europeans put real money on the table, another question is becoming unavoidable: what should they buy? Should Europe favour European arms and equipment, or continue spending much of that money on the American defence industry?
To me, the answer is clear: if Europe pays, Europe should benefit. Rutte, however, dismissed this as a “luxury debate” of the Brussels bubble. It isn’t. It is a fundamental question, and it goes to the heart of the emerging NATO 3.0 strategy.
The US is mulling a major shift in which Europe will have to take the lead in its own defence, pay more of the bill and deploy more of its troops, while Washington reduces its footprint to focus on the Pacific and China. That makes sense. It is a legitimate posture
But will the Trump administration allow Europeans to build up their own defence industries? If you listen to the words of the US ambassador to NATO, the answer is not quite. Will NATO 3.0 lead to an alliance of equals? I doubt it.
Mark Rutte believes he has learned to tame the beast. And he is convinced he is saving the alliance. If you ask me, he is doing the best job anyone can under the circumstances, and his Teflon skin is helping. It's cringey, but necessary.
Thank you for reading Off The Record make sure to subscribe here.

Ukraine’s FP-2 Strike Drones Destroy Russian Pantsir-S2 Air Defense System
Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian Pantsir-S2 air defense system using FP-2 strike drones, with footage showing the system burning before its ammunition detonated and tore the vehicle apart.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian open-source monitoring channel Exilenova+ on October 3, the Pantsir-S2 had been interfering with Ukrainian drone operations and preventing UAVs from reaching targets deeper behind Russian lines.
Video published by the channel shows a Ukrainian FP-2 striking the Russian air defense system at night. A fire subsequently broke out on the vehicle, followed by secondary explosions that destroyed much of the system.
Additional footage recorded nearby reportedly captured another FP-2 approaching the Pantsir-S2 after the initial strike. By that point, however, the system had already sustained extensive damage.
Images taken after the attack show the burned remains of the crew cabin and components of the rotating combat module scattered around the site.
Exilenova+ did not disclose where or exactly when the strike occurred. The channel said the Pantsir-S2 had been obstructing Ukrainian drones attempting to penetrate farther into Russia’s rear areas.
The Pantsir-S2 is an upgraded version of Russia’s Pantsir family of short-range air defense systems. It combines surface-to-air missiles with 30 mm automatic cannons and is designed to engage aircraft, missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles.
The S2 variant features an upgraded target-detection radar intended to improve the system’s ability to detect and track aerial targets.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian S-300 transport-loading vehicle carrying surface-to-air missiles, triggering a secondary detonation that completely burned out the vehicle.

Russia May Be Running Secret Mesh Relays Inside Kyiv to Guide Shahed Strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:01:47 UTC
19:01:47 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia May Be Running Secret Mesh Relays Inside Kyiv to Guide Shahed Strikes
Russian forces may be using a small number of radio relay devices operating inside Kyiv to establish temporary communication links with Shahed-type attack drones and adjust their flight during strikes, according to Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Beskrestnov said on October 3 that he believes Russian Mesh radio relays are periodically activated in the Ukrainian capital, potentially providing a short-term control channel for incoming drones.
“Right now, I insist that enemy Mesh radio relays are being switched on in Kyiv, providing a temporary short-term control channel for Shaheds to adjust strikes. Not many. Perhaps one to three. Such relays are difficult to find, but they must be searched for,” Beskrestnov said.
According to Beskrestnov, the presence of such devices could complicate efforts to protect Kyiv using electronic warfare systems, as the drones could retain a communication channel during the final stage of an attack.
He pointed to previous Russian strikes in Kyiv, including an attack on a Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) building, as evidence supporting his assessment.
“At the moment of the strike, there were no other Shahed relay drones in the sky. I also analyzed other strikes on Kyiv bridges and the possibility of organizing long-range Mesh channels from Russia at those moments,” he said.
Beskrestnov also raised concerns about Russian access to information on the location of Ukrainian air defense systems deployed around critical infrastructure. Images showing air defense equipment on Kyiv bridges have circulated online, while such deployments are difficult to conceal because tens of thousands of people use the crossings daily, he said.
As long as Russia maintains the ability to control Shahed drones in real time, Beskrestnov said, both infrastructure and air defense systems could potentially be targeted.
He argued that accurately striking individual structural elements of a bridge, such as supports or cables, would require a stable control channel that remains active until the final stage of the drone’s flight.
Beskrestnov stressed that his assessment of Russian relay devices operating inside Kyiv remains a hypothesis. Ukrainian specialists continue examining debris from downed Russian drones for evidence of alternative communication systems.
“Let me be wrong in my opinion about the relays,” Beskrestnov said. “I also want to say that we carefully examine all debris. We do not find any other ‘secret’ means of communication.”
The assessment follows earlier concerns over relay infrastructure outside Ukraine. On September 29, Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service said Belarus periodically activates relay systems that can strengthen communications for Russian drones during attacks on Ukraine.
In June, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko to dismantle relay equipment that Kyiv said was being used to support Russian drone operations.

Psychologists identify “collective anti-mattering” as a key driver of modern political grievances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:00:32 UTC
19:00:32 KST

New research suggests that when people believe their social group is treated as unimportant by others, they tend to report more anger about their group’s treatment and more anxiety about its future. These feelings were in turn linked to involvement in collective action, support for strong leadership, and, among White Americans, support for punitive policies. The findings were published in European Journal of Social Psychology.
The research examines a psychological concept known as collective anti-mattering. This is the belief that one’s specific social group does not count, is ignored, or is viewed as disposable by other groups or by society at large. It expands on the idea of personal anti-mattering, which describes the painful experience of feeling personally unnoticed or unvalued by other people. Research into personal feelings of unimportance, such as a 2021 study of adolescents and young adults, indicated that feeling like one does not matter to others is a unique form of distress that predicts loneliness and depression.
“The idea grew out of research on mattering, the basic psychological need to feel that we are noticed, valued, and significant to other people,” Nassim Tabri, an associate professor in the Department of Psychology at Carleton University, told PsyPost. “More recent work has examined anti-mattering, which is the belief that other people actively regard you as unimportant or insignificant.”
“We examined whether people can experience something analogous at the group level: not simply ‘I don’t matter,’ but ‘people like us don’t matter,'” he explained. “Historically marginalized groups may feel that their concerns or suffering are ignored by more advantaged groups or institutions, whereas members of historically advantaged groups may sometimes feel that their group is increasingly being overlooked or displaced.”
Tabri and colleagues proposed that this same feeling can occur at the group level and influence political life. When groups feel that they are morally invisible, they may experience two distinct emotional responses: group-based anger and collective angst. Group-based anger is a reaction to perceived unfairness in the present moment. It is the feeling that one’s group is being illegitimately devalued, which often motivates people to confront the source of the injustice.
Collective angst, on the other hand, is an anxiety focused on the future. It occurs when people fear that their group’s vitality, culture, or very existence might be in jeopardy. Previous work on group dynamics, such as a 2021 set of experiments, indicated that White people reminded of demographic changes, particularly those who saw race relations as zero-sum, felt more anxiety about their group’s future, which was linked to less support for progressive social movements and more anti-immigrant sentiment.
By studying collective anti-mattering, the authors sought to understand how feeling disregarded acts as a starting point for both anger and angst. They theorized that this single feeling could push marginalized groups to demand recognition and push advantaged groups to defend their status.
To test these ideas, the researchers conducted three separate studies using data from online panels, meaning the samples were not nationally representative. In the first study, they recruited 368 Black American adults who completed questionnaires measuring their sense of collective anti-mattering, individual anti-mattering, perceived injustice toward their group, group-based anger toward White Americans, and collective angst. Finally, participants reported how often they take part in collective action on behalf of Black Americans, such as demonstrations, and how much they agreed that their group needs a strong leader who will do whatever it takes to get things done for it.
The researchers found that collective anti-mattering was distinct from personal anti-mattering and strongly predicted both group-based anger and collective angst. It was also strongly correlated with perceived injustice, but statistical analyses showed the two were separate concepts.
The two emotions, however, predicted different outcomes. Higher levels of collective angst were associated with more frequent involvement in collective action, while anger did not predict collective action. Both collective angst and group-based anger predicted greater support for a strong leader, though the items measured broad support rather than specific authoritarian actions. Across the three studies, the statistical models explained only 6% to 12% of the differences in collective action, compared to 13% to 55% for strong-leader support.
For the second study, the researchers surveyed 552 Black British citizens living in the United Kingdom to see if the patterns would hold true in a different national context. The participants completed similar measures, focusing on their perceptions of how Black British people are viewed by White British people. They also answered questions about whether they felt White British people tried to control their group’s identity, a concept known as collective autonomy restriction.
The results of the second study showed that collective anti-mattering on its own was essentially unrelated to collective action, but it was again linked to both group-based anger and collective angst. Just as with the American participants, collective angst was the emotion linked to collective action. Both anger and angst were associated with support for strong leadership. The study also showed that feeling collectively disregarded is a separate experience from feeling that one’s group is being explicitly controlled or treated as less than human.
The third study shifted focus to a historically advantaged majority group. The researchers surveyed 399 White American adults, balancing the sample between Democrats and Republicans. This time, the collective anti-mattering questions asked participants how much they felt White Americans were disregarded by other Americans or by society in general. Along with measuring anger, angst, collective action, and strong-leader support, the researchers asked participants about their political attitudes, including their support for government bans on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives, as well as their support for persecuting undocumented immigrants, measured with statements ranging from praising the work of Immigration and Customs Enforcement to supporting the use of physical force and even executions.
Believing that White Americans no longer matter to society predicted higher levels of both group-based anger and collective angst, although average levels of collective anti-mattering were much lower among White Americans (about 2.1 on a 1-to-7 scale) than among Black Americans (about 4.0) or Black British participants (about 3.5). Collective angst was again linked to more involvement in collective action and stronger support for a strong leader. Unlike in the first two studies, anger was not linked to strong-leader support.
Group-based anger, however, was linked to different outcomes. Higher levels of anger were associated with stronger support for banning diversity initiatives and a greater willingness to support punitive measures against undocumented immigrants, while collective angst was not. These effects remained consistent even when the researchers adjusted their statistical models to account for whether the participant was a Democrat or a Republican. This differs from the 2021 experiments described earlier, in which anxiety about the group’s future, rather than anger, was linked to anti-immigrant sentiment.
“What struck me most was the consistency of the basic psychological pattern across groups who occupy very different structural positions in society,” Tabri said. “I was also struck by what we found when we expanded the range of political outcomes examined among White Americans. In this group, anger associated with perceived disregard was, in turn, associated with greater support for punitive and exclusionary political responses, including opposition to DEI initiatives and support for punitive treatment of undocumented immigrants. This suggests that the consequences of believing that one’s group does not matter may depend on the emotion involved and the broader social and political context.”
“I would characterize the findings as meaningful but not deterministic,” he added. “Collective anti-mattering showed moderate-to-large associations with the emotional processes we examined, particularly group-based anger and collective angst, but political attitudes and behavior obviously have many causes. The practical significance, in my view, comes less from any single effect size than from the consistency of the pattern across three samples and two countries. Perceiving that one’s group is disregarded appears to capture a psychologically meaningful form of group grievance.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. All three studies relied on cross-sectional survey data, meaning the researchers measured all variables at a single point in time. Because of this, it is not possible to establish a strict chain of cause and effect between feelings of disregard, specific emotions, and political behaviors.
“We found that collective anti-mattering was associated with particular emotions and political responses in theoretically meaningful ways, but we cannot conclude from these studies alone that making people feel that their group does not matter will cause those responses,” Tabri noted. “I would also caution against interpreting the findings as equating the experiences of advantaged and disadvantaged groups. Black Americans and Black British people may perceive disregard in the context of longstanding discrimination and structural inequality, whereas perceptions of disregard among White Americans can arise despite their group’s continued structural advantage.”
The researchers also emphasized how to view the study’s leadership questions. “Support for a ‘strong leader’ in our measures should not automatically be interpreted as support for authoritarianism,” Tabri said. “A strong leader can be understood as someone who protects or advances the group’s interests without necessarily rejecting democratic norms. This is one reason we distinguish strong-leader support from the more explicitly punitive and exclusionary outcomes we examined among White Americans.”
Additionally, the focus of the collective anti-mattering questions varied between the studies. In the first two studies, participants were asked about disregard from a specific majority group, while the third study asked about disregard from society more broadly. Future research could investigate whether feeling ignored by a specific group produces different political reactions than feeling ignored by social institutions as a whole.
Looking ahead, Tabri outlined plans to further investigate these dynamics. “An important next step is to establish whether collective anti-mattering actually has a causal influence on group-based emotions and behavior,” he said. “Experimental studies that manipulate perceptions of collective disregard, along with longitudinal studies that follow these processes over time, will help establish whether changes in collective anti-mattering precede changes in anger, anxiety about the group’s future, and political behavior.”
“One aspect of the concept that I think is especially important is the distinction between being treated unfairly and feeling that your group simply does not count,” Tabri said. “Injustice is about what is being done to a group; collective anti-mattering is about what people believe their group means to others—whether its concerns, welfare, and future are regarded as consequential. That distinction may help us understand some contemporary political grievances that are difficult to capture solely in terms of material interests or explicit discrimination. People and groups want not only fair outcomes but recognition that they matter.”
The study, “Collective Anti-Mattering: Belief That One’s Group Is Being Disregarded Fuels Collective Action and Authoritarian Leadership Support Among Both Advantaged and Disadvantaged Groups,” was authored by Nassim Tabri, Isabelle Boutros, and Michael J. A. Wohl.

‘The violence is off the scale’: staff and passengers at risk as assaults on UK trains soar to record high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:00:25 UTC
19:00:25 KST

When a train was halted outside Exeter St Davids station on Monday, rail staff leapt to one conclusion: there had been a violent incident on board.
“Someone will have kicked off,” one staff member said. “It happens all the time. My boss got head-butted recently.”
On this occasion, they were wrong – but their assumption told a tale. Figures released late last month showed the number of reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways had risen by a fifth, to a record high of almost 25,000 incidents in a year.
Staff in particular have felt increasingly under threat. While the total numbers reported by the Office of Rail and Road in 2025-26 covered threats, verbal abuse, and contact that might not have resulted in any injury, they included nearly 2,500 physical assaults on workers – an average of about seven every day.
Their unions said the numbers were horrendous, but unsurprising: the RMT and TSSA unions have campaigned for more staffed stations and policing, after the number of British Transport Police (BTP) officers fell by more than 10% between 2024 and 2026.
Many rail staff wear body cams to record and log incidents of violence. “I think it’s so sad that we have those,” said Dave*, a rail worker in south-west England. However, after 20 years in the job, he said: “The threats, the abuse, the violence we see is off the scale.”
Drink and drugs play a part, he added. “We’re also seeing a lot more people with mental health issues. If you’re out on the street you can steer clear, but if you’re on a train or a platform you can’t. Our workplaces are becoming more and more dangerous.”
‘Now it’s mostly bad days’
Steve, a guard based in the north of England, was punched in the head by a passenger: “It was my last train of the night. I’ve had to look away to see the door controls and the next thing I know, I’m waking up on the platform.”
Every guard gets verbally abused on a daily basis, he said, with behaviour worsening since the pandemic: “Now it’s mostly bad days, and you’re searching for good days, where nothing’s said, or nothing happens. The amount of times we’re getting threatened now with physical attacks, even when you walk through the train and say, ‘Tickets, please.’”
Even those working on the infrastructure can be on the receiving end. One rail contractor, Liam, based in Somerset, said: “We’re there working on the tracks and we sometimes get sworn at and even spat at. It’s just a minority, but somehow they think we’re responsible for slow journey times, cancelled trains. We’re in bright orange so we’re easy targets.”
The railway is by no means unique: bus drivers have faced repeated abuse and threats, as the Unite union has highlighted. Transport for London staff working on roads are issued with “spit kits”, or forensic saliva collection tubes, so common is that form of assault.
Violence against women and girls is of particular concern; at the Labour conference this week, the minister for buses and local transport, Simon Lightwood, described it as a “national emergency”.
Speaking alongside him, the mayor for the north-east, Kim McGuinness, said that as well as measures such as more staffing, lighting and CCTV, a crucial point for women was “knowing that if you raise an alarm something is going to be done. It’s a choice to use public transport or not … if you’re accepting 50% of the population don’t feel safe, that’s not good.”
The rail industry and police say some of the sharp rise in recorded assaults on passengers – up 36% last year – is due to greater reporting, including using discreet text messaging to the BTP.
But while many more incidents are now reported, plenty are not.
‘Tearful, angry and scared’
Emily, 24, was travelling home on a late-night train between Glasgow and Edinburgh last year when a stranger made a beeline for her. “He immediately tried to start a conversation and wouldn’t give up even when I showed no interest. He was asking what I’d been up to, whether I had a boyfriend, complimenting my outfit, and then it escalated really quickly.”
The man began rubbing Emily’s upper thigh and asking her intrusive questions about her sex life. “I froze and didn’t know what to do. I looked around but everyone else was oblivious. I tried to move but I was on the inside seat and he just grabbed my leg harder and leaned in towards me,” she said.
She managed to manoeuvre out of the seat and away from the man, who “shouted aggressively and called [her] a bitch”. Other passengers looked round but did not intervene. She moved to another carriage and arrived home shaken but decided not to report the incident.
“I wanted to just move on,” Emily said. “But I never used to think twice about getting on a train by myself at night and now I’m much more nervous.”
Edward, a trans man, was travelling home to Staffordshire with his partner, a trans woman, after a weekend in Wales. On a packed train from Aberystwyth, a man began loudly making homophobic comments and became confrontational.
“Normally in that situation I just walk on, but I physically couldn’t, we were so crammed,” Edward said. He finally yelled back, repeating: “You’re shouting homophobic abuse in front of your children.”
A railway worker eventually intervened and told the assailant and his family to move to another carriage. Edward chose not to report the incident to police, dissatisfied with the response to previous incidents. He now tries to avoid public transport: “I felt tearful, angry and scared afterwards.”
‘It’s put me off trains’
A fraction of passenger reports end up with arrest or prosecution. Last year, Sam was travelling north from London on a train packed with football supporters. As she tried to reach her reserved seat, a drunken man confronted her and pushed her backward.
She instinctively pushed him back. “Then I thought, what have you done?” she said. Other men began throwing beer cans while one held her by her rucksack. “I was being pushed and shoved … they were throwing punches as well.”
Amid the assault, one man deliberately grabbed her breasts. “I realised: ‘Oh no, I’m trapped on here with them for the next two hours’,” she said. “There’s nowhere to go. There’s nowhere to get off.”
Two BTP officers on the train got through to take a statement from Sam. The investigation was later dropped after police were unable to identify her assailant. 
The experience had a big impact, leaving her “not doing a lot of things I used to do. It’s put me off trains massively. I think if faced with a train like that, I would just not board it.”
The BTP assistant chief constable Ian Drummond-Smith said: “We will never tolerate violence or abuse directed at passengers or staff on the railway, and anyone committing these crimes can expect a robust response from us.”
He noted that when staff had body-worn recording, police brought offenders to justice in about 85% of incidents. “Anyone who witnesses violence or abuse on the railway should report it to us by texting 61016, or call 999 in an emergency,” he said.
The Department for Transport said the rise in assaults was “deeply concerning and unacceptable”. It has awarded a £63m increase in BTP funding by 2028-29, allowing more than 200 additional officers to be recruited, and investments in better CCTV and body-worn video. Dozens of new BTP officers will be specialised in tackling violence and intimidation against women and girls.
* Names have been changed

America’s Health Care Workforce Is in Crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:00:06 UTC
19:00:06 KST

Dr. Jonathan Tyes once struggled to imagine a future in medicine for himself. A first-generation college student and the oldest of 10 siblings, Tyes was raised by his grandparents in Cleveland. While studying biology at Morehouse College, he was a few credits from graduation when his grandmother died. Grief and financial hardship threatened to end both his education and his dream of becoming the first physician in his family.
Instead, he spent years rebuilding his path. He worked throughout school, served those in need as a community health worker, completed medical mission trips to Ghana, became a registered pharmacy technician, and refused to abandon his goal of practicing medicine. Eventually, as a non-traditional student in his mid-thirties, he got into medical school.
Though his family faced homelessness, gun violence, and other tribulations throughout his education, he stayed the course. Financial support from our organization, National Medical Fellowships (NMF), helped him remain enrolled and continue his training. Now, Tyes is an anesthesiology resident at the University of Buffalo, while at the same time pursuing a master of public health degree at Harvard.
His story is a testament to perseverance—but it is also a warning. America cannot afford to lose future physicians like Tyes.
The health care workforce emergency that experts have warned about for years is no longer approaching—it is here. Over the next decade, the U.S. is projected to face a shortage of more than 700,000 health care professionals, including physicians, registered nurses, and licensed practical nurses. At the same time, countries such as Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, and the United Arab Emirates are actively recruiting U.S.-trained clinicians through streamlined licensing pathways, placing additional pressure on an already strained workforce.
The consequences are being felt in every community. Whether you live in a rural town in Alabama or a high-rise in Manhattan, chances are you have experienced the shortage firsthand. You may have waited months for a pediatric appointment, spent hours in an emergency department hallway with an aging parent, or postponed care for your own chronic condition because the next available appointment was too far in the future. Today, the average wait time to see a physician is 38 days—nearly three times what many experts consider medically appropriate.
Health care is built on people, yet the nation’s largest employment sector is buckling under the weight of burnout, mistrust, underinvestment, and the lingering effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. According to a recent Harris Poll, more than half of health care workers are considering leaving their jobs, with many planning to exit the profession altogether. Fewer than 17% of physicians are under the age of 40, while roughly one in five is over 60.
The math isn’t adding up. We are losing experienced professionals faster than we are preparing the next generation. We are asking more of those who remain while offering them fewer resources and less support. Nowhere is this failure more visible than in rural and medically underserved communities.
If we fail to address the root causes of this crisis—professional burnout, crushing educational debt, and declining reimbursement—we will not have a health care system capable of caring for our growing aging population, regardless of ZIP code or socioeconomic status.
Yet instead of reinforcing the foundation, we are pulling bricks from the bottom. Federal health spending is being slashed. Programs that support research, expand access for low-income families, and strengthen public health infrastructure are being dismantled. Recent federal spending changes—including the passing of H.R. 1—are projected to increase the number of uninsured Americans, squeeze already fragile health systems, raise health care costs, and force community health centers and hospitals to shutter.
The impact extends beyond today’s workforce to tomorrow’s.
Changes to federal student lending that began in July 2026 will dramatically restrict access to financing for “professional” education. Medical students will face annual loan caps of $50,000, despite the fact that medical education costs exceed $286,000 at public institutions, on average, and approach $390,000 at private schools. Nursing students will face even tighter annual borrowing limits of $20,500, creating additional barriers to entering one of the nation’s most essential professions.
These policies risk pushing brilliant students away from medicine, nursing, and other health professions altogether. They will discourage careers in primary care and hollow out the very specialties communities need most.
And when we restrict who can afford to become a doctor or nurse, we ultimately restrict who gets cared for.
A health care workforce that reflects a broad range of socioeconomic backgrounds and lived experiences is better equipped to understand patients, build trust, and improve outcomes.
This moment demands collective action: We must reimagine pathways into health care careers, confront physician burnout head-on, and close the health and wealth gaps that weaken our system. We must prevent financial barriers from determining who has the opportunity to become a health care leader.
And most importantly, we must ensure that the next generation of health care professionals receives the financial, professional, and community support necessary to complete training and return to serve the communities that need them most.

We Must Fight Health Misinformation With Empathy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:00:05 UTC
19:00:05 KST

In November 2008, I was eight months pregnant, watching the election returns roll in. Somehow, I’d found a way to make myself even more uncomfortable: I was upside down on my couch. My head was on the cushions. My feet dangled above me. I strained to balance myself while trying to keep something called mugwort near my toes. My daughter was breech, and I was willing to try anything to help her flip, even if it meant turning the world upside-down.
I’d seen from a Google search that “moxibustion” with the smoldering herb might help with turning a breech baby. As a physician and scientist, I was well aware there was limited peer-reviewed evidence for what I was doing. I’d never heard of anyone prescribing moxibustion. But with the window narrowing for the birth I had hoped for, I was more willing to believe there might be something to it. Although I was skeptical, I thought, “It couldn’t hurt! Why not?”
My impulse to seek out and use unproven health information is not uncommon. New research released by the Edelman Trust Institute and our team at the Yale School of Public Health, where I serve as dean, shows that many of us are willing to look for health guidance in unreliable places.
In a world where information comes at us in fragments and trust in institutions is crumbling, it’s worth understanding what we believe and why. Our new analysis tested views on six unfounded health claims about subjects like childhood vaccines, raw milk, fluoride in drinking water, and so on. Huge majorities of the 13,000+ people surveyed, 70% globally, believed at least one of these claims. And the people who believed these claims weren’t simply those without exposure to science; most of them had taken a university-level or higher science course. Nor did susceptibility fall neatly along partisan or generational lines.
The search for alternative answers is far more mainstream than we tend to assume. Young or old, left or right—almost all of us are confused about some aspect of health information.
That’s especially true, the analysis shows, in moments of fear and uncertainty, when your life or the life of someone you love is on the line. In fact, those who frequently interacted with the health care system were more than 50% more likely to hold three or more of these unfounded beliefs.
Anyone who has endured the frustration of a complicated or persistent illness can understand why that might be the case. The longer you search for answers, the more uncertainty you encounter: ambiguous tests, treatments that don’t work, specialists who disagree. So people keep searching. They may rely on intuition or turn to friends for answers.
Increasingly, people also look online or turn to AI. In fact, nearly half of the respondents in our survey believe someone without medical training who is fluent with AI can perform at least one health-related task as well as or better than a doctor.
As a doctor, these findings concern me, but don’t surprise me. People crave empathy, humility, and active listening. AI—as well as friends, family, and social media—can provide that. Whether they provide accurate information is, however, up for debate.
Empathy alone isn’t, of course, a substitute for good data. Our analysis shows what may work in the face of confusion: recognizing that people are far more likely to accept good advice when they believe their concerns are truly heard. That principle applies not only to the exam room, but to anywhere public health asks people to place their trust in expertise.
What techniques seem to make a difference? People reported being more likely to take advice when they believe, first, that their concerns and experience have been taken seriously, when they believe that someone understands their community, and when they feel listened to.
As we collectively wade through a sea of conflicting health information, knowing whom to trust is genuinely hard. Misinformation flourishes in the petri dish of uncertainty, especially when misinformation offers simple answers to complicated questions. But our analysis shows that trust is not out of reach. In fact, nearly half of respondents said they’d seen doctors or medical experts build bridges and grow trust. This is where this analysis holds hope and shows us that there are paths forward.
As for me? In the end, my daughter did flip, albeit weeks later. I doubt the mugwort had anything to do with it. But I remember what I was actually looking for that night, and it wasn’t an answer. It was agency. Lighting that moxibustion stick was a little prayer that there was something I could do.
That impulse to find some certainty, control, and answers is deeply human. The more we understand that, the better chance we have of helping people find answers they can trust.

Spanish police clear Ceuta's largest migrant camp ahead of King and Queen's visit
