Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Police undertook Operation Trampolín on Sunday to clear a makeshift settlement on Ceuta's Trampolín beach, home to about 3,000 people living in poor conditions for more than two months.
Riot police from Spain's Police Intervention Unit (UIP), brought in from Seville, Granada, Malaga and other parts of the country, conducted Operation Trampolín on Sunday to clear the tents from the settlement that has seen the worst insecurity and tension of the crisis.
Officers from the Prevention and Reaction Unit (UPR) and intelligence units, both from Ceuta and elsewhere, also took part in it.
Police justified the operation by pointing to conditions at the site. The waters off Trampolín are contaminated, they say, arguing that safety cannot be guaranteed, and citing health risk concerns, alongside a rise in violent incidents.
To prevent trouble, officers sealed off all access points, preventing people from fleeing into the hills and heading off potential clashes.
Additional vehicles were also deployed, having been brought in from mainland Spain earlier this week. The vehicles, never before seen in Ceuta, included two BMR armoured vehicles and a Vamtac S3 off-road vehicle, according to El Faro de Ceuta. A drone was also used to monitor the operation from the air, as security was stepped up across the city.
Local police announced closures from around 7.30 a.m. on the roads between Benítez and Benzú. A National Police van was the first to arrive, shortly after half past seven, and the deployment began just before eight.
Just beforehand, there was music, street vendors and people only just waking up in the camp. Some migrants, already nervous, opted to run for the hills.
How the relocation is being carried out
Officers went from tent to tent and shack to shack informing occupants that they had to leave, while taking the tents down. An interpreter explained in Arabic where they would be moved to. Women and children were to be included in this first phase, although most of those affected are men.
The migrants are being taken by bus to the Tarajal CATE reception centre, where triage and identification are carried out. The first bus left shortly before 9.00, according to 'Radio Televisión Ceuta'.
It is expected that some may decide to return to their home countries, as several of those moved from Benítez did earlier this week. For now, reception facilities are available at Loma Colmenar, with room for more than 1,000 people.
This is the third such operation in a matter of weeks, following the two carried out in Benítez. According to the Higher Police Headquarters, the settlement is home to more than 3,500 people, and Sunday's operation is only a first phase.
The shortage of places remains the main obstacle. In mid-September, the port camp, built for 1,700 people, left more than 2,000 outside, who returned to the beaches.
The government has set 15 October as the deadline to complete the eviction, and the King and Queen are due to visit on the 13th.
The crisis began at the end of July, when more than 70,000 people crossed from Morocco, most of whom were sent back within a few hours.

Museum Vonk is "a testing ground for affordable bio-based construction"

Museum Vonk is "a testing ground for affordable bio-based construction"
Pigmented lime plaster colours the hempcrete facades of this wedge-shaped history museum in Eindhoven, completed by Dutch studio Studio Marco Vermeulen with a palette of biomaterials.
Located on the site of a former driving-school track in the Dutch city, Museum Vonk explores 10,000 years of regional history in a hands-on and interactive way.
It was constructed from reclaimed cross-laminated timber (CLT) and hempcrete facades, prefabricated in the Netherlands and finished with pigmented lime plaster. Hempcrete is a bio-composite material made from hemp and lime.
Studio Marco Vermeulen designed Museum Vonk as part of a merger of the existing open-air Prehistoric Village museum and the Eindhoven Museum.
The studio's design prioritised bio-based materials in homage to Prehistoric Village, which features artisanal buildings made from wood, clay and reed, but using a more high-tech approach.
This led them to use a reclaimed timber structure salvaged from Biobasecamp, a pavilion created by Studio Marco Vermeulen for Dutch Design Week 2019 that could be easily reused.
"We have been working with plant-based materials in our projects as much as possible for quite some time," studio founder Marco Vermeulen told Dezeen.
"The Prehistoric Village presents buildings dating from prehistoric times through to the Middle Ages, all constructed from wood, clay and reed – materials that were readily available in the immediate surroundings," he continued.
"As a result, these buildings are, in a sense, rooted in their environment. We wanted to achieve the same with the new building."
According to Studio Marco Vermeulen, one of the project's biggest challenges was working with the reclaimed CLT, as the contractor was initially hesitant.
"For the contractor, working with recycled CLT was initially somewhat unfamiliar," Vermeulen explained.
"Providing the necessary guarantees was an issue. The CLT therefore unfortunately had to be returned to the factory for inspection. After that, however, it was reused almost entirely in the new museum building without any problems."
The CLT elements that previously formed the upper side of the Biobasecamp and were left most weathered can be seen throughout the building, with colour differences and even some footprints celebrated as unique surface finishes.
"It creates a beautiful conceptual, but also tangible, connection between this new building and the promise of the Biobasecamp," reflected Vermeulen.
"The circle is now complete, as this temporary pavilion has been incorporated into a new building that is once again trying to take another step forward in bio-based construction."
Museum Vonk's wedge-shaped form and layered plaster finishes give the illusion that the building has been thrust out from the earth.
This look is enhanced by its accessible rooftop, which is covered in grass, plants and shrubs.
Visitors enter Museum Vonk from the park, which was created as part of the project. Once inside, they are greeted by an introductory show and exhibition that sit towards the centre of the building, as they do not require natural light or views.
The heart of the building is the "making shed", where visitors are invited to work together on creating objects and installations that represent Eindhoven's history and will become part of its displays.
This shed space sits at the building's highest point and opens onto the park and the Prehistoric Village museum.
It is also connected to the restaurant, which sits on the lower side of the building along with the staff offices, a conference room and the museum shop.
Finishing touches to the project include nesting spots for birds and bats, built into the hempcrete facade.
Asphalt from the former driving track was reused as a layer of crushed material in the museum's foundations, and a rainwater collection system provides water for the green roof.
A passive cooling strategy includes large ventilation hatches in the building's tallest areas, which allow warm air to escape. When it is cold, the hatches are shut, with heating and cooling provided through mechanical air-handling systems.
Studio Marco Vermeulen hopes that the project can demonstrate how accessible it is to build with biomaterials.
"The ambitions for this building were high, while the budget was limited," said Vermeulen.
"Nevertheless, we found ways to reconcile the two. As a result, the building became a testing ground for affordable bio-based construction techniques and natural climate control," he continued.
"Hopefully, it can serve as an inspiration, a catalyst and a reference – providing proof that bio-based, circular and nature-inclusive construction is possible."
Other public projects recently completed with bio-based material palettes include a trio of buildings by Jan Kattein Architects within a community garden in London, and nearby, a community food-growing hub by Material Cultures and Studio Gil.
The photography is by Ronald Tilleman.

Rural Data Centers Are in for a Big Federal Tax Break
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.
On January 1, a new tax windfall will kick in that could benefit scores of rural data center projects—all thanks to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Starting next year, projects sited in tracts of rural land across the country will be newly eligible for a set of specific corporate tax benefits under a program expanded by the bill. The new rules “may significantly lower barriers for large-scale, capital-intensive projects in rural areas—most notably hyperscale data centers,” said a statement from Ways and Means Committee chair Jason Smith last year. “The economic case for building data centers in designated rural opportunity zones becomes far more compelling” with the new program, he continued.
But experts warn that the results for rural communities could be mixed.
“Right now, the only requirement to get the benefits is capital investment,” says Emily Kraschel, a tax policy analyst at the Searchlight Institute, a public policy think tank. “However, that doesn't guarantee that that money is necessarily creating jobs or creating a local economic boost. You'd be more sure of that with a more traditional factory that requires lots of workers. But with a data center, that assumption goes a little wonky.”
During the first Trump administration, a bipartisan group of lawmakers proposed the creation of the opportunity zone program, which offers tax benefits for companies that choose to build projects in certain low-income census tracts. Last year, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act made a number of changes to open up the program in order to attract more investment to rural areas.
Kraschel and her colleagues from Searchlight have been researching data center projects that might qualify for these tax benefits, comparing the locations of data center projects in development with rural census tracts eligible for the new program. WIRED exclusively reviewed the research compiled by Searchlight and found more than 100 data centers under various stages of development in rural areas that could be eligible.
Searchlight used a very conservative database of under 700 data center projects that are planned or under construction to compile its research; other datasets put the number of data centers in development in the US at closer to 1,500. It’s very likely that the number of newly eligible projects is bigger, especially since more data centers are decamping from urban areas. Separate research from Pew found that while just 13 percent of operating data centers are located in rural areas, a majority of planned facilities—around 67 percent—are going rural.
Searchlight’s research comes as the backlash against data centers—including from rural and GOP voters—is reaching a fever pitch. Tax breaks for data centers being built by some of the most powerful companies in the world have become a flashpoint in these debates: Amazon recently made headlines for attempting to negotiate for a lower tax bill on one of dozens of data centers it plans to open in Mississippi, while The New York Times reported last week that Meta is writing off data center equipment under a federal tax break intended for research and experimentation.
In the scramble to try to regulate the industry, the opportunity zones aren’t going unnoticed. Last month, Senator Josh Hawley introduced legislation that would eliminate opportunity zone funding for data centers, claiming that he would help “ensure Big Tech companies don’t get tax breaks to build data centers on farmland.”
A project simply existing in a rural opportunity zone doesn’t mean the company automatically will get the tax benefits; the company has to create a specialized investment vehicle to kickstart the process. Because the tax break can be considered confidential IRS data, it’s next to impossible to know which companies are pursuing the benefits unless they voluntarily disclose.
The research Searchlight compiled shows some big names that could stand to benefit from the program. But high-profile tech companies, when contacted for comment on the program, seemed eager to distance themselves from yet another tax break story. WIRED reached out to Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, all of which are developing data centers in areas that could be eligible for the new program, to ask about their plans to take the tax benefits.
Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon all denied using the program. In a statement, Microsoft’s general counsel of infrastructure legal affairs, Rima Alaily, told WIRED that the company “does not use the opportunity zone program to invest in the purchase or construction of its data centers.” Similarly, Amazon spokesperson Julia Lawless said the company “does not actively seek out” land in opportunity zones for development, and that it has not claimed the tax benefit for its projects.
“If we locate in one of these areas, it's because our site selection criteria—from available land to access to talent—aligns with tracts that governments across all levels have previously identified for economic development; not because we utilized the OZ benefit,” says Lawless. “We have not used this program for our site selection and have no plans to add it to our criteria for our future decisionmaking process." Google did not respond.
There are many reasons why data center builders may be choosing rural areas, from moving away from community opposition to pursuing cheaper land. But it’s not out of the question that companies with lower corporate profiles than Microsoft or Amazon developing data centers may choose to opt in to tax benefits.
Nathan Jensen, a government professor at the University of Texas-Austin, says that he would be “very surprised” if some companies were not considering siting in rural opportunity zones as part of their decisionmaking process.
“It’s essentially free money,” he says.
Giving tax advantages to companies to build stuff to spur local economies is a good idea in theory. But the opportunity zone program has had mixed results in execution. There’s some evidence that the program has done little to actually drive investment to disadvantaged areas, and that many of the projects getting federal kickbacks would have happened even without the tax boost. (Overall, the government says the expansion of the opportunity zone program to rural areas will cost an estimated $40.9 billion over the next decade.)
There is no requirement for projects getting opportunity zone benefits to create jobs; the assumption is that they will do so, simply by siting in the community itself. This isn’t always the case for projects like storage facilities and warehouses, which, Jensen says, have been popular choices for developers working in opportunity zones. Data centers may create a number of jobs in the short term for their construction, but there’s an ongoing debate about whether or not they create a lasting new workforce over the longer term.
“Lawmakers need to decide what they really want out of these investments,” says Kraschel. “Do you want to use this as a way to get data centers away from population centers? Are they just looking for capital investment, or are they wanting things like jobs?”
Jensen, for his part, thinks it’s “interesting we have this program that's incentivizing an investment while states are trying to de-incentivize or even ban it.”
What We’re Writing
On Friday, Amazon rolled out a series of commitments in communities where it’s building its data centers, pledging $1 billion in investments in initiatives like free community college programs over the next five years. Importantly, the company also confirmed that it is no longer using nondisclosure agreements with public officials in communities where it’s building data centers. NDAs have been a huge flashpoint in the public backlash to data center development across the country.
I wrote about Amazon’s announcement; it will be interesting to see if this changes public opinion! (If you live in a community near an Amazon data center and have thoughts about this, I’m all ears: [email protected], or reach me on Signal at mollytaft.76.)
What We’re Reading
- There was a flurry of data-center-related activity on the Hill this week. First up: a long-awaited new bipartisan permitting bill has some big implications for data centers; Bloomberg has more.
- And a bill echoing the White House’s Ratepayer Protection Act failed in the Senate, after Democrats claimed it was simply lip service to help Republican senator Jon Husted. Husted is facing a tough reelection battle against Sherrod Brown in Ohio, where data centers have played a starring role. NBC covers the battle.
- In Pennsylvania, a data center is still struggling with local opposition even after offering residents $10,000 each to accept the project. The Wall Street Journal reports.
- There’s a new tool that estimates the energy use and carbon emissions from data centers, created by Sustainable AI Group. (We spoke to cofounder Boris Gamazaychikov about AI agents and energy use for a newsletter a few weeks back.) You can read all about it in Heatmap.

Hegseth Signals US Troop Shift From Europe to Americas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Some US military personnel and capabilities stationed in Europe could be redeployed to the Western Hemisphere or back to the American homeland, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth indicated on Saturday, Oct. 3.
According to The Hill, Hegseth linked the potential realignment to the administration’s demands for greater burden-sharing among European NATO allies, alongside an intensifying military campaign directed against drug cartels across Central and South America.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Well, we’re definitely expanding our presence and our footprint in Central and South America with partners, and because of the bold move the president made in Venezuela,” Hegseth stated, referring to the capture of former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.
“We have a whole new suite of options economically and militarily with partnerships.”
The defense secretary highlighted expanding bilateral security cooperation with regional governments including Ecuador, Honduras, Guatemala, and Panama.
Hegseth emphasized that implementing the administration’s National Security Strategy and National Defense Strategy requires allied European nations to assume primary responsibility for conventional continental defense.
“It makes it very clear that we want more burden sharing in Europe,” Hegseth said.
“And as we do that, a lot of – some of those capabilities are going to move elsewhere, either back home to the big, beautiful base that we’re going to build that we announced a couple of days ago, or to a different posture in the Western Hemisphere as we get after these designated terrorist organizations.”
Merz Makes Surprise Kyiv Visit, Pledges 1,000 Drone Interceptors
European posture review
Hegseth’s remarks follow his “State of the Force” address, in which he invited state governors and adjutant generals across the US to submit competitive bids to host what he termed the “next great American” military base.
The prospective realignment coincides with an overarching six-month Pentagon review of US force posture across Europe.
Scheduled to conclude in December, the assessment is evaluating mechanisms to transfer conventional deterrence burdens to NATO allies while reducing the roughly 80,000 American military personnel currently deployed across the continent.
Prior contingency scenarios reported by US defense media indicated that prospective drawdowns could affect between 25,000 and 40,000 troops, primarily from long-standing garrisons in Western Europe such as Germany, Italy, and Spain.
While the US does not maintain large-scale permanent military bases in South America, the administration has progressively deployed naval and air assets to interdict regional narcotics trafficking networks, which the White House has formally designated as national security threats.
Since September 2025, US armed forces have carried out at least 70 kinetic strikes targeting suspected drug-trafficking vessels across the Caribbean Sea and the Eastern Pacific Ocean, killing 234 individuals classified by Washington as narco-terrorists.
In recent weeks, US forces expanded interdiction operations off the coast of Ecuador to target maritime “floating refueling stations,” intercepting large commercial fishing vessels and removing their crews before destroying the ships with explosives.
Allied munitions strain
The potential redeployment of American capabilities away from Europe unfolds as allied governments confront widening delivery delays for contracted US weapon systems.
Washington has notified European and Indo-Pacific partners to anticipate postponements of up to five years for key precision-strike and air defense systems, as the Pentagon prioritizes replenishing domestic stockpiles depleted during combat operations against Iran.
Operational expenditures in the Middle East have consumed more than half of the US military’s inventory of advanced Patriot interceptors – leaving fewer than 1,700 missiles in reserve – alongside a third of its Tomahawk cruise missile inventories and roughly half of its THAAD interceptors.

How the aggressive lone star tick unleashed a hidden meat allergy on millions of Americans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- A lone star tick invasion is turning Martha’s Vineyard into ground zero for alpha-gal, a meat and dairy allergy reshaping daily life and medical care.
- Warmer climates and booming deer herds are fueling the spread of the ticks, which have been likened to ‘a cross between a lentil and a velociraptor.’
- Local officials, doctors and businesses scramble for answers, including meatless menus, while researchers chase distant solutions and a long-hoped-for vaccine.
WEST TISBURY, Mass. — Like a matador swirling his cape, Patrick Roden-Reynolds pulled a swatch of white flannel this way and that on the grass and leaf litter in my yard. After a minute or so, he plucked 11 tiny ticks from the cloth with tweezers, and stuck them on a lint roller.
“It’s like a plague,” he said, peering at his haul. “Ticks are everywhere now.”
I had asked Roden-Reynolds, a public health biologist, to inspect my yard because a lone star tick bit me as I was chopping wood last fall. It wasn’t painful, but after several weeks I developed alpha-gal syndrome, an increasingly common allergy to red meat, dairy and other mammalian food products.
Like many on Martha’s Vineyard, a resort island off Cape Cod that’s teeming with ticks this year, I bid a sad farewell to hamburgers, bacon and lamb chops. No ice cream. No pizza. My medicine cabinet became a minefield of animal-derived byproducts, including gelatin capsules and pain meds with lactose.
If I err, and I do, my legs sometimes itch so fiercely they feel on fire and I break out in hives. I grew ill one night just from the fumes of grilling meat. And I’ve got a mild case. Some victims suffer headaches, nausea, fever, diarrhea, vomiting or abdominal cramps so sharp that a friend calls them “knives in the stomach.”
Martha’s Vineyard, long known for attracting celebrities, has become the inevitable butt of memes as it battles the hostile arachnids. Editors from London to Hollywood, elated that blood-sucking predators are attacking A-listers on their private beaches, have posted lurid headlines about “Vegan Vampire” ticks and “Billionaires Under Siege.”
The mechanical chomping shark in “Jaws,” which was filmed on the Vineyard in 1975, invariably gets a mention. As in the thriller, anxious local leaders debated whether publicizing the peril would scare off tourists.
The island’s troubles are another reminder of the unexpected effects of climate change. Once confined to the Southeast, lone star ticks spread from Maine to Oklahoma in recent years as the climate warmed and as a decline in hunting led to an explosive growth in the number of whitetail deer, where lone stars find mates and breed.
The tick-borne allergy was discovered only in 2007, and researchers still can’t say why some immune systems go haywire and some don’t. A delayed reaction adds to the muddle because most victims don’t get sick until hours after eating, and weeks or months after the tick bite. There’s no known cure.
“It’s enigmatic enough that it’s almost the stuff of sci-fi or fantasy,” said Dr. Jeffrey Wilson, a University of Virginia School of Medicine allergist and immunologist who has treated nearly 1,000 alpha-gal patients. Many were dumbfounded to discover that food they’d enjoyed all their lives suddenly made them deathly ill.
1. Roden-Reynolds does tick surveys throughout Martha’s Vineyard. . 2. When Roden-Reynolds conducts tick surveys, he wears clothing permeated with the tick-killing insecticide permethrin.
“For a lot of people, this is antithetical to being American,” Wilson told me. “They say, ‘I want to go outside and do what I want to do. I want to eat a hamburger.’”
At a party on the Vineyard recently, I met Jean-Marc Dupon, a 61-year-old former French chef who can no longer work in a professional kitchen due to his alpha-gal. He was twice rushed to the hospital after his throat closed, he couldn’t breathe and his blood pressure plummeted — a severe allergic reaction called anaphylaxis.
He was so stricken when a local restaurant mistakenly grilled his food in butter, instead of oil, that he was unconscious when the ambulance arrived.
“It’s not just an inconvenience for me,” he said. “It’s a matter of life and death.”
The first alpha-gal fatality was confirmed in 2025 after Brian Waitzel, an otherwise healthy JetBlue pilot, died four hours after he ate a hamburger at a backyard barbecue in New Jersey. Experts say other deaths almost certainly have occurred.
It’s unclear how many people are affected, but in July, a study by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention concluded that an accurate tally would “far exceed” the CDC’s 2022 estimate of 450,000 Americans.
That study found 1 in 4 adults tested positive for alpha-gal in the five worst-hit states — Arkansas, Kentucky, Missouri, Tennessee and Virginia, or more than 4 million people. The counting is tricky, however. Only a small percentage of those who test positive, perhaps 15%, show symptoms.
Those who do often struggle to get help. A 2017 study in North Carolina found more than 90% of alpha-gal cases were misdiagnosed, often as food poisoning, because doctors were unfamiliar with it. My dermatologist in Washington, D.C., didn’t even know a blood test could measure alpha-gal antibodies.
Nancy Slonim Aronie, a writer and artist friend on the Vineyard, had a more alarming experience after she was rushed to a hospital in Boston in January for open heart surgery.
“The surgeon told me I might need a new heart valve, and that she had a cow valve she could use,” Aronie recalled. “And I said, ‘No, no, no, I have alpha-gal.’ And she said, ‘What’s that?’ And I thought, ‘Wow, my surgeon doesn’t know about alpha-gal.’ And then she said, ‘No problem, I think I have a pig valve on the shelf.’” And I’m like, ‘No pig!’”
In the end, she didn’t need a replacement valve. But she was treated with heparin, an anticoagulant derived from intestinal tissue of pigs. She broke out in hives, and “since then I’ve had really bad alpha-gal, much worse than before the operation.”
Lone star ticks, named for the white dot on the female’s back, haven’t hit California. But the western blacklegged tick, known as the deer tick in most of the country, is common in the state’s chaparral, grasslands and woods, and can transmit Lyme disease, babesiosis and other pathogens.
Luckily, those diseases can be cured by antibiotics or other remedies. Plus, an infected deer tick must keep its harpoon-like feeding tube in the bloodstream for 36 to 48 hours to transmit the bacteria that causes Lyme disease. That’s enough time for many to remove the tick.
A lone star bite, in contrast, instantly injects a galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose carbohydrate molecule into the blood. The sugar, found in most mammals but not in humans, prompts the antibodies that trigger an allergic reaction.
Lone stars are tough little buggers. Though low temperatures will plunge them into dormancy, they produce a type of antifreeze that lets them survive harsh winters. They can stay hours underwater, and have no natural predators. And they’ve been around since the dinosaurs.
“It’s the most aggressive tick in North America,” said Thomas Mather, professor of public health entomology and head of a tick research center at the University of Rhode Island. It’s also apparently the swiftest.
“If ESPN ever puts a tick race on TV, always put your money on the lone star,” he said.
1. Roden-Reynolds looks for ticks during one of his surveys.
Sensory organs in their eight feet and two antenna-like palps sense heat or carbon dioxide from people passing by, and they quickly climb aboard, piercing the flesh with long, barbed mouthparts.
“Think of them as a cross between a lentil and a velociraptor,” the National Society of Professional Surveyors, a group not normally known for purple prose, warns on its website. “These aggressive hunters,” it adds, “will actively pursue you across significant distances.”
On the Vineyard, local health officials call the threat a crisis. The Martha’s Vineyard Hospital has tallied an exponential rise in positive alpha-gal tests — 692 this year through August, compared with 742 last year, and up from only two in 2020.
“It is the most pressing emerging illness on the island right now,” Claire Seguin, president of the Martha’s Vineyard Hospital, told me. “It seems everyone I know has, or knows someone who has, alpha-gal syndrome, including here at the hospital.”
To ease pressure on the emergency room, the hospital opened a special outpatient clinic in June for tick-bite victims, and nearly 400 people were treated. The hospital also launched a $4-million research project into why only some people are affected and why their reactions vary so dramatically.
“Fear of tick bites rather than shark attacks now dominate the conversation,” agreed an op-ed in the Vineyard Gazette. “Like lead in the water in Flint, Mich., and the forest fires out West, the very fabric of our lives is being altered.”
“The situation is untenable,” Virginia Barbatti, executive director of Tick Free MV, a new nonprofit group that is trying to coordinate a response, told me. “What’s clear is everyone wants a path to solving this crisis.”
In response, school lunch menus were revamped to offer more meatless and dairy-free options. Restaurants in the island’s six towns, from the Sweet Life Cafe in Oak Bluffs to the Fish House in Edgartown, tweaked menus, recipes and how they cook.
“I switch out my pans, and I’m careful with knives and cutting boards to avoid cross contamination,” said Charlie Granquist, chef at Slough Farm. “I just know so many people with alpha-gal.”
He said his wife discovered her allergy only this spring when she “turned red as an Oompa Loompa” and went into anaphylaxis two hours after eating a hamburger.
At least nine companies sell pricey pesticide treatments or natural oil sprays for the backyard that are supposed to repel deer, or ticks, sparking an angry debate over whether they also endanger pets and pollinators. But other than avoiding tick bites, there’s no obvious solution.
“The holy grail is a tick vaccine,” Lea Hamner, an epidemiologist with a tick-focused program on the island, told an anxious crowd at one of the many public meetings focused on ticks. “People are working on it. But it’s a long way off.”
For now efforts are aimed at culling the vast deer herd. An aerial drone survey in March counted 4,681 white-tailed deer. It’s now probably closer to 6,000, far more than the 1,500 deemed optimal for wildlife management and tick control.
Officials have considered mass sterilization or hiring sharpshooters, but those options are wildly expensive. A treatment to eliminate ticks on deer, like a tick collar on dogs, shows promise. A proposed Roomba-like device to suck ticks out of the grass probably does not.
Hoping to boost the deer harvest, Massachusetts extended the Vineyard’s hunting season, which started Sept. 21, by six weeks, but most of the island’s 183 registered hunters only kill one or two deer a year — hardly enough to make a major impact.
But Brian Athearn, 54, is determined to try. An avid bowhunter, he shot 42 deer last year and hopes to take more this year. He donates the venison to food pantries because he has alpha-gal and his son “almost died from anaphylactic shock from two Advil gel caps,” he told me.
“I’m in it for revenge now,” he said.
Athearn has gone vegan, but I’m not there yet. I enjoy eating emu and ostrich, which taste surprisingly like beef. We also get pork chops that were genetically modified to remove the alpha-gal molecule, the byproduct of efforts to produce safe pig-based substances for pharmaceuticals.
When I’m futzing in the garden or hiking, I wear socks, pants and shirts permeated with the tick-killing insecticide permethrin. As insurance, I tuck my shirt in, pull my socks over my pant legs, and wear ankle-covering gaiters. It’s not high fashion, but I’ve avoided another bite. One friend wears her gaiters on the beach. I’m not there yet either.
On a recent afternoon I joined Roden-Reynolds, the public health biologist, as he surveyed an elderly couple’s yard in Chilmark, a tick hot spot. We both suited up in permethrin-infused clothes and gaiters, and he went to work with his white flannel flag, dragging it to and fro on the grass.
“We’ve gone from zero to crisis in five years,” he said as he stalked his prey.
He stopped after a few minutes to count his catch. “I’m just about getting a tick on every drag now,” he said. “There’s 11, 12, 13.”
He started up again but wiped his brow and quit when he hit 37.
Drogin is a special correspondent.

Supreme Court to weigh whether oil companies can be forced to pay for climate damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Supreme Court to weigh whether oil companies can be forced to pay for climate damage
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Justice Samuel A. Alito, a reliable conservative, withdrew from the case, making a 4-4 tie vote possible.
- In its new term, the court will also hear major cases on immigration and guns.
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court will open its new term Monday by hearing arguments on whether the oil and gas industry may be forced to pay damages for the scorching heat waves, wildfires and droughts that are blamed on climate change.
It’s a momentous question the justices have put off deciding for nearly a decade — and may do so again.
California joined more than two dozen blue states and municipalities in 2023 when it sued the five largest oil companies, alleging “decades of deception” over the danger of a warming climate.
They have “privately known the truth for decades but have fed us lies and mistruths to further their record-breaking profits at the expense of our environment,” California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta said.
Such climate-change lawsuits were patterned after the mass claims against the tobacco and opioid industries. Both were accused of concealing the dangers of their very profitable products.
But the climate suits have stalled. Judges have been divided over whether these potentially huge claims should be decided in federal or state court, and if so, under what law.
Last year, Boulder County, Colo., won a 5-2 ruling in the state Supreme Court that allowed its 2018 suit to proceed as a claim of a public nuisance, an unjust enrichment or a civil conspiracy. These are referred to as “common law” claims that are long-standing and traditional but do not rely on a measure approved by the Legislature.
California has sued five of the largest oil and gas companies in the world, alleging that they engaged in a ‘decades-long campaign of deception’ about climate change and the risks posed by fossil fuels.
The Colorado judges also said the climate-change suits are not “preempted” or blocked by federal anti-pollution laws because the suit for damages did not regulate greenhouse gas emissions.
The dissenters said the state court was giving Boulder a “green light to act as its own republic” to punish the Exxon Mobil Corp. for the impact of “global climate change.”
Appealing to the Supreme Court, the oil companies sounded the same theme.
“Boulder, Colorado cannot make energy policy for the entire country,” they said. A ruling for the county would “authorize all 50 states and tens of thousands of municipalities” to ask their local juries to “impose ruinous liability” on the fossil fuel industry, they told the court.
The Trump administration joined in support of the industry’s appeal.
“Our federal system would disintegrate if each state could tackle inherently national or international problems by forcing its regulatory prescriptions on the other 49,” the administration’s lawyers wrote.
In February, the justices voted to hear the case and decide whether federal law blocks state law claims for the “effects of interstate and international greenhouse-gas emissions.”
The court scheduled the case of Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil vs. Boulder County as the first of the new term.
Legal experts say the industry’s claim to be shielded by federal law is weak.
UCLA law professor Alejandro Camacho described the “preemption arguments as the latest and perhaps most ambitious effort to weaponize federal law to prevent polluters and fraudsters from paying for the harms they cause.”
Neither the Constitution nor the Clean Air Act provides such a shield, he said.
Legal experts on the other side question the notion that a public nuisance can be defined so broadly to include both the sale of a legal product and the impact on carbon pollution, much of it coming from China and India.
The outcome in the Supreme Court remains in doubt.
Last week, Justice Samuel A. Alito, a reliable conservative, announced he was withdrawing from the case. He did not say why, but he owns stock in other oil companies that could be affected by the court’s decision.
A broad ruling for Boulder would send a shock through the fossil-fuel industry and clear the wave of climate-change suits to proceed in state courts.
The industry may turn to Congress. Republicans in the House and Senate have introduced bills that would shield energy companies from such liability claims.
Similarly, a broad ruling shielding the oil companies probably would block all of the climate change suits, including California’s.
The justices may opt out of ruling, however.
When they granted review of the case, they asked the lawyers on both sides to weigh in on whether the high court had “jurisdiction” to decide the Boulder case.
Usually the U.S. Supreme Court reviews only final judgments handed down by state courts, and the Boulder case did not result in a final ruling.
And without Alito, the court could split 4 to 4.
Colorado ranchers struggling with severe drought and heat have filed a friend-of-the-court brief in a climate case that soon will be heard by the U.S. Supreme Court.
A decision based on a tie vote would affirm Boulder’s early stage victory but would not set a precedent that would govern other cases.
In its new term, the court also will hear major cases on immigration and guns.
Two of the cases test the Trump administration’s strict deportation policies. One denies bond hearings to people who entered the country illegally and may be deported.
In the past, the government usually offered bond hearings to those who could be held for months or even years while their claims were pending, so long as they could show they were not a flight risk or danger to the public.
But the Trump administration said it plans to detain tens of thousands of such persons indefinitely, even if they have no criminal record and pose no risk.
Government lawyers pointed to a provision of the 1996 immigration law that said people who entered the country illegally “shall be detained.” Previous administrations applied the mandatory-detention rule only to migrants who entered the U.S. illegally and were arrested near the border.
On Thursday, the court announced it will hear arguments on the mandatory detention policy, likely to be scheduled for January.
The other case involves so-called “third-country removals.”
The administration is determined to deport immigrants who have “final orders of removal,” many of whom have criminal records. But in some cases, they may not be sent back to their country of origin.
The policy of sending them to a third country has been condemned as harsh and cruel. Thousands of these people have been flown to impoverished countries that are dangerous and where they may be subjected to abuse.
The administration says it seeks assurances from those countries that the deported persons will not be not be abused or persecuted, but it refuses hearings for individuals.
More than 25,000 people have been expelled to ‘third countries’ under Trump, including to dangerous and conflict-ridden nations such as the Central Africa Republic.
U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy in Boston has ruled these deportees are entitled to a “meaningful notice” of where they are being sent and “meaningful opportunity” to contest this if they have a reasonable fear they will face persecution and torture.
Trump administration lawyers filed emergency appeals at the Supreme Court to set aside Murphy’s orders. They argued that the judge had gone beyond his authority, and the court’s conservatives agreed.
In December, however, the court will hear arguments from both sides on what the law calls for in such deportation cases.
Meanwhile, on Dec. 2, the court will hear a potential landmark on gun rights and and decide whether states may prohibit possession and sale of semiautomatic AR-15 rifles.
California and 11 other blue states have adopted such laws, often in response to mass shootings.
Gun rights advocates say these rapid-fire rifles are among the most popular weapons nationwide and should be protected as lawful under the 2nd Amendment’s right “to keep and bear arms.”
After turning away cases for a decade, the justices voted to hear 2nd Amendment challenges to the laws in Cook County, Ill., and the state of Connecticut.

Barabak: What's going to happen in the midterm election? Find out here. (Maybe)
Unknown

What’s going to happen in the midterm election? Find out here. (Maybe)
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Two of the country’s top political prognosticators see Democrats likely seizing the House and quite possibly the Senate.
- The guardrails Republicans were counting on to stem their November losses don’t seem to be holding.
There are few people, if any, who’ve tracked U.S. elections for longer or in greater depth than Charlie Cook.
Ever since 1984, when he started his eponymous political newsletter, Cook and his stellar crew of nonpartisan analysts have plumbed many thousands of races — for president, Congress, governor — following the money, sussing out the candidates, watching their ads and assaying the campaign landscape at a granular level.
Cook calls this midterm election the strangest he’s ever seen.
What appeared to be a fairly normal election for a president halfway through his term — a probable setback, as unhappy voters register their discontent — has the potential, Cook said, to turn into a disaster for Republicans. Big losses aren’t rare for the party in the White House. Democrats picked up 41 House seats in President Trump’s last midterm election, in 2018.
What’s unusual, Cook suggested, is the prospect of big Democratic gains when Republicans started out this election season with so many advantages. (And that was before the GOP set off on a gerrymandering jag at Trump’s behest.)
The four-seat gain Democrats need to win control once seemed all but out of reach. Odds are looking up, though the party still faces a tough path, with toss-up races in a half dozen (mostly red) states.
Roughly two-thirds of the Senate seats up in November are in states Trump carried in 2024. Five of the seven toss-up races are in states Trump won, several by double digits.
On the House side, Republicans maintain control by an exceedingly narrow margin, meaning there aren’t a lot of low-hanging districts for Democrats to aim for. As Cook rightly noted, “A party cannot lose a seat they don’t have.”
But Trump’s deteriorating approval rating, an unpopular war, persistent inflation and the president’s egotistical indulgences have jeopardized a number of GOP-held seats that normally would be automatic wins, including contests in such Republican strongholds as Alaska, Florida, Iowa, Ohio and even Texas.
“I’m not a meteorologist, but it’s kind of like three competing weather fronts collided,” Cook said. “One was Iran and gasoline, diesel prices going sky high ... Then there’s trade, tariffs, overall non-energy cost of living, tariff impact on farmers. And then the third is kind of the catch-all and it’s everything from ballrooms, reflecting pools, arches, vaccines, Medicaid cuts.”
We’ll get to predictions in a moment. (Patience, dear reader.)
First, let’s hear from Nathan Gonzales, another longtime election handicapper. He’s been tracking political contests nationwide for more than 25 years and edits and publishes Inside Elections — formerly the Rothenberg Political Report — another nonpartisan field guide to campaigns. Like Cook, he traffics in clear-eyed, dispassionate analysis, not partisan wish-casting or political spin.
Gonzales, too, sees a bad moon rising for Republicans.
Trump’s performance — his approval rating is flirting with record lows — “has inspired Democrats, turned off independents and created a group of apathetic Republicans,” Gonzales said, “and those are the ingredients for a good or great Democratic year.”
He noted Democrats don’t need a big wave to seize control of the House. A pickup of just three seats would flip the House, marking the seventh straight midterm election in which one chamber or the other changed partisan hands.
(For the record, there is no authoritative definition of a wave election, though it’s generally agreed the term applies to an election in which one party or the other gains a large and lopsided number of House and Senate seats.)
It’s beginning to feel a lot like 2006, Gonzales said.
“We had an unpopular Republican president, a war in the Middle East that drove up gas prices. Some members on Capitol Hill that were behaving badly,” Gonzales recalled. “I remember talking to Republicans after the fact and they admitted that, while they thought they had great research on Democratic candidates and they had a fundraising advantage, voters just didn’t care. Voters weren’t in the mood to listen to what they were saying about Democrats because they were so frustrated with what was going on with the status quo and the direction of the country.”
In that election, at the midpoint of President George W. Bush’s second term, Democrats gained six seats to take control of the Senate and netted 31 in the House, allowing the installation of Nancy Pelosi as the first female speaker in history. “A thumpin’,” Bush called it.
So, 2026.
Gonzales and his team of experts believe the House is most likely gone for Republicans, forecasting a Democratic gain of seven to 15 seats, unless the bottom falls out for the GOP and their losses climb much higher.
In the Senate, where Democrats need to pick up four seats to take control, Gonzales sees the chamber teetering on a knife’s edge, forecasting a Democratic gain of three to five seats.
“It’s too late to fundamentally change the trajectory of this election,” Gonzales said. “But if Republicans can boost Republican turnout, it might be enough to save the Senate.”
Stepping in for a complacent Congress, Democratic attorneys general are ready to fight efforts to undermine or overturn the Nov. 3 election. “We need to stay vigilant,” says Colorado’s Phil Weiser.
For his part, Cook agrees that Mike Johnson may be nearing the end of his speakership. The best-case scenario for the GOP would be keeping its losses to 25 House seats or less, Cook said, which is right around the average for midterm elections going back well over half a century.
“It starts getting into eyebrow-raising territory if it gets north of 35,” Cook said, “because that shouldn’t be possible with the few competitive districts we have now.”
As for the Senate, he suggested the best Republicans can hope for is a net loss of two seats, keeping the GOP barely in control. (A loss of three would mean a 50-50 split, leaving Vice President JD Vance poised to be the tiebreaker on close votes — and wouldn’t he love having to drop off the 2028 campaign trail to be on hand, just in case.)
Of course, there’s still an election to be held, votes to be cast and ballots to be counted.
Blue wave, tsunami or a pale sapphire puddle?
We’ll know in a little more than four weeks.

Hassan Salarieh, speaking at a ceremony marking Space Week at the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, pointed to progress in the country's space industry. He said very positive developments have occurred in recent years, especially over the past two years, which can be described as records in the field. He said Iran has reached historic milestones in many space industry development indicators, the result of teamwork across various bodies including the Ministry of Defence and Armed Forces Logistics, the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, universities, research centres and other institutions active in the country's space sector.
On recent achievements, Salarieh said Iran's first telecommunications satellite, Nahid-2, was successfully placed in orbit and most of its tests were successfully completed. Salarieh referred to heavy launches, saying the next success was the launch of the heaviest payload by the Simorgh satellite carrier, on which colleagues in the defence ministry are working. He said the simulator software test for the Saman orbital transfer block, presented by the Space Research Institute, was carried out with the Simorgh carrier. The Saman block, more advanced versions of which are under construction, plays a major role in reaching high orbits.
The head of Iran's Space Agency also announced the preparation of a new remote sensing satellite, saying Pars-2, a more advanced version of the Paya satellite, has been completed with imaging accuracy better than three metres and has been placed on the launch programme, with details to be announced.
He added that the first example of the "Shahid Soleimani constellation" was unveiled last year during the Ten-Day Dawn celebrations, and that the constellation is under construction and is among the communications ministry's most important space industry projects.

Supporters of the Al-Qaeda terrorist organization called for copycat attacks against Americans and Israeli passenger planes in a publication that referred to the September 11 attacks and praised Hammam al-Hammami, the flydubai co-pilot who attempted to hijack a flight. Four days after the attempted attack, Israeli authorities have yet to take responsibility for the failure or take steps to prevent similar incidents in the future.
The call was apparently published Friday and removed Saturday in the latest issue of “Al-Bayan,” a weekly publication launched by Al-Qaeda supporters in July. The New York Post reported that the issue referred both to the September 11 attacks and Wednesday’s attempted takeover of flydubai Flight FZ1073.
“The war is not over. Planes carrying Zionists, Americans and other infidels fighting Islam are still circling the skies and can be struck, as happened on September 11 and September 30,” the article threatened.
The article featured an image of a plane crashing into the World Trade Center towers on September 11, 2001, alongside an image referring to Wednesday’s attack on the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
“America and the Zionists have far more enemies today than they did in the past,” the article said. “Perhaps someone who does not believe in God will strike them, and his action will ultimately benefit Islam. The day will come when America’s evil empire will be destroyed.”
Despite the Al-Qaeda publication, no evidence has emerged that al-Hammami acted on orders from the terrorist organization or under the direction of any other outside party. Israeli security officials believe al-Hamami underwent a process of “Islamic radicalization” and acted on his own. However, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and U.S. President Donald Trump have both suggested that the co-pilot was directed by others.
From Syria to Australia to flydubai
Media reports provide a general picture of al-Hammami’s background. The Wall Street Journal reported that he grew up in Syria during the civil war that began in 2011, where his radicalization process apparently began.
According to Britain’s Guardian, the co-pilot later received a visa to Australia. A Sydney newspaper reported that he studied engineering in Melbourne for three years, until his visa was revoked.
He subsequently served as a pilot for Oman Air, although this has not been officially confirmed. After extremist materials were found in his possession, he was suspended from his position in 2024 and fired about a year later. He was hired by flydubai in early 2026.
ABC News reported that he is cooperating with investigators in the United Arab Emirates, where authorities have already declared the incident an act of terrorism. He testified that he had planned to crash the plane.
Investigation into Israel’s failure: 'There is no 100% security'
Whatever al-Hammami’s motives, the central question remains how a pilot holding Omani citizenship, whose background should have raised multiple red flags, was still allowed to fly to Israel. The agencies involved in conducting background checks on foreign crew members aboard flights to Israel are already blaming one another.
Prime Minister Netanyahu acknowledged that there had been a “loophole” that al-Hammami managed to exploit: A citizen of a country with no formal relations with Israel had been authorized to fly an aircraft into the country.
ynet has learned that investigators are examining whether al-Hammami had previously entered Israel as a pilot. That contradicts initial briefings immediately after the attempted attack, when Israeli officials denied that possibility. Transportation Ministry officials did not deny that al-Hammami may have flown to Israel before but said they currently have no information confirming it.
The Transportation Ministry, the body responsible for security checks, said it is not an intelligence agency and did not have the intelligence capabilities needed to vet the names of pilots and crew members on flights arriving in Israel.
Senior ministry officials said data on crew members arriving in Israel aboard foreign flights had not been retrieved or checked for about two years. Transportation Minister Miri Regev has already placed responsibility for the failure on the Mossad and the Israel Tax Authority.
During a briefing for reporters, the Civil Aviation Authority had no answer when asked how many pilots from hostile countries may already have landed in Israel and how passengers could be confident about boarding a foreign airline.
“We estimate there were none. But we have no certainty. There is no such thing as 100% security. Only if we shut down aviation entirely will everything be safe. We rely on local security.”

A new political storm is brewing for Erdogan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:51:35 UTC
18:51:35 KST

A new political storm is brewing for Erdogan
Until recently, it seemed that a split within the main, long-established opposition party (founded by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the architect of modern Türkiye) would play into the hands of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. Following a court ruling that removed Ozgur Ozel as the leader of the Republican People’s Party (CHP), his supporters broke away to form the Yeni Parti (New Party). The opposition suddenly found itself with two headquarters, two leaders, and a dispute over who rightfully owns its political legacy. However, September polls showed that a significant number of voters had followed Ozel. Yeni Parti took second place in surveys conducted by ASAL and GENAR. While it still has a long way to go to catch up with the ruling Justice and Development Party (AK Parti), the new movement can no longer be dismissed.
According to ASAL, if parliamentary elections were held, 33.8% of respondents would support AK Parti, while 23.6% would back Yeni Parti; that’s a gap of 10.2 percentage points. GENAR put support for the ruling party at 36.1% and Ozel’s party at 21.6%, recording a difference of 14.5 points. In both instances, AK Parti retained the top spot. Yet, for a political force established only in late July, the result is remarkable – especially considering that the CHP, under the leadership of Kemal Kilicdaroglu, garnered only about 6% in the same polls. The leadership of the party changed due to the court ruling, but judging by the surveys, the party failed to retain the bulk of its voter base.
To understand the origins of Yeni Parti, one must look back at the events of this spring. In May, a court annulled the results of the 2023 CHP congress – where Ozel had been elected chairman – and reinstated his predecessor, Kilicdaroglu. Ozel’s supporters viewed the ruling as interference in the affairs of the opposition. Turkish authorities deny allegations of pressuring the court and insist on the judiciary’s independence. The confrontation lasted several weeks until Ozel and 90 opposition MPs left the CHP. On July 24, they announced the formation of a new party. It immediately secured 91 parliamentary seats, becoming the largest opposition faction.
This demonstrates the unique nature of the current crisis. Yeni Parti emerged from a split within the opposition, yet it did not have to start from scratch. Ozel was supported by MPs, prominent politicians, and a portion of the organizational network that had worked for the CHP. He also retained the experience gained from the campaigns that delivered the opposition’s victory in the 2024 local elections. The new party allows the team to stay together and continue the fight, even though legal and political ties to the former party have been severed. For voters who supported Ozel prior to the court ruling, the shift to Yeni Parti appears logical.
At the same time, the September poll results also point to the party’s growth limitations. Erdogan’s AK Party maintains the lead in both polls, with a margin exceeding 14 points in the GENAR survey. It is too early for Erdogan’s supporters to speak of defeat, or for his opponents to anticipate an imminent change of power. However, the Turkish leader now faces a less favorable situation than might have emerged immediately after the CHP split. Erdogan’s main opponent did not just disappear along with his former party post, contrary to the predictions of many domestic experts. Ozel managed to shift the confrontation to a new arena and to quickly reclaim the role of parliamentary opposition leader.
The party’s future will depend on whether it can reach beyond the CHP’s traditional base of supporters. For now, the September figures can be interpreted either as a success for Ozel or as a redistribution of votes within the opposition. For example, a July study by GENAR put support for the CHP at 15.4% and for the then-nascent Yeni Parti at 14.5%. By September, the balance had shifted: Ozel’s party polled at 21.6%, while the CHP stood at 6.6%. These figures indicate voter migration between the two political forces. However, further polls and, ultimately, elections are necessary to confirm a sustained expansion of the opposition’s overall electoral base.
There is another issue that party ratings alone cannot resolve: Who will challenge Erdogan in the 2028 presidential election? Following the creation of Yeni Parti, Ozel reaffirmed his support for Ekrem Imamoglu – the mayor of Istanbul and a politician popular among Turkish youth – who is currently under arrest and facing legal proceedings. While Imamoglu remains a pivotal figure for opposition voters, his potential candidacy is complicated by a court case and the invalidation of his university degree, a requirement for presidential candidates. Ankara Mayor Mansur Yavas is also mentioned as a potential contender. While Yeni Parti boasts a prominent leader and a parliamentary faction, it is unclear who will be the opposition’s presidential candidate. And in a presidential campaign, this choice could prove far more significant than monthly fluctuations in party ratings.
Another challenge is that the Turkish opposition extends beyond Ozel’s party. Kilicdaroglu’s CHP party remains in parliament, while the pro-Kurdish DEM Party, the nationalist IYI Party led by Meral Aksener, and other forces also have their supporters. While all of them may oppose the incumbent president, they have different supporters and differing visions for the country’s future. Parliamentary elections allow each party to vie for its share of the vote; winning the presidency, however, requires an agreement capable of persuading the supporters of several parties to back a single candidate. The opposition already encountered this problem in 2023 – and ultimately suffered defeat.
Despite certain public fatigue regarding his long tenure, Erdogan retains significant political advantages. The ruling AK Party remains the leading party in the two abovementioned polls. Together with its ally, the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP, or Grey Wolves), it commands a stable electoral base, and the president continues to set the agenda for national politics. It is too early to say that Erdogan is in serious trouble, as the AK Party retains the top position in both surveys. However, Ozel has managed to retain a significant portion of the opposition electorate following the split within the CHP. If Ozel manages to attract voters who did not previously support the CHP, Erdogan will face a formidable rival.
The economic situation adds further tension to the situation. In September, the Turkish market faced a crisis involving investment funds and a sharp drop in asset prices. Against this backdrop, Zeynel Emre, a representative of Yeni Parti, leveled accusations regarding stock market transactions against AK Party Deputy Chairperson Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya and her husband. Kaya requested to be relieved of her party duties pending the investigation. While the allegations still require verification, the political impact is already evident: The new party is striving to position itself not only as a defender of its own rights following the split within the CHP but also as a force capable of posing uncomfortable questions to the authorities.
Yeni Parti has also encountered another problem: a dispute over its name. Another political organization, the Yenilik Partisi (Innovation Party), declared that the Yeni Parti name is too similar to its own and appealed to the prosecutor’s office. The matter eventually reached the Constitutional Court. On September 29, the court granted Yeni Parti 30 days to prepare its objections. No final decision regarding the name has been reached yet.
Looking ahead, Turkish politics faces another pressing issue: the upcoming presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled for 2028. The question of whether Erdogan can participate in the presidential race hinges on the timing of the election and constitutional regulations. An early vote called by parliament would allow him to run for another term, but such a decision requires a majority of 360 out of 600 deputies. The ruling bloc lacks the votes to resolve this matter unilaterally. Consequently, the outcome will depend not only on voter sentiment but also on negotiations between parties – including those currently on opposite sides of the political divide.
The latest surveys only show that following a painful rift within the opposition, Ozel has retained significant support. They do not reveal whether the Yeni Parti can catch up with the ruling AK Parti, find a presidential candidate acceptable to other forces, or bring about a change of power. For Erdogan, this means that he will have to monitor his new rival more closely. And for Ozel, it marks the beginning of a new phase in which he will have to transform his rapidly gained popularity into lasting political influence. Put together, these factors will determine the outcome of their standoff.

Costa’s coffee shops return to profit with iced drinks and matcha on the menu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:50:28 UTC
18:50:28 KST

Costa’s main coffee shop arm has returned to an operating profit after revamping its high street outlets and broadening its menu with iced drinks, matcha and fresher pastries.
The chain, which has 2,700 outlets in the UK and Ireland out of 4,000 globally, and employs about 20,000 people, also opened a net 50 new outlets in the UK last year – its first net increase in several years.
It plans a further 50 new UK outlets this year, including more drive-throughs and high street outlets.
Demand from younger consumers for decaffeinated coffee and other options is driving sales growth amid concerns about drinking caffeine in the afternoon, while there is heavy competition on classic coffees from companies such as Greggs, Gail’s, Caffè Nero and numerous smaller operators. Costa says it is now the largest seller of matcha via cafes in the UK.
The Costa Ltd arm made an operating profit of £20m in the year to 31 December 2025 after losses of £13.5m in 2024 and £5.8m the year before, according to accounts filed at Companies House. Revenues rose 5% to almost £1.3bn compared with 1% growth in 2024.
Philippe Schaillee, the chief executive of Costa, said the chain had experienced the strongest growth in visits in a decade.
Sipping a Velvetino, a low-calorie iced coffee popular with younger drinkers, Schaillee said: “The coffee shop is increasingly a destination for morning and afternoon. People not only want caffeine but iced herbal teas and those drinks that people will drink in the afternoon and evening.”
Showing off Costa’s new headquarters in St Albans, Hertfordshire, which will have space for 300 workers when it opens in January, he said it “really signals our confidence in the business”.
Costa plans to remodel about 250 stores a year after updating more than 1,200 of 1,700 company-owned outlets. That includes adding more digital self-order kiosks, which are already in 200 UK outlets.
The group is also selling more Podio office coffee machines, which launched in May and are intended to be “a barista in your office”.
Schaillee said Costa was already the UK’s third biggest brand in home coffee machines, and said the potential there was “limitless”.
Costa’s campaign to flag its strong performance comes after its owner, Coca-Cola, in February officially confirmed it had abandoned plans to sell the chain after bids failed to meet its expectations.
Coca-Cola had high hopes for Britain’s largest coffee chain when it bought it for £3.9bn in 2018 from Whitbread, the owner of Premier Inn hotels.
However, since then the chain has struggled in the face of rising costs, particularly the increase in coffee bean prices, and competition on UK high streets.
Schaillee said coffee production – and potentially prices – remained high and could be affected by the El Niño global climate phenomenon, which is affecting coffee and cocoa growers in Latin and South America. “We need to be prepared for that,” he said.

The story of a book in Gaza: A treasured possession given new lease of life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:46:48 UTC
18:46:48 KST

The story of a book in Gaza: A treasured possession given new lease of life
A team of book enthusiasts in Gaza is trying to keep Palestine’s literary heritage alive amid a genocide.
Aya al-Shawa, 10, sits in sixth grade at a school in northern Gaza, holding a book she recently received and what is now one of her most treasured possessions.
Before it reached Aya’s hands, it had a difficult journey. It once sat on a bookshelf before an Israeli attack demolished the building it was housed in, leaving it buried beneath the rubble. Then one day someone recovered it, cleaned it, sorted its pages and repaired them. The book then found its way to a new reader.
Amid the widespread destruction in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, books – one of the most vulnerable of all items – have become a rare commodity.
About 98 percent of school buildings in the Gaza Strip have been destroyed or damaged, according to UNICEF.
With approximately 700,000 children in Gaza deprived of regular in-person education since the war began in October 2023, books have also become a vital way for children to reconnect with learning.
UNESCO has documented widespread damage to cultural sites and institutions in Gaza, including libraries. With a “ceasefire” in Gaza since October 2025, during which there has been a relative decrease in Israeli bombing, books have begun to take a second life.
Mohammed Saad, 54, from Beit Lahiya, has spent more than 35 years collecting books, and before the war, he estimated that he had between 50,000 and 100,000 titles in his library.
On December 7, 2023, the library was destroyed.
After being displaced 16 times in total, Saad returned to Beit Lahiya again to see what remained of his book collection. From the rubble of his home, he began to pull out the surviving books.
“I risked my life to save these books from beneath the rubble,” Saad said.
He managed to recover about 12,000 books from the rubble and moved what he could to Deir el-Balah, where he erected a tent and established a library called Athar, meaning “impact” but also relating to antiquities or historical relics.
From the tent, Saad and his son Mohammed began cleaning and repairing the thousands of books in their possession.
But Saad’s goal is not only to save the books from damage. He also wants them to reach people, particularly children.
The library now sees children coming every day, looking for stories that might help them find some escape from their hardships.
They buy some of them at symbolic prices ranging from 5 shekels to 15 shekels ($1.63-$4.89), given that books have become unaffordable for most families.
Giving children access to books is a key reason for saving them in the first place: to keep knowledge accessible and give them a path back to reading and learning despite war and displacement.
But the books Saad rescues still face other dangers. Inside the tent, there is little protection from the sun, heat, humidity and rain.
“I saved them from beneath the rubble and from the fire. Today, I cannot save them from the rain,” Saad said.
Elsewhere, Omar Hamad, 30, a displaced person from Beit Hanoon in northern Gaza, has also been searching for destroyed libraries for books.
He traced the locations of libraries in northern Gaza and Gaza City and contacted their owners. So far, Hamad says, he and his team have extricated some 3,000 books.
Not all of the books came from rubble. Some were donated by the families of people who were killed and had private libraries, while the team bought or reprinted others.
Among the books Omar rescued was The Catastrophe of Palestine, printed in 1956. He found it in the destroyed Islamic University of Gaza library, where books were scattered among the rubble.
Retrieving the book was only the beginning of his task.
Omar and his friend Ibrahim cleaned the books, removed dust and traces of rubble, sorted and arranged the pages, and tried to repair whatever they could.
When a book required more specialised restoration, he turned to Jameel Mikdad, 71, in the Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.
Mikdad has worked in bookbinding and book repair for more than 45 years. His library and printing shop were destroyed during the war, but he continued working with limited resources, using his experience to rearrange pages, glue torn sections of the works, sew books and rebind them.
There is no single cost for repairing a book; it depends on the extent of the damage and the materials required. But the cost of materials has risen sharply.
Mikdad says a 3kg (6.6-pound) container of white glue cost 30-35 shekels ($9.78-11.48) before the war. Its price has now risen to 450-500 shekels ($146.74-163.05) due to Israel’s siege on Gaza and the damage caused by the war.
Repairing a damaged book can take two days to a week, depending on its condition. Sometimes the cost of repair can exceed the value of the book.
Not every book can be repaired. Omar says some of the books they found were 80 or 90 percent damaged and had to be left behind because they were no longer repairable or restorable.
At other times, they kept books that could no longer be read because bullet holes or fire damage made them witnesses to the genocide in Gaza.
“We took them with us so they could remain witnesses to this crime,” Omar said.
For the books that can be saved, Omar does not want them to remain on library shelves but to be distributed throughout a population known for their love of literature.
At the Phoenix Library, books are lent rather than sold. Readers can borrow one or two books a week after paying a refundable deposit of 50 shekels ($16.30). The library has books on literature, medicine, law, history, economics and science. There are also books for children and for students related to specialised fields of study.
Omar also organises initiatives to deliver books to students at schools, so they can be used once again for their original purpose: reading and learning.
Aya, 10, ends up with one such book: The Adventure of the Empty House by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle.
She sees the novel as a way of continuing her education when schools, often taking the form of a crowded tent, struggle to resume their role in teaching children.
And so, the journey of the book is complete.
It began on a shelf in a home or library in Gaza before the building was levelled in one of Israel’s thousands of air raids. It then remained beneath the rubble for months before being rescued by a person who risked their life to rescue lost books. It was then passed on to a restoration expert who repaired and cleaned it. Finally, it ended up in the hands of a student who will continue to love learning and overcome Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Ultimately, the book survived destruction and returned to its first purpose: to be opened and read.

Also, according to available data, the regulator instructed financial institutions to conduct comprehensive security checks, strengthen access controls, minimize external access to systems and enhance consumer protection measures.
It is also noted that attack methods, internet protocol addresses and other threat information will be rapidly shared throughout the industry to prevent further incidents
At the same time, regulators believe that the attacks may not have been directed at one specific institution, but rather involved the simultaneous scanning of several financial companies to search for vulnerabilities.

The turnout dropped 10 percent bellow the level of the last election in 2022. According to the Central Voter's Register, this time 42 percent of registered voters cast their ballots.
Bitter memories of that era have been revived by the recent death of Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic, who was convicted of genocide by The Hague tribunal for war crimes in Bosnia, and the subsequent hero’s funeral he received in Belgrade.
