2026-10-04
09:43:26 UTC
18:43:26 KST

Cornell University will examine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus after an outcry over the school’s handling of a student’s rape allegations, the Ivy League school’s president has said.
A civil lawsuit filed last month by the woman, who alleges she was drugged and raped in 2024 by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity, has prompted outrage and soul-searching at Cornell over its campus culture at the school in Ithaca, New York.
In a video message on Saturday, the Cornell University president, Michael Kotlikoff, said the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the future. That included “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”, Kotlikoff said.
“At their best, these organisations can provide students with friendship, belonging, mentorship and a powerful sense of community,” he said. “But being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility.“
The university would seek input, he said, from students, alumni and others on how to “preserve what is valuable about Greek life while strengthening individual accountability, transparency and a culture in which every member understands their responsibility to protect the safety and wellbeing of others”.
The lawsuit against Cornell, seven fraternity members and others, alleges that the school failed to adequately punish some of the accused students.
The accused men have denied all wrongdoing, the New York Times has reported.
Cornell has defended its handling of the matter, saying that in 2024 it launched a comprehensive investigation and barred the Chi Phi fraternity from campus. The school said it also imposed a range of disciplinary measures, including expulsions.
But “we must do better”, Kotlikoff said, adding: “We don’t have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves.”
He vowed that university officials would “be more transparent” about their actions related to the 2024 incident, but he did not detail specific initiatives that the university would take. “In the coming weeks, we will create additional opportunities for members of our community to ask questions and hear directly from university leadership,” he said.
The case has reignited scrutiny of how law enforcement and universities handle sexual assault complaints, with students questioning whether processes are enough to protect them. It has also drawn the attention of New York state officials, who have appointed a special prosecutor to investigate.
As the special prosecutor, Letitia James, the New York attorney general, investigates, new attention has been drawn to the findings of a state-mandated sexual violence survey conducted by Cornell in 2025, which found that 35% of female undergraduates who completed the survey reported that they had experienced nonconsensual sexual contact while at the university.
The 2025 version of the survey was the first to specifically include unwanted choking or strangulation in the definition of nonconsensual sexual contact involving force or incapacitation that students were asked about, in addition to nonconsensual penetration and/or sexual touching.

FlyDubai captain said “I had one more fight left in me” and opened cockpit door
Unknown

FlyDubai hero captain Smit Machchhar described to Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu how the attack started and how he managed to finally open the cockpit door after nearly losing his vision under the co-pilot’s repeated blows. “I knew I couldn't let the passengers die,” Machchhar said.
The FlyDubai hero captain revealed new details of his fight to save the passengers aboard flight FZ1073 in an emotional telephone conversation with Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, released by his office on Saturday evening.
The UAE, which is leading the investigation, said the co-pilot attacked the flight’s captain with the cockpit’s crash ax and tried to take control of the plummeting plane in a “terrorist attack” on Wednesday.
Captain Smit Machchhar told Netanyahu he felt he had “one more fight left” in him when in a critical state he reached for the cockpit door once again to save the 174 passengers and 6 crew members, while the co-pilot kept attacking him and putting the aircraft in a steep defence.
He described how the attack started saying that the co-pilot asked to pray in the cockpit which he did not consider an unusual request and “and out of respect for him, I didn’t look back.”
“After 4-5 minutes, I felt a heavy blow to the back of my head. My first thought was that catastrophic damage had been caused to the plane and something was wrong, but the blows kept coming one after another, and then I realized it wasn't the plane... it was the other guy who was with me in the cockpit," the captain described the attack.
Machchhar said his vision became badly blurred from the blows and he felt how the aircraft went into a steep descent. He tried to open the cockpit door once again, but the co-pilot kept closing it while passengers were trying to get in using the access code.
Netanyahu asked him if the door was closed with a pin mechanism and the captain answered that on the inside of the cockpit the door had a twist handle and that from the outside it could be opened with a code.
Machchhar remembered hearing the whooshing sound of the aircraft plunging downwards and the passengers screaming.
Realising what was happening, he told Netanyahu how he reached for the internal twist handle and with “a sharp, quick turn” managed to finally open the door, letting the passengers in who subdued the co-pilot and stabilised the plane.
The captain said that the co-pilot "locked the cockpit door and I was lying on the floor. I heard people screaming. I realized I had one last fight left: if I don't do this, I will die with the last of my strength, I opened the door, and people were already waiting right outside and jumped in".
“I knew I couldn't let the passengers die,” Machchhar said.
The Israeli prime minister told him that he is a hero with “an unbelievable courage, inviting him and Indian prime minister Narendra Modi to light a celebratory flame on Israel’s next Independence Day, the highest honour usually reserved for Israeli citizens.
“You are a true hero of the brave peoples of India and Israel, and you are a hero of the entire world. I wish you a very speedy and complete recovery," Netanyahu told captain Machchhar.
Israeli Ambassador to the UAE Yossi Shelley was at his bedside during the call and together with Netanyahu invited Machchhar and his family to visit Israel as soon as he is able, to receive the embrace and love that the entire country wants to give him.
Dubai's Crown Prince and UAE Minister of Defence Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid also visited Machchhar in hospital hailing the captain’s bravery, stating that he “embodied the highest degrees of courage, responsibility, and care for human life.”
“From us, and from the leadership of the nation, he has our full appreciation and praise. We are proud that he is part of our team, part of the story of our nation and part of what the UAE stands for a nation of compassion, a nation of peace and a nation of life,” Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed said.
In a new development on Sunday, British newspaper The Telegraph reported that the FlyDubai flight copilot, named by multiple media outlets as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, studied aviation at the UK-based Buckinghamshire New University.
The Telegraph said that during his time at the university, al-Hammami commented in social media posts that women should be “stomped on” and praised giving a woman a “pre-emptive slap.” He also appeared to praise Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, The Telegraph said.
The co-pilot used a crash axe against the captain and “attempted to carry out a terrorist attack”, the United Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said on Saturday, while the UAE president's diplomatic adviser Dr Anwar Gargash called the incident "a dangerous terrorist act".
Meanwhile on Sunday, regional officials said that the UAE authorities shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of the FlyDubai flight, including their nationalities, raising new questions over how the attacker evaded detection, the Associated Press reported.
According to AP, who quoted regional officials, Israel hadn’t raised red flags on any passenger or member of the crew.
Prime Minister Netanyahu later told the head of the National Security Council to appoint an examiner to review “all security aspects regarding foreign civil aviation to Israel.”
The Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, said the Transportation Ministry is responsible for vetting passenger lists from foreign flights. Transportation Minister Miri Regev told Israel’s public broadcaster Kan that the security agencies are responsible for flight security and that her ministry wasn’t given a list of passengers or any warnings.
Sharing the list is standard aviation procedure. But the head of aviation security at the Transportation Ministry, Dvir Rubenstien, told Army Radio that the ministry relies on local security checks and does not have the tools or the ability to run checks on each passenger on every flight.
Prime Minister Netanyahu said Thursday that Israel has long-standing agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from flying into the country if they are citizens of nations that don’t maintain diplomatic relations with Israel.
It also remains unclear how FlyDubai, a low-cost Emirati airline that operates flights between Israel and the UAE, had failed to identify the Omani pilot as a security risk and allowed him to fly the sensitive route to Israel.
Ahead of the elections at the end of the month, some opposition candidates have seized on the security failures to highlight what they perceive as negligence on the part of Netanyahu and his supporters. Transportation Minister Miri Regev is a member of Netanyahu’s Likud party and a staunch supporter.
“This is exactly what system collapse looks like,” Yair Golan, head of the opposition Democrats party, wrote on X. “A transportation minister who completely abandons our skies, and a prime minister who abandons national security.”
The UAE is leading the investigation and security agencies from four regional countries including Israel were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the United States and other Western governments, according to the AP.

Samuel: The Tsar Who Refused to Let Bulgaria Die
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:37:10 UTC
18:37:10 KST

On Saturday, Bulgaria laid to rest the remains of Tsar Samuel in the Basilica of St. Sofia, more than a thousand years after his death. The ceremony closed a diplomatic process that began in the 1970s. It also opened a new chapter in an older argument: who Samuel was, what his state was, and why his bones matter so much to three countries.
A state that refused to die
Samuel's story begins with a collapse. In 971, Byzantine Emperor John I Tzimiskes captured Preslav, the capital of the First Bulgarian Kingdom, after driving out the Kievan Rus who had occupied it. Tsar Boris II was taken to Constantinople and stripped of his regalia. Byzantium considered Bulgaria finished.
It wasn't. The western lands, centred on Macedonia, were never conquered. There, four brothers known as the Komitopuli, the sons of a provincial governor, Count (Komit) Nikola, took up the fight. David, Moses, Aron and Samuel launched an uprising around 976, after Tzimiskes died.
The brothers did not last long. David was killed by wandering Vlachs and Moses fell besieging Serres. Aron was executed on Samuel's orders along with most of his family, reportedly for negotiating with the Byzantines. Historians still disagree on whether this happened in 976 or 987. Only one of Aron's sons, Ivan Vladislav, was spared. That decision would come back to haunt the dynasty.
For years Samuel led the state as its military commander, while Roman, a son of the former Tsar Peter, held the title of tsar. Only after Roman died in Byzantine captivity was Samuel crowned, around 997.
Glory
The high point came in August 986. Emperor Basil II besieged Sofia, then known as Sredets, and failed to take it. On his way back, Samuel's army ambushed him at the pass known as Trajan's Gate. The imperial army was routed and Basil barely escaped. It was one of the worst defeats of his reign, and it shaped everything that followed.
Over the next decade Samuel rebuilt and expanded the state, from the Adriatic coast to Thessaly. He took Larissa after a long siege and moved the relics of its patron, St. Achillius, to an island in Lesser Prespa Lake. There he built a monumental basilica that became the seat of the Bulgarian patriarchate. His raids reached as far as the Peloponnese.
The long decline
Around 997, at the river Spercheios in central Greece, Samuel's army was surprised by the Byzantine general Nikephoros Ouranos and slaughtered. Samuel and his son Gavril Radomir survived, wounded, by hiding among the dead. Archaeologists believe a badly healed fracture on the left forearm of the skeleton now in Sofia may date from that night.
From 1001, Basil returned almost every year with a methodical campaign. Pliska and Preslav fell, then Vidin after an eight-month siege, then Skopje. Samuel kept fighting for another 13 years, without regaining the initiative.
The end came at Kleidion, in the Belasitsa mountains, on 29 July 1014. Basil's forces broke through Bulgarian fortifications and captured a large part of Samuel's army. According to the Byzantine chronicler John Skylitzes, Basil ordered 14,000 or 15,000 prisoners blinded, leaving one man in every hundred with one eye to lead the rest home. When Samuel saw them arrive at Prespa, he collapsed. He died on 6 October 1014.
A story worth questioning
The blinding is the most famous episode of Bulgarian medieval history and one of the least verified. Skylitzes wrote decades after the events. Michael Psellos, an earlier historian who covered Basil's reign, does not mention it. Many historians consider the numbers inflated, given the logistics of blinding and moving thousands of prisoners across mountain terrain. Even Basil's famous nickname, Bulgaroktonos or "Bulgar-Slayer," only appears in sources more than a century and a half after his death. A brutal act may well have happened. Its scale likely grew with the legend.
The fall
Samuel's death broke the state. In 1015, Gavril Radomir was murdered by his cousin Ivan Vladislav, the boy Samuel had spared. Ivan Vladislav reigned three years and left the Bitola inscription, in which he describes himself as Bulgarian by birth. He died besieging Dyrrhachium, modern Durrës, in early 1018. Weeks later his widow, Tsaritsa Maria, surrendered to Basil in Ohrid. The First Bulgarian Kingdom was over.
The bones
Greek archaeologist Nikolaos Moutsopoulos began excavating the Basilica of St. Achillius in 1965. In 1969 his team uncovered graves in the most honoured part of the church. One held the skeleton of a man of around 70, about 160 centimetres tall, with a crooked left forearm and a head wound, buried in remains of fine clothing and armour. Moutsopoulos attributed it to Samuel. Two nearby graves held remains he linked to Gavril Radomir and other members of the family.
The identification has its critics, mostly in Greece, who argue that the burial style and clothing point to later Byzantine elites. Bulgarian medievalists Dr. Konstantin Golev of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences and Prof. Pavlov, speaking on the Bulgarian History podcast before the ceremony, said they have little doubt. They point to the location inside Samuel's own patriarchal cathedral, the war injuries consistent with sources, and a grave protected for centuries by an arched niche that looters mistook for rock. According to Greek media, more recent anthropological and protein analyses also support the attribution.
Golev nevertheless warned that the remains should have been tested in full, including DNA, before reburial. Genetic analysis cannot prove the skeleton is Samuel's, but it can show whether the men in the neighbouring graves were close relatives. Once the bones lie in St. Sofia, he noted, the identification becomes the position of the Bulgarian state.
Significance
Bulgaria has a peculiar problem for a country with 13 centuries of statehood: it has almost no identified remains of its rulers or national heroes. Attributions for Khan Kubrat and Tsar Kaloyan remain disputed. The graves of Vasil Levski and Hristo Botev are unknown. Samuel now becomes the first medieval Bulgarian ruler whose burial place can be pointed to with reasonable confidence.
For North Macedonia, where Samuel is central to national historiography, the transfer is a blow. The joint Bulgarian-Macedonian historical commission had agreed that Samuel ruled a state most historians consider Bulgarian. Yet Skopje's official reaction stressed defending Macedonian identity, and parts of its media called the ceremony a spectacle.
Samuel's life, with its revival, brilliant victories, family bloodshed and collapse, has long been read as a mirror of Bulgarian history. His remains have finally come home. The arguments about him have not ended with the burial.

Who are the mystery pilots who successfully landed endangered Flydubai flight 1073?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Who are the mystery pilots who successfully landed endangered Flydubai flight 1073?
A passenger on Flydubai flight 1073 has described the actions of on-duty crew members who rushed into the cockpit to stabilise and land the plane after the co-pilot attacked the captain with a crash axe. The flight carrying 182 people en route to Israel Wednesday was able to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a descent so extreme that part of its rudder was torn away.
Who are the mystery pilots who stepped in to stabilise the Flydubai flight 1073 as it hurtled toward disaster?
As of Saturday, three days after the uniformed crew members rushed to the cockpit to steady the Israel-bound plane carrying 182 people after a sickening plummet, they still haven't been publicly identified. Flydubai has called them only on-duty crew members traveling on the plane. It’s not clear why the airline hasn't said more.
One passenger at the front of the plane, though, described the men’s actions in an interview with The Associated Press, giving one of the most detailed accounts of the yet-unsung heroes.
Read moreFlydubai hero pilot tells Modi 'I could not let all those people die'
“This is one of the miracles,” said Daniel Schlichter, who was seated in the second row.
“That not in every flight they bring two extra pilots. In this case, they brought them because they should have brought the plane back from Tel Aviv to Dubai, and this is the only reason they were there.” The practice is called deadheading.
The two men responded after screaming passengers discovered what was unfolding in the cockpit. They said the co-pilot was attacking the captain over and over, and blood was everywhere. The captain, while badly wounded, managed to unlock the cockpit door.
After a passenger grabbed the co-pilot and pulled him out, and others grappled with the man to subdue him, Schlichter said that one of the traveling pilots practically hurdled the scrum to enter the cockpit and seize the controls.
Read moreUAE investigators say Omani Flydubai co-pilot was planning 'terrorist' attack
“He was actually kind of jumping above the guys that were handling the terrorist, and he reached out to the pilot area and started to take over,” Schlichter said. “And then the other guy, the other pilot, joined in and they closed the door because they didn’t want anybody else to be there.”
Schlichter, like others, wasn’t sure where the two men had come from. But whoever the first one was, he moved very quickly.
“He acted really like a hero, taking over the plane and reacted like he understood exactly what is going on, and I think we owe him our lives not less than the other heroes that went on the flight,” Schlichter said.
Once the two entered the cockpit and closed the door, Schlichter wasn’t sure who did what inside. It took “quite a lot of minutes”, maybe 10 or more, to stabilise the plane after a descent so extreme that part of its rudder was torn away.
A mayday call was made as the men frantically sought a place to land.

Meanwhile, some of the frightened and wary passengers wondered about them and whether they could be trusted.
“After they managed to stabilise the airplane, actually they did not have any communication with us, and I have to tell you, I was worried about this,” Schlichter said.
He worried about an even worse situation – that the men might be “hijacking the plane into maybe Iran, or I don’t know where, because we’re actually not too far”.
But after about 45 minutes, he said, the pilots announced that they would be landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, and everything was going to be OK.
With that, Schlichter said, he decided to trust them. And it turned out to be true.

Germany to Provide Ukraine with €1 Billion in Military Aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:36:14 UTC
18:36:14 KST

Germany will provide Ukraine with €1 billion in military aid, along with an additional €350 million to help repair energy infrastructure.
Reuters reported the news.
According to German government officials, Chancellor Friedrich Merz is expected to announce the new support package during his visit to Kyiv on October 4. Germany and Ukraine are also expected to finalize an agreement on jointly producing various types of drones.
“I came to Kyiv today because Ukraine needs all the support we can give in the coming weeks. If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn against us,” Merz said, noting that Russian forces are bombing cities, residential buildings, and heating infrastructure.
The German chancellor is accompanied by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and a business delegation that includes executives from energy and defense companies, including Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defence, and Quantum Systems.
Merz is also expected to push for progress on reforms that Ukraine’s EU partners have called for, particularly efforts to combat corruption.
On Wednesday, following a phone call with Merz, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported that Ukraine and Germany would soon finalize an agreement on the production of drones, missiles, and related software.
A key priority will be the rapid production of drones designed to intercept Russian attack drones. The agreement will also cover the joint development and production of weapons with a range of more than 1,000 km, which Ukraine could use to strike targets deep inside Russian territory.
Overall, Germany has allocated a record €11.5 billion in aid to Ukraine for 2026. However, not all of this funding will go directly toward supporting Ukraine. For example, around €1.8 billion is planned to replenish Bundeswehr stocks after Germany transfers weapons to Ukraine. Another €688 million will be contributed to the European Peace Facility, which primarily reimburses EU countries for the cost of military aid they provide to Ukraine.
Germany’s Defense Ministry has received around €8.4 billion specifically for direct military assistance to Ukraine. An additional €515 million has been allocated to the Enable & Enhance Initiative Ukraine, which funds long-term contracts to produce weapons for Ukraine, supports the logistics of military aid, and finances repair hubs outside Ukraine.
The remaining funds are earmarked for non-lethal assistance, including demining and medical support, as well as treatment for wounded Ukrainian service members in Germany.
In 2027, according to the preliminary draft budget, the German government plans to increase funding for military assistance to Ukraine to a record €11.6 billion. Although the overall funding will formally increase by only €65 million, the new budget allocates €664 million less for replenishing Germany’s military stocks than in 2026. As a result, the share of direct assistance provided to Ukraine will increase significantly.

UN: Ukraine Civilian Casualties Surge 55% in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:33:00 UTC
18:33:00 KST

The United Nations (UN) has verified 15,280 civilian casualties in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026 as a result of Russian aggression, representing a 55 percent increase compared to the corresponding period in 2025, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk announced.
Addressing the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, Türk stated that the war results in an average of more than 400 civilian casualties each week.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Despite relatively static front lines, Russian forces have systematically directed strikes against residential apartment blocks, educational facilities, medical clinics, commercial shops, and railway infrastructure.
Türk specifically highlighted Moscow’s expanding deployment of high-explosive guided aerial bombs across the Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia regions. During the first eight months of the year, guided bomb strikes killed or wounded nearly 2,500 civilians, marking a 62 percent surge over the same period in 2025.
Characterizing Ukraine as a “laboratory of drone warfare,” the high commissioner appealed to the international community to halt the escalation.
Türk also expressed alarm over systematic bombardments targeting critical energy facilities and commercial enterprises, noting that strikes on food processing facilities have produced localized shortages of vegetables and dairy products across several provinces.
Russian Glide Bombs Strike Sumy Apartments, Injuring 7
In the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson region, Türk reported that approximately 2,000 civilians remain trapped without adequate access to food supplies, potable water, electricity, or municipal gas networks under an ongoing military blockade.
Conflict-related sexual violence and detention abuse
Türk also condemned a “shocking level” of conflict-related sexual violence documented against civilians and prisoners of war, noting that Russian forces and security services bear responsibility for 89 percent of more than 1,000 verified cases.
The high commissioner’s findings align with a comprehensive UN monitoring report spanning the period from February 2022 through July 2026, which documented 1,004 cases of conflict-related sexual violence in Ukraine.
The report attributed 892 of those violations directly to Russian military personnel, law enforcement agencies, and the Federal Security Service (FSB).
According to verified UN records, the documented victims of Russian abuse include 725 men, 151 women, and 16 children, with female victims ranging in age from 4 to 82.
Male victims consist predominantly of captured Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees subjected to beatings, electric shocks, genital torture, forced nudity, and sexual violence in detention facilities. Women and children were primarily targeted in occupied Ukrainian territories.
The UN report also attributed 112 documented violations to Ukrainian authorities, primarily involving the mistreatment of Russian prisoners of war. The findings noted that Ukrainian authorities have maintained cooperation with international investigators and enacted preventive measures, though formal accountability efforts remain limited.
Foreign fighters and third-country recruitment
Addressing recruitment pipelines sustaining Moscow’s frontline manpower, Türk revealed that representatives from his office conducted interviews with foreign prisoners of war from 36 countries currently held in Ukrainian custody.
Numerous captured foreign fighters reported that they were deceived, coerced, or recruited under misleading pretenses before being funneled into Russian military formations.
The testimonies reflect an institutionalized recruitment drive by Russian authorities utilizing expedited citizenship schemes, administrative residency mechanisms, and commercial intermediaries across Africa, the Middle East, and Asia to replenish combat units without declaring a domestic nationwide mobilization.

A tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz Sunday, a British maritime agency said, hours after Tehran warned there was no military solution to the Middle East conflict and the key waterway would remain closed until its conditions were met.
Iran has sought to impose control over the vital shipping lane since the start of its war with the United States and Israel.
It has repeatedly targeted vessels in the waterway that it accuses of transiting without its authorization, while the United States has struck ships allegedly attempting to skirt a counterblockade of Iranian ports.
An "unknown projectile" struck the ship but the crew were unharmed, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) said.
No environmental impact had been recorded from the attack, it added.
The agency did not specify the date of the incident, the vessel's origin or destination, or whether it was an oil tanker or LNG carrier.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which about one fifth of the world's oil and gas transited before the war, remains a key sticking point in negotiations between Iran and the U.S.
The latest attack came just hours after Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the Strait will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions set out in a June interim agreement are met, Iran's Nournews reported.
"The Americans, who say something different in the media, have recently put forward proposals through a mediator. But they must understand that the period of dragging out the process and dictating one-sided demands is over," Ghalibaf was quoted as saying.
"The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, are met."
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said separately Sunday there was no military solution to his country's conflict with the United States, with talks on ending the war apparently at an impasse.
"If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force," Araghchi said at a gathering of foreign ambassadors.
"There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions," he continued, adding "only negotiations based on justice and fairness" could end the conflict.
After a U.S.-Israel campaign of heavy bombardment failed to bring a decisive close to the war, Washington in recent weeks has dialed back military operations in favor of economic pressure.
The two sides agreed a memorandum of understanding in June aimed at providing a framework for a permanent resolution, but the deal collapsed, largely due to disagreements over Hormuz.
Iranian and U.S. officials last week held indirect talks on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, with Tehran saying it presented seven conditions for reopening the strait.
Trump, however, rejected the proposal, while leaving the door open both to further talks or renewed military operations.
Araghchi reiterated that a plan put forward by Tehran to resolve its dispute with Washington could lead to the Strait of Hormuz reopening within seven days if accepted.

Keurig Alta First-Look: No More Plastic K-Cups
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Opinions on Keurig’s K-Cup System fall into two camps: fans who value the convenience of a quick java hit and coffee purists who sideline it as flavored water. I land somewhere in the middle: I grind my own beans and brew them through a reusable filter, but I let the machine do the rest. So, perhaps, I’m the customer that Keurig has in mind with its new Alta system.
The Alta is Keurig's first single-serve coffee maker that uses plastic- and aluminum-free coffee pods—finally launching after years of development. If Alta takes off, we are likely seeing the beginning of the end for the disposable K-Cup, which launched in 1998.
Whatever your thoughts are on how the perfect cup should be made, for nearly 50 million homes in the US (and not counting the many more in offices), Keurig is coffee. For almost 30 years, we’ve been trained to ditch the old drip-coffee maker for disposable single-serve pods. But now, Keurig wants us to leave (eventually) the K-Cup and embrace the AltaRounds pod, a compostable, compressed coffee round that works the same: Drop it into the machine, press a button or two, and out comes joe.
During a presentation in New York City, Phil Drapeau, Keurig’s senior vice president of Future Coffee Systems, said customers wanted more than brewed coffee. They wanted to make fancy espresso drinks, from simple cappuccinos to salted caramel concoctions I sampled at the event (PSL fans, rejoice). But to do so, Keurig needed to invent an entirely new system.
“We wouldn’t be able to do any of that with K-Cup,” Drapeau says. “It will fail. You have to brew it at the right temperature and extract. You can’t be constrained by the K-Cup system.”
Robot Barista
If the K-Cup was about bringing Dunkin’ home, then the Alta is about mimicking brewing third-wave coffee in the kitchen. Keurig looked at how coffeehouse baristas brew espresso, and how it can simplify the process by applying the K-Cup experience.
With the AltaRound, you don’t need to measure and grind beans, tamp, or adjust pressure and temperature. The round is covered with a plant-based seaweed wrap that ensures the coffee stays compressed and fresh. After you insert it, pick a drink via the touchscreen, and the machine punctures the AltaRound and applies 10 bars of pressure to extract the liquid. Spent AltaRounds are dumped into a container.
The first-gen Alta coffee machine is sleek but enormous. It would take the space of my existing Keurig, coffee grinder, and Breville Bambino, and then some more. On the plus side, it has a built-in milk frother for drinks like lattes—it’s a separate process (a Keurig rep told me someone successfully made latte art with it)—and a built-in K-Cup brewer too. Keurig says this lets users keep brewing coffee styles not yet available in the Alta or if they want something quick. (At launch, AltaRounds come in single espresso, double espresso, and regular coffee.)
The machine is wonderfully easy to use, but the process from inserting the AltaRound to drinking takes some time. It's still faster than using a traditional espresso maker, and you do get flavorful coffee with that must-have crema on the surface. A fellow journalist/coffee enthusiast didn’t find it special, but for a K-Cup drinker like me, it’s a game changer.
Keurig is offering a bundle in the US that includes the Alta brewer (in four color choices), four boxes of AltaRounds, and Flur glasses for $500. The preorder has already sold out, which suggests strong interest. There’s no announcement on when the Alta will be on sale en masse and exactly how much (likely also $500, but without the bundled extras), but a pack of eight AltaRounds will cost $10 to $11. (Stay tuned for our full review.) With that high price, it will be some time before the K-Cup dies (well, plastic never dies) and the Alta takes its place.
It’s no secret that Keurig has been exploring a revolution in coffee pods to replace the K-Cup, and has already been beta-testing a prototype in homes. Customers have also been asking for something environmentally friendly that’s compostable and free of plastics and aluminum. (Foil wrappers and cardboard are still used in AltaRounds packaging.)
The K-Cup has been exhausted in terms of innovation. Specialty coffee for the Keurig doesn’t taste great (Nespresso does it better), and Keurig hasn’t been able to innovate beyond the K-Cup’s original intention: basic brewed coffee.
Beyond sustainability, the Alta’s technology echoes issues that plagued the K-Cup. To tell the machine which pod you inserted and to adjust the right settings, each AltaRound has a QR code that the brewer scans. In the past, Keurig ran afoul with consumers and advocates when it tried to implement a printer-toner-style DRM that would have shut out third-party pod makers. For now, Alta users can choose AltaRounds flavors from Keurig and Peet’s, both owned by the same parent company. Will Keurig allow other makers into the Alta system down the road, as it eventually did with the K-Cup? Time will tell if this is the pod revolution we’ve been waiting for.

Bosnia-Herzegovina votes amid divisive campaigns, EU bid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Nationalists top Bosnia-Herzegovina's divisive election
Published October 4, 2026last updated October 5, 2026
Bosnian officials reported a record-low turnout following the Sunday vote, with only 41.5% out of the country's 3.4 million voters taking part in the general election in Bosnia-Herzegovina.
Nationalist parties dominated races as citizens chose officials across multiple tiers of government; including members of the country's multiethnic, tripartite presidency.
With counting nearly concluded, Serb nationalist Zeljka Cvijanovic, Bosniak moderate leftist Denis Becirovic and Croat nationalist Darijana Filipovic have been announced as the winners of the presidential seats of their respective ethnicities.
Cvijanovic had been backed by the Republika Srpska's former secessionist leader Milorad Dodik, who was barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.
"I am declaring that we have won," Dodik told supporters in Banja Luka on Sunday night. He said his SNSD party had retained the Serb seat in the presidency and remained power in Republika Srpska.
With counting nearly over, Cvijanovic looked to have won with 55.6% of the vote.
Social Democrat Becirovic won the race for the Bosniak seat with 38.1% of the vote, while Croat Filipovic took 48.2% of the vote.
Nationalist and ethnic political division
Voters also chose lawmakers for the federal parliament and the heads of institutions for the country's two largely autonomous entities — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) and the Serb-run Republika Srpska (RS).
Currently, about 50% of Bosnia and Herzegovina's citizens are Muslim Bosniaks, 31% are Orthodox Serb and another 15% are Catholic Croat.
Between 1992 and 1995, more than two million people were displaced and nearly 100,000 killed in a civil war. Despite the country being peaceful for decades, ethnonationalist parties have kept divisions alive as a way to hold on to power. Many voters, however, say they want to move on from the war-era rhetoric.
The election comes at a time when the country is struggling with a number of challenges.
There's been an economic downturn, sluggish progress toward EU membership, and sustained political gridlock — with dominant ethnic parties from these entities repeatedly stalling decisions by the weak central government that binds them.
The election saw contests that pitted the Bosniak SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH against multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party.
Polls closed at 7 p.m. local time (1700 GMT), with preliminary results to be released later in the evening — though complex constitutional order and drawn out coalition talks mean that the true result of Sunday's election could remain unclear for months.
What is the system that governs Bosnia-Herzegovina?
The economic, administrative and political responsibilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina are divided between the multiethnic central government, the two semi-autonomous entities FBiH and RS, and the self-governing neutral Brcko district.
These entities are further split into several cantons and communities.
The complicated framework — divided along ethnic lines — was set up during the US-brokered 1995 Dayton Peace Accords, following the 1992-95 Bosnian war, itself a consequence of the breakup of Yugoslavia.
Milorad Dodik still powerful figure in Republika Srpska
In Republika Srpska, secessionist leader Milorad Dodik of the SNSD party remained the key figure of the election despite not being on the ballot.
Dodik, the former president of the Serb-majority entity, is barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.
Dodik-backed Savo Minic decisively won the Republika Srpska's presidency and RS increased its heft by taking 39% of the parliamentary tally, up from 34.6% in 2022.
After the vote, Dodik, who just returned from meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, thanked Putin and also credited "Donald Trump's magnificent victory" for keeping his political camp alive.
He added that "now, thanks to the new environment, we are political winners."
Dodik, wants close ties to Serbia and Russia and secession from Bosnia and Herzegovina.
"Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead, it is an impossible country," Dodik told supporters at the final rally of his in Banja Luka on Friday.
What is happening in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?
In the Muslim-Croat federation, Bosniak parties are advocating for a stronger central state.
The main Bosniak SDA party is focused on efforts to keep the country united against Serb separatism.
Bosnian Croats are also largely backing their ethnic parties, including the Bosnian branch of Croatia's ruling conservative Croatian Democratic Union.
Meanwhile, Denis Becirovic, the incumbent Bosniak presidency member, has vowed a renewed path to the EU and NATO.
Bosnia and Herzegovina has been a candidate for EU membership since 2022.
But the actual start of membership talks depends on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, including strengthening judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption laws.

Thousands protest in Spain after housing relief rejected
Unknown

Demonstrators fill a Madrid city square during a housing protest on Saturday. Photograph: Juan Barbosa/Reuters
Tens of thousands of demonstrators marched through Madrid and several Spanish cities on Oct. 3 demanding affordable housing after lawmakers voted down government-proposed tenant relief measures.
The protests extended a week-long crisis ignited by the eviction of 87-year-old pensioner Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid apartment. The parliamentary defeat marks another setback for Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, renewing pressure on his minority administration ahead of general elections scheduled for 2027.
Parliament rejected the legislative package on Oct. 2 after Catalan separatist party Junts joined the main opposition Popular Party and far-right Vox in opposing the measures. The rejected provisions included automatic renewals for rental contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants.
Government authorities estimated turnout in the capital at 70,000 people, while organizers placed the figure at 500,000. Demonstrators also staged rallies in Palma de Mallorca, Santander, Segovia, Toledo and Valencia, where police detained five individuals following clashes.
Hundreds of demonstrators continued occupying a tent camp established a week earlier in central Madrid. Police blocked far-right groups attempting to reach the site late Oct. 3 and detained three people, local media reported.
Valeria Racu, a spokesperson for the Tenants' Union organizing the mobilization, called for a nationwide general strike. Popular Party leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo urged Sanchez to call early elections, saying the country cannot endure current conditions.
Housing costs remain a central concern across Spain, where average rents have almost doubled over the past decade and property purchase prices have risen roughly 90 percent. Housing advocates said Abascal lived in her flat for seven decades before an investment firm acquired the property and sought a 275 percent rent increase, though public backlash prompted an agreement permitting her return at a reduced rent.

Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs speaks after the first exit poll results of the parliamentary election were announced during an election night event of his centre-right United List party in Riga on October 3, 2026. | Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’ United List has won the country’s parliamentary election by a wide margin, putting the pro-Ukraine leader in a strong position to remain in power.
With almost all votes counted following Saturday’s election, the center-right United List won around 35% of the vote — more than 20 percentage points ahead of the far-right Latvia First party, led by veteran politician Ainārs Šlesers, who opposes restrictive tariffs on Russia.
Preliminary results released on Sunday put United List on course for 42 of the 100 seats in the national parliament.
Advertisement
Despite the decisive victory — far stronger than pre-election polling suggested — Kulbergs will still need to negotiate with other parties to form a majority government.
Two partners in his outgoing coalition, the conservative National Alliance and center-right New Unity, cleared the 5% threshold and are set to return to parliament. They appear to have enough seats for a majority without the Union of Greens and Farmers, which fell below the threshold.
That gives Kulbergs a solid path to another pro-Ukraine coalition without having to seek support from Šlesers’ Latvia First, an option that had loomed over the election campaign, which was marked by high inflation, uncertainty around the troubled national airline airBaltic and instrumentalized migration orchestrated by Russia and Belarus.
Kulbergs became prime minister in late May after his predecessor, Evika Siliņa, stood down following a backlash over stray Ukrainian drone strikes.
The final stretch of Latvia’s election campaign also spilled into Brussels last week, where Kulbergs initially opposed an EU deal to remove Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the bloc’s sanctions list.
Latvia ultimately abstained, allowing the broader sanctions regime to be extended after a compromise among EU countries.

The Tower of David became a gathering place for Christian worshippers from around the world on Saturday night, October 3, when Eagles’ Wings presented its annual Awake Jerusalem music festival. The event brought international Christian artists to Jerusalem for an evening of music and worship, with a live broadcast by Daystar television, planned for audiences abroad.
The festival is a centerpiece of a ten-day visit led by Eagles’ Wings founder and president Bishop Robert Stearns in partnership with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. More than 550 Christian leaders from 51 nations arrived in Israel for the delegation, which began during Sukkot and continues through the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks.
For the organizers, the gathering at the Tower of David was intended to carry a message beyond the concert itself. The visiting leaders represent churches and networks that collectively reach tens of millions of Christians. Eagles’ Wings hopes they will return home with a deeper understanding of Israel, its people and the experiences of the past three years.
Organizers have described Awake Jerusalem as “more than a concert,” calling it “an encounter with God in the land of the Bible.” The event brought delegates together with Christian artists from across the world and was streamed through Christian television and media platforms, extending the gathering beyond those present in Jerusalem.
Among the visiting faith leaders were Bishop Dr. David A. Sobrepeña, Founder and Senior Pastor of Word of Hope Christian Church, one of the Philippines’ largest evangelical churches; Rev. Ricardo Castillo Medina, General Superintendent of the Assemblies of God in Costa Rica and President of the World Hispanic Assemblies of God; and Rev. Dr. Reinaldo dos Santos of Brazil.
High-level delegations from Nigeria also participated. They included His Majesty Ogiame Atuwatse III and Her Majesty Olori Atuwatse III of the Warri Kingdom.
The itinerary extends well beyond the festival. Delegates are due to meet with Israeli leaders, Israel Defense Forces and Foreign Ministry officials, as well as faith leaders, returned hostages and bereaved families. Eagles’ Wings organized the encounters to give participants firsthand perspectives on Israel and the challenges it has faced since October 2023.
A strategic briefing with Israeli officials and faith leaders will examine Israel’s security challenges and its position in the region. The briefing is intended to equip the visiting leaders with context they can bring back to their congregations and wider networks.
“We are here to let the people of Israel know that we are standing firmly by their side,” Stearns said. “We have come to add tangible actions to our prayers for Israel and Jerusalem, and to make a statement to our spheres of influence that an accurate understanding of and fervent support for Israel are of urgent importance in this hour.”
The delegation’s arrival during Sukkot adds another dimension to the visit. The festival drew visitors to Jerusalem from around the world, while this year’s gathering also falls just days before October 7. Eagles’ Wings has framed the trip as an opportunity for Christian leaders to meet Israelis personally and express solidarity at a time when the memory and consequences of the attacks remain immediate for many families.
For three decades, Eagles’ Wings has brought Christians to Israel to explore the roots of their faith and encounter the country firsthand. This visit places those encounters alongside public events that can reach audiences far beyond Jerusalem.
Awake Jerusalem provided the most visible moment of that effort: hundreds of leaders from dozens of nations gathered in one of the city’s best-known landmarks, then carrying their experiences home to communities across the world.

The sound of air raid sirens and explosions rang out in Ukraine's capital Kyiv on Sunday as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived for a visit to show support for President Volodymyr Zelensky amid escalating Russian attacks.
Merz will announce a package of measures including the release of 1 billion euros ($1.13 billion) in military aid and 350 million euros for repairs in the energy sector, German government officials said. A deal for joint production of various kinds of drones is also due to be finalised.
“I traveled to Kyiv today because Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks,” Merz said, adding that Russian forces were bombing towns, residential buildings and heating plants. “If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn against us.”
“I will tell President Zelensky today: 'You can continue to count on our help,'” Merz said.
Four air raid alerts were heard in Kyiv on Sunday morning, and explosions and air defense systems also sounded across the city.
One of the Russian strikes hit the Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River, damaging its roadway, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram. He said the strike had also damaged a hot water supply system in the area.
Russia has been attacking Kyiv's bridges since last week in an effort to disrupt links between the capital's two banks and logistics routes between central and eastern Ukraine.
MERZ SEEKS PROGRESS ON EU-BACKED REFORMS
The German chancellor is accompanied by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and an economic delegation including executives from Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defense, Quantum Systems and other companies.
Merz is also expected to press the Ukrainian government for progress on reforms requested by EU partners, including in the fight against corruption.
Zelensky said on Wednesday, after speaking to Merz by phone, that Ukraine would soon finalize a deal with Germany for the production of drones, missiles and related software.
A key focus of the agreement is expected to be the rapid production of anti-jet drones, which Quantum, a German defense-technology company, has successfully tested. Since the summer, Russia has used dozens of high-speed jet attack drones daily to target civilian and military infrastructure.
In April, Quantum and Ukrainian manufacturer WIY Drones announced the creation of Quantum WIY Industries, a joint venture to produce the Strila interceptor drone and related air-defense technologies.
INCREASED COOPERATION ON LONG-RANGE WEAPONS
The deal also involves the joint development and production of weapons with a range of more than 1,000 kilometers (600 miles) that Ukraine can use to launch attacks deep inside Russia.
On Thursday, Merz said Germany would not be intimidated by the rising number of hybrid attacks by Russia on European states.
Russia's Foreign Ministry said on Saturday that Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in Ukraine in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months. It warned foreign nationals and diplomatic staff against staying in or traveling to Ukraine.
Zelensky told Reuters on Saturday his country's armed forces would double down on their attacks on oil refineries in Russia in response to Moscow's “new doctrine” of escalating attacks on civilian infrastructure, which he said was aimed at forcing residents of Kyiv and other cities to flee.

Saudi Arabia quietly shelving NEOM Stadium, 2034 World Cup venue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:24:20 UTC
18:24:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia quietly shelving NEOM Stadium, one of 2034 World Cup venues
Saudi Arabia is quietly shelving plans to build one of its most ambitious stadiums for the 2034 FIFA World Cup, two sources familiar with the matter said, after delays and downscaling of the futuristic development housing it.
The NEOM Stadium was billed as an elevated arena in a glitzy 100-mile (160-km) steel and glass structure known as The Line, in turn part of the broader development known as NEOM.
NEOM was introduced about a decade ago as a centrepiece of de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030, an ambitious plan to diversify the economy and cut reliance on oil.
Yasir Al-Rumayyan, governor of NEOM's owner the Public Investment Fund, confirmed in April that The Line was no longer a priority, and said it was not vital before 2030, the original delivery target for its first phase. He denied any projects had been cancelled.
However, according to two sources, plans to build the NEOM Stadium have now been shelved indefinitely.
NEOM and the Saudi government media office did not reply to requests for comment, while Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Sports redirected questions to the World Cup 2034 Hosting Higher Authority.
The Authority said "substantial delivery" of construction milestones for the event was already taking place, but did not address questions around the NEOM Stadium and costs. It shared images of some of the other stadiums under construction.
Riyadh developing 15 venues for 2034 World Cup
The 2034 World Cup is seen as a marquee event for Saudi Arabia, which under the Vision 2030 programme has invested heavily in sports via wealth fund PIF. The tournament will be the first time a single nation hosts the expanded 48-team format.
Riyadh is working to build or renovate 15 venues across five cities, as well as dozens of training facilities.
MEED Projects, a Dubai-based construction industry market intelligence platform whose team of analysts tracks tenders and projects in the region, puts the total value of the projects at $22.7 billion in data shared with Reuters.
According to MEED, NEOM's stadium is expected to cost $2.5 billion. It lists the projected 46,000-seat stadium in its data as "on hold".
The stadium has no listed completion date, according to the data, which describes the remaining stadiums and facilities as in various stages of development, with completion expected between 2026 and 2033.
Saudi Arabia is under increasing pressure from the Iran war, which has led to heavy disruptions to energy shipments and damage to critical infrastructure, with the kingdom facing attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis.
Last week, the Ministry of Finance said it expected a fiscal deficit this year wider than previously projected and a real GDP contraction of 3.6% following a drop in oil activities.
Pivot from giga-projects
The geographic distribution of the stadiums adds to the challenge of delivering the projects, a third source said. That could further be compounded by some projects set to host stadiums being delayed or downsized, such as The Line or Riyadh's New Murabba development, the source added.
In January Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia has suspended construction of The Mukaab, a colossal cube-shaped skyscraper at the centre of the New Murabba.
Reuters also reported last year that the PIF was pivoting from its focus on costly giga-projects to endeavours with more immediate financial returns, a strategy later articulated by Saudi officials.
Still, other projects for the World Cup are progressing. The Aramco Stadium in the eastern city of Al Khobar is set to be completed by the end of this year and host its first game in January, for which tickets are on sale.
Work on other planned stadiums is going ahead, a fourth source said.

AA Photo
Bosnians headed to the polls on Oct. 4 in a general election dominated by ethnic divisions stemming from the 1990s conflict, choosing new leadership across a complex multi-tier system established under the 1995 Dayton peace agreement.
The central contest focuses on the three-member tripartite presidency split between Bosniak, Serb and Croat representatives, with competing political factions presenting opposing visions over national unity, regional autonomy and ethnic representation.
The US-brokered Dayton accord ended the 1992-1995 war by dividing the country into two semi-autonomous entities, the Serb-run Republika Srpska and a Muslim-Croat federation, connected by a weak central government.
In Republika Srpska, former entity president Milorad Dodik remains a dominant political figure despite receiving a six-year ban from the presidency following a conviction for overstepping powers. Dodik delivered separatist rhetoric during his party's final campaign rally, calling Bosnia an impossible state. Opposition candidate Branko Blanusa is challenging Dodik-backed candidate Savo Minic for the entity presidency.
In the Muslim-Croat federation, incumbent Bosniak presidency member Denis Becirovic campaigned on advancing European Union and NATO integration, while Croat parties demanded electoral changes to secure greater representation in selecting their member of the presidency.
Technical complications delayed voting across dozens of polling stations as election authorities introduced biometric identification and ballot scanners for the first time nationwide. Polls close at 7:00 p.m., with preliminary results expected late Sunday.

AI deciphered Napoleon’s secret message that is over 200 years old
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
12:23:21 EEST
18:23:21 KST

AI deciphered Napoleon’s secret message that is over 200 years old
Kyiv • UNN
Engineer Carter Church used GPT-6 Astra to decipher Napoleon’s 1809 letter. The message contained information about the troops and an order\r\nfor Marmont to prepare an offensive.
The mystery of Napoleon Bonaparte’s encrypted military letter remained unsolved for 217 years. Now AI engineer Carter Church, using the GPT-6 Astra model, deciphered the message in approximately six hours, reports UNN, citing Bild.
Details
According to media reports, the letter was sent in 1809 to General Auguste de Marmont. Napoleon instructed him to inform him of the strength and location of the French and allied forces, as well as to prepare for a march. At the time, the Austrian army was preparing to launch an offensive against France, while Marmont was stationed with his troops in Dalmatia, near present-day Croatia.
The original cipher key was lost. The text consisted of approximately 1,300 characters, with some symbols representing individual letters and others representing entire words. The AI first recognized the symbols in the scan, then matched them with a partially known cipher table and tested millions of variants until it obtained a meaningful French text.
The deciphered message provides information about the location and strength of the French and allied armies. Marmont is urged not to allow "a few troops or a rabble" to intimidate him and to prepare for an offensive.
Marmont later indeed left Dalmatia with his army and joined Napoleon’s forces during the campaign against Austria. After the victory at Wagram, he was made a marshal.
According to the researcher, deciphering such a code would theoretically have been possible without AI, but it would have required an enormous amount of time. Over 217 years, cryptographers had still failed to fully reconstruct the letter’s contents.

Le Pen stands by top ally Bardella as anti-Semitism claims hit star of French far right
French far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen has reiterated her "complete confidence" in National Rally (RN) leader Jordan Bardella, accused by investigative news outlet Mediapart of making anti-Semitic comments in 2013. But some analysts say the frontrunner in the Élysée Palace race may seek to distance herself from her protégé should the controversy end up damaging her campaign.
After one of the most meteoric rises in the history of French politics, Jordan Bardella, the 31-year-old top ally of Marine Le Pen, is fighting for his political life after allegations he made anti-Semitic comments as a teenager in 2013.
Just a week ago, all was looking rosy for Bardella, with polls predicting Le Pen is on course to win the presidency at the fourth attempt, and the young leader of her National Rally (RN) party subsequently set to take the job of prime minister.
But then came the bombshell allegations published on Monday by the Mediapart website, which accused Bardella of writing a string of anti-Semitic messages in 2013. On Thursday, it posted screenshots of the messages written on Facebook Messenger.
Bardella chose a strategy of all-out attack to deny the allegations, accusing his opponents of launching a "total war" to derail the RN's rise to the presidency and vowing to take Mediapart to court for publishing what he described as fakes.
Le Pen, addressing party MPs side-by-side with Bardella on Tuesday, echoed his denial.
Read moreFrance's Le Pen vows to 'counterattack' after top ally Bardella hit by anti-Semitism claims
But she fell into an uncharacteristic silence after the screenshots were published on Thursday, broken only by a brief comment of "I have complete confidence in Jordan" to La Tribune Dimanche newspaper this weekend.
According to the report, Bardella wrote, among other comments, in a chat: "The Jew has to dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them; a Zionist is necessarily a Jew, and fundamentally so."
'Pull the plug' on Bardella?
Bardella's defiance indicated that he hopes to ride out the crisis, with his future depending on whether Mediapart has more allegations in the pipeline and above all, Le Pen herself.
He has been instrumental in implementing her strategy of "de-demonisation" to try and rid the party of the toxic legacy of its founder, her father Jean-Marie Le Pen, who was openly anti-Semitic.
Read moreHow Jordan Bardella became France’s far-right poster boy
Bardella made an unprecedented visit to Israel in 2025, the first by a French far-right leader, in a bid to demonstrate the RN's new credentials.
He was invited by Amichai Chikli, a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's hard-right government, who has cultivated ties with several European far-right parties despite their history of anti-Semitism.
"Marine Le Pen had to back Jordan Bardella so as not to alienate voters who would not forgive her for abandoning him," said sociologist Erwan Lecoeur, a specialist on the far right.
But he added: "My belief is that Marine Le Pen will pull the plug on" Bardella, arguing that the more Bardella defends himself "the deeper he digs himself into a hole – taking the RN down with him".
The allegations also surfaced after months of reports of tensions between Bardella and Le Pen – notably over a policy to ban the Muslim headscarf in public – even though the tandem maintained an outward united front.
"I don't think she necessarily has to get rid of him," said Marta Lorimer, lecturer in politics at Cardiff University.

"They will try to use whatever they can to defend his position," she told AFP.
"But my suspicion is if we see Bardella ousted it is not going to be because of this but because of possibly broader tensions with Le Pen. For the time being that does not seem to be the case."
'Contaminate the candidate'
There have also been suggestions that some in the RN would like to see Bardella exit and be replaced as Le Pen's de-facto running mate by another figure such as Eric Ciotti, the leader of an allied far-right party, or her niece Marion Maréchal, who leads her own extreme-right movement.
Murmurs have also echoed on social media that the allegations could have come from within the RN, sparking a furious hunt for the "taupe" (mole).
Bardella has acknowledged what is at stake, saying that the aim is to "kill my political career".
His strategy of flat-out denial has also left him open to accusations of lying.
"Do we want a prime minister who is not only anti-Semitic but also lies to the French people in the face of damning evidence?" asked Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin.
Socialist leader Olivier Faure said: "We are dealing with two things here – his antisemitism and lying in politics. Neither is forgivable."
But with the RN lining up to back Bardella, Le Monde daily warned this had risks for Le Pen herself.
"The RN is closing ranks... in the hope that the storm will pass, at the risk of seeing the discredit attached to Jordan Bardella contaminate the presidential candidate," it said.

TEHRAN, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Iran's Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday the country is still ready to achieve a "just and honorable" solution through diplomacy, but it will give a "more crushing" response if the "enemies" once again resort to military actions.
Araghchi also highlighted Iran's seriousness and decisiveness in both defending itself and advancing diplomacy at a meeting with foreign ambassadors and diplomats in Tehran.
He expressed hope that the United States would choose the path of wisdom and rationality.
"There is no military solution, nor any solution based on further sanctions. Only a solution based on negotiation, justice, fairness, and diplomatic dignity can prove effective and provide a definitive resolution to end this war and the illegal and unjust aggression launched against Iran," he said.
Iran has received and replied to the U.S. proposal in response to its proposed plan to end hostilities, while some additional points are yet to be communicated to the United States, according to the Iranian Foreign Ministry.
Iran conveyed a proposed seven-day plan on Sept. 22 to cease hostilities and reopen the Strait of Hormuz to the United States through mediators on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
On Feb. 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz. The United States has also imposed a naval blockade as well as new sanctions on Iran.
A ceasefire was achieved between the warring parties on April 8. On June 18, Iran and the United States signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on ending the war in the region on all fronts.
Under the MoU, the two countries were scheduled to hold negotiations within 60 days, ending on Aug. 17, to reach a final agreement. However, the two sides failed to make sufficient progress toward a deal as tensions continued to escalate. ■

China sets sight on LA after record 169 golds at Asian Games: delegation official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
17:18:11 CST
18:18:11 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- China delivered an outstanding performance at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games and accomplished its mission of preparing for the Los Angeles Olympics, Zhang Xin, secretary-general of the Chinese delegation, said in a statement on Sunday.
China topped both the gold and the overall medal table for the 12th consecutive Asian Games, winning 169 golds, 89 silvers and 83 bronzes for a total of 341 medals, a record gold-medal haul for China at an Asian Games held outside China.
Zhang noted the delegation's performance in Nagoya showed four main characteristics.
Zhang said China's leading position in Asian sport was further consolidated. The delegation competed in 369 of the Games' events across 38 sports and 59 disciplines, winning gold in 38 of those disciplines and medals in 47, despite fielding fewer athletes and entries than at the previous Games in Hangzhou and facing a reduced number of medal events to contest.
The quality of China's results was also notable, Zhang said, with Chinese athletes breaking five world records, 11 Asian records and 22 Games records in sports with recognized records, including shooting, archery, athletics, swimming, weightlifting and track cycling.
"Winning performances in the women's javelin and hammer throw matched the gold-medal standards set at the Paris Olympics, while China's men's 200m freestyle, men's 4x100m medley relay and women's 200m individual medley all produced the world's best times so far this year," it read.
China also made gains in sports where it has traditionally lagged, according to Zhang. Triathlon delivered the country's best-ever Asian Games results across all three events, breaking Japan's long-standing dominance of the sport in Asia. The equestrian team won its first-ever Asian Games gold in team dressage, while China reclaimed the road cycling title after a 20-year gap and the men's individual modern pentathlon gold after 12 years.
Zhang stated that a new generation of Chinese athletes also emerged at the Games. Of the delegation's 815 athletes, 548, or around two-thirds, were competing at their first Asian Games.
"17-year-old Chen Yujie became Asia's youngest women's 100m champion, while 18-year-old Yan Ziyi won javelin gold with a single throw. 14-year-old Yu Zidi claimed three swimming golds, each breaking an Asian or Games record, and 19-year-old Zhang Zhanshuo equaled the Games record for individual gold medals at a single edition with seven swimming titles," he said.
Looking ahead to the Los Angeles Olympics, Zhang said the Nagoya Games had served its purpose.
"At this Asian Games, we have achieved our goals of testing our team, discovering new talent, identifying problems and conducting comprehensive training, further strengthening our confidence in achieving outstanding results at the Los Angeles Olympics," he said.
"After the Nagoya Asian Games, we will immediately shift to preparations for the Los Angeles Olympics, accelerate efforts to address our weaknesses, comprehensively improve our competitive level, and go all out to meet the challenge of the Los Angeles Olympics," Zhang added. ■

COLOMBO, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka's expenditure on fuel imports rose sharply during the first eight months of 2026, reaching 4.07 billion U.S. dollars, according to a report by the Central Bank of Sri Lanka dated Sept. 30, local media reported Sunday.
The figure was 1.55 billion dollars higher than the 2.52 billion dollars spent during the corresponding period of 2025, representing a year-on-year increase of 61.6 percent, according to local news outlet Ada Derana.
In August alone, fuel imports cost Sri Lanka 450.6 million dollars, up 76.5 percent from 255.2 million dollars in August 2025. The increase amounted to 195.4 million dollars compared with the same month last year.
Of the August fuel import bill, 321.9 million dollars were spent on refined petroleum, compared with 202.9 million dollars a year earlier.
The increase in fuel spending came as Sri Lanka's overall merchandise imports reached 1.91 billion dollars in August, up 12.8 percent year on year.
Total merchandise imports during the first eight months rose 24.1 percent to 16.56 billion dollars, according to the central bank. ■

'I want to spark new ideas': Architect Ma Yansong on designing the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:18:02 UTC
18:18:02 KST

Almost two decades after the ambitious architectural project began, George Lucas has finally unveiled his long-awaited Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles.
The 10,000 square-metre building, designed by Chinese architect Ma Yansong, resembles a spaceship, with its futuristic-styling intended to bring a wide range of visual storytelling together under one roof. Its galleries feature paintings, illustrations, comics, manga and film memorabilia.
Over the past 20 years, Ma has created dozens of visually striking projects in his home country and abroad, integrating nature with sleek, modern designs. He says he hopes this work will "spark curiosity and new ideas."
The main attraction for many visitors will be Star Wars as the opening exhibition includes Princess Leia's costume from The Empire Strikes Back, as well as Luke Skywalker's landspeeder, C-3PO and R2-D2.
But Star Wars accounts for only 7% of the entire collection.
Lucas, the creator of Star Wars and Indiana Jones, says the museum is intended to honour illustrators and artists who bring existing stories to life.
Drawing largely on Lucas and his wife Mellody Hobson's personal collection, it contains works by artists including Norman Rockwell and Banksy, alongside children's illustration, anime, manga and comic art.

Interview: Chinese climate cooperation helps advance Pacific climate action: Fijian scholar

by Xinhua writers Guo Xinhui and Liu Xiaoyu
SUVA, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- China's role in global climate governance is increasingly pivotal, and its practical and effective climate cooperation with Pacific island countries is helping advance climate action in the region, said Joseph Veramu, acting dean of the College of Humanities, Education and Law at Fiji National University.
In a recent interview with Xinhua, Veramu said China's efforts to promote technology transfer, fair climate finance and partnerships in renewable energy are helping bridge divides between developed and developing nations.
"Chinese electric vehicles are increasingly visible across Fiji," he said, citing solar installations, electric vehicle deployment, technical training and research exchanges as examples of practical cooperation.
"These initiatives have strengthened local energy access and reduced emissions," Veramu said.
The scholar also noted that China has consistently reaffirmed its commitment to multilateralism and climate cooperation grounded in equity and shared development.
"Even if their scales differ, the Pacific and China share common interests in adaptation, resilience, and sustainable livelihoods," he said.
Fiji, Tuvalu and Australia are partnering to deliver the official 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) Pre-COP ministerial meeting and Leaders' event from Monday to Thursday.
These events will bring global climate decision-makers to the Pacific ahead of COP31 scheduled for November, providing an opportunity to build momentum for negotiations while highlighting a range of Pacific priorities, including climate finance, adaptation, and temperature goals.
Veramu described the meeting as deeply symbolic.
It places the Pacific Islands at the center of global climate dialogue, ensuring that frontline nations speak directly to the world about the realities of rising seas, coastal loss, and community resilience, he said.
Veramu expected the upcoming event to provide an opportunity for the Pacific region and China to further cooperation in various areas.
"The region values China's constructive engagement and welcomes continued collaboration that strengthens resilience, innovation, and shared prosperity across the Blue Pacific," the scholar said. ■
