‘We do’: AfD firebrand Krah says Germany must carry Holocaust responsibility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:17:28 UTC
18:17:28 KST

German lawmaker Maximilian Krah, one of the most controversial figures in the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD), expressed regret during a visit to Israel over remarks he made about members of the Nazi SS, while seeking to convince Israelis that his party should not be viewed as antisemitic.
Krah, now a member of the Bundestag, sparked an international controversy in 2024 when he told Italy's La Repubblica that he would “never say that anyone who wore an SS uniform was automatically a criminal.” Asked whether members of the SS were war criminals, he said there had been a high proportion of criminals among them, but that not all were criminals.
Speaking to ynet Global in Israel, Krah described the episode as a “communication disaster” and said he regretted making the statement.
“Of course. It was a complete disaster,” he said when asked whether he regretted the remarks.
Krah maintained that his original response had come during a longer discussion about individual responsibility for crimes committed during World War II. He said his intention had not been to defend the SS, arguing that some young Germans had been conscripted toward the end of the war. Still, he acknowledged that the way he handled the exchange had been a serious mistake.
The remarks had major political consequences. At the time, Krah was the AfD's lead candidate in the European Parliament elections. The party barred him from further campaign appearances and he resigned from its federal executive board amid the fallout. The controversy also deepened tensions between the AfD and other European nationalist parties.
His visit to Israel comes as the AfD continues to face deep suspicion in the country over statements by some of its politicians concerning Germany's Nazi past and Holocaust remembrance. Krah acknowledged that such concerns exist but argued that the party and the broader European right have changed.
He presented the contemporary AfD as fundamentally different from the antisemitic movements historically associated with Europe's far right. Instead, he argued that hostility toward Israel and Jews is now increasingly found on the political left and linked his party's opposition to mass migration with what he described as the protection of Jewish communities.
Krah acknowledged, however, that the AfD has struggled to convince Jews and Israelis of that position and said the party needs to communicate its views more effectively.
He also addressed remarks by senior AfD politician Björn Höcke, who has faced repeated criticism over his rhetoric about Germany's Nazi past and once described Berlin's Holocaust memorial as a “monument of shame.” Krah said the AfD was formed by people from different political backgrounds and argued that rhetoric of that kind was now understood to be unacceptable.
Despite his effort to shift the focus toward future German-Israeli cooperation, Krah rejected the idea that Germany should free itself from responsibility for the Holocaust.
Asked whether Germany still needed to carry the guilt and burden of the Holocaust, he answered unequivocally: “We do.”
Krah argued, however, that remembrance alone could not sustain relations between younger generations of Germans and Jews. He called for greater emphasis on shared cultural, artistic and other projects that could give the relationship a positive dimension alongside Germany's responsibility for its past.
The German lawmaker said he was visiting Israel for the first time in about 14 years, partly because his son is spending a month in the country as an intern. He described the trip as an opportunity to reconnect with friends and revisit a country where he said he had long felt welcome.
Krah said he had not met Israeli government officials during the visit and had no direct contact with Knesset members. He said he preferred to wait until after Israel's election before pursuing political meetings, when the country's political landscape would be clearer.
He also suggested that the ideological gap between the AfD and Israeli society may appear larger from Germany than it does on the ground in Israel. German mainstream politics, he argued, is considerably further to the left than Israeli politics, leading him to characterize himself as a center-right politician by Israeli standards.
Krah said his reception in Israel had been positive, as had his son's experience in the country, despite the controversy surrounding his political affiliation.
His visit is also part of a broader effort to challenge the political isolation the AfD has faced in Israel. Krah said he intends to return and make his case directly to Israelis, arguing that German Jews in particular could serve as a bridge between the two countries.
For Krah, that means attempting to reconcile two messages that have often sat uneasily alongside each other in the AfD: acknowledging Germany's enduring responsibility for the Holocaust while arguing that today's nationalist right should no longer be judged through the lens of Europe's antisemitic past.

Du fioul dans les artères by French director Pierre le Gall won the award for Best Feature Film at the 22nd Zurich Film Festival (ZFF). In the documentary category, the Golden Eye was awarded to Bucks Harbor by Pete Muller.

Both prizes are worth CHF25,000. The Critics’ Prize for the best Swiss debut film went to Heinz Bütler’s documentary Ebjä! Adolf Wölfli, dedicated to the pioneer of Art Brut.

Nestle dairy whitener found unsafe, substandard by FSSAI; Nestle says product safe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:16:16 UTC
18:16:16 KST

A Nestlé India spokesperson said phosphorus occurs naturally in milk and is therefore present in milk-based products
NEW DELHI: A sample of Nestlé India’s Low Fat Dairy Whitener, collected from the premises of The LaLiT in Connaught Place, has been declared “unsafe and substandard” by a Food Analyst’s laboratory, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) said on Saturday. The sample was collected from M/s Bharat Hotels Ltd (The LaLiT), Connaught Place, FSSAI said. The regulator said the Food Analyst’s report found the product non-compliant under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.FSSAI said a copy of the laboratory analysis report was provided to the food business operator and a notice was issued regarding the non-compliant product. The operator was given an opportunity to appeal against the Food Analyst’s report within the prescribed period. FSSAI also directed that the identified product be immediately prohibited from sale.However, Nestlé India said the product is safe to consume and complies with all applicable regulatory requirements.A Nestlé India spokesperson said phosphorus occurs naturally in milk and is therefore present in milk-based products. The company said the FSSAI laboratory report reflects total phosphorus against the additive limit without accounting for the substantial natural phosphorus contribution from milk-based ingredients.
Nestlé said the product is in full compliance with prescribed limits for added phosphorus under the Food Safety and Standards Regulations, including on an “as consumed” basis. The company said it has been engaging with the authorities through the due process established under law and has shared data on other same or similar milk-based products to demonstrate the presence of naturally occurring phosphorus.
The LaLiT said the product was a packaged product procured from Nestlé India and that the sample was collected by FSSAI from the hotel approximately three months ago.Vivek Shukla, CEO, The LaLiT Suri Hospitality Group, said that after receiving communication from FSSAI, the hotel immediately took up the matter with Nestlé India, which assured it that the company would respond directly to FSSAI.The hotel said it simultaneously discontinued use of the product and removed all packets from its operations.“The matter concerning the product’s compliance is between FSSAI and Nestlé India and not with The LaLiT,” Shukla said, adding that the hotel had acted promptly after receiving the communication and remained committed to food safety protocols and compliance with FSSAI regulations.FSSAI’s public communication does not specify the particular laboratory finding or parameter that led to the sample being classified as unsafe and substandard.

Sarai Sarroca, director of regional weather service Meteocat, said on Saturday that the core of an exceptional weather system was over the Mediterranean and a "mini-hurricane" could move over land in Catalonia.
Flights were cancelled or delayed at Barcelona airport, La Vanguardia newspaper reported on Saturday.

Glasgow council workers face pay cuts in fire-and-rehire plan after union talks break down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:13:29 UTC
18:13:29 KST

Thousands of Glasgow council workers face being sacked and reappointed under less favourable terms in one of the UK’s biggest ever “fire-and-rehire” exercises, after union negotiations broke down once again this week.
About 23,000 workers – all of the council’s non-teaching staff – first heard they were affected last week when talks between the SNP-led council and the GMB, Unison and Unite unions fell apart. Those negotiations concerned a new pay and grading system designed to resolve historical pay equality issues. Unison refused to ballot its members on an offer that would mean pay cuts for 11% of council employees, prompting the council to begin issuing fire-and-rehire letters.
At the beginning of this week the fire-and-rehire plans were temporarily paused when Unison returned to the negotiating table. But when discussions collapsed again midweek, the council’s leader, Ricky Bell, suggested Unison members could still be fired and rehired while negotiations with GMB and Unite continued. Unison said it was seeking advice on the legality of its members being treated differently based on union membership.
An emergency motion by Green councillors to block the scheme was also rejected on Thursday by the council’s city administration committee, with the Glasgow Greens co-leader Anthony Carroll saying the city was “facing a genuine cliff-edge of one of the largest fire-and-rehire schemes in the UK being implemented”.
“We are angry and shocked that the SNP administration moved to fire and rehire all 23,000 staff last week despite its own government’s position,” he said, calling on Bell to personally rule out the move.
The deputy first minister, Jenny Gilruth, reaffirmed the Scottish government’s view on fire-and-rehire last week, saying “our position is that such a practice does not align with the principles and expected practice of fair work”.
On Friday, Gilruth chaired mediation talks between the council and Unison, securing a further pause to fire and rehire for the weekend. But the union said it must be taken off the table permanently for negotiations to be “productive and in good faith”.
For those affected, the week’s tumultuous events have caused anger and uncertainty. “It’s been handled terribly,” said one worker affected. “It’s like a rollercoaster ride of anxiety; we can’t plan for anything and nobody knows what’s going to happen next. We are all furious about how we’ve been treated.”
One person close to the negotiations said the unions were particularly aggrieved by “the blatant cynicism” of the council’s fire-and-rehire plans, which were communicated to staff in letters sent at the end of September, meaning a required 12-week notice period expires shortly before the practice becomes illegal in January under UK-wide changes to employment law.
“We’re talking about a so-called progressive administration who have spent years taking credit for ending the equal pay dispute,” they said. “It beggars belief they would treat workers who are already undervalued and overworked like this.”
In 2019, the council agreed to pay more than £500m to 8,000 mostly female workers who had been discriminated against by unequal pay structures. As seen in Birmingham in 2023, the authority risks financial ruin if it cannot agree a new pay structure after almost a decade of negotiation.
“We know equal pay is still an issue local authorities across Britain need to solve,” one union source said. “Council workers everywhere will surely be looking at what’s happening here and feeling very worried about what might happen to them next.”
Glasgow city council agreed in earlier negotiations to protect the pay of those facing wage cuts for an extra year, but Unison said they wanted a further year of protection alongside a number of other concessions.
Bell said in a statement: “I’m deeply disappointed that, despite the council putting a further year of pay protection on the table, Unison has once again chosen not to put this offer to its members. Taken together with improvements made since August, this represents a package well over £100m in extra pay for our staff.”
Bell said some of Unison’s remaining demands were “simply unworkable”.
Unison’s Glasgow city branch said: “We want workers who have waited decades for equal pay to receive every penny they are due. But we will not abandon workers facing devastating losses, or the thousands who still don’t know their outcome.”
They called for “a properly funded settlement that delivers equal pay without leaving thousands of other workers behind”.

As of Sunday morning, the post had received about 814,000 likes and more than 23,000 comments.
Jolie cited UN satellite analysis saying that as of June 16, 2026, 82% of Gaza’s structures had been damaged, with about two-thirds of the damaged buildings assessed as destroyed. She added that 1.98 million people, or 94% of Gaza’s population, require shelter assistance and essential items as winter approaches.
She also said humanitarian aid and shelter materials continue to face restrictions and delays, arguing that the satellite imagery provides an unusually clear view of the physical devastation but cannot convey what it means for civilians to live amid it, what happened to families who were killed or what daily life is like for those who survived.
Jolie called for shelter to reach civilians before winter, humanitarian assistance to be delivered at the scale required and medical supplies to reach hospitals. She also said conditions must be created to allow civilians to rebuild their homes, schools, hospitals and communities.
“The destruction is visible. The needs are known,” she wrote, concluding that the question now is whether those needs will be met.
Jolie tagged the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs and humanitarian aid organization INARA. She did not mention Israel or the war in the post.
The actress has repeatedly spoken out over the war in Gaza and has been involved in humanitarian activity for years. In January, she visited the Egyptian side of the Rafah crossing as part of what was described as a humanitarian tour for Gaza residents.
Arab media reported at the time that Jolie arrived accompanied by a representative of the U.S. State Department and the governor of Egypt’s North Sinai province. Egyptian reports said the visit was intended to examine aid options and the situation at Al-Arish Hospital.

Jolie had previously sharply criticized Israel’s military campaign in Gaza in the opening weeks of the war following Hamas’ Oct. 7 massacre. Majority of Swiss favour stricter gun control: survey
A clear majority of the Swiss population is in favour of tightening gun legislation, according to a survey.
There is broad support for compulsory psychological assessments before purchasing firearms.
This is the finding of a representative survey carried out by the LeeWas institute on behalf of 20 Minuten and Tamedia.
Some 70% of those surveyed favour more restrictive access to firearms and stricter regulations on their possession. Half of respondents said they were clearly in favour of these changes and a further 20% were “somewhat in favour”.
More
Swiss firearm laws: How Switzerland combines a passion for guns with safety
By contrast, 27% said they were “somewhat opposed” to tightening the law, of whom 18% responded to the survey with a clear and unequivocal “no”.
The public debate on this issue has resurfaced following several murders in Switzerland and the shooting that took place in early September in Aarau during a rave party, which claimed the life of a 22-year-old Italian woman.
More
One dead and five injured in shooting at rave in northern Switzerland
According to the survey, the introduction of a compulsory psychological assessment for the purchase and possession of firearms enjoys very broad support.
Some 80% of those surveyed said they were in favour of the idea of having to present such a medical certificate to own a firearm.
More specifically, when asked whether they considered such a rule necessary, 58% answered with a firm “yes”, 22% with a “somewhat yes”, while 17% were opposed.
Public opinion on the matter, however, varies according to gender and age. Tighter gun control laws are supported by 78% of women, compared with 61% of men.
Support rises from 62% among 18–34-year-olds to 79% among the over-65s. Geographically, support stands at 72% in both cities and urban areas, compared with 67% in rural areas.
The survey was conducted from September 24 to 27 and involved 10,858 people from all of Switzerland’s linguistic regions. The margin of error for the overall results is 2.5 percentage points.

Where life happens: New exhibit showcases everyday moments when something goes wrong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:07:26 UTC
18:07:26 KST

"A concrete truck that got stuck in front of an exhibition opening at a gallery is much more than a concrete truck that got stuck,” says Matan Ben Cnaan. “It’s an encounter between worlds that can’t possibly meet.”
The painting is called Shitty Day, and it hangs in his new solo exhibition at Rothschild Fine Art in Tel Aviv: ‘Everything’s wonderful,’ I said. I lied. The mixer stands at dusk on a wet city street, its chute lowered to the sidewalk. Beside it, a gallery window glows yellow, and figures crowd the light of an opening night. Outside, in the dark, a man stands with his back to us, a phone at his ear. On the asphalt behind the truck, a red warning triangle.
“I have a friend who tells me, ‘I think you’re the only painter or artist who’s interested in a concrete mixer,’” he says.
Ben Cnaan asks us to read Shitty Day like a detective. “It’s evening, so he’s probably been stuck there for many hours, because nobody pours concrete in the evening, you do it very early in the morning. And what happened to the concrete? It’s supposed to harden. He has already started unloading it onto the sidewalk, and he’s standing there, stuck, on the phone. It becomes a whole story. And it comes from trying to feel him, what helplessness this is.”
The exhibition, which runs until October 10, is full of moments like that one. It gathers some two dozen paintings, most of them painted this year and most of them small. In the title painting, a man standing in a narrow kitchen holding plastic shopping bags looks down at what has spilled on the floor at his feet.
Ron Bartos, who wrote the exhibition text, calls them “incident paintings”: a car stuck, fuel spilled, a watermelon split open on the floor of a market, someone waiting, someone angry, someone leaving. Not much happens. But something has already gone off balance.
BEN CNAAN (b. 1980) won first prize at the BP Portrait Award at the National Portrait Gallery in London in 2015 for Annabelle and Guy, the first Israeli to do so. The painting, which shows his friend Guy and his stepdaughter Annabelle in the blinding light of the Jezreel Valley, was inspired by the biblical story of Jephthah’s daughter. In 2017, he won the Haim Shiff Prize for Figurative-Realist Art, which brought a solo exhibition at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art.
Ben Cnaan made his name with large, meticulously staged scenes
In 2021, the Israel Museum showed his monumental painting The Bureaucrat (2018-2020), 2 by 4 m., alongside a text written about it by David Grossman, and in 2024, the Negev Museum of Art in Beersheba held a solo exhibition of his work. He teaches at Bezalel Academy of Arts and Design and at the University of Haifa, and his paintings are held in public and private collections in Israel and abroad.
Ben Cnaan made his name with large, meticulously staged scenes, many of them biblical stories recast with present-day Israelis. For The Bureaucrat, he assembled close to 100 people in a field and directed them, down to the last detail. The new paintings were found rather than staged, on the way to taking his children to school, by staying awake and attentive. “To listen with my eyes, with my whole body really,” he says. “Suddenly, in this marginal event, something happens that is much bigger than the event itself.”
In Not the Eggplant’s Problem, a man stands under the awning of a market stall, palms turned out, looking down at the watermelon that has just slipped from his hands and burst on the ground. The vendor looks at him. Next to him a woman, unmoved, holds out an eggplant to be weighed. Behind them the street is white with sun. The man stands in the shade, and the red of the split fruit at his feet returns in a market umbrella over his shoulder. “This moment, his watermelon smashed,” Ben Cnaan says. “But the eggplant doesn’t care. There’s also this humor in our DNA.”
“There’s a second of disaster,” he says. “You stand in front of the watermelon that exploded. What now? What do you do?” After October 7, he admits, he kept measuring such moments against the national catastrophe. “You come in with a kind of proportion. You got stuck for a moment, so what? But then you understand that such small things can happen to you that for you, right now, they are the worst thing in the world.”
The show’s title comes from Mashina’s 1990 hit “Az Lama Li Politika Achshav” (“So why do I need politics now”), written by Shlomi Bracha. “This specific line is so loaded,” he says, “because there’s a kind of self-recognition in it. He understands that he’s living in an illusion, that he said everything is fine, but everything is not fine.”
And it is not only about him. “It’s all of us. We lie to ourselves about a lot of things because it’s convenient to say everything is good. But no, everything is not good. There will only be hope if we acknowledge it.”
Choosing how to look at the world is political
THE WORKS are not political in the Left-Right sense, he says, though choosing how to look at the world is political, too. “In that sense, it’s very political. But it’s not a David Reeb painting. I don’t know how to bring the right arguments. There will always be someone who argues better. I know how to look with my own eyes and feel where it meets me: injustice, alienation, helplessness. And that is not a place for arguments.”
The formats have shrunk, some panels no bigger than 23 sq.cm., painted in oil on birch and linen. “Supposedly it’s easy to work small, but it really isn’t,” he says. “To suddenly squeeze a world into something so small, where every brushmark determines an expression. You have to be very, very precise.” When he first saw the gallery space, he admits, his knees buckled, and the works grew a bit since.
In Annabelle and Guy, the light of the Jezreel Valley is almost blinding. In the new paintings, most of the space is dark, and the light does the work. It comes from one place, a gallery window, a gap in the shutters, a sunlit street beyond an awning, and the figure often stands just outside it.
Many of the scenes have also moved indoors, into the artificial light of a garage, a laundromat, a food stall, a shop, or a room, and the crowd of The Bureaucrat thins to single figures, couples, and small groups. The staging, Bartos writes, remains as meticulous as ever, and what is left is what is essential: the lighting, the gestures, the relations between the figures, the objects, and the brushwork. Many of the paintings are silent. In one after another, the figure lowers its gaze.
Bartos points to Ben Cnaan’s virtuoso brushwork and an exceptional command of light and composition. Up close, the realism loosens into thick, quick strokes: the reflections on a wet street, the fruit in a crate, a curb painted yellow and blue are laid down in dabs of paint that settle into a scene only from a step back.
A shirtless man stands against a sunlit white wall, his skin burned copper, while a policeman beside him writes in a notebook. On a country road at sundown, a man leans on the door of a broken-down car as a young woman waits at the edge of the asphalt, her shadow stretched across the road. In a dim room, a shaft of greenish light cuts through the shutters onto a man at a piano, his back bare, while a woman watches from the doorway.
At times, Bartos notes, the silence gets a voice through the titles. Some are everyday speech: Nothing to Fix Here, You Here Too?, C’mon, What Am I Going to Do With You? Others come from musical memory, like Pretty Yardena and the exhibition title itself.
'I need to distill a moment that contains past, present, and future'
WHEN I TELL HIM his paintings look to me like films, he agrees at once. “It’s totally cinema,” he says. “But I’m not lucky. I don’t have the sequence, an hour and a half, 10 minutes, even one minute of development. I need to distill a moment that contains past, present, and future.”
One of the films that shaped his thinking is Quentin Tarantino’s Reservoir Dogs, where for long minutes the viewer doesn’t know what happened in the robbery, and then understands it doesn’t matter. “Everything that happens inside this hangar, that arena becomes the story itself,” Ben Cnaan says. “It’s the world.”
Take Nothing to Fix Here, in which a group of men gathers around a Volkswagen van stranded in a field. “You could make an hour-and-a-half film about three brothers, or three friends, who set out on a journey,” he says. “How do I turn that into one painting, so that it’s an hour-and-a-half film in one frame? That’s the challenge I keep trying to crack.”
David Grossman once told him that writers have the luxury of hundreds of pages. “I don’t have that luxury. I need one frame, one brushmark sitting in the right place, and that changes everything.” He thinks of Edward Hopper. “I don’t need all the thousands of tiles on the roof. I need the red roof in that place. My thing is to clean, clean, clean, so the viewer doesn’t get lost in a forest of details that don’t serve the essence.”
He is jealous of directors, he says, and would study directing now if he could. Staging The Bureaucrat, he had to improvise. “I don’t have 70 actors who prepared and read a script,” he says. “We gather in the field, I tell them the big thing, then I take key people aside. And then I see someone who isn’t quite there, and I whisper in his ear: You’re in line at the health clinic, the wait is getting longer, and you start losing patience.” Back in the studio, with thousands of photographs, he directed the scene all over again.
The Canadian photographer Jeff Wall also stages his pictures, catching the moment a man sticks out his leg and another man falls in the street. For Ben Cnaan, that is alienated. “I want to see the man who stuck out his leg, a moment after the other one has fallen. What is he thinking? Wait, what did I do? I didn’t even realize I’d stuck my leg out. What did I do? I acted on instinct. That’s the moment that preoccupies me. Now how do I reconstruct it, how do I stage it all over again? How do I touch it?”
He distinguishes between pity, “my tool for distancing myself from reality,” and compassion. “The hard one is compassion. There you have to be all in. You have to be able to feel the other person’s pain.”
BUREAUCRACY, THE SUBJECT of his monumental painting The Bureaucrat, is in his view “the policeman of compassion.” What preoccupies him is the moment a person stops seeing the human being in front of him, and the systems and procedures that make that possible.
He follows that question from any clerk behind a window all the way to Adolf Eichmann, not out of compassion for the perpetrator. “He was born a child. What led him to the point where he became arbitrary and murderous? I’m trying to understand at what stage he lost this thing.” He asks it of himself too, going back to his army service. “I didn’t hold up in every situation.”
Technique, for him, is never an end in itself. “The technique serves my voice,” he says. “Need is the mother of invention, and need is what justifies every brushmark.”
Visitors ask him why the people in his paintings are so sad. Not everyone is sad, he says; inside the darkness there is a lot of light. But a laughing figure is flat, and so is a crying one. “That happy figure, the glamorous Instagram profile, and you know it’s not a good life. I lied, exactly. So where does life happen?”
He answers himself: “In the middle.”
‘Everything’s wonderful,’ I said. I lied.■
Rothschild Fine Art, 2 Moshe Maor Street, Tel Aviv. 
Until October 10. For details: rgfineart.com

‘To laugh and cry’: New book combines biblical teachings with personal Oct. 7 reflections - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:07:02 UTC
18:07:02 KST

In his new book, After the Dust and Ashes, Fathom editor Calev Ben-Dor combines his own reflections and informed ruminations on October 7 with teachings on the Book of Job. Part biblical commentary, part Jewish approaches to grief, part literary reportage, and part personal memoir, the author describes how he seeks to provide a roadmap for finding meaning in the aftermath of the unimaginable: ways to live after the dust and ashes.
A member of the third cohort of Sacks Scholars, an initiative of the Rabbi Sacks Legacy, Ben-Dor teaches modern Israeli/Zionist thought and Jewish text at prestigious institutions in Israel and publishes essays at the Cardozo Institute. A former national security analyst at the Reut Institute and former Foreign Ministry policy planning analyst, he studied at the London School of Economics (LSE) and at Yeshivat HaKibbutz HaDati, among others.
Below is an extract from Dust and Ashes: October 7, the Book of Job, and Journeys from Grief to Hope, in which Ben-Dor quotes Rabbi Jonathan Sacks, saying: “It needs no courage to be an optimist, but it takes a great deal of courage to hope.”
From ‘After Dust and Ashes’
A quiet calmness had enveloped our Jerusalem neighborhood that Monday morning as I walked towards the hostage tent. The pizza store on the corner was closed, displaying the “Hersh Forever” bubble graffiti on its door. At the tent itself, dozens watched on a large screen as the remaining 20 live hostages were transferred from Hamas control to the Red Cross and then on to Israel, where in emotional scenes they reunited with their families. The names of all of them – both alive and dead – were written in chalk along the street.
A few days earlier, the Families’ Memorial Service had taken place in Tel Aviv’s HaYarkon Park. Organized by Kumu (Rise!), a movement founded by families of victims, hostages, and survivors, the memorial featured performances by artists and testimonies from bereaved families. One family was that of Gidi and Noa Chiel, who were killed near Mefalsim as they fled Nova. Their brother talked of how the loss had caused them and many other families to fall apart, but his mother quickly corrected him. “We have an incredibly deep hole in our hearts,” she said gently, “but we didn’t fall apart.”
As the event drew to a close, Kumu founder Yonatan Shimriz took the microphone. His own brother Alon had been a hostage before being tragically killed by IDF troops in Gaza along with Yotam Chaim and Samer Talalka in December 2023. To thunderous applause, he spoke directly to the hostages. “When you return, and the war ends,” he began, “our generation will take off its military uniform, shake off the dust from the burned houses, and wash off the debacles left by the previous generations. Our generation, that inherited a state bloodied, isolated, polarized and in pain, will be the one that will fix.”
Less than 48 hours later, as we awoke to heavy rain – the first of the season – the news emerged that a ceasefire deal had been achieved. The hostages were coming home.
For the first time in two years, there was a feeling that darkness was fading, that we could begin to breathe and to hope.
On Monday evening, as Sukkot ended and Simchat Torah began, my family returned to the Jerusalem hostage tent to celebrate in the place that had seen so much grief.
As we danced in circles in the car-less street, I thought of Hersh’s mother Rachel, who had recently spoken about Ecclesiastes, and its insight that a time and season exist for everything. “Yet now,” she said, “we are being asked to digest all of those seasons at that same second. It says there is a time to weep and a time to laugh and we have to do both right now … a time to tear and a time to heal, and we have to do both right now … a time to sob [and here she paused to sob deeply] and a time to dance and we have to do both right now.”
In the poem “A Man Doesn’t Have Time in His Life,” Yehuda Amichai wrote how Ecclesiastes was wrong. A man does not have time in his life for everything. “A man needs to love and to hate at the same moment, / to laugh and cry with the same eyes … to hate and forgive and remember and forget … to eat and to digest / what history / takes years and years to do.”
I thought too of Iris Haim, the mother of Yotam, killed by the IDF alongside Yonatan Shimriz’s brother, Alon. As I put my children on my shoulders to dance with the Torah, I tried to integrate Iris’ caution to “remember at every moment those who did not get to hug again. Those who starved and did not return, those who wanted and did not receive, the laughter of their fair-haired child.”
Sacks contrasted optimism with hope
In his book To Heal a Fractured World, Rabbi Jonathan Sacks contrasted optimism with hope. For Sacks, optimism was the belief that the world was changing for the better while hope was the belief that we could improve the world. “It needs no courage to be an optimist, but it takes a great deal of courage to hope.”
As we chanted the song “An Eternal People is not afraid of a Long Path,” I reflected how some families were rejoicing while others were marking the anniversary of their loved ones’ murder.
I tried to envision how we might hold these feelings together – the joy, grief, trauma, and relief, how to courageously choose hope in this yet unredeemed world, where even our joy is tempered.
I never imagined being able to laugh and cry with the same eyes, as Amichai suggested. But that night, on the streets of Jerusalem, it came naturally.
More details about the author at www.calevbendor.com
Calev Ben-Dror will be in conversation with Sarah Tuttle Singer at the launch of his book on October 7 at Begin Center. Public admission. Tickets available from the Begin Center.■
AFTER THE DUST AND ASHES:
OCTOBER 7, THE BOOK OF JOB, AND JOURNEYS FROM GRIEF TO HOPE
By Calev Ben-Dor
Fathom Journal Press

'Finding Peace in the Promised Land': From the Israel Trail to a new path for peace - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:06:50 UTC
18:06:50 KST

Is peace in the Middle East even possible?
Author Aryeh Green is passionately convinced that the answer is “Yes,” and in his latest book Finding Peace in the Promised Land, he lays out a bold and hopeful, yet deeply sensible and practical path forward, grounded in Jewish, Muslim, Christian, and universal values.
When a veteran Muslim-Arab Israeli journalist like Khaled Abu Toameh calls a book “a must-read for anyone who wants to understand the Arab-Israeli conflict and the path for peace and coexistence,” it is worth paying attention.
Green’s book earns that endorsement, as well as endorsements from others, including former ambassador Michael Oren, Middle East Forum President Daniel Pipes, Prof. Gil Troy, and Prof. Mohammed S. Dajani Daoudi, founder of the Wasatia moderate Islamic movement.
In a region long portrayed as a graveyard of peace plans, Green refuses to accept despair as our inevitable destiny and trailblazes a way forward.
A policy expert with decades of experience in Middle East affairs, including serving as senior adviser to Natan Sharansky, Green relates that he drew initial inspiration and motivation for this book from insights gained on his 1,050 km. solo trek along the entire length of the Israel Trail in 2014.
In his previous book, My Israel Trail, he recounts how the lessons learned on that grueling physical and spiritual journey – spanning the length of the country, from the Egyptian border to the Lebanese border – enabled him “to find a way out of the morass of despair and anger, resentment and sorrow,” and heal from a devastating divorce.
During that journey, Green realized that the transformative elements (humility, acceptance, gratitude, forgiveness, and purpose) that were critical to overcoming his personal challenges “can also be applied to much larger situations, such as national and international discord” – including the Arab-Israeli conflict.
The conceptual framework, “when distilled to its essence, calls for mutual respect, tolerance, understanding, love, and respect.”
This vision may sound pie-in-the-sky, but Green is actually very much a realist, taking full measure of sobering factors, such as the October 7 “murderous outrage carried out by Hamas ‘activists’ and 6,000 other Gaza civilians,” as well as the inescapable fact that many Arab and Muslim leaders, and even states “declare the obliteration of Israel as [their] central mission” and work actively with obsessive determination toward that end.
If that is the case, where does one find a basis for hope?
“There will never be real peace without a change in Arab and Muslim attitudes leading to acceptance, forgiveness, and a new sense of purpose, which includes peace and coexistence,” Green concedes. But importantly, “there exist normative and traditional Muslim thinkers/leaders who support such a change.”
A concrete 'to-do list' for both sides of the conflict
TO SUPPORT this mitigating trend, Green brings extensive proof from Muslim tradition and Arab culture and history, quoting statements from a significant sample of Arab/Muslim thought leaders throughout the Middle East who express a readiness for real peace. He cites the warm peace with the Abraham Accords countries as the most concrete and current demonstration of his thesis.
The five pillars mentioned above form the backbone and structure of this well-researched and extensively sourced book. They come with a concrete “to-do list” for both sides of the conflict – as well as for every individual interested in helping create a better future. Briefly, they are:
Humility: International diplomats and regional actors must admit their limitations. Humility begins with understanding one’s place in the universe while recognizing the deeply rooted, historical presence of the other. “Without humility, both sides fall into the trap of believing they can win everything.”
Acceptance: Accepting what it means to face the truth without denial. Jews must recognize that “Palestinian national identity, though shaped only in the last century, is now a fact.” For Arabs, this demands the unconditional acceptance of Israel’s foundational right to exist as a Jewish nation in its ancestral homeland.
Gratitude: Traditional media and political narratives focus on grievances, violence, and setbacks. Both sides need to reframe priorities, elevating appreciation of the many achievements they have already attained over resentment.
Forgiveness: “In the Middle East, forgiveness is almost absent from the political vocabulary… yet both Judaism and Islam honor forgiveness.” All parties here have wounds inflicted by wars, terrorism, massacres, and displacement. The refusal to forgive keeps the conflict simmering.
Purpose: “For Israel, purpose has long meant building a society rooted in the moral vision of the prophets while surviving in a hostile environment.” For too many in the Muslim and Arab world, however, purpose has been laser-focused on annihilating Israel. Fortunately, there are now leaders in that world working to redirect their destructive vision toward constructive goals, such as education, innovation, and growth.
The heart and soul of Finding Peace in the Promised Land is an impressively researched and meticulously documented deep dive into these five transformative steps, drawing judiciously from the region’s historical and religious sources, along with salient and often surprising statements from texts, leaders, and influencers from all streams of thought.
As just one example, Green identifies and spotlights a wide range of Islamic sources and scholars who conclusively debunk seminal harmful myths that portray Jews as interlopers and foreign intruders (European colonial implants) into the region that Arabs and Muslims consider “theirs.”
Re-examining and countering the invention of a native “Palestinian” people as indigenous, and bolstering the clear historical Arab and Muslim recognition of the connection between the land of Israel and the people of Israel as truly indigenous, naturally encourages a reduction of resentment and promotes conflict resolution.
Regarding the importance of acknowledging reality and the “acceptance” of Israel’s legitimacy, Green amasses an impressive array of supporting statements by Arab/Muslim luminaries, such as former Egyptian president Anwar Sadat, King Abdullah II of Jordan, United Arab Emirates Vice President Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid al-Maktoum, Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Zayed Al Nahyan, Oman Foreign Affairs Minister Yusuf bin Alawi, Islamic scholar Dr. Khaleel Mohammed, American Islamic Forum for Democracy founder M. Zuhdi Jasser, and others, as well as numerous verses from the Quran (with almost no repetition).
In addition, Green brings ample evidence that mindset changes have propelled transformative steps forward, historically, in various conflict-torn regions, including post-war Germany/Europe and Japan/Asia, among other places.
A how-to guide: From vision to blueprint
FINALLY, BECAUSE the book is, at its core, a how-to guide, and not merely a treatise on political theory, the final chapter takes us from vision to blueprint by laying out practical steps toward real peace.
In the field of education, for example, the mind- and soul-poisoning demonization of the UNRWA-style propaganda can be replaced by programs such as those offered by the Peace Research Institute in the Middle East, where students see the other side’s perspective presented honestly.
Tools that embody and foster shared purpose and cooperation on the large scale can include elements such as joint economic zones and bilateral infrastructure councils. And the book also zeroes in on things that readers can do on the grassroots level, starting today.
Green calls on individuals to begin now with these concrete suggestions:
Humility: Fostering this in daily encounters, including gestures of shared humanity toward creating an environment of mutual respect.
Acceptance: Recognizing that the other side’s presence is not temporary or illegitimate – can be promoted by acts such as attending each other’s weddings, shopping at each other’s markets, and sending children to joint extracurricular activities.
Gratitude: Cultivating this by recognizing benefits that come from the other side. It can be advanced by something as small as thanking a colleague from across the divide for help.
Forgiveness: Realizing that in many ways, we are all victims of this conflict, but we can learn to reduce the thirst for revenge and not let hatred own us.
Purpose: Encouraging this by participating in initiatives such as community dialogue circles, shared public service projects, cultural exchange events, and youth mentorship programs. These can help develop joint purpose and direction.
Green closes with a balanced call for steps to be taken by both the Israeli and Arab sides, but sums up the essential stumbling block underlying it all with the following declaration:
“Reality must be recognized. The Jews are indigenous to this land. Israel has acted almost exclusively in self-defense. No nation in history has taken greater care to protect innocents, even in enemy populations, in wartime.
“Yet these truths have been buried under layers of propaganda. The primary barrier to peace has never been ‘settlements’ or borders, or Israeli policy. It has been the continuous refusal of Arab and Muslim leadership to accept Israel’s existence and the legitimacy of its founding, and the systematic radicalization of their societies. Until this fact is faced, peace cannot begin.”
Finding Peace in the Promised Land is a valuable contribution to the body of literature on the Middle East, but as Abu Toameh wisely remarked at the recent book launch event at the Menachem Begin Heritage Center, it could have even greater value and impact if it were translated and made available in Arabic.
The reviewer is the author of The Dream’s Enough. ■
FINDING PEACE 
IN THE PROMISED LAND
By Aryeh Green
GreenHouse Press
215 pages; $15

Russia Rehearses Seizing Territory of Central Asian Neighbor in Massive 47,000-Troop War Games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:05:20 UTC
18:05:20 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Rehearses Seizing Territory of Central Asian Neighbor in Massive 47,000-Troop War Games
Russia rehearsed an offensive into the territory of a neighboring Central Asian state and the creation of a “security zone” there during the Center-2026 military exercises, which involved more than 47,000 personnel across multiple training grounds and the Caspian Sea.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Interfax on October 2, Russian forces practiced repelling an attack in the South Ural direction before switching to offensive operations intended to retake captured territory and establish a security zone on neighboring land.
“The coalition grouping of forces is repelling the main attack in the South Ural direction, has restored the situation, and since October 2 has been conducting offensive operations to liberate the captured territory and create a security zone on adjacent territory,” Russian Deputy Defense Minister Yunus-Bek Yevkurov told Russian leader Vladimir Putin during the exercises.
Russian officials did not identify the neighboring state involved in the scenario. Kazakhstan, however, is the only Central Asian country that shares a land border with Russia. It directly borders Russia’s Chelyabinsk region, where the main stage of Center-2026 was held, and also has access to the Caspian Sea, where another part of the exercises took place.
The drills ran from September 28 through October 3 and involved more than 47,000 military personnel across 11 training grounds and the Caspian Sea, according to Russian officials. Around 2,000 pieces of military equipment, 90 aircraft and helicopters, and 77 warships and support vessels were involved in the exercises.
At the Chebarkul training ground in the Chelyabinsk region, Russian forces deployed tanks, motorcycles, artillery, drones, aircraft, and other military equipment. A T-14 Armata tank was among the systems demonstrated during the exercises.
The Caspian Flotilla simultaneously conducted an anti-landing operation, while four Russian long-range aircraft practiced strikes against what the exercise scenario described as critical enemy infrastructure.
Military contingents from Belarus, China, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Pakistan, and Tajikistan also participated in Center-2026. Kazakhstan was represented during the exercises by an operational group.
Putin attended the drills at the Chebarkul training ground on October 2. Russian officials said units directly participating in Russia’s war against Ukraine were not deployed for the exercises, although the training incorporated battlefield experience gained during the invasion.
More than 2,000 Russian personnel who had fought in Ukraine participated in Center-2026, according to Russian Deputy Defense Minister Yevkurov, while equipment previously used on the battlefield was also incorporated into the drills.
The Center-2026 scenario therefore extended beyond defending Russian territory: after repelling the simulated attack, Russian-led forces were tasked with crossing into neighboring territory and establishing a security zone there.
Earlier, Ukrainian intelligence reported that Russia planned to train around 600 Chinese troops in 2025 using battlefield experience gained during its war against Ukraine. The program reportedly focused on tank warfare, artillery, air defense, and combat engineering, marking a broader expansion of military cooperation between Moscow and Beijing.

OPEC+ is to keep its oil production targets steady for November, a Reuters report says.
OPEC+ producers in the Persian Gulf have been pumping well below output targets in the face of continuing export disruptions from the US-Israel war on Iran. Their exports have fluctuated at 60 to 80 percent below normal levels in recent months.

Five innovative and practical modular furniture designs
Our latest roundup looks at modular furniture pieces that are both practical and surprising, ranging from an alternative to bespoke cabinetry to a furniture system made up of squishy balls.
Amoreba is comprised of hundreds of soft, upholstered balls that can be combined in a wide range of configurations.
Architecture and design studio Golem used custom-designed software to model three-dimensional surfaces for the modular furniture system, which the company says is tailored to "contemporary, non-conformist lifestyles".
Created by industrial design duo SF-SO, the metal shelves in the Thin collection are just 1.6 millimetres thick but can support the equivalent of a baby elephant in weight.
The slender modular shelving panels come in a variety of colours and have screws that slot through pre-drilled holes in the folded sections so that users can easily build the furniture themselves.
Modular furniture system by Lozi
This year's London Design Festival saw plywood specialist Lozi open up its Hackney Road showroom to reveal its new modular system, which includes clean-lined wardrobes and a fold-down bed.
The pieces are meant to be an alternative to bespoke cabinetry
They let users "mix and match individual standalone units to create a freestanding piece that mimics fitted joinery, like how Ikea sells their iconic Billy Bookcase design," Lozi founder Soroush Pourhashemi told Dezeen.

Omi Series 2 Stool by Omi Collective
The sculptural Omi Series 2 Stool, with its striking Klein-blue colour, was designed by Lagos studio Omi Collective as a reinterpretation of traditional African seating,
The six-legged stool can be divided into three standalone modules, which are connected by steel rods.
"We believe that the stool's modularity and its ability to be shared, taken apart, reassembled and adapted, naturally encourages community and shared ownership," Omi Collective founder Olorunfemi Adewuyi told Dezeen.

Advanced Concepts 2.0 furniture by Dubbeldam Architecture + Design
Toronto architecture studio Dubbeldam Architecture + Design's tech-oriented office furniture comprises a mobile work station, an under-desk pet holder and a ceiling system where coils descend from a grid to partition space.
The studio designed the modular pieces to be highly flexible.

‘It’s glottophobia’: Brazilians in Portugal battle for linguistic recognition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:00:24 UTC
18:00:24 KST

Not long after she started studying to become a nurse in Portugal, Iracema Ferreira began bringing a dictionary to her classes as a retort to accusations she was speaking Brazilian, not Portuguese. “It was to show that those words are in the Portuguese language dictionary,” she said.
A Brazilian speech therapist, Ferreira moved to Portugal in 2020 and later heard from several colleagues from her home country that the process of getting a licence to work in the European country was a dead end. The 45-year-old soon abandoned the idea of continuing the career she had practised for a decade and switched to nursing instead.
The speech therapists’ struggle for recognition underlines what Brazilians say is a wider strand of prejudice still embedded into Portuguese society against the language variant of its former colony. “It’s glottophobia,” said Tanise Anhaia, president of the Brazilian Speech Therapists Association in Portugal (AFBP), using a term to mean linguistic discrimination.
Barely any Brazilians have been awarded a licence to practise as a speech therapist in Portugal since 2019, according to the AFBP, which was set up last year. One of the two exceptions is a woman whose lawyer argued his client’s rejection was “totally incomprehensible, illegal and unconstitutional” and got it overturned.
For many Brazilians in Portugal the struggle will not come as a surprise. People from the Latin American giant make up by far the largest migrant group, numbering more than 480,000, according to the Portuguese migration agency, AIMA. (According to the Brazilian foreign ministry, the population is larger, at 628,000 in 2025.)
However, as the size of the group increases, so do the reports of xenophobia. In 2022, the commission for equality and against racial discrimination reported that “Brazilian nationality” was the most common basis of discrimination in the complaints they received, forming 34% of all complaints.
In 2023 Statistics Portugal reported that 55% of Brazilians said that they had suffered discrimination, the biggest proportion in terms of nationality.
Last year a Portuguese man was arrested after posting a video in which he offered 500 euros for each “Brazilian head” delivered to him.
A Brazilian woman who lives in the Lisbon district, who asked to remain anonymous, told the Guardian she had seen her then eight-year-old being punched by another child and told: “That’s for Brazilians to learn that they have to go back to their land.” Earlier, at a school meeting, she remembered a teacher saying “the kids were speaking too ‘Brazilianised’” and that they would themselves receive speech therapy.
The popularity of Brazilian YouTubers is leading to more young people emulating the speech of their favourite stars, say parents and linguists. In the 1980s there was a similar panic in Portugal over the popularity of Brazilian soap operas, said Afrânio Barbosa, dean of the Centre for Letters and Arts at Brazil’s federal university of Rio de Janeiro.
“Every time a Brazilian cultural product spreads in Portugal there is such a reaction. And you hear the same sentences: ‘They are worsening the Portuguese language’,” said Barbosa. “These are social reactions due to a colonial symbolic projection of the language, as if its legitimacy lay in its geographical origin and not in the historical demographic identity of its speakers.”
Brazil and Portugal are part of the Community of Portuguese Speaking Countries, which has the “diffusion of the Portuguese language” as one of its goals. Yet the question of whether the variants in practice are different languages or not splits linguists. “It’s a very complex discussion,” said Renato Basso, a professor of linguistics at the federal university of São Carlos who studies the history of the Portuguese language.
“The Brazilian Portuguese spoken by people with a university degree from the urban centres and the European standard are relatively similar.”
In schools it’s important that everyone has access to a “standard norm”, added Basso. However, linguists point out that even within Brazil and Portugal, people end up speaking differently depending on where they live and their social circle.
“If you get stuck with the idea that there is only one version of a language, everything gets too complicated,” said Basso.
That seems to be exactly what speech therapists are being told, however. When Anhaia sat the test to get a licence in 2021, there was no linguist present, just a speech therapist, she recalled. At the end, the examiner told her: “I won’t approve you because you don’t speak European Portuguese.” Anhaia will sit the test again this year.
Margarita Correia, a Portuguese linguist, said the requirement was “absurd”. The body responsible for the licences, ACSS, said that some candidates lacked the knowledge to assess the Portuguese population and that their university degrees were not equivalent.
The ACSS declined to comment. The Portuguese Association of Speech Therapists said its members did not have the authority to comment.
Álvaro Filho, a Brazilian journalist and writer who has lived in Lisbon since 2016, assembled chronicles of life as a migrant for his new book Eu Não Falo Brasileiro (I Don’t Speak Brazilian). One of them is about his son, whose teacher said that “he would just pass the class if he spoke Portuguese”.
“It’s implicit that when they say you speak Brazilian it’s because they don’t recognise this Portuguese variant as an equal. It’s worse,” he said. “It might become an autonomous version, but it has to be our decision, from Brazil.”

Own a mobile phone? Then you’re paying the ‘app tax’. It’s a racket and it’s time the UK faced Apple and Google down | Chi Onwurah
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:00:23 UTC
18:00:23 KST

Debates around big tech and digital regulation can sometimes feel distant from the everyday concerns of voters. But the power that a small number of global tech companies hold over our lives goes far beyond what most people realise.
As chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committee, I have spent years raising concerns about this: from the data they harvest and the digital “twins” they build of us, to the algorithms that decide what our children see.
But there’s a much less visible example of this imbalance of power sitting in the pocket of almost every smartphone user in Britain: the app tax. Apple and Google control the two app stores through which almost every mobile app in this country reaches its customers, and that position lets them set terms for app developers that most businesses would never accept from a supplier. Sell a subscription, game or piece of software through either app store and both companies now charge a commission of up to 30% on purchases made inside apps, regardless of what the product is or what it costs to make. With no alternative platforms, developers simply have to accept the terms set by Silicon Valley.
Developers are also prevented from telling users that a cheaper option exists elsewhere, known as “steering”. That restriction is enforced by Apple and Google to protect their own profits. For small British developers who might struggle to absorb the cost, that could be the difference between hiring their next engineer or not, investing in a new product or shelving it, or growing their business here or uprooting and building overseas instead.
Consumers pay the price, too. Research commissioned by the Coalition for App Fairness, as reported in the Daily Mail, indicated that British consumers pay approximately £700m per year to Apple and Google, a full £232m more than the companies paid in UK corporation tax last year combined. This is equivalent to around £55 annually for a household with four smartphone users. It is a cost built into the price of the product, invisible on any receipt, that has far more to do with market control and bolstering profits than anything the companies actually did to earn it.
My last job before coming into parliament was with Ofcom, the regulator for communications markets. I was responsible for assessing the competitiveness of markets, because it is through competition that consumers get choice. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has found that Apple and Google’s mobile platforms hold an effective duopoly, with at least 90% of UK mobile devices running on their mobile platforms. App developers have no choice but to distribute their product through the Apple App Store or the Google Play Store. If a developer happened to dislike Apple’s terms and another app store existed, they would take their app, and their customers, elsewhere, and the price would fall. But there is no alternative app store on an iPhone, and no practical route for Android users outside Google Play either. Apple and Google set the rules unchallenged.
Parliament anticipated this problem when, in 2024, it passed the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act (DMCCA) with cross-party support, giving the CMA genuine powers to force dominant platforms to change their behaviour. But, so far, the CMA has resorted to weak, voluntary commitments from Apple and Google rather than requirements it is actually obliged to enforce.
Its consultation on “steering”, which would finally let developers point users to cheaper options elsewhere, has now closed and a decision is due soon. Many are rightly nervous that this could end up with another voluntary gesture, rather than a binding rule, deemed acceptable.
But this moment also represents an opportunity. It will be one of the first serious decisions this government makes on big tech, and will likely determine the direction it takes on this issue. The prime minister has been clear, both before and since entering Downing Street, that tech sovereignty means reducing our dependence on a handful of overseas platforms. I want to see that instinct applied to decisions such as this.
This is not about being anti-technology or anti-growth. It is about whether British consumers, British developers and British regulators are able to shape the terms on which technology operates in our own market and influences our society. I urge the CMA to use the powers we gave it, and I urge my colleagues in government to back it in doing so.
- Chi Onwurah is the Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West and chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committee

Elusive ‘Geoneutrinos’ Are Building a New Map of Earth’s Volatile Interior
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
In a laboratory 2 kilometers underground, a crane lowers Matt Depatie, a detector technologist, through a hatch into a white-walled cavern filled with about 7,000 tons of ultrapure water that glows as blue as wiper fluid in the light. “Splashdown,” Depatie says over a radio as he steps into an inflatable raft waiting below.
Normally, the cavern is one of the darkest places on Earth, but today it is lit up for maintenance, offering us a rare chance to see inside. I peer through the hatch at Depatie as he paddles over to examine the submerged experiment. He’s inspecting a house-sized detector built to catch some of the most elusive particles known to physics: neutrinos.
This is the SNO+ neutrino experiment, buried deep within the Creighton mine at Snolab, an underground physics laboratory in Sudbury, Canada. SNO+ consists of an acrylic sphere lined with nearly 10,000 sensitive light detectors and filled with 780 tons of oily liquid scintillator, which flashes when lit up by energetic particles. The water around the device and the rock above it shield the detector from the glare of cosmic radiation, allowing the flickers of less common particle interactions to shine through.
Our whole journey down has been part of the crusade to maintain absolute darkness, even beyond the visible spectrum of light. As we descended the main shaft and walked through a rocky tunnel to the lab, our bodies and clothes collected minute amounts of radioactive radon dust. Before entering the main laboratory space, we tossed our mine clothes, showered, and changed into electric blue jumpsuits and hairnets to minimize the contamination we carried in with us. “The showers aren’t for you,” Depatie said as we changed, “they’re for the science.”
Such extremes are necessary when you’re trying to catch ghosts—in this case, ghosts that may help reveal the secrets of inaccessible regions deep within the Earth.
Neutrinos are the most abundant of all the particles that have mass. But that mass is tiny: just a millionth of the mass of an electron. With such little heft and a neutral electromagnetic charge, the particles hardly ever interact with other matter. Trillions of neutrinos—mostly those produced in the sun—pass through our bodies every second, yet after years of hunting them with detectors such as SNO+, researchers have captured only a few hundred thousand of their precious flashes.
Even more elusive—so much so that after decades of searching, scientists have detected only a few hundred of them—are geoneutrinos.
Geoneutrinos are produced in processes that heat the interior of the planet. This heat plays a major role in powering the flow of rocks in the mantle, which shapes everything from plate tectonics to Earth’s magnetic field. It comes from two main sources: heat left over from the planet’s formation, and heat produced by the decay of uranium, thorium, and potassium in the rocks of the mantle and crust. Without this second source, Earth would have long since cooled off and become a tectonically dead planet.
In counting geoneutrinos, physicists can get a direct measure of Earth’s vital heat-producing elements. “It’s the one thing we do that focuses on the Earth,” said Ryan Bayes, a particle astrophysicist at Queen’s University in Ontario who works on SNO+. “Everything else we do is more focused on what we receive from other places in the universe.”
The first detection of geoneutrinos, by an instrument in Japan called Kamland, was reported in 2005. In 2009, the Borexino detector in Italy reported catching several dozen more. In November 2025, SNO+ reported its first detection, bumping up the number of observed geoneutrinos by about 50.
What makes the detections at SNO+ special is the experiment’s location: These are the first geoneutrinos measured in the western hemisphere, offering a new perspective on Earth’s radioactive interior.
Major uncertainties remain in interpreting the results from these experiments, but researchers’ best estimates suggest that each site is measuring a different flux. “It could be that that’s the first hint that the mantle is not uniform,” said Mark Chen, a particle astrophysicist at Queen’s University and director of the SNO+ collaboration.
Geochemists have conventionally assumed that radioactive elements are distributed evenly throughout the mantle, because the flowing rock should mix everything together. But the measurements of geoneutrinos in different locations could hint that this is not the case.
The regions that seem to be producing the most geoneutrinos sit roughly above continent-size blobs of anomalously hot, dense material, known as large low-shear-velocity provinces, or LLSVPs, which seismologists have mapped on either side of the core. One is under Africa, the other under the Pacific Ocean. “There may be deep Earth structures in the mantle that are not understood,” Chen said. “It could be that [they] concentrate some kinds of elements.”
Neutrinos could one day offer new insight into the still mysterious origin of these deep structures and, more broadly, the patterns in the mantle that underlie many aspects of the Earth system. “It really would be a way to make a chemical map of the Earth’s interior,” said William McDonough, a geochemist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences who has long been a leading voice in the search for geoneutrinos.
The outstanding question is whether the geoneutrino measurements reveal differences between the areas of mantle below each experiment, or if the imbalance originates in the way the different experiments count their geoneutrinos. Researchers across the board say there’s still so much uncertainty that it’s impossible to say.
“If we take it at face value, we could say maybe the western hemisphere has a lot more radioactive material in it than the eastern hemisphere,” McDonough said. But there are reasons to be wary of these estimates. “Are the Italians right? Are the Japanese right? Are they both right? Or is something wrong?” he said.
The uncertainties associated with each detector’s results come from the sorting process that physicists go through to identify geoneutrinos, Bayes said. “They don’t just show up and say, ‘Hi, I’m a geoneutrino.’”
Scientists must eliminate signals from particles with too much energy, particles with the wrong measure of a property called helicity, and particles that they expect to see flowing from nuclear reactors. They must also eliminate geoneutrinos coming from Earth’s crust, with the largest contribution coming from the area within a few hundred kilometers of the detector. When those other detections are subtracted from the total count, the geoneutrino signal from the mantle should be all that’s left.
In general terms, the geoneutrino flux from the mantle seems to be very high at Borexino and very low at Kamland, though the uncertainties are great. A detailed geological interpretation of the SNO+ results is still in the works, Chen said, but so far scientists see a “pretty in-between” mantle below Canada.
A particular challenge for SNO+ scientists is understanding the neutrinos coming from the detector’s surroundings, including a basin formed 1.8 billion years ago by a giant impactor. “There are lots of unknowns in this geological area,” said Virginia Strati, a researcher at the University of Ferrara in Italy who helped develop a local model of radioactivity for Snolab.
Uncertainty also comes from estimates of the total amount of radioactive material heating the mantle. The flux of geoneutrinos suggests that these elements could contribute anywhere from just a small percentage of its heat to half of it—a discrepancy equivalent to the output of tens of thousands of nuclear power plants.
Both sources of uncertainty make it even more difficult to detect any differences between the chemical makeup of particular sections of the mantle. The difference in the geoneutrino flux expected from various distributions of radioactive elements “is very small, and is hidden in these uncertainties,” Strati said.
The detection at SNO+ comes at an exciting moment for geoneutrino research: JUNO, another huge neutrino experiment currently collecting data in China, is expected to report its first geoneutrino flux later this year, adding a fourth and notably richer view. With more than 20,000 tons of scintillator, the experiment—buried under a mountain outside the city of Guangzhou — is so large that it is expected to detect more geoneutrinos in its first year than the combined output of Kamland, Borexino, and SNO+ over decades.
Clearer estimates of the geoneutrino flux at each experiment could come from more detailed geological data, as well as further geoneutrino counts at each site. However, McDonough says the best thing would be to build a neutrino detector at the bottom of the ocean. It’s an idea McDonough has championed for decades.
Such a detector would be far from continental rocks, which are rich in radioactive elements; oceanic crust is also thinner and more uniform. Crust-related uncertainties go down so much that “you are in mantle-only territory,” he said.
The idea of an ocean-bottom detector, estimated to cost hundreds of millions of dollars, has seen little take-up from government funders to date. But McDonough is hoping he can make something happen in China, which has given the green light to other big geoscience projects. “It’s very possible,” he said. Until then, physicists will keep paddling around for answers deep underground.

‘A Talent for Murder’: Patricia Highsmith deserved something nastier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

‘A Talent for Murder’: Patricia Highsmith deserved something nastier
Adapted from the stage play Switzerland, Anton Corbijn’s film A Talent For Murder turns Patricia Highsmith into a character in her own fiction. It is an affectionate, but too gentle a tribute to a writer whose work was rarely known for its affection.
Patricia Highsmith’s permanent resting place in Cimitero di Tegna, a small municipal cemetery in canton Ticino, does not call attention to itself. The American novelist – the author, most famously, of the “Ripliad” series, five psychological thrillers set in Europe centered on the slippery character of Tom Ripley – is discreetly interned in a bare marble columbarium. Visitors have chosen stones over flowers to pay their respects.
A Talent For Murder, which premiered recently at the 51st Toronto International Film Festival and one of the highlights of Zurich Film Festival in September, casts Helen Mirren as the fractious writer shortly before her death, opposite Alden Ehrenreich as Edward Ridgeway, a young American editor sent to Switzerland to extract one final instalment in the Tom Ripley series.
Adapted from Australian screenwriter Joanna Murray-Smith’s play Switzerland, the script takes no small amount of pleasure in the games of submission and domination between the domineering Highsmith and the anxious Ridgeway, who might have arrived a few months later and simply left a rock.
“Perhaps you saw my email…” Ridgeway says to Highsmith, who, in 1995, we’re told, communicated almost exclusively via the Swiss postal service. It is a typical kind of interaction between an eager arts worker and an older artist who has seen it all. Attempts to bridge such divides are central to A Talent For Murder.
Murray-Smith’s play has been transposed from page to stage to screen, and, paying a modern kind of homage to Highsmith’s Ripley, A Talent For Murdercourts questions of imitation versus transformation at every opportunity. As Edward Ridgeway learns, the line between imposter syndrome and fake-it-till-you-make-it is razor thin.
Interview with a vampire
Director Anton Corbijn steps into a long and illustrious line of Highsmith cinema. Purple Noon (1960), The American Friend (1977), and The Talented Mr. Ripley (1999) are three standout adaptations of the Ripliad, while Hitchcock’s Strangers on a Train (1951, screenplay by Highsmith) and Carol (2015, based on a semi-autobiographical Highsmith novel, The Price of Salt) highlight the remarkable range of her work. Corbijn is no Hitchcock, but with A Talent for Murder he ambitiously reaches towards territory occupied by filmmakers such as René Clair or Anthony Minghella, even if he falls short.
After an awkward prologue on board a Swiss train, A Talent for Murder begins not with Highsmith, but rather an extended riff on Dracula (1897). Ridgeway takes the part of the young, naive North American arriving to sign a contract with the mysterious European in a remote location.
The film displays a curious commitment to this interlude, even having Ridgeway awaken with marks on his neck, with Highsmith-as-Nosferatu emerging as the obvious suspect. Although the extended allusion is swiftly abandoned, it immediately signals the film’s ambition – if not always its ability – to weave elements of pastiche into its storytelling.
After failing to shake off the indefatigable Ridgeway, Highsmith makes him an offer: if he can help her devise a suitably Highsmithian murder plot, she will sign on the dotted line. What follows is a film within the film, with Ehrenreich, stripped of his spectacles in Ridgeway’s imagination, recast as a Ripley stand-in ready to seduce the young heiress Clementine Balfour and murder the older relatives standing between him and her inheritance. Fiction, reality and fantasy soon begin to blur, intertwining throughout the film’s brisk 104-minute running time.
Vertigo, Cluedo, velcro
If viewers cannot help but compare Ehrenreich with his Ripley predecessors, or Corbijn’s postcard-perfect Ticino with the seedy sensuality of Mongibello, the fictional seaside village in Highsmith’s thriller The Talented Mr. Ripley, the film is extremely eager to work these gaps into its text. It needles the audience’s familiarity with earlier Ripley films while wringing what suspense it can from a familiar set of tropes.
When Ridgeway-as-Ripley must pass as an Ivy League man at a Balfour party, for instance, it is impossible not to watch Ehrenreich straining to fill the shoes of Matt Damon or Alain Delon. The result is a curious dual-layered tension that produces a distinctly postmodern vertigo. Such pleasures, however, cannot unfortunately substitute for genuine suspense.
>> The first Ripley adaptation (1960) was French, directed by René Clément and starring a young Alain Delon. Highsmith hated the moralist tweak in the end of the film. In her works, crime usually pays off.
Corbijn attempts to shift the postcard-sunny vision of Ticino into a darker register whenever the narrative slips into the film within the film. Yet even a violent seduction scene never quite escapes the feel of a game of Cluedo. The brisk match cuts that should keep tension taut too often resemble Velcro fastenings, lacking the precision they require. At the script level, a limp succession of twists fails to distract from an ending that is visible almost from the outset.
Ehrenreich must flick a switch between the film’s two narratives, while Mirren remains free to inhabit cantankerous grande dame mode throughout. Less generously, one might suspect that her abundance of audience-pleasing one-liners is among the chief reasons A Talent To Murder exists at all. “You’re a homo,” she taunts Ridgeway at one point, before the famously promiscuous lesbian adds, “I should know”, with an almost conspiratorial wink towards the audience.
>> The most recent (2024) filmic adaptation of The Talented Mr. Ripley is a Netflix production starring Andrew Scott:
Never meet your heroes
The film nevertheless blunts Highsmith’s sharpest edges in order to preserve its portrait of a difficult but brilliant artist. A throwaway remark about leaving New York to escape “the Blacks and the Jews” seems an obligatory nod to many prejudices that once led Highsmith to refer to the Holocaust the “semicaust.”
All the same, A Talent For Murder’s multi-layered exploration of imitation proves more fertile ground for reflection than for suspense, or for an honest characterisation of its main subject.
Acting and adaptation emerge as merely two more of Ripley’s games, where the difference between success and failure is little more than confidence. Somewhat awkwardly, and in one of the film’s best jokes, the same appears true of seduction and artistic ambition, as Mirren purrs in the ear of an unsettled Ehrenreich.
History is full of such missed encounters between generations. The renowned New York painter Duncan Hannah once recalled his excitement at meeting Lou Reed as a young man, only for the Velvet Underground singer to introduce himself by asking whether the artist would return to his hotel room and defecate in his mouth.
A Talent For Murder is nowhere near that nasty, which is unfortunate when dealing with a character as offensive as Highsmith. Faced with a difficult legacy, it would be unkind to say the film merely places a stone upon the author’s grave. It is, however, extremely careful not to disturb the dead.

Cranberry harvest booms in Estonia's bogs as pickers seek extra income
