Cranberry harvest booms in Estonia's bogs as pickers seek extra income
Estonia's bogs are full of cranberries this year, and there is no shortage of people eager to pick them. For some, it is a hobby; for others, a chance to earn extra money.
Cranberry pickers say the berries are good this year and plentiful. Even after making the long trip to the Emajõe‑Suursoo bog, you still meet many people who have also come to gather the large red berries.
Most pickers arrive by boat across Lake Peipus.
"Using a boat is convenient: if you pick a lot of cranberries, it's hard to carry them out of the bog. But with a boat, it's easy. The cranberries grow right near the water. You take a potato sack or a sugar sack, throw it into the boat, and haul it out. I think that's the main thing. And besides, boating is pure romance," said Tauno Laasik, initiator of the Peipsi Toit regional food network.
"It's much closer when you come by boat. If you go on foot, you have to walk almost two kilometers across the bog," said cranberry picker Jekaterina.
"For many, this is a hobby, but here at the edge of the bog there are quite a lot of people who pick cranberries to earn a bit of money for the winter. These are serious masters — they can pick 100 liters a day. Then they sell the berries to buyers and earn a decent amount as extra income for winter," Laasik added.
According to Kristel Vilbaste, who has studied cranberries for many years, more and more people prefer to sell their berries directly through social media rather than to collection points.
"I looked at the ads: prices range from €6 to €10. But some people don't notice that the price is listed per liter, not per kilogram. €6 per liter is almost €10 per kilogram. So you should pay close attention to what exactly you're buying. The berries are very good and tasty. We had a lot of rain this year, so they're juicy. And there was enough sun too," Vilbaste said.
She added that because of the large amount of water in the bogs this year, it's best to wear high rubber boots — and not forget a reflector, since berry picking often continues into the dark.

Bosnia Votes with Wartime Divisions Still Sominating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:55:00 UTC
17:55:00 KST

Bosnia was heading to the polls on Sunday after a general election campaign dominated by parties that identify closely with the ethnic divisions of its 1990s war.
Voters will elect a dizzying number of officials across multiple tiers of government, in a complex system that has held the partitioned country together since the 1995 peace deal.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Its key race will be for the tripartite presidency, split between Bosnian Muslims or Bosniaks, and the Serb and Croat ethnic groups, with frontrunners pitting visions of a united country against greater autonomy for the Serb-run entity while Croats seek greater political representation.
But the major parties’ repeated focus on war-era rhetoric and division was frustrating for some voters, activist Adi Selman of the Karton Revolucija protest group told AFP.
“I don’t think these new elections in Bosnia will change anything,” the 34-year-old said in the northern Bosnian town of Tuzla, ahead of the vote.
“The choice is limited to political parties that have already been around for 30 years and basically pick up votes by harping on about war, tensions, divisions and the past.”
The US-brokered Dayton agreement ended the 1992-1995 conflict but entrenched divisions that often paralyse decision-making.
It divided Bosnia into two semi-autonomous entities -- the Serb-run Republika Srpska (RS) and a Muslim-Croat federation -- linked by a weak central government.
After State Elections: Can Merz Keep His Job?
Serb strongman’s grip tested
On campaign posters and billboards in RS capital Banja Luka the face of the entity’s former president, Milorad Dodik, beams out.
He remains the central figure in the Serb entity despite not being on the ballot after being convicted for overstepping his powers and banned from the presidency for six years.
His regular separatist threats have led to repeated clashes with the central authorities and stymied hopes of political cooperation.
“Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead, it is an impossible country,” Dodik told the final rally of his SNSD party in Banja Luka late Friday.
Despite Dodik’s two decades of dominance in RS, researcher Adnan Cerimagic from the European Stability Initiative (ESI) told AFP that it was “not impossible” for opposition candidate Branko Blanusa to beat Dodik-backed Savo Minic in the race for RS presidency.
“Dodik and his colleagues cannot be sure that they will be able to ensure victory for their candidate,” Cerimagic said.
‘Never been worse’
In the Muslim-Croat federation, Bosniak parties are pushing for a stronger central state, with incumbent Bosniak presidency member Denis Becirovic pledging a renewed path to the European Union and NATO.
But Cerimagic said little had changed on that front in years.
“The ruling coalition at state level has made practically no positive progress since 2024, either on reforms or on bringing the country closer to the EU and NATO,” he said.
Croat nationalist parties are also pushing for electoral reform, demanding a greater say in choosing the Croat member of the presidency in the entity they share with the more numerous Bosniaks.
For 29-year-old environmental activist Sara Tusevljak, the political deadlock is a key reason many young Bosnians leave the country.
“I know quite a few young people who have left Bosnia precisely for these reasons, because they felt that their state, those in power, had nothing to offer them to make them stay,” she said in East Sarajevo, which is in the RS.
“I feel that, in some ways, the situation has never been worse.”
The start of voting was delayed in dozens of polling stations over technical issues, as the country rolled out biometric identification and scanning technology for the first time.
Polls close at 7:00 pm (1700 GMT) and first results are expected late Sunday.

Merz said this was so Ukraine could also target Russian launch pads. Increasingly this year we’ve seen long-range strikes from Ukraine landing deep into the heart of Russia. Ukraine has also targeted oil refineries and infrastructure in St Petersburg and Moscow.
Ukraine and Germany had also signed 15 agreements covering security co-operation as well as weapons production and procurement. They also finalised a deal expanding joint drone defence projects.
Merz said Germany would fund the making of drones aimed at intercepting Russia’s jet-powered drones which have been increasingly used by the Kremlin this year to get through Ukraine’s defences. This was urgently needed to strengthen Ukraine’s air defence, he said.
Zelenskyy said Russia had launched 900 such drones this week alone, of which Ukraine had only been able to intercept half.
Severe rains and flooding in Spain’s Catalonia region has led to the deaths of two people in towns north of Barcelona, local authorities say.
One person died when a wall at a campsite in Tordera collapsed and the other drowned in a flooded garage in Montornes del Valles, emergency services said.
At least one other person is also missing following the torrential rains overnight which trapped people in cars and prompted emergency rescues.
Spain’s Meteorological Office (AEMET) warned of “very heavy or torrential rainfall” in Barcelona and Girona on Sunday, noting the storm would be moving northwards and rain could “exceed 200 mm in 12 hours. Extreme caution is advised.”
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has also uregd residents to “avoid non-essential journeys” and follow directions from emergency services.
78 teachers and school staff injured says French minister
Some more detail from France’s Education Minister Edouard Geffray’s comments earlier where he said 400-500 schools would continue to be closed on Monday, following on from Friday’s shut down.
There are roughly 3,700 high schools, or lycees, across the country.
Geffray said lessons were being suspended because the security situation was still not stable enough following outbursts of violence last week amid mass demonstrations.
He claimed activists had infiltrated the protests, “hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence”.

Incinerated novels and destroyed warehouses: Russia’s war on Ukrainian books
Charlotte Higgins
My colleague Charlotte Higgins has written today’s Sunday read on Russia’s war on Ukrainian books:
On a Saturday morning in August, Viktor Kruglov, the co-founder and chief executive of the publisher Ranok, was at his headquarters in Kharkiv – the eastern Ukrainian city that, along with Kyiv, is the centre of the country’s publishing and printing industry. Built 15 years ago on the site of a former bread factory, the footprint of the premises is about 10,000 sq metres (107,640ft). Books were stacked 12 metres high on rank after rank of shelves.
Kruglov, along with five senior colleagues, were on the warehouse floor to discuss the approaching school year. The warehouse was holding 628,000 new schoolbooks. “It was the high season of distribution,” he said, “so we were checking all our processes: how to do it more successfully, how to do it in time.”
Russia strikes Kyiv bridge as German chancellor visits Ukraine in show of support
Pjotr Sauer
Russia has struck another major bridge in Kyiv as the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, arrived in the capital in a show of support for Ukraine.
A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, marking the fourth consecutive day that Russia has targeted bridges used by thousands of residents commuting between the city’s two banks. Video footage showed cars driving across the bridge as the drone plunged into the roadway and exploded in a burst of fire. Two people were injured in the strike, said Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.
The attack came shortly after Merz arrived in the city on an unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing of Ukraine as the country enters one of the most precarious periods since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Germany has become Ukraine’s biggest provider of military aid since Merz entered office in May 2025, surpassing the US as American support has declined.
The education minister says 400- 500 high schools will remain partially or fully shut following a week where riot police clashed with high school students as protests on classroom conditions have spread nationwide.
Lessons will be “totally or partly suspended” given the unrest, says Education Minister Edouard Geffray.
He said 24 schools had been “burned or ransacked” since the start of the movement.
At least 5,000 people, mainly teenagers, have been arrested while dozens of people, including students and teachers, have been injured. Unions are calling on teachers to strike.
The protests began last week in the Paris region, with students staging sit-ins over conditions like overcrowding in classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated buildings.
The rallies in some cases have become more violent with protesters wearing masks and setting off fires in the street and vidoes showing police officers using batons on students.
More protests had been scheduled for Tuesday this week, prompting law enforcement this weekend to say the situation had grown “out of control”.
Paris police chief Patrice Faure told students to abandon their school blockades to return to peaceful forms of protest and suggested to parents there was influence from “professional rioters”.
In the Bosnian capital, Sarajevo, Ismar Garasljevic, a 51-year-old high school teacher tells Reuters:
“More than 30 years after the war, the situation is still the same; we are talking about nationalism ... The same faces, the same story, constantly.“
There is this feeling of more of the same in the bitter ethno-nationalist politics in Bosnia.
There are multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party but also the major ethnically-based political parties in the Bosniak SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH.
They have been the ones in government so far but their differences in central government have blocked progress on measures like transparency laws which are needed for Bosnia to gain EU membership. It secured candidate status in 2022 but has progressed little since then.
Reporter Guy de Launey in Sarajevo also has this report from Bosnia on why so many young people have left the country in the past decade:
One local organisation that tracks emigration estimated that more than 600,000 people had left the country in the decade after the 2013 census, when the official population was 3.5 million.
“If I weren’t optimistic, maybe I would also move out,” said Timur Vilić, a 28-year-old municipal councillor in Sarajevo, who is standing on Sunday for election to the cantonal government. He represents Our Party – a multi-ethnic, non-nationalist, liberal movement that he admits faces a struggle to appeal to voters in a country dominated by ethnonationalist parties.
The problem for Our Party – and other non-nationalist movements – is that the young people who make up their support base are voting with their feet, rather than making their mark on ballot papers.
In theory, Sunday’s vote should be one of the great European festivals of democracy, with the election of no fewer than 14 prime ministers and five presidents. But the plethora of posts on offer reflects a fiendishly complicated system of governance.
The Dayton agreement’s creation of two powerful regional “entities” – with a weaker central government – was intended as a stopgap to ensure peace after the ruinous conflict of the 1990s. Instead, it has perpetuated the divisions in the country. Most Serbs live in the Republika Srpska (RS), while the Federation is home to most of Bosnia’s Croats and Bosniak Muslims. There is no incentive for the ethnonationalist leaders to change that situation – or to appeal to young people who see a brighter future outside the country.
“They don’t want young people to be interested, and young people are not interested in politics,” said Sarah Ćato. The 19-year-old student of political science and international relations is eligible to vote on Sunday for the first time – but she says that her age group feels unseen by the political mainstream.
“Young people don’t know how to vote or who to vote for because nobody’s standing for us,” she said, adding that the reluctance to engage in politics reflects its status as a “taboo subject” after the end of the conflict in 1995. “I think educating youth from middle school on how to be a good citizen should be mandatory.”
In Bosnia, ethno-nationalist politics are at the fore of today’s elections.
Voters are casting ballots today for the country’s three-person multi-ethnic presidency, lawmakers in the national parliament as well as the heads of institutions of Bosnia’s two powerful regional “entities”.
It’s a complicated governance structure – set up in the 1995 peace agreement that ended the preceding three-year civil war.
While Bosnia is one of the poorest countries in Europe after that devasating war, it has remained peaceful.
Still its politics remain divided along ethnic lines between the country’s Bosniaks, who are mainly Muslims, and its Serbs and Croats.
The entities – which are stronger than the central government – was set up to maintain that peace but have largely perpetuated the divison. Most Serbs live in the Republika Srpska (RS), while the Muslim-majority Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina is home to most of Bosnia’s Croats and Bosniak Muslims.
And tensions are rising between the two. Bosnian Serb leaders have pushed for the separation of their entity from the rest of Bosnia, and populist party figures like Russia sympathiser Milorad Dodik, said at a final rally on Friday night that modern Bosnia “is dead” and “doesn’t make any sense”.
Earlier, while visiting the science academy in Kyiv targeted by Russian drones on Monday, Merz decried the “war crime”.
“These barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop. These are daily war crimes,” the German chancellor said.
The National Academy of Science in Kyiv is just a few hundred meters from the German Embassy.
The German leader also issued a comment to Putin, telling him to “end this senseless war” and that “we are ready to talk”.
Zelensky noted that the strikes on Kyiv had continued even amid the chancellor’s visit.
Pro-Ukraine and EU Latvian PM wins parliamentary vote
In Latvia, the small republic right on Nato’s eastern flank, Prime Minister Andris Kulberg’s centre-right party has won the most support in the country’s parliamentary election.
The vote on Saturday had been dominated by concerns over neighbouring Russia as well as cost-of-living and economic issues- and saw about 51% turnout.
Kulberg’s United List party – which won 42 of the 100 seats in parliament, an unprecedented result- will now go about forming a coalition to govern.
Kulberg became prime minister in May after a political crisis over the handling of stray drones suspected to have come from Ukraine, brought down the governing coalition that was in place.
Kulberg, then in opposition, then secured parliamentary approval to lead a new coalition.
He has vowed to push on with his pro-Ukraine and EU direction. Latvia, a small country with a 1.8 million population, which borders both Russia and Moscow-allied Belarus has always supported Ukraine against Russia’s invasion.

Brazil goes to polls in decisive election for future of Latin America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:53:01 UTC
17:53:01 KST

The polls have closed in the first round of Brazil’s highly polarised and high-stakes presidential election that could change not only the direction of Latin America’s largest country but that of the entire region.
The election pits the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of Donald Trump and the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after his failed 2022 re-election attempt.
Late on Sunday Bolsonaro was leading Lula in partial results. With results in from almost 65% of the country, Bolsonaro had 49.8% to Lula’s 42.25%, while several other candidates stood in the single digits.
Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable. In recent days both have focused on persuading undecided voters in hopes of reaching 50% plus one vote; if neither does, there will be a runoff on 25 October.
Brazil is one of the few Latin American countries that still has a leftwing government after a wave of rightwing and far-right electoral victories across the region and the US takeover of Venezuela after the capture of Nicolás Maduro.
The 80-year-old Lula has positioned himself as one of the last regional leaders still willing to say no to Trump, and has recently accused the US president of trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour.
Like his father, who was Brazil’s president during Trump’s first term, Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, frequently praises the US president and has pledged to join the US-led anti-drug-cartel coalition that has killed dozens of people in airstrikes and carried out military operations across the region.
Voting on Sunday morning in São Bernardo do Campo, the industrial city where his political career began nearly half a century ago, Lula said: “People will have to choose between strengthening democracy and barbarism.” The incumbent played down polls released on Saturday that showed the race was wide open – they suggested either candidate could finish ahead and force a runoff, or even win outright on Sunday. “The poll that matters will be carried out today,” he said.
Flávio Bolsonaro, who voted in Rio de Janeiro’s north zone, urged supporters of other rightwing candidates to switch to him in a “protest vote”. “Our internal polls show people who would have voted for other candidates, who are also against Lula, already voting for Flávio Bolsonaro … I hope it’s enough to give us victory in the first round,” he said.
Claudinei Ferreira Viana, 45, a workshop manager in Pinhais in Paraná state, is one of the senator’s supporters. “My first choice would be Jair Bolsonaro but, since he is under house arrest and there is no other rightwing candidate strong enough to take on the current president, I’m going with Flávio,” he said.
At the beginning of the year, polls suggested Bolsonaro voters would have preferred a ticket led by the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas, or the former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro. But the former president chose his eldest son.
The campaign was also marked by a scandal in which the senator was caught on tape asking a banker accused of corruption for $26.8m (£20m) to fund a film about his father, as well as speculation that Bolsonaro might strip the country’s widely cherished patron saint of her status, but he has nevertheless remained highly competitive.
For many analysts, that reflects a combination of a straightforward transfer of his father’s voter base – Jair Bolsonaro lost to Lula by less than two percentage points in 2022 – and an anti-Lula vote, with the president still facing high rejection rates despite strong social and economic indicators.
The incumbent’s campaign has also been hit by corruption allegations – still under investigation – involving his son and a former aide, as well as a scandal involving supreme court justices, which, despite having no connection to Lula, is seen as fuelling an “anti-system” vote and by extension an anti-incumbent one.
Brazilians will also elect 27 state governors, members of state legislatures, all 513 federal congress members and 54 of the country’s 81 senators in Sunday’s vote.
AMC, 40, who asked to be identified only by her initials because she fears reprisals from the local conservative government where she works in the interior of Amazonas state, will vote for Lula on Sunday “because of the many programmes he created to support the most vulnerable groups”.
“Jair Bolsonaro weakened protections for Indigenous peoples, and everything Lula has done over the past four years to strengthen those protections and protect the Amazon would be seriously threatened if his son came to power,” she said.

Museums and archaeological sites to adopt new visitor system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:53:00 UTC
17:53:00 KST

Türkiye is modernizing its cultural heritage sites, with Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy confirming plans to install a next-generation visitor system at 216 locations by year-end 2026.
“With the new system, which we will implement with a domestic and national infrastructure, we will bring about a comprehensive transformation in many areas, from smart ticketing and digital visitor management to data security and new-generation museum applications,” Ersoy said.
According to a statement from the ministry, Ersoy received a delegation from Türk Telekom as part of efforts to create a new-generation visitor experience at museums and archaeological sites.
The meeting discussed the current status and implementation schedule of projects being carried out under a cooperation protocol signed between the Culture and Tourism Ministry and Türk Telekom.
Ersoy said in a post on his NSosyal account that they exchanged views on the implementation schedule and next steps for the project covering 216 museums and archaeological sites across Türkiye.
He said the project would bring cultural heritage together with the opportunities offered by technology and provide visitors with a faster, safer and higher-quality experience.
The project will establish an integrated digital structure covering areas ranging from ticket office operations and visitor services to data security and museum shops.
The new system will include smart ticketing, multichannel digital payments, artificial intelligence-supported data analytics, digital visitor management, audio guides, digital archiving, augmented reality and virtual reality applications.
Fiber infrastructure, widespread wireless internet systems and 5G integration will also be introduced to provide faster and more secure services to visitors. Strategic data related to cultural heritage will be stored on domestic infrastructure within Türkiye.
The digital transformation will also cover museum shops, cafeterias, sales areas and other visitor services, rather than being limited to entrance and ticketing systems.
Museum shops will offer products reflecting Türkiye’s cultural heritage, including traditional Turkish handicrafts, Turkish coffee and Turkish delight, Turkish carpets and traditional decorative arts. The ministry also aims to expand overseas sales of products supplied by artists certified as Intangible Cultural Heritage Bearers and traditional handicraft masters.
Under the new system, existing Müzekart cards that are still valid will remain unchanged. Once their validity expires, citizens will be able to use their Turkish identity cards as Müzekart.
After paying the Müzekart fee through e-Government or a mobile application, citizens will be able to enter museums and archaeological sites without waiting in line at ticket offices by having their identity cards scanned.

&quot;Dream Like a King&quot;: the seventh game as part of the &quot;Day with the Kings Team&quot; project took place in Ternopil
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
11:51:58 EEST
17:51:58 KST

"Dream Like a King": the seventh game as part of the "Day with the Kings Team" project took place in Ternopil
Kyiv • UNN
In Ternopil, 50 children played the seventh game of the "Day with the Kings Team" project with 11 Nyva footballers. The initiative supports children affected by the war.
On October 3, the seventh game as part of the social project "A Day with the Kings’ Team" by the Betking Foundation and its founder, Pavlo Zhurylo, took place in Ternopil. This time, 50 children and 11 professional footballers from the Niva Ternopil football club met on one pitch, UNN reports.
The match format is traditional for the project but unusual for professional football: a team of 50 children plays against 11 professional footballers. There is no distance between the professional athletes and the young players: they take to the pitch together, score goals, celebrate successful moments and simply enjoy football.
For the children, it is an opportunity to share a pitch with professional players and feel part of a real football match.
"I had been looking forward to this day, but I never thought we would play with footballers like this, for real. What I will remember most is the match and the fact that afterward we could talk to the players and get autographs. Now I want to train even more and one day play for a professional team too," said 11-year-old Sviatoslav Romanchuk.
Football that helps bring childhood back
"A Day with the Kings’ Team" was created specifically for children affected by the war. The participants include children of serving military personnel and fallen defenders, displaced children, as well as children from families that have experienced the consequences of Russian aggression.
The idea of the project is to give children, through sport, communication and positive emotions, an opportunity to leave their everyday worries beyond the football pitch for at least one day.
Before the match, the children trained together with professional footballers, and after the game they talked with them, took photographs, received autographs and were given presents.
"The war has taken many familiar things away from Ukrainian children, but it has not taken away their right to dream. That is why it is important for us to create moments when a child shares a pitch with professional footballers and sees that a big dream is not somewhere far away—it may be much closer than it seems. For some, this match will remain a vivid memory, while for others it will become an incentive to train, believe in their own abilities and not give up on their dream. It is for moments like these that we continue "A Day with the Kings’ Team," involve new football clubs and expand the project’s geography. We want as many Ukrainian children as possible to have this experience," said Betking Foundation founder Pavlo Zhurylo.
FC Niva also emphasizes that participating in the project gives the club an opportunity to be closer to children for whom football has already become a part of life.
"For our footballers, this is also a special match. On the pitch, you see not simply 50 children, but 50 young footballers who genuinely love this game. Perhaps for some of them, today’s meeting will become another incentive to continue training, work on themselves and dream of professional football. We are happy to be part of such a day and to see the children’s emotions firsthand," said Ivan Fedyk, head coach of FC Niva Ternopil.
From one match to a nationwide project
Ternopil became the next city on the map of "A Day with the Kings’ Team." Over the course of two years, the project has brought together more than 330 children from different cities across Ukraine.
Matches have taken place in Kyiv, Bucha, Rivne, Oleksandriia, Irpin and Uzhhorod. Professional football clubs joined the initiative and, for one day, became not athletes seen on screens and from the stands, but opponents and partners for the children on the football pitch.
The Betking Foundation plans to continue expanding the geography of "A Day with the Kings’ Team" and involving new football clubs in the project so that children from different regions of Ukraine can take part in such matches.
A Ukrainian project that has received international recognition
"A Day with the Kings’ Team" reached the final of the UN Global Compact competition "Partnership for Sustainable Development 2025."
In 2026, the project also received two Davos Communications Awards: gold in the "Best Sports or Entertainment Campaign" category and silver in the "Best Social Media Campaign" category.
For Betking Foundation, these distinctions represented international recognition of a Ukrainian social initiative that serves as a tool to support children and creates a space for them to communicate, gain new experiences, and dream.
About Betking Foundation
The Betking Foundation charity, founded by Pavlo Zhurylo and part of King Group, transforms social initiatives into real opportunities for children and young people. The foundation pays special attention to displaced children and those who have lost relatives due to the war, helping them through sports, education, and psychological support. Betking Foundation invests resources in creating a healthy and safe environment for children, helping them develop team spirit, gain new knowledge, and restore emotional balance. The foundation’s social mission is to create opportunities for the harmonious development and social adaptation of the younger generation.

66% of Hong Kong’s 8-year-olds could be short-sighted by 2028, experts warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

66% of Hong Kong’s 8-year-olds could be short-sighted by 2028, experts warn
Association finds 67 per cent of six-year-olds have insufficient hyperopic reserve, urging parents to start eye checks at age three
Two-thirds of Hong Kong’s eight-year-olds could be short-sighted by 2028, optometrists have predicted, citing a shrinking “hyperopic reserve” that normally helps delay nearsightedness.
The Hong Kong Association of Private Practice Optometrists released the findings on Sunday from a screening of more than 3,500 pupils at eight primary schools conducted between November and May, urging parents to begin comprehensive eye checks when children turned three.
The association found that 67 per cent of six-year-olds had less hyperopic reserve than the recommended standard of 0.75 dioptres (75 degrees), while 24 per cent were already short-sighted.

ADOB to enrich repertoire with Turkish works, new projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:51:00 UTC
17:51:00 KST

The Ankara State Opera and Ballet (ADOB) is preparing to meet audiences in the 2026-2027 season with a repertoire ranging from Mozart and Puccini to works by Turkish composers and modern dance productions.
ADOB Director Demet Gökalp told state-run Anadolu Agency that the institution reached around 110,000 audience members last season and aims to attract an even wider audience with productions spanning different genres in the new season.
Gökalp said they staged a busy program from October through the end of June last season, with performances not only at the Opera House but also at CSO Ada Ankara, museums and the Atatürk Cultural Center.
She said three key factors were taken into account when preparing the 2026-2027 repertoire: Audience expectations, the development of artists and support for Turkish composers.
“In selecting our repertoire, we prioritize the expectations of our audience, the development of our artists and supporting Turkish composers. We have shaped our new season with the aim of including Turkish works to encourage Turkish composers and support them in creating new works,” Gökalp said.
Gökalp said ADOB’s new season will open with Mozart’s “The Marriage of Figaro,” which was first staged in 1786. The opera will have its premiere at the Opera House on Oct. 3.
The new season will feature productions ranging from ballet and opera to modern dance and children’s shows. Gökalp said the ballet “Coppélia,” which was previously staged in Ankara but has not been part of the repertoire for a long time, will return to the stage.
Highlighting the importance they attach to Turkish works, Gökalp said the opera “Hekimoğlu,” with music by Tolga Taviş and a libretto by Bertan Rona, will be staged in Ankara on Dec. 12.
“Hekimoğlu” was previously staged by the Samsun State Opera and Ballet. “We will stage it in Ankara for the first time. I think it will be very good. We attach great importance to it,” Gökalp said.
HH Modern dance project ‘Alice in Wonderland’
Gökalp said the children’s repertoire would also be renewed, with the new production “Şekeronya” replacing “Barış Ormanı.”
She said a new modern dance project would be presented to audiences from the new year onward. “Alice in Wonderland” will be staged for the first time, with a foreign choreographer working on the production.
Gökalp said the operas “La Bohème” and “Lucia di Lammermoor,” which were carried over from last season, would also return, with a limited number of performances planned.
She added that the dance musical “Gangster” and the ballet “Harem,” which attracted strong demand in previous years, would continue to be staged this season.
Gökalp said some productions continuing from last season would be staged at the Atatürk Cultural Center to reach a larger audience. “Carmen” and “The Nutcracker” will be presented there.
“We have made new decisions to reach more audiences. These are major operations, but we are making the effort for our audience,” she said.
Gökalp said “The Nutcracker” would be staged in a larger venue because of strong demand, while “Carmen” would also go on tour in Denizli.
She emphasized that moving productions to different venues would allow them to reach a wider audience.
HH New Year’s concerts to be held at both Opera House and CSO
Gökalp said the concert program would continue in the new season, with New Year’s concerts being held at two different venues.
She said the absence of a New Year’s concert at CSO Ada Ankara last year had drawn criticism from audiences and that, following strong demand, a concert would be held at the Opera House on Dec. 30 and at the CSO Ada Ankara Main Hall on Jan. 4.
ADOB’s concerts at CSO’s Blue Hall will also continue. Gökalp said Friday concerts would generally feature the institution’s soloists.
She said the number of foyer concerts had been reduced because of the increase in the number of performances, while Saturday programs would feature more matinee and evening performances.
Gökalp also said ticket sales would begin earlier this season.
“Ticket sales will start earlier in the new season. In previous years, tickets went on sale 15 days in advance, but now sales will begin one month before the performances. I hope art lovers will follow the productions to be staged in the new season, and I recommend that those wishing to buy tickets for the limited number of performances act early,” she said.

Taliban Delegation Participates in Russia’s Center-2026 Exercises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:50:08 UTC
17:50:08 KST

A Taliban military delegation took part in Russia’s Center-2026 strategic military exercises at Moscow’s invitation.
The official page of the Ministry of Defense of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan reported the participation.
The Taliban representatives observed the drills and toured an exhibition showcasing Russian military equipment and weapons.
During the visit, the Afghan delegation also met with military representatives from other countries who had arrived for the exercises.
This is the first time that a Taliban military delegation has been invited to attend Russian military exercises as observers since the Taliban returned to power in 2021.
Center-2026 is a large-scale Russian strategic military exercise during which Russian forces practiced operations in the Central Asian direction and the Caspian region. Moscow invited military contingents and observers from dozens of countries to take part.
Military contingents from Belarus, China, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Pakistan, and Tajikistan participated in the exercises. Kazakhstan and the Republic of the Congo sent operational groups, while representatives of 33 other countries, including Afghanistan, India, North Korea, and Vietnam, attended as observers.
The delegation’s participation reflected the growing political and military ties between Russia and Afghanistan.
A key development in bilateral relations was the signing of a military-technical cooperation agreement. On May 27, 2026, Russia and the Taliban signed the agreement.
Russian Security Council Secretary Sergei Shoigu and Taliban Defense Minister Moulavi Mohammad Yaqoob Mujahid signed the agreement. The exact scope of the agreement remains unclear, as the document’s text has not been made public.
However, while explaining the agreement to the media, Russia’s special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, said it primarily covers refurbishing military equipment already in the Taliban’s possession. In the future, the two sides could conclude separate defense contracts.
The Russian side also said it was considering the possibility of establishing training centers for Taliban technical personnel responsible for maintaining military equipment.

Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:48:38 BST
17:48:38 KST

Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit
- Published
Major bridges in Kyiv have been hit by Russian drone strikes for four consecutive days, as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukraine's capital.
Two people were injured when the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge was struck on Sunday morning for the second day in a row, while the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times earlier in the week.
The latest attack came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a surprise visit to Kyiv in a show of support against Russia's continuing full-scale invasion.
Russia's military said it would be intensifying strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions. It earlier said it had hit the two bridges used to transfer Ukrainian troops.
Video footage of Sunday's strike, verified by the BBC, shows cars moving on Pivnichnyi Bridge as a drone crashes into it before exploding, creating a ball of fire. A cloud of black smoke can be seen rising above the bridge.
Other videos and pictures have emerged on social media showing a gaping hole in the middle of a traffic lane on the bridge.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were injured in the latest Russian attack. He earlier said that the Pivnichnyi Bridge's roadway was hit.
Kyiv's eight bridges across the wide Dnipro River link the western (right) and eastern (left) parts, and many of the capital's estimated three million residents rely heavily on the metro lines and trains to travel across the city.
Some 500,000 vehicles use the bridges every day.
The two struck bridges are still standing - but the damage and restrictions to traffic and public transport have caused gridlock in parts of the capital at times.
"To get from the left bank to the right one and back - it's just hell," Kyiv resident Roman told the BBC on Sunday.
Large numbers of commuters cross the river, especially on weekdays. Repair teams are working to fix the damage and officials say they are planning temporary pontoon bridges, ferry services and even a tunnel under the river to keep Kyiv connected.
Klitschko also said a separate Russian drone strike had damaged a heating main, adding that there would be a temporary lack of hot water in the north-eastern Desnyanskyi district as a result.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenksy said on Sunday morning Russian drones had also attacked a warehouse in the north-eastern region of Sumy, killing one person.
Meanwhile, in the central city of Dnipro, six people were injured after a communications facility was struck, he said.
Ukraine's Air Force said that overnight Russia had launched 135 drones, including 52 jet-powered ones. It said that 125 projectiles had been shot down.
As emergency services responded to the incidents, Germany's Merz met Zelenksy in Kyiv. They laid wreaths to Ukrainian soldiers who have been killed in the war.
Merz reaffirmed his country's support for Ukraine, writing on X: "Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I travelled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us.
"Germany's security also depends on the outcome of this war. That is why we are helping out of our own self-interest as well."
Zelensky later said that a new aid package worth more than €1.3bn (£1.1bn; $1.5bn) had been agreed with Germany.
"These are weapons that will help [us] right now, as well as support for our energy sector ahead of winter," he said.
As Merz was visiting Ukraine's Academy of Sciences building badly damaged in a Russian drone attack earlier this week, fresh air alert sirens were heard across the city. Two people were killed in that drone attack.
Since Merz became chancellor in May 2025, Germany has become the single largest donor to Ukraine.
He said the country "needs all our support in the coming weeks", adding: "If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us."
Zelensky said there would be "important agreements" made between Ukraine and Germany.
The Ukrainian president has made repeated appeals for Western allies to provide more military support to the country, including supplying advanced interceptors that can shoot down new jet-powered Russian drones and also ballistic missiles.
The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier this week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had earlier said his military was carrying out retaliatory attacks following Ukraine's strikes on Moscow's energy facilities, despite the fact that it was the Kremlin that had first launched such attacks.
Putin began a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.
The Russian foreign ministry on Saturday repeated a warning for foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv.
Responding to the warning, EU ambassador Katarína Mathernová wrote on X on Sunday: "The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe's support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!"
German ambassador to Ukraine, Boris Ruge, reacted to Mathernova's post with: "Amen - we're staying".
Earlier attacks on the Pivdennyi Bridge prompted Kyiv's defence council to hold a crisis meeting on Friday.
Klitschko warned that the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities.
Experts say Russian drones are unlikely to bring down the bridges - but repeated attacks will force their closure and risk weakening their structure, making them unusable.

More than 120 anglers compete for longest pike at Lake Saadjärv

More than 120 anglers compete for longest pike at Lake Saadjärv
Pike anglers competed at Lake Saadjärv on Saturday. Pike are crafty fish and less experienced anglers may end up with no catch at all.
More than 120 anglers gathered at Lake Saadjärv under a warm, summery sun to compete in the traditional "Saadjärve Haug" spinning competition for the 15th time. As only boats with engines of up to 10 horsepower are permitted on the lake in the Vooremaa Landscape Conservation Area, the day's fishing proceeded at a leisurely pace.
"The five longest pike count toward the result, with a minimum length of 52 centimeters. The lengths of the five pike are added together to determine the final result. Saadjärv is deep and large, with very clear water, so fishing here is difficult. You need to know the right spots and previous experience also helps," organizer Mart Toots said.
A total of 55 boat crews took part in Saturday's fishing competition at Lake Saadjärv, all trying to catch the longest pike.
"The fish are very finicky. You have to work the lure to entice them and they're very difficult to catch. Generally, if the fish aren't biting, there's nothing you can do to make them bite," Ivo said.
"We use something called a live sonar. It's a device that's like ultrasound underwater. It shows you how the fish are swimming in real time," Marcus said.
"We haven't had a single bite so far. It's been very poor. There are plenty of fish. They're picky, though, and don't want to follow the lure, so you have to work really hard," Kalmer said.
"It could be better, but we're actually happy with the three we've caught. When we first started 10 years ago, we didn't catch anything here at all," Margus said.
Although the day's average catch was around 60 centimeters long, Venno Viirsalu landed the longest pike, measuring 80 centimeters. Edgar Vaht and Allar Kukk took the overall victory, however, with their five pike measuring a combined 324 centimeters.

Operation Inherent Resolve: Reflecting on a Campaign that Shaped a Generation of RAF Personnel
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:43:27 BST
17:43:27 KST

As Operation Inherent Resolve concludes in Iraq, it closes a chapter that has shaped a generation of Royal Air Force personnel.
For more than twelve years, Operation Shader, the UK's contribution to the Global Coalition's campaign against Daesh, (Operation Inherent Resolve) has seen thousands of RAF personnel serve across the Middle East. From the humanitarian airdrops over Mount Sinjar in 2014 to the final stages of the campaign against Daesh, the operation became a defining experience for many of those who wore uniform.
As the Coalition mission transitions, it is an opportunity to reflect on the people, partnerships and achievements behind one of the RAF's most enduring operational commitments of the modern era.
For Group Captain Paul Hanson OBE, Typhoon Commander Air Wing, the moment represents an important milestone.
“It marks an important day in our collective history – the end of Typhoon operations over Iraq," he said.
"Operation Shader, as an overall mission continues - but Typhoon's part over Iraq has concluded."
What began in August 2014 with RAF Hercules aircraft delivering humanitarian aid to civilians trapped on Mount Sinjar evolved into one of the RAF's most sustained operational commitments. Over the following years, RAF personnel deployed across the region in support of Coalition efforts to defeat Daesh.
"When I think back over the last twelve years, I don't immediately think of aircraft or numbers. I think about people. I think about the young personnel who joined the RAF, completed operational tours and are now leading squadrons and teams themselves. I think about the pilots, engineers, intelligence specialists, force protection personnel, logisticians and support staff who quietly delivered excellence day after day. Tens of thousands of us served from CAOCs (Combined Air Operations Centre) to FOBs (Forward Operating Base), Akrotiri to Baghdad, Erbil to Al Assad. For many of us, we are defined by Operation Inherent Resolve and our fight against Daesh."
Group Captain Paul Hanson OBE
Typhoon Commander Air Wing
The campaign also spanned a period of significant change for the RAF, with capabilities entering service, maturing on operations and, in some cases, completing their final deployments.
"During Shader, the RAF used and retired E-3D, Sentinel, Tornado GR4, Reaper and C130," Hanson noted.
"Typhoon came of age as a proper multi-role aircraft and Storm Shadow strike asset leading the fight against Daesh."
Looking back, Hanson believes one of the campaign's defining achievements was helping create the conditions for Iraqi-led security.
"Today routine Combat Air Operations have finished with Daesh reduced to a level within which the Iraqis can address without our persistent support," he said.
The transition reflects years of partnership, training and cooperation with Iraqi Security Forces, with responsibility for security now increasingly held by Iraqi institutions.
Behind every deployment stood families and support networks who shared the demands of operational service, often across multiple tours and many years of commitment.
Hanson also highlighted the campaign's wider impact.
"We have stayed the course, and delivered a resounding success," he said.
"We have been instrumental in the territorial defeat of a twisted theocracy which threatened to upturn the Middle East permanently."
"And in doing so we have kept the streets of Britain safer, playing a vital role in disrupting ISIS terrorism abroad."
The conclusion of Operation Inherent Resolve marks an important milestone in the international campaign against Daesh and an opportunity to recognise the contribution of those who served.
"Operation Inherent Resolve will be remembered as a defining chapter in the RAF's modern history," Hanson reflected.
"The contribution made by those who served helped create the conditions for lasting security and delivered an enduring impact both in the region and at home in the UK."
While the military mission in Iraq has concluded, the UK's commitment to regional security continues. For the thousands of RAF personnel who served on Operation Shader, the campaign remains a defining chapter of service, professionalism and commitment over more than a decade of operations.

Finland investigates alleged war crime committed in Ukraine
Finland's National Bureau of Investigation is investigating an alleged war crime committed in Ukraine.
Source: Finnish public service media company Yle, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The police confirmed the information to Yle. Finnish law enforcement officials said the preliminary investigation began this year.
Yle notes that such a case is rare for Finnish law enforcement agencies.
The police are not currently disclosing details. In particular, they have not said when the crime may have occurred, who the victim is, or whether there are any suspects in the case.
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Finnish police collected evidence of alleged Russian war crimes. However, the police have not specified how they learned about this particular case.
The investigation launched this year remains the only case involving an alleged war crime in Ukraine currently being handled by the National Bureau of Investigation. Such cases are extremely rare in Finland.
Background:
- In August, the Helsinki Court of Appeal issued a ruling in a case concerning war crimes committed in Ukraine in 2014. It is currently the only such case to have reached a Finnish court. Russian national Voislav Torden was sentenced to 12 years and six months in prison.
- He was detained while attempting to enter Finland in 2023. A court refused to extradite him to Ukraine, citing poor conditions in Ukrainian prisons.

A shipping route near Helsinki, Finland, has been closed after an unidentified object was spotted in the water.
Finnish newspaper HS reported on this.
Around 7:20 p.m., the Finnish Border Guard alerted police after finding an unknown object in the water south of Kustaanmiekka Island, near the Suomenlinna fortress.
Authorities described it as a cone-shaped metal object.
The object was found on the Helsinki–Tallinn shipping route, which is used by passenger vessels, including the Viking XPRS ferry. The ferry’s crew was the first to spot the object.
Police, together with the Finnish Gulf of Finland Coast Guard, cordoned off the area and called in the Finnish Navy to identify the object.
During the night of October 4, the Finnish Navy preliminarily identified the object as a very old mechanical part of a ship’s structure.
Police emphasized that the object does not pose an explosive threat.
The object is expected to be towed to the Santahamina naval base for further examination.
Although this incident was related to the discovery of shipwreck remains, Finnish law enforcement and military authorities continue to closely monitor Russia’s activities, which currently pose a threat to Finland.

The EU will not scale back its support for Ukraine or alter the operations of its diplomatic presence in Kyiv in response to Russian warnings directed at foreign missions, European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand confirmed.
According to RBC-Ukraine and European Pravda, Wigand stated that the EU delegation to Ukraine continues to operate without changes in the capital, dismissing Moscow’s threats as an unsuccessful attempt to intimidate European governments and weaken Western backing for Kyiv.

“This is not the first time Russia has issued such threats. It shows that the Kremlin is losing the war and losing self-control,” Wigand said.
“The European Union will continue to support Ukraine, expose Russia’s irresponsible and dangerous actions, and steadily increase pressure on Moscow.”
The European Commission’s rebuff followed an official dispatch issued on Saturday, Oct. 3, by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Russia, which warned foreign citizens and accredited diplomats in Kyiv of “mortal danger” and pledged to sustain mass aerial bombardments across the capital.
Defense procurement tranches and air defense transfers
Wigand underscored that rather than retreating under Kremlin pressure, European institutions are accelerating military and financial assistance programs to reinforce Ukrainian resilience ahead of the winter heating season.

Operation Vivaldi Liberates up to 140 Sq Km in Donbas

Strengthening Ukraine’s air and missile defense architecture remains the primary operational priority for European defense coordinators.
To bridge delivery timelines while defense manufacturers scale up serial assembly lines, the EU is evaluating mechanisms to transfer surface-to-air interceptors directly from European national military stockpiles to Ukraine, with inventories to be replenished subsequently using funds allocated under the Ukraine Support Loan.
In addition to defense financing, Brussels is finalizing what officials describe as the most extensive sanctions package against Russia to date.
The diplomatic move follows the EU’s enactment on Sept. 28 of targeted restrictive measures penalizing individuals and entities involved in the unlawful transfer and deportation of Ukrainian children.
Unbroken diplomatic presence

The diplomatic exchanges unfold against an intensifying Russian aerial campaign aimed at degrading municipal utilities, transit infrastructure, and life-support networks across Kyiv.

Bosnia votes in one of world’s most complicated general elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:36:17 UTC
17:36:17 KST

Banned Bosnian Serb leader Dodik declares party victory in election
Voters cast their ballots for a dizzying number of officials across multiple tiers of government.
The party of banned Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik has retained its grip on power in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s predominantly Serb Republika Srpska entity, with his ally set to keep the Serb seat in the country’s three-member presidency.
Preliminary results from Sunday’s general election showed Zeljka Cvijanovic of the right-wing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD), led by Dodik, ahead in the presidential race.
The result reinforced Dodik’s political influence despite his conviction and ban from public office, leaving a party that has repeatedly challenged state institutions in a strong position.
Dodik was not on the ballot after being convicted last year of defying decisions by the international envoy charged with overseeing the 1995 peace agreement that ended the Bosnian War.
Speaking to supporters late on Sunday, he said his party would not alter course.
“No one should ask us to change our politics,” Dodik said, while also praising United States President Donald Trump’s 2024 election victory and thanking Russian President Vladimir Putin, a longtime ally.
Nationalist figures Cvijanovic and Darijana Filipovic, as well as leftist moderate Denis Becirovic, were leading the race as the Central Election Commission released preliminary results shortly after polls closed.
Becirovic, representing the Social Democratic Party (SDP-BiH), led the contest for the Bosniak seat. Cvijanovic of the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) led the race for the Serb seat. The Croatian Democratic Union’s (HDZ-BiH) Filipovic led the field for the Croat seat.
About 3.4 million people were eligible to vote in Sunday’s election to choose the three members of the country’s multiethnic presidency, legislators for the national Parliament and heads of institutions for the country’s two entities: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) and Republika Srpska.
Bosnia’s complex web of governing institutions was created by a US-brokered peace agreement in 1995 to manage the ethnic divisions between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats that gave rise to the 1992-95 war.
The major parties’ repeated focus on war-era rhetoric, and the division was frustrating for some voters, activist Adi Selman of the Karton Revolucija protest group told the AFP news agency.
“I don’t think these new elections in Bosnia will change anything,” the 34-year-old said in the northern Bosnian town of Tuzla ahead of the vote.
“The choice is limited to political parties that have already been around for 30 years and basically pick up votes by harping on about war, tensions, divisions and the past.”
“Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead; it is an impossible country,” Republika Srpska’s former President Dodik told the final rally of the SNSD in the entity’s capital, Banja Luka, late on Friday.
EU membership bid
In the FBiH, Bosniak parties are pushing for a stronger central state, with incumbent Bosniak presidency member Becirovic pledging a renewed path to the EU and NATO.
The European Union granted Bosnia candidate status in December 2022, but accession negotiations scheduled for 2024 were delayed as Brussels demanded the country pass stronger anticorruption laws and reform its judicial system.
Croat nationalist parties are also pushing for electoral reform, demanding a greater say in choosing the Croat member of the presidency in the entity they share with the more numerous Bosniaks.
Meanwhile, Russia is accused of slowing down the country’s path towards joining the EU, while also holding close ties with the SNSD, which favours secession for Republika Srpska, dominated by ethnic Serbs.
This general election is the first in the country to use new electronic tools to scan ballot papers and biometric fingerprint verification to reduce fraud.

By 2026, the K-12 Education Administration had provided about NT$15.8 million (US$496,514) in subsidies.
At participating schools, language instructors work with other teachers to design courses combining everyday conversation with food preparation, traditional children’s games, songs and dances, and festival-related activities, the education ministry said. Students develop their language skills and cultural understanding through hands-on learning and play.

Taiwan environment minister promotes urban forestry for climate adaptation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:33:31 UTC
17:33:31 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Environment Minister Peng Chi-ming (彭啓明) visited Taitung on Sunday to promote a national climate adaptation initiative that treats trees and urban forests as climate-resilience infrastructure rather than solely as landscaping.
Speaking at National Taitung University, Peng said Taiwan faces increasingly frequent high temperatures and extreme weather. The central government is working across ministries to expand the role of trees in cooling urban areas and improving living conditions, per UDN.
Peng said Taitung’s extensive forests and natural landscape make it well suited to expanding green infrastructure. He cited converting some school walls into green hedges and the “Green Point 100” initiative as ways to increase vegetation in populated areas and strengthen ecological corridors.
The ministry’s “Urban Forest Open Government” initiative calls for cooperation among central and local governments, businesses, schools, and communities. Its six strategies cover areas including climate data, tree management and maintenance, a circular economy, and public and corporate participation.
Under Green Point 100, the ministry plans to train community volunteers, connect civic groups with corporate ESG resources, and match volunteers with tree-care and adoption projects. The broader initiative emphasizes choosing suitable species and providing long-term care rather than simply counting the number of trees planted.
Peng also addressed the disposal of driftwood and pruned timber, a challenge in eastern Taiwan. He said the government would continue promoting wood-based power generation and recycling surplus timber as part of a shift from waste disposal toward life-cycle resource management, per UDN.
National Taitung University Vice President Hu Cho-chun (胡焯淳) said forests and lawns cover about 60% of the campus and that the university has incorporated sustainability into its administrative planning.
The meeting formed part of the government’s effort to establish a nationwide urban forestry system that reduces heat while providing ecological and social benefits.

Three weeks before the election, parties in the opposition are focusing on voters who could still shift between camps, including moderate right-wing voters, wavering Likud supporters, those considering staying home, and voters reluctant to back parties hovering around the electoral threshold, senior bloc officials said on Sunday.
"Everything has been stuck for a month," senior figures in the opposition said. After weeks in which a significant part of the political battle was also being fought within the blocs themselves, parties are now looking for seats they can bring in from outside their own camp.
According to senior bloc officials, studies and data held by the bloc's parties show no significant movement between the political camps in recent weeks. One senior official said the bloc's potential seats are among the moderate Right, including voters who oppose haredi draft evasion.
Those officials believe that if movement does occur, it is likely to come closer to Election Day.
Against this backdrop, parties in the bloc have recently sought to stop using political ammunition against one another. Party leaders decided to postpone the debate over their candidate for prime minister until after the election and, until then, focus on expanding the bloc.
Yashar's "largest party" campaign, which had largely targeted competition within the bloc, has also been toned down. The division of labor among the parties, however, is still not a binding agreement. Opposition officials said not all the parties are satisfied with the arrangement and not all are following it.
Eisenkot targets 'soft Likud voters,' Yisrael Beytenu looks beyond bloc lines
According to Yashar officials, Gadi Eisenkot's party has identified a pool of some 200,000 "soft" Likud voters, an internal term for voters weighing Likud, abstaining, Ofer Winter's People of Israel party, other parties, or Yashar itself.
The officials stressed that Yashar does not expect all 200,000 votes to move to the party. Rather, they represent a pool of undecided voters from which the party hopes to draw support.
According to Yashar officials, the party is also concentrating efforts on traditional voters and the moderate religious-Zionist public. The party has set a target of winning roughly two additional seats from those groups and, according to its internal assessments, already has support equivalent to about one to one-and-a-half seats from the religious-Zionist community.
A dedicated campaign headquarters led by Matan Kahana, fifth on the party list, is operating in Gush Etzion, Efrat, Givat Shmuel, and Ariel, among other places.
Yisrael Beytenu officials said the party is also looking for votes beyond the bloc's boundaries. According to the officials, the party has mapped cities, neighborhoods, and even polling stations where Likud previously received strong support and is focusing its activity there.
The officials said the party can identify the cities, neighborhoods, and polling stations where Likud won its highest levels of support and is conducting targeted activity there. The groups being targeted include secular and ideologically right-wing voters, disappointed Likud supporters, and Russian-speaking voters who previously backed Likud.
For now, senior bloc officials said the data available to them still shows no sign of the movement from the Right they are waiting for.
One senior official assessed that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would lose, but said the question for the bloc was whether it itself would manage to win. That was the official's political assessment, not a forecast of the election result.
According to bloc officials, their concern is the gap between opposition to Netanyahu and their ability to translate that opposition into voters crossing over from the rival camp.
Gantz, Blue and White not out of the race just yet
Benny Gantz is facing a different problem. Blue and White is consistently polling below the electoral threshold, and the party has now decided to appeal directly to voters who fear their ballots will be wasted.
Even before Gantz's public declaration, Blue and White officials said the decision had been made to remain in the race until the end. They said the party was confident it would not waste votes and was relying on internal polling.
On Saturday night, Gantz presented the figures he said underpinned the decision.
"According to our research, more than five seats' worth of voters want to vote Blue and White," he said.
He claimed that "fear of the electoral threshold is the only barrier."
Addressing undecided voters directly, he said: "If everyone who believes in our path votes, we will pass it by a wide margin."
Gantz also personally tied his name to the decision to remain in the race.
"When you see the ballot slip 'Blue and White led by Benny Gantz' at the polling station, you will know that we checked the data and we stand behind the decision to run. Your trust is sacred to me, and therefore your votes are safe."
He also invited journalists to examine the data.
"Come check us: Go over the data, and you will receive clear and transparent answers."
The five seats Gantz referred to are, according to him, a figure derived from Blue and White's internal research, not from polls published by the media.
The decision to remain in the race is also occupying the other parties in the bloc. As long as Blue and White remains below the electoral threshold in the Maariv poll, the possibility that votes cast for it will not count toward the distribution of Knesset seats remains part of the bloc's calculations.
Blue and White argues, based on its internal research, that its main problem is voters' fear of the electoral threshold. According to the party, some voters want to support Blue and White but refrain because they fear it will fail to cross the threshold.

Inside the ‘kill box’: The Yemenis who stayed behind in Houthi-held Mocha
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
08:31:29 UTC
17:31:29 KST

Inside the ‘kill box’: The Yemenis who stayed behind in Houthi-held Mocha
Yemenis trapped in the Red Sea port city speak of deteriorating conditions there.
Nabil watched from his balcony as a column of displaced people passed by at dawn on September 10, hours before Houthi forces entered Mocha, a Yemeni city on the Red Sea.
“People were terrified. There was fear everywhere,” he said.
Nabil, a daily wage labourer in his 40s, did not join them. He still lives in Yakhtul, a village north of Mocha, alongside relatives, none of whom has left their homes.
“Displacement is humiliation and homelessness,” he said. “I haven’t done anything wrong, so I have nothing to be afraid of, and I don’t belong to any side.”
Weeks after the Houthis took Mocha from forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, thousands of civilians remain in the district. The Houthis – an armed group that has controlled much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa, since September 2014 – have fought the government for more than a decade in a civil war that has drawn in a Saudi-led military coalition. No one knows how many people remain in Mocha, but according to Yemen’s last census in 2004 the city had 62,500 residents.
The government has declared Mocha a military zone and alleged that the Houthis have forced residents to demonstrate in support of the group or join its ranks.
Residents interviewed by Al Jazeera did not describe forced demonstrations, but one who asked not to be identified because he feared for his safety said three of his neighbours have been recruited and armed by the Houthis. They are now on the front lines fighting against government forces.
“Today my wife heard from a woman who came to our house that a Houthi-armed pick-up truck had kept coming to their home, wanting to recruit her sons, but she refused,” he said. “I know these people. They are our neighbours. One of her sons even spoke to me about it himself.”
The truck left after she refused, he said.
A refuge emptied
Mocha’s port lies about 75km (45 miles) north of the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a chokepoint for Red Sea shipping that the Houthis have repeatedly targeted since late 2023.
After government-aligned forces recaptured Mocha in 2017, the city became a refuge for Yemenis fleeing Houthi-controlled territory.
That changed in early September when fighting moved down the coast and families fled towards Aden, Taiz and Lahij. Many had already escaped Houthi rule once before.
On the evening of September 10, the government declared Mocha and its surroundings a “kill box”, a strike zone, warning that any Houthi movement there would be met with available firepower. Attacks began the following day.
Now residents say that leaving Mocha is almost impossible. “After the kill box was declared, the government opened the old al-Barh road so people could leave,” said Fuad, a 27-year-old pharmacist.
“Some got out, some were prevented by the Houthis and some stayed home, fearing the hardship of displacement.”
The Houthis have imposed a nighttime curfew on the city. Prices have soared, and power cuts have grown frequent, Nabil said.
A cooking gas cylinder has more than doubled in price to about 20,000 rials ($13), and a 50kg (110lb) sack of flour has risen by 8,000 rials ($5).
“A day’s work barely covers petrol and lunch,” he said. “Children have stopped going to school.”
Classrooms remain largely empty. “Parents and students are afraid of shelling or of their sons being thrown onto the front lines,” said Mansour, a teacher at a government secondary school who could not afford to flee with his family of seven.
“I am a teacher. I have nothing to do with politics,” he said. “In the end, we only die once.”
For Umm Khaled, a woman in her 60s whose husband is disabled and bedridden, leaving Mocha was never an option. “Where would I flee to? Look at my situation,” she said.
Her son, who had supported the family by fishing, joined the government-aligned National Resistance Forces for a monthly salary of 1,000 Saudi riyals ($267). He fled with them as the Houthis advanced, leaving behind his wife and two children, aged 15 and nine, in her care.
“Now they have fled, and we are lost,” she said. The local grocer has stopped extending credit, and the family survives on a sack of flour distributed by an aid group before the takeover. “Someone brings a fish, someone brings a yogurt and the rest is up to God,” she added.
Hassan, a 40-year-old fisherman who supports nine people, said he could not afford to leave the city. A ride to nearby Taiz costs up to 200,000 rials ($128). “Where would I go when I don’t even have my daily bread?” he asked.
Attacks and collapsed healthcare
Civilians have also been killed in the “kill zone”.
Before dawn on September 22, the bombing of a house in Mocha killed six members of one family, according to Mahmoud al-Otmi, a journalist with Saudi-owned Al-Hadath news channel whose relatives died.
Houthi-run media blamed Saudi air strikes. Saudi Arabia has not commented publicly.
Colonel Abdulbaset al-Bahr, deputy head of moral guidance in the government’s Taiz military command, said the kill box targets Houthi fighters.
“The kill box is for killing the militia, not civilians,” he said. “The statement did not ask civilians to leave the kill box area. Rather it asked them to stay in their homes and keep away from the militia’s barracks, positions and military gatherings.”
Sultan Mahmoud, the government-appointed director of the Mocha district, said no route out of the city was entirely safe as he accused the Houthis of targeting civilians.
Healthcare has nearly collapsed. On the day Houthi forces entered the city, Doctors Without Borders, also known by its French acronym MSF, said nearly all health facilities except Mocha General Hospital had stopped functioning. This was largely because staff had fled although about 30 health workers stayed behind, MSF told The National newspaper.
Residents said conditions in Mocha have since worsened.
“Doctors who were paid by organisations have stopped working because there are no salaries,” Nabil said. Fuad said the Houthis had placed hospitals under a security cordon and some medical equipment had been moved to Sanaa.
Aid has barely reached those who have stayed. Najib al-Saadi, head of the government’s executive unit for displacement camps, said his unit could not reach those in need.
“It is certain that there are families who could not flee because of poverty,” he said, accusing the Houthis of blocking humanitarian work. The International Committee of the Red Cross declined to comment.
In Yakhtul, Nabil said he would not leave, even if the fighting intensifies. “First, money is an obstacle,” he said. “And the house would be looted.”
