No room to roam: The cost of a crowded planet for wild animals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:56:48 UTC
16:56:48 KST

Over the past fifty years, the average size of monitored wildlife populations around the world has fallen by 73 per cent, according to WWF's Living Planet Report 2024. The report names loss and degradation of habitat as the most commonly reported threat, driven mainly by how the world grows its food.This finding raises a plain question. When animals lose the land, water and forest they depend on, what happens to them?A shrinking home, not a vanishing oneHabitat rarely disappears all at once. It is cut into pieces by farms, roads, canals, railway lines, power lines and growing towns. Each piece may still have trees and water, but it supports fewer animals than the original whole did.The 73 per cent figure also needs careful reading. It describes the average change across thousands of monitored populations. It does not mean that three-quarters of the world's animals are gone, or that three-quarters of species have disappeared. What it does show is a steady thinning, and the report describes such declines as an early warning of greater risk to species and ecosystems. The pressure it describes is gradual and widespread rather than the result of a single event, which is partly why it is easy to overlook. The report also notes that some populations have held steady or recovered where conservation has worked.
Not just about wildlife, it’s about the essential ecosystems that sustain human life
“This is not just about wildlife, it’s about the essential ecosystems that sustain human life,” said Daudi Sumba, chief conservation officer at WWF.What changes for an animal that loses spaceThe effects usually arrive in a recognisable order. Food and water become harder to find, so animals travel farther to reach them. Their routes cross fields, highways and railway tracks. Animals with large ranges, such as elephants and big cats, are affected first, because they need the most room.Smaller populations face a slower problem. When forest patches are cut off from one another, animals cannot move between them to find mates. Over time a small, isolated group becomes more vulnerable to disease and to sudden shocks such as drought or fire. Wherever forest meets farmland or settlement, animals and people also meet more often, and not always safely.Elephants outside the fenceIndia's elephants show how this plays out. The country holds about 60 per cent of the world's Asian elephants, according to the last census in 2017. Most of them do not live inside protected areas. Government and press figures put the share outside reserves at about 80 per cent. That share matters for everything that follows. A herd that lives mostly outside reserves has no boundary between it and the land that people farm, travel across and build on.For these herds, a journey between feeding grounds can pass through paddy fields, village lanes, rail lines and overhead power cables. Official data tabled in Parliament in 2024 shows what that means. Over five years, the leading cause of unnatural elephant deaths was electrocution, ahead of train accidents, poaching and poisoning. Odisha, Assam, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu reported the largest numbers of electrocution deaths.
The country holds about 60 per cent of the world's Asian elephants
The government has taken some steps in response. It has identified and ground-validated about 150 elephant corridors, the routes herds use to move between forests. The Railways and Environment ministries have also formed a standing committee to reduce deaths on tracks.Tigers on islands of forestTigers tell a more hopeful story, with a warning attached. The 2022 estimate counted at least 3,682 tigers in India, a record, spread across 53 tiger reserves. These reserves are among the best protected forests in the country.But the same assessment shows the limits of protection. Roughly a third of the reserves need stronger protection, habitat restoration or more prey for the tigers to feed on. A few reserves in Mizoram, Nagaland and Jharkhand reported almost no tigers at all. Summaries of the report also describe many reserves as small islands of forest, joined to one another by a limited number of corridors. A reserve with a healthy tiger population can send young animals out in search of territory of their own, and many of them end up in unprotected land among farms and villages.The record count and the weak reserves belong in the same account. Protection works where it is applied well, and the gaps appear where it is not.Where Kaziranga endsKaziranga's protection does not stop at the park boundary, and a new proposal from the Assam government has put that line under debate. The state wants to replace the default 10-km eco-sensitive zone (ESZ) around Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve with a site-specific zone of one to three kilometres. An ESZ is a regulatory buffer, declared by the environment ministry on a state's proposal. It is not an outright ban: depending on the notification, activities in it may be prohibited, regulated or permitted, and mining is among those most strictly restricted.
The state wants to replace the default 10-km eco-sensitive zone (ESZ) around Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve
Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma says the 10-km limit applies only because Kaziranga has not yet been finally notified. He argues it brings populated areas such as Kaliabor, Doboka and Jakhalabandha under restrictions, and holds up civic projects like a proposed stadium in Bokakhat. The state says the park's boundary and its UNESCO World Heritage status will not change, and that the 10-km zone stays in force until a new one is notified. Some residents agree. Hundreds rallied in support of the proposal on August 18, saying the current limits get in the way of building homes and basic infrastructure.The opposition and conservationists are not convinced. Congress state president Gaurav Gogoi led a protest at the Kohora range and alleged that the change could give legal cover to mining. The state government rejects the charge. Conservationists such as Jadav Payeng and Kavita Ashok point to the annual floods, when rhinos, deer and elephants move to higher ground outside the park. A smaller zone, they warn, could cut off those routes.A 2025 conservation assessment notes that a smaller zone is not necessarily a weaker one if it is designed to protect the most sensitive areas. Whether it does will depend on the final notification, which will decide whether wildlife corridors, flood escape routes and wetlands fall inside the line.Wetlands and the quieter lossesSpace does not only mean forest. Globally, freshwater species have seen the steepest declines in the WWF report, and wetlands are often among the first places to be drained or built over.The report points to Chennai, where rapid urban growth has led to a large loss of wetland area. Wetlands shelter birds, fish and amphibians, and they also soak up floodwater for the city around them. When they go, wildlife loses a home and people lose a buffer.The cost to peopleWhen space runs out, people pay too. Government data tabled in Parliament showed that elephants killed 2,853 people in India over five years, with the highest toll in 2023. Many of these deaths happened in places where farms, villages and elephant routes overlap. The elephant deaths and the human deaths come from the same stretches of land, where both now depend on the same ground.The Environment Ministry has issued guidelines on managing human-elephant conflict, and it says compensation is provided for losses. These measures respond to the damage after it happens. They do not by themselves restore the space that animals have lost.Where space is being rebuiltSome efforts aim at the cause. West Bengal has begun a community programme called Gajamitra, or Friends of Elephants, in which local people take part in reducing conflict. Conservation scientists have also suggested low-cost methods for farmers, such as planting chillies, ginger or citrus around fields, which elephants tend to avoid, or placing beehives along field edges.The WWF report also records progress in India, where it says some wildlife populations have stabilised or recovered. It credits government initiatives, careful habitat management, scientific monitoring and community involvement. At the global level, the report calls for more effective conservation along with changes in food, energy and finance systems.
What the evidence points toThe picture from India and from the world is consistent. Animals do not simply move on when their habitat shrinks. Their numbers thin out, they wander into danger, they come into conflict with people, or they disappear from places they once held. Where land is protected, connected and shared with the people who live beside it, some populations hold their ground or recover.
Animals do not simply move on when their habitat shrinks. Their numbers thin out
India's own examples point in both directions: electrocutions and train deaths on one side, a record tiger count and recovering populations on the other. The difference lies largely in whether land is protected and linked together, and whether the people who live beside wildlife are part of the plan.The question on World Wildlife Day is how much room is left for wildlife, and who decides what happens to it.

Japan’s island-defense glide missile seen at Camp Fuji
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:56:26 UTC
16:56:26 KST

- New video shows Japan's Type 25 Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile launcher arriving, raising into firing position and withdrawing at Camp Fuji.
- Japan deployed the missile to Camp Fuji on March 31 and plans new units in Hokkaido and Kyushu during fiscal 2026.
New video from Camp Fuji shows Japan’s Type 25 Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile launcher driving onto a firing site, raising its missiles into launch position and packing up again, giving a rare look at how the country’s first domestically built long-range strike missile is operated.
The three-minute clip was posted on X by Japanese military photographer @yahou5, who described it as the full sequence from arrival through moving into firing posture to withdrawal. It shows a heavy 8×8 truck carrying two large missile canisters on its back. The post was tagged with Camp Fuji and the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force’s Fuji School, which runs the service’s artillery training.
Japan deployed the weapon to Camp Fuji in Shizuoka Prefecture on March 31, the same day the Defense Ministry gave it its official name. Developed as the Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile for island defense, it was redesignated the Type 25 HVGP, also known as 25HGP. The unit at Camp Fuji is the Field Artillery Training Unit, which is using the first systems to train crews and work out how the weapon will be used.
Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said at the time that the deployment, together with the Type 25 surface-to-ship missile sent to Camp Kengun in Kumamoto, was the first time domestically produced stand-off missiles had been delivered to Japanese military units. Stand-off weapons are meant to hit an enemy force from outside the range of its own weapons.
The HVGP works differently from a cruise missile. A rocket booster carries it to high altitude, where the warhead section separates and glides toward the target at very high speed, maneuvering on the way down. That combination of speed and an unpredictable flight path makes it harder to intercept than a conventional ballistic missile. Japanese outlet Jiji Press has described it as a type of hypersonic glide weapon, flying at more than five times the speed of sound.
The Defense Ministry says the current Block 1 version has a range of several hundred kilometers. Japanese media have reported figures of up to 900 km (560 miles). The ministry is developing longer-range versions, with a goal of 1,000 to 2,000 km, and a later Block 2 with a more advanced glide body is planned for the 2030s.
The launcher made its first public appearance at the Fuji Firepower Review, Japan’s largest annual live-fire demonstration, at the East Fuji Maneuver Area on June 7. There, it raised its two launch tubes upright to show its firing posture. No missile was fired.
Camp Fuji is only the first stop. The Defense Ministry plans to form new HVGP units at Camp Kamifurano in Hokkaido and Camp Ebino in Miyazaki Prefecture on Kyushu during fiscal 2026, which ends in March 2027.
The deployment has drawn attention from local officials. The ministry told the town of Oyama, home to Camp Fuji, that launch equipment would be stationed there, but it has declined to say whether warheads are kept at the base.

Türkiye’s exports surge by 15.54 percent year-on-year to $25.98 billionin September.
Türkiye’s exports in the January-September period rose 5.2 percent year-on-year to a record $211 billion, Trade Minister Ömer Bolat announced.
Speaking in Istanbul on Oct. 3 while unveiling September foreign trade figures, Bolat said the country’s rolling 12-month goods exports had increased to $283.7 billion in September.
“This is also an annual goods export record,” he said.
Recalling that the 2026 Medium-Term Program (OVP) target was $282 billion, Bolat said: “We have surpassed the OVP target with three months still remaining in the year.”
Bolat also said that rolling 12-month services exports had reached $125.4 billion as of September.
The minister further noted that a record was set for September exports.
“September goods exports of $26 billion represent the second-highest monthly figure on record. The highest was $26.3 billion in December 2025,” Bolat said.
According to Trade Ministry data, exports increased 15.4 percent year-on-year in September to $25.98 billion, while imports rose 5.9 percent year-on-year to $31.21 billion.
The foreign trade deficit narrowed 24.8 percent year-on-year to $5.23 billion in the month.
In the January-September period, imports climbed 5.4 percent year-on-year to $282 billion, while the foreign trade deficit widened 5.8 percent year-on-year to $71.03
billion.
“Despite the rise in imports driven by higher commodity prices, the increase in the foreign trade deficit remained more limited than initially anticipated at the outset of the war,” Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said in a social media post, commenting on the latest trade data.
“Even amid the impact of geopolitical tensions, we expect the current account deficit-to-GDP ratio to remain at a manageable level of 2.6 percent,” said Şimşek.

OPEC+ Set to Keep November Oil Output Targets Steady, Sources Say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:53:24 UTC
16:53:24 KST

OPEC+ agreed to keep oil production targets steady for November at a meeting on Sunday, the producer group said, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments are unlikely until next year.
Seven core members of the group comprising the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia made the decision for November in a brief online meeting on Sunday. The core members are Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman.
Gulf OPEC+ producers have been pumping well below output targets in the face of continuing export disruptions from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, with exports fluctuating at 60% to 80% of normal levels in recent months.
“The OPEC+ group of seven kept their production ceilings unchanged, in line with market expectations. That said, despite rising flows through the Strait of Hormuz, their output levels remain well below quota,” said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo.
“Consequently, the oil market remains tight.”
Oil prices had dropped on Friday after European leaders agreed to U.S. President Donald Trump's request to release diesel reserves. Even so, Brent crude remains above $100 a barrel, up from about $73 before the Iran war started in late February.
OUTPUT HIKES HAVE BEEN LARGELY ON PAPER THIS YEAR
The Iran war has also delayed the group's output capacity review — crucial to determine members’ 2027 output quotas — because it has thrown estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, industry sources told Reuters last week.
OPEC+ has been raising output targets for much of 2026 after years of production cuts, but most of the increases stayed on paper because of the Middle East conflict.
The seven core OPEC+ members pumped 25 million barrels per day in August, up 630,000 bpd from July, yet still roughly 5 million bpd below prewar levels in February, OPEC data shows.
The seven hold their next meeting on Nov. 1.
OPEC+ still has about 2 million bpd of output cuts in place covering most members. It needs the result of the capacity review to decide how to distribute increases and any changes to output are unlikely before 2027, sources have said.
A separate OPEC+ ministerial group called the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee (JMMC), which does not decide policy, also met on Sunday to review the market.

The defense and aerospace industry’s exports amounted to a total of $6.93 billion in the January-September period, rising 15.6 percent.
Türkiye’s defense and aerospace industry exports increased 15.6 percent year-on-year to $6.93 billion in the January-September period, accounting for 3.28 percent of the country’s total exports, data from the Türkiye Exporters’ Assembly (TİM) showed.
In September alone, defense and aerospace exports climbed 10.7 percent year-on-year to $634.1 million. The sector accounted for 2.44 percent of the country’s total exports.
Over the past 12 months, defense and aerospace exports reached $10.94 billion, marking a 29.9 percent year-on-year increase and representing 3.86 percent of Türkiye’s total exports.
“Behind these figures are our high value-added products, engineering capabilities, production capacity and the partnerships we have developed across different geographies around the world,” said Haluk Görgün, head of Türkiye’s Defense Industries Secretariat.
The automotive industry maintained its position as the country’s top exporting sector in September, with exports totaling $3.94 billion.
The sector’s exports in the January-September period rose 3.1 percent year-on-year to $31.15 billion.
Among the top exporting sectors in September, chemicals and chemical products ranked second with $3.07 billion in exports, while the electrical and electronics sector came third with $2.06 billion.

New U.S. Army tank and fighting vehicles spotted during live-fire testing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:50:36 UTC
16:50:36 KST

- Footage shared by U.S. Army CTO Alexander Miller shows the M1E3 Abrams tank and two XM30 infantry fighting vehicle prototypes firing live rounds.
- Miller also saw the Mobile Tactical Cannon and robots from Operation Jailbreak Falcon Fury shooting down drones.
New footage shows the U.S. Army’s next-generation M1E3 Abrams tank and two prototypes competing to replace the Bradley infantry fighting vehicle firing live rounds, one of the first public looks at the vehicles in action.
The footage was shared on LinkedIn by Alexander Miller, chief technology officer to the U.S. Army chief of staff. Miller wrote that he went hands-on with the M1E3 pre-prototype, one of the XM30 offerings, the Mobile Tactical Cannon and some new optics, and watched robots from the U.S. Army’s Operation Jailbreak Falcon Fury shoot down drones. He did not say where the event took place or name the units involved.
The M1E3 is the U.S. Army’s redesign of its main battle tank, launched in 2023 after the service cancelled a planned SEPv4 upgrade to the current Abrams. The first early prototype was unveiled at the Detroit Auto Show in January. It has an uncrewed turret with an autoloader, a three-person crew seated in the hull, digital controls and an open systems architecture meant to allow quick hardware and software updates. Four pre-prototypes built by Roush are due to reach the 1st Armored Brigade Combat Team, 1st Cavalry Division, known as the Iron Horse brigade, at Fort Hood, Texas, later this year, with General Dynamics Land Systems delivering more.
The XM30 Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicle competition pits General Dynamics Land Systems’ Wolf against American Rheinmetall’s Lynx-based design. Both companies delivered their first prototypes at the end of August and the start of September, and each is building eight. The two designs are headed to the same Iron Horse brigade for soldier testing, including a National Training Center rotation in spring 2027, and the U.S. Army could pick a winner after that.
The Mobile Tactical Cannon is the U.S. Army’s program to replace the towed M777 howitzer with a wheeled, self-propelled 155 mm gun that can fire and move quickly. In August, the service picked Hanwha Defense USA’s K9 Mobile Howitzer, ordering six prototypes with an option for 12 more.
Miller used the post to argue that cheap, numerous systems still matter alongside expensive ones.
“Mass still matters. Pretending that it doesn’t is risk blindness and academics. To take and hold land you need mass – affordable mass, with autonomy, mission planning at superhuman scale and speed, and execution at echelon,” said Alexander Miller, chief technology officer to the U.S. Army chief of staff.
“We should always make the first engagement with any adversary a trade for blood and steel. Their blood, our steel,” Miller said.
He also pointed to the networks behind the vehicles. Miller said the Next Generation Command and Control program provides the data platform for tools and applications, while the Integrated Battle Command System-Maneuver handles fire control and asset management for counter-drone sensors and weapons. Cheap, attritable drones flow to units from the Defense Innovation Unit’s Drone Dominance Program through a drone marketplace, he wrote.
Power is a growing problem for troops in the field, Miller added.
“Soldiers draw between 60-120W depending on their loadout. That’s nearly continuous. When you get to a squad you’re at almost a kW of draw – that’s before drone batteries,” Miller said.
He said mobile power that does not give away troops through visual, acoustic or infrared signatures is critical.
Operation Jailbreak is the U.S. Army’s push to make sensors, weapons and software from different companies work together, starting with counter-drone and air defense systems. Miller did not say which robots took part or what weapons they used against the drones.
The U.S. Army has not said when M1E3 testing with the Iron Horse brigade will begin or released results from the live-fire event.

Latvian PM on track to lead pro-Ukraine coalition after election win
RIGA, Oct 4 - Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs was set to retain power and form a pro-Ukrainian coalition after his centrist United List secured the biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence in 1991.
With 97% of ballots counted after Saturday's election in the NATO and European Union country bordering Russia, United List was on 35.3%, enough for 42 seats in the 100-seat parliament.
A businessman and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which stray Ukrainian military drones flew undetected into Latvia.
Latvia's economy has underperformed its Baltic neighbours for more than a decade and Kulbergs has vowed to improve governance, cut red tape and reduce public spending, political scientist Roberts Kits said.
"Kulbergs played on being a get-things-done type of guy and has persuaded the voters that he can do things differently, bring some fresh energy," he said.
"This means the responsibility is huge. People expect him to deliver, but the question remains whether he has the team to do it."
United List appeared able to secure a parliamentary majority with either the nationalist National Alliance or the liberal Progressives, Kits said.
"(Kulbergs) is smart, let's hope that something will be better, that he will change what can be changed", Aina Sturmane, 78, a pensioner, told Reuters in Riga on Sunday.
No Latvian government has survived a full term, and Kulbergs will face an uphill battle holding together the United List, a loose alliance of small parties and independents, said political scientist Janis Ikstens.
PM PLEDGES TO MAINTAIN HARD LINE ON RUSSIA
Kulbergs pledged continuing support to Ukraine and to keep a hard line towards Moscow.
"Any economic ties with Russia makes us weak. Yes, it can bring some extra money, but it's a weakness Russia might exploit," he told reporters at his party's headquarters on election night as supporters celebrated the scale of the win.
"It's remarkably good. I was not expecting such a result," Kulbergs said.
Voter turnout was 51.8%, down from 59.4% in 2022, underscoring disappointment with politicians in Latvia, Ikstens said.
United List was followed by the populist, MAGA-style Latvia First, which was on 13.1%. Latvia First had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority in the run-up to the vote.
Third in the ranking was the pro-Russian Sovereign Power party, on 11.7%, followed by the National Alliance, which promotes a hardline approach to the Kremlin, at 8.9%.
Throughout his campaign, Kulbergs promised moreanti-drone capability for Latvia and to maintain defencespending at 5% of gross domestic product, one of the highestlevels in NATO.
His pro-Kremlin rivals said Latvia should stop any aid toUkraine and instead focus on tackling cost-of-living issues,particularly among the country's Russian-speaking minority.
Although pro-Russian parties increased their representation, Kits said they remained sidelined and were unlikely to influence government policy.
Latvia's ethnic Russian minority is split between thosewho oppose Moscow's war in Ukraine and others who voice frustration with policies at home aimed at limiting their influence on public life, which many of them see asdiscriminatory.
Latvia, with a population of 1.9 million, is sandwichedbetween the Baltic Sea and Russia and Belarus to the east, withEU and NATO allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south. REUTERS

U.S. Air Force adds $12M for AI agents on doomsday plane
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:43:42 UTC
16:43:42 KST

- The U.S. Air Force added $12.1 million to Scale AI's contract for agentic AI on the E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center, raising it to $44.3 million.
- The work runs through Nov. 5, 2027, with $5 million in fiscal 2026 research funds obligated at award.
The U.S. Air Force has added $12.1 million to a contract with Scale AI to develop artificial intelligence agents for the E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center, the new “doomsday plane” meant to keep U.S. leaders in command of the military, including nuclear forces, if ground command centers are destroyed.
The modification raises the total value of the San Francisco company’s contract from $32.2 million to $44.3 million, the U.S. Department of War said. The work will be done in San Francisco and is expected to run through Nov. 5, 2027. The U.S. Air Force obligated $5 million in fiscal 2026 research and development funds at award.
The notice does not say what tasks the AI agents will perform aboard the aircraft, whether they will run on the plane itself or on ground systems that support it, or how much human control will be built in.
Agentic AI goes a step beyond chatbots that answer questions. These systems can plan and carry out multi-step tasks on their own, such as gathering and sorting information, drafting options or managing workflows, with people supervising or approving key decisions. On a command aircraft packed with communications gear and a battle staff, that could mean helping crews handle large volumes of messages and data during a crisis, though the U.S. Air Force has not described its plans.
The original contract was awarded earlier this year through the Air Force Research Laboratory’s Information Directorate in Rome, New York. The latest modification was issued by the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Hanscom Air Force Base, Massachusetts.
The E-4C will replace the E-4B Nightwatch, a fleet of four heavily modified Boeing 747-200s that first flew in the 1970s and serve as the National Airborne Operations Center. The aircraft are hardened against the effects of nuclear blasts and can be refueled in flight, allowing them to stay aloft for long periods while the president, defense secretary and senior commanders direct forces from the air.
Sierra Nevada Corp. won a $13 billion contract in April 2024 to build the replacement. The company bought used Boeing 747-8I airliners from Korean Air and is converting them in Dayton, Ohio, adding protection against radiation and electromagnetic pulse, new communications antennas, computers and mission systems. The first E-4C test aircraft flew on Aug. 7, 2025, and flight and ground testing is continuing through 2026 before mission equipment is installed. Deliveries are scheduled to finish by July 2036.
Scale AI, best known for labeling data used to train AI models, has become a major supplier of AI tools to the U.S. military. In March 2025, it won the Defense Innovation Unit’s Thunderforge project to bring AI agents into military planning and operations, working with Anduril and Microsoft. Earlier this year, the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office raised the ceiling on another Scale AI agreement from $100 million to $500 million. Meta holds a minority stake in the company.

Nothing stolen, lights left on: Finland probes MPs’ home break-ins amid Russia tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:42:40 UTC
16:42:40 KST

Finnish authorities are investigating a series of suspicious break-ins at the homes of members of parliament, incidents Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said could potentially be linked to a foreign power.
Parliament Speaker Jussi Halla-aho said lawmakers had been informed of a “significant” number of break-ins and signs of attempted intrusions at the homes of several politicians, prompting an investigation.
“I cannot comment precisely on the number of suspicious cases known to us, but in any event it is a significant number,” Halla-aho told a news conference. He said the incidents appeared to have taken place over an extended period, with the first believed to have occurred about a year ago.
“At this stage, there is no information about the motive or who is responsible,” he said.
Asked whether a foreign power could be behind the suspected break-ins, Orpo said it was “entirely possible. It is certainly possible these days.”
“If someone is trying to undermine stability in Finland, our sense of security or, for example, our support for Ukraine, it achieves the opposite result,” he added. “It only strengthens our unity.”
The investigation was announced after Finnish newspaper Ilta-Sanomat reported last week that members of parliament had been warned several days earlier about possible break-ins.
President Alexander Stubb said an “attack on a member of parliament is an attack on democracy.”
“It must not be allowed or accepted in any form,” he told reporters at a ceremony marking the launch of Finland’s new F-35 fighter jets in Rovaniemi in the country’s far north.
Most of the known incidents occurred in the Helsinki area and targeted politicians from different parties, both men and women.
Halla-aho said it was possible the intruders had deliberately left clear signs that they had been inside the homes. Finnish media reported cases in which doors were left open, lights were left on or objects were moved to make the intrusion obvious and unsettle the occupants.
One member of parliament reportedly returned home to find that someone had used the toilet and failed to flush.
Because the intruders apparently left without stealing anything or causing major damage, the incidents have raised suspicions that the objective may have been intimidation or psychological pressure against senior Finnish officials.
The investigation comes amid growing tension in northern Europe over fears of possible Russian military action against countries in the region, particularly the Baltic states of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, all former Soviet republics and now NATO members.
Finland, which maintained military neutrality for decades, joined NATO following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The move angered the Kremlin, particularly because Finland shares a 1,340-kilometer border with Russia, the longest Russian border held by any EU or NATO country.
Meanwhile, Finland’s government and Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen survived two separate no-confidence votes in parliament on Friday following criticism from opposition parties over the minister’s visit to Israel.
The Social Democratic Party filed a no-confidence motion against the right-wing government, accusing it of inconsistency in its Middle East policy. A separate motion by the Greens, backed by the Left Alliance and the Social Democrats, targeted Häkkänen personally.
Häkkänen survived by a vote of 114 to 61, while the government won its vote by 93 to 62.
The criticism followed Häkkänen’s September visit to Lebanon and Israel. In Israel, he met Defense Minister Israel Katz, primarily to discuss purchases of Israeli military equipment, including the David’s Sling missile defense system.
Finland and Israel signed a deal for the system in November 2023 amid Finnish concerns over a possible future conflict with Russia. Opposition parties also criticized Häkkänen for not meeting Palestinian representatives during the trip.
“It is still unclear whether Minister Häkkänen raised Israel’s violations of international law” against the Palestinian population during his visit, the Social Democratic Party said last week.
Häkkänen defended the visit, saying it was essential to Finland’s security.

North Korea fires intermediate-range missile, claiming evasive flight and AI features
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:41:31 UTC
16:41:31 KST

Japan’s military said the missile landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone, while South Korea's military, which often accuses the North of exaggerating its capabilities, said it travelled more than 700 kilometres.
North Korea announced Saturday that it had test-fired an intermediate-range ballistic missile, claiming the weapon can manoeuvre in flight to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan.
The launch comes as tensions between the two Koreas run high over landmine explosions along their border.
Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said her brother oversaw the test. She called the missile "strategic", a term that suggests it is meant to carry nuclear warheads. She also claimed it can alter its trajectory at low altitudes and has unspecified artificial intelligence capabilities, which she said would make it extremely hard to intercept.
Japan’s military said the missile landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone, while the South Korean military, which often accuses North Korea of exaggerating its military capabilities, said the missile travelled more than 700 kilometres.
North Korea claims new missile capabilities
According to South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff, the North Korean missile was fired early Saturday from the eastern coastal Wonsan area. Japan's Defense Ministry later put the distance at roughly 680 kilometres.
In her statement, Kim Yo Jong pointed to the gap between the two US allies' figures as proof that they could not follow the missile in flight.
"Whenever we applied the wavelike trajectory mode to missiles, the enemy failed to track the targets from their first skip points," she said. "There is no way to avoid this attack."
The launch followed a day after she mocked Seoul's demand that Pyongyang apologise for the 21 September landmine explosions. The blasts went off about 10 metres south of the military demarcation line and wounded three South Korean soldiers.
A joint inspection by South Korea and the US-led United Nations Command concluded that North Korea had planted the mines, and the command later found that Pyongyang had breached the armistice that halted the 1950-53 Korean War.
Seoul has also asked the North to stop fortifying the border with mines and anti-tank barriers. That work has sped up since Kim Jong Un dropped the goal of reconciliation in 2024 and branded Seoul a permanent adversary.
Kim Yo Jong, who may be the second most powerful person in Pyongyang, called Seoul's demands "utterly pathetic" on Friday and rejected any North Korean responsibility for the blasts, warning of retaliation if the South fires on troops working along the border.
Pyongyang's weapons tests are piling up
The Wonsan launch is the newest in a string of recent military displays, which also include missile tests, live-fire drills and the commissioning of a new warship. Kim Jong Un is showing off his expanding nuclear programme even as Washington urges a return to diplomacy.
Wonsan also hosted the Sept. 20 test of what state media described as a hypersonic missile system. It belongs to a family of weapons built to overwhelm missile defences in South Korea and Japan, including solid-fuel intermediate-range missiles first revealed in 2024.
South Korea's military said it had raised its surveillance level for further launches and was sharing information closely with Washington and Tokyo. The US Pacific Command said the launch "does not pose an immediate threat to American personnel or territory or to our allies."
Kim has mostly turned his back on diplomacy with the US and South Korea since his nuclear talks with President Donald Trump broke down in 2019. He has shifted his focus to Moscow, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons to back Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine. After years of heavier testing, his arsenal of nuclear-capable missiles now includes long-range systems that could potentially reach the U.S. mainland and shorter-range ones that threaten South Korea and Japan.
In August, Trump scaled back a large joint exercise with South Korea, apparently hoping to restart talks.
North Korea has brushed off the overture, insisting that Washington first end its "hostile policy", a phrase Pyongyang uses to describe US-led sanctions and joint military drills with South Korea.

Taipei mayoral candidates clash over framing of drug policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:37:40 UTC
16:37:40 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) and incumbent KMT Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) have clashed over drug policy, despite both supporting existing needle-exchange and methadone programs.
The controversy intensified after Shen discussed international harm-reduction approaches, including community centers, clean needles, and methadone treatment. Chiang responded in a Facebook post Saturday that drug policy must maintain a clear distinction between drugs and medicine, per CNA.
Chiang clarified Sunday that he supports methadone treatment and clean-needle policies but opposes drug decriminalization and community centers that provide drugs. He also supports stronger action against drug smuggling, trafficking, manufacturing, and use, along with expanded anti-drug education.
Shen has argued that harm reduction should form part of a broader strategy combining prevention, treatment, and law enforcement. He noted that needle-exchange and methadone programs are already established public health measures in Taiwan.
Taiwan introduced its harm-reduction program after HIV infections rose sharply among people who inject drugs. The Centers for Disease Control began implementing needle-exchange and methadone treatment programs in 2005, after which new HIV infections among people who inject drugs declined sharply, per a health ministry press release.
CDC Director-General Lo Yi-chun (羅一鈞) cited a National Taiwan University College of Public Health study that estimated the two programs prevented 13,664 HIV diagnoses among people who inject drugs between 2005 and 2020. It projected that they would prevent another 10,821 diagnoses from 2021 through 2040.
The measures cost an estimated NT$21 billion (US$660 million) from 2005 through 2020 while saving about NT$404.1 billion in HIV-related medical costs, according to Lo. He said every NT$1 invested could save about NT$19 in medical costs and added that disease prevention should not be viewed through a partisan lens.
The dispute centers on how harm-reduction programs fit within broader drug policy and how candidates communicate the distinction between treatment and decriminalization.

Across China: From import replacement to global exporter, Chinese harvester maker sweetens sugarcane business
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
15:34:17 CST
16:34:17 KST

by Xinhua writer Zhang Yunlong
ZHENGZHOU, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- "People say a woman fears marrying the wrong man, while a man fears choosing the wrong trade. I definitely chose the wrong trade," Zhang Changxian, 59, said with a laugh.
When Zhang began developing a sugarcane harvester in 2008, he expected challenges. He did not expect it would take eight years to bring the machine to market.
For years, the engineer-turned-entrepreneur and his team spent harvest seasons testing and redesigning prototypes in cane fields in Chongzuo, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. The city is about 1,600 km from his factory in Luoyang, central China's Henan Province.
During one field test, a steering linkage snapped in a muddy patch. In many others, the machine struggled with cane flattened by typhoons.
Today, machines made by his company, Luoyang Chenhan Agricultural Equipment Technology, account for about half of China's sugarcane harvester market by volume, the company says. They are also drawing buyers overseas, from Southeast Asia to Latin America.
The company's rise comes as China's sugar industry seeks to cut costs and improve competitiveness through mechanization.
China has long relied on imports to bridge a wide gap between domestic sugar output and demand. In the 2024/25 marketing year, the country produced about 11.2 million tonnes of sugar and consumed about 15.7 million tonnes, according to the Chinese Agriculture Outlook Committee under the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs. Imports totaled about 4.6 million tonnes.
According to Zhang, major sugar-exporting countries such as Brazil generally enjoy lower production costs, with large-scale mechanized farming being one of the key factors.
Rising labor costs have added to the pressure on China's sugar industry. When Zhang entered the industry in 2008, a worker could harvest about one tonne of cane a day for 25 to 30 yuan (3.7 to 4.5 U.S. dollars). Today, the same work can cost 180 to 250 yuan, he said, while harvested cane sells for around 500 yuan a tonne.
As labor costs climb, demand for mechanized harvesting has grown. One Chenhan harvester, Zhang said, can now cut more than 100 tonnes of cane a day, roughly the work of 100 laborers.
When Zhang started, nearly all harvesters in China were imported. His team decided to develop equipment tailored to local conditions. But building a domestic harvester proved far harder than many had expected.
Unlike in Brazil and Australia, where cane is often grown on large plantations, China's major sugarcane regions typically have sloping terrain, with smaller and more fragmented fields.
Many major agricultural machinery makers focused on larger markets for wheat, corn and rice equipment, while sugarcane harvesting was a niche segment with significant technical challenges. With no established supply chains or mature domestic components for sugarcane harvesters at the time, Zhang's team had to design and test many critical systems themselves.
Each year offered only a narrow testing window because cane is harvested in a specific season, so a design flaw found in the field often meant waiting another year for large-scale trials.
After nearly three years without a breakthrough, Zhang put the project on hold for a while. Experts, including his former mentor, advised him to give up, he recalled.
A turning point came in 2011 when the team resumed work and shifted from an earlier whole-stalk harvesting approach to a chopped-cane system better suited to Chinese field conditions.
"At times we nearly ran out of money," Zhang said. To keep going, he used money set aside for his daughter's education and later mortgaged property to fund development.
Chenhan completed its first harvester in 2015. The machine entered the market a year later and sold more than 30 units in 2016, rising to more than 150 the following year.
Overseas expansion began in 2019. The company has since exported machines to countries including Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia, Costa Rica and Venezuela. Exports account for about one-fifth of revenue and are growing steadily, Zhang said.
Many foreign buyers are drawn by lower prices and the company's willingness to customize equipment. Customers in the French overseas department of Reunion, for example, requested tracked harvesters able to work on volcanic soil. The company developed a specialized tracked machine to reduce ground pressure and optimized its cooling systems for the island's tropical climate.
Looking ahead, Zhang said the company is exploring smarter controls, hybrid power systems and lower fuel consumption.
"Many people told us Chinese companies couldn't make a sugarcane harvester," Zhang said, recalling the early doubts. "We made it, and now we're exporting it." ■

Dozens detained at Communist Party rally in Moscow
Police in Moscow detained about 60 people at a rally held by Russia’s Kremlin-friendly Communist Party, the party has said.
The party said in a statement that the detentions happened as the rally was ending, and that its Moscow branch was working to get those who were detained – mostly young people – released.
The rally marked the anniversary of the Kremlin’s 1993 crushing of a parliamentary uprising.
The Telegram news channel Ostorozhno Novosti said protesters chanted slogans including “Freedom for political prisoners,” “For fair elections,” and “Down with the Tsar.”
The rally came as public frustration has been simmering in Russia during the intensifying Ukrainian drone attacks deep inside the country.

"For months, Russia has been trying to isolate Ukrainians in Oleshky from the outside world, even obstructing the delivery of food to people facing severe shortages," Sybiha said on X.
Drones carrying food packages fly over a location given as Oleshky, in Kherson Oblast, in footage released by Ukrainian military officials. Credit: Reuters

Ukraine believes Russia shared jet-drone technology with North Korea
Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky says he believes Russia has shared jet-drone technology with its longstanding ally North Korea,
In recent weeks, Russia has sharply increased its use of jet-drones against Ukraine, which so far has no effective means of countering them other than using combat aircraft.
Asked if Russia had shared with North Korea the technology behind its latest generation of jet-powered drones, Zelensky told journalists: "Yes, of course".
"They (Russia) are sharing with North Korea all the technologies. I don't know about the ballistic and etc, but I think, yes, because North Korea helped them with missiles," he added.
Earlier in the war, North Korea supplied Russia with millions of artillery shells, and it has since provided ballistic missiles that Moscow regularly uses to attack Ukrainian cities.
India pushing for bigger role in Russia-Ukraine talks
India is seeking a greater role in brokering an end to the Russia-Ukraine war, Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar has said at a Munich Security Conference in New Delhi.
"We have been advocating (dialogue and diplomacy) for many years, and in recent months we have got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy, so we have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard," Jaishankar said.
Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (left) visited Kyiv on September 3. Credit: Efrem Lukatsky, AP
The minister, who made his first solo trip to Ukraine in September, said India was "trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping".
But he said India was also "going beyond that", including discussion on grain and energy exports and "on non-attack possibilities".
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin have close ties, and the pair met in New Delhi in September.
Germany's Merz announces new aid for Ukraine in Kyiv
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has announced a new aid package for Ukraine worth more than 1.3 billion euros ($1.5 billion) during a visit to Kyiv.
About 1 billion euros ($1.1 billion) of the package is military aid, including long-range strike weapons, combat drones and satellite technology, “so that Ukraine can also target Russian launch pads,” Merz said at a news conference.
Germany is also providing some 350 million euros ($395 million) in energy aid ahead of winter for generators, substations and repair work, he said.

Report: Israel's Transportation Ministry warned foreign-flight security was 'too big' for its security division
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:25:16 UTC
16:25:16 KST

In mid-2025, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu unequivocally placed responsibility for the security of foreign airlines flying to Israel with the Transportation Ministry and its Security Division. Behind the scenes, however, officials in the division strongly opposed the move, arguing they lacked the necessary tools, authority and budget.
Despite those concerns, no one raised a formal alarm. Neither the security agencies nor the ministry’s Security Division intervened, and the division did not approach the security services for assistance.
According to a report aired Sunday morning by Army Radio, the Shin Bet relinquished responsibility for securing foreign flights in 2021, while the Transportation Ministry failed to assume that responsibility in practice. The State Comptroller reportedly pointed to the issue in a classified May 2024 report that remains under gag order.
The comptroller’s report prompted the security cabinet in May 2024 to order the National Security Council to establish a team with the Transportation Ministry, Civil Aviation Authority, Shin Bet, Mossad and Finance Ministry to examine the security framework for civil aviation to Israel.
The National Security Council conducted a year-long review, during which disagreements emerged within the Transportation Ministry. The NSC and Shin Bet pushed for the ministry to assume responsibility, a position also supported by Civil Aviation Authority Director Shmuel Zakai.
But according to the Army Radio report, Transportation Ministry Security Division chief Avri Cohen argued in internal discussions that the responsibility was too heavy and that the issue was beyond the division’s capabilities, voicing his objections to Zakai.
“During the discussions, a scenario was raised in which all it would take was for a Syrian migrant who had moved to Britain to board a plane. He would look British, not Syrian, and we would not know,” a source familiar with the discussions was quoted as saying.
“There were major blowups, confrontations and strongly worded letters, but Regev, Director-General Ben Zaken and the head of the Civil Aviation Authority did not listen,” the source said.
In mid-2025, Netanyahu ultimately ruled that responsibility would be transferred to the Transportation Ministry and its Security Division.
A year and a half later, according to the report, no one has approached the security agencies to request assistance. The Shin Bet and Mossad, for their part, have not expanded their responsibilities or offered such assistance.

Ossoff and El-Sayed: Two Senate races and what they say about the Democratic Party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:21:26 UTC
16:21:26 KST

Ossoff and El-Sayed: Two Senate races and what they say about the Democratic Party
Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democratic favourite, is running for re-election in Georgia in the 2026 US midterms while Abdul El-Sayed is a Senate candidate in the battleground state of Michigan. The two Democrats have very different profiles and platforms, underscoring divergences within the party. They could also determine the party's future ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
Top Republicans have had it in for Senator Jon Ossoff and Abdul El-Sayed, both Democratic candidates for the US Senate, for a while now. As the November 3 midterms approach, campaign battles get more stinging, bruising – and at times, amusing.
Ossoff, the incumbent senator from Georgia running for re-election, has long been in President Donald Trump’s sights. But the 37-year-old Democrat can give as good as he gets.
Just months after Trump called the Georgia Democrat “Senator Os(jerk!)off” in a Truth Social post, Ossoff hit home with a quip on the president’s zealous aide, Natalie Harp. While accusing Trump of not wanting to “do the job”, Ossoff remarked that the US president simply wants to “build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace".
Read more‘She’ll never leave me’: Who is Natalie Harp, Trump’s most devoted aide?
The Republican response came swift and hard, with White House communications staff labeling Ossoff a “lightweight”, “Jon Jackoff” and “the biggest cuck loser”, among other epithets.
El-Sayed, who is running in Michigan, has also been the target of virulent attacks. At the Republican midterm convention in Texas, Senator Ted Cruz accused El-Sayed, whose parents are Egyptian immigrants, of seeking to implement Sharia law. Hecklers in the crowd roared back, “He should be shot,” sparking headlines in the US press. Weeks later, Cruz was at it again. In an interview with a conservative radio show, the Texas senator warned of a “green-red alliance of Marxists and Islamists” who are “taking over” the Democratic party.
Two candidates, two states, one goal
In the 2026 US midterms, Ossoff and El-Sayed are both trying to defend Democratic seats in high-stakes races. The Georgia senator is running for re-election after serving his first term in the US senate. In Michigan, El-Sayed is running for the seat vacated by outgoing Democratic Senator Gary Peters.
The two candidates also happen to be running against two Mikes: Ossoff’s Republican opponent is Mike Collins, who currently holds a seat in the US House of Representatives. El-Sayed is taking on Mike Rogers, a former FBI agent, veteran and staunch Trump ally.
As Senate candidates, Ossoff and El-Sayed have very different profiles.
The Georgia politician is ahead in the polls and is viewed as a rising Democratic star, a potential “hot presidential possibility” for the 2028 White House race. Feisty, media savvy and with choirboy looks, Ossoff is the country’s youngest serving senator and the only Democrat in the chamber to be seeking re-election in a state Trump won in 2024. Within the party, Ossoff is viewed as a moderate Democrat, capable of appealing to a broad base of voters in one of America’s right-leaning southern states.
El-Sayed, on the other hand, has never held elected office. The 41-year-old physician and public health expert is considered a left-wing politician, part of a wave of progressive Democrats focused on affordability and state services.
But in a battleground state that is home to cities with major Muslim communities such as Dearborn, “the capital of Arab America”, his position on the Israeli-Palestinian crisis often overshadows his economic justice messaging – and grabs global headlines. El-Sayed narrowly won his party’s nomination in August after a nasty primary against his pro-Israel rival Haley Stevens that exposed bitter divides within the party. In a state that regularly sends Democrats to the US Senate, the Michigan race is considered a tossup.
Read moreDemocrat El-Sayed narrowly wins Michigan primary
They are two candidates running in different states, but both are critical to the common Democratic goal of attempting to wrest control of the Senate in the November elections. “They're both important states where Democrats have sometimes struggled, perhaps Georgia more than Michigan, but they’re both seen as important wins for Democrats," said Matt Duss from the Center for International Policy and a former foreign policy adviser to Senator Bernie Sanders, who is a leading progressive in the Democratic party.
"Obviously, Abdullah El-Sayed is an Arab Muslim who is taking a much more progressive populist approach. But Ossoff has been a leader on the issue of anti-corruption, which is a major issue in American politics, and particularly for the progressive left. So they've both been offering what will be really important arguments for the party going forward.”
Left or right or in-between
The 2026 midterm race has increased attention on a progressive, leftward trend in the Democratic party that has picked up steam since Trump returned to the White House last year.
Democratic Socialism – a largely anodyne political ideology in many parts of the world, but which has long been stigmatised in the private capital-driven USA – is now the subject of polls and headlines across the country.
In barely two weeks, for instance, a Gallup poll found that Socialism is more popular than ever, with 43 percent of Americans holding a positive view. But The New York Times, citing another poll, informed readers that roughly half of US voters view socialism unfavourably.
For many Democratic strategists, that means a "Socialist" label is not a problem in primary race, but broadening a Socialist candidate's appeal in a general election could remain a challenge.
“In some ways, these are more differences in tone and manner and style rather than in policy,” said Richard Johnson, a US politics and policy expert at Queen Mary University of London.
While Ossoff is widely viewed as a moderate, Johnson notes that, “what people call moderate Democrat today is not what people called a moderate Democrat 20 or 30 years ago. Twenty or 30 years ago, a moderate Democrat was much more to the right of a moderate Democrat today because the whole party has moved much more consistently to the left.”
‘About three letters’
The party’s leftward move has put the focus on the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), a political group founded in 1982 that spent decades in obscurity before the 2016 presidential primary catapulted Sanders to national prominence before his defeat to Hillary Clinton. While Sanders calls himself a democratic socialist, the Vermont senator is not formally affiliated with DSA.
The group got a boost in 2018, when DSA member Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez won the New York primary and went on to win a House of Representatives seat. A high-profile breakthrough came in late 2025 with the election of Zohran Mamdani as New York City mayor.
Since the DSA is a movement that aims to promote progressive issues and not a political party, it can be a source of messaging gymnastics and sometimes panic for Democrats on the campaign trail. In a CBS interview last week, Florida's Democratic Senate nominee Angie Nixon stressed that "this is not about three letters" amid Republican criticism of her DSA membership. Nixon was one of the big surprises of the 2026 Democratic primaries, when the African-American self-described “former single mama” overcame a vast fundraising disadvantage to defeat former military officer and fellow Florida Democrat Alex Vindman.
While most analysts place El-Sayed on the left of the political spectrum, the Michigan candidate is not a DSA member. “El-Sayed has made it clear that he is not a Socialist. He describes himself as a capitalist who understands capitalism, that’s where his critique of capitalism comes from. But still, he is arguing for many things that DSA argues for. So, however he may identify himself, there is a formation behind him that includes the DSA that sees his message as consistent with their broader agenda,” explained Duss.
US Mideast policy on the ticket
A distinctive feature of the 2026 midterms race is the prominence foreign policy has played on the campaign trail. That’s largely because Trump’s Iran war has seen an overlap of domestic and international issues.
“The Iran war is raising gas prices, impacting the global economy and the US economy. But it's also feeding into a longstanding sense among many American voters, both Democrat and Republican and Independent, that America has been wasting time, resources and energy on all of these wars, particularly in the Middle East,” said Duss.
“But in the Democratic side, especially, I think Gaza continues to be a very severe tension point between the progressive left and the conservative establishment,” he added, referring to Israel’s military onslaught on the Palestinian enclave after the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack.
In Michigan, while El-Sayed’s platform is focused on providing healthcare and cost-of-living issues, the spotlight in the bitter primary race was on the two candidates’ positions on Israel.
His Democratic rival, Stevens, ran on a pro-Israel platform and raised a record $60 million, around half of which came from sources affiliated with pro-Israel lobby group, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). El-Sayed criticised Stevens for taking AIPAC donations, calls Israeli military onslaught in Gaza a genocide and opposes unconditional US aid to Israel. Stevens supported continuing US aid to Israel without conditions.
“The Democratic party is changing quite a lot on this issue. The party used to be pretty much as pro-Israel as the Republican Party. Now many Democratic voters are much more sceptical on Israel. There are elements where you can see the grassroots moving the party in a direction that's different from where it has been in the last few decades,” said Johnson.
Following El-Sayed’s primary win, Michigan Democrats – including Stevens and establishment figures such as Senator Elissa Slotkin, who holds the state’s other seat in the chamber – have rallied behind their candidate in the race against Republican Mike Rogers.
But it’s been a tripwire issue. El-Sayed has had to downplay his relationship with leftwing influencer Hasan Piker, who campaigned with him during the primary. Barely weeks after his primary victory, the Democratic candidate apologised to the state’s Jewish Democratic caucus for comments he made after a synagogue attack in March.
The controversies have sparked debates over whether El-Sayed, who won the primary by just 15,000 votes, can sway undecided voters and an estimated 130,000 Jewish Americans who live in Michigan, 61% of whom identified with or leaned Democrat, according to a 2021 study.
It also fuels Republican attacks as they eye a crucial Senate seat in a battleground state. Shortly after El-Sayed was projected to win the August primary, Trump declared it was “great news” for the Republicans in a Truth Social post. “El-Sayed, a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel, is the projected winner in this race with the Socialist,” Trump wrote. Rogers, El-Sayed’s Republican opponent in the Senate race, released a statement claiming that after spending “years hunting terrorists” he was now “running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11”.
“There's been so much attention on El-Sayed being an observant Muslim and much of it is, unfortunately, very bigoted and inflammatory,” said Duss. “Going back to 9/11, there has been an unfortunate tendency to see Muslim Americans as a source of threat. I completely reject that. And I think many Americans reject that.”
‘An almighty battle’ within the party
Ossoff, whose father is Jewish, has managed to negotiate the minefield of the Mideast crisis in US politics relatively unscathed.
On the Senate floor, Ossoff has attempted a balancing act between supporting Israel’s right to defend itself while criticising the humanitarian impact of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Gaza policies.
Last year, for instance, Ossoff voted to block a proposed US arms export to the Israeli police. But he also voted against another resolution that would have blocked the sale of air-to-ground munitions to Israel. “Despite my opposition to Prime Minister Netanyahu’s conduct of the war in Gaza, I believe the United States must continue to support the Israeli people,” said Ossoff in a press statement. Both resolutions were introduced by Sanders and failed the floor vote.
“Georgia is a more conservative state [than Michigan], Senator Ossoff has a read on his own politics,” said Duss, while noting that Ossoff’s vote to block arms exports to the Israeli police “took some courage”. The former foreign policy adviser to Sanders admitted that, “Personally, I wish he would go farther. I think he can go farther, and I would expect that if he wants to play a role as a leader in the Democratic Party in the future, he is going to need to go farther.”
In terms of policy shifts, Johnson believes the 2026 midterms will have a limited impact even if the Democrats manage to take over Congress. “I think government shutdowns in the US will be more likely to happen. If they win, the Democrats will use bargaining over budgets basically to try to extract some policy concessions over Trump, perhaps on immigration or such issues. But I think these will be fairly modest policy changes,” he explained.
The real impact of the November elections, Johnson predicts, will be the Democratic bench or the likely party candidates the midterms propel into the 2028 presidential race.
If El-Sayed and Ossoff win their respective races, the two men could influence their party’s future trajectory, according to experts.
“If El-Sayed wins the Senate, I think he is well very well-positioned to play a major national role, perhaps not running for president right now, but he is a very skilled candidate, a very courageous voice. And the United States is changing,” said Duss.
While Ossoff has dismissed speculation about his presidential ambitions, analysts believe the Democratic “star of the south” could be a strong candidate for the 2028 White House race.
“If Jon Ossoff is going to become the next [presidential] nominee, I think he’ll have a hell of a fight on his hands because I think the left of the party is going to really want someone that they view as a less compromising figure politically,” said Johnson. “The next Democratic primary is likely to see an almighty battle between the moderates and the left of the party.”

‘Gyanesh ka resignation to lekar rahenge’: Congress steps up protest against CEC Kumar
NEW DELHI: The Congress on Sunday announced a protest in Delhi calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. In a post on X, the party said its supporters would gather at India Gate at 5 pm before marching to Jantar Mantar.“Koi kitna bhi zor laga le.. Gyanesh ka Resignation to lekar rahenge. Chaliye, Sham ko milte hain. 4th October. 5 PM onwards. India Gate to Jantar Mantar,” the post read.
Earlier on Saturday, nearly 200 protesters were detained in connection with demonstrations at Jantar Mantar demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, officials said. Delhi Police also registered cases over Friday’s protest under provisions related to disobedience of orders and obstruction and assault of public servants.On Saturday, protesters marched from Patel Chowk towards Jantar Mantar, where police and paramilitary personnel had erected barricades and deployed additional forces to prevent them from reaching the designated protest area.Police invoked Sections 223(a), 221, 132 and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) in connection with Friday’s protests. The provisions relate to disobedience of a lawful order issued by a public servant, obstructing a public servant in the discharge of public functions, assault or use of criminal force to deter a public servant from performing his duty, and acts carried out by several persons in furtherance of a common intention, respectively.
The All India Students’ Association (AISA) had called for fresh mobilisation on Saturday, a day after nearly 1,000 people were detained during protests in and around Jantar Mantar. Many of those detained on Friday were later released.AAP’s student wing, the Association of Students for Alternative Politics (ASAP), also staged a protest on Saturday. The organisation alleged that some of its volunteers were detained and taken to different parts of Delhi in a bus for several hours before being brought to Jafarpur police station.AAP Delhi president Saurabh Bharadwaj questioned the continued detention of the student volunteers. Delhi Police did not immediately respond to the allegations.The latest action came a day after Delhi Police registered at least three FIRs in connection with Friday’s protests. Two FIRs were registered at Parliament Street police station and one at Connaught Place police station under Section 223 of the BNS for alleged disobedience of an order issued by a public servant.Ahead of Friday’s protest, police had imposed prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) across the New Delhi district. The order prohibits gatherings of five or more people, processions, demonstrations, picketing, dharnas and slogan shouting without prior written permission.
Around 5,000 police and paramilitary personnel, including more than 10 companies of paramilitary forces, were deployed across central Delhi on Friday. Barricades were erected at several locations, while drones were used to monitor crowded areas.Officials said police had received inputs that around 4,000 to 5,000 people could gather for the protest.The protests have also taken place amid a political debate over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise. The Election Commission has maintained that differences of opinion within the poll panel are part of institutional deliberations and that its orders follow established statutory procedures.
