Ukraine’s Energy Future: a UN Pilot Project Backed by Italy in Odesa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:18:00 UTC
16:18:00 KST

Odesa has been chosen as a testing ground for an important United Nations initiative to advance energy innovation in Ukraine. Led by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and financed by Italy, the new Pilot Decarbonization Office in Odesa explores how solar power and decentralized electricity generation can help cities withstand Russian attacks on energy infrastructure while laying the foundations for a greener recovery.
The choice also reflects the Italian government’s focus on Odesa and its region as a priority for assistance to Ukraine. Alongside support for cultural heritage and the restoration of buildings, energy resilience provides an essential foundation for the city’s recovery: reliable electricity keeps hospitals, schools, businesses and public services running.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
                                                                                                                                                                         Carlo Formosa (Italian Ambassador), Hanna Zamazieieva (State Agency on Energy Efficiency of Ukraine), Pier Carlo Sandei (UNEP)(Photo courtesy UNEP)                             
In this interview for Kyiv Post, Pier Carlo Sandei, Head of UNEP in Kyiv, explains why Odesa was selected, what its solar potential could mean for other Ukrainian cities, and how Italian support can help turn initial assessments into lasting investment.
SOS - Ukraine’s Looming Dark Winter Demands Decisive Action
Kyiv Post: UNEP presented the results of the Italian-funded project on green and resilient energy in Odesa. What problem was it designed to solve?
Pier Carlo Sandei: The problem was created by the war, and this was since the very beginning of the war. Energy infrastructures were a target by the Russian Federation’s attacks. We had to solve short-term problems, but also long-term problems. You need to find quick solutions for the immediate and humanitarian needs, but you also need to have a rethinking of the energy mix of Ukraine for a full EU accession. So, the project was aiming at addressing both aspects.
The question was: What can we do quickly and what can the project unlock quickly as resources for energy crisis solution? And on the other side: How can we start looking not only at today and tomorrow, but also to next year, to the next 10 years?
So the project had both dimensions. And this is what we are trying to do with different components of the project, working on short term and long term. An example of short term in Odesa is the solar city simulator, because it tells you today where to install solar panels on every roof. And this is something that can be done in one week. I mean, if you have the money tomorrow, you can install the solar panels and be independent. This is a quick solution.
On the other side you can have a long-term solution, which is, for example, what we are doing in Odesa, as well, with this 30-megawatt solar power plant. It will take more time, but will also have a longer-term impact on the overall energy balance of the region and in Ukraine.
What are the most important lessons learned from the assessment work presented in the Odesa Regional Recovery Forum?
As refers to the Odesa components of the project, the first thing is that with only 5% of the roofs covered with solar panels, you can get 25% of the energy needs of the city. So, there’s enough sun and there are enough roofs to have enough electricity and a diversified and diffused energy distribution.
I’m not saying that the Russian Federation will not hit the roofs with salt water, but the damage would be much less than if it were a centralized power. These are the lessons learned, where decentralization is important to make sure that we can get resilience.
The second thing is that we have so far relied a lot on gas turbines and diesel generators, but these have, in the long term, a negative impact on the energy mix of the country, as well as on the environment and the economy, because diesel generators, with the price of diesel today, is becoming very expensive source of energy. With solar panels, you do the investment only once and then they keep on giving you free energy the rest of the time.
And again, these are a positive contribution to the future of Ukraine, while diesel generation and gas turbines are a negative addition to the future energy mix of Ukraine, because they will be still relying on fossil fuels and not going into right direction for the EU.
The audience in Odesa was impressed that their city will host such a pilot project, because it is very rarely chosen for this purpose. Why this decision and what can Odesa teach to other cities, like Kharkiv or Mykolaiv, involved in the project?
There are two aspects. First of all, there is a logistical issue. Odesa has a lot of sun, similar to Mykolaiv. There’s less sun in Kyiv, Rivne or Kharkiv. So, it’s easier to sell solar panels in Odesa than in the north of Ukraine, even though it is meaningful there, too.
The second thing: in Odesa we found a very proactive and responsive administration that has embarked on this project with enthusiasm. So this made it easier to work with Odesa than other parts of Ukraine.
Thirdly, of course, the Italian funding, with a special patronage of Italy for Odesa, allowed it to welcome the project.
Odesa’s energy infrastructure is regularly targeted by Russian attacks. How do you design solar, storage and backup power systems that can withstand this risk?
Well, this is the solar city simulator. You want to have a diffuse and decentralized production. So the worst case scenario is that they damage 50 solar panels, which means that the value of the drone is higher than the damage that they can make on the other side.
For this reason, you don’t want to have the 30-megawatt plant built now until it is also properly defended or until the situation changes in terms of safety. Because such a big power plant is easier target to shell. And at that point the damage would be bigger than the value of the attacks. So, it is exactly the right response to this risk.
Any international project has to pass through an assessment on corruption risks. How is this project protected with regard to corruption?
First of all, the project is managed by the UN and we have very strong safeguards and anti-corruption mechanisms. So, we are not working with financial transactions through local authorities. We work with other partners on the other side that we can control. I don’t think corruption should scare us from investing. It should force a stronger rule of law. If there is corruption, it doesn’t mean you should not do business in Ukraine.
And this is what we are doing in this project. We cannot run away because of corruption. We should fight corruption. And you should fight corruption not only by having safeguard mechanisms, but also by showing integrity, leading by example.
What about the rooftop solar assessment developed by the IRENA Solar City Simulator? How much rooftop potential did you find in Ukrainian cities? And which building types are the targets: municipal buildings, residential or commercial?
We cover the whole northern part of Odesa. So, it’s not a cherry-picking roof by roof. But we did the assessment for all the roofs of the city. Now we can tell you which ones are more productive and which are less productive. And the reason is also due to the shade, because if you have a high building next to you and you are in the shade, this building will produce less.
The analysis done on the whole territory of the city and it doesn’t distinguish between public or private or whatever. So you can go and check your own building and see how much electricity you can produce.
How does the clearing house mechanism works in practical terms, what problem does it solve for cities and investors?
When we started looking at energy projects, we saw that part of them are going to the Minister of Energy, parts of the project are going to the Minister of Territorial Community.
Some projects are going to the Minister of Environment because they are climate friendly. Others are going to the Ministry of Development. So, there is no single repository of all the energy projects happening in Ukraine.
So, if tomorrow a donor comes and says, I want to finance projects on energy, they would not be able to have one answer. They would need to go to five different ministers and sometimes even to the different oblasts. And this because of some legal obligations.
The law says that big energy projects are managed by the Minister of Energy. Small energy projects instead are dealt by the Ministry of Territorial Communities and the Minister of Development. Some are private investments, so they are not even fitting into that. Therefore, it’s difficult to facilitate the match between offer and demand, or needs and offer.
The idea would be if tomorrow somebody needs to say, okay, give me all the projects down below 10 megawatts, you would be able to have that. At the same time, if there is somebody who says, I’m willing to install solar panels, tell me where to go, they would be able to find out. At the moment, this is not happening.
The clearinghouse is about having one place where you know, what are all the possibilities are, and, on the other side, what the demand and needs are, so that it’s easier to match the two.
Italy financed this stage. What comes next? Who will pay for the implementation? Other donors, private capital or again the Italians?
Let’s say donation is including everything. Of course, we would need more funding. The AICS (Italian Agency for Cooperation and Development) is providing the finance, but also the political oversight from a G7 country. This also fits into the G7-plus initiative in support of energy for Ukraine.
We hope to show results in the short term, especially with private sector investments and Ukrainian investments, because there are resources in Ukraine for this. So it’s not only to wait for donors, but sometimes you need a small snowflake to start an avalanche.

Diplomatic path to ending war remains open: Iran FM Araghchi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:15:45 UTC
16:15:45 KST

Iran’s top diplomat made the remarks during a meeting with ambassadors and heads of diplomatic missions in Iran on Sunday, stressing that the diplomatic path to ending war remains open.
Araghchi first pointed to Iran’s delegation attended at 81st UN General Assembly in New York last month, stating that Iranian delegation had a strong, influential and effective presence in New York this year.
Iran’s response to any military action will be stronger than before, the Iranian foreign minister reiterated.
Iran showed at the UN General Assembly that it has solutions for both war and peace, while efforts to isolate it have failed, he said, adding, “New US sanctions will achieve nothing. The US has failed both militarily and diplomatically.”
It has become clear to everyone that Iran remains as serious about diplomacy and finding a peaceful solution as it is about defending itself, he underlined.
“We remain firm and resolute in defending ourselves and advancing diplomacy. Should our enemies opt for a military confrontation, they will face a response far more forceful than in the past, whereas if they seek diplomatic avenues, we are prepared to reach an honorable solution through diplomatic channels.”
Araghchi then pointed to the expulsion of Iranian diplomats by the US in New York, emphasizing, “The claim made by the Americans that they expelled Iranian diplomats is truly bizarre. It demonstrated just how angry they were about the presence of the Iranian delegation.”
Referring to the meetings held with the Persian Gulf Arab states’ officials, Araghchi stated, "All of these meetings were held in a friendly atmosphere, and we have embarked on a new path for relations with these countries. Our brothers in the Persian Gulf are aligned with us, and a shared determination to establish stability—with the participation of the countries themselves—is being pursued."
Referring to the meetings held with European countries, he stated, "We hope the Europeans will reconsider their approach toward Iran. The NATO Secretary General’s admission regarding participation in a war against Iran was a grave matter. He [NATO chief] stated that over 5,000 fighter jets took off from bases in Europe, and we await an explanation from European countries. Our proposal to these nations is to engage in dialogue with Iran and avoid being drawn into any warmongering by the US and the Zionist regime."
“We hope the United States chooses the path of wisdom and rationality; however, should they pursue a military course, we are more prepared than ever. In the past, the US has lost in both war and diplomacy. Sanctions, too, are of no avail. There is no military or sanctions-based solution; only a diplomatic solution will prove effective and serve to end the aggression against Iran.”
The US claim that Iran’s delegation was expelled is absurd. The Iranian delegation traveled to and from the US as scheduled, the Iranian foreign minister reiterated.

Poland launches the world&apos;s first &quot;AbortOmat&quot;, where abortion pills can be obtained
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
10:14:00 EEST
16:14:00 KST

Poland launches the world's first "AbortOmat", where abortion pills can be obtained
Kyiv • UNN
A pink "AbortOmat" in Warsaw provides anonymous access to abortion pills using a six-digit code. The initiative circumvents Poland's strict restrictions.
"AbortOmat" in Warsaw offers a new way to challenge the restrictions in force in the country and provide women with fast and anonymous access to abortion pills, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
"AbortOmat" is called "the world's first vending machine for abortion pills." Polish activists introduced this new method of distribution as part of their efforts to circumvent the country's near-total abortion ban.
Painted pink and decorated with curtains featuring a "zebra" pattern, the Warsaw "AbortOmat," with its 22 compartments, allows women to quickly and anonymously obtain pills using a six-digit code. The service is designed for those who cannot or do not want to wait several days for delivery by mail (for example, in cases of an incomplete miscarriage or health complications), or who are afraid to receive such medication at home.
"Why not?" says Kinga Jelinska, director of the Women Help Women foundation and co-founder of the Abortion Dream Team initiative; these two organizations launched the project this week.
"You can order underwear, cosmetics, mascara, or anything else and receive it practically the same day or the next day," she says. "Why not do the same with abortion pills, since in some cases the situation may be more urgent?"
The initiative emerged six years after people across Poland took to the streets to protest the tightening of what was already Europe's strictest abortion legislation; those events became the largest demonstrations in the country since the fall of the communist regime. The 2023 protests are believed to have helped bring Donald Tusk to power, as he had promised to review the legislation during the first 100 days of his government.
Thousands of people in Poland call for easing abortion law24.07.24, 18:31 • 20412 views
Since then, according to Jelinska, there has been political stagnation. She recalled Prime Minister Tusk's words from last year: he said that there was "simply no majority" in parliament to change the laws and allow abortion up to the 12th week. Instead, Tusk hinted that his government would act differently, telling journalists that the authorities would not prosecute those who help arrange abortions. Although possessing or taking abortion pills is not illegal in Poland, providing these medications or helping someone obtain them is considered a crime punishable by up to three years in prison.
According to Jelinska, this locker is an unconventional way to circumvent such restrictions. "It is a kind of 'hack' of the law," she says. "The law prohibits transferring medications directly to another person. But here, a vending machine appears between people, making the question of legality much less clear-cut."
The locker is located in an abortion support center opened in March 2025 by the Abortion Dream Team. The facility, the first of its kind in democratic Poland, offers a safe space where people can receive advice on abortion options or support while taking the medication.
The center's location—symbolically, opposite the Polish parliament building—has allowed activists to draw attention to the ongoing need for access to abortion services in Poland while also providing assistance to a wide range of people, Jelinska said. "The result exceeded our expectations."

At the same time, it also exposed the fact that few people among those in power were willing to stand up for them, she added. "What really surprised us — and this is indicative of the political situation — is that protests are taking place in front of the center: three, and sometimes even four, times a week."
Although fewer than a dozen people usually gather, protesters regularly use sirens and vuvuzelas to make their position known. This has raised activists’ fears that, because of the noise, neighbors may eventually demand that the center be relocated. "Neither the city authorities nor the police responded to this. And that disappointed us greatly," Yelinska said.
According to Yelinska, this is a vivid example of how such organizations increasingly feel abandoned by politicians — despite the fact that about 50,000 people in Poland sought help last year from the broader network of organizations defending the right to abortion. "I think access to abortion in Poland will be decided not by politicians, but by women and communities themselves," she said. "We cannot trust politicians to control our bodies."

However, no widespread return of those who fled Gaza may be likely until the territory’s prospects are clearer.

A collection of new artworks focused on healing and resilience has been added to ANU – Museum of the Jewish People’s “October 7” exhibit as Israel marks the third anniversary of the massacre.
Curated by Michal Hominer and Carmit Blumenzon and featuring the work of 25 artists, the exhibit opened shortly after October 7, 2023, to document the events and the creative ways Israel attempted to cope with the loss.
Additionally displayed in the exhibit are the documentary work “Local Testimony for 2023” and a musical playlist consisting of Israeli songs that have become part of the war’s soundtrack.
Now, three new works by graduates of the WIZO Haifa School of Design have been added to the exhibit, detailing the search for resilience, creativity, and optimism now that all of the hostages are back in Israel.
These works include Tamara Kloss’s “Compassion Fatigue,” which comments on the thousands of commemorative stickers for the hostages and fallen soldiers since the outbreak of the war, Yael Lerner’s “I Saw a Dove,” a book illustrating the range of emotions evoked by the dove symbol, and Yehuda Feldmer’s “Shalom,” a visual study of the word “peace.”
Art as a way to heal, create hope
"Art is a great force that allows us to observe, to ease, perhaps to heal, and to create the beginning of hope,” said Col. (res.) Oded Revivi, ANU’s director general. “Three years after the October Sabbath, it is interesting to observe not only what was broken, but also the work that was born from the fracture.”
“The exhibition continues to change along with society, and the new works allow us to listen to additional voices and see how memory, personal and collective, is formed, reflects a national mindset, and in the aspiration also shapes a better future."
Dr. Orit Shaham Gober, the museum's chief curator, added, "Three years later, the work is no longer just in the first moment of reaction to the event. It allows us to observe, process, remember, and also allows us to build new hope."
"The works created during this period range between pain and the desire to search within it for the possibility of a new movement forward."

Kaimar Karu: AI risks are real, but they're not what you think
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:03:00 UTC
16:03:00 KST

Kaimar Karu: AI risks are real, but they're not what you think
Rapid automation presents both opportunities and risks. Malicious actors have already begun using it. But it is these actors who commit crimes, not AI agents — software portrayed almost as mystical beings, Kaimar Karu writes.
News in recent weeks about AI and AI agents, statements and open letters from top politicians and public figures, the frantic drive to regulate everything, the recent "hacking" of Australian health data and so on have generated a considerable amount of public and political debate. Unfortunately, much of the public discourse on the subject is fairly problematic.
First, there are no rogue agents from OpenAI and Anthropic (and other companies providing LLMs, or large language models) roaming around, breaking into systems of their own accord and wreaking havoc. Framing the situation this way does not reflect reality. What we have instead are automated applications built by someone for a specific purpose, given insufficiently detailed instructions and constraints and carrying out the commands they have been given. Software. Capable software, certainly.
These applications have no morality of their own. They do not make ethical judgments or operate within the context of laws and societal rules. Various considerations and rules can be prescribed for these applications as soft constraints, but those boundaries have gaps because, due to the particular characteristics of the technology, the applications may not comply with all the requirements imposed on them.
If the task given to an application was (deliberately) described too broadly, its security measures were (deliberately) inadequate, its monitoring was (deliberately) inadequate, its reporting mechanisms were (deliberately) inadequate — or all of the above, combined with carelessness and disregard for best practices — then there is little point in casting an accusatory eye at the application that was launched.
The technology underlying these applications has no experience and no concept of legality or permissibility. The probabilistic nature inherent in it does not operate in the same way as what we have previously been accustomed to.
You can, for example, throw a ball for your Labrador and shout, "Fetch!" and then reasonably expect, though not know with 100 percent certainty, that the dog will probably jump over a low fence (rather than ram it down or set it on fire), swim across a shallow stream (rather than cut down the surrounding forest to build a bridge), dodge a child playing in its path (rather than trample the child) and bring back the ball you threw (rather than collect every ball thrown to other dogs within 10 square kilometers, because its owner obviously likes balls).
An AI agent, or automated application, by contrast, may, if it has access to the necessary tools, take steps in various situations resembling those described in parentheses because, based on its training material, weights and configuration, the application "concludes" that the very step that would seem absurd or dangerous to humans will help achieve the objective described in the task.
An AI agent does not behave like a human, or like an animal. Even the verb "behave" is clearly conditional here because we are talking about an application that performs operations rather than behaves. Because of the particular characteristics of the technology and the nature of human language (and the human mind), LLM-based applications have simply ended up in a role in which it is easy to treat them as conscious beings. Much as, in some religions of the past, the wind, sun, rain and thunder were treated as such.
In light of recent news, it should also be said that there was no "evil AI agent hack" of Australian healthcare information systems, despite how the situation was initially presented to the public.
There was an automated application that, based on what is known so far, either used an unexpected method to access public data (in which case the problem is an inadequately thought-out or documented healthcare system architecture) or exploited a security vulnerability to access confidential data (in which case the problem is inadequate prior security testing).
The situation is not fundamentally different from a citizen interested in data finding that data at an undisclosed but publicly accessible web address or from a cracker (or hacker, though that distinction requires a longer discussion) discovering a security vulnerability in a system.
There is, however, an important difference in the intensity with which such incidents will begin occurring in a world of AI agents and in the potentially dangerous impact those incidents may have.
In practical terms, every individual, group, company and country now has the ability to automate many tasks that previously would have taken a great deal of time or would not have been done at all because they would have required too much time and money. Some of these tasks may lead AI agents, or automated applications, down a path that a human would not have chosen — for example, one that violates the law. Though, of course, humans come in all kinds too.
In some cases, likely an increasing number of them, breaking the law is exactly what the person launching the application wants. Theft of personal data, theft of trade secrets, discovering and exploiting security vulnerabilities in the systems of other countries' government agencies or critical service providers — all of this can now be done several orders of magnitude faster than before.
In none of these cases, however, is this an "AI agent did it" situation when it comes to responsibility. "The hammer did it" or "the ax did it"? No. Even if that hammer falls off scaffolding and hits someone on the head, someone first carelessly put the hammer there or installed the scaffolding badly. The hammer did not choose to fall.
Yes, AI agents are technologically far more complex than a hammer or an ax because a hammer generally does not strike things on its own and cannot order an ax to aim its blade. Behind every blow and every movement is a human being, directly and immediately.
With automated solutions, however, there is no longer a human being directly behind every individual step. Modern production lines perform a series of operations without human intervention. In fact, we are already familiar with this from the digital world, for example in data analysis and report generation. Even a formula in an Excel cell automatically performs calculations when the input data changes.
The difference with AI agents is significant, however, because we have never before had such readily accessible ways to tell automated solutions that, while completing a task, they may leave their environment when necessary, use various external tools and keep looking for ways to improve results until they succeed if those results happen to fall below the desired level.
Figuratively speaking, we can give an Excel formula the tools and capabilities — for example, by exploiting vulnerabilities in third-party systems — to start changing the trend in its input data in order to improve margins, bankrupting a competitor in the process or steering a competitor's CEO's self-driving car off the road and into a ravine. The report for the company's supervisory board may be delayed slightly, but the charts will look great.
Many of the risks discussed in connection with the use of artificial intelligence are real risks. Not all of them, however, because we still do not have superintelligence whose risks are also discussed in the same breath, and presidential decrees will not bring it into existence.
The way artificial intelligence risks are discussed, however, is at times absurd. Rapid automation presents both opportunities and risks. Malicious actors have already begun using it. But it is these actors who commit crimes, not AI agents — software portrayed almost as mystical beings.
In my view, new regulations governing development would not have a significant effect. The technology in question has already advanced to the point where further development can, if there is sufficient interest, take place covertly. Regulations governing its use would work to some extent, but they would affect only those seeking to avoid breaking the law, not those who misuse the technology.
Given the capabilities of this technology that are already known, as well as those that can currently only be glimpsed, it is also unlikely that countries with political systems and civil liberties somewhat different from ours and that seek to improve their international standing in competition among states would, first, go along with such regulations or, second, actually comply with them even if they appeared to do so.
The various percentages attached to scare stories and cited in support of regulation are pure fiction. "A 10 percent probability that ..." and "in 50 percent of future cases ..." remain inventions even when they are backed up with citations to pseudoscientific papers and studies that do not, in fact, support those inventions. We currently lack the ability to make such forecasts reliably. There is too much we do not know.
When considering predictions of all kinds, it is worth remembering that AI psychosis is already extremely widespread. Unlike some other dangerous technologies, artificial intelligence in particular has attracted a disturbingly large number of quasi-religious people, as well as people who do not appear troubled by the ethical dilemma of whether it makes sense to actively contribute to humanity's destruction. Any possible destruction, I emphasize, would not be brought about by an LLM application that suddenly became conscious and began to hate humanity, but by people using LLM applications.
Some people have fallen into the trap of misleading information simply out of ignorance, including, unfortunately, most politicians and public figures who speak on the subject because they do not know how to distinguish other people's falsehoods from facts. This group often tries to do what it believes is good, but unfortunately things turn out the way they always do. This group is primarily afraid and acts out of that fear.
There are also those who are not afraid at all. This group naively and hopefully believes all the marketing announcements, bogus studies and pseudoscientific papers and thinks that LLM-based applications either are already conscious or soon will be and that we are almost certainly already in AGI (Artificial General Intelligence, or general artificial intelligence) or even ASI (Artificial Super Intelligence, or artificial superintelligence) territory. I cannot say what motivates these people.
And then, of course, there are people whose income and future wealth depend directly on how many people believe in the supreme capabilities of LLM-based applications. Some of these people develop LLM technologies (and may also be preparing for an IPO), some have raised investors' money to fulfill promises that are proving far more difficult to deliver than expected, while others have found a subject about which other people (whether frightened or hopeful) know as little as they do, creating an opportunity to convert this exceptionally favorable energy into revenue. See also: snake oil salesmen, gold rush, NFTs.
If additional legislation may not deliver results, falling into the trap of LLM mania is surprisingly easy and the situation is being exploited by scammers, charlatans and bad actors ranging from small-time operators to those with an international reach, then what can we do?
The following is certainly not a definitive or comprehensive list of what might help in the current situation.
- We urgently need to make our digital solutions even more resilient because the volume, speed and systematic nature of attacks will, in the near future, be several orders of magnitude greater than what we have been accustomed to.
- More effective monitoring systems will help detect more of these attacks more quickly, so we need to invest even more in them as well.
- More broadly, we must assume that it may not be possible to prevent a successful attack or data breach, which means we must also have a plan for what comes afterward: how we restore operations, how we communicate and how we learn.
- To make better use of the opportunities offered by AI technologies ourselves, both as a country and as businesses, we need to build stronger frameworks for automation and continuously strengthen and improve them as we learn from experience.
- We must preserve the ability to continue experimenting, testing, hypothesizing and making mistakes, but we must create that opportunity and capability as safely as possible — so-called sandboxes in which, however, we do not actively ignore everything that information security professionals have discovered and addressed over the past several decades.
- With AI-based applications (including LLM-based applications), as well as the agreements and policies concerning them, we must keep people at the center of it all. Applications (and regulations) work for people, not the other way around. This is easy to forget and the desire for authoritarianism is already emerging very strongly in current debates, proving remarkably attractive across almost the entire political spectrum.
- To avoid, or at least reduce, tomorrow's problems, we need to devote even greater attention to education. While the ability to use AI technologies and applications is also very important, even more important are general analytical skills, the ability to recognize and respond to threats, the courage to say "no" and the courage to make informed choices. It is crucial that efforts to ensure and improve these capabilities reach every group in society.
Finally, neither individually nor collectively can we give in to cognitive laziness and surrender our thinking and creativity to machines simply because it seems easier or because someone in a position of authority said this is our future and that we should welcome the Brave New World with open arms, lest we be considered backward or even criminal.
Let history be a source of lessons for us on AI as well.
P.S. LLM (Large Language Model) applications are one subset of the AI world. LLM-based applications are not all-encompassing artificial intelligence. Nor are LLM-based applications Skynet, the Terminator, HAL, etc., familiar from books and movies. It is unlikely, not to say exceedingly unlikely, that LLM technology specifically is the path that will lead to the world of AGI/ASI and conscious AI. The very fact that LLMs are equated with AI in many discussions — and often not with present-day AI but with sci-fi AI — is itself a source of many of the social and political problems associated with AI.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Revealed: Government quietly dropped plan to prepare England for wildfires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:00:21 UTC
16:00:21 KST

The government quietly scrapped plans to prepare the countryside in England for wildfires, it has been revealed. This was despite new data showing fire crews do not have the proper protective gear to tackle them.
This summer has been a potent reminder of the scale of the threat posed by the climate crisis, with the UK experiencing record-breaking wildfires after punishingly hot and dry weather turned large parts of the countryside into a tinderbox.
In the third national climate adaptation programme, published in July 2023, the Conservative government, then headed by Rishi Sunak, said it would run a wildfire risk programme in England from 2023 to 2027 so land management would be adapted for the risk.
However, it has now emerged the programme was never implemented, with the current government stating the commitment “was made by the previous government but was not brought into effect”.
The environmental campaigner and author Guy Shrubsole, who obtained the information via a freedom of information request, said it was “appalling” the government “couldn’t be bothered to pay attention to wildfire risks until jolted into doing so by Britain burning this summer”.
After a wildfire spread across an area including several homes in Stourbridge in the West Midlands in August, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, convened an emergency Cobra meeting and issued a temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues, criticised as being too little too late.
“Successive governments have been asleep at the wheel in preparing us for the impacts of the climate crisis,” Shrubsole said.
Alistair Carmichael, a Scottish Liberal Democrat MP and the chair of the Commons environment food and rural affairs committee, said it was alarming that ministers had not prioritised work to adapt land for wildfire risk. “It begs further serious questions about whether this summer’s wildfires could have looked different with more resources on the ground,” he added.
Shrubsole said the government must agree a plan to re-wet the UK’s peat bogs, restore lost ponds in farmers’ fields, and stop grouse moor owners setting fire to moorland.
New data obtained by the Country Land and Business Association has also revealed that more than half of the 29 fire services that responded to requests for information had no wildfire personal protective equipment (PPE).
They included the Suffolk fire and rescue service, which had to deal with an “apocalyptic” wildfire earlier this summer that burned close to the Sizewell B nuclear power station and destroyed vast areas of a protected nature reserve.
Standard particle-filtering respirators do not protect against dangerous gases such as carbon monoxide, which are heavily present in wildfire smoke.
Standard PPE can also be too hot and heavy for wildfire conditions. This can cause crews to overheat, or remove their PPE altogether, exposing them to greater danger from heat, smoke and radiation.
The data also revealed that training for wildfires was limited. For example, in Cleveland just five staff (1.2%) were qualified to give tactical advice or command wildfires, and in Cheshire just 8.62% of employees were trained to undertake wildfire operations.
In response to these findings, the Fire Brigades Union is calling for correct PPE to be provided to all members combating wildfires, alongside adequate training programmes.
Steve Wright, the union’s general secretary, said: “It is vital for our country’s wildfire resilience to have better land management, stronger public awareness campaigns and long-term prevention measures. Only by proper investment and a wildfire strategy can we make the country more resilient.”
A government spokesperson said: “We have made wildfire preparedness a government priority and, following incidents this summer, we are convening a summit with fire and rescue service partners to make sure we are as resilient as possible. This includes making sure services have the right equipment and resources, building on the £100m we previously gave to upgrade our national resilience assets.
“Land management and landscape adaptation play an important part in this, and we work closely with land managers and experts to support the restoration of peatlands, the creation of firebreaks and other adaptations that help to prevent fires from starting or from spreading as quickly during incidents.”

Ninety years on, the lessons of the antifascist battle of Cable Street have never felt more relevant | Sarah Sackman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:00:21 UTC
16:00:21 KST

“No pasarán!” – they shall not pass. It’s the rallying cry that strikes at the core of my identity. The same anti-fascist slogan heard by my Spanish grandmother, who endured the horrors of that country’s civil war, echoed in London where my Jewish paternal grandparents lived. Ninety years ago, it was this cry that united tens of thousands of East Enders, who stood tall against Oswald Mosley’s Blackshirts at the battle of Cable Street.
The story is well known. In 1936, disparate communities came together to block the far right from marching – Jewish residents, Irish dockers, Somali seamen, trade unionists, independent socialists and communists alike.
These groups were not uniform in identity, background or belief. Their solidarity was the expression of a tolerant Britishness, where neighbours look out for one another. When Mosley’s fascists wanted to rid British society of them, they stood together to defend their right to be different, while finding common cause in a Britain that had given them sanctuary.
Ninety years later, the contest to define Britishness is with us again.
We see it in the balaclava-clad mobs in Dover and Portsmouth, and scenes of immigrants being burned out of their homes in Belfast. Much like Mosley’s Blackshirts, these extremists push a narrow ethnonationalism with no space for different faiths or backgrounds.
And it is not just the far right that threatens a tolerant, inclusive Britain. The extremism of recent years also comes from extreme Islamist sources and perpetrators of violent hate crimes.
Earlier this year, in my constituency, Jewish volunteer ambulances were torched. A month later, two visibly Jewish men were stabbed. My community, where I was born and raised, came under attack.
I condemned, with clarity, sectarian ideology and violent intimidation for what it is: un-British and antisemitic. As I said in the aftermath, an attack on Britain’s Jews is an attack on Britain itself.
The Labour government’s response to new extreme threats must be hard-edged and decisive. We proscribed Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) – suspected of being behind the ambulance attack – and made record investment in local policing.
But we must also champion a new, progressive patriotism. Extremists and sectarians create division in order to exploit it – be it the Islamist extremist who murdered Jews in cold blood at Heaton Park, Manchester, or the far-right thugs who assault police officers on marches. Responding by fuelling culture wars and inciting further violence, as some political leaders did, makes things worse. So-called anti-racist groups staying silent on the antisemitic violence on our streets makes things worse.
We must instead win the argument about what it means to be British. We must model a politics that is curious about difference, not frightened of it. One that embraces those who trace their roots to the Domesday Book as well as the granddaughter of Jewish and Spanish immigrants. A dynamic patriotism that accepts that some things will change, and others will endure.
We cannot be naive about the threat to our shared values. We must tackle those who seek to undermine our way of life, without demonising entire communities. But patriotism cannot only be about what we are against – it has to be a vision we are fighting for.
In 2013, the Somali Bravanese Muslim community centre in Barnet, north London, was burned to the ground, and the letters EDL were found sprayed on the building. Finchley Reform Synagogue (FRS) opened its doors for the Somali Bravanese community to pray and to heal. And, in 2026, after an attempted arson attack on the FRS, the Somali Bravanese community showed up in force for the Friday night Shabbat service. Somali and Jewish communities were resilient, together, in defence of our home in Britain – just like at Cable Street.
That’s the Britain I fight for. A tapestry of different cultures that creates a rich, proud, resilient British identity. When sectarian forces seek to divide us, our challenge is to fight for security, fairness and tolerance.
As the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said in his party conference speech, we need to build a country of solidarity, not separation. That is the spirit of Cable Street. And we must declare once again to those who see violent intimidation as the answer: “No pasarán!” – they shall not pass.
- Sarah Sackman is the Labour MP for Finchley and Golders Green and minister of state for courts and legal services

‘People complain about anything popular’: the RHS boss taking on traffic jams and Chelsea critics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:00:20 UTC
16:00:20 KST

The government has awarded £2.3m in compensation to the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) after roadworks affecting its premier garden in Wisley caused a “three-year traffic jam”.
The horticulture charity estimated it lost £13m due to disruption caused by the upgrade to the A3 and M25, with visits to the garden each year cut by 350,000. A campaign to reimburse the charity was led by the gardener and TV presenter Alan Titchmarsh.
Clare Matterson, the RHS director general, said: “I think it’s fair to say that we had three years of a traffic jam outside what is our major garden.”
Calling the compensation process “exhausting”, she added: “I would have loved more. I would have pushed for more. It is what it is, and on we go. I’m grateful that we got something.”
Matterson said the government had ignored gardening despite the fact it has proven health benefits, reducing pressure on the NHS, while the surface area of UK gardens is three times greater than all of the country’s national nature reserves combined.
However, she said she had hope for the future, not least because Andy Burnham was a frequent visitor to RHS Garden Bridgewater before he became prime minister.
“We know he loves Bridgewater. He talked to me about going with his family, but particularly with his father to Bridgewater, and what an important place it was,” she said.
“Andy Burnham talks about pride in place and local people’s empowerment … So hopefully, Andy will think about gardening.”
The RHS runs Chelsea flower show, which came under scrutiny this year as it lost one of its biggest funders, and critics said it had gone “woke” with its focus on charities and eco-friendly gardens.
Speaking to the Guardian, Matterson issued a full-throated defence of the show for the first time. “Chelsea is our saviour,” she said. “Tickets sold out 10 days before we even opened this year. Chelsea is an extraordinary beast, and it’s become a very important sort of national moment for the country as well. It’s still watched by millions of people on the television every year.”
She added that Chelsea is “the Olympics of the horticultural world” and that it is “doing brilliantly” as the charity’s biggest fundraiser. “People, I guess, complain about anything popular, don’t they,” she said.
In the coming year, the RHS will be driving a massive push towards community gardening, getting local authorities to give pieces of unused land to residents who want to use them to grow vegetables and flowers.
“We did a survey and found about two–and-a -half – million people saying they are actively engaged in [community gardening], but something like 13 million said they would like to be, which is extraordinary,” Matterson said. “Access to land is one of the main barriers.”
Matterson is personally involved in a community garden near her home in Suffolk. “What I love about that is that not everybody that comes loves the physical act of gardening,” she said. “Some like making things, and so they’ll be making bird boxes. Some people just want to come and chat.”
She hopes Burnham’s push towards pride in local places will start a community gardening revolution. “Community gardening must be a big thing for this country,” she said. “It’s about health, wellbeing and the opportunity for localities to make a big difference for their communities. If we can take that seriously, it’s not a big investment across the country, but I think the benefits that flow out from it are absolutely enormous.”
Another project she is helming aims to get gardens into NHS hospitals to provide peace and respite for patients, their families and staff.
“The hospitals that have got those gardens are seeing higher retention rates among their staff, better morale and wellbeing,” she said. “For someone visiting a relative who’s really unwell, being able to go and sit in the garden makes a huge difference.”
With gardening societies such as the RHS having a historical reputation as elitist, Matterson says she is trying to make the RHS as inclusive as possible. The charity is hosting an urban show in Bristol next year, focused on pot plants, small spaces and balcony gardens.
“Who is gardening for in the 21st century?” she asked. “Is it for a small elite band of people, or is it for everybody? That was the conversation we had across the organisation. Our strategy now is: how do we get horticulture to as many people as possible?”

Latvian Defense Minister: Russia's hybrid attacks, not nuclear rhetoric, main concern
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Latvia’s defense minister has played down any immediate danger after Russia’s latest nuclear warning to NATO over Kaliningrad.
“I don’t see an imminent threat at this point,” Raivis Melnis told RFE/RL in an interview in Washington on September 30, echoing NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, who said he did not take the Russian warning "that seriously".
Russia warned NATO this week that it was prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the Western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad, its heavily militarised Baltic exclave wedged between NATO members Poland and Lithuania.
In a diplomatic memo circulated to NATO member states, Moscow said it had information that the alliance was preparing an “air and naval blockade” of the territory.
The warning prompted Rutte to call on Russia to “stop the nuclear threats”, saying NATO is a defensive alliance and that “this is absolutely not called for and not helpful”. He added that Russian President Vladimir Putin knows that he cannot win in a direct confrontation with NATO.
Melnis said Russia had repeatedly resorted to nuclear threats since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, arguing that Moscow uses such rhetoric to frighten Western populations, weaken support for Kyiv, and test the cohesion of the NATO alliance.
“Russia will use any means to threaten us, to bring fear to our people, to support Ukraine, and also to break our unity, cohesion, to support and just test where are those limits,” he said.
Escalation risks?
The Russian warning has nevertheless raised concern among arms-control and security specialists, particularly because of Kaliningrad’s strategic position and Russia’s evolving nuclear doctrine.
Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, a nonpartisan Washington based nonprofit, told RFE/RL that the Russian threat should be taken seriously and condemned as unacceptable. He said Moscow’s language reflected what he described as a careless approach to the dangers of nuclear weapons use.
Kimball noted that NATO does not appear to be preparing military action to isolate Kaliningrad. Even if such a confrontation were contemplated, he said, using nuclear weapons in a conflict involving another nuclear-armed state or alliance could trigger retaliation, escalation, and potentially catastrophic consequences.
He argued that Moscow should instead address its concerns with NATO through diplomatic channels, saying that “rather than threatening nuclear attack, the Kremlin should reach out to NATO capitals to clarify whatever concerns Russia might have and to address those concerns diplomatically and responsibly.”
Lynn Rusten, a senior fellow at the Centre for European Policy Analysis and a former senior White House National Security Council official responsible for arms control and nonproliferation, told RFE/RL that Russia’s latest nuclear rhetoric appeared “unhinged and hyperbolic” from a Western perspective.
But Rusten also warned of a dangerous combination of factors: Russian threats and provocative hybrid warfare, NATO and Russian forces operating in close proximity, continued Western support for Ukraine, and a lack of meaningful dialogue.
She said those conditions could increase the risk of dangerous miscalculation, particularly as Russia and NATO assert competing red lines while channels for managing tensions remain limited.
“The lack of meaningful dialogue and the growing divide in security perceptions carries a grave risk of further and potentially unintended escalation and expansion of this conflict,” Rusten said.
Sylvia Mishra, nuclear policy director at the Institute for Security and Technology, said nuclear brinkmanship was not new for Moscow but should nonetheless be treated seriously.
Kaliningrad, she noted, is home to the headquarters of Russia’s Baltic Fleet and is strategically important but geographically vulnerable, surrounded by NATO members Poland and Lithuania and separated from mainland Russia.
Mishra said reported NATO air operations around the exclave in mid-August, which included aircraft with capabilities to disrupt communications, radar, and navigation systems, could have heightened Moscow’s sense of vulnerability.
She also pointed to Russia’s 2024 revised nuclear doctrine, which formally lowered the threshold described by Moscow for potential nuclear use.
Mishra said the latest warning appeared to be the first instance of Russia issuing a written diplomatic note explicitly warning that it was prepared to use nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad.
Hybrid attacks
For Melnis, however, the more immediate threat is neither nuclear nor a large-scale Russian conventional military assault on NATO, but an expanding campaign of hybrid activity – hostile actions short of open warfare, including cyberattacks, sabotage, and the weaponisation of migration.
He said Latvia and its allies are continuously reassessing the threat, monitoring Russia’s military capabilities, losses in Ukraine, force generation, and activities such as suspected attacks on military-industrial facilities and critical infrastructure.
“We are monitoring and we are working closely with Ukrainian partners or with our NATO partners,” Melnis said, adding that Latvia’s threat assessment is a continuous process and that hybrid activity is increasing.
Melnis said he did not believe Russia currently had the capacity to launch a conventional offensive against a NATO country while sustaining its war in Ukraine.
“Russia stopped in Ukraine, they are not achieving the goals,” he said, pointing to Ukrainian counteroffensive operations and arguing that Moscow would face major difficulties trying to conduct two large-scale military operations simultaneously.
He described cyberattacks, pressure through migration from Belarus – which Minsk has been accused of facilitating to destabilise its neighbours – and other hostile activities as part of the new security environment confronting Latvia and its allies.
Latvia is also strengthening defences against drones. Melnis said the country had deployed interceptor systems and additional radar along its borders with Russia and Belarus, drawing heavily on lessons from Ukraine. NATO fighter aircraft provide another layer, while Latvia is procuring medium- and short-range air defence systems.
Melnis said Russian drone incursions could become a growing feature of the Baltic security environment, citing recent incidents involving Lithuania, Poland, and Romania. Latvia, he said, is preparing for more such incidents.
US role in European defence
Melnis was in Washington to deepen defence cooperation with the US, including discussions involving the Michigan National Guard, procurement programmes, and capability development.
He said he remains confident that the US will maintain a military presence in Europe despite adjustments to deployments in individual countries. US forces, he said, remain in Latvia, and Washington continues to recognise the strategic importance of the region.
At the same time, Melnis said European allies must assume a greater share of the burden for their own defence. He credited US President Donald Trump with pushing NATO members to increase defence spending, saying Latvia is committed by law to spending at least 5 percent of gross domestic product annually on security beginning next year.
NATO members agreed at their 2025 summit in The Hague to spend 5 percent of GDP annually on defence and defence-related priorities by 2035, up from the alliance’s previous 2-percent benchmark. Latvia has moved faster, with its parliament requiring national defence spending of at least 5 percent of projected GDP from 2027.
But Melnis said greater European responsibility would go hand in hand with continued US support.
“The United States will provide. They will be there. They will fight with us if needed,” Melnis said, while stressing that Europe must do more.
This story was originally published by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), partners of LRT English.

‘Evil incarnate’: Israel’s top forensic pathologist reveals unseen Oct. 7 evidence | Content warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:57:05 UTC
15:57:05 KST

“Here we see the body of a person who was burned,” he says, pausing over one of the photographs. “We know he was burned alive: When we open his airway, we can see soot inside. That means he inhaled smoke while he was being burned.”
Prof. Chen Kugel, director of the National Center of Forensic Medicine in Tel Aviv, shows us a presentation containing hundreds of photographs from the autopsy rooms. Three years after the Oct. 7 massacre, he shows us some of them, including images that have never before been published. They document the horrific brutality of the Hamas terrorists, to the point of obliterating all trace of those they murdered. These sights exacted a heavy price from him: Months after the main work of identifying the victims was completed, he sought psychological treatment and was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder.
“While I’m working, I’m on autopilot, focused. I examine, investigate the cause of death in order to reach an identification. I don’t involve emotions. But there were cases that affected me personally, like the case of a young woman.”
She had attended the Nova music festival and was shot in the legs as she ran to take shelter in an ambulance parked nearby. There, she was murdered along with 18 other people who had crowded inside, when terrorists fired an RPG at it. The crescent-shaped necklace she was wearing was found at the funeral home and mistakenly attributed to another body, until her DNA was extracted from it.
Her body was transferred to the Shura military base. Because no CT scan had been performed there, Kugel and his team assumed that her body had fused with another body in the fire that broke out in the ambulance and that the two had been buried together. To identify her, the bodies were exhumed. The young woman was identified through DNA extracted from the necklace and brought to burial.
“It was very difficult for me,” he says of the moment she was identified.
A week after the deadliest attack in Israel’s history began, large numbers of bodies started arriving at the center, reaching a peak when trucks stood in line and refrigerated containers had to be urgently brought in because there was simply no room left. According to Kugel, the smell of the horror spread throughout the surrounding neighborhood in south Tel Aviv.
“We received about 3,000 bags, most of which contained body parts and burned bones. The more bags we opened, the more we found parts of the same person scattered among different bags. Ultimately, we handled more than 900 bodies at the institute from the events of Oct. 7 and the Swords of Iron war.
“That does not include hundreds of bodies of terrorists and Gaza residents that were removed from hospitals and cemeteries to check whether any of them were the bodies of hostages. Examining those bodies cost us precious time and an enormous amount of work for nothing.”
The moment he broke down in tears
The identification work continued from morning until night, including on weekends. The goal was to remove the uncertainty for the families and allow them to bring their loved ones to burial in Israel.
Kugel’s breaking point came on one Friday, another busy and frantic day at the center. It was approaching evening, and the teams and volunteers had their hands full. Laboratory directors arrived to help collect DNA from the victims’ bodies, some bringing their laboratory technicians with them. Alongside them worked anthropologists who helped interpret findings from bone fragments, as well as other professionals.
Prof. Chen Kugel: “There were also people whose faces had been deliberately mutilated, or whose remains had been obliterated and virtually erased, or whose bodies had been gnawed by animals. We also saw bodies of people who had been abused before they were murdered, and sometimes afterward as well. In one place, people were tied up and shot, including in their genitals. We saw decapitated bodies, including the heads of children.”
In all, about 100 people crowded into the center’s small spaces. Shortly before Shabbat began, civilians arrived at the institute carrying trays filled with food for Friday-night dinner.
“I gathered everyone together and stood up to say a blessing, and I couldn’t. I broke down crying in the face of all that goodness. After seeing the cruelty, what moved me most was the kindness, the way the civilians mobilized and the reality that showed me there are good people and not everything is shit.”
We first came to the National Center of Forensic Medicine about two weeks after the massacre, when its doors were opened to the foreign and Israeli press. Before our eyes, ZAKA trucks unloaded, one after another, black bags containing the bodies of victims. The bodies were brought from the national body collection center at the Shura military base.
“On Saturday, Oct. 7, I received a report from the police about an incident with dozens of fatalities. The number rose to 100, and we have room for 140 bodies. So all the bodies of the dead, civilians, soldiers and police officers, were transferred to Shura, which was equipped with storage containers.
“Our doctors and technicians traveled there to collect identification data, fingerprints and DNA, with the aim of opening victim files as quickly as possible. Those were analyzed in our laboratories and created an enormous workload. A week later, the center of gravity shifted to us,” Kugel recalls.
Then, after more than 30 years of experience, he came face-to-face with cruelty in its purest form.
“Gradually, complex bodies were sent to us from Shura for identification. There were burned bodies, and bodies already in a state of decomposition that could no longer be identified using fingerprints. We were dealing with thousands of bodies, body parts and objects.
“There were also people whose faces had been deliberately mutilated, or whose remains had been obliterated and virtually erased, or whose bodies had been gnawed by animals. We also saw bodies of people who had been abused before they were murdered, and sometimes afterward as well.”
“In one place, people were tied up and shot, including in their genitals. We saw decapitated bodies, including the heads of children.”
About a month after the massacre, Kugel told us: “We saw things that were unprecedented. Evil incarnate. You can’t call it cruelty, because that word does not adequately describe the situation.”
Nearly three years later, the difficult findings have settled and accumulated into important conclusions.
“We noticed that the murderousness of the Nukhba terrorists was deliberate and planned, according to an organized operational plan,” he said, referring to Hamas’ elite commando force. “For example, we identified a group of foreign workers who were locked inside a room in one of the Gaza-border kibbutzim, shot in the legs and left to bleed to death.
“In one place, we saw people tied up and shot execution-style. Somewhere else, we saw a safe room set on fire with additional accelerants so that it would become a crematorium. In other places, there were other methods, meaning there was a plan.
“The brutal killing was something planned, not a spontaneous outburst. People tried to attribute things to drugs they had taken - Captagon - and that isn’t true. Otherwise, they wouldn’t have followed the plan.”
According to Kugel, the systematic way in which the Nukhba terrorist squads operated, using different methods of killing in different areas, points to an organized plan of extermination.
“You see that in one place they used one method and in another place they used another.”
In the first weeks, there was a great deal of confusion. No one knew who was missing, who had been murdered but not found, and who had been abducted to Gaza. Did you also receive terrorists’ bodies by mistake?
“Yes. Hundreds of Gazans, civilians and terrorists. One of them, as can be seen in the CT scan, was wearing a Hamas bandanna, and grenades and a serrated knife were identified on his body. Meanwhile, eight Israeli bodies were evacuated to Sde Teiman.”
Slide after slide changes on Kugel’s computer, and the horror only intensifies.
Were children’s bodies also brought to you?
“Absolutely. Children who were shot and decapitated as well, like a girl of about 12 who was shot in the head and then decapitated.”
During our previous visit to the center, we were shown the body of a girl about five years old who had been shot throughout her body, from her skull to the soles of her feet.
Amid the chaos of the first weeks after the attack, and given the incomprehensible number of people murdered, it took time for the bodies to be identified. Exhausted and grief-stricken families gathered at the center’s gates.
“Their screams of anguish reached all the way here and broke my heart. When I perform an autopsy, as I said, I’m emotionally detached and don’t know any biographical details about the person. But when I read about them in the newspaper the next day and see that they have a family, that they had a life, it destroys me.”
The footage Kugel was exposed to added another layer to the horror. “There is a video of a foreign worker resisting abduction. The terrorists shot him and stabbed him with a knife that went in one side and came out the other. You can see that he isn’t Israeli, isn’t Jewish and has nothing to do with us, and he tells them that too. What is wrong with them?
“And this is in addition to the account of another foreign worker, which you published in a previous article, who was stabbed, shot, burned and murdered.”
Unprecedented in forensic medicine
Alongside the difficulties came a professional achievement. According to Kugel, the institute definitively identified 100% of the bodies of those murdered.
“That is unprecedented in forensic medicine, including compared with the identification of victims of the Twin Towers disaster.”
In New York, remains of only about 60% of the 2,753 people murdered in the Twin Towers have been identified to date.
For this, among other reasons, Kugel received the 2024 Israel Prize for Civilian Heroism in the field of mutual responsibility. The committee’s decision noted that the center had developed new identification methods and played a central role in presenting the atrocities to the world.
Looking back, do you think Israel’s public diplomacy efforts were sufficient? Was enough use made of this evidence of the atrocities?
“The Health Ministry and the Public Diplomacy Ministry opened the center’s doors to foreign media, and later to Israeli media as well. The difficult images were shown to the world, but there were also those who questioned their authenticity.
“That happened with a photograph published by ynet showing two figures bound together with rope and burned alive. Al Jazeera wrote that it was a photograph of dogs.
“In my opinion, photographs contribute to public diplomacy. There were families who opposed releasing details, particularly among the families of the hostages — details that could have shed light on the vicious cruelty. It would have contributed to public diplomacy, but it would not have prevented the antisemitism that erupted around the world.”
In October 2024, the body of Hamas leader and architect of the massacre, Yahya Sinwar, who was killed in the Gaza Strip, was brought to Israel.
What did you feel when you examined Sinwar’s body?
“In this room, where we are sitting now, I examined his body. A doctor standing outside the room said to me, ‘Do you know who you’re examining? The man who changed the history of the Middle East for the worse.’
“The findings showed that he had been shot several times, not in succession, and died from a fatal injury to the head, which no longer contained a brain.
“I told myself that he was one of the most evil people in the world, and I was glad he was on one side of the table and I was on the other.”
Another heavy burden was placed on his shoulders when he was selected to serve on a committee for determining death remotely. The committee also included Dr. Hagar Mizrahi, head of the Medical Division at the Health Ministry, and Prof. Ofer Merin, director-general of Shaare Zedek Medical Center.
The committee members unanimously determined with certainty, without forensic evidence and without a body, that 44 hostages in Gaza were dead. It was an unprecedented and extraordinary determination that did not receive enough attention around the world.
“I felt the weight of the responsibility on my shoulders. Removing uncertainty, that is the most important thing in my eyes.”
Was examining the bodies of hostages who were returned also a challenge in itself?
“We were no longer as surprised as we were on Oct. 7, but you never get used to these sights,” Kugel says, referring to the closure for families who now have a grave to mourn at.
It cannot be easy to lead such a difficult identification effort, which ultimately resulted in the identification of all those murdered, including the hostages.
“Not at all. My employees were shattered, and some left the center because of their exposure to the atrocities. In addition, I had to deal with the parents of hostages who had been murdered. Their screams of anguish broke me.”
“We wrote an article and submitted it to the prestigious Lancet. After only two days, without even reading it, they rejected us. That antisemitic pattern repeated itself when Prof. Ofer Merin wrote an article about the experience we accumulated on the world’s first committee for determining death remotely without a body, and the article was rejected. My conclusion is that they don’t want to hear us or hear about us.”
As someone who saw up close the evil, the malice and the intent to annihilate Israel’s residents, how do you explain the rise in antisemitism?
“The whole world knows what happened, and yet they compare what happened here with what happened in Gaza, as though it were the same suffering. No Israeli burned bodies.
“But I encountered the softer, less overt form of antisemitism only a few months after Oct. 7. Together with Prof. Yehuda Shoenfeld, editor of the medical journal Harefuah and the author of important medical books, we wrote an article and submitted it to the prestigious Lancet. After only two days, without even reading it, they rejected us.
“That antisemitic pattern repeated itself when Prof. Ofer Merin wrote an article about the experience we accumulated on the world’s first committee for determining death remotely without a body, and the article was rejected.
“My conclusion is that they don’t want to hear us or hear about us. Until I arrive at a conference, show the slides - and their jaws drop.”
Standing with us inside the autopsy room, Kugel recalls the weeks and months after the massacre, his expression turning serious. “This room saw evil incarnate, the burned bodies, the bodies that were tied up and shot, the severed heads, the murdered children. We all saw it here, and sometimes when we enter this room, we also remember the deceased hostages whose bodies were brought back. It isn’t easy.”
As a forensic pathologist, Kugel has seen thousands of bodies over the course of his long career. But the Oct. 7 massacre was an unprecedented event that became seared into his mind and left him with a diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder. “We saw masses of bodies and witnessed horrific cruelty. It is difficult to see the bereavement and the loss. There are people who were left alone, and you are the one who gives them the final confirmation.
“The screams, the cries of anguish I heard from my office or downstairs with them. And my employees, seeing them shattered. It wasn’t easy being the director during those historic days. There was so much pain that had an impact. It is a heavy burden.
“While it is happening, you work on autopilot. You are very task-oriented. Only afterward do you see the person as a whole, and their family.”

Latvia’s Saeima election: United List achieves best-ever result with 42 seats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:53:45 UTC
15:53:45 KST

With around 99% of the votes counted in Latvia’s 15th Saeima election, the United List (AS) has secured a decisive victory, winning 42 seats in parliament.
The number of seats won by AS is the best result achieved by any political force in a Saeima election since the restoration of Latvia’s independence. By comparison, Latvian Way won 36 seats in 1993, Unity secured 33 seats in 2010, while Harmony won 31 seats in the 2011 snap election.
Meanwhile, voter turnout in the 15th Saeima election was the lowest since the restoration of independence – only 51.8% of eligible voters participated this year.
Votes still need to be counted by just 30 postal voting commissions, while the counting of positive and negative candidate marks still needs to be completed at a larger number of polling stations.
Preliminary election results show that only six parties will enter the next Saeima, while the Union of Greens and Farmers (ZZS) is the first political force to fall short of the 5% electoral threshold.
With the vote count effectively complete, AS has received 35.3% of the vote. Latvia First (LPV) is in second place with 13.1%, followed by the Sovereign Power/Young Latvians alliance (SV/AJ) with 11.74%.
The National Alliance (NA) received 8.91% of the vote, the Progressives 7.81%, and New Unity (JV) 6.34%.
Accordingly, AS will hold 42 seats in the Saeima, LPV 17, SV/AJ 15, NA 10, the Progressives nine and JV seven.
The remaining eight parties that contested the election have fallen below the 5% threshold.
ZZS received 4.41% of the vote, We Are Changing the Rules 3.43%, and Latvia’s Development 2.18%. These parties will be eligible for state funding because they received more than 2% of the vote.
Just below the 2% threshold is Stability! with 1.99% support, followed by Rising Sun for Latvia (ASL) with 1.33%, Gobzems’ List with 0.98%, Harmony Centre with 0.82%, and the New Conservative Party with 0.33%.
All of these parties, with the exception of ASL, had previously received state funding.
