Bosnia votes as pro-Russian politician looms large over race and a stalled EU bid dominate election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:53:37 UTC
15:53:37 KST

Around 3.4 million eligible voters in Bosnia headed to the polls to choose the three members of the country’s multi-ethnic presidency, lawmakers for the national Parliament, and heads of institutions for the country’s two entities.
Polls have now closed in Bosnia’s general election on Sunday, where preliminary results remain unclear, and the country is waiting for further updates in the coming hours to get a clearer picture of the outcome.
Some 3.4 million voters were eligible to choose the three members of the multi-ethnic presidency, national lawmakers, and leaders of the country's two entities: the Muslim-majority Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska.
The complex system of institutions was created by the US-brokered 1995 peace agreement to manage divisions among Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats.
Early reports show voting was delayed at several polling places due to problems with new digital voting technology, which was introduced to address earlier concerns about vote tampering. Bosnia's Election Commission made this decision to prolonge the 7 p.m. voting cutoff at polling stations that experienced problems.
The election comes as many citizens in the multiethnic Balkan state face everyday problems, while some leading politicians stoke the war-era tensions that have kept the country divided since the 1992-95 conflict.
By 3 p.m. around 27% of voters had cast their ballots, according to the commission, a decrease from 35% at the same time during the last national election.
New election security measures
For the first time, authorities were using electronic voter identification and ballot scanning to curb the irregularities and organised manipulation that undermined confidence in earlier elections.
Most of the 75 parties running are organised along ethnic lines. The Bosniak nationalist Party of Democratic Action has campaigned on keeping Bosnia united against Serb separatism, while many Bosnian Croats back ethnic parties such as the local branch of Croatia's ruling Croatian Democratic Union.
Izetbegovic, who was beaten by Becirovic in 2022, is seeking a third term as president of the centre-right SDA, the largest Bosniak party in the nation.
Many disillusioned citizens say politicians use nationalism to avoid tackling real problems like low living standards and the exodus of young people. Mostar voter Ivan Silic said nothing has improved since he first voted and that politicians live well while everyone else's situation stays the same.
Dodik looms large despite not being on the ballot
Despite not being on the ballot, the campaign has been dominated by Milorad Dodik, the pro-Russian, separatist former president of Republika Srpska. Dodik is banned from public office after being convicted of defying the international envoy who oversees the peace agreement.
Fresh from meeting Russia's president Vladimir Putin in Moscow, Dodik leads a party, the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, that is likely to win in Republika Srpska.
At a final rally Friday in Banja Luka, attended by Russia's ambassador, Igor Khalabukov, Dodik declared Bosnia is "dead" and "an impossible country". "It doesn't make any sense," he stressed.
Off the ballot for the first time in almost 30 years, he is still in command and is present across the country's media, says Dragan Bursac, an analyst. In Bursac's view, the ban is not working, and Dodik is exploiting it.
Ethnic tensions continue to rise
Bosnia has been peaceful in recent years, but its politicians have kept ethnic divisions alive. Bosnian Serb leaders such as Dodik have pushed for their entity to break away, raising Western fears of renewed instability.
The Balkan nation remains one of Europe's poorest countries, still recovering from a war that began after it declared independence from Serb-led Yugoslavia and ethnic Serbs took up arms to carve out their own state. That conflict killed more than 100,000 people and displaced millions.
The country is formally seeking European Union membership, but progress has stalled despite EU efforts to push its leaders toward reform.
Major powers continue to influence socio-economic and political life in the small Balkan nation. Russia is holding down the EU's efforts to expand its membership throughout the Balkans, including Bosnia, while continuing to back the Republika Srpska.
While a $1.5 billion pipeline project to import US liquefied natural gas is being pushed by a corporation with ties to the Trump administration as part of the US's efforts to gain influence.
And recently, wartime wounds were reopened by public tributes in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs to Ratko Mladic, the wartime army commander who died in late August while serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes.
Bosnian Serbs regard him as a hero, despite his UN court conviction over the killing of more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica in 1995.
Senior Bosnian Serb officials attended his funeral in Belgrade, drawing sharp EU criticism and angering Bosniak politicians.

Operation Vivaldi Liberates up to 140 Sq Km in Donbas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:51:00 UTC
15:51:00 KST

Ukrainian forces have liberated between 125 and 140 square kilometers of territory during the ongoing Operation “Vivaldi” in the northern Donetsk region, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with Reuters.
Zelensky described the counteroffensive along the Lyman axis as a major tactical success that remains underway, noting that delaying the operation until units were adequately prepared allowed Ukrainian forces to achieve substantial territorial recoveries while minimizing personnel losses.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Vivaldi is a very successful operation. It is not finished yet. As of today, approximately 125 to 140 square kilometers have been liberated,” Zelensky said in comments released by the presidential administration.
“Our military wanted to start this operation a year ago, but at the time it was not sufficiently prepared. Fortunately, we decided to postpone it briefly, and now we have good results and fewer casualties.”
According to Zelensky, Russian casualty rates across the theater surged over the past two to three months from an average of 30,000 to 32,000 personnel monthly – comprising roughly 21,000 to 22,000 killed alongside severely wounded soldiers – up to approximately 42,000 casualties per month.
Lyman operational direction
The territorial gains in the Lyman sector follow consecutive operational phases commanded by Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps.
Recent combat actions in the municipality involved joint clearance operations conducted by the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade alongside border guard detachments, including the 3rd Border Guard Detachment named after Yevheniy Pikus and the 10th “DOZOR” Mobile Border Detachment.
Merz Makes Surprise Kyiv Visit, Pledges 1,000 Drone Interceptors
Operational footage released by corps leadership showed units clearing contested settlements and evacuating captured personnel under continuous enemy observation.
Tactical integration
A foundational element of Operation Vivaldi has been the extensive frontline deployment of unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) and robotic systems operating ahead of maneuver infantry.
During his consultations with operational commanders, Zelensky emphasized that fielding automated robotic complexes in high-threat sectors proved instrumental in breaching defensive belts and preserving Ukrainian personnel.
The operational focus reflects a broader state policy initiated in early 2026 prioritizing the integration of ground robotic systems to replace personnel in logistical, evacuation, and combat breach roles.
The Verkhovna Rada supported the transition by enacting statutory exemptions eliminating value-added tax (VAT) on the procurement and import of ground robotic equipment to accelerate deliveries to frontline formations.
Ukrainian units have conducted tens of thousands of logistical supply runs and wounded casualty evacuations using tracked and wheeled ground platforms, utilizing automated units to navigate artillery corridors and minefields that remain impassable for conventional transport.

What a US-China thaw could cost India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:47:36 UTC
15:47:36 KST

What a US-China thaw could cost India
When the leaders of the world’s two largest economies meet, the whole world watches the theatrics, the body language and the substance. Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the US and summit with President Donald Trump took place against the backdrop of a surge in China’s global trade, while Trump has been struggling with falling approval ratings at home.
The high-stakes summit centred on symbolic gestures, personal rapport, and major economic and technology tensions. It yielded few breakthroughs on structural disputes. The most tangible outcome was an agreement to extend a critical trade war tariff truce by an additional two months, shifting the deadline to mid-January 2027. China’s export boom defied Trump’s tariff campaign.
From a position of strength, Xi was in no rush to make concessions while Trump was constrained by the costly Iran war that was hurting both his popularity and American wallets. The tariffs to address a trade imbalance with China were actually “killing” the US.
View from Delhi
Few nations have been monitoring the proceedings in Washington with greater scrutiny than India, as Xi-Trump discuss AI governance, tariff truces, critical minerals, regional maritime flashpoints, Taiwan and Indo-Pacific security. The outcome could affect New Delhi’s trade ambitions, supply chains, border security, Quad strategy, energy costs and influence.
New Delhi has been closely monitoring shifts in bilateral ties and supply chain vulnerabilities, and wondering about regional security frameworks like the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad). Indians have been also wondering why they were being singled out for 100% tariff for trading with Russia, while China was being wooed due high US economic dependences. As China has grown in global stature, it was clear that economic and military strength brings prestige and respect.
The largest and oldest democracies, India and the US, were meant to have congruence of interests and common global perceptions. That a day would come so quickly when the US would woo the communist arch rival and competitor from a relative position of weakness, was not anticipated.
At the core of it all, for some time now, India’s calculations have been based on an enduring fear of the emergence of a US-China “G2.” Something that could position India as a “second fiddle.”
The new emerging duopoly could establish a bilateral framework to partition spheres of influence, resolve global disputes, and manage international security above the heads of leading middle powers or an aspiring great power like India. China could get emboldened towards Asian dominance. Early signals were visible during Trump’s second term that Washington preferred a highly transactional foreign policy. Trump’s tariffs were bound to actually give greater leverage to China which monopolizes critical minerals and technologies and has a balance of payments advantage with all.
Despite structural mistrust between the US and China, these baby-steps towards managed coexistence present challenging outcomes for India. On the other hand, a total breakdown of US-China relations would be even worse for New Delhi and the world.
Washington’s policing failures around the world over the decades, and now never-ending Iran war, have lowered America’s global standing and influence. The tariffs have caused a level of distrust in New Delhi. NATO allies and West Asian friends of the US are running helter-skelter looking for alternative security arrangements and umbrellas.
For a long time India was hoping US support for technology and military capability building would allow it to remain a peer to China in Asia. A cosy bilateral understanding between Washington and Beijing could marginalize India’s diplomatic leverage. India also risks diluting regional bargaining power. In fact, US-China competition also indirectly supported India’s “strategic autonomy.”
In the recent past, India was looking for alternative sourcing through what is called the ‘China Plus One’ manufacturing strategy. American industrial giants that have been eager to exit China dependence have been investing billions of dollars into Make-in-India, especially in consumer electronics, pharmaceuticals, automotive parts, and solar equipment. This has helped boost manufacturing’s share of India’s GDP and expand the country’s exports.
But now if Xi and Trump move towards a comprehensive trade deal, securing American industry interests, then the move towards India could slowdown. A transactional Trump has been vocal about India’s protective trade policies and domestic market restrictions. He may now push for opening India’s agriculture and technology sectors to American firms. Global commodity price volatility is also being watched closely by India. A reconciliation between Washington and Beijing could stabilize global demand, and be good for New Delhi.
China controls roughly 70% of global rare-earth element extraction and nearly 85% of refining capacity. Essential for military hardware, electric vehicle batteries, wind turbines, and advanced electronics, they give Beijing significant leverage over Washington. Any US-China understanding on critical minerals will be good for the world and India.
Just days before the bilateral summit, on September 18, Trump signed into law a bill that allows a 100% tariff on top buyers of Russian energy, primarily China and India. Days later, the US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that Washington and Beijing had extended their Busan Agreement until January 10, 2027, under which the two sides agreed to avoid new tariffs and trade restrictions on each other.
Will India receive a similar concession? For now, it remains exposed to the tariff threat. Does Trump see India as a softer target? While US threatens India and Brazil, it is more considerate towards China because Beijing exercises much more leverage. Peter Navarro, an American economist and Trump’s senior counsellor for trade and manufacturing, at one point called Ukraine ‘Modi’s war’ - because of New Delhi’s oil imports from Russia. Nobody in Trump’s administration has ever tried to call the Ukraine crisis ‘Xi’s war’. Recall that in July 2025, Washington spared China but imposed an additional 25% on India for buying Russian crude. There is thus increased suspicion that India is in the crosshairs while Beijing keeps escaping US scrutiny.
The US has been concerned about AI malpractice by China and has sought structured AI safety dialogues. India, which aims to become a global hub for AI deployment and digital public infrastructure, is monitoring the discussions closely, so that it does not lose the early mover advantage.
India’s Indo-Pacific strategy relies heavily on the Quad alongside the United States, Japan, and Australia. But under Trump 2.0, the grouping has faced growing uncertainty, with the US president clearly favoring bilateral deals over multilateral frameworks. If Washington ends up softening its position on the South China Sea in exchange for economic concessions, it would send a deeply troubling signal — not only to New Delhi, but to the wider world.
As China becomes a peer power with the US, a weakening American position on Taiwan could embolden the People’s Liberation Army (PLA). While India’s immediate focus remains sovereignty over its territory along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) and its influence across South Asia, an emboldened PLA could be a threat for India. It could weaken India’s position on the painstaking negotiations after the 2020 border conflict. Beijing might become less accommodating toward Indian border positions. Conversely a stable China-US relationship could also bring stability in China-India relations, and reduce the trust deficit. India also does not want Chinese or US influence in South Asia as it considers it detrimental to its security.
India hopes that the Xi-Trump discussions bring stability to the global energy trade. Spiking oil prices are already worsening India’s current account deficit and driving domestic inflation.
Reenergized US-China relations could reduce Russia-China dependency on each other. Russia may then edge closer to India.
Long strategic game
The export juggernaut that Trump sought to tame has kept roaring in what economists are increasingly referring to as ‘China Shock 2.0’. China’s global trade surplus is on pace to top $1 trillion for a second straight year. The Trump administration thought they could use massive unilateral pressure to force China to make concessions, but that did not occur.
The US president had hoped to use the pending $14 billion arms package for Taiwan as a “negotiating chip” with Beijing. With Xi clearly in the driver’s seat it will further unnerve US allies in Asia, especially Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, Taiwan, and the Quad partners. Washington’s resolve to defend Taiwan is again in question.
Washington also sees Xi as uniquely able to exert pressure on Iran to negotiate, but Xi has shown little inclination to do so. Beijing is selling billions of dollars’ worth of goods to Iran through sanctions-evasion. Xi had urged the US and Iran to return to negotiations to end the war, but Xi has not publicly commented on Chinese support for Iran. China is moving from indirect influence to signalling readiness for a direct role. Could China become the next mediator in the US-Iran war?
Xi pressed Trump on Taiwan saying he hoped the US would “handle the Taiwan question with prudence.” Meanwhile, Senate Democrats criticized Trump for failing to publicly address China’s military pressure on Taiwan and called for the immediate delivery of approved military aid and arms sales to the island.
In his characteristic way, Trump said America was “very happy” about Xi’s visit, and hoped that China is “very happy also.” Xi said the US-China relationship had developed into a constructive one of “strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity,” thus positioning Beijing as an equal to the US on the global stage.
“In some ways, the best thing that we accomplished in this visit is to continue the conversation,” US Ambassador to China David Perdue told Fox News. Showmanship of bonhomie and current positive mood in the relationship could be temporary, given disputes over technology controls, rare earth exports, agricultural trade, and over Iran, Russia, and Taiwan.
The US and China remain strategic competitors across trade, technology, security and geopolitics, yet both governments have simultaneously demonstrated an interest in preventing competition from degenerating into confrontation. There was a talk about a possible hotline between the two countries, and some sort of a broad deal for sharing a progress report of sorts. Nothing of that sort happened.
Xi Jinping is playing a long strategic game. Washington continues to be at war and mired in multiple geopolitical and domestic crises. Beijing is quietly consolidating its economy, political control, restructuring its military and expanding its strategic footprint. China does not need to defeat America, it may only need to outlast American attention. “America is very happy about this visit, and I’m sure China is very happy also,” Trump said. Whether India is happy will be dissected in the corridors of power in New Delhi.

- Analysis: Brigginshaw's NRLW legend remains eternal
1. Origin wingers make uncharacteristic errors
It doesn't matter how much experience you have, every player feels some sort of pressure on grand final day.
And the pressure of a grand final was on display in the opening minutes, with a pair of State of Origin representatives making uncharacteristic errors.
Sydney Roosters winger Jayme Fressard had a proper shocker to begin the grand final, failing to gather the opening kick-off and nudging it into touch.
As the ball came to the NSW State of Origin rep, she tried to trap it with her foot but kicked the footy over the sideline.
The Roosters were able to defend their goal-line and then it was a Broncos Origin rep to have a shocker.
It was Fressard's opposing winger, Julia Robinson, who dropped the ball stone cold in her own half, which gifted the Roosters a golden chance to open the scoring.
Unlike the Broncos, the Roosters were able to score when winger Brydie Parker fielded a great cross-field kick from five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher and touched down in the corner.
2. Tarryn Aiken takes over in 7-minute blitz
The Roosters were dominating the grand final in the first half, as multiple errors from Brisbane kept them under immense pressure.
But Brisbane's goal-line defence was one aspect of their game that was withstanding the impressive Roosters.
That was until Sydney halfback Tarryn Aiken, who missed last year's decider due to an ACL injury, produced three moments of brilliance in a 7-minute stretch that led to a trio of tries for the Roosters.
First Aiken grubbered for herself and when the ball bounced off the arm of Brisbane winger Kerri Johnson, the Sydney halfback caught the ricochet and scored the game's second try.
Four minutes later, Aiken was setting up the third try of the match. The halfback lined up at lock in an attacking scrum 10 metres from Brisbane's goal-line. Aiken passed from the base of the scrum to the left, wrapped around and retook the footy, then gave a perfect short pass to captain Isabelle Kelly who charged over.
The Roosters then charged down the field again and when a sixth tackle play looked to be coming unstuck, it was Aiken again who produced a great kick which Brisbane's Deleni Paitai fumbled, and the Tricolours regathered and Fressard scored in the corner.
3. Brigginshaw on report in her farewell game
The trailblazing career of Ali Brigginshaw, someone who has been instrumental in the growth of women's rugby league, came to an end with an NRLW grand final.
But the legendary Broncos, Maroos and Jillaroo might have considered herself lucky not to have been sin-binned in her farewell game.
With the Roosters on top, Brigginshaw was desperate not to let Aiken put in an attacking cross-field kick.
Aiken did, which led to a try, but Brigginshaw's low dive resulted in her clattering into the planted leg of Aiken.
A hit under the knee led to Aiken landing hard on her back and could have easily resulted in Brigginshaw being sent for a 10-minute break on the sideline.
But referee Belinda Sharpe decided that putting Brigginshaw on report was the only action necessary, which really is academic considering this was her farewell outing.
4. Dally M medallist pulls off one of season's best tackles
Down 26-0 early in the second half, Brisbane's misery looked destined to continue when the Roosters were about to cross over for what would have been their seventh try of the grand final.
A high bomb from the Roosters was allowed to bounce, the ball took a wicked turn and landed in the arms of Brydie Parker, and a brilliant flick pass on the inside looked set to end with Jessica Sergis scoring in the corner.
But Brisbane's captain and fullback Tamika Upton, the Dally M medalist this season, produced a try-saving tackle as good as any seen this season.
The Brisbane number one screamed across in cover and was able to twist her body in the tackle and make sure she was under the ball as Sergis fell to the line.
With Upton around her like a snake, Sergis was unable to get her arm free and ground the ball. It didn't change the outcome, but it was another example of why Upton is the best player in the competition.
5. Roosters complete first perfect season in 101 years
The Roosters came into Sunday's decider with plenty of confidence.
They had won 30 of their previous 31 NRLW matches. There only loss was last year's grand final, to the Broncos, denying them an undefeated season.
But the Tricolours regrouped in 2026, won every match on their way to the decider, then exacted revenge with a commanding win to complete the perfect season.
The Sydney Roosters became the first men's or women's side in top grade rugby league to go the entire season without suffering a loss since the 1959 ST George Dragons.
That Dragons team recorded 17 wins, and one draw, on their way to a fourth consecutive premiership, in a dominant era of 11 straight titles.
But the 2026 Roosters NRLW side had no draws, just 13 wins from 13 matches. The last team to win every match in a season was South Sydney, way back in 1925.

Economic Watch: China trade ties carry significant weight for U.S. West Coast ports
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:45:30 CST
15:45:30 KST

by Julia Pierrepont III, Gao Shan
LOS ANGELES, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- With China accounting for about 55 percent of trade at the Port of Long Beach and roughly 40 percent of business at the neighboring Port of Los Angeles, stable relations between Washington and Beijing are not an abstract diplomatic concern for the two busiest container ports in the United States.
That deep trade linkage means shifts in U.S.-China ties can quickly ripple through cargo flows, jobs, consumer supply chains and investment across Southern California, according to the heads of the two ports.
"Stable and constructive relations between the United States and China are important to the global economy, to American consumers and businesses, and to the reliability of international supply chains," Noel Hacegaba, CEO of the Port of Long Beach, told Xinhua.
The two ports, located side by side in San Pedro Bay, form the largest container gateway in the United States and anchor a vast logistics network of dockworkers, truckers, warehouses, railroads, retailers and exporters.
China has been Long Beach's largest trading partner by cargo volume for decades and now accounts for about 55 percent of the port's imports and exports, Hacegaba said.
He described Long Beach as "a vital link in the Pacific trade corridor," connecting Chinese manufacturers and exporters with U.S. consumers, businesses and distribution networks, while also serving as a gateway for California goods headed to China.
At the Port of Los Angeles, ties with China are similarly deep. Gene Seroka, the port's executive director, said China accounts for approximately 40 percent of its business, more than two and a half times that of its next-largest trading partner.
"China remains a critically important trading partner for the Port of Los Angeles, and our longstanding relationships with Chinese ports have opened the door to cooperation that goes well beyond moving cargo," Seroka said.
Trade with China remains central to both ports. A more stable bilateral relationship would help protect cargo flows, jobs and consumer supply chains. China is also one of the leading export markets for California goods, Hacegaba said.
Beyond cargo volumes, the ports are expanding cooperation with Chinese counterparts in areas including cleaner shipping, digitalization and supply-chain resilience.
Seroka cited work with the ports of Shanghai, Guangzhou and, more recently, Shenzhen on green shipping corridors and other initiatives aimed at cutting emissions and making global trade more efficient and resilient.
"These port-to-port partnerships are a good example of how practical cooperation can deliver meaningful benefits on both sides of the Pacific," he said.
As the Port of Los Angeles handles more than 10 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) annually, while the Port of Long Beach processed a record 9.9 million TEUs in 2025, the scale of the two ports underscores the wider economic stakes.
Together, they handled about 31 percent of U.S. containerized international waterborne trade in 2025 and support 2.4 million jobs nationwide. ■

United List leads in Latvian parliamentary election: preliminary results
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
14:44:40 CST
15:44:40 KST

RIGA, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- The United List, led by Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, took a large lead in the country's parliamentary election, preliminary results released Sunday morning showed.
According to the Central Election Commission, with about 93 percent of the votes counted as of 6:35 a.m. local time (0335 GMT), the United List had secured 35.44 percent of the vote, followed by Latvia First with 13.22 percent and Sovereign Power/Alliance of Young Latvians with 11.73 percent.
The National Alliance, the Progressives and New Unity had received 9.09 percent, 7.24 percent and 6.18 percent, respectively. The Union of Greens and Farmers had garnered 4.62 percent, slightly below the 5-percent threshold required to win seats in parliament.
The vote count was still underway, and the rankings and distribution of seats could change. The commission said the official results would be confirmed by Oct. 19.
Voting in the Latvian parliamentary election began on Saturday morning, with 1,428 candidates vying for 100 seats in the 15th Saeima, or parliament. A total of 14 political parties and party alliances took part in the election.
About 807,000 of the country's approximately 1.558 million registered voters cast ballots, putting voter turnout at about 51.81 percent, according to the commission.
Under Latvia's electoral system, 100 seats in the parliament are allocated through proportional representation. Each political party or political alliance must obtain at least 5 percent of the vote to enter parliament.
According to the country's constitution, after the new parliament is formed, the president will consult with the political forces entering the parliament and invite the candidate for prime minister to form a new government. The new government must be approved by a vote of confidence in the parliament before it can assume its duties. ■

Malaysia seeks Türkiye’s tourism expertise to deepen Muslim-friendly travel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:43:54 UTC
15:43:54 KST

Malaysia is looking to Türkiye's experience in managing historical heritage and developing transit tourism as the two countries explore greater cooperation in faith-based travel, according to the head of Malaysia's Islamic Tourism Center.
Mohammad Faisal bin Abu Suaib Khan, director-general of the centre, told Anadolu that Türkiye's experience in combining tourism with the preservation and commercial use of historical sites offers lessons for Malaysia.
"Türkiye has experience in managing heritage. The way you monetise historical monuments, and at the same time get the funding to upgrade, take care of and manage them, is very important because conservation is very costly," Faisal said.
"We can learn from the way you do business and, at the same time, how you conserve certain monuments and make them good tourist spots," he said.
Both Türkiye and Malaysia seek to expand their already significant tourism industries while tapping into the growing global Muslim travel market.
Türkiye generated $65.23 billion in tourism revenue in 2025, up 6.8 percent from the previous year, according to the Turkish Statistical Institute.
Museums and archaeological sites recorded nearly 65.9 million visits in 2025, an increase of 6.8 percent year-on-year.
Malaysia welcomed 42.2 million international visitors in 2025, up from 38 million a year earlier, according to Tourism Malaysia, and is seeking further to expand the sector through its Visit Malaysia 2026 campaign.
Türkiye's transit tourism
Faisal said his own experience travelling through Istanbul demonstrated another Turkish tourism practice that Malaysia could potentially adapt.
During an about eight-hour layover in Istanbul while travelling to Kazan, Russia, he and a colleague were offered a city tour by Turkish Airlines.
"They brought us from the airport to the city, then on a cruise to see the historical monuments along the Bosphorus Strait [officially Strait of Istanbul], with a little bit of the historical story about every building and the historical part of the Golden Horn," he said.
The program also included a meal before the passengers returned to continue their journey.
"It was a very nice offer because they gave us a small, simple gift that made us want to come again," he said.
"The way they crafted the trip was like giving us a teaser, a very good teaser, so that we would come again and stay in Istanbul and enjoy more."
Faisal said he would like to see Malaysia develop a similar model for passengers spending long transit periods at Kuala Lumpur International Airport.
"I wish that we could do the same thing for tourists who are transiting through KLIA or KLIA2, so that we can bring them to Kuala Lumpur, let them enjoy it, and then they will come again," he said, referring to Kuala Lumpur International Airport Terminal 1 and Terminal 2.
"This is something interesting for us to learn from Türkiye."
Cooperation can be both ways
Faisal stressed that cooperation would not be limited to Malaysia learning from Türkiye, saying Kuala Lumpur also has experience, particularly in establishing structured standards for Muslim-friendly tourism.
"We can learn from there, but, like I said, we can also share something," he said. "It can be bilateral – both ways."
Malaysia's Islamic Tourism Center, an agency under Malaysia's Ministry of Tourism, Arts and Culture, develops standards, research, training and capacity-building programs for Muslim-friendly tourism and hospitality.
"We focus on Muslim-friendly tourism and hospitality. We do the standards and also capacity building, training and research," Faisal said.
One of its key initiatives is the Muslim-Friendly Tourism and Hospitality Assurance and Recognition, which recognises tourism businesses meeting specified requirements for serving Muslim travellers.
More than 500 businesses and services in Malaysia are registered as Muslim-friendly, including 73 hotels, 39 travel agencies, 11 spa centres and 390 tourist guides.
Faisal said Malaysia's experience with such standards could complement Türkiye's established tourism infrastructure.
"We have the Muslim-friendly assurance recognition, so people who go to Türkiye can find and have a trusted hotel that is Muslim-friendly," he said.
Türkiye already has a substantial Muslim-friendly tourism market, supported by its Islamic cultural heritage and widespread availability of halal food, mosques and accommodation catering to Muslim travellers.
"Türkiye has a very good Muslim and Islamic history, so it will be very easy for Türkiye to get enrolled in this program and, at the same time, reach the Muslim-friendly market," he said.
Expanding Muslim-friendly tourism beyond Muslim countries
Malaysia received 9.7 million Muslim visitors in 2025, with the figure targeted to reach 15.2 million by 2030, according to the centre's data.
The recognition framework is expanding internationally, with the centre developing cooperation in markets including Russia, Taiwan, Indonesia, South Korea and Brazil.
Faisal said Muslim-friendly standards could be particularly valuable in non-Muslim-majority countries, where travellers may have more difficulty identifying suitable hotels, restaurants and other services.
"For non-Muslim countries, we work with the halal certification bodies. Their product now is halal certification, so we add another product, which is the Muslim-Friendly Assurance Recognition," he said.
"They can offer a variety of hotels and halal restaurants. Instead of selling only one product, they can add Muslim-Friendly Assurance to hotels."
"The tourists who go to these non-Muslim countries can be happy because they know they have certain products. We give them assurance and, at the same time, provide the products they need and fulfil their needs," he said.
'We grow together because the market is the same'
Faisal said closer cooperation between Türkiye and Malaysia could also encourage travelers to combine the two destinations rather than viewing them as competitors for the Muslim tourism market.
"It can be two ways," Faisal said. "Certain people can come to Türkiye and then come to Malaysia, or someone going from Malaysia can stay in Türkiye before going to a third country."
"We also share and grow together because the market is the same. Instead of fighting for the market, we can grow together," he said.

This photo shows an Amazon Web Services data center adjacent to single-family homes in Stone Ridge, Virginia. AFP Photo
Amazon has pledged more than $1 billion over five years for U.S. communities that host its data centers, the latest tech giant seeking to win over residents increasingly hostile to the AI-fueled construction boom.
The "Built Together" program, unveiled by Amazon Web Services chief Matt Garman in a 3,000-word blog post on Oct. 2, will fund free community college degrees and trades training as well as energy-efficiency upgrades for schools and homes.
The company also announced a "Data Center Commitment," promising that its facilities will not drive up local electricity bills and that it will publish annual figures on energy and water use.
Garman said AWS would stop using nondisclosure agreements with government agencies on its projects, a practice that has become a major flashpoint for the movement opposing data centers.
Microsoft made a similar move in March, the first major tech firm to do so.
He also took aim at what he called myths about data centers, disputing as false arguments that they drive up power costs, deplete water supply and cause pollution from diesel fumes.
Citing "widespread reports," Garman said some countries were deliberately seeding misinformation in the United States to slow construction — an argument also made by the Trump administration.
Disinformation researchers and fact-checkers say such claims overstate the role of foreign influence campaigns in a grassroots movement that spans the political spectrum and nearly every U.S. state.

On Sunday, the U.S. Navy aircraft carrier "George H.W. Bush" arrived at the Thai resort island of Phuket; approximately 4,800 service members are on board, having been given an opportunity to rest after six months of participating in U.S. operations in the Middle East, UNN reports, citing Reuters.

The sailors will take part in cultural and community events in Phuket, including excursions and a football match between teams from the United States and Thailand.

Thailand is the only U.S. ally in mainland Southeast Asia with which the United States has a formal mutual defense treaty.

Assisi marks 800th anniversary of Saint Francis's death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:40:01 UTC
15:40:01 KST

Ceremonies and events are being held in Assisi throughout the day in honour of Italy's patron saint. The festivities form part of the Franciscan Jubilee Year, proclaimed by Pope Leo XIV.
This Sunday, 4 October, marks the 800th anniversary of the death of Saint Francis of Assisi, Italy's patron saint. From this year, and for the first time since 1977, 4 October once again becomes a national holiday.
To mark the occasion, the city of Assisi is celebrating this historic anniversary by exceptionally bringing together all of Italy's Regions and provincial capital municipalities, with 18 Regions and just as many municipalities already represented.
More than 3,000 pilgrims and tourists have arrived in the city to take part in the celebrations, which culminate in an address to the Nation by the President of the Republic, Sergio Mattarella, from the loggia of the Sacred Convent.
Events to celebrate the 800th anniversary of Saint Francis
The day of prayer and festivities follows a tightly scheduled programme that began at midnight on Saturday with the festive ringing of the bells. At 6.00 a.m. mass is celebrated for the community of friars, presided over by the Minister General, Friar Carlos Alberto Trovarelli, followed at 6.50 a.m. by the offering of prayers at the Saint's Tomb.
The arrival of President Mattarella is expected by 9.45 a.m. for the solemn mass in the Upper Basilica, presided over by Cardinal Matteo Maria Zuppi. During the celebration, attended also by ambassadors and representatives of accredited countries, Umbria will offer the oil and the mayor of Assisi, Valter Stoppini, will light the votive lamp on behalf of all Italian municipalities. This will be followed, at 11.20 a.m., by official speeches and, at noon, by the live broadcast of Pope Leo XIV's Angelus prayer on the giant screens in the square.
Cultural initiatives linked to Saint Francis
Alongside the institutional and religious ceremonies, major cultural initiatives have been organised, starting with the exhibition "Saint Francis at the Porziuncola", open to visitors until 25 October 2026.
The exhibition is hosted in the Porziuncola Museum at the Basilica of Santa Maria degli Angeli, which for the occasion has created a new entrance by refurbishing the ancient 15th-century cloister, once a traditional passageway for the friars. This exhibition itinerary, curated by the director Friar Saul Tambini and Donatella Vaccari, offers visitors a profound immersion in Franciscan iconography from its origins in the 13th century.
For the first time, the exhibition brings together the breviary of Saint Francis and that of Saint Clare, highlighting the deep bond between these two key figures of the early Franciscan movement. Visitors can admire paintings and relics, such as the famous portrait-relic attributed to Cimabue, which tradition holds was the lid of the Saint's first coffin, and the table on which Francis greeted death in song.
Among the works on display is also the Crucifix of the suffering Christ painted by Giunta Pisano around 1236. The entire cycle of exhibitions and celebrations forms part of the Franciscan Jubilee Year, proclaimed by Pope Leo XIV, which began on 10 January 2026 and is due to conclude on 10 January 2027.

AI needs safety layers like nuclear plants: Ex-OpenAI engineer

15:40:00 KST

There have been numerous reports about AI agents going rogue.
Another former OpenAI employee has added his voice to a chorus of frantic calls to make AI safe, saying the industry must mimic the aviation or nuclear power sectors with their layers of safeguards to avoid disaster.
In an article published in The Atlantic Magazine, David Robinson echoed warnings from inside and outside the AI world that its agents are being developed so fast and becoming so smart they could soon elude control and conceivably wipe out humanity.

He argued that cutting-edge AI labs need to operate like the aviation or the nuclear industry with layers of redundant safeguards and careful planning "so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster."

7 Bulgarian idiosyncrasies that are puzzling to foreigners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:36:54 UTC
15:36:54 KST

Author
Veneta Nikolova
News
7 Bulgarian idiosyncrasies that are puzzling to foreigners
Sunday 4 October 2026 09:10
Sunday, 4 October 2026, 09:10
PHOTO pixabay
Font size
Bulgaria is a beautiful, safe and secure country, Bulgarians are welcoming people, ever ready to show the world their best. But there are some Bulgarian idiosyncrasies that a foreigner finds hard to understand. Here are some of them:
“Do not embarrass yourself in front of foreigners!”, is something Bulgarians say often, though of late, ironically. But, typically, foreigners are taken care of and pampered. Why? So as to dispel even the hint of a doubt that Bulgarians are not hospitable – a point of honour for any Bulgarian opening the door of their home to a foreigner. And, yes, sometimes they overdo it, treating their guest as an old-time friend, refusing to take a “no” for an answer if they do not join them for the family meal, or for feasting into the small hours, or they will insist on tagging along everywhere you go to show you the local sights…
PHOTO pixabay
Nod for “No” and shake your head for “Yes”. When they first come to Bulgaria, foreigners may find they are at sea when they see us answering their questions. Why? Because when we nod and shake our head it means the exact opposite of what it means in the rest of the world. In Bulgaria, nodding means “no”, and shaking your head from side to side means “yes”.
Bulgarians rarely smile, they do not like to show emotion in front of a stranger. This somber expression, which we are rarely actually aware of, makes a deep impression, and is often taken to be a sign of bad manners and a cold heart. But having got to know Bulgarians’ true character, foreigners quickly change their minds and even regret having been “taken in” by appearances.
PHOTO BGNES
Feasting and partying until dawn. If there is one thing Bulgarians have mastered to perfection it is the art of “letting their hair down” and partying, come hell or high water. Foreigners are left puzzled as to how, in the poorest country of the EU, restaurants and bars are always full – from the pub in the obscurest village to the trendy cafes, taverns and gourmet restaurants in big cities.
PHOTO pixabay
Leave your shoes at the door! If you are invited to someone’s home, there is one thing you should know – Bulgarians are finicky about hygiene. So, you should be ready to be asked to take your shoes off at the door, so as not to bring street dirt into the house. You might even be handed a pair of soft slippers, to make you feel at home…
PHOTO pixabay
Bulgarian cuisine is spicy, often salty, sometimes greasy, and more often than not Oriental. True, shopska salad, banitsa, mixed grills, chips with grated cheese are all appreciated by our guests from abroad.
But sometimes the spicy, salty, hot food with lots of herbs may be too much for them. And they are not always very keen on the kinds of food and drink that are so popular in this country, like boza, salty ayryan, tripe soup, headcheese or grilled pork ears, and a host of other weird, sometimes insipid, or too spicy or greasy kinds of food that are so alien to the foreign palette.
A splash of water in front of your feet for “God speed!” Traditionally, Bulgarians believe in the purifying life-force of water. So, don’t be alarmed if, just as you are leaving for the airport, the family you have been staying with suddenly splash some water onto the floor in front of your feet. When a family member leaves the home for some special event – like the first day of school, prom night, an exam, a wedding or a trip abroad - Bulgarians invariably splash some water at the front door, with a ritual wish of “God speed” or “Good luck”. But there is one thing you should know – never go back to fetch a passport forgotten on the nightstand, because the magic will be gone, and your good luck will fizzle away!

Estonian men's football team takes first Nations League victory over Luxembourg
The Estonian men's national football team earned its first Nations League victory of the year, defeating Luxembourg 1-0 at home in a heated match.
Estonia made a lively start and took the lead after just five minutes. Mattias Käit collected the ball inside the Luxembourg penalty area and saw his low effort saved, but the rebound fell to Rasmus Peetson, whose powerful follow-up took a deflection on its way into the net.
Maksim Paskotši had another good opportunity just a few minutes later after Patrik Kristal picked him out with a deft backheel, but he was unable to make the chance count. Luxembourg then began to take control, dictating the tempo for much of the next 15 minutes and getting into dangerous positions around the Estonian goal without finding a finish.
Estonia wrestled back the initiative around the half-hour mark but could not add to its advantage, sending the hosts into the break with a 1-0 lead.
Luxembourg emerged with renewed energy after halftime and tested Estonia with several efforts from distance, though none found the net. Estonia soon regained the upper hand and Luxembourg goalkeeper Anthony Moris was called into action in the 63rd minute, producing an excellent save to keep out Peetson's header.
The pressure continued and just a few minutes later Moris was forced into another fine stop when Kristal let fly from distance.
The closing stages grew increasingly heated, with Estonia captain Karol Mets among those booked. The yellow card means he will miss the fourth match against Iceland. Luxembourg continued to threaten late on, but Estonia held firm to protect its 1-0 lead and secure its first Nations League victory following two draws.
"After two very close draws where we could have achieved more, we definitely wanted to win. We didn't want to come away from here with anything less. We wanted to give the fans and ourselves something to celebrate and we managed to do that," Estonia captain Karol Mets told ERR.
"We've been together with the same group for a long time and have grown together. Time is a very important factor. We've been given time to make mistakes, develop and grow together. We're starting to see the first fruits of that now. The work continues."
Estonia will host Iceland on Tuesday, October 6, with the match available to watch on ERR's channels.
Iceland cruised to a 3-0 home victory over Bulgaria on Saturday and tops the group with seven points, with Estonia second on five. The group winner will earn automatic promotion to League B of the Nations League.
"I'd say it's 50-50. Given the team they have, Iceland is a slight favorite going into the match, but we're playing at home — and I hope we get as many fans as we did today — so anything is possible. We've got good momentum and need to keep it going," Mets added.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Trump tariffs a mixed bag for US auto industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:34:00 UTC
15:34:00 KST

President Donald Trump looks on before speaking during a visit to the Peterbilt Motors truck plant in Denton, Texas, on Oct 01, 2026. AFP Photo
President Donald Trump has claimed a "roaring comeback" in American auto manufacturing following aggressive trade policy, but analysts view the cumulative impact as more of a mixed bag.
Since Trump returned to the White House, General Motors, Toyota, Ford and other carmakers have announced plans to expand U.S. plants or shift production from overseas to make use of underutilized factories, as the industry navigated measures such as a 25-percent levy on imported autos.
But as the president's allies in the Republican party look ahead to mid-term elections in November, the gains to the U.S. carmaker profile look more incremental than decisive, and are accompanied by a drag in spending in some cases due to trade uncertainty.
"It's a partial win," Stephanie Brinley, an automotive analyst at Mobility Global, said of the lift from Trump's tariffs to the U.S. auto industry.
Auto industry experts view the unsettled nature of Trump's trade measures as a hindrance to bigger wins. This defect has most recently surfaced in the dust-up between the United States and Canada that has clouded the prospects of the North American trade agreement, known as the USMCA.
In August, a top Honda executive said the company was operating near full capacity at its North American facilities and wanted to build a new plant, but might pivot if the fog around USMCA persists.
Moreover, the disruptions from tariffs and Trump's reversals of U.S. policies favoring electric vehicles have weighed on the U.S. auto supplier sector, which provides parts and technology and employs some 930,000 people in the United States.
There has been "a noticeable slowdown" in investment by suppliers due to policy uncertainty, including on tariffs, said Tyler Harp, an industry economist at the Center for Automotive Research (CAR).
Investment by suppliers plunged from more than $8 billion in the first quarter of 2025 to around $600 million in the two subsequent quarters before recovering somewhat, according to CAR data.
"Suppliers are more exposed to tariffs," Harp said. "They're not in a position to absorb them as well as automakers."
After falling for much of 2025, U.S. auto employment has been on an upswing for most of 2026. In September, the sector had just under 1.8 million workers, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
That's almost one percent more than the level in January 2025 when Trump took office, but more than 2 percent below the peak level from the last decade, in July 2024 when Joe Biden was president, according to the BLS.
U.S. auto production has also been broadly stable, but isn't expected to rise until around 2030, when GM's $4 billion investments in Michigan, Kansas and Tennessee come into force, along with Toyota's $3.6 billion plan to move Tacoma pickup production to Texas from Mexico.
Global Mobility projects that U.S. car production will be 10 million vehicles in 2026, about the same as last year, but rise to around 11.3 million in 2030, according to Brinley.
"There is definitely an increase in there and it is partially related to tariffs," she said, noting that in some cases automakers are reconfiguring plants or making use of underutilized capacity.
A brand-new plant such as the one floated by Honda must be used for decades.
"Plants aren't put in the ground with the expectation of lasting a presidential cycle," Brinley said. "The tariffs have an impact, but it's just not the only input."
Suppliers have ranked changes in government trade policy as the industry's "greatest threat" over the next 12 months, according to surveys from MEMA, the Vehicle Suppliers Association.
In the most recent report, nearly 80 percent of companies ranked trade policy changes among the four top threats, alongside weakness in the US economy, an external or "black swan" event, and poor vehicle sales.
The industry has recovered only about half of tariff-policy-related costs, a "sustained margin drag that is likely to weigh on supplier financials," according to a commentary from Deloitte accompanying the survey.
The industry is following a "discipline-over-growth playbook" while shifting more investment to automation and robotics, Deloitte said.

The dream of normalization with Saudi Arabia clouded Netanyahu’s judgment - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:29:15 UTC
15:29:15 KST

Exactly three years ago, two weeks before the October 7 massacre, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stood before the UN General Assembly and delivered a hopeful speech about the transformation ushered in by the Abraham Accords.
“They brought Arabs and Jews closer together. We see it in Jewish weddings in Dubai, in the dedication of a Torah scroll in a synagogue in Bahrain, in visitors flocking to the Museum of Moroccan Judaism in Casablanca. We see it in lessons about the Holocaust taught to Arab students in the United Arab Emirates,” Netanyahu said.
But for Netanyahu, the Abraham Accords were merely the appetizer before the main course: Saudi Arabia. “I believe that we are at the cusp of an even more dramatic breakthrough – a historic peace between Israel and Saudi Arabia.”
Such an agreement, Netanyahu said, would advance the end of the Arab-Israeli conflict, encourage additional Arab states to normalize relations with Israel, and improve the prospects for peace with the Palestinians.
Indeed, normalization with Saudi Arabia appeared to be within reach. Two days before Netanyahu’s appearance at the UN, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman said in an interview with Fox News, referring to normalization with Israel: “Every day we get closer.”
A 2024 investigation by The Atlantic described how, in the fall of 2023, the Biden administration was moving closer to a broad agreement that would include Israeli-Saudi normalization, a US-Saudi defense pact, and American assistance for a Saudi civilian nuclear program.
The shift in the Saudi position on normalization had been developing for years, but it had gathered momentum since at least 2018, when MBS was quoted as telling Jewish leaders in the US that “in the last several decades the Palestinian leadership has missed one opportunity after another and rejected all the peace proposals it was given... It is about time the Palestinians take the proposals and agree to come to the negotiations table or shut up and stop complaining.”
MBS added that the Palestinian issue was not at the top of the Saudi government’s priorities.
Meeting between MBS, Netanyahu
Moreover, in 2020, Netanyahu met MBS on Saudi soil. It was the first time that a meeting at such a senior level had taken place in Saudi Arabia. In March 2022, MBS told The Atlantic: “We don’t look at Israel as an enemy; we look to them as a potential ally.”
This background is important because it helps illustrate just how close normalization with Saudi Arabia appeared to be before October 7. An agreement with a country of such immense political, economic, and religious importance in the Arab and Islamic worlds would have overshadowed even the Abraham Accords.
When warnings arrived from Egypt and the UAE about Hamas’s preparations – as well as the message of an “earthquake” conveyed by Yahya Sinwar through Palestinian politician Sufian Abu Zaida – they reached a prime minister who not only suffered from excessive confidence in Israel’s ability to deal with the Hamas threat but was also dazzled by the prospect of an achievement that seemed increasingly within reach.
The very fact that Egypt and the UAE maintained such close intelligence ties with Israel also diverted attention from the warnings toward the hubris generated by Israel’s cooperation with a number of key Arab states.
For Hamas, Israeli normalization with Saudi Arabia represented nothing less than a strategic threat. In the minutes of a Hamas leadership meeting held on September 26-27, 2023, less than two weeks before the attack – and shortly after the statements by MBS and Netanyahu – Sinwar spoke of the need for an “extraordinary action” to bring about a strategic shift.
Sinwar believed that, given Saudi Arabia’s importance, Saudi normalization could lead additional Arab and Muslim states to follow suit and produce a new regional order with Israel at its center.
Moreover, it could push the Palestinian issue off the agenda and undermine the “resistance project.” Sinwar argued that Hamas could not acquiesce in this process and that confrontation had to be intensified, particularly over Jerusalem and al-Aqsa.
Thus, even if planning for Operation al-Aqsa Flood – October 7 – began much earlier and was driven by other considerations as well, the normalization issue played a major role in determining the timing of the operation.
Just as Hamas sought to disrupt the Arab Peace Initiative, announced at the Arab summit in Beirut on March 28, 2002, by carrying out the devastating terrorist attack at the Park Hotel in Netanya the previous day, during the Passover Seder, so too did it seek to sabotage the normalization process through its military operation.
On the Israeli side, warning papers issued by research institutes – and perhaps by intelligence agencies as well – failed to identify the threat that normalization posed to Hamas. In many assessments, it was the internal rift within Israeli society resulting from the judicial overhaul that was seen as posing a threat to Israel’s national security.
Another example appeared in Israel Weekly War Summary published by the Israel Defense and Security Forum. Its main headline on October 5, two days before the attack, declared that “Israeli-Saudi normalization seems closer than ever.”
The same briefing also analyzed the escalation initiated by Hamas along the Gaza border but portrayed it as an attempt to pressure Israel and Qatar into granting economic concessions, without connecting it to Saudi normalization.
Three years after October 7, it is becoming increasingly clear that the question of normalization with Saudi Arabia lay at the heart of the calculations and thinking on both sides.
Sinwar, on the one hand, and Netanyahu, on the other, understood the strategic importance of the process: One sought to sabotage it, while the other did everything in his power to advance it. The former succeeded in his mission, while the latter failed – precisely because of the desire to keep the situation calm and prepare the ground for the normalization initiative.
The writer teaches in the Department of Islamic and Middle Eastern Studies at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. He is a member of the board of Mitvim – The Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies – and a member of the Coalition for Regional Security.

Did the pager operation change the Middle East? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:28:58 UTC
15:28:58 KST

The unequivocal answer is yes. But the story is far more complex than a one-word answer.
The operation had two main achievements. The first was psychological. It restored Israel’s standing as a security power capable of carrying out operations that had seemed unimaginable or impossible.
After October 7, it demonstrated to the region in which we live that Israel had recovered and was capable of penetrating even its enemies’ most sensitive systems. This was enormously important for Israel’s deterrence. Hezbollah, the strongest and most important militia in the Shi’ite axis, suddenly found itself in deep distress and embarrassment.
The psychological dimension was also reflected in the message conveyed to Israelis themselves. Following the October 7 massacre in the south, and the disappointment of northern residents who had been under fire for 11 months, there was a need to rebuild Israelis’ trust in their security establishment. The pager operation made a significant contribution to this effort: it restored Israelis’ sense of capability and, to some extent, opened the door to further daring operations, from the elimination of Hezbollah’s leadership to operations in Iran.
The second achievement was operational. Thousands of Hezbollah operatives were injured by the pagers and communications devices, and the Radwan Force’s chain of command was subsequently hit as well, when Ibrahim Aqil was eliminated along with 14 commanders from Radwan Force brigades three days after the pager operation.
This blow helped neutralize capabilities and skilled personnel that had been developed over many years to carry out Hezbollah’s firepower and invasion plans. It damaged the organization’s morale and operational functioning and later made it easier for the IDF to operate in southern Lebanon against infrastructure prepared for an invasion of Israel.
The pager operation, together with the elimination of Hezbollah’s leadership and the blow to the Radwan Force, formed part of a chain of events that changed the Middle East, from the revolution in Syria to the Israeli strikes against Iran. One of the main lessons was that terrorism can and must be fought without fearing its imagined power.
The Shi’ite axis was exposed in its weakness, and it became clear that it could be confronted in different arenas and through a variety of means. In Syria, this created the timing for Ahmed al-Sharaa’s revolution. He had been waiting in Idlib for an opportune moment and seized it once he understood that Hezbollah, Basher Assad’s principal ally in the region, had been weakened.
But Hezbollah has not disappeared. The large-scale military model it built before October 7 has been severely damaged: its broad plan to invade the Galilee has been neutralized, its ground forces in southern Lebanon have collapsed, and its firepower array no longer exists on the scale originally planned. Nevertheless, according to Alma Center assessments, it still possesses as many as approximately 15,000 rockets and missiles and continues to invest in expanding its drone capabilities.
In general, Hezbollah is devoting considerable efforts to its military reconstruction. It is recruiting and training new operatives, updating operational plans, gathering intelligence, and restoring weapons systems. Weapons smuggling from Syria continues, including rockets, advanced anti-tank missiles, UAVs, and additional components. At the same time, efforts are also underway to manufacture and repair weapons inside Lebanon.
Meanwhile, the failure of the Lebanese government and the Lebanese Armed Forces to fulfill their commitment to disarm Hezbollah continues to be exposed time and again. Even in 2026, the organization was able to sustain several months of rocket and drone launches into Israeli territory, albeit on a smaller scale than in 2024.
Therefore, the question today is not only whether the pager operation changed the Middle East, but whether that change can be preserved and steered in the right direction.
There are two challenges: how to prevent the reconstruction of the Shi’ite axis while also preventing it from being replaced by a radical Sunni axis comprising Syria, Qatar, and Turkey. Perhaps it would be more accurate to frame the question this way: How can actors interested in reaching arrangements with Israel be strengthened, while those seeking to destroy it continue to be weakenedת and even defeated?
The international system has a significant role to play. As long as it does not adopt an uncompromising approach toward murderous ideologies, terrorism, and hatred of the West, Israel will continue to face pressure preventing it from “finishing the job” and allowing terrorist organizations to survive, rebuild, and grow stronger.
This may be the final lesson of the pager operation: even when we are stronger, and the terrorist organizations are weaker, we must not count on pulling another “rabbit out of the hat.” The pager operation was a one-time event planned over many years. Its achievement must be preserved through a consistent and sustained policy of uprooting terrorist organizations. This should be the policy in Gaza, in Lebanon, and toward Iran.
The Israeli government should lead this effort together with local actors such as the Lebanese government and international actors such as the United States.

The US and Israel must come to Saudi Arabia’s aid - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:28:43 UTC
15:28:43 KST

Saudi Arabia has never been the strong and powerful state it is often portrayed as.
In 1979, the Iranian revolution placed at the helm of a more populous neighbor a Shi’ite revolutionary and theocratic leadership that loathed the Sunni Kingdom, not least for its long-standing suppression of Saudi Arabia’s Shi’ite minority in the south along the Yemen border and, more critically, the Shi’ites who populated the same region in which the Saudis produce most of their oil.
The Saudis were quick to acknowledge Iran’s dire threat. Saudi’s support of Iraq during the Iran-Iraq War (1980-1988) kept then-president Saddam Hussein’s Iraqi regime afloat. Their investment clearly paid off: the harried, tired Iranian mullahs and the Revolutionary Guard, for all their ideological ardor, refrained by and large from attacking Saudi Arabia directly for the next decade.
But that was the last time Saudi Arabia engaged (however indirectly) successfully with the Iranian threat.
Since then, it has all been downhill for the Saudis as Iran expanded its militia proxies in nearby countries both to produce a ring of fire over Israel but also to transform in the long run the Gulf states into Iranian vassals that would pay financial tribute (or more simply, protection money) into Iranian coffers.
Lebanon was probably the first battle zone in the Iranian-Saudi proxy war; the Saudis clearly lost to the Iranians. The Saudi’s in vain tried mobilizing the Sunni minority, along with their Christian-Maronite counterparts, to fight the rising Shi’ite militias, first “Amal” and later Hezbollah, who were backed by the Alawite Assad regime in Syria, Iran’s only Arab state ally.
For a while, it looked like the Saudis had succeeded with the creation of a government headed by the pro-Saudi Rafic Hariri, backed by the Sunni community and most of Lebanon’s Christian political forces.
The Saudis soon realized that in the Middle East at least, the military and terrorist power Iran and its proxies possessed would prevail over Saudi’s financial clout. Hariri was assassinated in 2005, in a demonstration of force on Beirut’s streets.
Three years later, Hezbollah cowed the Lebanese parliament into changing the rules of the game so that it would give it essentially the decisive say in Lebanese government and politics. The Saudis backed out of Lebanese politics, leaving the Lebanese population to bear the costs of the war Hezbollah initiated in 2023 against Israel in support of Hamas.
Graver still were the losses on the Iraqi and Yemeni fronts, both battle zones on Saudi Arabia’s long borders. Unfortunately for Saudi Arabia, the United States got rid of the Hussein Sunni regime that served as the counterpoise to the Iranian threat.
The Saudis in vain tried to support the minority Sunni militias, even possibly ISIS, to prevent Iraq’s Shi’ite majority from taking over and consolidating its regime.
Meanwhile, the Iranians used the threat ISIS posed to the new Shi’ite regime in Iraq to create powerful Shi’ite militias that would control the Iraqi political elite and the state apparatus as it did in Lebanon. Once again, the Saudis backed off in defeat.
Protecting the free world
In Yemen, the Saudis directly confronted the Houthis backed by Iran in a war that lasted six years to little avail. The Saudis, in 2022, sued for a truce, and the air force ceased its attacks on the Houthis, though the Kingdom continued to support the official Yemeni government the Houthis ousted from Sanaa, the capital, and most of Yemen’s populated areas.
And recently, in one more regional war not of Saudi-making, Saudi Arabia is witnessing Houthi advances that give them increasing control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait through which much of Saudi oil and gas transits and, more critically, greater control of the Red Sea, in which the Houthis can jeopardize Saudi Arabia’s major pipeline and the Yanbu port from which the oil is exported to Europe through the Suez Canal.
Yet even more ominous is the possibility that the Houthis will make a surprise attack in Saudi Arabia’s vast and unpopulated south (and if populated, it is mostly by a Shi’ite population) and advance along Route 10, the Saudi highway that links the south to the massive Saudi oil fields and its capital, Riyadh.
The aim would be not to take over the capital but to advance to the point of directly threatening the oil fields and processing plants and thus force the Saudis to acknowledge defeat and become a tributary state of Iran and its Houthi proxy.
The US and Israel, acutely aware of the possibility of surprises in the Middle East (the Hamas attack on Israel, the fall of the Assad regime, for example), must prevent this possibility at all costs.
They must closely monitor Houthi movements, quickly establish intelligence to distinguish between Houthi forces and civilians fleeing from the Houthis, especially as the Houthi forces may disguise themselves as civilians, and stop the Houthis even at the price of boots on the ground.
An Iran backed by Saudi financial clout is a nightmare for the free world, a “free” world where only two states amongst so many, the US and Israel, are ready and able to protect, at least in the Middle East. Preventing the fall of Saudi Arabia is vital to protecting the free world.
The writer is a senior researcher at the JISS and professor emeritus at Bar-Ilan University.

IEA: 325 million barrels of oil from strategic reserves released
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:28:00 UTC
15:28:00 KST

A boat of the Berlin Water Police (Wasserschutzpolizei) sails past a storage facility for oil products in Berlin, Germany, on April 22, 2026. AFP Photo
The International Energy Agency said on Oct. 3 that member countries had so far released 325 million barrels of oil and oil-derivative products from strategic reserves, from 400 million barrels promised in March.
The update came a day after G7 countries, in coordination with the IEA, agreed to immediately release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil to ease global energy supply concerns caused by fallout from the US-Iran war.
The G7 did not say whether the 100 million barrels included the outstanding 75 million barrels from the March IEA commitment, or came on top of that.
The U.S. government of President Donald Trump has been pressuring allies to release diesel reserves to ease a spike in prices for the fuel, being felt in America and elsewhere.
Restricted diesel supplies is one of the consequences of the war in the Middle East. Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, part of the fightback against Moscow’s strikes, have also affected the market.
The IEA said in a statement on Oct. 3 that “around 325 million barrels of the IEA collective action announced on March 11 have so far been released, representing over 80 percent of the 400 million barrels originally pledged in the action.”
The March pledge was offered up by the IEA’s 32 member countries, a grouping that includes all the G7 nations: of Britain, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan and the U.S.
The G7 countries on Oct. 2 agreed to release over the next four months 100 million barrels of oil and oil-derivative products, “including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days”.
They also said there would be no ban on diesel exports between them -- heading off a threat Washington had brandished, and which Trump later said would not be enacted.

Russia attacked Ukraine with 135 drones: the number of downed targets is increasing, hits were recorded at 5 locations
Kyiv • UNN
Russia launched 135 unmanned aerial vehicles from various directions, including 52 jet-powered ones. Air defense shot down or suppressed 125 enemy targets.
During the night of October 4, Russia attacked Ukraine with 135 attack drones of various types, while Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 125 enemy targets. This was reported by the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, UNN reports.
Details
According to available information, the attack began at 18:00 on October 3. Russian forces deployed 135 drones, including Shahed, "Gerbera," "Banderoль"/"Dan-T," and "Parody"-type decoy drones. Of the total number, 52 drones were jet-powered.
The drones were launched from the areas of Oryol, Kursk, Millerovo, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as from the temporarily occupied Donetsk and Crimea—from the area of Hvardiiske.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces. According to preliminary data, as of 08:30, air defenses had shot down/suppressed 123 enemy Shahed-, Gerbera-, and other types of drones, as well as 2 "Banderoль"/"Dan-T" drones.
In addition, according to available information, enemy air attack weapons were recorded striking 5 locations, while the debris of downed targets fell at 5 locations.
The attack is ongoing; several enemy UAVs are in the airspace. Follow safety rules!

Ukraine will eliminate its wartime budget deficit before the end of the year, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced in an interview with Reuters.
Zelensky stated that negotiations conducted by Ukrainian officials in Brussels had produced a viable framework to manage the state’s short-term financing gap while maintaining steady procurement for the armed forces.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Over the past several months we worked on our financial deficit. We will close the current deficit by the end of the year,” Zelensky said in comments released by the presidential administration. “We still have some issues to work through, but we will close the deficit.”
The president described resolving the shortfall as a major success for Ukraine, his negotiating team, and European partners, emphasizing that stabilization of the state budget was achieved through joint fiscal adjustments and credit mechanisms.
Frontloading EU loans and 2027 drone contracts
Zelensky explained that the government intends to advance portions of European credit allocations originally scheduled for 2027 into early January, ensuring that domestic defense contractors receive early capital allocations to maintain uninterrupted production lines.
“It was not easy. We worked with our budget, with our partners, especially the European Union, and we will also try to partially use loan funds for next year,” Zelensky said. “We will bring this closer to January and use this money to order drones for January and February 2027. My team returned from Brussels and reported. Everything is working well. I hope that this will continue.”
Vilnius Airport Closes as NATO Jets Scramble Over Suspected Drone
The drive to secure early procurement funding follows discussions between Ukrainian economic officials and European counterparts in Brussels, where Ukrainian Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko outlined long-term financing requirements for the coming fiscal year.
Marchenko previously cautioned that Ukraine could face a prospective financial shortfall of approximately €69 billion ($78 billion) in 2027, projecting requirements of roughly €40 billion ($45 billion) for defense operations and €29 billion ($33 billion) to maintain civilian state administration and public services.
Reform conditionality and frozen asset discussions
The planned deployment of credit lines unfolds as Brussels manages disbursements under the EU’s €90 billion ($102 billion) support loan facility covering the 2026-2027 period.
Under the framework’s 2026 allocation of €45 billion ($51 billion), the European Commission has disbursed approximately €15 billion ($17 billion). European officials have emphasized that subsequent payment tranches remain linked to verified reform benchmarks, focusing on anti-corruption enforcement, judicial governance, and public administration transparency.
European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos noted during donor coordination sessions that completing statutory reforms remains the primary mechanism for unlocking committed funding pipelines, urging Ukrainian institutions to coordinate closely to meet technical criteria.
Concurrently, European capitals have debated proposals to utilize immobilized Russian sovereign assets to support Ukraine’s defense and recovery.
While Kyiv has advocated using portions of the roughly €210 billion ($239 billion) in Russian central bank reserves immobilized across Europe – principally held in Belgium through the Euroclear depository – member states including Belgium, France, and Italy have urged caution regarding potential legal liabilities and financial market stability.
To supplement bilateral budgetary aid, European institutions are also integrating Ukraine into wider industrial initiatives. The European Commission approved €325 million ($368.6 million) to fund five European Defence Projects of Common Interest (EDPCI), with Ukraine participating in four collaborative frameworks.
