Hong Kong’s IPO haul more than doubles to HK$388b in first 9 months: Paul Chan
Finance chief says amount raised has surpassed whole of 2025, while HKIC’s CEO says over 30 portfolio firms preparing to apply for listings this year
Funds raised through initial public offerings in Hong Kong more than doubled year on year to over HK$388 billion (US$49.4 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, already surpassing the total amount for the whole of last year, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po has said.
Adding to the positive outlook, Clara Chan Ka-chai, CEO of the government-owned Hong Kong Investment Corporation (HKIC), noted on Sunday that more than 30 of its portfolio firms were preparing to apply for Hong Kong listings this year.
Paul Chan also revealed in his weekly blog that the average daily turnover on Hong Kong’s stock market from January to September stood at HK$272.9 billion, representing 6.4 per cent year-on-year growth.
“The yields of long-term US bonds have risen to a 24-year high, which has heightened investor concerns over global economic prospects and inevitably dampened recent sentiment in the Hong Kong stock market,” he said.

Narva‑Jõesuu to build €1.2 million tennis and padel center

Narva‑Jõesuu to build €1.2 million tennis and padel center
At the initiative of the Narva‑Jõesuu tennis club and with support from European Union funding, a racket‑sports center with four tennis courts and two padel courts will be completed there by next summer.
The center will give both local residents and visitors better opportunities for sports and help enliven the Narva‑Jõesuu town center area.
Narva‑Jõesuu actually has the longest tennis history in Estonia. The first tennis club was founded 117 years ago by summer visitors from St. Petersburg, and before World War II the town had six tennis courts.
After the war, decline began, and the resort town's last tennis court became overgrown by the end of the previous century, explains Erki Jaanson, board member of the Narva‑Jõesuu tennis club.
"The same thing happened as in other small towns. It wasn't a priority sport, nor was it an Olympic sport for a long time, so the Soviet era did its work," Jaanson said.
Now Narva‑Jõesuu is one of the last resort towns in Estonia to bring back major tennis.
At the initiative of the local tennis club, a racket‑sports center is being built near the seaside, with four tennis courts, two padel courts, and space for several more courts if the project gains momentum.
"Everyone I've spoken to is eagerly waiting for these courts and promises to come play. One goal is definitely to have a summer base for Kadriorg, where training camps can be held," said Jaanson, who also heads the Kadriorg tennis club.
"A few years ago, the situation in Viljandi was such that to hold a training camp there, you had to book the courts three years in advance. Things have improved somewhat now because so many padel courts have been added and the player groups overlap a bit. The situation has normalized," he explained.
Tennis players are not jealous of padel's success.
"I'm rather glad that a somewhat simpler sport has emerged alongside tennis. It also works the other way — some people reach tennis through padel," Jaanson said.
Construction has already begun in Narva‑Jõesuu, and the tennis courts are taking shape.
According to Jaanson, it took more than ten years from idea to implementation.
The undertaking is expensive, because at least four tennis courts are needed to practice properly and host competitions.
The Narva‑Jõesuu racket‑sports center will open next summer. Building the courts costs €1.2 million, most of which is covered by European Union support.
--

Elections have begun in Bosnia, the results of which could affect the country&apos;s bid to join the EU
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
09:17:00 EEST
15:17:00 KST

Elections have begun in Bosnia, the results of which could affect the country's bid to join the EU
Kyiv • UNN
Bosnians are electing the presidency, parliament and local authorities amid interethnic tensions. The elections are accompanied by glitches in the new electronic system.
On Sunday, Bosnians will take part in elections whose results could affect the country’s bid to join the European Union, as well as the influence that the United States and Russia seek to exert over this small Balkan state, UNN reports, citing AP and Reuters.
Details
General voting began in Bosnia on Sunday morning. Most citizens of this multiethnic Balkan country are focused on everyday problems, while some leading politicians are stoking wartime tensions that have kept the country divided since the brutal 1992–1995 conflict.
About 3.4 million voters in Bosnia are electing three members of the country’s multiethnic presidency, members of the national parliament, and heads of government bodies in the two entities: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (where Muslims constitute the majority) and Republika Srpska (where ethnic Serbs predominate).
Bosnia has a complex system of governing bodies created as a result of the 1995 peace agreement brokered by the United States. Its goal was to resolve the ethnic disputes between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs, and Catholic Croats that caused the war.
On Sunday morning, Associated Press journalists reported numerous polling stations where voting failed to begin on time due to problems with the new digital voting technology — a measure introduced to address previous problems with the falsification of results.
Pro-Russian Dodik retains influence despite being absent from the ballot
A pro-Russian politician who, although not running personally, played a leading role in the campaign and intensified divisions that are raising fears of a new wave of instability became the focus of the election race.
Milorad Dodik — a nationalist and former president of Republika Srpska (where Serbs make up the majority of the population) — has been barred from holding public office after being found guilty of failing to comply with the decisions of the international representative overseeing implementation of the 1995 peace agreement.
Dodik’s party, the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, is likely to win the election in Republika Srpska; the politician himself has just returned from Moscow, where he met with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
During his party’s final campaign rally, held on Friday evening in Banja Luka (the administrative center of Republika Srpska), Dodik told supporters that Bosnia was "dead." "It is an impossible country. It makes no sense," Dodik said at the rally, which was also attended by Russia’s ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Igor Kalabukhov.
Analyst Dragan Bursać noted that although Dodik is appearing on the ballot for the first time in nearly 30 years, he "still runs the process. He is everywhere."
"He has flooded the media space not only within the entity of Republika Srpska, but throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is obvious that measures to remove him from political life are not working — instead, he is using them to his own advantage," Bursać said.
Voting is taking place amid rising interethnic tensions
Although peace has prevailed in Bosnia in recent years, politicians continue to fuel divisions between Bosniaks (mostly Muslims), Serbs, and Croats. Leaders of the Bosnian Serbs, such as Dodik, insist on separating their entity from the rest of Bosnia, raising concerns in the West about a possible new outbreak of tensions.
Bosnia — one of Europe’s poorest countries — is still trying to recover from the consequences of the war that began in 1992 after it declared independence from the former Yugoslavia (which was dominated by Serbs) and an armed uprising by ethnic Serbs who sought to establish their own state and join Serbia.
More than 100,000 people were killed in the conflict, and millions became internally displaced persons.
Bosnia officially seeks to join the European Union, but the integration process has stalled despite the EU’s efforts to encourage the country’s divided leaders to cooperate in carrying out reforms.
On the eve of election day, Durak Miler, a resident of Bosnia’s capital Sarajevo, said that the politicians in power "are simply poisoning people with their speeches."
"It is time for us to change the old faces," he said. "They have been in charge for 35 years already... I think that whoever replaces them will work better in the interests of pensioners and low-income people."
Painful memories of the war were recently intensified by public commemorations in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs of wartime military commander Ratko Mladić, who died at the end of August while serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes.
Bosnian Serbs regard Mladić as a hero, despite the fact that a UN court found him guilty of the mass murder of more than 8,000 Muslims (men and boys) in Srebrenica in 1995 and of other atrocities.
Senior Bosnian Serb officials attended a memorial service for Mladić in Belgrade, drawing sharp criticism from the EU and outrage from Bosnian politicians.
Electronic election security measures introduced
The authorities are using electronic voter identification and ballot scanning for the first time to prevent violations or organized manipulation that previously cast doubt on the fairness of elections. Salko Bijavica from the southern city of Mostar expressed satisfaction that "every vote will be counted," as well as hope that these changes would give people faith in the fairness of elections.
Most of the 75 political parties in Bosnia taking part in the elections are formed along ethnic lines: some operate in the Serb-controlled Republika Srpska, while others operate in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, where Bosniaks and Croats predominate. These two entities are united by shared central authorities—the presidency and parliament.
The Bosniak nationalist "Party of Democratic Action" focused its campaign on preserving Bosnia’s unity and opposing Serb separatism. Bosnian Croats also largely support parties representing their ethnic community, including the Bosnian branch of Croatia’s ruling conservative party—the "Croatian Democratic Union."
Polling stations will close at 19:00 local time.
Many disillusioned citizens believe that politicians use nationalist rhetoric to avoid addressing important problems, such as low living standards and the mass exodus of young people from the country.
Ivan Silic from Mostar said: "I have seen no improvements since I started voting."
"We all know who is living well," he added. "They (the politicians) are better off, while for the rest of us everything remains the same as before."

Estonia's crisis preparedness improves, but shelter shortage remains critical
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:17:00 UTC
15:17:00 KST

Estonia's crisis preparedness improves, but shelter shortage remains critical
Estonia's preparedness for major crises is steadily improving, but much remains to be done, according to both the interior minister and the Rescue Board. The biggest challenge is the shortage of shelters in Estonia.
At New Year's, a large part of Tallinn was left without water for several hours. Since spring, drones that strayed from Russian airspace have entered Estonia. These are just a few examples of the kinds of crises Estonia is currently preparing for.
According to Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200), the situation is most critical when it comes to shelters. There are currently just over 300, a small fraction of what Estonia needs.
"We have picked the low-hanging fruit, meaning we have identified and marked the existing shelters so people know they are there, but now comes the next challenge. We actually need to adapt spaces in buildings that already exist for use as shelters," Taro said.
However, converting the basements of apartment buildings into shelters has not proved particularly popular. Various grants are available, but they are not being used. Tallinn, for example, has €1.5 million in its budget this year for apartment associations.
"We still have money available. Apartment associations could take this issue a little more seriously. We are currently offering to cover 70 percent of their costs for adapting basements and carrying out electrical, plumbing and ventilation work, provided the total is around €10,000," Tallinn Deputy Mayor Tiit Terik (Center Party) said.
More public shelters are also being added. In Tallinn, most are located in the city center, but options become increasingly limited farther toward the outskirts.
"In the future, we also want to establish mobile shelters in places like these. We plan to bring them into Tallinn's urban space next year," Terik said.
Starting this year, all new large buildings, including apartment buildings, must be built with a proper shelter.
The Rescue Board, however, is concerned about how well schools and kindergartens are prepared for crises.
"The situation in schools and kindergartens today is still very worrying. We have not done much preparation there and we need to address this so that children are always protected while they are at school or kindergarten. Frankly, there are no major plans at the moment. It will probably only be in a couple of years, using European Union funding, that we will actually be able to start adapting these spaces," Rescue Board Director General Margo Klaos said.

Bosnia and Herzegovina holds elections for new president, lawmakers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:09:47 UTC
15:09:47 KST

Voting began on Sunday in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s general elections, with more than 3.4 million registered voters eligible to choose new leadership and lawmakers at several levels of government.
Polling stations opened at 7 am local time (0500GMT) and are scheduled to close at 7 pm, according to the Central Election Commission (CIK).
A total of 3,414,364 voters are eligible to vote in the elections, which are held every four years.
Voters will elect the Bosniak, Croat and Serb members of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s three-member presidency, as well as members of the state-level Parliamentary Assembly.
They will also elect lawmakers to the House of Representatives of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, one of the country’s two entities. The National Assembly of Republika Srpska is the other.
Voters will also choose the president and vice presidents of Republika Srpska and members of the 10 cantonal assemblies in the Federation entity.
A total of 518 officials will be elected.
Bosnia and Herzegovina has a complex political system established under the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, which ended the 1992 - 1995 war.
The country consists of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, as well as the self-governing Brcko District.
10 candidates seek seats on tripartite presidency
Ten candidates are competing for the three seats on the presidency.
Voters in the Federation can vote for either a Bosniak or Croat member of the Presidency, while voters in the Republika Srpska entity elect the Serb member.
Incumbent Denis Becirovic, Bakir Izetbegovic, Semir Efendic and Fahrudin Radoncic are running for the Bosniak seat.
Darijana Filipovic, Zdenko Lucic and Slaven Kovacevic are competing for the Croat seat, while incumbent Zeljka Cvijanovic, Marinko Bozovic and Nebojsa Vukanovic are running for the Serb seat.
Twelve candidates are also competing for the presidency of Republika Srpska.
The CIK approved 75 political parties, 29 coalitions and four independent candidates.
More than 7,000 candidacies have been registered at all levels of government.
New election technology used for first time
The election also marks the first nationwide use of new voting technology designed to improve the identification of voters, counting of ballots and transmission of results.
Biometric voter verification, ballot scanners and video surveillance systems are being used at around 4,500 polling locations.
After their identities are checked, voters will undergo fingerprint verification. Voting will continue to be conducted using paper ballots, which will be scanned before being placed in ballot boxes.
Data from the scanned ballots will be transmitted directly to the CIK, allowing preliminary and incomplete results to be announced at around 8 pm, earlier than in previous elections.
The ballots will also be counted manually.
The election commission has said additional checks will be conducted if there is a significant discrepancy between scanned and manually counted ballots. If the discrepancy remains, the manual count will be accepted as the official result.
Bosnian diaspora participates in elections
A total of 48,078 voters registered to cast ballots by mail, marking one of the lowest levels of diaspora registration in recent election cycles.
Voting is also taking place at 20 Bosnian diplomatic and consular missions in 13 countries, including Germany, Austria, Croatia, Serbia, Slovenia, Switzerland, Belgium, Denmark, Sweden, the Netherlands, Norway, the US, Qatar and Jordan.
The number of registered voters is slightly higher than in the 2022 general elections, when 3.37 million people were on the electoral roll.
In the 2022 elections, Becirovic was elected as the Bosniak member of the presidency, Zeljko Komsic as the Croat member and Cvijanovic as the Serb member.
Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence in 1992, and its first elections following the war were held in September 1996.

Merz visits Kyiv as Russia urges diplomats to leave
Unknown

06:07:28 UTC
15:07:28 KST

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky (L) and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz (2nd L) visit damaged building of the Ukrainian Academy of Science in Kyiv on October 4, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Germany's chancellor arrived in Ukraine's capital on a surprise visit to demonstrate European support in the face of an upsurge in attacks. (AFP Photo)
Russia struck another major bridge in Kiev on Oct. 4, soon after Germany’s chancellor arrived on a surprise visit to show European support in the face of an upsurge in attacks.
Air raid sirens blared repeatedly across the Ukrainian capital throughout the morning, including as Friedrich Merz met President Volodymyr Zelensky at the National Academy of Sciences, which was hit by a Russian attack drone on Sept. 28.
Zelensky told him that people in Kiev were suffering “terrible nights and days” from the relentless attacks and called Ukraine’s Russian adversaries “absolute barbarians.”
“We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place,” noted Merz.
“These barbarous attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop. These are war crimes that are being committed daily here.”
Kiev Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a strike had damaged the road surface on the Northern Bridge, one of several connecting the eastern and western parts of the city over the Dnipro River which have been struck in repeatedly in the last four days.
Klitschko has said that Kiev, largely spared from the devastation wrought near the frontlines in nearly five years of conflict, should now be on a war footing due to the upsurge in attacks.
A spate of round-the-clock attacks has hit residential areas, petrol stations, schools, rail and communications infrastructure while near-constant air raid sirens disrupt daily life and put people on edge.
Merz said as he arrived that Ukraine “needs all our support in the coming weeks.”
“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he added.
Ukraine wants more Western military support, including advanced interceptors to shoot down Russia’s new fast-moving, jet-powered drones.
The Russian Defense Ministry on Oct. 4 vowed to ramp up its strikes on “military and military-industrial facilities” plus “related infrastructure in Kiev” and elsewhere after Zelensky this week said Ukraine would intensify its own attacks against oil facilities that it says supply Moscow’s troops.
Merz this week called for NATO and European unity against Russia as well as his own country, where the far-right, Moscow-friendly AfD opposition is on the rise.
There have been increasing fears in Europe that it could find itself in Russia’s crosshairs.
On Oct. 3, Moscow warned foreigners and diplomats to leave Kiev, saying “massive” new airstrikes would hit the city.
It made a similar threat in May but leaders from Ukraine’s allies have continued to make visits.
“The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe’s support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!” EU ambassador Katarina Mathernova wrote on X on Oct. 4.
Mathernova told AFP separately that “nobody is moving,” although European embassies always had contingency plans, she added.

Object that halted Helsinki–Tallinn ferry traffic turns out harmless
An object found in the sea that halted ship traffic from Helsinki on Saturday evening is likely part of an old shipwreck, Finnish authorities said. The shipping lane was reopened overnight.
At 7:20 p.m. Saturday, Finnish police received a report from the Border Guard about a funnel-shaped metal object in the southern part of the Kustaanmiekka Strait, in a shipping lane used by passenger vessels. Police and the Coast Guard then cordoned off the area. Police asked the Finnish Navy for assistance in identifying the object, Finnish public broadcaster Yle reported.
Fintraffic, the agency responsible for monitoring maritime traffic, told Finnish news agency STT that the restricted sea area was south of Särkkä and Suomenlinna and west of Vallisaari. Ships arriving at and departing from the Katajanokka terminal and the Olympia Terminal in Helsinki's South Harbor are among those that pass through the area.
Finnish police has ongoing operation in Gulf of Finland since 8pm local time, ferry traffic between Estonia and Finland temporarily stopped as the shipping lane is closed by authorities. Place is near Kustaanmiekka just outside Helsinki, no further info given. https://t.co/Mt9mR3X56Z
— Aki H Heikkinen (@akihheikkinen) October 3, 2026
The Finnish Navy, which arrived to identify the object, said its preliminary assessment was that it was a very old mechanical part from a shipwreck. The Helsinki Police Department said in a statement issued at around 2:30 a.m. that the object was not an explosive device.
Authorities lifted the restrictions on the sea area and police left the scene.
The object will be towed to Santahamina for further examination at a later date, Yle reported.
A passenger aboard Viking Line's XPRS told the newspaper Ilta-Sanomat on Saturday evening that the vessel was unable to depart Helsinki for Tallinn on schedule because of the discovery. The ship was due to depart at 8 p.m., but according to Yle, it did not leave the port until 2 a.m. Sunday.

====================================================================================================

Party conference will be more upbeat than last year, Tories say – but that’s not the whole story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:00:20 UTC
15:00:20 KST

The forthcoming Conservative conference will be, almost everyone in the party agrees, notably more upbeat and unified than last year. There is a similar consensus that Kemi Badenoch is doing well as party leader. That is, however, not the whole story.
“The mood is better but the facts are still very poor,” one Conservative MP said. “We are still a distant third in the polls, and if there was an election tomorrow we would lose, and badly. That means the mood is overhyped.”
This is the inescapable shadow over the Tory gathering in Birmingham, which begins on Sunday. Almost two years since Badenoch was elected leader, her party is still polling lower than it did in 2024, when it suffered a catastrophically poor election result.
There is, of course, context behind her MPs’ patience, not least the fracturing of the political landscape and the rise of a new competitor on the right in Reform UK.
But while Badenoch’s future is secure for now, there is concern among some Tories that her dogged focus on winning back support from Nigel Farage’s party, with little on offer to more centrist voters, poses both political and reputational risks.
“We need to be attracting as many voters who left us for the Lib Dems as Reform, and I don’t personally think we have got the balance right,” a shadow minister said.
“There is an economic offering, but they don’t want us to be so intolerant on social issues. The way we are going, we risk being seen as the nasty party again.”
The phrase “nasty party” was coined by Theresa May in 2002, when the then party chair warned activists against focusing on too narrow a voter base and targeting other parts of society with punitive policies.
Even if Badenoch has learned to prioritise core policy and walk away from culture war arguments, it seems she has not fully absorbed May’s lessons about not punching down.
In recent weeks, the Tories have pledged to bar non-Britons from social housing, strip UK citizenship from dual nationals convicted of serious crimes, and cut some benefits payments to a “subsistence” level, with restrictions preventing the money being used to buy alcohol or tobacco.
The main pre-conference policy offering was in a similar vein: a pledge to slash overseas aid to pay for 50,000 new prison places.
There are plenty of Conservative MPs who don’t view this as a problem. “I’ve not heard any colleagues say they were worried about the nasty party stuff,” one said. “In contrast, a lot of constituents say they are very worried about welfare costs.”
One of the paradoxes of Badenoch’s tenure is the relative lack of open dissent, even on totemic ideas such as the commitment to leave the European convention on human rights (ECHR) to enact more rigorous deportation policies.
This is, in part, because many of her MPs respect the way Badenoch has taken time over decisions and sought to make her case, with the ECHR plan prefaced by a 185-page report by David Wolfson, the shadow attorney general.
But its is also a function of the apparent lack of appetite for a fight from centrist Conservatives such as the One Nation group, most of whom are either outside parliament, lying low on the backbenches or co-opted into the Badenoch project, as with Tom Tugendhat, made shadow foreign secretary in a recent mini-reshuffle.
“The thing about the One Nation group is that we never actually did anything,” one centrist MP said. “We got together and metaphorically held hands from time to time, but that was about it.
“Either way, everybody seems to be pulling together now. It’s not quite yet the Blues Brothers on a mission from God, but there’s a real sense of purpose. There are no factions, no five families. The arguments have stopped.”
This end of the arguments – at least for now – is in part down to Badenoch’s improved performance. While last year’s party conference was widely seen as make or break for a leader who had started shakily, she is now feted by Tory MPs for her performances in the Commons.
Her personal poll ratings are also on the rise, even if this is a relative achievement – Badenoch’s net favourability score with YouGov has gone up by 20 points, but remains at a lowly minus 15. Similarly, when voters are asked to describe her, common epithets include not just “strong” but also “mean” and “cold”.
Last year’s conference was also overshadowed by comments from Robert Jenrick, the then shadow justice secretary, who was accused of amplifying toxic nationalism after he complained about “not seeing another white face” in a part of Birmingham where the event was taking place.
There is no risk of this happening again, given Jenrick defected to Reform three months later, having been sacked by Badenoch for plotting against her.
“We are very unified, and a lot of that coincided with Jenrick going. We have outsourced our toxicity to Reform,” a shadow minister said. “But there is more to it than that. This time last year, Reform and Keir Starmer were both talking about us as being dead or irrelevant, and we’re not. Kemi has had a lot of cut-through.”
What public dissent does exist often comes from Prosper UK, a centrist grouping launched earlier this year by Andy Street, the ex-West Midlands mayor, and Ruth Davidson, who formerly led the Scottish Conservatives.
Among its vice-chairs is David Gauke, the May-era cabinet minister, who says Badenoch must pay more attention to “politically homeless” moderate Tories who helped the Liberal Democrats win dozens of seats in southern England in 2024.
“There’s a set of the electorate that don’t feel the party has spoken to them for at least 10 years, and Conservatives need to start doing that,” he said.
“There is no route to a Conservative majority that does not involve winning back seats in Oxfordshire and Surrey and other parts of the home counties.”
Badenoch’s calculation, according to Tim Bale, professor of politics at Queen Mary, University of London, seemed to be to try to stop Reform running riot, and then hoping Reform implodes and Andy Burnham’s government slumps.
“It is a risk, but what else have they got?” he said. “But I can’t see how it’s going to work for them and where the votes are going to come from.
“They seem to be overstating the extent to which voters think even Badenoch is a good thing. She’s still in negative territory. They have gone from a situation in which they got 24% of the vote in 2024 and they’re now, at best, on just over 20%. If this is what success looks like, I’d love to know what failure is.”

‘They call every week’: the phishing attacks targeting past victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:00:20 UTC
15:00:20 KST

When the British actor Lisa Riley was preparing to travel to the US last year, she applied online for an Esta so she would not need a visa. After finding the site through a Google search she filled in her passport, bank and personal details and waited for the confirmation, which normally takes just under an hour.
When it failed to arrive, she emailed an address from the site where she had paid and got back a message unlike any she had seen before, with a link to a website that displayed a jumble of words and letters.
It was then she realised she had been scammed. But that was just the start of her problems, which persist to this day. She has been repeatedly targeted by criminals, receiving text messages and calls many times every week.
Riley was the victim of a fraud where criminals create websites similar to the legitimate one run by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP). After fooling unsuspecting applicants they pocket a fee and use the personal details of victims for later scams.
Riley lost £16 – the cost of an Esta back then – but says there has been a huge increase in the number of scam calls and texts she has received in the 17 months since the fraud happened.
Often the person claims to be from her bank with queries about a money transfer. “Calls are once a week, easy – sometimes twice a week,” she says. “And the texts even more often.”
Research from Nationwide building society suggests that 15% of people have given personal information to something who later turned out not to be genuine, leaving them open to future frauds.
“Criminals do sadly retarget people after an initial scam,” says Annya Burskys, head of fraud operations at Nationwide. “They take the personal information they have gained and either sell it on to other scammers or use them to make follow-up bank impersonation calls, texts and emails appear more convincing.”
What it looks like
The fake Esta site that stole Riley’s personal details looked very similar to the official one and showed up high in search results, she says.
“The webpage was absolutely identical so there was nothing that would remotely make me fearful up until [I realised],” she says.
Criminals can use AI to recreate legitimate government sites and will frequently use key words such as “Esta”, in the domain name to try to portray legitimacy.
A spokesperson for the US CBP says some sites may demand action by the applicant quickly, a common tactic by criminals to try to get people to act without thinking something through.
What to do
Only use the official Esta website, which has a .gov address, or the mobile app.
“Applicants should protect their Esta confirmation number and payment details, retain application records, and review financial statements for unauthorised charges,” says the CBP spokesperson.
“Suspected fraud should be documented and reported promptly to the applicant’s financial institution and appropriate local government reporting channels.”
In the UK that means telling your bank and Report Fraud.
If you have inadvertently handed over your personal details you are at risk of future scams, so be alert to unexpected calls, texts or emails, says Burskys.
“Don’t feel pressured to act. A genuine call or message from your bank will never ask you to move money, never ask you to share codes, and will never tell you what to say to your bank or friends, family,” she says.
“Take a moment to verify who you’re speaking to and contact your bank directly using trusted contact information from your bank card or search for the official website if you’re unsure.”

Alone with the stars, lynx and wolves in ‘Empty Spain’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:00:20 UTC
15:00:20 KST

As photographed at night from a satellite, or the International Space Station (ISS), the Iberian peninsula looks encrusted with lights along its coastal edges. Madrid forms a big pulsing cluster near the centre, while surrounding hinterlands appear as something of a void. Ever fewer people live out in Castile and León and Extremadura, adjoining regions that cover much of what is known as La España Vacía, or “Empty Spain”.
Not many visit either, or at least not compared with Barcelona and other glowing nodes of the tourist circuit. So, while the big ports and resorts struggle to manage surplus holidaymakers, there is room for plenty more out west, toward the Portuguese border. Some have been following the stars that way lately, under the auspices of an astrotourism initiative called Extremadura Buenas Noches.
A route map plotted point-to-point between optimal stargazing sites leads to distant outposts like La Siberia (so-called because it felt that remote to workers who laid down the first roads and railways in these parts) and the Corral de los Lobos, an ancient stone enclosure on a hilltop, built to trap wolves when they outnumbered the farmers and shepherds around here.
Corral de los Lobos also lies in one of the rainier reaches of the Spanish interior, and the weather has mostly closed over the night sky when I go up to look. But even through breaks in the clouds, I can see the ISS pass in its elliptical orbit. Beyond that, Jupiter. And, much farther out, the Milky Way.
“Big region, small population, almost no light pollution,” says forestry engineer and nature guide Alberto Garzón Fernández the next day, on a misty hike through Garganta de los Infiernos, a nature reserve named for the fearsome sound of water through its gorges.
There are no other forms of pollution either, it seems. We look down into gigantic cauldrons of granite known as marmitas, where the River Jerte swirls like soup in a pot around eroded rock smooth as brushed steel. The lichen across the wet surface is a luminous green, “a bioindicator of clean air”.
“Extremadura is, no doubt, the most natural and healthy place to live,” Garzón says. His claim extends to non-human natives, not least the birds, and he points skyward to the ghostly profiles of honey buzzards and griffon vultures floating in the vapour off the peaks above. Thanks to “sound management”, as he puts it, the Spanish imperial eagle is now seen in much healthier numbers up there.
The Iberian lynx population, meanwhile, is climbing steadily from dangerous lows of a few decades ago in neighbouring Monfragüe national park, where Garzón was born and raised. And the Iberian wolf – hunted and displaced almost to extinction before recent, belated protections – has been making a comeback over the flanking Gredos mountains.
That’s close enough for their howls to be heard again from the Corral de los Lobos, on those same clear nights when “the stars look so close you could touch them”, says Garzón. The return of these signature species gives him hope for our own. “To me, they represent our capacity to do things right, but we so often wait until the last minute.”
If this region has felt the benefit of a minimal human presence lately, it’s hardly untouched by the increasing hazards of our time. The heatwave-borne wildfires of 2025 burned through nearly 20,000 hectares (49,400 acres) of the Jerte valley’s famous cherry orchards. All that damage is bound to affect the harvests to follow – one of the few events to draw a crowd to this area. “It will still be beautiful,” says Sara Cudero Morcuende at Alimentación Sara, a grocery store in the nearby mountain town of Valverde de la Vera.
Her shop is so well stocked with local delicacies that the place would make a killing if transplanted to, say, east London: figs and olives from surrounding groves, sweet and hot paprika dried over open fires, all sorts of cherry jams and liqueurs. But her town, like many in the region, has lost thousands of residents in recent years.
There’s a gothic-romantic hush to the cobbled streets below Valverde de la Vera’s ruined and overgrown castle. The quietude, the quasi-abandonment, may yet enhance the appeal to those passing through, though it can’t be good for business. “A few more customers would be nice,” says Cudero, but otherwise the town has only a couple of tapas bars, a few guesthouses, and no hotel.
For my part, I make use of Spain’s state-owned parador network, which tends to offer surprisingly affordable rooms in converted convents and palaces, mostly within the medieval walls of the nearest comparatively big cities. The provincial capital, Cáceres; Trujillo, with its dreamlike hilltop fortress; and Plasencia, with its two half-cathedrals (one never fully demolished, the other forever unfinished), make good, solid bases.
Fun fact: there are more pigs than people in these regions, including the black, acorn-fed pigs of the dehesa forest, whose meat becomes the world-renowned jamón ibérico. Including, too, the very chunky fellow I encounter in La Alberca, enjoying a siesta in a sty that is also a kind of shrine. Custom dictates that a single fat pig be allowed to wander and eat at its leisure for seven months of each year, until it’s raffled off for the feast of San Antón in January. In the past, that porker was invariably eaten, but some recent winners have apparently kept them as pets.
La Alberca is also known for its gorgeous three-storey houses with half-timber facades, the legacy of Christian settlers from Burgundy, who came to occupy territory reconquered from the Moors 1,000 years ago. The encircling mountains are called the Sierra de Francia for that reason, their slopes thick with oak forests that yield many fine species of mushroom.
“You can eat them all,” says biologist and guide Marino Esteban (La Alberca visitor centre operates hikes into the forest), on a walk through woods that look more like French or even English countryside. “But some you can only eat once.” This is his way of saying that certain types are toxic. This is also to say that a massive meal at Meson de San Martín – a stonebuilt tavern that seems the only place open in nearby village San Martín del Castañar – is not all about the ham.
There’s plenty of that, but also plenty of the freshly picked penny bun mushrooms grilled with garlic salt and olive oil, not to mention the chestnuts, cheeses, tomatoes and potatoes of surrounding farmlands, and the red wine made from native rufete grapes – as good as anything I’ve tried from more domineering production regions such as La Rioja and Ribera del Duero.
And here’s the big secret I learn on this little road trip: you can often eat and drink better and cheaper in “Empty Spain” than in most of the busier quarters. This was one of the great lunches of my life, I tell the cheery chef, Alfonso Buenaventura Calvo. His wife and co-owner Belén answers for him: “Of course it was.”
The trip was provided by the Spanish tourist office, Turismo Extremadura and Turismo Castilla Y León. Accommodation provided by Paradores). For stargazing, see extremadurabuenasnoches.com. Aventura Jerte offers tours with Alberto Garzón Fernández

‘You have 10 minutes to decide’: answering the life-changing call to become a kinship carer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:00:20 UTC
15:00:20 KST

Clive vividly remembers the day when, without warning or time to work out what he was really letting himself in for, he became a kinship carer.
“The social worker left, the door closed and Savannah was lying there in a carry cot, wrapped up in a pink blanket. She looked so calm and so comfy, absolutely oblivious about what’s just happened.
“There was this eerie silence in the house. It was just me and her and a little suitcase with some belongings in it. I burst into tears. I’m a teacher, but training as a teacher does not prepare you for looking after a baby.
“I didn’t know how to change a baby’s nappy, I didn’t have a push chair, I didn’t have a cot, I didn’t know where she was going to sleep. I didn’t have anything.”
A few hours earlier, Clive, a primary school headteacher, had taken a call at work from children’s services. He assumed it would be about one of his pupils, but it was about his six-week-old niece. Would he, as a family member, take her into temporary care?
“So I, quite blase, said: ‘Yeah, no problem at all. I’ll need to put a few things in place, so just give me a couple of days.’ They were like: ‘No, she needs to come to you today. We need to drop her off at four o’clock.’
“I was kind of like: ‘Well, what happens if I don’t say yes today?’ They said they’d have to come up with ‘other options’. So I started to panic: what if she goes into foster care or for adoption? So I said yes – and deal with the consequences later.”
“I went home and just sat there waiting. It was a bit bizarre because I don’t think I’ve ever been home at 3.30pm on a school day before. And then social care came, dropped her off. And that was that.
“I’d only ever invested in my career. I was career-driven all the time. And then a baby was sprung on me that I’d never planned for.”
Clive, then 32, would now admit he was naive about the consequences of the decision that changed his life. Nine years on, with the “temporary” stay having become permanent, “Uncle Clive” is Savannah’s legal guardian, though she is in regular contact with her birth parents. He adores her, and theirs is a heartwarming kinship success story. She still has the pink blanket. But the path, he admits, while joyful and fulfilling, has not always been smooth.
“I would do it all again. It’s the best thing that could have happened for my niece. But at times it’s been quite isolating and exhausting.”
More than 141,000 children in England and Wales are like Savannah, being raised by kinship carers. These are normally relatives, like Clive, or family friends who step in to prevent children whose parents can no longer look after them from entering the care system.
Despite the dependence of children’s services on kinship care – twice as many children enter kinship arrangements as are fostered – it remains startlingly informal, with few of the practical, legal and financial supports that accompany fostering or adoption. Often it can seem kinship care is invisible to policymakers.
Clive’s experience – being given just hours to make a momentous decision about whether to take over care of a loved one – is far from unusual. A new survey by the care charity Kinship found that four in 10 carers were given less than an hour to make a decision. A further fifth had less than 24 hours.
Alan and Julie, both 65, were given 10 minutes to decide whether they would care for their severely disabled grandchild Ella, who was then 10 months old. They had just got back home to Leeds after a holiday when they got the call from social services.
“They said: ‘This place closes in 10 minutes. We need to know if you are prepared to take the child on, or they will go into local authority care and you will probably never see them again,’” Alan recalls. “Of course, it was a no-brainer. We said we’d take her on straight away, as we would any of our grandchildren.”
Having made that snap decision, almost all kinship carers report that it changes their lives profoundly. The ramifications are broad and not always immediately appreciated, and official support can be patchy or nonexistent. Overnight, there is an extra person in the home to feed and clothe, who may have suffered trauma and have special needs. There is often an unexpected strain on finances, carer health and wider family relationships.
Many kinship carers give up work, often at the request of social services. Clive was terrified he would have to abandon his career. He worried he wouldn’t be able to pay the mortgage if that happened, and if he lost the house, Savannah would be taken into foster care.
He was lucky: his school was incredibly supportive and allowed him to work flexibly – he recalls bottle-feeding Savannah while delivering a staff training session. He also has a strong network of friends and family. But he knows from support groups organised by Kinship that other carers are not so fortunate.
Leasa, 56, and Oly, 57, from west London, say that having made the snap decision to care for their nephews, Jake and Luke, they had to fight for support they expected would be automatic. With their own son at home, there were suddenly five people crammed into their tiny two-bed flat, but the council didn’t seem interested.
Oly recalls he had once enquired about becoming a foster carer, but was told he stood no chance because his home was not big enough. That didn’t seem to matter when it came to kinship care. When he asked his housing association landlord about moving to a bigger flat, just before his nephews arrived, there was little sympathy. “I was told: ‘Why are you making your house overcrowded?’”
Leasa and Oly are still in the flat, and for the past five years, they have slept on a sofa bed in the lounge. The room is crammed with storage boxes, and is also where the couple’s nephews do their homework. The arrangement works partly because Oly works night shifts and Leasa, who is a nanny, works during the day.
“Some of our friends sat us down and said: ‘What are you doing? Where will you find the money to look after these kids?’ My mum thought I was crazy,” says Leasa. “What people with the power to do something need to understand is that kinship care really does upend your life, physically and emotionally.”
Looking back, Oly says they were naive. Eventually, with the help of a lawyer, they got a bigger financial allowance. They don’t regret becoming kinship carers for a minute, but the nagging feeling remains that social services exploited their goodwill.
“I feel a bit blindsided by the council,” says Oly. “Sometimes, I think: why didn’t you tell us (about the support available). It didn’t have to be like this, right?”
Clive says: “Kinship carers are like the shadow of the care system. We are not well recognised, not well understood or appreciated, and the system almost takes advantage of that. That’s what it feels like.”
The chief executive of Kinship, Lucy Peake, says kinship carers save £4.3bn a year that the state would otherwise spend on children’s homes and foster care.
“Relatives often say they are told that if they don’t step in, children will go into care,” Peake says. “They step up to do the right thing for children. Kinship carers regularly tell us they felt under pressure to make a decision without enough time, information or clarity about the support available to them.
“It’s time their extraordinary contribution to children and our society is recognised,” she adds.
Earlier this year, the government launched a three-year pilot scheme in seven local authorities giving kinship carers a financial allowance in line with foster carers for the first time. Foster carers currently receive between £170 and £299 a week, depending on where they live and the age of the child. The children’s minister, Josh MacAlister, said the pilot recognised “the vital role [kinship carers] play ensuring families can stay together”.
Kinship welcomes the scheme, but points out it covers just 5,000 children. “Unlike foster carers who receive months of preparation and ongoing support, kinship carers have no notice and get little support, forcing many to lose jobs, pensions, savings and even their own retirement to keep a child they love out of the care system,” says Peake.
Research shows kinship care is not only cheaper than residential or foster care, but more likely to lead to better outcomes for the child while helping them retain a strong sense of family and identity. Yet the latest Kinship survey found many carers were struggling financially, falling into debt and relying on food banks.
For all the stress, many enthuse about the joy kinship caring has brought. Alan talks about lying on the floor next to Ella, watching her smile as he sings Beatles songs to her. She is non-verbal and is only just learning to walk aged nine, but “she has a way of showing us things”, Alan says proudly.
Clive says he is often asked at conferences to name his greatest achievement. Once he would have said turning a school around or becoming a headteacher at 28. Now, he says, “keeping my niece in the family means more than any of those accolades”.
For Oly, “the best thing is when I look at the boys and they are laughing from the heart. They didn’t do that when they first came. They were in shock. So when I see that laughter, and feel those hugs … yeah, that fills my heart.”

Ministers explore how to stop regional leaders misusing planned new spending powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
06:00:19 UTC
15:00:19 KST

Ministers are mulling over how to ensure that England’s regional leaders do not misuse their newfound spending muscle, as Whitehall prepares to devolve more revenue to local levels.
Ideas under consideration include a new select committee in Westminster, enhanced reporting rules and a new audit body focused on local and regional government.
The Guardian understands the idea has even been mooted of allowing spendthrift mayors to be recalled by the electorate, as can happen to rule-breaking MPs.
The government will publish a white paper on “rewiring the state” later this month, setting out detailed plans to hand over more income tax revenue to regional mayors.
Rachel Reeves suggested the idea in her Mais lecture earlier this year, and it has been adopted by Andy Burnham’s government, which sees devolution as a big part of its growth policy.
However, officials are concerned about how to ensure local leaders are fully accountable for what they do with the additional cash – including in between elections.
Meg Hillier, the chair of the Treasury select committee, said she believed hers would be the right body to scrutinise the use of the additional spending powers.
“It’s clear that one of the prime minister’s key ambitions is to take spending power out of Westminster and hand it to local leaders,” the Labour MP said.
“It is absolutely critical, though, that strong, clear scrutiny structures are established which match this move to localism. It would be reckless to hand out new powers without ensuring there are transparent mechanisms to hold mayors to account for their decisions.”
Hillier added: “One way to do this is to establish clear lines of authority running through departments and up to ministers, which will allow existing select committees to judge this work.
“A core role of a select committee, particularly the Treasury committee which I chair, is to ensure politicians are publicly held to account for how they decide to spend taxpayers’ money. That is just important at a local level as it is on a national scale.”
The Audit Commission, which had the specific task of overseeing local government spending, was abolished in 2015, with its role split across several other bodies.
As well as shoring up accountability, it is understood there have been lengthy discussions in government about how to balance the need to incentivise local leaders to encourage economic growth, with the imperative to ensure funding is stable over time.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies said last week that the government should use “equalisation payments” to prevent the funding of areas with the highest share of income tax, such as London, pulling ahead of other regions.
David Phillips, the IFS’s devolution expert, said: “With more skin in the game of economic growth, mayors will be more incentivised and empowered to support growth through local policies and investments. But careful design will be needed to prevent richer areas’ funding unfairly pulling ahead.
“The government must also decide how big a gap in funding it is willing to see between ‘winners’ and ‘losers’ in the years ahead.”
Burnham has made clear his intention of accelerating devolution, with his new No 10 North office focusing on the regional aspects of growth policy.

Long-Range FP-9 Missile Ready This Fall, Zelensky Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:57:00 UTC
14:57:00 KST

Ukraine’s domestically developed FP-9 ballistic missile, designed to reach targets at distances including Moscow, will be operational this fall, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced in an interview with Reuters.
Zelensky stated that he contacted the leadership of Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point to urge the expedited finalization of the FP-9, following the combat debut earlier in the week of the shorter-range FP-7 tactical ballistic missile.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I told them: where is my FP-9? We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be [ready] this autumn, I am confident,” Zelensky said.
The president added that Ukraine plans to intensify precision strikes against Russian oil refineries to counter an expanded aerial campaign by Moscow aimed at forcing residents to evacuate Kyiv and other urban centers ahead of winter.
Citing intelligence documents, Zelensky said Russian President Vladimir Putin approved an operational directive expanding strikes against a wider array of civilian targets, including roads, transportation links, schools, and hospitals.
“We have seen the documents and we know that they permit attacks on infrastructure, logistics, roads, schools, hospitals to force people to leave the capital, to leave different cities. This is the goal of the operation,” Zelensky said, attributing the shift in Russian tactics to frontline pressures and personnel losses in the Donbas.
Russian Billionaires Fund 1% of State Budget in ‘Voluntary’ War Levy
Zelensky emphasized that while Ukraine will respond to Moscow’s attacks on its energy grid by targeting Russian energy infrastructure, Ukrainian forces will not conduct indiscriminate attacks on civilian sites.
“We must react in any possible way. To their attacks on our energy sector, we must respond with strikes against their energy sector. Above all – on oil refineries: that is what provides them money for this war. But we will certainly not, as they do, strike any civilian facilities,” Zelensky said.
Deep-strike operations and overnight engagements
Zelensky confirmed that Ukrainian forces carried out long-range strikes early Saturday morning, Oct. 3.
According to the president, the overnight strikes engaged Russian Iskander missile launcher positions and personnel in the Bryansk region alongside targets in the Samara region.
“Over the past 24 hours, our long-range capability worked effectively against facilities operating for the aggressor’s war machine,” Zelensky stated on social media, adding that Ukrainian operations also produced new results in the Black Sea, without disclosing operational specifics.
The confirmed strikes follow an ongoing campaign by Ukrainian defense forces targeting rear logistics, air surveillance networks, and missile batteries deployed in Russian border regions.
Fire Point development and the FREYJA initiative
The deployment timeline for the FP-9 follows Ukraine’s first operational combat use of the FP-7 tactical ballistic missile on Thursday, Oct. 1.
Manufactured by Fire Point, the baseline FP-7 carries a 150-kilogram warhead across an operational reach of approximately 200 to 250 kilometers.
Fire Point founder and chief designer Denys Shtilerman previously compared the platform to the US-manufactured Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS), noting that the sovereign weapon is produced at roughly half the acquisition cost with domestic manufacturing spanning rocket motors and flight guidance systems.
Fire Point officially announced the development of both the FP-7 and the longer-range FP-9 in September 2025, conducting initial flight trials of the FP-7 in February 2026.
Prior to its combat deployment, Fire Point Chief Executive Officer Iryna Terekh confirmed that the FP-7 had completed roughly 15 test launches and final Defense Ministry certifications.
The defense contractor also serves as the industrial hub for the European FREYJA initiative, launched in July alongside nine partner nations to build low-cost ballistic missile interceptors.
Under that program, Fire Point is developing the FP-7.X high-speed interceptor variant, aiming for unit production costs below €1 million ($1.2 million) to reduce reliance on scarce US-supplied Patriot batteries ahead of planned operational interception trials in 2027.

Bosnians head to the polls Sunday in elections that could impact how much influence Russia has over the small Balkan nation, with separatist Serb leader Milorad Dodik dominating the campaign despite his ban from public office. Bosnia and Herzegovina, a country marred by ethnic tensions, has struggled to recover since its brutal 1992-95 conflict.

Polls opened Sunday morning in Bosnia and Herzegovina for a general election in which most citizens of the multi-ethnic Balkan nation are focused on everyday problems, while some mainstream politicians are whipping up war-era tensions that have kept the country divided since its brutal 1992-95 conflict.
Around 3.4 million voters in Bosnia are choosing the three members of the country's multi-ethnic presidency, lawmakers for the national Parliament, and heads of institutions for the country's two entities: the Muslim-majority Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Republika Srpska, which is dominated by ethnic Serbs.
Bosnia has a complex web of governing institutions that were created by a US-brokered peace agreement in 1995 in an effort to manage the ethnic divisions between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats that gave rise to the war.

On Sunday morning, Associated Press journalists reported seeing multiple polling places where voting could not begin on time due to difficulties with new digital voting technology, a measure introduced to address earlier concerns over vote tampering.
Taking center stage in the contest is a staunchly pro-Russian politician who, despite not appearing on the ballot, has dominated the campaign and inflamed divisions that have sparked fears of renewed instability.
Milorad Dodik, the separatist and nationalist former president of the Serb-majority Republika Srpska, has been banned from holding public office after being convicted of defying decisions by the international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace agreement.

Just back from a trip to Moscow where he met with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Dodik's party, the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, is likely to win the election in Republika Srpska.
At his party's final election rally Friday night in Banja Luka, Republika Srpska's administrative capital, Dodik told supporters that Bosnia “is dead".
"It is an impossible country. It doesn’t make any sense,” Dodik said at the rally, which was also attended by the Russian ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Igor Khalabukov.
Dragan Bursac, an analyst, said despite Dodik not appearing on the ballot for the first time in nearly 30 years, he “is still in command. He is everywhere."
“He is all over the media, not only in the entity of Republika Srpska, but in all of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is obvious that these measures to ban him from political life are not working, and he is using them,” Bursac said.
While Bosnia has been peaceful in recent years, its politicians have kept alive the divisions between the country's Bosniaks, who are mainly Muslim, and its Serbs and Croats. Bosnian Serb leaders like Dodik have pushed for the separation of their entity from the rest of Bosnia, which has led to concerns among Western countries that tensions could once again spill over.

One of the poorest countries in Europe, Bosnia is still struggling to recover decades after the war that started in 1992 after Bosnia declared independence from the Serb-led former Yugoslavia and ethnic Serbs took up arms to carve out their own state and join Serbia.
The conflict killed more than 100,000 people and displaced millions.
Bosnia is formally seeking to join the European Union, but progress toward membership has been stalled despite EU efforts to encourage Bosnia's divided leaders to work together for reform.
Ahead of Election Day, Durak Miler, a resident of the Bosnian capital of Sarajevo, said governing politicians “just poison people when they talk”.
“We should change the old faces,” he said. “They have been governing for 35 years ... I think whoever comes next will work better for retired people and the poor.”
The country's wartime wounds were recently revived by a public homage in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs to the wartime army commander Ratko Mladic, who died in late August while serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes.

Bosnian Serbs view Mladic as a hero despite his conviction by a UN court over the massacre of more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica in 1995, and other atrocities.

Authorities are for the first time using electronic identification of voters and scanning of ballots to prevent irregularities or organized voter manipulation, which have cast doubt on the fairness of previous elections.
Salko Bijavica, from the southern town of Mostar, said he is glad that “every vote will be counted”, and that the change will give “hope to people that elections will be fair”.
Most of Bosnia's 75 political parties running in the election are organized along ethnic lines in the country's Serb-controlled Republika Srpska and the Bosniak-Croat Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The two entities are bound together by the central presidency and Parliament.
The Bosniak nationalist Party of Democratic Action has focused its campaign on efforts to keep Bosnia united against Serb separatism. Bosnian Croats, too, largely support their ethnic parties, including the Bosnian branch of Croatia's ruling conservative Croatian Democratic Union.

Former Palestinian Authority minister Sufian Abu Zaida, who last month said he had conveyed a warning message from Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar to Israel just weeks before the October 7 massacre, said he did not make that revelation to influence the Israeli election on October 27.
“I did not choose the timing of the reporting in the Israeli media about that message from Sinwar,” he told The Jerusalem Post, referring to the Haaretz expose. “I’m a mediator; I’m not responsible for when and how such information is released.”
According to a Haaretz investigative report published last month, a warning that “Hamas was planning a major event” was delivered to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu by UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan (MBZ).
The Prime Minister’s Office denied the claim.
“I’m not interfering in the elections in Israel and didn’t have any intention to do so,” said Abu Zaida, the mediator referred to as “Coal Eyes.”
While the reported conversation between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and MBZ has generated intense buzz and heightened political debate in Israel, Abu Zaida said he was responsible only for relaying to the Israelis the message he had received from Sinwar: “Before the end of September, I will have cards on the table that would cause an earthquake concerning the negotiations, and they [the Israelis] should prepare themselves to empty the prisons.”
Asked what those cards were that Sinwar was speaking about in his threat, he said, “I don’t know.”
October 7 was 'reckless gamble,' outcome was 'devastating' for Palestinians
Abu Zaida, a former Fatah official originally from the Jabalya refugee camp in northern Gaza, served as a mediator between Hamas and Israel through back channels for about a year prior to the October 7 massacre, trying to reach a deal for the exchange of two Israeli soldiers and two civilians held by Hamas in Gaza in return for the release of Palestinian prisoners from Israeli jails and steps to ease humanitarian conditions in Gaza.
After receiving the mid-September 2023 message from Sinwar, he said he had turned to his close associate, Mohammad Dahlan, who heads the Democratic Reform faction.
“I consulted him before passing it on to the Israelis,” he said. “Dahlan asked me: ‘Are you sure that Sinwar wants you to deliver it to Israel?’ I told him, ‘Yes.’”
Abu Zaida then informed Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) officials about Sinwar’s message.
Hamas’s massacre was “a reckless gamble based on mistaken calculations and assessments,” he said. “The outcome was therefore devastating for the Palestinian people.”
“Looking back, none of the objectives Hamas had put forward as reasons for the attack – especially Jerusalem, the prisoners, the blockade on Gaza, and the settlements in the West Bank – were achieved,” he added. “In fact, the opposite occurred.”
Abbas concerned about losing elections, says Abu Zaida
Abu Zaida said he was not convinced that the elections for the Palestinian Legislative Council, announced by PA President Mahmoud Abbas for November 28, would be held as planned.
Abu Zaida, who is affiliated with the faction led by Dahlan, a political rival of Abbas, said he believes Abbas is concerned about losing the elections.
“When Abbas sees the ongoing political talks, consultations, and maneuvers among opposition Palestinian factions, he realizes that there is a political risk for him,” he said.
“He [Abbas] understands that Fatah, under his leadership, could lose power,” he added. “So, he would try to first explore how things are developing, specifically to what extent the opposition factions are influential and strong, before making any decisions about moving forward with the elections.”
Abu Zaida described Dahlan as a Palestinian leader with charisma and influence in many circles. When asked about his prospects of replacing Abbas and becoming president, he said: “It is for Dahlan to decide whether to run for the presidency, and in any case, the Palestinian people should make that decision at the ballot box. This is also Dahlan’s position.”
Dahlan, once a senior Fatah official and security chief, was expelled by Abbas from the movement’s central committee and has lived in exile, mostly in the UAE, since 2011. He broke with the official Fatah movement and established his own faction, known as the “Democratic Reformist Current.”
In recent months, discussions have taken place among Palestinian factions opposed to Abbas, including Dahlan’s camp, Hamas, and possibly other factions, aimed at uniting under a joint national list ahead of the Palestinian Legislative Council elections.
According to people familiar with the matter, while no final decision has been made to form such an opposition bloc, efforts are likely to continue, posing a political challenge to Abbas’s leadership.

IDF to equip combat engineering vehicles with Iron Fist active protection against anti-tank threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:53:12 UTC
14:53:12 KST

IDF Ground Forces Commander Maj.-Gen. Nadav Lotan is advancing a series of major changes to Israel's ground forces based on lessons learned from the October 7 attacks and the ensuing war, with a new plan focused on increasing the independence and operational continuity of brigade combat teams maneuvering deep inside enemy territory.
At the center of the plan is a decision to integrate the Iron Fist active protection system into heavy combat engineering equipment and bulldozers, providing the vehicles with additional protection in the field.
Under Lotan's plan, the IDF will expand brigade-level stocks of military equipment, ammunition, and weapons to reduce brigade combat teams' dependence on outside support while maneuvering and remaining deep in enemy territory.
The plan also emphasizes alternatives to digital systems, including command-and-control systems with backup capabilities that will allow troops to continue operating in the event of communications disruptions or electronic warfare.
One of the most significant and rapidly advancing force-building efforts under the plan concerns the Combat Engineering Corps, particularly the number of heavy engineering vehicles available to it, with a broad focus on bulldozer platforms.
Updated figures show that the IDF currently has some 450 heavy engineering vehicles, in addition to approximately 80 Indian-made vehicles used primarily in defensive sectors.
Iron Fist system to provide active protection against anti-tank threats
At the height of the intense fighting across the various fronts, heavy engineering vehicles proved to be at the forefront of IDF troops maneuvering deep into enemy territory. They cleared the way into the heart of Gaza City, Khan Yunis, Rafah, Wadi Saluki, the Litani River area, the Beaufort Ridge, and elsewhere.
The heavy vehicles that opened routes deep into enemy territory faced unprecedented threats, including powerful explosive devices, anti-tank missiles, drones, mortar shells, rockets, and terrorist cells that attempted to attack the vehicles directly.
Those threats took a heavy toll on Combat Engineering Corps units. According to data obtained by Walla, Israel’s enemies have destroyed 32 heavy engineering vehicles since October 7.
Following those figures and an extensive staff review that examined several possible protection solutions, the Ground Forces made a significant decision to integrate the Iron Fist active protection system into the protective package for the heavy vehicles.
The system will provide Combat Engineering Corps crews with an additional critical layer of active protection, particularly against anti-tank missiles, allowing ground maneuver operations to continue under fire while reducing damage to the vehicles.
Iron Fist, manufactured by Elbit Systems, is an active protection system designed to protect armored fighting vehicles and engineering vehicles.
The system combines radar and electro-optical sensors to detect approaching threats in real time, including anti-tank missiles and rockets. When the system detects a threat, it launches an interceptor that detonates and destroys the incoming threat from a safe distance, without endangering the protected vehicle or nearby troops.

China Focus: China's cat parks seek lasting, sustainable homes for strays
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
13:49:25 CST
14:49:25 KST

Cats are seen at Chongqing Firefly Bay Cat Harbor Park in Chongqing, southwest China, Oct. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Yanxia)
CHONGQING/HARBIN, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- When Chongqing Firefly Bay Cat Harbor Park opened on New Year's Day in southwest China, it had just over 600 cats. More than eight months later, the number has passed 1,000.
By September, the 30,000-square-meter riverside park had rescued or taken in more than 1,300 cats, while over 240 had been adopted. As the number of cats grows, so do the demands on the park -- from veterinary care and staffing to finding enough space for new arrivals.
"The first thing is to keep the daily operation running," said Jian Ning, who oversees offline operations at the park. "We have to survive first before talking about anything else."
The park sits on what was a long-idle site near Nanbin Road in Chongqing Municipality. The local government provides the land rent-free, while the operator earns revenue from admission fees, spending inside the park and rent paid by businesses on the site.
A ticket costs 19.9 yuan (about 3 U.S. dollars). During the city's hot summer, when fewer people visit the outdoor park, daily attendance averages just over 300. On its busiest day, however, the park received 8,000 visitors.
Veterinary care accounts for roughly one-third of operating costs, Jian said. Current revenue is enough to keep the park running day to day, but making a profit remains difficult.
"If we had to pay normal rent, the operating pressure would be much greater," Jian said.
The park now employs 51 people, including animal-care staff, security guards and cleaners. Most employees who work directly with the cats are in their 20s. All are paid, full-time staff.
"We don't expect people to work simply for love," Jian said.
Most members of the park's core team are from stray-cat rescue groups. They had seen rescue efforts struggle with a basic problem: expenses kept mounting, while funding often depended on donations, subsidies or rescuers paying out of their own pockets.
The team therefore decided to open the site to visitors, hoping revenue from ticket sales and other businesses could help cover the cost of long-term care for rescued cats.
The park sums up the idea in a lighthearted slogan: "Cats work to support themselves."
The experiment is unfolding alongside a sizable pet economy. China had 126 million pet dogs and cats in urban areas in 2025, including 72.89 million cats, while the urban dog-and-cat consumer market reached 312.6 billion yuan, according to the 2026 China Pet Industry White Paper (Consumption Report).
Yet space has a limit. Jian estimated that the park could accommodate 2,000 to 3,000 cats. If the population approaches that level, she said, new admissions will have to be reduced.
The park does not encourage people to relocate stray cats that are regularly fed in residential communities, as they have already grown accustomed to those surroundings, Jian said.
Scientific research also suggests that managing free-roaming cat populations requires more than one-off interventions. A 12-year controlled study published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that sustained, high-intensity neutering across contiguous areas could reduce cat numbers, while immigration and other compensatory effects could weaken the impact. The researchers recommended combining the trap-neuter-return method with complementary measures such as adoption and resource management.
Adoption certainly provides another outlet. Applicants face strict requirements, however, and the park conducts follow-up checks. None of the more than 240 adopted cats have so far been returned.
Visitors, meanwhile, must adapt to rules designed around the animals. Children under six are not admitted, and staff ask visitors not to chase cats or pick them up against their will. Jian said disputes over scratches and bites have become less common as visitor guidance has improved.
The park may stop admitting visitors once more than 3,000 people are inside. So far, the flow of people in and out has made that unnecessary.
Some 3,000 kilometers away in northeast China, another cat park is testing a similar combination of animal rescue and tourism on a smaller scale.
Scarlett's Friends, Heilongjiang Province's first cat-themed park, opened on Aug. 28 at the Yabuli Ski Resort in Harbin and is now home to 150 rescued stray cats.
The cat park occupies a site that had stood idle for years and gives Yabuli, long known for winter skiing, another attraction for the warmer months.
Before entering areas open to visitors, the cats must be neutered, vaccinated, treated for parasites, and assessed to determine whether they can adapt to interaction with people. Sick cats are moved to an isolation area, while a partner veterinary hospital provides regular health support.
Winter in Yabuli brings temperatures far below freezing. Indoor activity areas and cat houses have been equipped with air-source heating systems, and the cats will spend most of the winter indoors, said Liu Guangpeng, deputy general manager of Harbin Yabuli Tourism Investment Group Co., Ltd.
Ning Xiaofeng, general manager of the group, said stray-cat rescue that relies solely on continued spending is difficult to sustain. By linking the park with tourism, the operator aims to use tourism revenue to help cover the cost of caring for the cats while providing them with a stable home.
Liu said the park would limit visitor numbers rather than compromise the cats' welfare.
"Even if there were no visitors, we would still make sure the cats were properly cared for," he said. If crowds exceeded the park's capacity, it would introduce reservations and limit entry.
Similar ideas have begun to appear in local policies. In February, the eastern Chinese city of Nanjing in Jiangsu Province issued guidelines encouraging pet-related tourism while calling for stray animals to be managed via capture, neutering, return or adoption. The document also said eligible animal-protection groups could receive support through government service purchases and public-interest programs.
Back in Chongqing, Jian explained that relying entirely on subsidies, donations or unpaid work would not be sustainable.
"Only by using commercial operations to support rescue can we keep this going in the long run," she said.
During Chongqing's hot summer, the park stays open until midnight. As temperatures fall in the evening, visitors arrive to see the cats and enjoy the riverside night view.
Many simply sit and wait.
"Here, you don't have to talk or please anyone," Jian said. "You can just sit on the steps, and maybe a cat will come over, rub against you or fall asleep in your lap." ■
